title: Mamdani, Paris already knows where 'globalize the intifada' ends up - comment
body: Some of the protesters in Paris on Saturday didn't stay on the ground. They climbed the Monument to the Republic, the bronze Marianne at the center of Place de la République, and stood above a crowd of tens of thousands.Reuters photographer Jack Taylor caught them up there. In his picture, two flags fly side by side over the square: the French tricolor and the Palestinian flag.The people below had come to protest the cost of living, worsening public services, and the state of French schools. Those are French problems, and serious ones. So what was the Palestinian flag doing up there next to the tricolor?Saturday's demonstrations turned into some of the worst violence France has seen in years. Rioters burned cars, looted shops, and attacked police officers. By Sunday, nearly 1,800 people had been arrested across the country, according to Reuters.More than half a million people took part in the demonstrations, the overwhelming majority of them peacefully, over real problems: French classrooms are short of teachers, and families are struggling with living costs.I want to be careful with the answer. The flag proves less than some people were already claiming. It shows that protesters brought the Palestinian cause to a demonstration about French problems. It doesn't tell us whether anyone carrying it had a hand in the arson or the attacks, and we don't know that yet.On Sunday, the Combat Antisemitism Movement shared a video it said showed a Paris synagogue vandalized during the unrest. It opens on what looks like a small prayer room. The Torah scroll is still standing in its wooden ark. Around it, the furniture has been shoved out of place, and things are lying all over the floor.The synagogue was reported to be in the 19th arrondissement, a district in northeastern Paris. Nobody has independently confirmed what happened there, when the video was filmed, or whether it had anything to do with Saturday's riots. I've watched too many frightening clips get treated as fact before anyone bothered to ask what happened, and I don't want to add another one.Still, it bothered me. On Saturday, the Shabbat, a synagogue is a pretty ordinary place. People pray, complain that the rabbi's sermon ran long, and ask about each other's kids. Nobody there should have to wonder what happened at a political demonstration earlier that day.This is how the conflict travels. When it reaches Paris or New York, it rarely finds an Israeli official to shout at. It finds Jews, and it works on them in two steps. First they're made to stand in for Israel. Then they're made to answer for it. I learned how the first step works on a Paris street in 2015.Ten hours in Paris after 2015 terrorist attacksIn February 2015, I spent 10 hours walking through Paris and its suburbs in a kippah and tzitzit, the ritual fringes worn by observant Jewish men. It was a few weeks after the terrorist attacks at the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo and at the Hypercacher kosher supermarket, where four Jews were murdered. A photographer followed me with a hidden camera. A security guard came along and stayed out of sight.I was covering the Jewish world for the Israeli news website NRG and the newspaper Makor Rishon at the time, and we wanted to see what ordinary Jewish life felt like on the streets of Paris.We started in the center of Paris, where the worst I got was the occasional stare. Then we headed into other neighborhoods and out to the suburbs, and the mood changed. People cursed at me and threatened me, and some spat. Someone shouted “Viva Palestine” as I walked past. In one neighborhood, our security guard, who had been keeping out of sight, decided it was getting dangerous, and we got out.I hadn't said a word about Israel or carried a flag, and nobody asked what I thought of the Israeli government. Apparently my kippah had already answered for me. That's the first step: to the people shouting at me, a Jew walking down a Paris street had become Israel.What still gets me is how young some of them were, teenagers barely older than children, who seemed to know almost nothing about Jews except what they'd picked up on the street.The video went viral. Millions of people watched it, and for a while I was the guy explaining on television around the world what it felt like to walk through Paris in a kippah.Attacking a synagogue to send a message to IsraelOne Saturday morning in August 2024, two cars went up in flames outside the Beth Yaacov synagogue in La Grande-Motte, a seaside town near Montpellier in southern France. One of them had a propane tank inside.Firefighters found more fires at two of the synagogue's entrances. Five people were inside, including the rabbi, and none of them were hurt. A police officer who walked up to the scene was injured when the tank exploded.French prosecutors later said the suspect had admitted carrying out the attack to support the Palestinian cause and to provoke a reaction from the Israeli authorities. He denied wanting to kill anyone, though he acknowledged he had wanted to frighten people.I still find the logic hard to follow. A man angry at Israel set fire to a synagogue in southern France and expected it to influence decisions made in Jerusalem. The people who prayed there had no say over Israeli policy and no special line to the prime minister's office. They were Jews, and as far as he was concerned, that was enough. It was the same first step I met on the street in 2015, this time carried out with fire.After the attack, Yonathan Arfi, president of CRIF, the body that represents French Jewish institutions, spoke to my colleague Michael Starr. He said French Jews lived with the knowledge that some people saw them as legitimate targets in a battle being fought thousands of kilometers away.French Jews have lived with this since the Second Intifada, which began in 2000, long before October 7, 2023. In those years, attacks on Jewish schools, synagogues, and individuals became common for Europe's largest Jewish community.Ilan Halimi was kidnapped, tortured, and murdered in 2006 because he was Jewish. In 2012, a terrorist murdered Rabbi Jonathan Sandler, his two sons, and 8-year-old Myriam Monsonego at a Jewish school in Toulouse. In 2025, France recorded 1,320 antisemitic incidents, according to the Interior Ministry. That was down from the year before and still historically high.The second step does its damage more quietly. A CRIF study published in July looked at the experiences of 30 Jewish schoolchildren interviewed in 2024. Many said they felt pressured to answer for Israeli policies, sometimes by classmates who barely understood the conflict. Some hid that they were Jewish or avoided talking about Israel at all.These are teenagers worried about grades and friends, and they're being asked to defend decisions made by the Israeli cabinet. I'm not sure most of the ministers could explain all of those decisions. A Jewish kid in a Paris classroom is expected to.What a rabbi told New York Mayor Zohran MamdaniEarly in his campaign, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani resisted calls to condemn the slogan “globalize the intifada.” Intifada, he argued, means uprising, and some activists use the word to describe resistance to oppression.In September 2025, he told MSNBC's Al Sharpton that his views had changed. A rabbi, he said, had told him the slogan reminded her of bus bombings in Haifa, and that she feared extremists could terrorize Jews in New York.She was describing exactly how the intifada travels. He said he now saw a gap between what some people meant by the phrase and its impact on Jewish New Yorkers, and that he would discourage its use.I'll give him credit for that. It means he can't say nobody explained it to him. The rabbi could have added the Park Hotel in Netanya, where a Palestinian suicide bomber walked into a Passover Seder in March 2002 and murdered 30 people.For Israelis who lived through the Second Intifada, the word means buses blown up in Jerusalem and Haifa and restaurants turned into murder scenes. So when someone calls for that to be globalized, I'd like to know what exactly they're planning to export.Mamdani's supporters may mean demonstrations, civil disobedience, or solidarity with Palestinians. Fine, that's politics. But we hear the bombings, and calling it an “uprising” doesn't change what we hear.Last month, his administration announced a strategy to combat antisemitism, including $6.4 million in grants for hate-crime prevention and support for victims, along with more money for security at synagogues and other houses of worship. I hope it helps.Earlier this month, I wrote that his security grants and cultural programs would leave a central part of the problem untouched: the hostility Jews face over their attachment to Israel. That part depends on Mamdani himself, and on whether he tells people on his own side when their language or behavior has crossed a line.On a Wednesday evening in November 2025, two weeks after Mamdani won the election, Nefesh B'Nefesh, which helps Jews move to Israel, was holding an event at Park East Synagogue on Manhattan's Upper East Side.Outside, police put up barricades between protesters and a group of counterprotesters. Some of the protesters chanted “globalize the intifada” and “make them scared.” Inside, the event went on.The next day, his press secretary said he had discouraged the language and would continue to do so. The same statement said sacred spaces “should not be used to promote activities in violation of international law.”When the news site Jewish Insider pressed his team on what that meant, it said it was referring to the organization's promotion of settlement activity beyond the Green Line, the pre-1967 armistice line.So the Jews inside heard a crowd chanting about making them scared, and the next day the mayor-elect's office suggested they'd misused their own synagogue by promoting settlements.The protesters had made them stand in for Israel. The incoming mayor's office then asked them to answer for it. Which part of that evening, exactly, was their fault?Even the Union for Reform Judaism, whose leaders are hardly automatic supporters of every Israeli government, condemned the intimidation and criticized his response.Anyone can protest Israel's policies. Jews going into a synagogue should be able to get there without being threatened, and a mayor should be able to say so without adding a “but.” It isn't a hard sentence to write.Young child in Paris understood the presence of antisemitism The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is part of ordinary life in France now. It comes up in classrooms and neighborhood conversations, and in arguments between people who have never been to Israel.I have plenty of disagreements with my own government, as regular readers of this column know. A Jew in France or New York should be able to hold any opinion about Israel, or none, without being tested on it before walking into a synagogue.One moment from those 10 hours in Paris is stuck in my head, much more than the insults.A young boy saw me walking by in my kippah and asked his mother what I was doing there. Didn't I know I might be killed?He seemed genuinely worried about me. The boy knew nothing about the hidden camera or the security guard. All he saw was a Jew walking through his neighborhood. Young as he was, he already understood what that could mean there, and he was afraid of what might happen to me.He'd be a young man now, and I wonder whether he remembers that afternoon as well as I do.As for the teenagers who spat at me, I'd like to know whether any of them ever got to know a Jewish person, learned something about Jewish history, or rethought what they had been taught.Eleven years later, there's violence in France's streets again, and French Jews are looking at videos like the one from the 19th arrondissement.Mamdani has said he wants Jewish New Yorkers to feel safe. I hope he means it. He can show it the next time someone chants “globalize the intifada” outside a synagogue, by condemning it plainly, with no second sentence about the people inside.People can support Palestinians without reaching for the worst years of the Second Intifada. And kids in Paris and New York deserve to meet Jews as neighbors before anyone teaches them that every Jew is a stand-in for Israel.I still wonder what that boy's mother told him. I hope it was something kind.

title: Iran's IRGC exploits women through sex trafficking, uses children to fund proxy wars, report finds
body: Iranian women, undocumented migrants, children, and refugees are being exploited by the Islamic Republic, specifically the IRGC, to finance and support its proxy wars across the region, according to an analysis published last week by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).Ella Rosenberg, a senior research fellow at the JCFA and a member of the Dvorah Forum, said Iran's legal framework allows the regime to project an image of compliance with international anti-trafficking regulations while relying on flawed legislation that falls short of international standards and fails to adequately protect victims.She noted that the Islamic Republic conflates human trafficking with migrant smuggling, and the regime has consistently refused to ratify the 2000 United Nations Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons (the Palermo Protocol).IRGC directly benefiting from sex trafficking, Israeli study findsBeyond failing to protect victims, Rosenberg assessed that the IRGC directly benefits from human trafficking. She noted that the IRGC uses the sex trafficking sector, often facilitated by the regime through temporary marriages, as a major source of income.Rosenberg described Iran as a source, transit, and destination country for the sex trafficking of women and girls, citing widespread poverty, systemic corruption, and economic mismanagement as contributing factors.She argued that Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code, which permits girls to marry at 13 and even younger girls to marry with parental permission and court approval, has helped normalize the sexual exploitation of minors.Rosenberg also linked the practice of nikah mut'ah, a temporary marriage contract agreed upon for a predetermined period, to the exploitation of vulnerable women and girls for the benefit of organized trafficking networks.Trafficking networks move victims within Iran and across its borders into neighboring countries, including Iraq, with the alleged support of the IRGC, according to Rosenberg. She said that the scale of cross-border sex trafficking could not be sustained without the IRGC's complicity, given its role in border control and the intelligence apparatus's oversight of internal security checkpoints and airports.Adding more weight to her analysis, human rights groups, including the IHR Monitoring and Evaluation Framework and HRANA, have documented allegations that IRGC commanders accepted bribes to facilitate the passage of trafficking victims.Rosenberg added that the IRGC profits directly from the exploitation of Iranian women by taxing the commercial sex trade.IRGC exploiting Afghan, Pakistani refugeesIn addition to financially benefiting from human trafficking, the JCFA report said that the IRGC's Quds Force and the Basij systematically traffic undocumented migrants, refugees, and children to “sustain their proxy wars across the Middle East.”The IRGC exploits vulnerable populations, particularly Afghan and Pakistani refugees, to recruit fighters through deception, financial coercion, and threats of deportation, she said. Individuals harvested from these communities are coerced into joining proxy militias like the Fatemiyoun and the Zainabiyoun Brigades, for deployment in foreign countries like Iraq.Additionally, in violation of international law, the Basij systematically recruits and coerces Iranian children as young as 12 into military indoctrination and combat support roles. This was argued to be a severe form of human trafficking, as the recruitment exploits children's vulnerability to coerce them into hazardous, involuntary servitude in military environments.Though JCFA warns of the abuse of children aged 12 and up, The Jerusalem Post has previously reported on the death of an 11-year-old Basij member who was killed at a checkpoint in Iran.Rather than directly profiting from the trafficking of vulnerable individuals into the IRGC, Rosenberg suggested, the financial gain can be categorized as cost avoidance rather than revenue.She argued that instead of deploying trained members of the IRGC, which the regime would have to pay and has invested in, the system can deploy underpaid or unpaid vulnerable groups who are deemed disposable because of their lack of funded training.Such deployments were estimated to save the Islamic Republic billions of dollars in military expenditure, freeing funds to be redirected into the IRGC's domestic corporate monopolies and regional terrorist financing networks.Again, Iran's “tax” system also allows it to benefit from migrants transiting from Pakistan and Afghanistan who are hoping to reach Europe through Iran and Turkey.Such migrants are also routinely subjected to debt bondage, extortion, and forced labor in Iran's informal agricultural and construction sectors to pay off exorbitant smuggling fees by criminal networks that pay protection money to the IRGC. This alone is estimated to generate billions of dollars for Iran's shadow economy.Focus on Iran's nuclear program may distract from IRGC human trafficking Rosenberg noted that Iran was able to continue to exploit these systems as sanctions from the EU and US have primarily focused on Tehran's nuclear proliferation, ballistic missile development, support for regional terrorism, and suppression of domestic dissent. Failing to also sanction the IRGC and the front companies it uses for human trafficking continues to provide Tehran a lifeline.Given that the funds raised by human trafficking are often liquid, Rosenberg also alerted to the fact that it was hard for international systems to monitor how much wealth Iran is accumulating through these sources.Individuals involved in facilitating or covering for regime-backed smuggling networks can therefore continue to travel, use regional banks, and manage front companies without fear of asset freezes or international arrest warrants.To prevent Iran from continuing to profit from human trafficking, Rosenberg advised that the US Treasury Department utilize the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act to designate IRGC border commanders, Basij recruitment officers, and complicit Iranian law enforcement officials for their roles in labor and sex trafficking.She added that the European Commission must also use the Sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (AMLD6) to require European financial institutions to aggressively monitor illicit financial flows generated by Iranian trafficking networks.

title: Israeli court orders charity officials to repay NIS 1.85 million over diverted cancer donation
body: The Haifa District Court has ordered seven people who ran two linked charities to personally repay NIS 1.85 million after finding that a donation intended to help children and teenagers with cancer was diverted to another organization and spent outside its approved purpose.Senior Judge Ron Sokol ruled that the officials breached their duties by allowing the transfer, submitting misleading reports and failing to account adequately for the money. His October 8 decision also found that substantial sums were paid unlawfully to the charities' leading figure, attorney Galit Pauker Shemesh, as salary and rent.The ruling, announced by the Justice Ministry on Sunday, concerns the charities, Keren L'Chaim and Keren L'Chaim L'Yeladim V'Noar (for children and youth), both ordered by the court to close in 2024.All seven must repay the money, and any one of them can be required to cover the full amount still owed. Interest and inflation adjustments will be added from April 2019. They were also ordered to pay a total of NIS 20,000 in legal costs.Donation intended to support children with cancerThe money came from the estate of Helen Hatab. Her estate administrator told the court that she had been a teacher and had suffered from cancer, leading him to propose using part of her estate to support children and teenagers with the disease.A family court approved the arrangement in March 2019. The program was to provide educational support during illness, guidance for recovering patients and funding for equipment, medicines and treatment through the original Keren L'Chaim charity.But the bank details supplied for the transfer belonged to the newer organization, Keren L'Chaim L'Yeladim V'Noar. The family court did not approve transferring the donation to a different charity or using it for a different purpose.The First International Bank of Israel (FIBI) initially refused to transfer the money after identifying the mismatch between the approved recipient and the account. The charities subsequently opened accounts at Bank Mizrahi-Tefahot, where the donation was deposited in the newer charity's account in April 2019.Sokol also found that a document submitted to FIBI had been altered to replace the original charity's registration number with that of the newer organization.Charity officials defend spending on hostel renovationsThe seven argued that the money had supported legitimate charitable work, principally renovations at Beit Keren, a hostel for at-risk girls in Hadera. Pauker Shemesh maintained that the estate administrator had approved redirecting funds, that she had provided evidence of the renovation costs and other expenses, and that her salary and rent payments were justified and approved.The other six argued that they had volunteered, received no personal benefit, and relied on Pauker Shemesh and professional advisers to oversee the finances.The court rejected those defenses. The approved cancer-support program could not simply be replaced with another charitable project without the required approval, Sokol found. He concluded that transferring the donation and changing its purpose were intended to evade scrutiny of the original charity and allow the officials to continue handling donations without restrictions.The officials said that roughly NIS 1m. had been spent on the hostel, but did not provide sufficient invoices, plans or other evidence to establish that expenditure. A promised expert assessment of the work's value was never submitted.Sokol accepted that some renovation work had taken place. In calculating the repayment, he deducted NIS 41,621 for that work, using the amount recorded in the charity's financial report.Court orders repayment of salary and rentPauker Shemesh was separately ordered to return NIS 180,390 in salary and NIS 112,110 in rent, plus interest and inflation adjustments. Any salary and rent she returns will reduce the total amount the seven must repay.Sokol acknowledged that the officials had genuinely wanted to help people in need and had done so for years. But he found that the money had also been used improperly for personal benefits, mainly for Pauker Shemesh, and that the other officials' failure to oversee spending had allowed this to happen.“We cannot accept the respondents' claim that they are exempt from any duty merely because they acted as volunteers,” Sokol wrote.Trusting that nobody was pocketing money was no substitute for checking that donations were used for their intended purpose, he added.

title: Bonei Zion Prize honors Olim rebuilding Israel after the war as North American Aliyah hits records
body: When Hamas terrorists tore through the farming communities of the Gaza border on October 7, they left behind burned sheds, wrecked machinery and fields no one could harvest. Within days, Danielle Abraham, a London-born Olah who had spent years bringing Israeli agricultural expertise to countries battling drought and food insecurity, turned her attention homeward and launched ReGrow Israel to get those farms running again.The initiative has since expanded to farms and communities damaged by the war in the North. This year, it earned Abraham the Global Impact award at the 12th annual Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize, and her story captures what this year's prize is about.The Bonei Zion ("Builders of Zion") Prize recognizes Olim from English-speaking countries whose professional achievements and community leadership have made a lasting impact on Israeli society. This year's eight recipients were selected from hundreds of nominees from Australia, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States. They are being honored at a moment when Israel is still rebuilding from war, and when more North American Jews than ever are choosing to follow in their footsteps.A record year for AliyahThe Bonei Zion Prize lands in a year that Nefesh B'Nefesh says is shaping up to be one of its strongest since the organization was founded in 2002. More than 1,100 North Americans made Aliyah through Nefesh B'Nefesh in August alone, a monthly record for the organization. "It's record-breaking for us," Marc Rosenberg, Nefesh B'Nefesh's vice president of Diaspora partnerships, told The Jerusalem Post at Ben-Gurion Airport as another 150 Olim landed.Approximately 2,700 North Americans had made Aliyah by the end of August, and the organization expects the total to pass 4,000 by year's end. Rosenberg said interest in Aliyah has been climbing by three to five percent annually in recent years.Many of the newcomers are heading to precisely the regions that bore the brunt of the war: around 650 of this summer's North American Olim moved to the periphery in the North and South. For prize sponsor Sylvan Adams, himself a Nefesh B'Nefesh Oleh who made Aliyah a decade ago, the connection between the honorees and the new arrivals is the point."In the wake of the immense challenges Israel and Jewish communities around the world have faced over the past year, these stories of commitment, resilience, and contribution carry even greater meaning," said Adams, president of the World Jewish Congress Israel Region. "At a time when we are working to encourage greater Aliyah and strengthen Israel through the vision of bringing one million new Olim to Israel, these honorees embody the very best of what Aliyah represents."Builders in every fieldAlongside Abraham, this year's Bonei Zion Prize recipients span science, education, social welfare, sport and diplomacy.In the Community & Non-Profit category, the prize goes to Naomi Stuchiner, founder of Beit Issie Shapiro, one of Israel's leading organizations serving people with disabilities and their families, work whose importance has only grown as Israel confronts the physical and emotional toll of the war.Rabbanit Chana Henkin, founder and chancellor of Nishmat, is recognized in Education for building one of the country's foremost institutions of advanced Torah learning for women. In Science & Medicine, Dr. Philip Klipstein, senior principal scientist in the R&D division of SemiConductor Devices (SCD), is honored for his contribution to Israel's high-tech and defense-technology base.Ami Baran, president of the Israel Athletics Association, receives the award in Culture, Art & Sports, while content creator Barak Swarttz, founder of GRIT for Good, is recognized in Young Leadership, representing a new generation of Olim using digital platforms to make an impact.The Bonei Zion Lifetime Achievement Award goes to Prof. Marta Weinstock-Rosin, the pioneering neuropharmacologist who developed the Alzheimer's drug Exelon. Her research has had a profound global impact on neuroscience and medicine.This year's Special Recognition Award is presented to Amb. Ron Dermer, former Israeli ambassador to the United States and former minister of strategic affairs, for his decades of public service, including his role in strengthening the US-Israel alliance and advancing the Abraham Accords.Why they stayRosenberg has argued that the bigger Aliyah story is less about what is pushing Jews out of North America than what is drawing them to Israel: family, values, community and a sense of belonging. The Bonei Zion honorees are the long-term proof of that pull. Nefesh B'Nefesh, which works in partnership with Israel's Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, the Jewish Agency for Israel, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael and Jewish National Fund-USA, has helped nearly 100,000 North American Olim settle in Israel and reports a 90% retention rate."Each of this year's recipients exemplifies the values of dedication, innovation, and Zionism, and together they are a living embodiment of the vitality and strength that Aliyah continues to bring to the State of Israel," said Rabbi Yehoshua Fass, Nefesh B'Nefesh co-founder and executive director.For Adams, the message to the thousands landing at Ben-Gurion this year is simple. "Each year, the Bonei Zion Prize reminds us of one of Israel's greatest strengths," he said, "the extraordinary people who choose to build their lives here and, in doing so, help build the future of the Jewish state."Written in collaborations with Nefesh B'Nefesh

title: BBC's Responsible AI chief previously jailed over immigration offenses, found with al-Qaeda manual
body: An Algerian national formerly found to be in possession of an al-Qaeda training manual and who was later sentenced to nine months in prison for immigration offenses is now the BBC's principal data scientist in the Responsible AI division.This was first reported by The Telegraph on Saturday, and then independently confirmed by The Jerusalem Post.The case involves Hicham Yezza, who was working in an administrative role at the University of Nottingham when, in May 2008, university staff discovered a copy of an al-Qaeda training manual on his work computer and alerted the authorities.The document had been sent to him by his friend, postgraduate student Rizwaan Sabir, who was researching Islamist terrorism and allegedly wanted help printing it.On May 14, 2008, both men were arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 and detained for around six days. They were released without charge, after Yezza maintained that he had no involvement in terrorism and said the document had been sent to him for printing, not for operational purposes.The Nottingham Two arrests and immigration convictionThe case sparked outrage from academics and civil-liberties campaigners, and the case became known as the “Nottingham Two” arrests.Following his release from the terrorism investigation, Yezza was immediately rearrested under immigration legislation, and authorities sought to deport him to Algeria.In 2009, Yezza was sentenced to nine months in prison for an immigration-related offence involving his claim to have valid permission to remain in Britain. He was released after five months, and is now a British citizen.On returning from prison, Yezza launched Ceasefire Magazine, which describes itself as an independent political and cultural publication motivated by “a belief in the free exchange of radical and ground-breaking ideas.”On his LinkedIn, Yezza listed himself as editor-in-chief of the magazine from September 2010 to September 2021. Since his departure, the magazine has become significantly less active. Its most recent article appears to be a May 2025 Comment piece titled “Dispossession resistance is a natural law right of the Palestinian people.”The piece, by Asim Qureshi, refers to Hamas as a “faith-based movement” and said, “Until the entirety of the Zionist colonial entity and all its settlements are dismantled, the Palestinians will be entitled to exercise their natural law right to resist their dispossession and recover what was unlawfully stolen.” However, as Yezza has apparently taken a step back from the magazine, no relationship can be drawn between him and its current content.Yezza's BBC career and previous anti-Israel statementsOutside of Ceasefire Magazine, Yezza served as an editorial consultant for Al Jazeera from November 2017 to June 2019. He then spent three years and 10 months at the BBC in an editorial capacity, first as a Middle East and North Africa (MENA) expert and then as a senior journalist in BBC Monitoring's central editorial Data Hub team.In his time as a MENA expert, Yezza reported on the war in Gaza despite his previous anti-Israel stances.As of July 2025, he is the principal data scientist for Responsible AI at the BBC, “helping guide and shape how the BBC approaches and applies responsible AI use across the organization.”Prior to his employment with the BBC in 2021, Yezza was an active commenter on social media, frequently speaking about the “occupation and apartheid” in Israel.Many of his posts in the year 2018 revolved around Israel, his support for Palestinian resistance, and his defense of Jeremy Corbyn against accusations of antisemitism.He also tweeted that rockets being fired from Gaza into Israel were “resist[ance].”The Post reached out to the BBC for comment.

title: Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new defense minister and veteran of its missile program?
body: Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi as the country's new defense minister on Sunday. His rise to the position in recent weeks is important. It helps stabilize Iran's top defense leadership amid rising tensions in the Gulf. Iran expects more fighting to break out with the US or Israel. It is therefore trying to shore up its defenses at home and prepare for operations in the region.Akhlaghi is believed to have a background in Iran's missile program and its broader defense industry. Given the Islamic Republic's attempts to rebuild its industrial defense base, this matters.Reuters noted that Ketabchi is replacing Majid Ebn al-Reza, who took over in an interim capacity after then-defense minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed by US-Israeli strikes in February.The Iranian parliament widely supported Akhlaghi's appointment. He has said he will rebuild the country's defense sector.Iran International, a media outlet critical of the Iranian regime, said that Akhlaghi was born in 1958. He studied chemical engineering at the Amirkabir University of Technology.Akhlaghi then earned a master's degree in strategic management from the Malek Ashtar University of Technology, an institution affiliated with Iran's Defense Ministry.Iranian state media provided a short bio, noting that “his previous positions include heading the Shahid Bakeri Industrial Group and serving as managing director of the Aerospace Industries Organization.”Akhlaghi worked in Iranian defense industries for over four decadesPer the Iran International report, Akhlaghi “entered Iran's defense industries in the early 1980s and spent more than four decades in technical, industrial, and managerial positions, according to Iranian state-linked media.”It added that “much of his career has involved solid-fuel missile propulsion systems and the management of industrial facilities associated with ballistic missile development.”The new defense minister also worked at the “Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, a subsidiary of the Aerospace Industries Organization involved in Iran's ballistic missile program.”He became the head of the Aerospace Industries Organization in 2014 and then headed the Defense Industries Organization.Akhlaghi played a role in Iran's Fateh-110 missile project, Iran International reported, as his “close relationship with Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam, a founder of the [IRGC's] missile program, was central to his involvement in developing Iran's missile industry.”New Iranian defense minister sanctioned by UN for involvement in missile programThe new defense minister was sanctioned for his role in the missile program. In 2007, the UN listed Akhlaghi on a sanctions list “as an individual involved in nuclear or ballistic missile activities.”This was because he was listed as “head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, which is designated under resolution 1737 (2006) for its role in the ballistic missile program (designated under IRe.066),” the UN said.The US Treasury Department also sanctioned Akhlaghi in 2008. He is well known for his role in Iran's missile program. He has also been involved in procuring items for the program.The person now in charge of Iran's defense ministry is uniquely positioned to try to rebuild its missile program.In March, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that “after 20 days, I can tell you – Iran today has no ability to enrich uranium, and no ability to produce ballistic missiles.”Recent reports, however, indicate that Iran is rebuilding its missile program and has also repaired many missile launchers.

title: EU condemns West Bank settler attacks targeting diplomats, Palestinians during olive harvest
body: The European Union "strongly condemns" attacks by extremist settlers in the West Bank, including attacks against European diplomats, the bloc's foreign policy spokesperson said on Sunday.The statement came a day after Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian civilians, European diplomats and a French mayor in the West Bank."We take positive note of statements by several Israeli representatives who condemned the attacks, but we expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists," the EU spokesperson said.The incident in question included a group of European diplomats who claimed to have been attacked by Jewish settler extremists on Saturday.Netanyahu cautioned against ongoing 'campaign to smear Israel'Following the report, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a statement saying that "serious accusations require serious evidence."Masked men reportedly attacked European diplomats in the West Bank."We urge caution before drawing conclusions from today's reports that European diplomats were attacked by masked Israelis in Judea and Samaria. Any violence against diplomats is unacceptable. The more serious the accusation, the greater the demand for compelling evidence," the Prime Minister's Office said in a statement.The statement by Netanyahu also claimed that the reports come amid a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge."The Prime Minister's Office: ALLEGED ATTACK ON EUROPEAN DIPLOMATS: SERIOUS ACCUSATIONS REQUIRE SERIOUS EVIDENCE. We urge caution before drawing conclusions from today's reports that European diplomats were attacked by masked Israelis in Judea and Samaria. Any violence against diplomats is unacceptable. The more serious the accusation, the greater the demand for compelling evidence. Here is what we know: - The diplomatic delegation entered a sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination with the IDF, as officially confirmed by the military. Such coordination is essential to protecting visiting diplomats and preventing violence. - The visit included Bernard Baudoux, a French Communist Party mayor who previously raised the Palestinian flag over his municipal building, prompting French authorities to order its removal. - Published footage shows masked individuals confronting a diplomatic vehicle. Separate images show a smashed window and a person lying on the ground. These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility. Those circumstances remain under investigation. - Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible. These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge. We may see further allegations in the coming days. By the time the evidence is fully examined, the reputational damage from premature conclusions may already be done. We call on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay, and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria.— Prime Minister of Israel (@IsraeliPM) October 17, 2026"We may see further allegations in the coming days. By the time the evidence is fully examined, the reputational damage from premature conclusions may already be done," the statement continued, adding that the PMO has "called on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay, and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria."

title: Israeli patients' blood samples allegedly taken without consent for research, hospital says
body: Kaplan Medical Center in Rehovot filed a police complaint over suspicions that blood samples were taken from patients without their informed consent as part of a research study in the hospital's cardiology department, the hospital said Sunday.The complaint followed preliminary findings that raised concerns about possible misconduct during the study.Hospital management also notified the Health Ministry of the suspicions and the immediate steps taken in response.Medical services in the cardiology department are continuing as usual, the hospital said, adding that measures have been put in place to ensure continuity of care and patient safety.Previous complaint involving cardiology department directorThe latest complaint follows a separate complaint against Professor Kobi George, head of the cardiology department, concerning the alleged shortening of an internal medicine residency under his supervision.According to the report, a committee was established after a resident doctor at the medical center alleged that residency records had been falsified to allow cardiology residents to bypass the required internal medicine training period while appearing to have completed it.That complaint is also under review.

title: How could Israel help Saudi Arabia defend against the Houthis - and at what cost? - analysis
body: There is increased discussion about how Israel might help Saudi Arabia against the Iranian-backed Houthis. How might such help take shape, and what might be most effective?This comes amid wider questions about whether Saudi Arabia will join the Abraham Accords. Questions about this have come up since the accords began in 2020. So far, Riyadh has taken a wait-and-see approach, preferring that Israel make positive moves on the Palestinian issue.Now, US President Donald Trump has said that Saudi Arabia may be accepting help from Israel. Asked about whether he thought Saudi Arabia might normalize ties with Israel, he said, “I think they will. Israel's been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” The comments were made days after Saudi Arabia appeared to downplay whether Israel would support them.The context for this latest development is the Houthis' increased attacks on Saudi Arabia. America has not joined the fighting but may be supporting the Saudis in various ways, such as via intelligence.The US has so far chosen not to join strikes on the Houthis. The Trump administration carried out strikes on the Houthis in March and April 2025. The administration eventually concluded that it was better to do a deal with the Houthis than continue strikes.On Sunday, Walla had a piece by Amir Bohbot, asking whether Israeli aid to Saudi Arabia would be an opportunity or a potential powder keg.“Security sources confirmed to Walla that the quality of Israeli intelligence is improving, but at the same time the Houthis are causing heavy damage. The security establishment is aware that there is an opportunity to strengthen relations, but is not addressing the issue for fear of inflaming the situation,” Bohbot reported.The Turkish pro-government media outlet Anadolu Agency noted on October 13 that “Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has rejected an Israeli push to join the military campaign against Yemen's Houthi group, despite efforts to secure Riyadh's approval through US mediation.”Anadolu Agency said it based this on a report in Haaretz. “Another source familiar with the matter said Israel hoped military cooperation with Saudi Arabia would strengthen bilateral ties and pave the way for a future normalization agreement,” the report said. “There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the report.”Saudi Arabia needs Israeli aerial defense systemsYnet noted on Sunday, in a piece by Ron Ben-Yishai, that “the Saudis urgently need early-warning radar systems and air defense batteries capable of countering different types of aerial threats, including Iron Dome, David's Sling, and even Arrow 2 interceptors.”“The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and explosive-laden drones, requiring a combination of defensive capabilities,” he added.This analysis noted that “Trump sees a chance to revive Saudi-Israel normalization as the Houthis strike Riyadh; Israel is sharing intelligence, but Riyadh's demand for Palestinian statehood talks and Israel's need for its own defenses make a deal far from certain.”It also added that Trump may see an “opportunity for greater Israeli assistance, potentially generating enough goodwill in Riyadh to persuade the Saudis to abandon their longstanding condition for normalization: negotiations with the Palestinians toward a two-state solution. For now, however, there is good reason to doubt that Trump's comments signal a meaningful breakthrough in Israeli-Saudi relations.”Walla noted that “security sources confirmed that as time goes by, the contribution of Israeli intelligence is increasing, with the Houthis in the background causing heavy damage to the Saudis throughout the country.”The report goes on to say that “as first published in Walla, the IDF is assisting Saudi Arabia on the intelligence front in the fight against the Houthis in aspects of warning, target banking, and building a situational picture.”“Israel sees this as a positive process that will intensify once the US decides how it will decide on the Iranian issue,” it said.America, Walla said, is facing this dilemma: “If the US attacks Iran, the latter may attack the countries of the region, including Israel. If America continues with the economic sanctions (there is a slim chance of a political agreement without further conflict), this could also lead to escalation in the region.”Houthis targeted shipping they claimed was linked to Israel after Oct. 7The overall story now points to potential increased Israeli involvement and support. It's worth noting that the Houthis began attacks on Israel soon after October 7. The Houthis began by attacking ships they claimed were linked to Israel.The Iranian-backed group said that it was targeting Israeli ships and vessels linked to Israel, although many of the ships attacked had no direct Israeli ownership or operational connection.One of the most prominent incidents occurred on November 19, 2023, when Houthi forces seized the Galaxy Leader, a vehicle carrier, in the Red Sea.Armed men boarded the ship from a helicopter and diverted it to Yemen. A Japanese company operated the vessel and, through its ownership structure, was linked to Israeli businessman Abraham Ungar. None of its 25 crew members were Israeli nationals. They remained detained until January 2025, when the Houthis released them following the Gaza ceasefire agreement.The seizure marked the beginning of a wider campaign against international shipping. The Houthis subsequently expanded their declared targets to include vessels traveling to Israeli ports and ships associated with American and British interests.The Houthis also carried out ballistic missile attacks on Israel. Israel responded by striking dozens of Houthi targets in 2025. This shows that Israel has already launched a campaign against the Houthis. The US has also carried out a campaign.Notably, Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis since 2015. That means that all the players know the Houthi threat and capabilities. The Saudis have worked with Egypt, the UAE, and others in the past against the Houthis.It appears that Riyadh will work again with Egypt and the UAE. Israel has ties with the UAE and Egypt via peace treaties. Israel also already works closely with the US Central Command.Any cooperation against the Houthis can strengthen regional defense ties and infrastructure. This helps defend against Iranian-backed threats and Iran's direct threats. For instance, when Iran carried out large missile attacks on Israel in 2024, many countries cooperated against the threat.

title: Is the concert residency slowly replacing traditional touring?
body:
Going on tour as a major artist is like mobilizing an army for an offensive that will last months, if not years. A battalion of semi-trucks needs to be wrangled to transport gear from city to city. Buses need to be rented for the act and crew. Hotels, airfare and/or private jets have to be booked. Often, multiple stages plus sound and lighting rigs must be assembled, so that while a show is happening in one venue, things are already being set up at the next. Support staff, from caterers to chiropractors, have to be mobilized. Backstage amenities must be organized. Merch needs to be sourced, transported and replenished throughout the tour.
Audiences demand a spectacle for their concert dollar, so productions have to be wilder and more technologically advanced while remaining portable. And because touring is an artist’s major source of revenue, everyone is on tour, driving up the cost of renting gear, trucking and roadies. Touring has never been more expensive and fans are very close to that red line when it comes to what they’ll pay to see a show. Raising prices isn’t an option anymore, yet expenses keep climbing. Of great concern is the skyrocketing price of diesel fuel for all those trucks and buses.
Then there’s all the red tape and paperwork. Having to advance shows in different cities and different countries. Crossing borders with loads of gear and personnel who may have, er, issues. Visas. Currency conversions. Settlements. The accounting complexities are enormous.
Then there’s the human toll. Being away from home and living out of hotels, backstage lounges and airports is very hard on the mind, body and spirit. It’s to the point where many musicians are questioning whether touring is worth it anymore , especially when it comes to emerging talent, indie musicians, or those in the middle class of the music industry.
What if there were a better way that was cheaper, easier on the artist and could provide a superior experience for the audience? Enter the residency.
Las Vegas was the pioneer in this area. As far back as the 1950s, casinos and hotels began booking long-term engagements for entertainers ranging from Sinatra and the Rat Pack to Liberace to Elvis. Since people were already flocking to the city to gamble, why not give them another way to spend their money? Artists loved it because everyone came to them. Vegas is still king of the residency, hosting strings of shows by Céline Dion, Britney Spears, Janet Jackson, Bruno Mars, Garth Brooks, Lady Gaga, Adele, Shania Twain and dozens more.
The Sphere is the latest iteration of the Las Vegas residency, providing an immersive experience that you can’t get anywhere else in the world (well, until the new one opens in Abu Dhabi). It’s also very lucrative for artists. U2 played 40 shows over weekends and grossed US$245 million. The Eagles made US$290 million over 58 shows (so far), pulling in around US$5 million per gig. By the time their stand finishes in January, the overall gross will be close to half a billion . Metallica, No Doubt, Dead & Company, Phish and a few others have also had great paydays, all without having to move from a single venue. Margins expanded. ROI went through the roof.
The live music industry is falling in love with residencies for this reason. Why spend money going to fans when you can entice the fans to come to you?
Live Nation experimented in Munich in the summer of 2024. A temporary stadium was built within a space dubbed “Adele World.” Construction cost €40 million and featured 250 tons of stage equipment and the biggest LED video screen ever constructed, all for just ten shows. Through the month of August. It was an insane success, attracting 750,000 people. Gross sales were never released to the public, but it’s whispered that Adele walked away with US$50 million. Then the whole venue was taken down.
Long stays in arenas and stadiums have become increasingly common. Taylor Swift’s Eras tour had two stretches: one for three nights and another for five, at Wembley Stadium in London. Coldplay did 10 nights at Estadio River Plate Buenos Aires before completing a 16-night run at Wembley Stadium. Shakira completed a 13-show stint in Madrid in a temporary venue attracting 55,000 people per night, grossing at least US$200 million . To put it another way, she attracted more money and people to the city than F1 and a visit by Pope Leo XIV.
Next year, the Backstreet Boys have 12 shows booked for the Rogers Centre in Toronto. And Oasis has 11 sold-out nights at Etihad Stadium in Manchester along with four grand finale shows at Knebworth Park in September 2027. And Céline Dion is set for a 26-concert residency at Plentitude Arena in Nanterre, France.
In each case, the act commands the fans to come to them. And because transportation/setup/teardown costs are greatly reduced, profits must be astronomical.
While this is all fine and good for the artist, this isn’t much of a deal for fans. While residencies may hold down the price of a concert ticket due to lowered operating costs (well, we’ll see), fans increasingly have to pony up for new expenses like airfare and hotel. Wanna see your favourite band live? Forget about them coming to you. You now have to go to them.
Meanwhile, governments are loving residencies because of the economic impact they can have on a city. The promotion of music tourism has become a priority in some spots. In the U.K., for example, people traveling to shows brought in £11.2 billion at last count. Since the ABBA Voyage avatar show debuted in London in May 2022, it has brought in nearly US$3 billion.
Other countries are getting on board with music tourism, too. Egypt (the pyramids are always a great venue), Chile, India and Australia are all working on plans. Just this past week, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the American Music Tourism Act into law. By creating a welcoming atmosphere for music tourists, you just know that managers, promoters and artists are going to try to capitalize on the opportunity with more residencies.
The one hold-out might be U2, a band that, outside of The Sphere opportunity, has always been determined to bring their music to their fans around the world, even though the operating costs of their tours has been insane. Both The Joshua Tree Tour and the ZooTV Tour almost bankrupted the band. The 360 Tour required three “claw” stages to be custom-built at the cost of US$30 million each. Rumours are that their next tour in 2027 will run over several years and consist of up to six legs. It sounds like an old-school world tour that will travel the planet like the old days.
Meanwhile, everyone else might want to get used to budgeting for more than just a concert ticket to see your favourite band. You may have to go to them.

title: J Mascis has nothing better to do
body:
Dinosaur Jr. frontman J Mascis is known as something of a slacker guitar god. He stands stoically onstage, barely moving, as he seemingly effortlessly works through deft guitar solos and lopsided riffs. Unfortunately, Mascis has developed a similar reputation as an interview subject, quietly sitting and offering deft nonanswers.
That’s not to say that Mascis can’t be funny or charming. As our interview was winding down and I was thanking him for his time, he started to loosen up a bit. He told me about his youth as a mini golf “enthusiast.” “I had a 3-foot putt for the win” at a mini-golf tournament, he said, but “that’s when I realized that I was a choker … When I was 11, I choked.” And that’s when he decided, “I should maybe not do sports.” So, instead of becoming a professional mini golfer, Mascis went on to form one of the most important bands in alternative rock.
While most of his contemporaries have called it quits or are just going through the motions onstage for a paycheck, the original lineup of Mascis, bassist Lou Barlow, and drummer Patrick Murphy are still regularly putting out new LPs of reliable rockers. But Mascis says there isn’t any grand secret to the band’s longevity. Over 40 years deep, he says, “I guess we have nothing better to do.”
What, for an interviewer, can come off as frustrating indifference might actually be the key to Mascis’ staying power — for better or worse. Creatively and professionally, his modus operandi seems to be rolling with the punches and not overthinking things.
For the new record There Near, he said, the band “just didn’t push it.” There were no eight-hour marathon studio sessions. They weren’t meticulously fine-tuning basslines or trading Logic sessions back and forth remotely. Mascis would roll in with fully prepared demos and the band would immediately start recording, even as Barlow and Murph were still learning their parts, “on the off chance that it comes together quickly.”
The same sort of relaxed approach also informs Mascis’ gear choices. He said, “I am kind of a tube purist guy, but it’s just also kind of inconvenient sometimes,” so he uses whatever works. That means while he mixes and masters to tape, he’s also tracking in Pro Tools.
When it comes to designing signature instruments with Fender, he’s just as easygoing. “I try to, you know, do the important things that I want, but not make it too complicated … I think it’s better to keep it kind of cheap … just so people can do what they want with it.” The neck is his biggest concern, he said. “I’m a sucker for jumbo frets and, you know, if the neck is good and the frets and stuff, that’s the main thing. Most of the other stuff, you know, you can swap out if you want.”
But that somewhat lackadaisical attitude has also caught him some heat. Two years ago, Mascis released a video for his solo track “Old Friends” that was made using generative AI. Speaking with The Verge, he finally publicly addressed the controversy. “Yeah, just some kid did it,” he said. “I thought it looked cool, so… Yeah, that’s dipping my toes into the... I don’t do much with videos.” He trailed off repeatedly while answering before finally admitting, “But yeah, I guess that’s a slippery slope.”
Similarly, he said that while he doesn’t believe there is a place for AI in music making, we have to acknowledge that it’s here whether we like it or not, and “I guess we’re learning how to deal with it. And hopefully it won’t kill us all.”
About the only thing that Mascis could muster strong feelings about was the band’s infamously loud live shows. (Dinosaur Jr.’s recent performance at the tiny Baby’s All Right is what finally convinced me to start packing earplugs.) “I noticed the audience too seems more desperate for something kind of reality-based,” he said, letting a touch of his purist heart show. “We don’t have in-ear monitors or click tracks. We have amps and you know, just, I think some people are responding to the reality of it. Like they really need something that’s not, you know, computer-generated or something.”
He bemoaned the lack of amps onstage (Mascis plays in front of three full stacks, even in a 280-person-capacity club) and the reliance on high-tech front-of-house setups. “It’s very weird. Now, soundmen create the sound instead of capture the sound,” he said. Of course, his recognition of the visceral power of live music and directly connecting with an audience makes his indifference to AI all the more baffling.
Dinosaur Jr. are currently touring the US behind There Near, which is out now.

title: Warnock wants Democrats to focus on the South. He’s starting in Mississippi.
body: JACKSON, Mississippi — Raphael Warnock is racing to get Democrat Scott Colom elected in deep-red Mississippi. It’s part of his bigger bet on the South. Colom, a charismatic local prosecutor, is within striking distance in the polls of unseating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. And in the absence of more dedicated resources, Warnock himself is trying to fill the gap by directing money and donors to the race. He has raised over $500,000 directly into Colom’s campaign committee, according to a person with direct knowledge of his efforts, granted anonymity to share private details. And, over the course of four separate fundraisers, has tried to steer Senate Democrats’ top donors to the race. In April, he told attendees at a Democratic donor breakfast that he thinks the party is “sleeping on” the Mississippi contest, prompting surprised laughter from the crowd, according to a recording of the event obtained by POLITICO. “I'm going to ask you to resist the Democratic tendency to ignore the South,” he told the assembled donors. “And for our own sake, for the sake of us having a possibility of winning over time, I think we can win in Mississippi if the conditions are just right.” Warnock, who is also widely seen as a potential presidential contender, is trying to capitalize on an incredibly unfavorable midterm environment for the GOP that has put more and more traditionally red states into play. He has been criss-crossing not just Mississippi, but the broader South, to convince Democrats to expand into the region and shore up their support with Black voters ahead of 2028. The time is ripe, he said, for a “new kind of Southern strategy” — a play off of former President Richard Nixon’s plan for Republicans to best Democrats in the region in the late 1960s that capitalized on white backlash to the civil rights movement. It’s been a hard sell so far, particularly in Mississippi: Republicans control all levers of state government, and Trump handily won by 24 points in 2024. The last time Mississippians sent a Democrat to the Senate was 1982. Even though national Democrats speak highly of Colom’s candidacy, their resources to compete on an expanded Senate battleground map are already strained, and money has been prioritized in more expensive, high-profile contests like Iowa, Alaska and Maine. The half-million Warnock has raised for Colom is 15% of the $3.5 million he’s managed to raise over the cycle. It’s still a strategic move on Warnock’s part: An upset win by Colom would boost the Senator’s own profile as he continues to leave the door open to running for president. And even if Colom loses, the South is a treasure trove of delegates for 2028 — and Black voters dominate the region in Democratic primaries. Pressed whether he’s interested in the White House himself, Warnock evaded, saying he’s “trying to think and pray about the highest and best use of my skills.” “I’ve been at crossroads many times, and in the moment, I've always known what to do,” he added. Other Democrats see the work as helpful regardless of what Warnock does in 2028. “The ’28 chatter is something he will listen to, but I don't think it's something that's part of a checklist he's marching towards,” said Georgia Democratic strategist Andrew Heaton, who has worked on Warnock’s Senate campaigns. “Regardless of what happens on that front, ’28 is going to be a very busy year because — especially if he decides not to run — I think there's no question he's planning on running for the Senate again.” Free from the constraints of reelection this year, Warnock has traveled across the Carolinas, Mississippi and his Georgia home to support local candidates and pitch a vision of his party’s future that runs through the region that launched his political career. In interviews with POLITICO on the campaign trail, Warnock drew parallels between Democrats’ 2020 wins in Georgia — his own, Sen. Jon Ossoff’s and former President Joe Biden’s — and the conditions he sees emerging in the Magnolia State for Democratic growth. Those kinds of wins will disappear from the horizon if Democrats fail to invest now and in the Black voters who are core to the party’s coalition, he argued. Mississippi, where over 35% of the population is Black, would be key to the Democratic Party’s efforts to win back voters of color, as many shifted toward Trump and Republicans in 2024. Strong Democratic candidates have reached around 45% of the vote in the state in recent years, but none have been able to punch through for a victory in Mississippi, which has a long history of extremely polarized voting along racial lines. But in the wake of the Supreme Court’s decision to gut the Voting Rights Act, there are signs Black voters are surging to the polls in higher numbers — and some Democrats hope that could remake the state’s politics. “It is in the interest of the party to invest in the base and have the base understand that the party understands that these are loyal Democratic voters, and Black voters want what other voters want,” said Warnock. “They want the same kind of prosperity and opportunity that all families want.” Colom was more blunt. Asked if he equates ignoring Mississippi and its Senate race to the party ignoring Black voters, he said: “Yeah, of course, 100 percent.” Democrats have not been averse to flooding money into traditionally red states in the final stretch of the campaign, but Mississippi has not yet made it high on that list, where Colom still faces an uphill battle to close the gap with Hyde-Smith. Building out the statewide grassroots infrastructure that has proved effective in places like Georgia takes time and resources, which have yet to land in Mississippi at a significant scale this cycle. “Democrats are investing in Mississippi, but not enough. And, I think, certainly not as much as I think we should, and not as much as we could,” Warnock said in an interview between campaign stops in the state. He was in somewhat of a rush: between a fundraiser for Colom and an event with local faith leaders, Warnock wanted to visit the home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights era titan who was shot and killed in the car port of his Jackson home in 1963. “We're playing enough here to force the other side to compete in Mississippi, and that is an improvement, but it's not enough,” he said. Colom himself has begged national Democrats to focus on his race. “Mississippi has really always been competitive. It just hasn't got the attention, the resources it deserves,” Colom said in an interview at his campaign headquarters. Some has come: American Bridge, a Democrat-aligned super PAC, pumped over $2 million into the race earlier this month, and earlier this week the New York Times reported that a single megadonor is set to split $7 million of his personal wealth between Colom’s race and others. Several top Democrats have made an effort to signal their support. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg plan to visit the state before Election Day. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and his Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, Kirsten Gillibrand, have each hosted separate fundraisers for Colom, according to a source familiar with the events, granted anonymity to share private details. And Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, a DSCC vice-chair, campaigned with Colom in Mississippi. Colom’s campaign committee outraised Hyde-Smith’s over the summer, posting $1.3 million to her just over $640,000 . But it pales in comparison to the tens of millions that have flooded into other states. In separate statements, spokespeople for the DSCC and Senate Majority PAC lauded Colom as a strong candidate, but said they were constrained by how much they could spend. Both groups said they were monitoring the race “closely.” Republicans are still publicly maintaining their confidence in their hold on the seat. Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, tied Colom to Washington Democrats in a statement and said the campaign “planned for Colom to have plenty of resources. We are executing our own campaign plan with that in mind.” One day after his sojourn in Mississippi, Warnock was presented with a stark contrast in what Democrats are capable of when they devote resources to a Southern state. He was in North Carolina on Thursday, where Democratic Senate nominee Roy Cooper is dominating his Republican opponent , Michael Whatley, in fundraising and polling. As one of Democrats’ top candidate recruits of the cycle, Cooper has attracted significant resources and national attention from the outset of the race. But Mississippi and North Carolina are two enormously different states, in population, income, and demographics — and that change didn’t happen overnight. Democrats began significantly investing in the state ever since President Barack Obama’s 2008 victory there and ramped up their efforts after the GOP-led state government redrew the state’s congressional maps in 2013. “It's taken a lot over the last 13 years,” Rep. Valerie Foushee (D-N.C.) said on the sidelines of a party canvass kickoff in Durham. “Our eye has never been taken off the ball, and because we believe that we could make that change, that we needed to be the change that we wanted to see, we have put that in action now, and we're going to win because of it.”

title: Article of Faith: The acceptable sacrifice (2), By Femi Aribisala
body:
In the tabernacle Moses built, the inner court was reserved for consecrated priests (descendants of Aaron) to perform sacrifices. The Holy of Holies was off-limits. It was a no-go area. It was a sacred space within the Temple where the Ark of the Covenant was placed, protected by a heavy veil. Only the High Priest could enter there, once a year, on Yom Kippur. This restriction represented the high holiness required to approach God’s presence.
If any man violated these restrictions, he died on the spot. This is what happened to Nadab and Abihu when they offered strange fire in the temple. Priests entering the inner court and the holy of holies had a rope tied around their waist. If they died as a result of ritual impurity or because of sins of disobedience, they were then pulled out with the rope around their waist.
However, what is impossible with man is possible with faith in God.
Assuredly, I say to you, if you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you. Matt 17:20).
Therefore, Abel could offer an acceptable sacrifice to God before the Law of Moses. He did this by faith.
By faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts; and through it, he being dead still speaks. (Heb 11:4).
But by the grace of God, David, the man after God’s heart, also found a way to bypass God’s legal limitations. He was not an Aaronite, and neither was he a Levite. He was from the tribe of Judah. Nevertheless, his faith in God made a way for him to offer an acceptable sacrifice to God.
Enter into (God’s) gates with thanksgiving, and into His courts with praise. Be thankful to Him, and bless His name. (Psa 100:4).
God sent me to pray for a man sick with cancer. But after I prayed for him, God did not heal him. His parents sent for me. They said that after I prayed for him, he became better. But then he became so much worse. Could I come back to pray for him? God told me to go back. But I struggled with God. I told Him, “If You wanted to heal him, You could have done so the first time I prayed for him.” “Why do I have to pray a second time?” “If you want to kill him, just kill him without involving me.”
So, God said, “Don’t pray for him again.” “Just show him a video.” God said, “Go to the shelf, and I will show you which video you are to show him.”
When I got to the shelf, He asked me to stretch out my hand and take a videotape. When I did, I took one entitled, “If Satan Can’t Steal Your Joy, He Can’t Keep Your Goods.”
I watched the video and understood why it was relevant. Jesus says:
Therefore, you now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and your joy no one will take from you. (John 16:22).
I copied the video and took it to the man on his sickbed. But when I played the tape, it only played for 10 minutes. There was a power cut, so the recording stopped. Not to worry. I told him about the message in the video. “Rejoice.” Thereafter, for two hours, I sang praises to God with the sick man and his family.
Two weeks later, the man died. Then, I changed gears with God. I told Him it did not matter whether those He sent me to pray for lived or died. He can heal them, or He can kill them if He wants to. My business is to touch and pray; healing is His department.
When I reached that juncture, God told me to sing a song:
“I will enter His presence with thanksgiving in my heart, I will enter His courts with praise I will say this is the day that the Lord has made I will rejoice for He has made me glad.”
When I sang that song, God switched on the light. I now have perfect understanding of the matter. Indeed, I was sent to heal the sick man. But his healing was spiritual. God was taking him home to Himself. God’s message to Him was to enter His heavenly gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise.
What God required of the man was a sacrifice of praise.
“Thus says the Lord: ‘Again there shall be heard in this place — of which you say, “It is desolate, without man and without beast” — in the cities of Judah, in the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man and without inhabitant and without beast, the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voice of those who will say: “Praise the Lord of hosts, for the Lord is good, for His mercy endures forever” — and of those who will bring the sacrifice of praise into the house of the Lord. For I will cause the captives of the land to return as at the first,’ says the Lord. (Jeremiah 33:10-11).
The sacrifice of praise is acceptable to God. It is offered joyfully even under the most inconvenient circumstances. God does not accept praise that is not offered joyfully.
Why are you cast down, O my soul? And why are you disquieted within me? (Psa 43:5).
No matter the vagaries of life, God requires us to offer to Him joyful praise:
Because Your lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise You. Thus I will bless You while I live; I will lift up my hands in Your name. My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise You with joyful lips. (Psa 63:3-5).
My lips shall greatly rejoice when I sing to You, and my soul, which You have redeemed. (Psa 71:23).
Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy; and on the harp I will praise You, O God, my God. (Psa 43:4).
Women like to dance. But make sure you are dancing on the inside
David resolved to build a house for God. He insisted God was too important to dwell in a tabernacle. However, God told David he could not build Him a temple because he had killed too many people and his hands were full of blood.
But God said through Isaiah that He does not desire a Temple built by fleshly men.
Thus says the Lord: “Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool. Where is the house that you will build Me? And where is the place of My rest? For all those things My hand has made, and all those things exist,” says the Lord. “But on this one will I look: on him who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at My word. (Isa 66:1-2).
God sent men to destroy every temple built by men.
Believe Me, the hour is coming when you will neither on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, worship the Father. You worship what you do not know; we know what we worship, for salvation is of the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth; for the Father is seeking such to worship Him. God is Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth. (John 4:21-24).
Coming to Him as to a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God and precious, you also, as living stones, are being built up a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. (1 Pet 2:4-5). NKJV
Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone defiles the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are. (1 Cor 3:16-17).
God also cannot accept sacrifices made by sinful men. What He desires from men is love and mercy. That is the first and great commandment.
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ (Matt 22:37).
But you cannot love God unless you are born again.
I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. (Hos 6:6).
Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance. (Matt 9:13). CONTINUED.
