title: Call of the Wilde: Cole Caufield shines with two goals as the Montreal Canadiens outlast the Buffalo Sabres in overtime
body:
For the second time in five days, the Buffalo Sabres and Montreal Canadiens went to overtime at the Bell Centre, and for the second time, the Canadiens won it. Cole Caufield with an absolute stunner of a shot upstairs on a breakaway led the Canadiens to a 4-3 win.
It was the first game of the season for Oliver Kapanen. He looked solid. The last time Kapanen looked as talented as he did on Saturday was about game 60 last season, before he hit the wall for the rest of the season and the playoffs.
Kapanen had that trademark intelligence. He was on a two-on-one looking confident with Kirby Dach. With Kapanen, Dach looked good for the first time this season.
If Kapanen finds his better game, it would be a giant boost for the Canadiens who are looking for a 12th forward that doesn’t bring the team down. Another night and another goal for Bolduc. On the power play, it was Bolduc in the bumper position, and he deflected a point shot from Nick Suzuki for a tally.
The top line was in outstanding form. They scored on strong work from the first-forechecker Juraj Slafkovsky. He managed to get behind the net right after the defender on the dump-in. He chipped it to Cold Caufield who scored his fourth goal of the season. Once again, it was from an angle most players wouldn’t even attempt to shoot.
Even after a 51-goal season, goalies still aren’t prepared for Caufield to shoot from anywhere. Caufield understands that he’s got a great chance when the goalie isn’t prepared. He’s pretty good, too, when they are prepared.
Caufield won it on a breakaway away from centre in overtime. He looked shot all the way and sniped it so quickly in and out of the top corner, Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen didn’t even move.
The Suzuki line had its best contest of the season. The Expected Goals total was stunning. They had a 99.3 per cent share. Suzuki is one of the best players in this league. It’s a rare night that he is outdone by his opposite, even though he faces the best centres in hockey.
Injuries are always bad, there’s no argument to that, but, strangely, injuries can also lead to some accidental discoveries. The day-to-day injury of Mike Matheson has led to the returning Kaiden Guhle lining up with Alexandre Carrier.
The result is both of these defenders are playing their best hockey. They look right together. They compliment each other. They understand each other. They have great chemistry. Midweek, Guhle played 25:25 in one of this highest ice times on record for a game.
He was the game’s first star. Guhle has returned to action looking like he didn’t have surgery at all; nor miss training camp. With Carrier, they dominate the game. They rarely get into trouble. Carrier doesn’t get hit as much either.
Their best moment of the night was on the penalty kill in a tied game with one minute remaining. Both boxed out beautifully to keep the shots to the outside. They are becoming a shutdown pair.
Lane Hutson and Noah Dobson also look good together. Both pairs had a 60 per cent share in Expected Goals.
The only reason the Canadiens have these two outstanding pairs going right now is the Canadiens were destroyed by the Carolina Hurricanes when Dobson and Matheson were together. It was that awful night that was step one in this positive change.
It’s been interesting to watch the Canadiens try to bring another defender into the fold since trading Jayden Struble. It has not gone as well as planned. The Canadiens felt that they could trade Struble because Adam Engstrom and David Reinbacher are ready to go.
Engstrom auditioned first, and he was abysmal. In one contest, two goals went off his body when he wasn’t boxing out, and he had very little awareness of the danger. Engstrom continued to make terrible decisions when he had plenty of time and space.
Saturday night, they tried Reinbacher. He was a mess on the first Sabres goal. He retrieved the puck just inside his own blue line. He felt so panicky he threw the puck up ice only about ten feet, without looking who happened to be there. Sadly, for Reinbacher, it was two Sabres.
Buffalo, immediately, came back on the counter-attack, and the Canadiens were caught believing they had possession. Reinbacher then compounded the first error by making another one just as bad.
He didn’t take his man at all, basically, standing in front of the net by himself looking around. The result was a Josh Norris goal. Reinbacher is a much better player than this, but he was anxious, and his decision making completely left him.
The rest of the evening Reinbacher was acceptable, and the coaching staff thought he was reliable enough because with five minutes left, in a 3-3 game, Reinbacher was on the ice. That’s as big a vote of confidence that a player in his first game at home in the NHL can get.
It hasn’t been a great start to the season for Montreal. They are near the bottom of the standings in the Atlantic Division. However, they shouldn’t fret. Underneath the surface, the Canadiens have metrics that show they are playing extremely well.
Using analytics, such as Corsi and Expected Goals, the tale of the tape is excellent. The Canadiens made the playoffs the last two seasons with shockingly bad Corsi. They were 28th in 2025 and 23rd in 2026. They made the playoffs on the back of good goaltending.
This season, it’s the complete opposite. The Canadiens are one of the best teams in the league in advanced metrics. They have won the Corsi and Expected Goals battle all season long, except in the Carolina Hurricanes game when they were dominated.
Overall, Montreal this year is fifth in Corsi. The Canadiens are playing more in the other team’s end than they have in a decade and a half. The longer the season goes, the more this statistic matters. The last three winners of the cup were first, fourth, and second in Corsi.
The issue is goaltending where the Canadiens have had a terrible time so far. Montreal is 29th of 32 teams in Goals Saved Above Expected this season. Jakub Dobes will find his game. When he does, the excellence in Corsi will show up as wins on the scoreboard.
Brian Wilde, a Montreal-based sportswriter, brings you Call of the Wilde on globalnews.ca after each Canadiens game.

title: Peru pauses the K2. South Korea must wait for South America
body:
Peru has not formally closed the door on the South Korean K2 Black Panther, but the programme has been politically and budgetarily paused. Defence Minister Rafael Belaúnde has said that the army has not submitted an investment project, the purchase is not included in the 2027 budget, and any future replacement for the T-55 should go through an international tender. This does not mean that the K2 has failed. It means that South Korea must wait longer for a real breakthrough in South America.
The Peruvian case is more interesting than the simple line that there is no money for Korean tanks. In December 2025, the Peruvian Army, FAME and Hyundai Rotem signed a framework agreement covering the possible future acquisition of 54 K2 Black Panther tanks and 141 K808 White Tiger armoured vehicles. But this was not yet a state-financed executive contract. It was a political and industrial route towards procurement, not procurement itself.
Belaúnde has now stopped that route. The previous logic was based on a strategic FAME-Hyundai Rotem arrangement. The new one returns to three basic questions: does the army have a formal requirement, does the state have funding, and will the process be competitive? At the moment, the answer is no.
It would still be wrong to write that Peru has abandoned the K2. Hyundai Rotem remains present in the country, the K808 is already part of the relationship, and three K2 tanks were brought to Peru for demonstrations. The problem is different: the 54 K2s are not today an approved modernisation programme. They are an ambition without money in the next budget.
This does not change the wider assessment of the K2. It remains one of the most interesting main battle tanks available on the market. Its strength is not only the platform itself, but also the offer around it: fast deliveries, industrial flexibility and willingness to build local participation. In a market where many European programmes are delayed, that matters.
The actual users of the K2 are South Korea and Poland. Poland is now the key export reference point. The first stage gave the Polish Armed Forces rapid deliveries of K2GF tanks. The more important stage is K2PL with the Polonised version, with Polish industry involved in production, maintenance and further development. This is why the Polish programme is so important for Hyundai Rotem. It is not only a contract, but also a test of whether the K2 can become a European industrial project.
If K2PL succeeds, Poland will become the main European reference centre for the tank. That will matter for states that do not want to wait many years for future European platforms or rely only on the Leopard 2 ecosystem. For South Korea, Poland is therefore not just a customer. It is the gateway to credibility in Europe.
Interest in the K2 does not stop with Peru. During Defence24Days in Poland, Armenia was visibly engaged in discussions with the Korean side about possible future strengthening of its land forces, including armoured capabilities. This does not mean that Yerevan has a K2 programme. It shows, however, that the Korean tank is already treated as a serious option by states looking for rapid modernisation.
France is not considering buying the K2. Paris has its own armoured tradition, its Leclerc experience, its view of MGCS and its own work on future systems. But France cannot ignore the Korean model. The K2 shows that a non-European producer can offer a modern tank, quick production and industrial partnership. For France, it is not a procurement option. It is a competitive signal.
That is the wider meaning of the K2. Germany has the Leopard 2 network. The United States has the Abrams and political weight. France wants to preserve its own heavy-armour competence. South Korea comes with a simpler message: a modern tank, fast production and readiness to adapt the platform industrially.
Peru could have been a breakthrough because an entry into South America would have given Hyundai Rotem more than another contract. It would have created a first major foothold in a region where several armies still operate older tanks and where land-force modernisation has often been delayed.
For now, that scenario has been pushed back. Peru is not saying that the K2 is a bad tank; nevertheless, there is no investment project, no funding in the 2027 budget and no procedure that would make the K2 the selected successor to the T-55.
The K2 can be attractive, modern and industrially flexible, but even the best offer cannot replace a state budget decision. Poland had the Russian threat, an urgent need to rebuild armoured forces and a political decision to buy quickly. Peru has old T-55s and clear interest in the K2, but not yet an approved programme.
It must be underlined that the K2 remains one of the strongest export tanks in the world, and Poland is becoming its most important European laboratory. But South America will not open automatically. If Peru returns to the issue, the K2 will be one of the natural candidates. If it does not, Hyundai Rotem will need another opportunity to prove that the Black Panther can become not only a European success, but also a global armoured product.

title: Czech companies interested in Ukraine's reconstruction – Chamber of Commerce representative
body:
Tomas Kopecny, Special Representative for Ukraine at the Czech Chamber of Commerce, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Czech exports to Ukraine are growing and will continue to grow. Exports also essentially mean participation in reconstruction projects. This means that Czech companies are getting involved and investing in Ukraine," Kopecny said.
According to him, Czech businesses are showing considerable interest in Ukraine's reconstruction, despite the fact that Czech partners do not expect peace or a ceasefire agreement in the near future.
Kopecny noted that during the first four years of Russia's full-scale war, Czech entrepreneurs had repeatedly visited Ukraine on business missions. Several such visits have also taken place this year, including a business mission to Dnipro focused on the construction of shelters.
At the same time, Czech companies are developing partnerships with Ukrainian businesses in the Czech Republic itself, he said. In October, a delegation representing more than ten Ukrainian technology and industrial companies, universities, research institutions and clusters took part in the MSV 2026 International Engineering Fair in Brno.
By the end of the year, the Czech Chamber of Commerce plans to organize two more large-scale missions involving dozens of entrepreneurs from several cities.
A major business mission to Ukraine led by Czech Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade Karel Havlicek is scheduled for November.
"This mission is the culmination of previous initiatives, while also involving state representatives at the highest possible level. […] Dozens of entrepreneurs are expected to take part in the mission," Kopecny said.
He identified energy, infrastructure and agriculture as the main areas of cooperation.
The delegation will include companies that are major producers and investors in the energy sector, including Moravske naftove doly (MND), RSJ, Gentec and Agregat. Skoda Transportation is actively involved in infrastructure projects, while Czech company Agromino operates in Ukraine's agricultural sector.
Kopecny also noted that earlier this year, Deputy Prime Minister Havlicek described Ukraine as an important partner for the Czech Republic, and that these statements have been accompanied by concrete steps. He expressed hope that the security situation would allow the planned events to go ahead.
"The government is taking only slightly fewer practical steps than its predecessor. For example, the budget for funds intended to help rebuild Ukraine has been increased, whether through guarantee programs or export insurance. […] The Czech government is actually supporting these companies when it comes to civilian cooperation. They simply do not talk about it because they have chosen this policy," he said.
As previously reported, Ukraine and the Czech Republic remain in contact on further steps to develop cooperation, particularly in infrastructure reconstruction and joint projects to restore local communities.

title: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
body:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
How it started
The first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.
Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.
While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.
The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.
How it’s going
Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.
Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.
It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa.
Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms.
Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints.
What happens next
As the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere.
Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards.
Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip cities of their core police, zoning, and emergency response powers. States will also have a say, and sometimes that may complement or conflict with their own cities. Even airport authorities are getting in on the action, proposing their own slate of rules for robotaxis. AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere.
By the way
* Even if the feds pass a sweeping national framework, like the proposed SELF DRIVE Act, cities and states would still keep their authority over local road usage. In other words, cities are going to be the main arbiters of robotaxi permission for the foreseeable future.
* Texas may be the Wild West, with fewer rules governing self-driving cars than most states, but California is still the gold standard. Securing a deployment permit from the California Public Utilities Commission, for example, is viewed by the industry as a definitive safety validation.
Read this
* Streetsblog reports that Uber and Waymo have spent more than $15 million on lobbying state officials in New York.
* Tesla had to change the name of its Full Self-Driving software to “Assisted Driving” to win approval from European Union regulators, Reuters reports.
* Tesla provided first responders in Austin three days of training and emergency guidebooks on how to interact with its Cybercabs, according to The Daily Texan.

title: If you have the scratch, they have the scares
body:
Chanthal Harris owns Long Dark House in Alexandria, Virginia. Ryan Benk/NPR News hide caption
The horror biz is booming, as recent Weekend Edition reporting has made clear. But not everyone wants to be up close and personal the with the IRL frights of a haunted house or spooky corn maze. Many would rather experience nightstalkers, goblins and witches that can't escape the theater or TV screen, or zombies and werewolves that won't lunge off the pages of a book.
Chanthal Harris owns Long Dark House in Alexandria, Va. It's a bookstore devoted exclusively to horror and the supernatural. It's been doing business for just over a month and Harris says she already has steady traffic from both genre stalwarts and first-timers.
"You know, I think people are looking for things that they wouldn't normally find in a lot of other places. I've had people comment about the curation and how they're finding something unexpected," Harris says. "And I'm also surprised at how many people are trying to dip their toe into horror."
Harris is no newbie herself: books and horror have been constant companions.
"My love of horror started from an early age. And I joke, but I do truly blame my parents because my dad was a[n] avid reader. He probably takes responsibility more for my fantasy/sci-fi love, but my mother always loved horror," Harris says.
"To me it was completely normal. I didn't think of it as a spooky thing."
So after a career in aviation, Harris decided to follow her passion and open Long Dark House.
"It's exceeded my expectations and, you know, could be the season. But I just am so appreciative that people are as excited about these genres and this experience as I am. And so anytime someone walks through the door, I'm a little surprised and happy and grateful," she says.
The numbers say Chanthal Harris shouldn't be very surprised. Market research by Nielsen says profits from the genre have jumped almost 26-percent year over year.
And the numbers are good for films as well.
Last May, Backrooms — about a horrifying liminal space that exists beyond our own reality — smashed box office records.
With just a $10 million budget, petty cash for Hollywood, it grossed over $400 million worldwide. The feature film started as a short on YouTube . And It's just one title from the newly-merged studio Blumhouse Atomic Monster .
Actor Chiwetel Umeadi Ejiofor portraying Clark in Backrooms. A24/Blumhouse Atomic Monster hide caption
Abhijay Prakash and Michael Clear head up the studio. Prakash is Blumhouse president. Clear is the president of Atomic Monster and leads the studio's emerging directors program. The merged studio retains separate leadership teams.
"We're drawn like moths to a flame to things that are scary," Clear says. "We reached out to Kane Parsons who had created the short and at the time he was 15 or 16; he was still in high school."
Despite the headlines Blumhouse Atomic Monster garnered for hiring Parsons, Clear adds it's not really all that new for them.
"We've always kind of scoured a variety of sources, particularly for filmmakers who have a sense of how to scare people. Going all the way back to one of the first movies we produced, Lights Out , David Sandberg, the director of that film, was actually himself a YouTube creator," Clear says.
"They say it's hard to describe what scary is but I know it when I see it."
Abhijay Prakash says the COVID-19 pandemic had an outsized impact on the horror film industry.
"Horror as a share of the box office…pre-COVID, was never more than 10% of the box office. Then after COVID though, it's occupying a much larger share. It's over 15%, almost 20% last year and this year. And inside of that we are over half of that box office," Prakash says.
"So our market share is over 50% of the horror box office. And that's where we're focused. We live and breathe it."
Our friends over at the Recreational Fear Lab theorize people are flocking to fear more these days because the real world has been just so darn scary.
But Michael Clear thinks it could be a bit more complicated than that.
"I agree it's part of it, but I also think that one of the things that shifted [is] the bar has been rising for what people need or what draws people to the theatres. It's been rising consistently over the last 10, 15 years," Clear says.
"Maybe all the isolation has just driven people towards more social activities," he adds. "People are craving collective experiences. We're finding more now than before the pandemic that people are going to movies in larger groups. And it just so happens that our genre, because it's participatory — if we do our jobs right, we're getting reactions, audible reactions from the audience — and it can be more fun to experience that with your friends."
"Scary stories in the dark," Abhijay Prakash underlines. "[It] has delivered for thousands of years."
While Blumhouse Atomic Monster makes its bid to reign supreme in theaters, many scream queens and kings are finding bite-sized horror scrolling social media. And often, those scary shorts are the products of AI.
"Personally, I think that, you know, anything that makes filmmaking more democratic can can be great. You know, people who find tools that can enable them to create it will allow more people, more talented people, to enter the space," Michael Clear says.
He cautions that audiences want things to feel authentic, as though the horror on the screen is genuine.
"When it comes to our movies, I think one of the things that just happens to be a characteristic of our genre is that the things that are scariest are the things that feel the most real. So really, when you get down to the way that AI images or whatever may impact movies, you know, our focus is always on doing things as real as possible. Doing things as practically as possible," Clear says.
Abhijay Prakash told The Ankler early this year that his goal for Blumhouse Atomic Monster is to be the Disney of fear.
"Every place that consumers engage with scary stories is a place that we as a business, as a company obsessed with horror and scary stories will be. And then it's only a question of the business model," Prakash says.
Prakash says the studio is exploring creating an attraction from its Five Nights at Freddy's franchise and he also points to the popularity of the stage version of Paranormal Activity .
"So that really is a guiding principle for our company. We want to be everywhere where horror is relevant and it's taking a bigger and bigger place in the culture," Prakash says.
Michael Clear says the idea isn't just to cater to existing fans of the genre, but to grow the fanbase for all things spooky itself. "We like to think that we can provide a kind of gateway horror," he says.
Next week we get a lesson in horror storytelling from one of the most prolific writers in the genre — Stephen Graham Jones.

title: Hormuz Strait to be reopened if US accepts Iran’s conditions
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi says the strategic Strait of Hormuz will be reopened if the United States accepts Iran’s terms and conditions.
Speaking on the sidelines of the meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC)’s Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad on Sunday, Iran’s top diplomat emphasized that the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened after the United States accepts Iran’s conditions.
In response to a question on Iran’s conditions and the possibility of a revision in the country’s nuclear positions, Araghchi stated that Iran’s conditions are entirely clear and have been presented to the American side in the form of a seven-point plan.
If there were any real sincerity on the US side—which there isn't—the way forward would be clear, he underscored.
Referring to the meeting of the OIC’s Council of Foreign Ministers and the transfer of its chairmanship to Iraq, he stated that Iraq, as a friendly and neighboring country, has special significance for the Islamic Republic, and its success in leading the Organization of Islamic Cooperation is also of paramount importance.
Turning to the participation of OIC’s member states in this meeting, Araghchi underlined that the meeting was highly received with approximately 20 foreign ministers and over 20 deputy foreign ministers from member states attended this prestigious event.
Emphasizing the necessity for the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) to play a constructive role in resolving disputes among Muslim nations, he stated, "I raised the issue during meetings with the prime minister and foreign minister of Iraq and also the newly-appointed secretary-general of the Organization.”
Regarding the meeting’s final statement and resolutions, Araghchi stated, "At present, the resolutions have not yet been adopted, and the drafting of the final declaration is not yet complete. Our colleagues have been working over the past few days to contribute to the formulation of all the resolutions."
In response to a question regarding Iran’s conditions and the possibility of a revision in country’s nuclear stance, the foreign minister stated, "Our conditions are entirely clear and have been presented to the American side in the form of a seven-point plan. The American side has also offered its own views, which we are currently reviewing."
If the US meets those conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen on the sixth day, and negotiations will resume on the seventh day, IRan's top diplomat reiterated.

title: Sybiha: 76 Energy Strikes Prove Moscow Flouts Ceasefire
body:
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has warned that Russia is systematically expandeing targeted strikes against Ukraine’s power grid while feigning interest in diplomatic initiatives, stating that 76 targeted attacks on energy infrastructure over the past week prove Moscow has honored no commitments.
Writing on X on Sunday, Oct. 18, Sybiha stressed that offering economic accommodations or easing sanctions under such conditions only equips the Kremlin with fresh revenue to underwrite ongoing military operations ahead of winter.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Its message could hardly be clearer – Moscow has not abided by any obligations,” Sybiha stated, noting that tens of thousands of Ukrainian families remain without electricity as international partners attempt to explore avenues to conclude the war.
The foreign minister reiterated figures disclosed earlier in the day by President Volodymyr Zelensky, pointing out that Russian forces carried out 76 targeted attacks against Ukrainian energy facilities since US President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” one week ago.
Sybiha added that over the preceding seven days alone, Russian forces deployed nearly 2,700 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs (KABs), and 66 missiles across Ukrainian territory, with the vast majority of missile systems consisting of high-speed ballistic weapons directed at municipal utilities.
Ukraine’s top diplomat observed that the Kremlin is pursuing an asymmetric strategy engineered to secure international sanctions relief without altering its operational conduct or military objectives on the ground.
According to Sybiha, Moscow seeks “sanctions relief without changing its behavior, preservation of profits without accountability, and the imitation of diplomatic efforts without any commitment to stop killing Ukrainians.”
Addressing international allies and policymakers in Washington, Sybiha cautioned that lowering the economic costs of Russian aggression while civilian infrastructure faces daily bombardment directly undermines prospective peace efforts.
“Easing economic pressure under these circumstances risks giving the Kremlin additional resources to finance its war,” Sybiha emphasized.
“It is time for our partners to draw the necessary conclusions. Any serious effort to end this war must increase pressure on Moscow, restrict the revenues financing its aggression, and strengthen Ukraine’s ability to defend its cities and energy infrastructure.”
The foreign minister underlined that Russia bears unilateral responsibility for prolonging the conflict, dismissing the notion that commercial accommodations can incentivize de-escalation.
“Reducing the cost of its aggression while it continues attacking Ukraine will not bring peace,” Sybiha concluded. “It can only make further aggression easier to finance.”
Sybiha’s public remarks arrive amid sharp transatlantic disagreements over the Trump administration’s recent foreign policy maneuvers toward Moscow.
On Friday, Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to waive mandatory statutory penalties, including 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties targeting global purchasers of Russian hydrocarbons, just 48 hours before their scheduled implementation.
The waiver follows an Oct. 9 bilateral commercial arrangement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin , under which Moscow agreed to deliver refined diesel onto international markets through 2027 to curb fuel benchmark inflation.
The shipments were authorized under a general license issued by the US Treasury Department.
While White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers argued that enforcing statutory sanctions now would impede ongoing diplomatic efforts to broker a peace settlement, Ukrainian officials have strongly contested that assessment.
Both Zelensky and Sybiha have warned that granting Moscow access to international energy markets injects direct hard currency into the Russian state budget during active military operations, validating the Kremlin’s calculation that its war effort is yielding economic dividends rather than consequences .

title: RAF Jets Log Near Misses With Suspected Drones at High Altitude
body:
British military jets encountered suspected drones on at least two occasions this year while carrying out exercises, a newspaper has claimed.
British news outlet The Telegraph reported on Friday that aircraft from the UK’s Royal Air Force (RAF) had near misses with the objects in February while flying many times above the legal height limit for commercial drones.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The outlet cited RAF incident logs it had seen.
News of the suspected drone encounters comes amid heightened concerns in Europe over apparently increasing levels of Russian hybrid warfare and espionage activity aimed at undermining NATO unity and reducing support for Ukraine.
The first incident took place on Feb. 18 while an RAF Airbus Voyager tanker aircraft was refueling a Typhoon fighter jet near Norfolk above eastern England, with the Voyager pilot reporting that the “potential drone” flew so close to the plane that it made the pilot “instinctively duck”, according to The Telegraph.
The incident reportedly occurred at an altitude of around 17,000 feet (5,181 meters) – well above the legal limit of 400 feet (121 meters) for commercial drones in the UK.
The second encounter took place just days later, on February 23, when a Typhoon fighter jet pilot taking part in dogfighting exercises spotted a “black circular object (similar in size to a car tire) pass directly above him”, according to the report cited by The Telegraph. That incident reportedly occurred at an altitude of about 12,500 feet (3,810 meters) about 30 miles (48 kilometers) off the coast of England.
There has been no confirmation on what the objects were or where they originated.

title: NDLEA intercepts N6.98bn tramadol shipment at Lagos port, arrests suspects across states
body:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has intercepted 8,725 kilogrammes of powdered tramadol worth more than N6.98 billion at the Apapa port in Lagos, after discovering that a shipment from India, declared as maize starch, contained the controlled drug.
In a statement shared with PREMIUM TIMES on Sunday by the agency’s Director of Media and Advocacy, Femi Babafemi, the consignment comprised 349 bags, which laboratory analysis confirmed contained tramadol hydrochloride.
Mr Babafemi stated that at the Tincan port, officers also seized 55 kilogrammes of Canadian Loud, a strain of cannabis valued at N165 million. The substance was concealed in a Toyota Sienna inside a 40-foot container.
In Lagos, NDLEA operatives raided a store in Idumota and arrested Elizabeth Chidera Kalu. They recovered 10,600 ampoules of diazepam and 6,500 tablets of Molly, according to the agency.
Two men were arrested in separate operations in Mushin. Idowu Daudu, 35, was found with 59.95 kilogrammes of cannabis, while Ahmed Oniyinde, 35, had 61.23 kilogrammes.
Officers also intercepted a truck travelling from the Trade Fair market along the Iyana Oba axis. A search revealed 18,000 tablets of 250mg tramadol hidden in cartons labelled as Rambo insecticide.
The agency identified the suspects as Tajudeen Adeduntan, a loading manager, and his assistant, Azeez Sikiru.
In Edo State, six suspects were arrested during raids conducted between 15 and 16 October in Warake, Ivhiaro, Ewe and Irue communities in Owan East Local Government Area.
Grace Ehimeka, 85, was found with 179 kilogrammes of cannabis, while Ayo Aigberadion, 53, had 220.8 kilogrammes.
The other suspects were Ali Garba, 57, who was found with 5.852 kilogrammes of cannabis; Habib Braimoh, 45, with 100 grammes; Musa Mubid, 35, with two kilogrammes of cannabis, seeds, tramadol, Swinol and diazepam; and Hope Okoro, 35, with 237 grammes of Loud.
Ms Ehimeka’s arrest comes weeks after PREMIUM TIMES reported the rearrest of another elderly woman, Uloma Sunday, 83, in Abia State.
Ms Sunday was arrested on 7 October, months after she and her daughter, Chisom Uchechi, 32, were convicted in a drug-related case.
The pair were arrested in May 2025 after officers recovered 50 grammes of methamphetamine, 522 grammes of cannabis, 260 grammes of fresh cannabis leaves and 12 grammes of tramadol. They pleaded guilty and were sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment or a fine of N200,000 each. Both paid their fines and were released.
During her latest arrest, Ms Sunday was allegedly found with methamphetamine and Colorado, a synthetic cannabinoid, concealed around her waist in a wrapper.
The NDLEA said intelligence reports indicated that she operated a drug joint where criminal suspects gathered and terrorised residents. The agency did not state whether she had been charged over the latest seizure.
The cases involving Ms Sunday and Ms Ehimeka are separate. The agency has not linked the two women.
In Ondo State, officers destroyed a cannabis farm covering three hectares in the Okemoro Isinbode camp forest on 17 October. The plants were estimated to weigh 7,500 kilogrammes.
Five suspects were arrested during the operation: Asikpo Ekpeyoung, 43; Solomon Okpani, 22; Ubong Friday, 35; Joseph Friday, 22; and Ekenimi Seth, 35.
Officers also recovered 92 bags of cannabis weighing 1,267 kilogrammes, 11 kilogrammes of cannabis seeds and three kilogrammes of fresh cannabis stems. The recovered exhibits weighed 1,281 kilogrammes, separate from the plants destroyed at the farm.
In another operation, officers arrested Okunebe Ndidi, 53, in the Ameyinti area of Owo on 16 October. They recovered 25 bags of cannabis weighing 375 kilogrammes.
In Bauchi State, officers intercepted Shamsu Garba, 35, at Ragwam village in Katagum Local Government Area on 14 October. He was travelling in a Volkswagen Golf wagon carrying 894,800 pills, identified by the agency as tramadol capsules and Exol-5 tablets.
On the same day, officers recovered 291 blocks of cannabis weighing 265 kilogrammes from an abandoned vehicle at Tudun Natsira, along the Bauchi-Gombe road.
In Kano State, Ali Abdullahi, 38, and Ibrahim Adamu, 23, were arrested along the Zaria-Kano road on 13 October with 30,100 tablets of tramadol, 225mg.
A day later, officers arrested Murtala Dayyabu, 54, on Niger Street in the Malan Kato area with 100,000 tablets of Exol-5.
At the airport, a 16-year-old passenger, Fatimah Ahmad, was arrested on 16 October while preparing to board an Ethiopian Airlines flight to Jeddah via Addis Ababa.
The agency noted that she was carrying 511.75 grammes of cannabis concealed in a gallon of palm oil.
Ms Ahmad reportedly told officers that her cousin, Abubakar Yahaya, had given her the substance. He was subsequently arrested at the airport car park.
In Kaduna State, officers arrested Mohammed Sani, 48; Zaharadeen Shafiu, 29; and Yakubu Abdullahi, 20, during a raid in Kayimi village. They recovered 496.5 kilogrammes of cannabis.
At Food Palace on Ali Akilu Road, officers arrested John Ayo David, 39, with 49,500 tablets of tramadol, 225mg.
In Abuja, Odo Jonas Ejike, 42, was arrested in Utako on 17 October with 29,500 tramadol capsules, the agency said.
The agency also held awareness programmes under its War Against Drug Abuse (WADA) campaign at schools and other institutions in several states.
The activities took place at Nawar-Ur-Deen High School in Ogboro, Oyo State; Elf Junior Secondary School in Bojude, Gombe State; Cherubim and Seraphim Primary School in Ikorodu, Lagos State; Harmony Secondary School in Lokoja, Kogi State; and Government Secondary School in Ikot Ansa, Calabar, Cross River State.
Other sessions were held at Rivers State College of Health Science and Management Technology in Port Harcourt, Mesh International School in Benin City, Edo State, and Abu Hanifa Academy in Kano Municipal.
NDLEA chairman Buba Marwa commended officers involved in the operations, including personnel at the Apapa and Tincan ports, the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, and the agency’s commands in Lagos, Edo, Bauchi, Ondo, Kano and the Federal Capital Territory.
He urged them to sustain efforts against drug trafficking and abuse.

title: Central Pelion: 7 Villages Between Forest and Aegean Sea
body: PELION, October 2026 — Central Pelion tempts visitors in all 12 months, with forest villages, a ski centre, old churches and pebble beaches. The Mountain of the Centaurs also offers trails for every level, while its taverns showcase fine local produce. Chania and Drakeia, the gateway to central Pelion Chania is the closest village in central Pelion to the ski centre at Agriolefkes , 12 kilometres from Portaria. As its name suggests, it once had inns, or hania, for travellers and muleteers. Today, because of the ski centre, Chania is full of shops, hotels, ski hire stores and taverns serving traditional dishes. About 8 kilometres away lies Drakeia, another village of central Pelion. The drive winds through chestnut and beech forests, with stunning views of the Pagasetic Gulf . Spread across the slope since 1615, or even earlier, Drakeia has an upper neighbourhood of old houses. It also has two plane-shaded squares and a traditional bakery. Its churches include Agios Georgios, with paintings by Pagonis, and Agios Spyridon, with a carved iconostasis. Road signs call Drakeia a “martyr village”, because German forces executed 118 people here in reprisal for resistance activity. Kissos and the story behind its name At 550 metres, Kissos ranks among the most beautiful small villages of central Pelion, hidden in forests of chestnut, beech and plane trees. Its major sight stands on the main square: the church of Agia Marina. This three-aisled basilica is one of the most representative church monuments on the mountain. Due to its fame, many people travel to Kissos to admire it. Kissos Locals still call the village “K’so”. However, the name does not come from ivy, which is kissos in Greek. According to the historian Yanis Kordatos , it is a corruption of chrysos, the Greek word for gold. That may reflect its past under Ottoman rule, when Kissos was a thriving main village of central Pelion. A local workshop turned chestnut wood on lathes to make wooden plates sold abroad. The village also prospered from silk and from skoutia, cloths woven with goat hair. A forest village with a legendary plane tree Tsagarada, the forest village of central Pelion, spreads across four neighbourhoods: Agios Stefanos, Agia Kyriaki, Agia Paraskevi and Taxiarches. They lie far apart, so it hardly feels like a classic village. Its story began in the 16th century, when people from the beach at Karavostasi moved uphill to escape pirates and, later, the Turks. As a result, they hid their homes deep in the forest. The plane tree in Agia Paraskevi square, Tsagarada, central Pelion, on Saturday 16 May 2015. Photo: Rob Stoeltje/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 By the mid-19th century, many residents had emigrated, mostly to Egypt. Some wealthy Egyptiot Greeks later funded fine buildings, roads, aqueducts and stone fountains in Tsagarada. For many years, it has been the most popular village in central Pelion, with dozens of hotels and restaurants. Its closeness to beaches such as Mylopotamos, Papa Nero and Fakistra also helped it grow. The heart of the village is Agia Paraskevi. On its large square stands a giant plane tree, with a trunk 14 metres around. Local legend puts its age at 1,000 years. Beside it, the church of Agia Paraskevi blends local architecture with neoclassical touches. In the small Taxiarches square, in contrast, the monumental church dates from 1786, and its carved Venetian-style iconostasis from 1749. An old harbour below castle ruins During the 19th century, Damouchari offered the only relatively safe harbour on the eastern side of the mountain. It had warehouses, shops and the Turkish customs house. Because of this port, many residents of Tsagarada and Mouresi became sailors. A cape splits it into Old and New Damouchari. Although much has changed since 1970, when few people knew of it, it keeps its charm. Spring and autumn are the best seasons to visit this corner of central Pelion, since summer brings crowds. On a rocky hill 25 metres above the sea stand the ruins of a castle. Without any excavation, firm facts are scarce. Even so, most accounts call it Byzantine, adding that the Venetians used it for a time. Near the car park in Damouchari stands the chapel of Agios Nikolaos, built or renovated in 1744. Many credit its early 19th-century frescoes to Pagonis. Look for the dog-headed saint, as well as the faded Last Supper. Mouresi and the beaches of Agios Ioannis Officially Mouresion, the village goes simply by Mouresi in central Pelion. It offers wide Aegean views, with hundreds of places to stay nearby, many on the road down to Agios Ioannis. Once you stroll its square, the church of Agia Triada wins you over, framed by giant linden trees. Renovated in 1776, it has a carved iconostasis and unusual purple-burgundy door and window frames. Folklorist Kostas Liapis notes that Mouresi flourished in the late 18th century, when residents raised silkworms and made skoutia. Below it, Agios Ioannis, once the landing for Kissos, has plane trees and a huge white pebble beach. Its family holiday tradition began with youth camps run by the Thessaloniki YMCA from 1928. Large hotels followed from 1930, then contractors gave it its present shape during the military junta . Near the Mouresi road, the chapel of Agios Ioannis Prodromos has a pebble floor and crypto-Christian symbols on its iconostasis. Papa Nero beach lies right beside Agios Ioannis, while Plaka beach sits on the other side. Source: travel.gr The post Central Pelion: 7 Villages Between Forest and Aegean Sea appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Mahama announces plans for airstrips in regions without airports
body: President John Dramani Mahama has announced plans to construct airstrips in regions without airports to improve emergency air travel and facilitate urgent medical evacuations. Western North, which currently has no operational commercial airport, is expected to benefit from the initiative. The President announced the plan during a courtesy call by chiefs from the Western North Region, explaining that the proposed facilities would provide landing sites for aircraft during emergencies. He said regions without existing airports would be provided with airstrips measuring approximately two kilometres in length, alongside small control offices to support aircraft operations. “We are going to provide an airstrip in every region that does not already have an airport. Sometimes there are emergencies, and sometimes medical evacuations are necessary. At the moment, some regions do not have landing sites for aircraft,” he said. President Mahama explained that regions with existing airports would not require the additional facilities, while those without airports would benefit from the planned infrastructure. “Regions that already have airports are covered, but those without airports will receive landing strips. They will be about two kilometres long and will have a small control office so that aircraft can land in the region in an emergency. Western North will be one of the beneficiaries,” he added.

title: Rubio says Ukraine does not have access to Starshield
body:
According to Ukrinform, he told this to reporters at Joint Base Andrews before departing for India and Uzbekistan.
At the same time, he said Ukraine currently does not have access to the Starshield system.
According to Rubio, Starlink is a commercial product, while Starshield is a defense and military product.
"I mean that that [Starshield] is something that the United States military uses. It's not at this moment available to Ukraine and that's under conversation. It's under discussion right now how they would want to use it," he said.
Rubio denied that the United States was involved in reducing Starlink's operating speed in Ukraine.
"We had nothing to do with it. Nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened. But my understanding is it's [Starlink's operating speed] been restored. It's back to where it was before. So that's Starlink though. They were using Starlink for their drones," he said.
Asked about restoring Starshield's operation, Rubio replied that the system was a separate product and had nothing to do with Ukraine.
"Starshield is a totally different product. Starshield is a contract with the U.S. military. It had nothing to do with Ukraine. I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield. They do not have Starshield now. They've asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment," Rubio said.
As Ukrinform reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Starlink's operation in Ukraine was being restricted to speeds of 161 km/h, making it impossible to use the system on interceptor drones designed to take down jet-powered Shahed drones.
Ukraine's chargé d'affaires in the United States, Denys Sienik, said Ukraine was awaiting an official response from the Pentagon and SpaceX regarding the full restoration of the Starshield satellite system's operation, adding that its performance remained unstable.
According to The Telegraph, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was the one who approached U.S. President Donald Trump with a proposal to restrict Starlink's operating speed in Ukraine.

title: Violent Protests in France : 1 Dead, 1,200 Arrested, 150 Police Injured
body: Widespread clashes, arson and looting marked protests across France on Saturday, leaving one rioter dead, 1,200 people arrested and 150 police officers injured. The death occurred in Paris after a person suffered cardiac arrest on Boulevard de Magenta and died outside a first-aid station. A 17-year-old in Saint-Étienne lost a hand after allegedly picking up a police grenade. The looting continues in Paris pic.twitter.com/usieB9ZHhf — Visegrád 24 (@visegrad24) October 17, 2026 Masked rioters set fire to Limoges Town Hall, stormed Marseille City Hall, attacked the CNews headquarters, and damaged buildings including Lyon’s tourist office and town halls in Lille and Grenoble. Serious clashes also took place around Place de la République in Paris. Attendance estimates differed: organisers and the CGT union claimed 800,000 participants, while the Interior Ministry put the figure at 550,000. Around 110,000 took part in Paris. . @elonmusk predicted what's happening in France: “If you get lots of immigrants who oppose Western values, you are setting yourself up for civil war.” pic.twitter.com/hBq7qbQMiL — Dr. Eli David (@DrEliDavid) October 18, 2026 Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and President Emmanuel Macron said those responsible for the violence and destruction would be prosecuted. Lecornu stated that “no one will impose their political agenda through violence.” The government pointed to elements on the Left amid the fallout. The post Violent Protests in France : 1 Dead, 1,200 Arrested, 150 Police Injured appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: 'You are the real target': Netanyahu warns Iran developing ICBMs, nuclear weapons to target US
body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran was developing intercontinental ballistic missiles and pursuing nuclear weapons with the aim of threatening American cities, telling FOX News on Saturday that the US, rather than Israel, was the Iranian regime's ultimate target.Netanyahu argued that Iran's ambitions extend beyond Israel, warning that the regime intends to target both the US and Europe if it succeeds in destroying Israel. He said Iran's development of long-range missiles and pursuit of a nuclear arsenal were intended to place American cities at the mercy of the regime."They understand that if they can destroy Israel, then they can conquer the Middle East, control the waterways of the world... and then proceed to the next target, which is you. That's why they're building intercontinental missiles: to reach the United States," Netanyahu said."This is a regime that chants death to Israel, death to America. You are the real target. And I think we are well on our way to achieving this, with President Trump's brilliant leadership, both military and, then, economic blockade."The prime minister explained that the Iranian regime views the US as "the great Satan" and Israel as the "little Satan," before directing a remark at European countries.He said he "hoped our European friends are not offended; you are seen as the middle-sized Satan, you are mediocre in so many ways.""Iran would be a nuclear power as we've never seen in the entire world, because they don't have this careful calculus of cause and benefit. Because they are so fanatic. So you can't win them over, you can't buy them out," he said.Netanyahu also described the Iranian regime as a "malevolent power" operating alongside what he called the "Three Hs": Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis."They are the arms of this toxic octopus. And it's not Iranian people; they are great people," he added.Eliminating the Iranian threat was the first of three priorities Netanyahu outlined for his next term if reelected in the October 27 Knesset election, alongside expanding the Abraham Accords and establishing Israel as a global leader in artificial intelligence."First, we will achieve the complete elimination of the Iranian threat to Israel, to America, and to the entire world," Netanyahu said.Expanding Abraham Accords as a key objective"Second thing is to expand the historic Abraham Accords that [US President Donald] Trump and I forged here with four Arab states," Netanyahu continued."There are many more that are waiting in this precise moment, because they saw our strength, our power and fortitude. And they want to join us. So let's create an axis of peace and moderation against these barbarians who shoot their own people," he said.Netanyahu also said he plans to "forge a different future, a different Middle East, and also a different world" if reelected.Artificial Intelligence to help humankindNetanyahu's third priority focused on artificial intelligence, and the prime minister said he agreed with Trump on both the dangers the technology poses and its potential benefits for humanity."I plan to seize the future with the 'Neverland AI,' the 'super intelligence,' as the president calls it. He is absolutely right; they are dangerous, but their possibilities in health, in agriculture, in transport, and in education," he explained."You can personalize AI for every child; they have their own potential, and you can give them the best teachers on the planet. We are doing it today in Israel, and we intend to be the world leaders in that area too. These are all amazing things," he added.Netanyahu also pointed to Israel's economic performance, which he described as among the strongest in the developed world."By the way, the economy, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), is leading all the Western countries, the OCD countries, with the greatest growth. That's after three years of war. I want to push that even further, bring a better future to Israel, to our neighbors, to our great ally the United States."

title: Trump Envoys Push Russian Gas Transit in Ukraine Peace Talks
body:
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have urged Ukraine and European allies to consider resuming Russian natural gas transit through Ukrainian pipeline infrastructure as a key economic element of a prospective peace settlement, The New York Times reported.
According to officials familiar with the discussions, the proposal was presented by the Trump administration during high-level consultations with President Volodymyr Zelensky and senior European policymakers.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The initiative has encountered firm opposition across European capitals, particularly in Germany, where officials warn that reviving reliance on Russian hydrocarbons undermines continental energy security.
American negotiators argue that restoring Russian pipeline flows to Europe would provide the Kremlin with a commercial incentive to halt military operations, while generating valuable transit revenues for Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction. Washington also anticipates that sustained inflation and elevated energy costs will eventually prompt European consumers to demand cheaper supplies.
The proposal forms part of a broader, long-term settlement architecture being explored by the White House, encompassing future NATO -Russia relations, post-war security guarantees for Kyiv, and territorial arrangements.
Some Ukrainian and European officials briefed on the discussions suggested that Washington could seek a share of the commercial proceeds generated from the restarted gas trade.
A White House spokesperson confirmed that the administration’s peace proposals incorporate economic incentives for both Moscow and Kyiv to encourage a durable armistice.
According to sources cited by The New York Times, discussions between American and Russian representatives have also touched upon the sabotaged Nord Stream 2 undersea pipeline across the Baltic Sea .
One source familiar with the backchannel contacts described restarting intact segments of Nord Stream 2 following a peace accord as the “simplest step” to stabilize regional gas balances.
However, White House officials formally denied that reviving the Baltic pipeline project had been actively discussed in recent engagements.
The gas transit proposal follows earlier economic inducements presented by Witkoff and Kushner during multilateral talks in Miami, which included unfreezing up to $100 billion in immobilized Russian state assets, authorizing a Middle Eastern buyout of Lukoil’s foreign operations, and easing sanctions on Belarusian potash.
The prospect of restoring Russian pipeline supplies has provoked decisive resistance in Berlin, formerly the largest purchaser of Russian natural gas in Europe prior to the February 2022 full-scale invasion .
During diplomatic consultations held in Florida, Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz , pushed back forcefully against the initiative. German officials emphasized that Russian gas remains Russian regardless of whether transactions are structured through intermediary traders or third-party brokers.
Former German Economy Minister Robert Habeck warned against repeating past strategic mistakes, emphasizing that Germany has fundamentally adapted its energy architecture away from Moscow.
“Europe, and especially Germany, must never again become dependent on Russian gas. We saw how unreliable Russia was,” Habeck stated.
The diplomatic friction unfolds against intense domestic political debate within Germany. The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party , which has polled near 30 percent in recent nationwide surveys, has campaigned heavily on restoring direct imports of cheap Russian gas to curb consumer inflation and lower industrial electricity tariffs.
German and European officials maintain that restoring energy flows to the Kremlin would undermine European sanctions packages and generate billions of dollars in hard currency that underwrite Moscow’s defense industry, complicating ongoing transatlantic negotiations over post-war security frameworks.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Herzog meets Bahrain's foreign minister in Azerbaijan as Baku emerges as a regional hub - analysis
body: President Isaac Herzog's meeting with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani in Baku on Wednesday highlighted Azerbaijan's increasingly important role in regional diplomacy. At a time when relations across the Middle East remain strained, the Azerbaijani capital has become a meeting point for countries that do not always find it easy to talk to one another.The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) summit, hosted by Azerbaijan. According to Herzog's office, the two discussed strengthening the Abraham Accords and expanding regional cooperation. Herzog also met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev to discuss bilateral relations and regional security.For Azerbaijan, an emerging middle power, the meetings reflect a diplomatic role that has developed over the years. The country maintains close relations with Israel while preserving strong ties with Turkey, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and other Muslim-majority countries. Its ability to work with governments whose interests sometimes conflict has made it a useful venue for sensitive discussions.Azerbaijan's diplomatic role allows for 'reconciliation without a public stage'Joseph Epstein, director of the Turan Research Center and a senior fellow at the Yorktown Institute, describes this approach as “reconciliation without a public stage.”“Azerbaijan established relations with Israel in 1992 and has kept them intact through two Karabakh wars, the war in Gaza and years of pressure from Tehran and Ankara,” Epstein said. “The partnership covers security, trade, technology, and energy, and Baku built it without cutting a single tie to the Arab and Muslim world.”According to Epstein, Azerbaijan's relationships with Israel and Muslim countries gave it a diplomatic role well before the Abraham Accords were signed in 2020.“Israeli and Arab officials could meet there years before because no one saw Azerbaijan as Israel's enemy or as its client. Every side trusted the host,” he said.That relationship has also helped manage tensions between Israel and Turkey. In April 2025, Israeli and Turkish security delegations met in Azerbaijan for talks aimed at establishing a mechanism to prevent military incidents in Syria, where both countries have strategic interests. The Prime Minister's Office publicly thanked Azerbaijan and President Aliyev for hosting the discussions.The talks did not resolve the broader disagreements between Jerusalem and Ankara, but they demonstrated the value of maintaining a direct channel even when political relations are strained.“The same logic now applies to Turkey and Israel,” Epstein said. “Baku is Ankara's closest ally and one of Jerusalem's closest partners, and it uses that trust to keep the two from drifting into confrontation.”After its victory in Karabakh, Azerbaijan took another step in this strategy, moving from military success toward normalization with Armenia. Negotiations over a peace treaty, border delimitation and the opening of transport links reflect Baku's stated aim of consolidating its gains through a new regional framework rather than military force alone.The process has also created opportunities for normalization between Armenia and Turkey. Without reduced tensions between Baku and Yerevan, progress between Armenia and Turkey would have been considerably more difficult.Azerbaijan emerging as a middle power in the Middle EastProfessor Ze'ev Khanin, head of the Post-Soviet Conflicts Research Program at the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, sees Azerbaijan's emergence as a middle power as a model distinct from the formal framework of the Abraham Accords.Baku continues to develop relations with Israel despite the escalation of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and pressure from Iran and Turkey. For Israel, Khanin argues, this makes Azerbaijan not merely a partner but a rare example of a durable bridge between the Jewish state and the Muslim world.Herzog's visit also underscores Azerbaijan's growing importance to the United States and the West. Washington's recognition of the country's role in regional stability was reflected in the strategic partnership charter the two governments signed in February 2026, which emphasized their shared interest in peace and security in the South Caucasus.For Baku, this presents an opportunity to consolidate its position as a diplomatic intermediary. For Israel, Turkey, Armenia, and the Arab states, it highlights the availability of a venue for dialogue even during periods of regional tension.Azerbaijani officials involved in the country's foreign policy present Baku's diplomatic approach as pragmatic rather than ideological. In this view, Azerbaijan does not require governments to endorse its political model or make public concessions as a condition for dialogue. Nor does it seek to turn diplomatic contacts into public propaganda campaigns.This approach helps explain why Israel, Turkey, the Gulf Arab states, and Armenia can engage with Azerbaijan despite their sometimes conflicting interests, without necessarily turning such contacts into domestic political controversies.This role is especially important as the Middle East faces continued tensions over Gaza and Iran and a wider crisis of trust among regional governments. The Abraham Accords demonstrated that normalization is possible, but their durability depends on more than formal agreements. It also requires countries willing to maintain relationships when political rhetoric hardens.Azerbaijan has become one such country, preserving its partnership with Israel while maintaining contacts across the Arab and Muslim world.Herzog's meeting with the Bahraini foreign minister in Baku therefore carried significance beyond diplomatic protocol. Israel and Bahrain established diplomatic relations under the Abraham Accords in 2020, but their relationship came under strain following the outbreak of the Gaza war in October 2023.The meeting showed that, despite a period of cooling relations, Jerusalem and Manama can still engage in direct dialogue, with Baku providing a venue for their talks.For Israel, the encounter offered an opportunity to preserve and strengthen the Abraham Accords. For Washington, it underscored the importance of maintaining regional diplomatic channels. For Azerbaijan, it reinforced its growing status as a middle power and an independent center of influence.As Prof. Khanin puts it, “Baku can offer a venue for dialogue between governments that have reasons to maintain contact despite their disagreements. As regional tensions continue, Azerbaijan's experience suggests that diplomatic influence does not always depend on brokering a major peace agreement. Sometimes, maintaining relationships and providing a place where difficult conversations can continue is an achievement in itself.”

title: Macron to address France tonight amid unrest — Le Monde
body:
PARIS, October 18. /TASS/. French President Emmanuel Macron will deliver a televised address to his fellow citizens a 9:00 p.m. Moscow time (6:00 p.m. GMT) in connection with the October 17 unrest, Le Monde quoted the Elysee Palace as saying.
On October 17, mass demonstrations against rising fuel prices and declining purchasing power took place in Paris and throughout France. According to the organizers, 800,000 people participated, while the Interior Ministry put the figure at 550,000. In some cities, the protests erupted into riots and clashes with the police. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 1,800 people across the country were detained and promised that the government would continue to pursue everyone who participated in the riots and ransacking.

title: Russia supports GCC’s efforts to prevent full·scale war in region — Lavrov
body:
MANAMA /Kingdom of Bahrain/, October 18. /TASS/. Russia supports the peacekeeping efforts of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), which are aimed at preventing a full·scale war in the Middle East, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at a ministerial meeting of the Russia-GCC strategic dialogue.
"Russia supports the ongoing peacekeeping efforts, including those of the countries represented here, [efforts] that are aimed at preventing a return to a full·scale war in the region," he said.
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) is a regional organization comprising six countries: Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, Oman, and Saudi Arabia. The organization’s goal is to expand cooperation among the member countries in all areas and to develop common positions on key international and regional issues. The GCC charter says that its members are "united by a common historical and cultural development and a similarity of political systems" (all member countries are monarchies).

title: Gulf countries call on Russia to support their participation in negotiations on Iran
body:
DOHA, October 18. /TASS/. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) expects Russia to use its ties with Iran to encourage it to comply with the UN security council resolutions and to support the participation of Arab states in talks on the Iranian nuclear program, said Bahrain’s Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani.
"We expect the Russian Federation to use its ties with Iran to encourage it to fully comply with [UN security council] resolution 2817 and to support the participation of the countries of the Cooperation Council in any negotiations or agreements related to Iran’s nuclear and missile programs," al·Zayani said at the 9th joint ministerial meeting within the framework of the Russia-GCC Strategic Dialogue. According to him, the states of the region are most likely to suffer from Tehran’s programs, which is why their participation in the negotiations is necessary.
He also expressed gratitude to Moscow for its coordination within the UN Security Council. "We also appreciate its participation in aligning the chairman’s statement adopted by the security council on October 15, condemning the ongoing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia," the minister said.
Al·Zayani hopes that Moscow would support a draft resolution submitted by Saudi Arabia to the UN security council. The document is aimed at protecting the civilian population, stopping the rebels’ attacks, and curbing the sources of their financing and armament, the minister noted.
In Manama, under the chairmanship of al-Zayani, the 168th meeting of the Council of Ministers of the GCC is being held at the level of heads of foreign policy departments. On October 17, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in the kingdom on an official visit. The session is scheduled to include the ninth joint ministerial meeting within the framework of the Russia-GCC Strategic Dialogue, during which the participants will discuss the development of multilateral partnership, coordination on regional security issues, and the international agenda.

title: Mitsotakis: Greece Now Has a Strong Voice in Europe
body: Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Greece is using its stronger position in Europe to benefit both Greek and European citizens. In his weekly review, he highlighted three Greek proposals that received backing from EU leaders at the recent Summit: An emergency adjustment of European fiscal rules so countries with surpluses, like Greece, can provide targeted support to households and businesses during the energy crisis. A European mechanism to counter hybrid threats on the migration front, such as those seen in Evros in 2020 and recently in Ceuta, Spain. A stricter framework of age limits for children’s access to social media. “All of these are Greek proposals that are becoming European policies,” Mitsotakis said. “Europe must move faster on all three fronts.” He also outlined domestic measures against the energy crisis. Heating oil is being subsidised by 40 cents per litre, shared between the state and refineries, and the heating allowance is rising by 30%. This brings the price to €1.55 per litre (around €1.35 for those receiving the allowance), supporting nearly 1.2 million households. Motor fuels will see temporary cuts of 20 cents on diesel and 10 cents on unleaded petrol until October 31, applied directly at the pump. Mitsotakis said the government will continue monitoring international developments and keep reserves for further support if needed. The post Mitsotakis: Greece Now Has a Strong Voice in Europe appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: What the next WHO director-general must learn from Nigeria’s health reforms, By Chinedu Moghalu
body:
Progress is nonetheless visible. By October 2026, the National Health Insurance Authority reported that 80,000 women had received emergency maternal care by August, while health insurance enrolment surpassed 23 million by September… The more important lesson, however, is not the numbers themselves but the accountability model behind them. Effective reform means tracking resources from allocation to release and from release to service delivery. It requires assessing service quality and asking whether households can genuinely afford care. WHO can help countries adopt common metrics and independent oversight mechanisms, while ensuring that the consequences of unmet commitments are visible to those who control financial resources.
When WHO elects its next director-general in 2027, member states will also consider proposals to reshape the wider global health system. Development aid is shrinking, the United States has withdrawn from WHO , and governments are increasingly asking international agencies to align behind national health plans.
National plans can provide a common framework for government, donors, and development partners. But a plan alone cannot guarantee that funding reaches frontline facilities, that clinics are properly staffed, or that patients receive quality care. The next director-general must demonstrate how WHO can help countries not only design ambitious plans, but also finance and deliver what those plans promise.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has strengthened WHO’s tools for collective action. Under his leadership, the organisation expanded pandemic intelligence, scientific guidance, workforce training and support for technology transfer. Member states amended the International Health Regulations , adopted the Pandemic Agreement , and committed to increasing assessed contributions .
Having guided the WHO through the COVID-19 pandemic, Tedros also inherited the difficult aftermath. Funding reductions have left the organisation with fewer staff and a smaller budget to sustain many of the gains achieved during that period.
As at 31 March, only 73 per cent of WHO’s 2026–27 base budget was financed , and just 41 per cent was projected to be financed flexibly . While earmarked contributions keeps many programmes, it often leaves critical gaps in independent technical guidance and country support.
The challenge extends beyond WHO. Development assistance across all sectors declined by 23.1 per cent in real terms in 2025 . Meanwhile, the World Bank projects that reductions in aid could outweigh increases rising government health spending, leaving 80 per cent of low-income countries and 40 per cent of lower-middle-income countries with less combined government and donor funding in 2030 than they had in 2024.
This reality makes transition planning more important than ever. Before external funders withdraw, countries and partners must identify who will finance treatment, immunisation, disease surveillance, and other essential services. The US–Nigeria health agreement offers one example, preserving significant bilateral support while Nigeria gradually increases domestic health expenditure.
The Accra Reset panel has proposed a simple principle: “One Plan. One Budget. One Platform.” Building on the Lusaka Agenda and Africa CDC’s efforts to strengthen national ownership and regional capacity, the proposal seeks greater alignment across the global health ecosystem.
The Accra Reset panel has proposed a simple principle: “One Plan. One Budget. One Platform.” Building on the Lusaka Agenda and Africa CDC’s efforts to strengthen national ownership and regional capacity, the proposal seeks greater alignment across the global health ecosystem.
Yet major institutions, including Gavi, the Global Fund, development banks, and bilateral donors, still operate through separate grant cycles, procurement rules, and reporting requirements. Their governing boards retain the authority to harmonise these mechanisms around costed national programmes. That work should advance in parallel with the wider architecture review commissioned at the Seventy-Ninth World Health Assembly (WHA79) , whose recommendations will be considered in 2027.
