The Seventy-Ninth World Health Assembly also adopted an Economics of Health for All strategy, providing health ministers with a stronger framework for engaging finance and planning authorities on investment, growth, and financial protection. Its amended health-worker recruitment code of health workers likewise encourages destination countries to invest measurably in the health systems that train the professionals they recruit… Nigeria’s Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) offers another useful lesson by linking procurement, regulation, and industrial policy within a single conversation.
Nigeria illustrates just how demanding genuine coordination can be. The National Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and Health Renewal Compact bring together primary healthcare, financing, workforce development, health security, and local manufacturing and supply systems under a single framework.
The expanded compact assigns responsibilities across federal, state, and local governments, while also incorporating development partners and civil society within a sector-wide approach. Joint reviews and independent verification mechanisms help reinforce accountability. Even so, no federal agreement can by itself recruit health workers, stock medicines, or ensure the release of state budget allocations.
Progress is nonetheless visible. By October 2026, the National Health Insurance Authority reported that 80,000 women had received emergency maternal care by August, while health insurance enrolment surpassed 23 million by September.
The more important lesson, however, is not the numbers themselves but the accountability model behind them. Effective reform means tracking resources from allocation to release and from release to service delivery. It requires assessing service quality and asking whether households can genuinely afford care. WHO can help countries adopt common metrics and independent oversight mechanisms, while ensuring that the consequences of unmet commitments are visible to those who control financial resources.
The Seventy-Ninth World Health Assembly also adopted an Economics of Health for All strategy , providing health ministers with a stronger framework for engaging finance and planning authorities on investment, growth, and financial protection. Its amended health-worker recruitment code of health workers likewise encourages destination countries to invest measurably in the health systems that train the professionals they recruit.
Nigeria’s Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) offers another useful lesson by linking procurement, regulation, and industrial policy within a single conversation. Regional manufacturing and pooled procurement can strengthen health systems, but only if regulatory institutions guarantee quality and purchasers have access to reliable products at affordable prices.
Meanwhile, negotiations on the benefit-sharing annex remain incomplete, preventing the Pandemic Agreement from opening for signature. Although the agreement envisions rapid financing provisions at the onset of health emergencies, the proposed coordinating mechanism still requires clear operational rules and dependable funding.
The next Director-General should therefore bring governments and financing institutions together around plans that are fully costed, tested, and actionable. These plans should include sustained investment in surveillance systems and laboratory networks, predefined triggers for releasing emergency funds and procuring medical supplies, equitable access to diagnostics, vaccines, and treatments, and safeguards to ensure continuity of routine health services during outbreaks.
Many of the governments that vote on WHO’s budget also sit on the boards of Gavi, the Global Fund, and major development banks. Nigeria’s Health Compact provides a practical framework for comparing the policies they approve with what actually happens on the ground: whether budgets are released, whether care improves, and whether households can afford essential services.
WHO’s 2025–28 programme already recognises the interconnected nature of modern health challenges, including climate-related risks, prevention, primary healthcare, financial protection, and emergency preparedness. The next Director-General must now help member states distinguish between the technical functions that require reliable, predictable funding and the country-level activities that WHO is uniquely positioned to deliver.
Among the seven candidates currently seeking the office , several themes are emerging. Belgium’s Hans Kluge advocates stronger country offices and more flexible financing. Saudi Arabia’s Hanan Balkhy emphasises scientific independence, emergency preparedness, and regional capacity. Indonesia’s Health Minister, Budi Gunadi Sadikin , highlights WHO’s convening power in support of costed national plans and regional procurement cooperation.
Qatar’s Hanan Mohammed Al-Kuwari calls for a more independent and sustainably financed WHO, alongside a review of the organisation’s three-tier structure. Spain’s María Neira places prevention and environmental health at the centre of her vision. Armenian paediatric oncologist Gevorg Tamamyan has stressed the importance of patient outcomes. China’s Song Li has been presented by her government as a strong advocate for multilateral cooperation, although a detailed public programme has yet to emerge.
Despite their differences, all candidates face the same fundamental challenge: explaining how WHO will finance its core functions while influencing the grant and investment decisions that shape health outcomes in lower-income countries.
Many of the governments that vote on WHO’s budget also sit on the boards of Gavi, the Global Fund, and major development banks. Nigeria’s Health Compact provides a practical framework for comparing the policies they approve with what actually happens on the ground: whether budgets are released, whether care improves, and whether households can afford essential services.
The next Director-General should extend that level of scrutiny beyond Nigeria. WHO’s own country support should be assessed alongside donor grants and public spending, creating a clearer line of sight between commitments, financing, implementation, and results. That is ultimately the lesson Nigeria offers the world: health reform succeeds not when plans are written, but when promises are funded, delivered, and measured.
Chinedu Moghalu is a lawyer, strategic communications expert, and public policy adviser with over two decades of leadership across government, international organisations, and development institutions. Currently, senior special adviser to Nigeria’s coordinating minister of health and social welfare.

title: Ukraine targets Russia with more than 1,000 drones, striking oil terminal
body:
Russian officials said oil facilities were struck in the massive attack.
LONDON and MOSCOW -- Ukraine overnight launched a massive aerial attack, sending hundreds of drones toward targets in Moscow and St. Petersburg, and striking a major oil terminal again despite pressure from President Donald Trump to end such attacks.
Drones struck a major oil terminal in St. Petersburg as well as a large data center, with videos posted online appearing to show fires burning. Video also appears to show a drone striking a huge bridge in the city.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said it had shot down some 1,015 drones near Moscow and several other western regions, making the attack one of the largest of the war. The attack also appeared to be the biggest St. Petersburg has witnessed.
St. Petersburg’s governor, Alexander Beglov, confirmed the attacks in the city, in a post on Telegram, writing, "Emergency services continue to work on extinguishing fires at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District."
One person was killed and five others were injured in St. Petersburg, Beglov said, saying that apartment buildings and homes had been damaged in the attack.
Two transformer substations were struck in Yanino, in the Leningrad region, Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said, adding that about 20,000 people were without electricity on Sunday morning. Russia media reported the attack was one of the largest the region had witnessed since the start of war.
The strikes on the oil terminals also underline that Ukraine has returned to attacking Russia's oil industry after pausing to adhere to Trump's "energy ceasefire." The Kremlin never abided by that "ceasefire."
Ukraine had reluctantly halted the refinery attacks under pressure from Trump, after he announced last weekend that the two sides had agreed to the "ceasefire" and following his deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
It comes as Trump this week moved to further ease pressure on Putin while escalating it on Zelenskyy. Trump on Friday waived a sweeping new sanctions package passed by Congress. The sanctions law named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham would have significantly expanded measures targeting Russia’s oil and gas industry.
Zelenskyy has criticised the move, saying it encourages Putin to keep fighting. He suggested on Saturday he believed Trump would likely move to further ease sanctions on Putin, saying the diesel deal was just the first step.
This week Ukraine also reported Elon Musk’s crucial Starlink internet system had been abruptly restricted on its drones, disrupting its military’s operations, with concerns in Kyiv the move was intended to further pressure it. There was also anxiety among officials in Ukraine that Trump may move to limit intelligence sharing providing warning about Russia missiles launches.
Russia has continued to heavily target Ukraine's energy infrastructure without pause despite Trump’s declaring the two sides had agreed to the "ceasefire" last weekend.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday morning accused Russia of "deliberately" launching at least 76 attacks on energy or oil and gas targets over the last week. He said Russia had launched attacks overnight on substations in four regions, including Odesa.
"Tens of thousands of families remain without power," Zelenskyy said on social media. "Energy workers and repair crews are working virtually around the clock to restore electricity supply."
Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight killed at least two people and injured at least a dozen others, he said.
"In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic," Zelenskyy said. "The main targets of these strikes are energy facilities -- the Russians are trying to cause a blackout. And America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements."
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Russian drones hit western Ukraine as nationwide attacks kill 10, injure 73
body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 10 civilians and injured 73 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Oct. 18.
Russia launched an Iskander-M ballistic missile, 180 Shahed drones, including 26 jet-powered Shaheds, as well as S-8000 and Banderol loitering munitions, also known as Dan-T, and Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force reported.
Ukrainian forces intercepted 152 drones, including 16 jet-powered drones. Russian strikes hit 20 locations, while falling debris was reported at four other sites.
Three western Ukrainian oblasts came under Russian attack on the morning of Oct. 18, continuing Moscow's recent pattern of targeting critical infrastructure across multiple regions.
In Volyn Oblast, in northwestern Ukraine, Russian drones attacked an industrial facility in the town of Manevychi, sparking a large fire, acting regional Governor Roman Romaniuk said .
Warehouses and production facilities caught fire, with the blaze covering a large area and generating heavy smoke. No casualties or injuries had been reported as of the latest update.
The attack marked the second strike on an industrial facility in Manevychi in three days. An earlier Russian attack on the Agrofrukt LTD facility on Oct. 16 killed one person and injured eight others, Manevychi Mayor Oleksandr Havryliuk said .
In western Ternopil Oblast, Russian drones attacked an energy infrastructure facility near the settlement of Staryi Vyshnivets, Governor Taras Pastukh said . The strike left some consumers without electricity. No casualties had been reported at the time of his statement.
Russian forces also launched a large-scale drone attack on Rivne, in northwestern Ukraine, targeting civilian infrastructure, regional Governor Oleksandr Koval said . The strikes sparked fires at the impact sites. No casualties had been reported as of the latest update.
In Odesa, Russian forces struck the roof of a multistory residential building on the morning of Oct. 18, injuring two people, including a 14-year-old girl, regional Governor Oleh Kiper said .
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed seven people and injured 14 others, Governor Vadym Filashkin said . Most of the casualties were reported in Sloviansk, where multiple houses were damaged.
Russian attacks in Kherson Oblast injured 32 people, including one child, regional Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said . Russian forces targeted critical infrastructure, social infrastructure, and residential areas across the region.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured four others, regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said . Russian forces launched 10 missiles at the city of Zaporizhzhia. Over the past 24 hours, they carried out 808 strikes on 53 settlements across the region.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people and injured five over the past 24 hours, according to the regional military administration. Russian forces carried out nearly 50 attacks across the region, damaging or destroying civilian infrastructure.
In Kharkiv Oblast, 12 people were injured in Russian attacks, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said . Russian forces struck Kharkiv and nine other settlements using ballistic missiles, drones, glide bombs, known as KABs, and a multiple-launch rocket system.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, three people were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said . Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times using drones and artillery.
Russian forces again targeted critical infrastructure in the city of Dnipro on the morning of Oct. 18. Information about possible casualties was still being clarified, Hanzha said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, one person was injured when a Russian Geran drone struck a residential yard, regional Governor Viacheslav Chaus said .

title: Zelensky: Russia has attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure 76 times since Trump announced truce
body:
According to Ukrinform, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported this on Telegram .
"Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ago, Russia has deliberately attacked Ukraine's energy and oil and gas sectors 76 times," he said.
The head of state noted that substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi and Odesa regions were targeted last night alone.
Zelensky stressed that Russian strikes have left tens of thousands of families without electricity, while energy workers and repair crews are working virtually around the clock to restore power.
Overnight, Russian forces also attacked residential buildings in various regions of Ukraine. According to him, 12 people have been injured so far, including two children. Two people were killed. Zelensky expressed his condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims.
In the morning, Russia also struck an agricultural enterprise in the Volyn region. All relevant services are currently working at the scene.
According to Zelensky, energy infrastructure is the main target of these attacks, as "the Russians are trying to cause a blackout."
"And America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting. It is because of this position of Russia’s that the war continues, not because Ukraine is rightfully defending itself. It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps," he said.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

title: Britain yet to fill twenty-seven posts at Norfolk command
body: Britain has taken command of NATO’s Atlantic headquarters with twenty-seven of its own seventy-one posts there still unfilled, and the Ministry of Defence does not expect to complete them until the end of 2027, according to written evidence submitted to the Defence Committee. The Ministry of Defence supplied the figures in answer to follow-up questions from the committee’s High North inquiry, after members asked for the percentage and actual numbers of British-allocated NATO posts at the headquarters that are currently filled. The department said: “The UK holds over 1000 NATO posts, which are currently filled at around 90% – one of the highest fill rates in the Alliance. Fill rates naturally fluctuate as posts are created, filled and rotated. The UK holds 71 out of the 494 Joint Force Command Norfolk (JFC Norfolk) posts; 44 of these have already been filled, with the remaining 27 posts due to be filled by the end of 2027. The UK will assume command of JFC Norfolk from the United States in September 2026, when General Nick Perry will take up the 4* Commander (COM) role.” Joint Force Command Norfolk is the NATO headquarters responsible for the North Atlantic, established in 2019 and declared fully operational in 2021 as the alliance reckoned with Russian submarine activity returning to Cold War levels. It is the only NATO command headquarters based in North America, co-located with the United States Second Fleet at Norfolk, Virginia, and its area of responsibility covers the sea lines of communication between North America and Europe that any reinforcement of the continent depends on. General Nick Perry took up the four-star Commander role in September, putting a British officer in charge of the headquarters that would run the Atlantic in a crisis. The Royal Navy has long argued that anti-submarine warfare in the Greenland Iceland United Kingdom gap is where Britain contributes most distinctively to NATO, and the command appointment follows that logic. The post Britain yet to fill twenty-seven posts at Norfolk command first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Stalled wind farm project in Katsina typifies Nigeria’s struggle to build renewable-energy industry
body:
For more than two decades, Nigeria has pursued renewable energy as part of the solution to its electricity crisis.
The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) reported that the average supply from grid-connected power plants was about 5,400MW in the fourth quarter of 2025, while World Bank data put the access rate at 62.5 per cent in 2024.
Authorities have tried to expand power generation through solar and wind projects. However, the 10MW Lambar-Rimi wind farm project in Katsina State shows how difficult it has been for the country to turn plans into functioning power assets.
The Katsina State Government began the project in 2005. Since then, the facility has changed ownership twice, the first time in 2007 when it was taken over by the federal government.
After the takeover, the federal government awarded a contract in 2010 to a French company, Vergnet S.A., to build the wind farm within 24 months. The farm would have 37 turbines, each to deliver about 275 kilowatts of electricity. The contract included offshore components valued at €18.5 million and onshore components valued at N494 million.
Safe to say the project did not go according to plan.
The project encountered several setbacks in a state facing severe security challenges. Following the abduction of a French commissioning engineer, the company obtained approval to transfer components of the work to a local contractor, Credco Nigeria Limited.
The revised arrangement increased the contract to €20.85 million offshore and N573.90 million onshore.
By 2016, a government budget implementation report stated the progress made in the project to include the delivery of two 7.5MVA transformers, restoration of a vandalised 33kV line, completion of foundation work, installation of towers and turbines, and construction of medium-voltage rooms.
It said outstanding works included the overhead line linking the wind farm to the 33kV network and an injection substation at Liyafa.
The 2017 government budget implementation report later described the project as about 95 per cent complete.
However, six years later, in 2023, Kano Electricity Distribution Company (KEDCO), the designated off-taker of power from the wind farm, described the wind farm as only 80 per cent complete.
In an article published on 31 August 2026, the Nigerian Wind Energy Council (NWEC) said years of inactivity had left the Lambar-Rimi wind farm’s turbines degraded and in need of extensive rehabilitation.
In April 2025, the Katsina State Government requested to reacquire the facility. The federal government approved the transfer, with the Minister of Power, Adebayo Adelabu, explaining that it was in line with the Electricity Act 2023 and the emerging role of states in the electricity markets.
In September 2025, Katsina announced the reacquisition of the wind farm and its plans to hybridise it with a 10MW solar plant.
The state has since said it was working with Vergnet to assess the turbines, electrical systems, and grid infrastructure. The state government expects the hybrid facility to come on stream in the fourth quarter of 2026.
The twists and turns in the Lambar-Rimi wind farm story demonstrate how Nigeria has struggled to produce and distribute enough electricity for its 240 million people.
PREMIUM TIMES sent several calls and messages to the Special Adviser on Power and Energy to the Katsina State Governor, Abubakar Ibrahim, seeking details of the current status of the facility, the funds committed and whether progress had been made towards the planned commissioning. The officials did not respond to the inquiry.
PREMIUM TIMES also made several attempts to reach officials at the Federal Ministry of Power for clarification on why the project has not been completed in over 15 years.
The calls were not answered, and the ministry did not respond to the text messages either.
Many other large renewable-energy projects in Nigeria have remained at different stages of development for years.
They include the 100MW Maraban Pushit wind farm in Mangu Local Government Area of Plateau State, promoted by JBS Wind Power Limited.
A World Bank project document records that the company had secured a 45-year land lease, conducted environmental impact assessment studies and obtained provisional approval to evacuate electricity through a 132kV substation at Makeri in Plateau State.
The project appeared in regulatory records in October 2012, 14 years ago, but has not developed into an operating utility-scale wind farm. Publicly available records reviewed for this report did not establish how much has been spent on the project or whether public funds were committed.
Solar projects in Nigeria have a similarly mixed track record.
The 50MW Onyi project in Kokona, Nasarawa State, associated with Afrinergia Power Limited, received a generation licence in April 2016. Global Energy Monitor lists the project as cancelled, inferring cancellation occurred in June 2024.
A 75 MW Kankia solar project in Katsina State was promoted by Pan Africa Solar Limited, with JCM Capital listed as the project owner. The Nation newspaper reported in July 2016 that the company and the federal government had signed a power purchase agreement for the project, with a proposed investment of $146 million.
NERC records show that Pan Africa Solar received a generation licence in December 2014, which expired in December 2024. The regulator lists the project as non-operational, while Global Energy Monitor classifies it as cancelled, with cancellation inferred to have occurred in February 2025.
However, despite the lack of success in some renewable energy projects, others have been successfully completed. A 10MW solar project in Kumbotso, Kano State, developed by the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA), was commissioned in 2023. This project shows that utility-scale renewable projects can be delivered when financing, project management, evacuation infrastructure, and an identifiable market align.
In an interview with PREMIUM TIMES, NWEC’s Research and Operations Consultant, Ojodomo Odiniya, noted that Nigeria lacks an ecosystem capable of turning power resources into bankable projects.
He identified policy and regulatory uncertainty, grid constraints, financing, inadequate wind-resource data, weak institutional coordination, and land and community issues as major barriers.
Investors, he said, need a predictable pathway from resource assessment and land acquisition through permitting, procurement, financing, power purchase agreements, grid connection and long-term operation.
Mr Odiniya prescribed a systematic development of the sector. He said this could also begin with localising parts of the renewable-energy value chain instead of trying to manufacture an entire wind turbine immediately.
He said foundations, civil works, tower fabrication, electrical installation, transportation, engineering, operations, and maintenance could provide entry points for Nigerian companies.
“The point is not to begin with a fully Nigerian-made turbine. It is to ensure that each project creates capabilities that can be used by the next project,” he said.
The consultant also warned against developing generation without the transmission infrastructure required to evacuate it.
For future wind projects, Mr Odiniya said site selection should consider not only wind strength but also grid access, logistics, security, land and lifetime operating costs.
North African economic powerhouse, Egypt, shows what happens when projects are developed alongside the institutions and infrastructure required to support them.
In written responses to questions from PREMIUM TIMES in September, Jauad El Kharraz, senior advisor to the TERAMED Initiative and former executive director of the Regional Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency, said Egypt’s expansion followed a sequence of institutional decisions that reduced uncertainty for investors.
Egypt’s Electricity Law, Law No. 87 of 2015, provided a framework for the country’s electricity market and allowed greater participation by private generators.
Egypt had also introduced a separate Renewable Energy Law, Law No. 203 of 2014, which established mechanisms for developing renewable-energy projects.
The country first used feed-in tariffs to encourage private investment in renewable energy and develop projects such as the Benban solar park.
It subsequently moved towards competitive auctions and build-own-operate arrangements as the market matured. Egypt’s New and Renewable Energy Authority (NREA) lists feed-in tariffs, competitive auctions, build-own-operate projects, and independent power producer arrangements among the mechanisms used to develop renewable-energy projects.
That progression mattered because developers were not simply being asked to build renewable plants. They were being given a clearer framework for how electricity would be purchased and how investment could be recovered.
The Benban experience illustrates the effect.
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) says it invested more than $1.1 billion in 16 photovoltaic plants at Benban, with a combined capacity of 750MW.
The plants were connected to Egypt’s national electricity grid in 2019. The bank also supported Egypt’s move from feed-in tariffs towards competitive renewable-energy auctions.
Mr El Kharraz said Egypt also addressed some of the infrastructure problems before they could become bottlenecks.
The New and Renewable Energy Authority, he said, helped make land available in resource-rich areas, while the government invested heavily in transmission.
According to figures he provided, Egypt’s 500-kilovolt transmission lines increased from 2,364 kilometres in 2014 to 8,250 kilometres by late 2024, while substation capacity increased to about 48,000 megavolt-amperes (MVA).
The lesson for Nigeria is that a renewable-energy project cannot be treated as an isolated generating asset. The land, transmission system, power purchaser, financing structure, approvals and maintenance arrangements must develop around it.
Egypt’s model also relied heavily on development finance.
EBRD financing helped establish the Benban pipeline, while the bank worked with Egyptian authorities on the design and implementation of competitive renewable-energy tenders.
Mr El Kharraz said Egypt used sovereign-backed arrangements, standardised contracts, risk-sharing mechanisms and development-finance institutions to reduce the risks private investors faced.
He said some of these institutional principles could be adapted to Nigeria, including standardised bankable power purchase agreements (PPAs), clean-energy corridors with prepared land and grid connections, and more coordinated permitting.
For Nigeria, the answer is not to copy Egypt’s model wholesale.
Tobi Oluwatola, associate partner at AP3 Advisory, noted that Egypt’s large, centralised renewable-energy parks developed within a different electricity-market structure. Nigeria, by contrast, has increasingly relied on commercial and industrial projects, mini-grids, and other decentralised systems.
He said Nigeria needs contracts that give investors the confidence that electricity will be purchased, that there are credible buyers capable of paying for the power, and transmission infrastructure and mechanisms for managing foreign-exchange and other risks.
Mr Oluwatola said Nigeria could adapt elements of the Egyptian experience, including pre-permitted renewable-energy zones, standardised power-purchase arrangements and local-content requirements tied to public procurement.
The common lesson from both experts is that a renewable-energy project cannot be treated as an isolated generating plant.
Land, financing, contracts, transmission, regulation, and the electricity market have to develop around it.
Segun Ajayi-Kadir, director-general of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), told PREMIUM TIMES that Nigerian companies can produce or assemble some renewable-energy equipment, including solar panels, mounting structures, cables and battery packs.
However, specialised technologies and several critical inputs remain heavily dependent on imports.
Government figures cited by officials put Nigeria’s solar technology import bill at more than N400 billion in 2025 and more than N200 billion in the first half of 2026.
Mr Ajayi-Kadir said manufacturers face high financing costs, foreign-exchange instability, expensive and unreliable electricity, infrastructure gaps, skills shortages, and uncertainty over demand.
Manufacturers are reluctant to invest heavily without predictable demand, while renewable-energy developers often turn to imported equipment because local suppliers cannot yet provide sufficient scale, technology, or competitive pricing.
The government’s Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) programme could help break that cycle by creating predictable demand.
The programme targets electricity access for more than 17.5 million Nigerians through thousands of connections and mini-grids.
Another example is the proposed Solarge Nigeria Limited solar manufacturing facility, established by the Rural Electrification Agency (REA), Infrastructure Corporation of Nigeria (InfraCorp) and Dutch company Solarge BV.
The proposed facility is designed to link manufacturing to a guaranteed market, with plans for local-content growth and procurement commitments.
Mr Ajayi-Kadir said localisation should nevertheless be gradual.
Nigeria, he said, can begin with solar-module assembly, mounting structures, cables, battery packs and other balance-of-system components before moving into more sophisticated technologies.
For wind, immediate opportunities are more likely to lie in steel towers, foundations, electrical installation, engineering and maintenance than in manufacturing complete turbines.
The government’s Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) programme could help break that cycle by creating predictable demand.
The programme targets electricity access for more than 17.5 million Nigerians through thousands of connections and mini-grids.
Another example is the proposed Solarge Nigeria Limited solar manufacturing facility, established by the Rural Electrification Agency (REA), Infrastructure Corporation of Nigeria (InfraCorp) and Dutch company Solarge BV.
The proposed facility is designed to link manufacturing to a guaranteed market, with plans for local-content growth and procurement commitments.

title: 4 New Air Defense Towers Built Near Putin’s Valdai Residence
body:
Four additional air defense towers have been erected near the Valdai residence of Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Novgorod region of Russia, with the closest structure situated roughly 400 meters from the main residential compound, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Russian service reported .
Satellite imagery analyzed by investigative journalists revealed that the newly constructed elevated platforms expand an already dense protective perimeter surrounding the presidential retreat.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
With the addition of the four new towers, the total number of specialized air defense towers identified in the immediate vicinity of the Valdai compound has grown to approximately 30.
The installation of elevated ramparts and stationary towers across Russian territory is engineered primarily to host short-range surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems, such as the Pantsir-S1, elevating radar and kinetic engagement equipment above regional forest canopies to detect and intercept low-altitude strike drones.
The Valdai estate, located on Lake Valdai approximately midway between Moscow and St. Petersburg, serves as a heavily fortified private retreat frequented by Putin and his inner circle.
The construction of the four new towers marks the latest phase in a progressive militarization of the airspace safeguarding the presidential retreat against asymmetric Ukrainian drone incursions.
In early April, investigative reports based on satellite imagery confirmed that Russian engineering units had completed seven new stationary air defense towers mounting Pantsir systems around the Valdai complex between late 2025 and March 2026.
Over subsequent months, secondary rings of fortified positions were established along surrounding access routes and peripheral forested areas.
Concurrently, Russian security agencies reinforced ground-level defenses around the complex. In early June, independent Russian media outlets, including Meduza and Agentstvo, verified the installation of anti-drone netting systems over transport routes and truck staging facilities in the Valdai district, approximately nine kilometers (5.6 miles) from the compound.
Defense analysts from the Conflict Intelligence Team (CIT) observed that the netting arrays – technologies widely employed along frontline sectors in Ukraine to shield vehicles from loitering munitions and first-person view (FPV) drone drops – were deployed around Valdai to protect security convoys and control access corridors amid Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign .
The continuous reinforcement of the Valdai residence forms part of a broader, systemic effort by Russian defense planners to erect dense, layered air defense networks around high-value leadership compounds, strategic command hubs, and the Russian capital.
In late June, satellite reconnaissance revealed that Russian forces established a fortified S-400 long-range surface-to-air missile position fewer than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from the Kremlin in western Moscow.
Constructed across a 4.5-hectare concrete platform near Moscow State University’s Innovation Science and Technology Center – the flagship project of the Innopraktika Foundation directed by Putin’s daughter Kateryna Tikhonova – the site incorporates S-300 and S-400 missile launchers alongside a 40V6MR mobile radar mast designed to detect low-flying aerodynamic targets.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Farmers in Yambio call for better markets, storage
body: Western Equatoria State officials, the Azande Kingdom and development partners have called for increased investment in agriculture to boost commercial farming, improve food security and raise farmers’ incomes. The call was made on Friday during World Food Day celebrations at Freedom Square in Yambio, where farmers exhibited produce, including maize, rice, honey, vegetables, chickens and goats, while highlighting challenges such as inadequate storage facilities and limited market access. Joel Binza, a representative of Star Trust Organization, said the exhibition enabled farmers to sell directly to consumers, reducing reliance on middlemen and potentially increasing their earnings. Abakr Rajab, the Food and Agriculture Organization’s (FAO) field officer in Western Equatoria, urged the government, development partners and humanitarian agencies to coordinate efforts to tackle hunger and strengthen farmers’ resilience. He called for improved access to quality seeds, agricultural inputs and technical training to increase production. Tadeo Mario Sasa, prince of the Azande Kingdom, said greater investment in farming, storage and transportation is needed to move farmers from subsistence production to commercial agriculture. He said the kingdom is working with the government to facilitate access to farmland. Western Equatoria State Agriculture Minister Gibson Bullen Wande urged development partners to provide farming tools, improved inputs, technical assistance and mechanized equipment. He also called on the Azande Kingdom to make sufficient land available for cultivation. World Food Day is observed annually on Oct. 16 to raise awareness of hunger and promote food security and nutrition. Western Equatoria’s Green Belt supports the cultivation of maize, rice, groundnuts and cassava. The state has agricultural potential, but limited storage and market access remain challenges for farmers. The post Farmers in Yambio call for better markets, storage appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Two German courts now hold Google liable for what its AI overviews say
body:
Google tried to overturn a landmark Munich ruling on liability for AI search summaries by appealing, then quietly settled. Now a second court has applied the same reasoning. Google's AI answers count as the company's own content, and Google is responsible for them.
In late May, the Munich Regional Court I ruled in a widely watched case that Google is directly liable for the content of its AI-generated search summaries. Google's AI had falsely linked two Munich-based publishers to fraud schemes. The judges classified AI Overviews not as mere search results but as Google's own statements, meaning the company itself has to answer for them.
Instead of hiding behind the role of a neutral middleman passing along third-party information, Google would have to own the unlawful statements its AI produces. For a search feature that constantly generates new answers, that's a legal risk that's hard to quantify. If this view holds up, it could call into question the entire business model of AI search in Germany and shape the debate in other countries too. Ad
The distinction between a search reference and original content could also have consequences beyond false factual claims. If AI answers count as Google's own content, the publishers whose texts Google uses to generate those answers might eventually assert their own claims. That wasn't part of the Munich case, but it's a logical next step. Ad
As THE DECODER has learned, the appeal Google publicly announced was never carried through to a decision. The case ended in a settlement instead, meaning no higher court ever weighed in on the Munich reasoning. Why the settlement was reached and whether money changed hands is unknown. Neither Google nor the affected publisher would comment. The court also declined to weigh in on the broader significance of its own ruling beyond this specific case.
The Munich judges' legal reasoning isn't dead, though. In a decision dated September 24, 2026, the Aachen Regional Court barred Google from spreading certain false statements and explicitly relied on the Munich ruling's reasoning. Google can challenge the injunction. The decision isn't final yet. Ad
In this new case, a physician in Aachen fought back against serious false claims in Google's "AI Mode" search feature. The doctor had worked as chief physician and professor of neuroradiology from 2010 until late June 2026. On August 28, a colleague alerted him that Google's AI was explaining his departure by citing an alleged sexual assault against his secretary. When users ran additional searches using terms like "suspension," "termination," and "court proceedings," AI Mode returned detailed, multi-paragraph fabrications. It even invented a complete legal aftermath.
None of the allegations or proceedings had anything to do with the doctor. The AI had taken events involving a different former university professor and pinned them on him, something the Aachen court could confirm from its own records since the criminal case had actually been brought against someone else. Cases of AI misattribution like this have been documented before . Ad
Even though the doctor described the mix-up in detail in late August and asked Google by email to remove the content, the company said in mid-September that it would take no action. A formal legal demand sent the same day also went nowhere. Google confirmed receiving it, but according to the court, the false AI-generated texts were still live. Ad
The Aachen Regional Court then banned further spread of the three disputed text variants. Because the false claims could seriously damage the doctor's professional reputation, the court acted on an emergency basis without hearing Google first. If Google violates the order, it faces fines of up to 250,000 euros per violation.
The most significant part of the Aachen decision is how closely it tracks the Munich reasoning, suggesting a consistent legal view is forming across German courts. Google uses its AI to produce its own statements rather than simply making third-party information findable. "The respondent provides AI-generated search and is therefore also responsible for the answers generated in this context," the court wrote.
Aachen even cites the Munich ruling directly, noting that Google's AI produces "independent, new, and substantive statements based on an evaluation and combination of content from various third-party websites."
Google could check such statements, the court said, for example, by comparing AI output against the source websites it used. The Aachen judges added that had Google confronted its own AI with the doctor's objections, the system would have caught the errors itself.
Both cases raise the question of what long-term legal strategy Google is pursuing with its AI search features. If German courts keep classifying the company as a publisher of false statements and Google keeps dodging precedent through what are likely financial settlements, that creates a perverse incentive.
For specialized law firms and affected parties, it could turn into a lucrative business model. They could probe AI search with targeted queries until the language model stitches together false, potentially defamatory statements, then file for an injunction and negotiate a settlement. These systems are easy to manipulate.
Of course, Google can afford to make individual cases disappear this way for years, since binding precedent only happens when at least one side pushes the legal process all the way to the end. But Google's motivation likely goes well beyond liability for individual false claims. If a top court were to rule that AI answers count as original content, the publishers whose texts feed those answers could assert their own claims too. In the most extreme scenario, Google would have to compensate the creators behind its sources for every AI-generated answer. That would upend the economics of AI search entirely.

title: Russian drone strikes minibus in Kharkiv region, injuring two
body:
According to Ukrinform, Andrii Kanashevych, head of the Kupiansk District Military Administration, announced this on Telegram .
"On October 18, at around 08:30, a UAV attack on a minibus on the Velykyi Burluk-Nova Oleksandrivka road injured a 49-year-old man and a 55-year-old woman," Kanashevych wrote.
According to him, the injured are receiving medical assistance.
He also reported that on October 18, a medical facility building in the settlement of Velykyi Burluk was damaged in a UAV attack.
As Ukrinform reported, 12 people were injured in Russian attacks in the Kharkiv region on October 17.

title: US Goes on the Offensive in Central Asia
body:
It’s dealmaking time: despite the roiling geopolitical tensions embroiling Washington on several fronts, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio headed to Central and South Asia late Saturday to boost commercial ties – and gain an edge over Russia and China.
With the US mired in its war with Iran, and the conflict in Ukraine showing no signs of abating, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America, smack in the middle of the US midterm election campaign.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
He has largely ceded control of the contentious Iran, Ukraine and Gaza situations to US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Rubio was instead leading a massive delegation of 200 business leaders to Uzbekistan, where he will take part on Monday in a ministerial meeting of five Central Asian countries.
“This is an important relationship,” Rubio said shortly before his departure, calling the trip a strategic visit. “There’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.”
A senior State Department official told reporters on Friday that Rubio was demonstrating Washington’s goodwill toward the “deepening partnership across Central Asia,” especially in the energy sector.
Central Asia is a resource-rich region as vast as the European Union but only boasts a population of about 80 million people.
“We’ve been planning this for several months, and it’s an incredible opportunity to bring the United States into a region of the world that is vitally important,” said a second senior US official, on condition of anonymity.
During his visit to the Uzbek city of Samarkand, an emblematic stop on the historic Silk Road, Rubio will participate in a C5+1 meeting with ministers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
In November 2025, Trump welcomed the leaders of those countries to the White House.
The former Soviet republics remain linked to Moscow by energy pipelines, as well as security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of the war in Ukraine -- with China reaping the benefits.
Beijing is the main trade partner of all five Central Asian nations.
Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.
The US also has made sourcing rare earths and improving its energy mix key parts of its foreign policy.
The US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor – who also serves as the special envoy for Central and South Asia -- has repeatedly emphasized the need for Washington to have better ties across the region.
After his visit to Uzbekistan, Rubio will head to India, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are industrial hubs and major international port cities.
It will be the secretary of state’s second official visit to India this year, after a May trip to New Delhi and Kolkata, signifying Washington’s push in the region.
“We’re very close” to a trade deal with India, the second senior US official said of negotiations that have dragged on for months.
Last February, the two sides reached a provisional agreement aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian products.
But just a few days later, the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s tariffs, which fueled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.
Ever since, Washington and Delhi have been locked in negotiations.
Relations were rattled when Trump imposed 25 percent tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.
In Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio will offer the new US brand of so-called “commercial diplomacy” in his meetings with Indian business leaders.
He will notably raise plans by the Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries to finance a refinery in Texas. Reliance is led by billionaire Indian tycoon Anant Ambani.

title: Wase mobilises stakeholders to tackle insecurity
body: Member representing Wase Federal Constituency in the House of Representatives, Ahmed Idris Wase, has mobilised traditional, political and community leaders in Bashar Chiefdom to address security challenges threatening socio-economic activities in parts of Wase Local Government Area of Plateau State. The meeting, held on Saturday at the palace of the Rekna of Bashar, Alhaji Abdullahi Idris, brought together security personnel, community leaders, youth advocates and village chiefs to discuss ways of tackling insecurity in the area. The meeting focused on building a united front against criminal activities, particularly banditry, in border communities and mining areas within the chiefdom. Addressing the stakeholders, Wase said lasting security could not be achieved through military intervention alone, stressing the need for grassroots intelligence sharing and cooperation among community members. Soldiers killed as military van runs into ISWAP landmine in Borno Mining Marshals deny involvement in operation linked to miners’ deaths His mobilisation efforts followed the deployment of an Intervention Battalion of Special Forces to the Bashar base by the Nigerian Army. Wase had commended the Army leadership for the deployment, which is expected to strengthen security operations in the area. Community leaders are also said to be engaging with the newly deployed troops to improve cooperation between residents and security personnel. In a recent briefing on its strategic security plans, the Bashar traditional leadership pledged to strengthen intelligence gathering through direct communication channels between village heads and security operatives. The traditional leadership also identified the need to monitor mining sites to address security concerns associated with unregulated activities and the presence of unauthorised operators in the area. The initiative forms part of Wase’s broader legislative efforts to address insecurity in Plateau State. He had previously sponsored motions of urgent public importance in the House of Representatives, calling for federal security deployments and humanitarian assistance for displaced persons in the southern part of the state. The Bashar Chiefdom Community Development Association (BACCODA) expressed optimism that the collaboration between Wase and the traditional council would contribute to restoring peace and protecting lives and property.

title: How employment is changing at Anthropic
body:
Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.
What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment.
This report draws on comprehensive internal Anthropic data covering employment, AI use, output metrics, employee surveys, internal communication patterns, employee calendar data, and hiring decision records. It contextualizes these quantitative data with 17 employee interviews.
We find that even as the company grows, relative hiring in junior technical positions has slowed. Productivity for both engineers and non-technical employees has leapt up and did so sharply when they adopted coding agents. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgment relative to specific technical expertise. A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible. One engineer described work as facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” Employees at Anthropic remain critical. But the nature of their contributions has changed.
Anthropic has responded to these changes by setting up an early warning system to track jobs at risk of disruption, and as jobs evolve the company has prioritized internal redeployments. These actions, taken at the frontier of both AI development and workplace change, show how specific organizational commitments can shape the impact of AI on employment. But they also raise difficult questions about exactly what those commitments should be.
Anthropic has expanded rapidly. But it has hired less per dollar of revenue than an earlier generation of large tech companies. At five years old, Anthropic takes in between 2–4 times as much revenue per employee as Meta and Google as they crested in their own rapid growth. 1
What jobs are missing? Within Anthropic, discussion of a decline in demand for junior technical employees emerged in core technical functions in January 2026. The teams that relied most heavily on Claude in their own work found that writing code and finding bugs could increasingly be offloaded to Claude. Newly capable models accelerated this perception: “the thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for.”
By April, engineering and research teams had deemphasized hiring for lower band technical positions. When surveyed in the same month, a majority of managers described hiring for a different set of skills due to AI. Around a third of ML and a fifth of SWE managers reported hiring less due to AI.
The shift in employment shares is striking. Figure 1 shows that the share of junior-level employees in technical departments at Anthropic slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025. The proportion of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Postings for juniors have fallen particularly sharply since December 2025.
At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it. Part of this shift is the natural expansion of business functions as the company scales. Part could reflect coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves. For example, a sales representative designed a custom dashboard and pipeline tailored to their work: “a build like this was out of my wheelhouse, especially with the UI, connecting all the tools, the MCPs. But I built this probably in three to four hours, just iterating on it.” Coding-focused AI agent sessions for non-technical employees (identified as those with no code commits at baseline, excluding new hires) leapt from 2 per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.
Yet this shift in hiring composition is not only a story about automated coding allowing it to diffuse to other domain experts . Within technical departments, the share of employees not actively coding (defined as those making no code commits in the prior 30 days) fell by almost half over the year through April 2026. Part of this is due to a thinning share of non-engineers: the ratio of engineers to product managers, for example, sits at around 17 to 1 and has increased since 2025. The number of commits from managers has also doubled. The supervising and coordinating roles within technical teams increasingly involve building and shipping code.
One area in which non-technical hiring has not accelerated is in the administrative functions that typically scale with a company’s size. A combination of agent assistants, automated review and ticket service outsourcing has left Anthropic clerical-light even as it has grown rapidly. A financial manager built a purchase request review agent and explained to colleagues “it's just trying to find the things that take a lot of hours so they can focus on the other stuff.”
Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we've already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.
These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025. Whole teams have also been reallocated as they handed off their work to agents. Consider one product design team, which wrote content like the greetings on Claude.ai: “Hello night owl;” “Coffee and Claude time?” In spring 2026, the team developed a context graph that effectively guided agents to write compelling product content. This “scaled the team out,” its manager explained, but also raised the question of what was left for human writers. The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude. “Writers who used language to drive human behavior are now using it to drive Claude behavior.”
Are these shifts attributable to AI? At Anthropic, humans are a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents. Based on agent session telemetry, in March 2026, the sum of autonomous and interactive agent work hours leapt past human work hours for the first time. Part of this is fleets of agents conducting industrial-scale software engineering, filling in myriad routine tests and checks, conducting maintenance on a growing mass of infrastructure code, and driving concerted campaigns to translate massive codebases. But even narrowing in on the agents deployed by individual employees, as in Figure 2, by August the agents worked 6 times as many hours as their human handlers.
Anthropic is a software producer, and the vast bulk of tokens flowing through these agents is spent producing software code. Dashboards monitor fleets of agents operating across the company. But personal assistant agents also monitor employee calendars and messages, scheduling, sending to-do lists accumulated from incoming messages, and automatically briefing employees on the people and purpose of their upcoming meetings. Tokens touch a growing range of everyday work tasks.
What do all of these tokens amount to? Figure 3 plots output over time for a range of job functions with measurable output. Consistent with prior reports surveying Anthropic engineers and describing automation of model training and research , code commits per engineer have risen the fastest, coming in at 5x their velocity as six months ago. Data scientists are also querying the growing mass of Anthropic data more, asking Claude agents to get real-time metrics to dashboards and decisionmakers. But Figure 3 shows that even non-technical employees saw output rise as coding agents diffused: lawyers processed more contracts; accounts payable ushered through invoices; salespeople closed more deals.
But is all of this due to Claude usage? During this same period, the company saw explosive business growth. It is easier to close deals when you sell a strong model. To assess the independent effect of AI, we compare the output of employees who adopt agentic coding tools to those who have not yet adopted the tools. This lets us compare employees working in the same month at the company, and therefore exposed to a similar business context, but approaching it with different tools. Note, however, that tool adoption is not random: if employees on the cusp of driving some big new project decide to tool up for it, for example, this would bias our estimates.
We follow 192 engineers over time as they adopt coding agents, compared to 74 engineers who do not adopt agents during the period studied. Figure 4 shows that in the months following adoption, the amount of code that engineers add rises sharply. More code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact . To test for AI code slop, we study code commits made at Anthropic. We compare code committed by the same employee, in the same month, in the same coding directory, but written by coding agents rather than written directly by the human employee. There are many dimensions of code quality, and AI errors may be harder to identify than human ones. But we find no difference in rates of lines of code subsequently removed or reverted.
Figure 4 also looks at what happens after an engineer adopts their first fully autonomous agent. Those who adopt were already on a steeply upward trajectory compared to non-adopters. This suggests that employees shifting toward fully autonomous agents were already ramping up their output.
Do these patterns go beyond coding, into a broader transformation of knowledge work? Anthropic sales representatives steadily adopted AI agents starting last September. Figure 4 shows that after sales representatives adopt agents, they close deals with more clients. Part of this pattern could be driven by representatives with more sales opportunities selecting into automation. But it could also reflect automation of logging and routine communication. One account executive explained that Claude automations handled email drafting and customer management software integrations, replacing around 20% of their prior work tasks. Another noted that similar automations freed them up to focus on face-to-face time, letting them talk to 30% more of their customers than was previously possible: “anytime you do anything a second time, you're kind of like, okay, how can I use Claude to make it so that I don't have to do it a third time?”
Beyond sales, an Anthropic lawyer built a series of Claude automations to scan risks and opportunities, triage legal questions and take first passes through public-facing copy for legal review. A recruiter used Claude to help with candidate sourcing, tracking applications and an analysis that would have taken “maybe a couple of weeks,” freeing him to redesign outdated interview questions and meet with more applicants.
All of this suggests that as AI capabilities improve, it impacts a wide range of jobs across Anthropic. Descriptively, we see junior employment slowing in jobs that use Claude for the most complex tasks (Figure 5).
Heavy AI adoption reshapes more than employment and productivity. It also drives continual changes in work processes, generating new tasks and shifting employees’ perceptions of their workplace. One employee described this as the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything” and another that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.” An internal employee survey asked whether work processes at Anthropic made respondents as productive as possible: 44% of employees agreed in late 2024; 58% by November 2025 (in April 2026, 75% answered yes, but the question weakened by dropping “as possible”). As of August, employees at Anthropic expected that AI will be able to do 75% of their work by 2030, compared to 28% for other Americans.
These ratcheting productivity expectations are dramatized by the cadence of internal model releases. As soon as a new model is available, Anthropic employees start tackling harder problems in interactive coding agent sessions. We measure this with an automated Claude grader rating deidentified sessions’ task demands based on depth, scope and number of systems implicated. The share of tasks above the 90th percentile of difficulty for the old model rises sharply by around 30% (from 10% to 13% of all tasks) and stays elevated in the weeks following model releases. The easy end of tasks given to agents changes little.
Spiraling agent productivity translates into output pitched across humans’ screens and attention. One engineer compared this to babysitting:
They're like, I need my juice box opened and it's an emergency that my juice box is opened. And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding. [...] When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.
In the April 2026 survey, an open-ended question about how AI has impacted day-to-day work, 27% described productivity gains from Claude tools and 20% described their role shifting from actually doing work to managing Claudes.
Amid this model-driven acceleration, human attention is a constant bottleneck. In interactive, multi-turn sessions, the vast majority of agents’ session time is not spent working at all, but spent waiting. We track idle time by subtracting each agent’s active working time from each interactive session’s total wall-clock time. Claude sessions amount to around 80% idly waiting for human input. As one engineer put it, people are “bottlenecking the agents.”
How much time exactly would be needed to read all of Claude’s output from interactive sessions? For each interactive session, we convert each session’s agent output token to word count, assuming average human reading speed. Figure 6 shows that technical functions have seen the volume of coding agent output leap up over the last six months. But even for non-technical groups, interactive Claude sessions are outputting enough content to take up over half of the work week. The deluge of Claude text needs organizing.
One solution to this deluge is rising automation. But this requires work of a different kind. Written standing instructions for agents grew from a few hundred in July 2025 to 8,500 a year later. One engineer set up an agent chief of staff to triage agent requests. Another wrote a performance review for their Claude team: “Hey, let’s talk about what is and is not working about our communication style.” Recruiters built integrated dashboards with agents surfacing problems and initiating actions. A lawyer shifted their attention from reviewing legal questions to doing “SEO for legal advice, you need to write frameworks that [clients’] agents discover.”
Figure 7 shows that this kind of meta-work leapt from 10% of the average employee’s interactive Claude sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. Much of this rise was due specifically to agent management: writing specs for multi-agent runs, looping one agent to review another’s output, and monitoring pipelines. Across functions, human involvement increasingly abstracted from a particular piece of code or writing to the tooling necessary to get agents to do their tasks effectively.
Despite increases in agent reliability and these significant investments in tooling to supervise them, human trust and accountability remains critical. One employee explained that, increasingly, chasing down bugs “uncovers these organizational or systemic or tech debt things that actually require some amount of human convening and decision-making and governance to solve.” In interview after interview, employees described face-to-face coordination as indispensable. Based on calendar data, the median employee spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Part of this reflects the growth of the company, and a shift toward meeting-intensive non-technical roles. But even among employees in technical individual contributor roles, meeting time is up 16% over the past year. Big-picture strategic questions touch a broad range of leveraged positions, and typically require debate and engagement with others. A break from managing the agents typically looks like jumping into a meeting.
Broadly, both technical and non-technical roles have seen implementation parts of their job automated (writing code, identifying bugs, logging progress, drafting emails). Engineers described becoming leaders and managers of agents; non-technical employees described doing more and more of the strategic parts of their job: “that 20% that was strategic becomes 90% of the job.” But for many non-technical roles, core implementation work is also interpersonal: a sales call, an interview, cross-functional alignment on a complex problem. All of this remains human.
Consider too the Slack channels that provide both the front page and backchannels of Anthropic communication. Agents diffused through Slack and eventually appeared in nearly half of active, public channels. Figure 8 zooms in on the communication network of a single large department, drawing on all public Slack channels that department members interacted through. It links both human and agent participants by whether they participated in a Slack thread. The figure shows the remarkable rise of agents, as orange dots blossom and dominate the network.
Agents appear disproportionately in dedicated channels for Claude-human interactions, rather than messaging a lot in incumbent human channels. The underlying structure and density of human communication changes little. Agents did not replace human interaction, but rather added to it: human threads in this department sustained the same number of human responses, while additionally layering on agent responses. Agents become teams for a single employee, rather than nodes with high connectivity to many employees at once.
As humans work amid a growing fleet of AI agents, they face pressure to shift human work into agent-visible channels. If a decision is made in an in-person meeting, and no notes or report-out appears, agents are missing crucial context for updating their goals and assumptions. An employee explained how having their name on a months-old document about Claude swag meant agents kept bringing requests for t-shirts and mugs, long after their responsibilities had changed. Private work, in unlogged meetings and direct messages, is invisible, confusing and discouraged in an AI-heavy workplace. One researcher described this default toward openness as critical to Anthropic’s thoroughgoing integration of AI: “most organizations do not run that way and I think that's a big shift because leaders have to defend feedback out in the open.” The need to feed AI context requires observability of human work and decisions.
Who will thrive in a workplace like this? Shifts in the content of work at Anthropic also show up as changes in the skills that hiring managers prioritize in hiring decisions. We used an automated coder to process hiring manager interview score cards for thousands of employees hired at Anthropic since 2024. These comments are qualitative reactions by interviewers assessing candidates’ performance. The clearest change is increased emphasis on whether candidates have demonstrated creative use of AI tools. In 2024, hiring managers noted candidates' track record on AI tooling in around 5% of assessments for technical roles, and 7% for non-technical roles. By 2026, these rates had tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical roles. Hiring managers increasingly focus on whether candidates effectively use AI.
Deeper changes in assessment are also visible. Among interviews for technical candidates, the single biggest increases were in comments on applicants’ autonomy and judgment. Discussion of domain expertise shrank as a share of overall assessment. As one manager explained, “I expect models to continue to be jagged, so for my team I want them to be fungible across domains.” Similarly, for non-technical candidates, customer and mission orientation increased, while discussion of execution skills fell. Increasingly, hiring managers assess applicants based on their judgment and commitment, rather than the domain-specific skills and execution automated by AI tools.
The deep adoption of AI at Anthropic makes it a useful case. As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift as it has in prior waves of technological change. The railroads gave us the managerial corporation, steam power allowed factories, and personal computers delivered the startup. What new organizations will tool-using, reasoning LLMs require, and what will be our role in them? One possibility is single-person startups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue. Another is companies built by AI genius CEOs employing human agents only to wield pipettes and testify before Congress.
Anthropic does not look like either of these. It has tripled in size in the last year. It is no longer a small startup. It has also not ceded executive control to its models. Written Slack debates and in-person meetings steer everything from company strategy to team decisions, with little input from AI agents. Keeping human work visible across the company ensures autonomous agents reason from fresh context. Individual contributors orchestrating teams of agents look more like managers in terms of the knowledge they need and the interdependencies in their work. Working and deciding in the open is critical at an AI-intensive organization.
As employees increasingly see their work as managing teams of Claudes, they spend more time building the tools needed to do this effectively in their own distinctive domains. This experimentation means that employees are continually automating their own tasks away. In some roles, they are increasingly removed from the object-level work that originally built their skills. As agents sprint through workflows, human attention and judgment are a bottleneck that the system strains against. From sales to legal, human employees are expected to do more and different tasks. Roles broaden to include building products, managing agents and tackling the strategic and interpersonal work that remain beyond the scope of the best LLMs.
These changes in the organization and content of work have appeared alongside declining shares of junior technical roles in headcount, hiring, and posting. Hiring managers increasingly focus on applicants’ autonomy and judgment, rather than execution and narrow expertise. Overall, Anthropic’s revenue growth relative to its employment growth has sped past even the rapid early productivity growth of a prior generation of technology companies.
Reading these patterns forward and out across the economy suggests that AI diffusion could risk worker displacement. Prior work also finds that AI-native startups and AI-adopters are flatter and employ fewer entry-level employees. What can we learn from Anthropic about how to manage AI upheavals in a way that serves the humans working around them?
Here we want to proceed carefully. There are many parts of Anthropic’s employment practices that cannot be replicated across the economy.
But three features stand out. First, widespread stock ownership gives employees a strong interest in the company’s success. Of course, this is an easy posture for a company that has seen substantial increases in valuation. For many firms, shared ownership may be insufficient or otherwise undesirable. But it is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout. If individual contributors are expected to “manage agents,” “make VP-level decisions” and be “their own business line,” as interviewees put it, then aligning their interests with the organization is crucial. The post-World War II union-management settlement forged in the 1950s rested on exactly this kind of bargain: labor unions like the United Auto Workers and the United Steel Workers allowed management prerogative over work reorganization (and even intensification) in return for pay increases tied to productivity increases and to a rich array of benefits. Whatever the new deal between AI-affected employees and their employers, a mechanism to share benefits of adoption is essential. At Anthropic, workers codify their expertise for the machine, see their work routines constantly roiled and disrupted, and have seen a large part of their job become speedreading the output of their AI collaborators. They do not do this for free.
Second, Anthropic is standing up an ongoing early warning system to monitor jobs facing AI-driven transformation. A series of role-level metrics for demand and productivity are read against AI capabilities and use. These aggregate metrics help flag where work is shifting. An early warning system allows the company to start reallocating affected employees to jobs with a skills fit that may be less immediately at risk. As companies across the economy reorient to an accelerated pace of work reorganization, effective systems for guiding internal employee reallocation will become increasingly valuable. Turning to the external labor market to meet every new task demanded by AI advances will be a stronger bottleneck the faster AI advances. In this report, we found increased mobility between departments, changing work content, and employees shifting to new tasks as old ones were automated. Building systems to flexibly reallocate workers internally will be critical for AI-intensive organizations.
This commitment to internal worker reallocation raises important tradeoffs. A well-functioning labor market should shift workers into their most productive positions, whether that is at their current employer or another one. Commitments to reallocate incumbent workers could make employers hesitant to take a risk on hiring new employees. In normal economic conditions, particularly intensely competitive ones, such commitments could be costly.
But prioritizing reallocation forces AI-adopting companies to consider ways that AI can create new tasks for new products and new markets, rather than funneling AI applications into replacing human workers to save on labor costs.
