This could help employers resist the temptation of ‘ so-so’ or ‘ inefficient ’ automation in which AI or other technologies just barely outcompete human workers: employers replace human workers, imposing substantial social costs in lost income for displaced workers, while delivering minimal productivity benefits.
From what we see in Anthropic, both novel and persistently human tasks remain alongside intensive AI use. Uncertainty about the future set of these tasks should recommend preserving a flexible workforce. As one Anthropic executive noted, “a workforce that is anxiously worried is not a workforce doing its best work.”
None of these actions will prevent powerful AI from disrupting jobs. And indeed none directly address the slowdown in junior hires documented in this report. Employment protections for incumbents will not benefit those not hired to begin with. Private action on the part of employers must come alongside farsighted government policy around retraining and income support. Such policy should be guided by a clear picture of the scale of workplace transformation that AI can bring.

title: Kiev’s resistance and agony not to change course of events — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. The Kiev regime is in its death throes and is trying to resist, but this cannot change the course of events, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, when asked by TASS about Moscow’s response to the massive attack by Ukrainian drones on St. Petersburg.
"Some final signs of agony are being observed. The Kiev regime is resisting. But this cannot change the course of events," he said.
He noted that Moscow is constantly responding to Kiev’s actions -- systematic, massive strikes are being carried out, and they are yielding results.

title: Ukraine loses about 1,200 servicemen in special military operation zone over past 24 hours
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Ukraine lost 1,185 servicemen in the special military operation zone over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
Ukraine’s losses in the area of responsibility of the North battlegroup amounted to over 195 servicemen, West up to 240, South up to 175, Center up to 350, East over 195, and Dnepr up to 30 military personnel.

title: Russia strikes transport infrastructure used by Ukrainian army
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Russian troops struck transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, a warehouse of military·technical equipment, and drone production workshops within the last 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
"Operational-tactical aviation, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops, and artillery of the military groupings of the armed forces of the Russian Federation have inflicted damage on transport infrastructure facilities used in the interests of the armed forces of Ukraine, a warehouse of military-technical equipment, assembly workshops, storage and launch sites for long-range unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as temporary deployment points of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," it said in a statement.

title: Russia shoots down seven Flamingo missiles and 1,256 Ukrainian drones over past day
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Russian air defense systems shot down seven Ukrainian long·range Flamingo missiles and 1,256 Ukrainian aircraft·type drones over the past day, the Defense Ministry said.
"Air defense systems shot down seven long·range Flamingo cruise missiles and 1,256 unmanned aircraft of aircraft type," it said in a statement.
According to it, since the start of the special military operation, Russia has destroyed 674 aircraft, 284 helicopters, 265,145 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 anti·aircraft missile systems, 31,279 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,792 multiple rocket launcher systems, 36,750 field artillery pieces and mortars, and 74,862 units of special military automotive equipment.

title: Thwarted Arson at Lithuanian Starlink Site Triggers Security Review
body:
An overnight arson attack targeting a Lithuanian logistics facility storing Starlink satellite communications equipment was thwarted by security measures, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius announced on Sunday, Oct. 18.
Writing on Facebook, Sinkevičius confirmed that the attempted sabotage occurred shortly after midnight, but failed to inflict damage because national intelligence and security services had alerted the enterprise in advance.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Today after midnight, another incident occurred – an attempt was made to set fire to a Lithuanian company where Starlink communications equipment is stored,” Sinkevičius stated.
“The security services had warned this company of prospective attacks, security had been reinforced, and the attempt was unsuccessful.”
Following the attempted arson, Sinkevičius announced that he is convening an emergency session of the National Security Commission on Monday, Oct. 19.
The high-level security meeting will address the attempted facility attack alongside a separate aerial provocation detected early Sunday morning, when an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle breached Lithuanian sovereign airspace.
“It is necessary to determine where the drone flew from and where radar systems first began tracking it,” the prime minister explained.
“The findings of the services following their examination of the debris will also be critical. Furthermore, we will consider granting our services additional statutory powers to neutralize drones.”
Sinkevičius emphasized that Lithuanian security agencies are monitoring the activities of hostile foreign states with heightened vigilance, coordinating protective protocols to shield critical infrastructure, civilian enterprises, and high-value supply chains.
The thwarted attack in Lithuania coincides with an escalating campaign of state-sponsored hybrid warfare , physical sabotage, and airspace incursions directed against the Baltic states and Poland .
Allied intelligence agencies have repeatedly warned that Russian military intelligence (the GRU) and recruited proxies have intensified efforts to target European logistics hubs, supply warehouses, and communications nodes supporting Ukraine’s civil and military defense.
On Friday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned following European Council consultations that Moscow could escalate hybrid attacks, sabotage operations , and border provocations against Poland and the Baltic nations before Christmas, highlighting transit corridors for fuel, food, and dual-use equipment as prime targets.
Lithuanian security officials have noted that commercial satellite terminals, particularly Starlink equipment destined for government and defensive deployment, represent high-priority targets for hostile reconnaissance and interdiction given their vital role in sustaining frontline communications and emergency utilities.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Russia’s strikes on Ukraine aim to reduce potential of Kiev regime — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Russia’s strikes against Ukraine are meant to undermine the strike potential of the Kiev regime, Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in response to a question from TASS.
"The strikes are intended, in fact, to reduce the strike potential of the Kiev regime. This is yielding results," Peskov said, when asked whether a symmetrical Russian response to Kiev’s strikes on St. Petersburg should be coming.

title: Russia’s response to Ukraine’s strikes is ongoing — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Moscow’s response to the Ukrainian strikes is ongoing and the Russian strikes are systematic and massive, Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in response to a question from TASS.
"It [Russia’s response to Ukraine’s strikes] is ongoing; strikes are constantly being carried out, they are systematic, they are massive," Peskov said when asked whether Russia’s symmetrical response to Kiev’s strikes on St. Petersburg should be expected.

title: Support for Takaichi cabinet down below 50% for first time — Kyodo poll
body:
TOKYO, October 18. /TASS/. For the first time since coming to power in October 2025, less than half of the Japanese -- 49.1% -- have expressed support for the government led by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a Kyodo news agency survey said.
Over a third of the participants, or 33%, did not support Takaichi’s cabinet, while 17.9% of the respondents abstained from answering.
Almost 58% of the respondents believe that the prime minister was too late with dismissing Kazuo Yana, the minister of agriculture, forestry and fisheries, who found himself at the center of a scandal after threats to cut state funding for the local authorities, which did not support him in the latest general elections. He was also suspected of violating electoral legislation by providing free buses to transport his supporters during the elections.
At the same time, 54.7% of those surveyed believe that the Kazuo Yana scandal will have some degree of impact on the future political fate of the Takaichi government. According to Kyodo, this incident could become the main reason for the decline in the cabinet’s popularity.
More than 65% of the polled said they are concerned about the government’s plan to reduce the consumer food tax from the current 8% to 1% for two years, Takaichi’s pre·election promise, which was generally met with approval. However, the respondents now fear that the tax cut will undermine the country’s finances and will hurt other social spending.
The survey was conducted on October 17 and 18 across Japan by phone. The number of participants is not specified.

title: Lysenko wins track cycling world championship in keirin discipline
body:
SHANGHAI, October 18. /TASS/. Russian athlete Alina Lysenko has become the winner of the track cycling World Championship in the keirin discipline.
German athlete Lea Sophie Friedrich came second and United Kingdom’s Emma Finucane third.
Lysenko, 23, is the 2026 European champion and the bronze medalist at the 2025 World Championship.
The World Championship in Shanghai will end on October 18.

title: Russia has something to offer to Global South in trade and economy — deputy PM
body:
BANGKOK, October 18. /TASS/. Russia is ready to transfer its technologies, provide services, sell goods, and help the countries of the Global South develop, Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk said in an interview with TASS after participating in the autumn session of the governing bodies of the IMF and the World Bank.
"Today Russia is a country that can actively share knowledge, actively transfer its technologies, provide services, sell goods, and help other countries develop. And, first and foremost, of course, we are talking about the countries of the Global South, with which we are developing our trade and economic ties. This is why we are interested in this cooperation," he said.
Overchuk said that at one time the World Bank’s international country rating "Doing Business" played a significant role in improving the business climate in various countries around the world, including Russia.
"Our work on this rating was coordinated by the Agency for Strategic Initiatives. Many federal executive bodies and regions were involved in it," he said.
"Indeed, thanks to that systematic work we have significantly improved the business environment in the Russian Federation, reduced the costs associated with the interaction between the state and business, and became stronger and more competitive. Now a new World Bank rating is emerging, aimed at improving the business environment, and this is also useful work.".

title: Police detain 1,800 people during unrest in France — Interior Ministry
body:
PARIS, October 18. /TASS/. The French law enforcement agencies have detained more than 1,800 people during the large·scale protests and clashes with the police, said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez.
"At the moment, 1,800 people were detained; an investigation is underway to identify those responsible so that they can be brought to justice," Nunez wrote on X.
He added that more than 500 law enforcement officers were injured during the rallies.

title: Lavrov meets with Saudi Arabian foreign minister in Bahrain — Russian Foreign Ministry
body:
MANAMA /Kingdom of Bahrain/, October 18. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is meeting with Saudi Arabian Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud on the sidelines of a ministerial session of the ninth Russia-GCC strategic dialogue, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
The ministers met in September in Moscow to discuss the dangerous escalation in the Middle East, including in connection with the deteriorating conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Houthis. The Saudi foreign ministry clearly said that Riyadh is not talking about "closing the diplomatic track" and remains in favor of a political solution to the problems in the region, but will not hesitate in matters of self·defense. Lavrov called the Houthis’ attacks on civilian facilities in Saudi Arabia unacceptable and described their chosen course as counterproductive.

title: Northern Bahr el Ghazal women seek greater role in elections
body: Women in Northern Bahr el Ghazal state have called for greater representation in political decision-making and the upcoming general elections, urging political parties to honour commitments to women’s participation in leadership. Angelina Agau Thiep, a women’s rights activist based in Aweil, told Radio Tamazuj on Sunday that women could help improve public services and promote development if given opportunities to participate in decision-making. “The election of leaders means the delivery of services to communities and improving people’s lives. If we women are part of the process as decision-makers, it will be a guarantee for development and service delivery,” she said. Awut Kuel Kuel, a member of the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM), said women in the state had been sensitised about the elections and that some plan to contest governorship and legislative seats. “We have sensitised women and the people of Northern Bahr el Ghazal state to prepare for the upcoming elections, and many women will contest for governorship and legislative positions,” she said. Awut urged voters to choose candidates who would prioritise security, peace, child protection and development. “I want every South Sudanese to be careful when selecting leaders because the elections are important for us, our children, development, security and peace,” she said. Angelina Achan, a representative of a women’s group in Aweil West County, cited the construction of the county headquarters under former commissioner Abuol Akok as an example of women’s contribution to public leadership. Achan said Akok had overseen the construction of the headquarters using concrete materials, contrasting the project with the work of previous commissioners. South Sudan is scheduled to hold its first general elections since independence on Dec. 22, 2026, after repeated delays. The 2018 peace agreement provides for at least 35% representation of women in government institutions, while the National Elections Commission says 35% of seats in the national and state legislative assemblies are reserved for women under the electoral system. However, the implementation of commitments to women’s representation has faced criticism from women’s rights advocates, who say women remain underrepresented in leadership. The post Northern Bahr el Ghazal women seek greater role in elections appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Russian forces attack critical infrastructure facility in Dnipro
body:
According to Ukrinform, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration, said this in a post on the Telegram messaging app.
"The enemy has again attacked a critical infrastructure facility in Dnipro," Hanzha said.
He added that information about possible casualties was being clarified.

title: US Tech Curbs on Kyiv Expose Allied Dependency
body:
Relations between US President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky have once again cooled : early this week the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s (AFU) access to US data on Russian missile launches was restricted, which delayed the triggering of air raid sirens. The functionality of Starshield – the military version of the satellite-based internet service Starlink – has also been limited. Europe’s media draw their own conclusions.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Europe is still a long way from strategic independence, Die Welt (Germany) rails:
“Europe can’t even offer Ukraine an alternative to Starlink that is in any way comparable. It’s the same when it comes to the critical shortage of American Patriot air-defence missiles. The people of Ukraine are paying for Europe’s ignorance and incompetence with their lives. The way Trump’s people have behaved in recent days is the final warning shot for Europe. No government in its right mind can allow itself to become dependent on American systems like Starlink or Palantir for military or critical infrastructure.”
Hospodářské noviny (Czech Republic) explains why Trump appears to be siding with Russia:
“The US has significantly more influence over Ukraine than it does over Russia – and this is the main reason why it often demands far greater concessions from Ukraine than from the aggressor, namely Russia. Trump can threaten Zelensky with measures that would have a crushing impact, such as blocking arms deliveries or halting the sharing of intelligence. Trump wants to secure a peace deal; he’s not interested in the details. The easiest way to exert pressure is on the party to the conflict that will feel that pressure most directly.”
Ukraine remains dependent on the US’s military support, says The Economist (UK):
“There are no practical alternatives to what America provides. ... Europe is years away from American levels of missile production. ... Ukraine has no alternative to American sensors and satellites, which map Russian spoofing, jamming, and troop movements, helping the Ukrainians plan and conduct drone attacks. Ending such co-operation would cripple Ukraine’s ability to take the fight to Russia.”
This disastrous turn of events has a silver lining, columnist Pierre Haski explains on France Inter (France):
“The positive aspect of this crisis is that it brings clarity to the relations between the US and the wider Europe. ... It is an important lesson for those Europeans who continue to purchase US equipment and make their security dependent on decisions taken in Washington. Until the day when a president’s whim leads to a satellite signal being cut off or an aeroplane’s computer system being disabled. Achieving strategic autonomy has never been more urgent.”

title: Ukraine’s Delta system proves NATO compatible at sea
body: Ukrainian personnel ran maritime operations through the Delta combat system at NATO’s REPMUS 2026 exercise in Portugal, integrating every asset transmitting data to NATO standards including uncrewed aerial, surface and subsurface systems and radars, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence. The ministry said the exercise “again confirmed DELTA’s compatibility with NATO systems and brought Ukrainian solutions closer to standardization.” All assets transmitting telemetry in line with NATO STANAG 4817 were successfully integrated. REPMUS, the Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems exercise, is run annually by the Portuguese Navy and is the largest international exercise focused on employing uncrewed systems in maritime operations. This was Ukraine’s third year taking part. The ministry said partners and allies “practiced the joint employment of unmanned aerial, surface, and subsurface systems and tested interoperability within multinational forces” , with the Ukrainian team drawn from different services and branches and coordinating its activity through Delta. Ukrainian specialists trained alongside allies in reconnaissance, maritime area monitoring, manoeuvring, and escort and simulated engagement exercises, and shared combat experience with partners on the employment of uncrewed systems in the maritime domain. On how the system performed, the ministry said the Ukrainian team noted “DELTA’s uninterrupted operation under unstable connectivity, as well as the ease of streaming in the Vezha module compared with other platforms.” Delta served as the primary command and control platform at REPMUS 2025, when it integrated more than a hundred uncrewed systems across multiple domains. Delta is the situational awareness and command system Ukraine built during the war, assembling a common operating picture from drone feeds, sensors, radar and reporting from units, and pushing it to commanders on ordinary devices through a browser. It has become the backbone of Ukrainian targeting, and the ministry has previously said it records more than six thousand six hundred enemy targets hit every day. Running at a NATO exercise on NATO standards carries consequences well beyond the exercise. STANAG 4817 governs how uncrewed systems exchange command, control and telemetry data within the alliance, and a system that speaks it can plug into allied formations without a translation layer. Ukraine has been pressing for its battlefield software to be treated as an alliance asset and not merely a national one, and performing at REPMUS three years running builds that case in front of the navies that would have to adopt it. The Royal Navy has been a regular participant at the Troia range where REPMUS runs, through NATO’s Dynamic Messenger exercise which follows it and which turns the experimentation into operational trials. British uncrewed maritime work has been moving in the same direction, with the Royal Navy’s autonomy programmes and the Atlantic Bastion effort both built on connecting crewed and uncrewed platforms into a single targeting network. The post Ukraine’s Delta system proves NATO compatible at sea first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Why can't airlines fly wherever they want? The freedoms of the air explained
body:
An airline has the aircraft, passengers willing to buy tickets and airports ready to handle its flights. Yet it may still be legally unable to operate a route.
Unlike many other businesses, an airline cannot simply identify demand between two countries and start selling tickets. International commercial aviation is built around traffic rights granted by governments, mostly through bilateral or multilateral agreements.
These rights are commonly known as the "freedoms of the air," a system whose origins date to the Chicago Conference of 1944 , which established the framework for modern international civil aviation.
Today, nine freedoms are commonly used to describe what an airline can do, ranging from crossing another country's airspace without landing to operating domestic flights entirely within a foreign country.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
But they are not nine progressively granted rights that every airline automatically receives. The first five have their origins in agreements negotiated at Chicago, while the sixth through ninth developed as convenient definitions for other forms of traffic rights. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) itself refers to the latter as "so-called" freedoms.
The First Freedom is the simplest: the right for an aircraft from one country to fly through the airspace of another without landing.
A Argentine airline flying to Europe, for example, may need overflight rights from countries crossed along the route even though it has no intention of landing there.
The Second Freedom allows an aircraft to land in another country for non-commercial purposes, such as refueling or maintenance, without picking up or dropping off revenue passengers or cargo.
This was particularly important when early long-range aircraft could not fly many international routes nonstop. Technological stops have become less common as aircraft range increased, although the right remains relevant.
The two freedoms were incorporated into the International Air Services Transit Agreement signed in Chicago in 1944. They are distinct from the commercial rights that allow airlines to actually sell transportation in another country.
The Third and Fourth Freedoms form the foundation of conventional international airline networks.
The Third Freedom allows an airline to carry passengers and cargo from its home country to another country. A Brazilian airline flying passengers from Sao Paulo to Lisbon would be exercising this right.
The Fourth Freedom allows it to bring passengers in the opposite direction, from the foreign country back to its home country.
These rights are normally negotiated together and explain why opening an international route involves more than obtaining airport slots and regulatory approval for the aircraft operation itself.
Governments determine which traffic rights are exchanged, and air service agreements can also regulate designated airlines, routes, capacity and other conditions.
The Fifth Freedom is where the system becomes more interesting. It allows an airline to transport passengers between two foreign countries when that sector forms part of a service originating or terminating in the airline's home country.
Imagine a US airline operating New York-London-Paris. Third Freedom rights would allow it to carry passengers from the United States to UK. With the necessary Fifth Freedom rights, it could also sell tickets between London and Paris.
This explains some seemingly unusual flights found around the world, where an airline competes on a route that does not touch its home country.
The crucial distinction is the right to carry local traffic. An airline can be authorized to land at an intermediate airport and continue to another country without necessarily being allowed to sell tickets between those two points.
ICAO defines the Fifth Freedom precisely around this ability to take on and discharge traffic in another country on a service connected to a third state.
The Sixth Freedom reverses the logic. Instead of carrying passengers between two foreign countries on a flight extending beyond its home country, an airline transports them between those countries through its home market.
A passenger traveling from London to Bangkok through Dubai on Emirates, for example, is carried from the United Kingdom to the United Arab Emirates and then from the UAE to Thailand.
This model is fundamental to the global hub-and-spoke networks built by airlines such as Emirates, Qatar Airways, Turkish Airlines and Singapore Airlines.
Yet the Sixth Freedom is not normally a separate traffic right granted by an agreement. ICAO describes it as a combination of Third and Fourth Freedom rights: one permits the airline to bring the passenger into its home country and another allows it to carry the passenger onward.
The Seventh Freedom goes further. It allows an airline to operate between two foreign countries without the service originating, terminating or even passing through its own country.
Under such an arrangement, a Brazilian airline could theoretically operate Lisbon-Paris as an independent service, without the aircraft continuing to São Paulo.
That distinction separates it from Fifth Freedom operations. The aircraft does not need any operational connection with the airline's home country.
Seventh Freedom rights are substantially less widespread for passenger services, although liberalized aviation markets and some agreements provide them under particular circumstances.
The Eighth and Ninth Freedoms concern something governments have traditionally guarded much more closely: allowing a foreign airline to transport passengers domestically.
The Eighth Freedom, also called consecutive cabotage, allows a foreign airline to carry passengers between two points within another country as part of a service connected with its home country.
Imagine a British airline operating London-New York-Chicago and being permitted to sell New York-Chicago tickets. The domestic sector remains connected to an international service originating in the United Kingdom.
The Ninth Freedom removes even that connection. It allows the foreign airline to operate a domestic service entirely within another country. A British carrier could, for example, base an aircraft in the United States and sell New York-Chicago tickets without the flight having any connection with Britain.
The European Union provides one of the clearest examples of how different aviation can look when these traditional barriers are removed.
Creation of the EU single aviation market during the 1990s eliminated commercial restrictions on routes operated by EU airlines within the bloc. An airline licensed in one member state can operate routes between other EU countries and domestic services inside another member state.
That is why an Irish airline such as Ryanair can base aircraft in Italy and operate domestic Italian routes without those flights having to originate in Ireland.
The arrangement effectively provides freedoms that would be extraordinary under the traditional bilateral system but have become routine inside the EU aviation market.
Outside such liberalized markets, cabotage remains much more restricted and frequently becomes a subject of political and economic debate.
Even possessing the relevant traffic right does not automatically produce a new route.
Air service agreements can determine which airlines are eligible to operate, what points can be served and under what conditions. Airlines may still need operating permits, airport slots and approvals from aviation authorities, among other requirements.
Codeshares also do not create traffic rights for the airline whose code appears on the ticket. The rights governing the physical operation belong to the carrier operating the flight.
This is why two apparently identical routes can face very different regulatory circumstances depending on the nationality of the airline and the agreements between the countries involved.
More than 80 years after the Chicago Conference, the freedoms devised as international aviation was taking shape still help determine whether an airline can fly over a country, land there, carry its passengers home, continue beyond it — or sell a simple domestic ticket between two cities within its borders.

title: Russian forces hit apartment building in Odesa, injure child
body:
Serhii Lysak, head of the Odesa City Military Administration, announced this on Telegram , Ukrinform reports.
According to him, a residential building was damaged.
Lysak later provided further details about the Russian attack.
"The enemy struck a high-rise residential building in a densely populated area of Odesa. A 13-year-old girl was injured. Medical personnel are providing her with the necessary assistance," he said.
According to Lysak, the roof caught fire and apartments on the top floor were damaged.
All relevant emergency services are working at the scene.

title: NIOA and MBDA sign agreement to assess Australian production of Deluge one-way attack munition with up to 500-kilometre range
body: Deluge is intended to complement more complex weapons by allowing forces to attack defended targets in large numbers at a controlled cost. MBDA plans to produce the first batch for France’s Directorate General of Armaments, or DGA, in 2027. Deluge has a three-metre wingspan, carries a 50-kilogram-class payload and uses a turbojet engine. MBDA lists a speed of approximately 400 kilometres per hour and a range of up to 500 kilometres. The munition follows a mid-altitude flight path and navigates autonomously to predefined target coordinates. Launched from the ground in coordinated salvoes, it is designed to force repeated engagements and maintain pressure on enemy air defences. MBDA describes Deluge as an attrition weapon that adds volume to long-range strikes alongside higher-end effectors. Its design also allows rapid updates and adaptations as battlefield requirements change. The airframe is designed for manufacture and assembly using existing mass-production facilities. MBDA is working with civilian industries to support high output rather than relying solely on specialised defence manufacturing capacity. Deluge uses a standard warhead and fuel to simplify compatibility and storage. NIOA said the design can use M795 casings of the type that its Rheinmetall NIOA Munitions joint venture will manufacture in Maryborough, Queensland. The joint venture’s casing production is covered by a recently announced A$72 million Australian Government contract. That provides a potential link between existing Australian munitions investment and the proposed Deluge manufacturing work. “NIOA is pleased to have signed this MOU with MBDA, further reinforcing the relationship between our companies that started with our cooperation on the Mistral VSHORAD system,” said NIOA Group chief executive Rob Nioa. “The Deluge One-Way Attack Munition is well adapted to the current and future low-cost mass effect requirements of the Australian Defence Force.” Previously known as One Way Effector, Deluge completed its first prototype flight in September 2025. An initial live-firing test followed in November 2025. Those milestones led to a first contract with the DGA, establishing a path to production. MBDA says its industrial approach is intended to support high-rate manufacturing and rapid introduction into operational units. The Australian memorandum builds on an agreement signed by NIOA and MBDA in November 2025 to assess domestic warhead production for the Mistral missile family. The Deluge agreement concerns potential Australian manufacturing rather than a confirmed local production programme or an Australian Defence Force purchase.

title: Accra Rehabilitation Centre appeals for more support beyond food donations
body: The Accra Rehabilitation Centre is appealing for additional support, including teaching materials, to help meet the needs of its inmates. The appeal follows a five-day corporate social responsibility exercise by Melcom Ghana, through the Melcom Care Foundation, which provided 1,000 hot meals to five care institutions across Accra. An inmate at the centre, Eric Badudiwoh, welcomed the donation but said more assistance was needed to support the centre’s work. “We need more, more, more, more help. We need teaching materials… So, when we sit one on one, we can voice all this out, so that you can take it, and then whatever area you want to help, you’re welcome,” he said. Mr Badudiwoh encouraged potential donors to engage directly with the centre to understand its needs and identify areas where they could offer further assistance. Public Relations Officer of Melcom Ghana, Joseph Kpormegbey, said the Melcom Care Foundation was established to reflect the company’s commitment to giving back to society. He said the foundation was inspired by the vision of the late chairman of Melcom Group, Bhagwan Ramchand Khubchandani, who believed in giving back to society. “This week, we decided to visit selected orphanages and this Accra Rehabilitation Centre, so that we give back to society as part of our corporate social responsibility,” he said. Mr Kpormegbey said the company was pleased to support the institutions, acknowledging the challenges involved in running care facilities. “It’s not easy running a children’s home or a rehabilitation centre. That is why we believe that giving them the support will go a long way to assist them,” he said. Responding to concerns about the need for additional resources, including teaching and building materials, Mr Kpormegbey said the foundation had taken note of the requests. “Melcom is always doing its corporate social responsibility. So, once we have heard them, we have taken it in good faith,” he said, adding that the company would work towards providing the necessary assistance. The five-day exercise, which ran from October 5 to 9, 2026, provided 200 hot meals each to five selected institutions, bringing the total to 1,000 meals. The other beneficiaries were Osu Children’s Home, Teshie Children’s Home, Blissful Children’s Home and Nyamedua Children’s Home.

title: Russian Strike Hits Odesa High-Rise, Injures 2
body:
A Russian strike on Sunday hit a multi-story residential building in a densely populated district of Odesa and severely damaged regional energy infrastructure, injuring two civilians – including a 13-year-old girl – and cutting electricity to more than 24,000 households on Sunday, Oct. 18.
Head of the Odesa Regional Military Administration Oleh Kiper confirmed that incoming fire hit an urban residential neighborhood, igniting a blaze across the roof of a high-rise residential building and damaging upper-floor apartments.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Emergency responders, municipal utility teams, and medical crews deployed to the impact zone to extinguish the roof fire and administer medical assistance. Authorities established an operational emergency headquarters on-site to assist displaced residents and assess structural damage to the building.
Officials confirmed that two people sustained injuries in the residential strike, including a 13-year-old girl who received medical care.
Concurrently with the attack on the regional center, Russian strikes targeted electrical infrastructure across the wider Odesa region, inflicting significant physical damage on power distribution and transmission equipment.
Private Ukrainian energy operator DTEK reported that the bombardment inflicted extensive destruction across targeted energy facilities, noting that technical assessments and subsequent equipment repairs will require substantial time to execute.
“The destruction is extensive. Restoring damaged equipment will require time,” DTEK stated in an operational advisory.
To protect grid stability and prevent uncontrolled systemic failures, electrical dispatchers enacted emergency power shutdowns across impacted districts.
The disruptions left 24,100 households without electricity across the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, Izmail, and Bolhrad districts in southern Odesa region.
The strikes on Odesa’s residential sector and electrical grid form part of an intensified Russian interdiction campaign targeting Ukrainian life-support networks and municipal utilities ahead of winter.
Earlier on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Russian forces had carried out 76 targeted strikes against Ukrainian energy and oil-and-gas installations over the preceding seven days, noting overnight impacts on electrical substations across Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Air India’s new chief Tewolde Gebremariam puts safety, reliability and profitability at the centre of turnaround
body:
MUMBAI. Air India’s incoming chief executive and managing director, Tewolde Gebremariam, has laid out an agenda centred on safety, operational reliability, sustainable profitability and greater organisational efficiency, signalling a shift towards execution and financial discipline in the airline’s next phase of transformation.



Addressing employees at his first company-wide town hall in Mumbai on September 28, Gebremariam acknowledged the progress Air India had made over the preceding four years but said considerable work remained before the airline could establish itself among the world’s leading carriers.

The former Ethiopian Airlines chief called on employees to take collective responsibility for safety, improve punctuality and baggage handling, communicate transparently with passengers during disruptions, generate additional revenue and identify opportunities to reduce costs. He also stressed the importance of operating as “one Air India Group”, with greater coordination across businesses and more efficient use of the airline’s fleet, network and resources.

The town hall was an important early indication of the management priorities Gebremariam intends to pursue as he succeeds Campbell Wilson. It came at a time when Air India is attempting to translate extensive investments in fleet modernisation, corporate integration and network expansion into measurable

improvements in service quality and financial performance.

The central message was that expansion alone would not be enough. Air India must build a stronger operational foundation, restore passenger confidence and ensure that growth generates sustainable returns.

Safety: the non-negotiable priority

Safety was the foremost concern in Gebremariam’s address. He told employees that every activity undertaken by the airline must meet safety requirements and that responsibility for maintaining high standards rests with everyone, not just the safety department or senior management.

“Everything we do must be safe,” he said.

He called for a workplace culture in which employees feel empowered to raise concerns, report irregularities and flag potential hazards without hesitation.

“If you see something, say something,” he told employees, adding that a stronger reporting culture would strengthen the airline’s overall safety culture.

The emphasis on reporting is significant in aviation, where early identification of technical faults, procedural lapses and other hazards can help prevent incidents. A robust safety culture requires employees to communicate concerns promptly and management to investigate them thoroughly and take corrective action.

For Air India, this means reinforcing standard operating procedures, strengthening coordination among flight operations, engineering, maintenance and ground-handling teams, and ensuring that safety concerns are addressed without delay.

It also requires management to distinguish between honest reporting of mistakes or hazards and deliberate violations of established procedures. Employees must have confidence that raising a legitimate concern will lead to appropriate action rather than being ignored.

The airline’s safety performance is under particular scrutiny following the fatal crash of an Air India Boeing 787 shortly after take-off from Ahmedabad in June 2025, as well as subsequent operational incidents. The pressure to demonstrate improvements in safety oversight, technical capability and regulatory compliance has consequently intensified.

Gebremariam’s message therefore establishes safety as the foundation on which the airline’s commercial ambitions must rest. Fleet expansion, new routes and improved financial results cannot substitute for consistently sound operational practices.

The real test will be whether the emphasis on speaking up is translated into effective reporting mechanisms, stronger technical oversight, adequate training and measurable improvements in safety management.

Reliability and customer confidence: getting the basics right

Gebremariam identified operational reliability as the second major priority, emphasising that customers should be able to depend on Air India for punctual departures and arrivals, proper baggage handling and transparent communication when flights are disrupted.

“Our customers should remember Air India for its reliability,” he said, according to reports of the town hall. He stressed that when disruptions occur, the airline must communicate openly and recover quickly.

The message reflects a fundamental challenge for Air India: rebuilding passenger confidence requires consistent performance across the entire travel experience, not merely a modern fleet or an expanded international network.

Delays caused by weather, airspace restrictions or technical issues cannot always be avoided. However, airlines can improve their ability to manage such disruptions through effective planning, adequate operational reserves, timely communication and coordinated decision-making.

For Air India, reliability will depend on several interconnected functions:

 	Aircraft availability: Ensuring that maintenance schedules, engineering support and spare-parts availability minimise avoidable aircraft-on-ground situations.
 	Crew and flight planning: Improving coordination so that disruptions do not cascade across subsequent services.
 	Airport operations: Strengthening turnaround procedures, ground handling and baggage delivery.
 	Passenger communication: Providing timely, accurate information and practical assistance when schedules change.
 	Disruption recovery: Making decisions quickly to restore operations while treating affected passengers fairly.

These improvements are particularly important as the airline expands its international network. Longer routes, complex connecting itineraries and aircraft operating across multiple time zones can magnify the consequences of a disruption.

Gebremariam’s emphasis on reliability suggests that Air India must make operational performance a shared responsibility across departments. Punctuality and baggage delivery are visible to passengers, but achieving them depends on the effectiveness of systems and processes operating behind the scenes.

Profitability: a sharper focus on revenue and costs

A third major priority was to improve Air India’s financial performance by increasing revenue and exercising tighter control over expenditure.

Gebremariam identified opportunities across the international network, commercial activities and cargo business. He also highlighted the importance of improving network efficiency, optimising aircraft deployment and ensuring that the airline’s operations are appropriately balanced.

The emphasis comes against a difficult financial backdrop. According to media reports, the Air India Group recorded a consolidated net loss of ₹22,238 crore in FY2025-26, compared with ₹10,859 crore in FY2024-25. The figures underline the scale of the challenge facing the new management.

Air India has invested heavily in rebuilding its business, but its long-term viability will depend on its ability to turn increased capacity and improved services into stronger financial returns.

Generating more revenue from existing operations

One important opportunity lies in improving the commercial performance of the airline’s existing network.

Revenue depends not simply on how many passengers fly, but also on fares, passenger mix, seat occupancy, route economics and the effectiveness with which aircraft capacity is deployed.

A key industry measure is revenue per available seat kilometre (RASK), which indicates how much passenger revenue an airline earns for the capacity it offers. Improving this metric requires a combination of sound pricing, effective revenue management, an appropriate route mix and the ability to attract passengers willing to pay fares that support profitable operations.

Air India can also seek to improve returns from its international connections, where coordinated schedules and effective hub operations can help attract passengers travelling between different regions.

Cargo provides another potential source of revenue. Better utilisation of cargo capacity, stronger commercial relationships and improved integration between passenger and cargo operations could help diversify earnings.

However, these opportunities will need to be assessed against market demand, competition and operating costs. Additional revenue is valuable only when it contributes positively to the airline’s overall financial performance.

Cost control must involve every employee

Gebremariam also argued that cost management should not be regarded as the exclusive responsibility of the finance department or senior executives.

“Cost management is not just the responsibility of leadership or the finance function. Every employee can contribute to savings, and those savings add up across an organisation of our scale,” he said.

Air India was also considering programmes to reward employees whose suggestions deliver measurable cost savings and operational efficiencies.

This approach could encourage employees to identify waste, streamline administrative processes, improve resource utilisation and suggest practical ways of reducing avoidable expenditure.

In an airline, even relatively small improvements can have significant cumulative effects because of the scale of operations. Better aircraft utilisation, fewer avoidable delays and more efficient procurement can improve financial performance across a large network.

But cost discipline must be applied carefully. Cutting expenditure on maintenance, training, safety equipment or other essential functions could undermine the very operational standards the airline is trying to strengthen.

The objective, therefore, is to reduce inefficiencies while preserving the investment required for safe operations, reliable services and sustainable growth.

Disciplined expansion: Growth must be profitable

Gebremariam acknowledged the substantial opportunities available to Air India because of India’s economic growth, demographic profile, geographical position and large overseas diaspora.

These factors provide a strong foundation for expanding international connectivity and strengthening India’s position in global aviation. However, he cautioned that growth must be sustainable and supported by the airline’s operational capabilities.

“Growth is the oxygen of business. But growth must also be profitable and sustainable,” he said.

The distinction is important for an airline that has committed substantial capital to aircraft acquisition, cabin upgrades, technology and network development.

Expansion can increase revenue and market presence, but it also brings additional costs. New routes require suitable aircraft, trained crew, engineering support, airport arrangements and sufficient demand. If these elements are not aligned, additional capacity can place pressure on margins rather than improve profitability.

Gebremariam’s approach appears to be that Air India should match its expansion plans to the readiness of its people, fleet and network.

That means ensuring that aircraft are available when required, operational teams have the necessary resources and routes can generate adequate returns. It also means examining the performance of existing services rather than assuming that adding capacity will automatically produce better results.

The objective is not to abandon Air India’s global ambitions, but to ensure that the airline builds scale without compromising operational reliability or financial sustainability.

Building ‘One Air India Group’

Gebremariam also stressed the importance of operating as “one Air India Group”, with streamlined processes and greater synergies across its businesses.

The Tata Group’s consolidation of its aviation operations has already reshaped the structure of Indian aviation. Vistara was integrated into Air India, while Air India Express and AIX Connect were combined under the Air India Express brand. The resulting group has a broader operating base and a larger platform for international and domestic growth.

But corporate consolidation is only the first step. The benefits must be realised through effective integration of systems, teams, commercial processes and operational planning.

Greater coordination could help the group improve aircraft utilisation, reduce duplication, strengthen procurement and align network planning. It could also improve connections between services and create opportunities to generate more revenue from passengers travelling across multiple routes.

At the same time, integration requires a common culture and clear accountability. Employees from different legacy organisations must be able to work effectively together, while management must ensure that decision-making remains responsive and operational responsibilities are clearly defined.

Gebremariam’s emphasis on a unified group suggests that he sees organisational efficiency as an important part of Air India’s turnaround.

His remarks did not announce another merger. Rather, the stated objective was to streamline operations and capture synergies while maintaining a strong focus on customers.

Geopolitical tensions and fuel prices add to the challenge

The new chief executive also acknowledged the external pressures facing Air India, including geopolitical developments, airspace restrictions affecting Indian carriers, elevated fuel prices and uncertainty in international markets.

These factors can affect both costs and operational planning.

Airspace restrictions may force airlines to take longer routes, increasing fuel consumption and flight times. Longer journeys can also affect crew scheduling, aircraft utilisation and the timing of connecting services.

Fuel-price volatility is another major concern because fuel represents a substantial component of airline operating expenditure. Even when an airline improves its internal efficiency, sharp increases in fuel costs can erode margins.

Uncertainty in international markets can also complicate decisions about route expansion, aircraft deployment and pricing.

These challenges make disciplined planning particularly important. Air India must balance the need to grow its international network with the flexibility required to respond to changing geopolitical and commercial conditions.

Its ability to manage external disruptions while maintaining reliable service will be a significant test of the new management team.

Why Gebremariam’s appointment matters

Gebremariam brings extensive experience in airline management, international network development and operational transformation. During his tenure at Ethiopian Airlines, he oversaw a major expansion that helped establish the carrier as one of Africa’s leading airlines.

Tata group

The Tata Group announced his appointment on August 5, 2026, citing his experience in managing large-scale airline transformations, improving operational performance and building international aviation businesses. He was selected to succeed Campbell Wilson as Air India moved into what the group described as a new phase of growth and execution.

His experience at Ethiopian Airlines is relevant because that carrier developed an extensive international network and strengthened Addis Ababa’s position as a connecting hub for passengers travelling between Africa and other parts of the world.

Air India has a different set of opportunities and constraints. It operates in a highly competitive domestic market, serves a large international passenger base and must integrate businesses while managing significant capital requirements and heightened expectations on safety and service.

Gebremariam’s experience may help Air India strengthen operational processes, technical capabilities and network efficiency. But the results will depend on his ability to adapt those lessons to the airline’s specific circumstances and deliver improvements across a much larger and more complex organisation.

From rebuilding the airline to delivering results

The town hall acknowledged the contribution of Air India’s employees to the transformation undertaken since the airline returned to Tata Group ownership in January 2022.

Gebremariam thanked the workforce for its role in the changes of the preceding four years, including the merger and integration of Air India and Vistara. He also said that considerable opportunities remained to improve the airline and strengthen its global position.

His message points to a transition between two phases of the turnaround.

The first phase focused on rebuilding the foundations: consolidating businesses, ordering new aircraft, modernising the fleet, upgrading the passenger experience and creating a platform for expansion.

The next phase requires those investments to deliver consistent results. Aircraft must be deployed efficiently, operational disruptions reduced, passengers treated well and revenues improved relative to costs.

These objectives are interconnected. Better maintenance planning can improve aircraft availability. More reliable flights can strengthen passenger confidence. Improved network coordination can increase the value of connecting traffic. And greater operational efficiency can help reduce avoidable costs.

For employees, this means a stronger emphasis on accountability and collaboration. For management, it means setting measurable priorities and ensuring that departments work towards common objectives.

For passengers, the ultimate measure will be whether Air India becomes safer, more dependable and more responsive to their needs.

The road ahead

Gebremariam’s first town hall was an early statement of intent rather than a detailed public announcement of new financial targets or a comprehensive restructuring plan.

Its significance lies in the priorities he chose to emphasise: safety first, operational reliability, sustainable profitability, disciplined growth and a more integrated airline group.

Air India continues to face substantial challenges, including financial losses, competition, operational complexity and the need to rebuild passenger confidence. Its investments and expanded network provide opportunities, but they do not guarantee success.

The airline will need to demonstrate progress through tangible improvements in safety practices, punctuality, customer service, aircraft availability, revenue performance and cost efficiency.

The wider significance of the town hall is that Air India’s next phase will be judged increasingly by execution rather than ambition alone.

The test for Gebremariam will be whether he can turn Air India’s expanded scale and substantial investments into a consistently reliable, customer-focused and financially sustainable global airline.

title: NLNG Dividend Delay Hurting States, Says Makinde
body: Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, has criticised the delay in releasing Nigeria LNG (NLNG) dividend funds due to states, saying the development is affecting subnational development plans and long-term infrastructure investment. Makinde spoke at the 2027 Budget Stakeholders’ Consultative Engagement held at the Olola Ogunlana Hall, International Conference Centre, University of Ibadan on Saturday. He said each state was expected to receive ₦250 billion from the NLNG dividends but claimed the funds would not be released until after the 2027 elections. “Each state was supposed to get ₦250 billion. We had already identified projects that would expand Oyo State’s economy. But they have now said the money will not be paid until after the election. Is the election more important than the people of Nigeria?” the governor asked. Makinde said the delay could affect states’ ability to sustain infrastructure projects and respond to rising costs of governance. He disclosed that Oyo State’s monthly wage bill had risen from ₦4.5 billion in 2019 to ₦18 billion in 2026, while inflation had significantly increased the cost of major projects. The governor said the timely release of the funds would help states manage these pressures, sustain ongoing projects and maintain economic growth. On the state’s development priorities, Makinde said his administration had recognised infrastructure as a foundation for economic growth, adding that investments in the sector had increased the value of assets across Oyo State. He said the next phase of development would require prudent financial managers to maintain and improve the institutional reforms already established, rather than simply increasing the number of engineers. Makinde also said his administration would implement about 30 per cent of the 2027 budget, noting that a new government would take over on May 29, 2027. He thanked residents for their support, saying that over the past seven years, budgeted projects had enjoyed a 70 per cent chance of implementation. On agriculture, the governor defended his administration’s tractorisation policy, saying the decision to scrap the loss-making government tractor unit and privatise tractor services had improved farmers’ access to mechanisation. The Speaker of the Oyo State House of Assembly, Adebo Ogundoyin, commended the governor for making public consultation part of the budget process, saying people-centred budgeting had improved project execution. The Secretary to the State Government, Musibau Babatunde, said the administration had moved from ad hoc budgeting to a performance-driven model, recording more than 70 per cent budget performance in 2026. He said the consultative process, which began in the three senatorial districts before expanding across the state, now includes feedback mechanisms, quarterly budget tracking and mandatory compliance by ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs). According to him, MDAs must demonstrate how they incorporated public contributions from stakeholder engagements before they can defend their budgets at the pre-treasury stage. Earlier, the Commissioner for Budget and Economic Planning, Ayobami Ojo, described the engagement as a platform for building consensus on development priorities. He said the 2027 budget should be based on realistic revenue projections, prudent expenditure and effective resource allocation. Participants, including local government representatives, student unions, farmers, persons with disabilities, religious leaders, civil society groups, artisans and market associations, offered recommendations on roads, security, welfare and project maintenance. The event was attended by Deputy Governor Bayo Lawal, Chief of Staff Akinwale Akinwole, Head of Service Adenike Fashina, government officials, traditional rulers, labour leaders and youth groups, among others. The post NLNG Dividend Delay Hurting States, Says Makinde appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Egypt pledges support for Saudi Arabia as Houthis warn Cairo against military intervention
body: Egypt 's top security body on Sunday pledged “all necessary and possible forms of support” to Saudi Arabia . It met hours before parliament convened to vote on authorising President Abdel Fattah El Sisi to help defend the kingdom against attacks by the Houthi rebels in Yemen. The National Defence Council, chaired by Mr El Sisi at Al Ittihadiya Palace in Cairo, said Saudi Arabia's security was inextricably linked to Egypt's own and to wider Arab national security. The support would help the kingdom defend its security and territory, as well as the Islamic holy sites, the presidency said. It cited the “escalating unacceptable attacks” on the kingdom and called for more diplomacy to calm the region. The statement did not mention troops. But Mostafa Bakry, an MP and TV host close to the state, said on X that the council had approved sending forces to Saudi Arabia on “a defensive mission”. The Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, Speaker of Parliament Hisham Badawy, Defence Minister Lt Gen Ashraf Zaher and intelligence chiefs attended. Under Article 152 of Egypt's constitution, the President cannot declare war or send the army on a combat mission abroad without consulting the council. He also needs the approval of two-thirds of MPs. Parliament's rules require the vote to take place in an urgent closed session. The emergency sitting was set for 1pm on Sunday. The House has a majority of pro-Sisi legislators who are widely expected to approve the request, as they have backed previous policies championed by the President. Mr El Sisi made the request on Saturday. “It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed,” he said. Egypt would act only if Riyadh asked, he said in a speech at the Military Academy. “We do not want to fight or attack anyone. We will only defend Saudi Arabia,” he added. The move drew a swift warning from Sanaa. Yahya Al Raei, speaker of the Houthi-run parliament there, wrote to Mr Badawi on Saturday. The Houthi-controlled body is not recognised internationally. “We categorically reject Egypt being dragged” into “the same trench as the takfiri forces and the Israeli occupation entity,” he wrote. Such a path “would pose a grave danger to its national security,” he said, urging Cairo to take a “courageous stance”. He accused Riyadh of waging “aggression and siege” against Yemen for more than 12 years. He said it had walked away from a peace road map and ended a period of calm by striking Sanaa airport. The letter was carried by the Houthis' Al Masirah TV. Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had shot down two ballistic missiles fired at Khamis Mushait and three drones over Riyadh and the Eastern Province. The Houthis have launched 20 attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport since October 1, coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said on Thursday. Attacks on Saudi airports have killed 19 people and wounded 364, he said. The deadliest, on October 10 in Riyadh, killed 13, including an Egyptian flight attendant. The coalition also said it intercepted a missile aimed at Madinah on Thursday. The Houthis denied firing it. The UN Security Council condemned the attacks as “escalatory” that same day and backed the kingdom's right to self-defence. Cairo's move also comes as a new alliance takes shape around Riyadh. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on August 7 . The pact provides that an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. Riyadh activated it on October 5, and Pakistan said the partners would send the “agreed military forces” to the kingdom. While Egypt is not yet a member, Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said last week that joining was “under serious consideration”. Cairo has long been wary of binding pacts. Joining one could strain its ties with Iran and its peace treaty with Israel, while potentially drawing Egypt into a war with the Houthis. Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping have already caused heavy losses in Suez Canal revenue . Over the past week, many commentators have cited Egypt's costly intervention in Yemen in the 1960s as a reason not to rush into such an agreement. Instead, Cairo has taken smaller steps. On August 13, it joined a Saudi-led naval coalition set up after the Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi shipping. Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015. In July 2020, MPs voted unanimously in a closed session to allow combat missions abroad as fighting in Libya neared Egypt's western border. Approval of the request would not, in itself, mean that troops would be deployed.

title: The North Shekarau Claims to Speak For Does Not Exist
body: By Hassan Husaini, mni Senator Ibrahim Shekarau, former governor of Kano State, recently declared that the entire North is solidly behind President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election in 2027. He made this declaration under the banner of a group called “Arewa for Asiwaju” (A4A), flanked by other former governors and political associates from the All Progressives Congress. The question that immediately arises is simple: which North is Shekarau speaking for? It cannot be the North of the farmer in Zamfara who has not accessed his farmland for two consecutive planting seasons because armed bandits have made the roads and fields unsafe. It cannot be the North of the mother in Borno whose child is among the 5.5 million people in the northeast whom the World Food Programme cannot reach with lifesaving food assistance. It cannot be the North of the trader in Mubi paying N1,850 per litre for petrol while customers can barely afford to buy. And it certainly cannot be the North of the young man in Katsina or Sokoto who watches his community bury victims of attacks the federal government has not been able to prevent, let alone prosecute. The North Shekarau speaks for is the North of the APC. It is a North defined by political office, by access to power, by networks of former governors and serving senators who have gathered under the A4A umbrella to mobilize votes for a president whose administration has presided over the most severe humanitarian crisis in northern Nigeria in a decade. It is a North of convention halls in Abuja, of press conferences, of secretariat commissioning ceremonies attended by vice presidents and party chairmen. It is not the North that exists outside the perimeter of those events. Shekarau and his colleagues have every right to form a political campaign group and support whomever they choose. But they do not have the right to claim that their political preferences represent the collective will of a region of nearly 100 million people, many of whom are struggling to survive the consequences of the very policies their group exists to promote. When Shekarau says the North is “solidly behind” Tinubu, he is not describing a political reality. He is attempting to manufacture one, using the authority of his former office to create the impression of northern consensus where none exists. The data does not support his claim. The World Food Programme reports that 36.3 million Nigerians are acutely food insecure, with the crisis concentrated in Borno, Adamawa, Yobe, Katsina, Sokoto, and Zamfara. In the northeast alone, 6.2 million people are food insecure, but WFP can only reach 740,000, leaving 5.5 million without lifesaving assistance. The Famine Early Warning Systems Network projects Crisis-level food insecurity across much of northern Nigeria through January 2027, driven by conflict, high fuel costs, and eroded household purchasing power. The security situation is no better. Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026 documents 2,938 abductions in the Northwest between July 2024 and June 2025—over 60 percent of all reported incidents nationwide. Zamfara alone recorded 1,203 abductions. In the Northeast, Boko Haram factions resumed deadly attacks, killing at least 57 people in Borno in May and 60 more in September. The Nigerian authorities have failed to arrest or prosecute those responsible. The North Shekarau describes as solidly behind this administration is a North where communities bury their dead without justice. Shekarau’s group has compiled a catalogue of infrastructure projects to counter claims of neglect. Roads and bridges and gas pipelines are not nothing. But they are not food in the stomach of a child in Sokoto. They are not safety for the farmer in Katsina who cannot harvest his crops. They are not the accountability the families of the 52 people killed in Plateau State in April 2025 still await. When the basic conditions of survival are deteriorating for millions, a list of construction projects is not a rebuttal. It is a distraction. The A4A group’s composition reveals the problem. Its leadership is drawn overwhelmingly from former governors and political officeholders who governed northern states in the past and now seek to shape the region’s political future. The group claims representation from all three northern zones, with deputy coordinators for the Northwest, Northeast, and North-Central. But representation on a letterhead is not representation of the people. Shekarau, Badaru, Lalong, Shema, Bello, Namdas—these are not community organizers who emerged from the grassroots. They are political veterans who have spent decades navigating the corridors of power. Their claim to speak for the North rests entirely on authority they once held in office, not on any current mandate from the people they claim to represent. The political arithmetic Shekarau and his colleagues are attempting to impose is also not as settled as they would have the public believe. Dr. Umar Ardo, convener of the League of Northern Democrats, has predicted Tinubu may secure less than 10 percent of northern votes in a free and fair election. This is a partisan prediction, dismissed by pro-Tinubu groups. But the very fact that such a prediction is being made—and taken seriously enough to require rebuttal—demonstrates the North is not the monolith Shekarau describes. If the entire North were solidly behind the president, there would be no need for a group like A4A. The group’s purpose is not to celebrate an existing consensus but to create one. Its existence is an admission the consensus does not yet exist. There is a deeper issue than political strategy. When northern leaders who have held high office gather to pledge votes for a sitting president, they are not speaking truth to power. They are speaking power to the people, telling northerners what they should think and how they should vote while ignoring what they are experiencing. The role of a former governor who claims to represent the North should be to tell the president what the North is going through, not to tell the North what the president is doing for them. Shekarau and his colleagues have reversed that relationship. They have become messengers of the federal government to the region, rather than representatives of the region to the federal government. This is a familiar pattern in Nigerian politics. Former governors and political heavyweights convert their followings into bargaining chips for access to the center. They offer the votes of their people in exchange for influence, contracts, and the continuation of their own relevance. The people themselves are abstractions in this calculus—voters to be mobilized, statistics to be cited, a region to be claimed. The suffering of that region is an inconvenience to be managed with press releases and catalogues of achievements, not a reality to be confronted with honesty and urgency. Shekarau and his associates are not unique in this. They are part of a political class that has learned to survive by attaching itself to whoever holds power, regardless of what that power does to the people. But they should be named for what they are: political opportunists whose primary loyalty is not to the North, not to their constituents, and not to the truth, but to their own continued relevance in a system that rewards loyalty over accountability. In a sane political environment, leaders who preside over or endorse policies that produce mass hunger, insecurity, and destitution would face consequences at the ballot box. In Nigeria, they are instead rewarded with campaign platforms and secretariat commissioning ceremonies. The North Shekarau speaks for is a convenient fiction. It is a North of political elites who have decided their interests and the president’s interests are aligned. It is a North that exists in press statements and speeches delivered at party headquarters. It is not the North that is hungry, that is unsafe, that is waiting for government to do the job it was elected to do. That North cannot be summoned into existence by a press conference. And it should not be spoken for by those who have no intention of listening to it.

title: UAE signs agreement to hold 2029 World Bank and IMF meetings in Abu Dhabi
body: The UAE has formally signed the agreement to host the 2029 annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Abu Dhabi. The deal, signed at the conclusion of the IMF and the World Bank 2026 annual meetings in Thailand, is a mark of growing international confidence in the UAE’s economic and financial ecosystem, the UAE Ministry of Finance said in a statement on Sunday. The formal pact to host the meetings also reinforces the status of the UAE – the Arab world’s second-largest economy – as a global financial hub that is helping to shape the stability and future of the global economic system. Mohamed bin Hadi Al Hussaini, Minister of State for Financial Affairs, and Khaled Balama, governor of the Central Bank of the UAE, signed the agreement in the Thai capital, Bangkok, with the World Bank president Ajay Banga and the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva. “The signing of the agreement marks a significant milestone, reflecting … confidence in the UAE’s readiness, the efficiency of its infrastructure and financial system, and its ability to host major international events of strategic importance,” Mr Al Hussaini said. The hosting of the event in the UAE will provide global financial leaders and decision-makers with a platform to explore how to advance the financial and monetary stability agenda as well as build development finance, the minister added. The UAE’s selection to host the event builds on the country’s track record in hosting major economic events. Scheduled to be held in October 2029, the summit will return to the Emirates for the first time in more than a quarter of a century. Dubai hosted the meetings in 2003. Participation in the annual meetings has continued to grow over the years, with more than 10,000 in-person and virtual attendees welcomed at each event. Country group meetings, civil society forums and press conferences with the World Bank president and IMF managing director are also held. They are closely watched by financial experts and policymakers from around the world. The World Bank-IMF annual meetings are traditionally held at their headquarters in Washington DC, and every third year a member country is selected to host them. London was the first city outside the US to host the meetings in 1947, while the UAE and Turkey remain the only countries in the Middle East to have hosted them. “The UAE has built institutions and infrastructure with a spirit of bold ambition and partnership, cementing its role as a global hub for economic dialogue,” Mr Banga of the World Bank Group, said. “Abu Dhabi is a fitting host for the annual meetings where our focus is on development impact, and delivering jobs, growth, and financing at scale.” The meetings usually bring together finance ministers, central bank governors, policymakers and economic experts, private sector representatives, civil society, media, and academics from more than 190 countries to examine the challenges and opportunities facing the global economy. The IMF and World Bank also release their outlook for growth and financial stability, and discuss future policy direction that supports inclusive and sustainable development. “The UAE has become an important hub for ideas, finance, innovation and international co-operation,” Ms Georgieva said. The 2029 meeting in Abu Dhabi will provide an opportunity to discuss the “challenges and opportunities ahead and help shape a better future”, the IMF managing director added.

title: Chelsea Keeper Set for Spell on Sidelines After Jaw Surgery
body: Chelsea goalkeeper, Emiliano ‘Dibu’ Martinez, has undergone successful surgery for fractured jaw and will be out for an undisclosed period. The English Premier League club disclosed Martinez’s medical condition in a statement that detailed the sequence of events leading to the injury. Martinez collided with an Everton defender during Saturday’s EPL match the Blues won 2-0 at the Toffees Hill Dickinson stadium. The Argentine goalkeeper was stretchered off after a lengthy delay, and moved to the hospital in Liverpool for further assessment. EPL: Manchester City remain perfect with Ipswich win Akor Adams winner ends Venezia Serie A losing streak Surgery was performed at the hospital following the confirmation of a fractured jaw, and the club assured the goalkeeper of its support during recovery. “Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez has undergone successful surgery on a fractured jaw.
