Martinez was injured following a collision midway through the second half of our 2-0 victory over Everton at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on Saturday. “Martinez was taken to hospital for further assessment, which confirmed a fractured jaw that required surgery. “Everyone at Chelsea wishes Emi a speedy recovery and will support him throughout.” Martinez, who revealed he expects to be out for a few weeks, kept his first Chelsea clean sheet in seven matches for the club he joined at the start of the season.

title: Warrior disposal dates withheld on security grounds
body: The Ministry of Defence has refused to say when each of the seventy-eight Warrior infantry fighting vehicles removed from the fleet in the past year was disposed of, according to an answer given in Parliament. Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the dates on which each vehicle was disposed of, following an answer of 7 September. Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The answer to Question 23452 explained that the seventy-eight Warrior Infantry Fighting Vehicles removed from the reported fleet between 2025 and 2026 have been disposed of in accordance with Defence disposal policy. It would be inappropriate for me to provide exact disposal details, such as dates or variants as to do so could, or would be likely to, prejudice the capability of our Armed Forces.” The number leaving the fleet has been confirmed, but not when they went or which variants they were, so the rate at which Warrior is being drawn down cannot be read from the published record. The FV510 Warrior entered service in 1988 as the British Army tracked infantry fighting vehicle, carrying a section of dismounted infantry behind a two man turret armed with the 30mm RARDEN cannon. A programme to rebuild the fleet around a stabilised 40mm cased telescoped cannon, the Warrior Capability Sustainment Programme, was cancelled in March 2021 after more than a decade of development and around £430 million of spending, and the vehicle has been running down since. The post Warrior disposal dates withheld on security grounds first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: NPFL: Ranchers Bees part ways with Coach Usman Abd’Allah
body: Ranchers Bees have announced it has parted ways with Technical Adviser Usman Abd’Allah by mutual agreement. The NPFL club also confirmed that Abd’Allah left with some of his technical crew. It, however, did not list the members of the crew retained. “Ranchers Bees Kaduna confirms that the club has parted ways with Technical Adviser Usman Abd’Allah and some members of the technical crew by mutual agreement.” Chelsea Keeper Set for Spell on Sidelines After Jaw Surgery Akor Adams winner ends Venezia Serie A losing streak Abd’Allah’s exit comes less than 48 hours after Ranchers Bees lost 3-1 to Shooting Stars in Ibadan. The newly promoted club becomes the second NPFL club to sack its coach in the 2026/27 season. Abd’Allah was previously relieved from his role as Technical Adviser with Remo Stars at the end of last season after only six months, relegating the NPFL champions 12 months after their first-ever league title. Ranchers Bees had been on a five-match winless run before the club management pulled the rug off Abd’Allah’s feet nine matches into the season. Ranchers Bees are battling relegation early in the season, sitting in 18th place on the NPFL log with eight points from nine matches played so far.

title: FRSC Ogun Sector Commander Oludare Ogunjobi Dies After Brief Illness
body: The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) has announced the death of its Ogun State Sector Commander, Corps Commander Oludare Ogunjobi, after a brief illness. The announcement was contained in a statement issued in Abeokuta, the state capital, by the command’s Public Relations Officer, Afolabi Odunsin. Describing his death as a great loss, Odunsin said Ogunjobi would be remembered for his service, leadership and commitment to road safety administration. “His passing is a great loss to the Corps, his colleagues, and the entire road safety community. He will be remembered for his service, leadership, commitment to road safety administration, and dedication to the mandate of the Federal Road Safety Corps,” he said. Odunsin said Ogunjobi contributed to efforts to promote safer roads, improve public enlightenment, strengthen stakeholder engagement and enhance compliance with traffic regulations during his service. The command expressed condolences to his family, loved ones, colleagues and associates, describing his death as deeply regrettable. It added that details of the funeral arrangements would be communicated in due course. The statement prayed for the repose of Ogunjobi’s soul and strength for his family, the Corps and others affected by his death. The post FRSC Ogun Sector Commander Oludare Ogunjobi Dies After Brief Illness appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Soldiers to remain in nine cleared forest reserves to prevent galamsey – Mahama
body: President John Dramani Mahama has announced that soldiers will remain stationed in nine forest reserves cleared of illegal mining to prevent operators from returning to the sites. He said the decision followed previous experiences in which illegal miners returned to the reserves after military personnel deployed to flush them out had withdrawn. President Mahama said all nine forest reserves previously designated as red zones because of extensive destruction and the presence of heavily armed illegal miners had been cleared, with troops deployed to protect the areas. “We have now cleared all nine of those red zones. There are no galamsey operators in those forest reserves, and we have stationed soldiers there to ensure that the illegal miners do not return. The soldiers will remain in those areas,” he said. The President made the remarks during a courtesy call by chiefs from the Western North Region, where he called for stronger collaboration with traditional authorities to sustain the fight against illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey. He said previous efforts to clear some forest reserves had failed because illegal miners returned shortly after soldiers withdrew, leaving forest guards to resume responsibility for protecting the areas. “Whenever forest guards went there, they were fired upon, and some lost their lives,” he said, highlighting the dangers faced by personnel tasked with protecting the reserves. President Mahama urged chiefs to support the government’s efforts, particularly in communities where young people and some traditional authorities had resisted operations by the National Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee on Illegal Mining (NAIMOS). He said the cooperation of traditional authorities was crucial because they lived among the people and were better positioned to help address the local factors sustaining illegal mining. Mahama raises concern over deaths during operations The President also expressed concern about incidents in which soldiers had discharged firearms during enforcement operations, resulting in deaths. He stressed the need for stronger community engagement and collaboration with traditional leaders to prevent further casualties while protecting forest reserves and water bodies. GoldBod, military to support forest restoration On efforts to restore degraded lands, President Mahama said GoldBod had begun engaging the military in a programme to reclaim destroyed forest areas and replant them with trees. Under the programme, bulldozers would be used to level degraded land, while the Forestry Commission would work with the military on reclamation and reforestation. The initiative forms part of broader efforts to restore areas damaged by illegal mining and protect the country’s forest resources. GH¢400m allocated for Blue Water Guards President Mahama also announced that the Finance Minister had allocated GH¢400 million in the 2027 Budget to recruit additional Blue Water Guards to patrol water bodies and intensify the fight against illegal mining. He said the guards had been instructed to destroy changfang machines used for illegal mining whenever they encountered them. According to the President, several machines had already been destroyed, helping to clear many major river channels. However, he noted that illegal mining in tributaries continued to contribute mud and silt to the rivers, underscoring the need for sustained enforcement and monitoring. President Mahama said the government’s response must go beyond enforcement to address the economic circumstances pushing young people into illegal mining. He emphasised the importance of combining security operations, environmental restoration and community collaboration to sustain the fight against galamsey.

title: Russia’s Rassvet Network Threatens Ukraine With Real-Time Strike Control
body:
Russia is deploying its low-Earth orbit satellite network “Rassvet,” which could enable Russian operators to control strike drones , reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and low-cost cruise missiles in real time across Ukraine within roughly six months, presidential adviser on defense technologies Serhii Beskrestnov has warned.
Speaking to the Associated Press , Beskrestnov – widely known by the call sign “Flash” – described the emerging satellite communication constellation as Moscow’s foremost technological threat, warning that its operational deployment poses acute security hazards for both Ukraine and broader European defense architectures.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
According to Beskrestnov, Russian engineers are tailoring the satellite communications architecture to guide Shahed-type loitering munitions, tactical reconnaissance UAVs, and lower-cost missile systems such as the Banderol and Dan-M.
Continuous real-time satellite links would permit remote operators to adjust flight trajectories, alter terminal approach angles, and dynamically retarget munitions in mid-air, substantially degrading the effectiveness of Ukrainian electronic warfare (EW) countermeasures and radio-frequency jamming systems.
“They will be able to attack the entire country in real time and do so with extreme precision,” Beskrestnov cautioned. “This will truly be a major catastrophe for everyone.”
Moscow has not yet established uninterrupted satellite coverage over Ukrainian sovereign airspace. Current orbital mechanics allow Rassvet satellites to provide temporary data links for windows of approximately 30 to 40 minutes as individual spacecraft transit overhead.
However, Beskrestnov estimated that continuous, 24-hour satellite connectivity over Ukrainian territory could materialize within approximately six months as additional orbital planes are populated.
In early October, Russian commercial satellite developer “Bureau 1440” showcased three operational user terminals engineered for the Rassvet architecture. Defense analysts assess that these compact transceivers could be integrated into the fuselages of long-range loitering munitions and cruise platforms to maintain persistent data uplinks.
Ukrainian defense planners and technical services are formulating countermeasures, including international sanctions targeting component supply chains.
Beskrestnov emphasized that technical countermeasures face significant hurdles because domestic teams must engineer protective systems against an orbital network that is not yet fully active, whereas Russian specialists previously calibrated jamming techniques against an established, functioning Starlink network.
“When Russia begins using it for strikes against our infrastructure, we must already have developed defensive means, manufactured them in volume, and deployed them,” the presidential adviser stressed.
The warnings from Beskrestnov reinforce concerns voiced earlier in the week by former Ukrainian intelligence officials regarding Moscow’s pursuit of a sovereign low-orbit communications backbone.
Major General Ilya Pavlenko, who served as deputy chief of the Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate ( HUR ) from 2015 to 2020, said that Moscow’s low-orbit network constitutes a direct conventional and hybrid threat to European stability .
Pavlenko noted that compact Rassvet terminals integrated into turbojet drones – especially those manufactured in subterranean production sites – could theoretically enable long-range precision strikes deep into Western Europe managed remotely from command centers in Moscow.
Developed by Bureau 1440, the Rassvet broadband constellation is projected to operate at an altitude of approximately 800 kilometers (497 miles), delivering theoretical throughput rates of up to 1 Gbps with signal latency around 70 milliseconds using 5G non-terrestrial network protocols and inter-satellite laser cross-links.
Lower orbital trials near 500 kilometers offer potential latency reductions down to 30 milliseconds, drastically compressing guidance response loops.
Russia executed two orbital launches carrying 16 Rassvet-3 satellites each in 2026 aboard Soyuz-2.1b carrier rockets from the Plesetsk cosmodrome.
While technical anomalies affected several payloads – including one satellite de-orbiting prematurely and others failing to attain designated altitudes – Moscow has outlined plans to deploy 292 spacecraft by 2027 and expand the constellation to 924 units by 2035.
Ukrainian diplomacy has actively targeted the network’s legal operating parameters. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed that Kyiv petitioned the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) to formally exclude Ukraine’s sovereign territory from Rassvet’s designated service footprint, arguing the platform is being built exclusively to coordinate military aggression.
Concurrently, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Beijing is assisting Moscow’s satellite initiatives , stating that Chinese entities are collaborating on orbital communications systems similar to Starlink to accelerate Russia’s technological parity on the battlefield.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Two armed robbers jailed 40 years with hard labour in Bekwai
body: The Bekwai Circuit Court has sentenced two men to 20 years’ imprisonment each with hard labour for robbing a motorbike at Edwenase, near Jacobu, in the Amansie Central District of the Ashanti Region. The convicts, 23-year-old galamsey operator Emmanuel Adams and 22-year-old Okada rider Vincent Aidoo, alias Kakai, were sentenced by the court presided over by His Honour Isaac Appiatu. Speaking to Adom News correspondent Isaac K. Normanyo at the court, the Ashanti South Regional Police Command Court Officer and Acting Public Affairs Officer, ASP Lloyd Baidoo, said the two committed the robbery on October 4, 2026, within the jurisdiction of the Bekwai Circuit Court. ASP Baidoo said the sentences amounted to a total of 40 years’ imprisonment with hard labour, with each convict serving 20 years. He cautioned the youth against engaging in robbery and other criminal activities, warning that anyone arrested for such offences would be prosecuted and dealt with according to law.

title: I’ve paid over N7bn as compensation to property owners — Uba Sani
body: Governor Uba Sani has disclosed that his administration has been paying compensation to property owners whose structures were affected by ongoing road constructions in the last three and half years. The Governor disclosed that Kaduna State Government has compensated approximately 4,865 households at a cost of about ₦7 billion across the three senatorial zones since he assumed office. He made this known at the flagging off of property compensation payment to 865 households, amounting to approximately N2 billion, for the construction of Zaria, Giwa, Shika township roads on Saturday. In his address at the event, Governor Uba Sani pointed out that ‘’since taking office on May 29, 2023, we have remained guided by the conviction that development must advance human dignity.’’ ‘Operate Within The Law’, SSG Counsels Kaduna Governing Boards Kaduna To Establish Post Basic Nursing College In Rigasa ‘’Infrastructure gives physical expression to progress, but the fairness with which it is delivered determines whether citizens experience government as a source of reassurance and opportunity,’’ he added. According to him, the reconstruction ‘’ of 11 township roads within Zaria and Sabon Gari Local Government Areas, alongside the Giwa and Shika township roads, reflects our determination to improve connectivity and expand economic activity.’’ ‘’These investments will ease movement, support commerce and bring communities closer to schools, healthcare and other essential services. Their enduring value will be measured by the opportunities they create and the quality of life they help secure,’’ he said. The Governor however recalled that as project progressed, homes, businesses and public utilities were identified within the designated rights-of-way. ‘’We therefore recognised that proceeding responsibly required us to address the human consequences of construction with the same seriousness applied to its engineering requirements,’’ he argued. Speaking at the event which held at Waziri Lawal Primary School, Angwan Iya in Zaria city, the Governor said that ‘’today, we commence the distribution of compensation cheques amounting to approximately ₦2 billion.’’ ‘’These payments are intended to support affected families as they relocate, rebuild and reorganise their livelihoods. ‘’Compensation fulfils an obligation owed to citizens whose property is required for public development. Its purpose is to ensure that the benefits of improved infrastructure are not secured through avoidable hardship for those directly affected,’’ he argued. Governor Uba Sani commended the owners of the 865 affected households across Babban Dodo to Kofar Kuyan Bana, Rimin Tsiwa to Kofar Gayan, Tudun Wada, Giwa Township and Shika township for their patience. ‘’We understand that relocation involves uncertainty, expense and the disruption of familiar surroundings. Your willingness to engage constructively has helped us pursue these projects with greater understanding of their impact on your lives,’’ he added. The Governor who also commended the surveyors, valuers, engineers and community representatives whose diligence supported the assessment process, also directed relevant utility agencies to expedite the safe relocation of water, electricity and telecommunications infrastructure.

title: Alberta separation referendum ‘not very likely’ new poll shows
body:
Less than one-quarter of Albertans support proceeding to a binding vote on separation, but support for the other nine questions on Monday’s referendum may be higher, a new survey shows.
An Ipsos poll conducted exclusively for Global News suggests seven in 10 Albertans say they plan to vote for Alberta to remain a province of Canada in the upcoming referendum, holding steady from previous polling conducted in September.
The proportion of voters who said they would vote for Alberta to begin the legal process of holding a binding referendum vote on separation increased three percentage points from September to 23 per cent.
That support is highest among men (27 per cent), those aged 35 to 54 (27 per cent) and those living outside Calgary and Edmonton (29 per cent).
“We’re seeing only about a quarter of people in Alberta saying they give support for this, but there’s a fair amount of diversity in the opinions among the people that we interviewed depending on where they lived and what their demographic background is,” Darrell Bricker, chairman of Ipsos Canada, told Global News.
Ipsos conducted online interviews with 801 Albertans between Oct. 13 and 16.
Only five per cent of voters remain undecided and two per cent say they will not vote, but Bricker said even if all of those respondents ultimately voted yes on referendum day, it would not be enough to trigger a separation vote.
“Whether or not it is only a quarter of the population that decide that they’re going to vote yes. Still not a small number. That’s a pretty big number,” Bricker said.
Premier Danielle Smith has said that if voting goes the way polling suggests, she expects everyone to accept it and move on . Leaders of the independence movement contest that.
But the premier has also asked Albertans to vote yes to the first nine questions, saying it would give her more leverage to negotiate for the province with the federal government.
“What we’re seeing is that the status quo relationship with the rest of the country is not something that’s particularly popular in Alberta at the moment,” Bricker said. “They don’t see the solution to that status quo situation as being separating from the country. But I expect that some of those other questions might get themselves majorities on election night.”
The first nine questions are related to immigration and the constitution .
A previous poll conducted for Global News in September found a strong majority (76 per cent) of Albertans were aware there were several questions in the upcoming referendum. Eighty-one per cent of Albertans said they planned to vote in the referendum with 62 per cent saying they will vote on all 10 questions.
Global News will have in-depth team coverage on both broadcast and streaming online.
Anchors Dallas Flexhaug and Carole Anne Devaney will be joined by veteran political reporter and Ottawa bureau chief David Akin for results analysis, along with insights from a political panel hosted by anchor Blake Lough, and reporters on the ground.
From 8 p.m. MT to midnight, our Decision Alberta Referendum 2026 coverage will air on Globalnews.ca, as well as on YouTube and our Global TV app that is available on streaming services Prime Video, Apple TV, Roku, and select smart TVs.
Starting at 9 p.m., the special will also begin airing live on all Global News stations in Alberta.
The precision of Ipsos polls containing online data is measured using a credibility interval. In this case, the overall poll of 801 Albertans is accurate to within +/- 4.2 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, had all adult Alberta residents been polled. The credibility interval will be wider among subsets of the population. All sample surveys and polls may be subject to other sources of error, including, but not limited to coverage error, and measurement error.
– With files from Global News’ Jace Maki and Karen Bartko

title: COMMENTARY: On immigration, Danielle Smith is closer to Canadians than Mark Carney
body:
On Monday, Albertans will vote in a province-wide referendum on a series of questions about the province’s future, and the question drawing the most attention is whether to hold a second referendum on separation; Ipsos’ current polling suggests Albertans will reject that possibility, with only 23 per cent saying they will vote to trigger the second vote and 70 per cent saying they will vote to stay part of Canada . But the outcome on nine other themes – immigration, federal programs and greater provincial autonomy – is far less certain.
Looking only at the immigration-related questions, Ipsos polling conducted in September found that a majority of Albertans supported giving their province greater control over immigration (65 per cent) and denying access to federally funded programs to people who do not have legal status in Canada (59 per cent). In our polling, we tested support for the concept, not the actual referendum question, so the results reflect how Albertans feel about these issues in general.
Most interestingly, however, Albertans aren’t the only ones who feel this way. In fact, Canadians outside Alberta are more likely to support these proposals than Albertans.
As it stands, 74 per cent of Canadians outside of Alberta supported giving their province more control over immigration, and 67 per cent supported denying access to federal programs to those who do not have legal status. This suggests that Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has captured the public mood of both Albertans and the broader population. A national debate on immigration will likely follow, especially if the Alberta referendum delivers majority support for some of these policy proposals.
Indeed, former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney, an avowed federalist and one of the loudest voices for the “no” side on the separation question, is calling for such a debate, and there is increasing evidence that Canada’s consensus on immigration is becoming a ballot box issue .
This could put Alberta’s government at odds with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government.
The federal immigration minister recently signalled that Canada plans to open its immigration targets to allow more immigrants, despite housing affordability remaining a concern. Other concerns remain, as polls consistently show that affordability is a major issue. And Alberta is now proposing to wrest control over immigration from the federal government and create two classes of social support – one for those without status, and one for those with it. Our poll suggests Canadians agree with both propositions.
Overall, people are thinking about how we should approach immigration – and the costs associated with it – amid a housing and affordability crisis. For her part, Smith has urged Albertans to vote “yes to the nine,” arguing that immigration costs are prohibitively expensive, while Carney has called on Albertans to vote no. While they are on the same side on Alberta’s future in Canada, they differ on how to approach immigration, despite finding common ground on issues such as pipelines and supporting the growth of Alberta’s energy industry.
Remarkably, especially for a Liberal prime minister in Alberta, Albertans view Carney most favourably, while they view Smith least favourably. On immigration and provincial rights, though, Smith appears to share most Canadians’ view, not Carney.
Whatever happens tomorrow, the Alberta referendum will shake up Canada. Alberta separatists have made it clear they will not let the issue go and will treat the “stay or leave” vote’s result as a permanent decision on their project, so that issue is unlikely to go away quickly, no matter the result. The debate over Alberta’s future within the federation has obscured how it might operate if it decides to remain.
If Smith wins a majority on some or all of the “other nine” questions, we might expect her to believe she has a mandate from the population to act. She may try to work with other premiers to raise these issues with the federal government and obtain more direct control over immigration and provincial rights from Carney.
She will have an ally in Quebec premier-elect Paul St.-Pierre Plamondon, who has pledged to use the early days of his premiership as leader of an overtly separatist party to advance provincial interests, having deferred a referendum on separation until when President Trump leaves office.
During the recent Quebec provincial campaign, the incoming premier also promised to cut the number of immigrants being allowed into the province, seeking even more powers than what Quebec already enjoys through a 35-year-old agreement giving Quebec more control on immigration than most provinces have. These are powers Smith is seeking for Alberta as well.
Smith, too, has reason to pick a fight with Ottawa. Some members of her own party feel she hasn’t gone far enough on separation. They are opposing her vow to not revisit the issue if Monday ends with a vote for the status quo, and some separatist supporters vowing to oust her at the upcoming leadership review. She has campaigned fiercely for a strong Alberta within a united Canada and said she voted “no” on that question. But she has voted “yes” to the other nine. If the separation question was designed to appease her base, the other nine may reveal her true ambitions: to secure more control for Alberta over immigration, control costs, and ensure that only those legally allowed in Alberta receive taxpayer-funded services.
The results on those questions, not only for Albertans but for all Canadians and far more than Alberta’s future in Canada as a province, may be the most consequential issues to emerge from tomorrow’s election, and the ones that will shape debate across Canada for the next year and beyond.

title: Stun grenades, water cannon deployed to disperse haredi protesters blocking Highway 4 near Yavne
body: Israel Police used stun grenades and deployed a water cannon to disperse haredi (ultra-Orthodox) protesters from the extremist Jerusalem Faction (Peleg Yerushalmi) who blocked Highway 4 in both directions near Yavne Interchange on Sunday morning, Israeli media reported.The highway was reopened to traffic after about two hours of protests, which were sparked by the arrests of two IDF draft evaders over the weekend.Approximately 40 to 50 protesters unexpectedly blocked the highway during the morning rush hour, despite the demonstration being publicly scheduled to begin at 4:00 p.m., police said.The sudden blockade brought traffic to a standstill in both directions, disrupting the morning commute for drivers traveling to work.Confrontations broke out between protesters and motorists caught in the blockade, with some drivers clashing with demonstrators after they could not continue their journeys.חרדים קיצונים מהפלג הירושלמי חסמו הבוקר בהפתעה את מחלף גן יבנה במחאה על מעצרי העריקים. חלקם התעמתו עם אזרחים אחרים במקום | תיעוד @daniel_grovais https://t.co/w2mCgsASHu— כאן חדשות (@kann_news) October 18, 2026Police declared the demonstration illegal and said officers were working to "reopen the road and restore order."Authorities urged motorists to avoid the area and use alternative routes, advising drivers to consult navigation apps for updated traffic information and follow instructions from police officers stationed at the scene.המשטרה מודיעה שכביש 4 נחסם לתנועה בשני הכיוונים באזור מחלף יבנה עקב הפגנת החרדים הקיצוניים @eli_hirschmann | https://t.co/3YtKSfOSG9 https://t.co/2pOXX6zTOx— החדשות - N12 (@N12News) October 18, 2026Israel authorities ramp up arrests for draft evadersPolice emphasized that while they recognize the right to protest, they would not tolerate public disorder, interference with freedom of movement, or conduct that could endanger public safety.In recent months, the Israeli security establishment has ramped up arrests of haredi draft evaders, ultra-Orthodox men who refuse mandatory IDF service on religious grounds despite not having received official exemptions from the military.In response to the arrests, haredi groups have organized multiple protests throughout Jerusalem and central Israel, with demonstrations frequently disrupting traffic and resulting in confrontations with police.The issue of haredi military enlistment has also become a central point of contention in the 2026 Knesset election campaigns, as political parties debate the enforcement of military service requirements and exemptions for yeshiva students.Maya Zanger-Shamir contributed to this report.

title: F-35A is not enough. Infrastructure as the bottleneck of nuclear sharing
body:
F-35A squadrons are not in themselves a guarantee of participation in NS, because although in Poland we also have the previous DCA (Dual-Capable Aircraft) model, the F-16, Polish participation in NS is still shrouded in fog. This is because in Poland, politics has outpaced planning.
Let’s start with what we already have. Since May, the first Polish F-35As have been stationed at the 32nd Tactical Air Base in Łask. Eight of the 32 ordered had arrived by October, and the type itself has been certified to carry B61-12 bombs since 2023. Then there is politics: on 27 August, Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski announced that the government had secured the possibility of joining the DCA programme, which he called a first step towards nuclear sharing, and a month earlier, the head of the National Security Bureau (BBN), back from Washington, spoke of great openness on the American side.
The Husarz is not the only Polish candidate, by the way. The B61-12 has also been integrated with the F-16, including the C/D version, and it was precisely these aircraft that carried out the nuclear mission in Belgium and the Netherlands for years. We have 47 Block 52+ jets, which are being upgraded to the F-16V standard. The thing is, the type’s compatibility with the bomb does not make it a carrier yet, because you need the right equipment and the certification of the aircraft, the crews and the whole unit. So it turns out we potentially have two carriers and ground infrastructure for neither of them.
This is where the problem with how we talk about the issue arises. In the public debate, it goes like this: there is an aircraft, there is consent, the rest is a formality. But that is not true. The aircraft, although expensive, is actually the easiest part of the whole puzzle, because you buy it in a standard configuration, and adapting it comes down to wiring, software and certification. Much harder is what has to be built on the ground and what cannot be bought off the shelf.
To understand what we are missing, it is enough to look at the countries that have been flying this mission for years. Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Italy and Turkey host around a hundred American bombs at their bases, and none of them sits in an ordinary warehouse. The weapons rest in underground vaults of the WS3 system (Weapons Storage and Security System), built into the floors of hardened aircraft shelters. This means the bomb does not leave the protected facility until the moment it is loaded onto the aircraft. There are no such vaults in Poland, nor in the Baltic states.
The vault is only the beginning of the list. Custody of the weapons lies exclusively with the Americans, and at host-nation bases, this is the job of the Munitions Support Squadrons (MUNSS), usually 125–150 personnel strong. They are responsible for receiving, storing, maintaining and protecting the bombs until an authorised order to release them is received. Such a unit will not fit into a container by the fence, because it needs its own facilities, a separate security zone, secure communications with the American and allied command systems, and facilities for the technical maintenance of the weapons. The host has plenty to do as well: security forces, trained and certified crews, weapons personnel and recurring inspections; whoever fails an inspection has the capability suspended.
Someone will say that Łask already has American certification. That is true, because in March the base received certification of its infrastructure for F-35 operations, covering hangars, technical facilities and security systems. It is a significant achievement, but it concerns protecting the aircraft’s secrets, not nuclear weapons. These are two separate sets of requirements and one cannot replace the other.
How long it takes to build such infrastructure is best seen in examples from Western Europe. The first is RAF Lakenheath in Britain, from which American bombs were withdrawn in the first decade of this century. The base had 33 vaults from the 1990s, which were mothballed but still existed. The decision to restore the mission was most likely taken in 2021; the first trace appeared in 2022 in the budget documents of the NATO Security Investment Programme (NSIP), and by February 2025, 22 of the 33 shelters had been modernised. So even where the infrastructure was in place and the base is used by the US Air Force, the reactivation alone took several years.
The second example is Büchel in Germany, which has hosted American weapons for decades. Adapting the base to the F-35 alone was supposed to cost 1.2 billion euros, and according to the German Defence Ministry, it will swallow around 2 billion, with the infrastructure due to be ready in 2027. Berlin, for its part, said from the start that complex American security requirements were among the sources of risk.
The conclusion for us is an uncomfortable one. If countries that have vaults, personnel, procedures and decades of practice need years and billions just to keep the capability, then what about Poland, which would be starting from scratch? For comparison, NATO’s last programme to modernise storage sites in Europe took thirteen years and cost 384 million dollars, and we are talking about facilities that were already standing.
What we hear about most often is an intermediate solution. William Alberque, a former senior NATO official, considers it more likely than permanent storage, and the idea is to certify the Polish F-35s and designate selected bases as Dispersed Operating Bases. The weapons would only reach them in a crisis or on the eve of war, and in peacetime there would be no warheads in Poland. This fits the line sketched out by Deputy Minister Zalewski, which is participation in the mission without a permanent stockpile.
The trouble is that a dispersal base without prepared infrastructure remains an entry in a planning document. To receive weapons within hours, you need to have in advance a place for their temporary storage that meets American standards, and on top of that, positions for the custodial personnel, communications, security forces and rehearsed procedures for receiving the shipment, loading and releasing the weapon. All of this has to pass certification in peacetime, because a crisis is not the moment for a first inspection.
Then there is survivability. Łask and Świdwin lie within range of Russian ballistic and cruise missiles stationed in the Kaliningrad Oblast and in Belarus, and flight time is counted in minutes. A base to which nuclear weapons are moved in a crisis becomes a first-priority target. Whether it will deter anyone at all therefore depends on things that seem far removed from the subject: layered air and missile defence, hardened shelters, rapid runway repair and the ability to disperse aircraft to other airfields. Without this, an adversary may conclude that the whole capability can be switched off with a single conventional strike. Instead of stabilising the situation, it invites pre-emptive action.
First, it is not Warsaw that sets the pace. Weapons storage infrastructure is funded by NATO through the NSIP, the standards are set by the United States, and the allies have to agree to expand the network of bases. We can lobby and push, but we will not build this on our own.
Second, a lot can be done with our own resources and there is no need to wait for anyone. These include air defence of the bases, shelters, physical protection, training of crews and ground personnel, and wider participation in the Steadfast Noon exercises. These are investments that will pay off regardless of what happens with nuclear sharing, because they raise the resilience of the air force in every scenario.
Third, it is worth changing how we measure progress. Whether things have really started moving is not shown by more declarations or more Husarz jets on the apron in Łask. It will be shown by line items in American and NATO budget documents, tenders for construction work at specific bases and the arrival in Poland of American personnel specialising in nuclear weapons handling. Until that happens, Polish participation in NS remains a story with no action behind it, and the Husarz jets in Łask are simply very good aircraft without a nuclear mission.

title: [Inside the Newsroom] China’s envoy: Sounds like a threat, walks like a threat
body: Since 2026, the Chinese embassy in Manila has made it normal to issue strong, sometimes incendiary, statements against Philippine agencies and officials, including the nationally-elected kind. It’s language that has teetered close to gutter-level, particularly when it’s the exchanges between its deputy spokesperson Guo Wei and Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, who speaks for the Philippine Coast Guard on the West Philippine Sea. Yet it was still quite surprising — even if it was arguably expected — for Beijing’s top diplomat in the Philippines, Ambassador Jing Quan , to say the Philippines “should feel fortunate” that China doesn’t use force in its maritime disputes. If it did, the veteran diplomat said, “we may easily win.” “But no, we will not choose to use force. We love peace,” he told reporters on October 15, on the sidelines of a forum. Jing went on to mention regions in the world — Gaza and Venezuela — where conflicts launched by Israel and the United States, respectively, have triggered instability in the region. The ambassador conveniently left out two other major conflicts in the world: the Israel and US war on Iran, and Russia’s war on Ukraine. The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), in a rare strongly-worded but terse statement, chastised Jing for his remarks. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is expected to summon the Chinese envoy for the second time in less than a year over the same remarks, which he characterized as a “threat.” The Chinese embassy has pushed back against the DFA through a statement and against Marcos through a vaguely-worded tweet (“Is this a threat?” to caption a longer clip of the chance interview with the media). In the five-minute interview, Jing goes on about the importance of dialogue in Asia, including within Southeast Asia, which is negotiating a South China Sea code with China. But the minutes preceding and succeeding that one line about the use of force doesn’t really take away from how out-of-pocket it was — to insist that Manila should be grateful that its superpower neighbor “loves” peace because, if it did not, it would handily win. Because the reality on the ground and at sea is that a “peace-loving” China can still inflict harm — economically and physically. Filipino personnel have been injured, to varying degrees, from the water cannons the China Coast Guard (CCG) uses to drive away maritime missions to key features in the West Philippine Sea. Literal blood has been shed by soldiers inadvertently injured during confrontations — a finger was severed in Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal in June 2024, and one soldier sustained a head injury just in July 2026. Earlier in October, the medical evacuation of a soldier with appendicitis took 10 hours because the CCG insisted on their way of doing things during the mission. Fisherfolk in Zambales, Palawan, and other fishing communities that have historically relied on the West Philippine Sea speak of dwindling catches or the lack of any opportunity to fish at all. During embeds in Navy warships on West Philippine Sea missions, I’ve come to almost expect the presence of a Chinese navy warship. I have to actively remind myself that while this has become the norm, it should not be accepted as such. Such is the “reset” that Marcos signalled and Filipino diplomats have aspired for since the beginning of 2026. The information ecosystem when it comes to discussions on the West Philippine Sea and the disputes between the Philippines and China is, no doubt, full of noise — many of it the manufactured kind that’s designed to obfuscate from the facts on hand. Information and influence operations want to wear down the Filipino soldier and civilian’s spirit to wanting to defend what is the Filipinos’ by spotlighting Chinese narratives: that resistance is futile, or that it’s a binary choice between war and peace. I sometimes find myself having to discern whether a statement from either the embassy or a Philippine government official ought to be highlighted and amplified. He-said-he-said and tits-for-tats are easy and fun to draw out, sure. But they don’t always help readers make sense of what’s going on between the two countries in terms of maritime, political, or diplomatic issues. Recently, journalism students interviewed me for a school project. At one point, they asked me: How do you sift through the noise in diplomacy when, in some cases, either side has their own truth that they want amplified? The answer can be simple, I told them. You go back to what international law, including the 2016 Arbitral Award, says. In reconstructing events that are not available for the public or even journalists to see, you talk to the widest range of sources, including those who could be adversarial to your personal beliefs. You probe, you ask — and then you second-guess yourself. Rinse, repeat. In conversations with sources, there have been worries that, in all the noise, advocates and experts — even the most earnest ones — are in danger of losing the plot. The burden then falls onto the bureaucrats, the credentialed experts, and journalists who’ve done their homework to sift through propaganda, spin, and political noise, and stay laser-focused on key truths: that Manila must defend its entitlements and claims in the West Philippine Sea while also trying to keep okay ties with a sometimes-renegade Beijing. For the military, that means keeping vigilant, especially with the 2028 presidential elections forthcoming, while still keeping itself free of partisan and electoral politicking. It means amping up its external defense posture, which, 15 years since the revised AFP modernization act, means focusing on logistics and supply chains. What good are new and shiny military toys when there’s little space to service them? We recently published a two-part report on the military’s modernization and defense self-reliance efforts. Because as we keep close track of both escalating rhetoric and confrontations in the West Philippine Sea, it’s important to keep an eye on how the Philippines’ maritime frontliners are preparing for any and all eventualities, including scenarios they would never wish on themselves. title: The Kila affair: Duty of care runs both ways, By Babafemi A. Badejo
body:
This is where I part company with the idea of a “soft landing”. I am yet to see what the elements of such a landing would be, or with whom it would be negotiated. Is it with the newspaper, so that it stops publishing? Is it with the anti-corruption agency, so that it stops asking? Neither is ours to give away.
For a few weeks now, one subject has competed with fuel prices, insecurity and the latest in the shifting alliances of thieves a.k.a political parties for the attention of Nigerians. It is the case of Anthony Kila, the television regular and reportedly suspended pro-chancellor of Michael and Cecilia Ibru University, whom PREMIUM TIMES has reported to be a professor that no recognised university ever made.
The matter raises questions that go well beyond one man. How should a society treat a person at the centre of such a storm? Should a “soft landing” be found for him? Is he simply an easy target, and who will be next?
These are fair questions, and they deserve a considered answer. Mine is simple enough. We must look after the man. We must not look away from the matter.
Let me first set out what we are talking about, for the benefit of anyone who has been away from Nigeria or from the internet.
On 3 October, PREMIUM TIMES published an investigation reporting that it could find no recognised academic institution that had conferred the rank of professor on Mr Kila, who has for years been introduced on television and in newspapers as a “Jean Monnet Professor of Strategy and Development.” A week later, on 10 October, the paper went further. Its second investigation alleged that the problem was not only the professorship but the academic qualifications claimed by Mr Kila, from the first degree to the doctorate.
Mr Kila has not kept quiet. He has reportedly insisted that he is a professor, that he stands by his title, and that “the facts and documentation will speak for themselves”. He has also said that he has instructed his lawyers to review the publication. That is his right. In the meantime, the university whose governing council he chaired has suspended him, and the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) is reported to have set up a team to look into the matter.
I must say this plainly: Mr Kila remains innocent until proven otherwise. Nothing here has been tested in a court of law. But we are also well past the stage of “if.” Specific allegations, published in considerable detail, are on the ground. They will not go away because some of us find them uncomfortable.
The case of Jason Arday is fresh in the mind, and it should be. Arday, celebrated in 2023 as the youngest black professor in the history of the University of Cambridge, resigned on 5 August after allegations of plagiarism and questions about parts of his biography. In his resignation statement, he said that relentless accusations, speculations, and public commentary had taken a profound toll on him and those he loved. Nine days later, he was found dead at the age of 41.
Nobody should wish that sort of ending on anybody. I certainly do not wish it on Anthony Kila. We like to think of ourselves as a tough people, but shame is a heavy load, and none of us knows the weight that another person can carry.
So, Nigeria must prevent an Arday outcome. Mr Kila’s family and friends owe him a duty of care. They should stay close, support him and, where necessary, get him professional help. If the State eventually invites him for questioning, the State will owe him that duty too. And the rest of us can discuss the issue without making sport of a man in trouble. Ridicule is not accountability.
Still, the two cases are not the same, and we should not pretend that they are. Arday was a black man at the top of a British system in which blacks are about one per cent of the professoriate. Many people, including the Chancellor of Cambridge, who spoke of a “racist feeding frenzy”, saw the avalanche of coverage as race-based witch-hunting. Others reject that reading. It is an argument for Britain to settle. Nothing of the sort arises here. This is a Nigerian newspaper asking a Nigerian about titles used in Nigeria. Nor are the allegations alike. Arday held a chair that a real university conferred on him, and the questions concerned his thesis and parts of his biography. With Mr Kila, the question is whether the titles exist at all. What the two cases share is the human being at the centre.
So, Nigeria must prevent an Arday outcome. Mr Kila’s family and friends owe him a duty of care. They should stay close, support him and, where necessary, get him professional help. If the State eventually invites him for questioning, the State will owe him that duty too. And the rest of us can discuss the issue without making sport of a man in trouble. Ridicule is not accountability.
I would add one thing. Mr Kila is reported to be heading to court to seek civil remedies. I am glad of it. It is a creditable path, and one that Arday did not take. A man who is preparing his case is a man who is still standing. If his friends want to help him, they can contribute to his legal fees.
But the Duty of Care is Not a One-way Street
This is where I part company with the idea of a “soft landing”. I am yet to see what the elements of such a landing would be, or with whom it would be negotiated. Is it with the newspaper, so that it stops publishing? Is it with the anti-corruption agency, so that it stops asking? Neither is ours to give away.
PREMIUM TIMES has done its part and should continue to do it. If there are errors in its reports, they should be corrected, for the sake of accuracy and posterity. If it has more to publish, I, for one, would not discourage its editors. Mercy to the man does not require silence about the matter.
More importantly, Mr Kila also owes something. He owes it to the students and parents of a university whose council he chaired. He owes it to the television audiences who took his analysis more seriously, given the title that came before his name. He owes it to those of us who paid attention to his views.
I count myself among them. He and I were on the same side, over Zoom, in an association that campaigned for the restructuring of Nigeria. He was its general secretary until it packed up. I listened to him with respect.
A friend of his has publicly asked him to come clean and answer the questions raised. This is good advice from a good friend. He is, of course, free to stay quiet and leave everything to his lawyers.
And since this is Nigeria, let me say the obvious. We have a long history of injunctions: against further publication, against investigation, even against an invitation by the police. It would be a pity if this case took that familiar road. A court is a place to prove one’s claim, not to prevent the question.
There are several familiar arguments for looking the other way in a case like this. He is brilliant and prolific, so he measures up to the title anyway. We live in a post-certificate world. He is not in public service, so why the hullabaloo? He is only being hounded because of his outspoken public commentary.
None of these persuade me. If a man is brilliant, he does not need a borrowed robe. If certificates no longer matter, nobody should need to claim one. And one does not have to be on the government payroll to hold a position of public trust.
So here is where I stand. Let his family and friends hold him close. Let PREMIUM TIMES finish its work and correct whatever it got wrong. Let the ICPC do its job without fear or favour. Let our universities look inward and verify before they certify or appoint. Let Mr Kila have his day in court, with every presumption in his favour. And let him, in the meantime, show Nigerians the documents he says will speak for themselves.
I have long defined corruption as the betrayal of public trust. That goes beyond being a public official. My 3X3X3 framework looks for corruption, and for the means of curbing it, across the three arms of government, the three tiers of government and the three sectors of society: public, private and social. The public sector is primus inter pares , the first among equals, because it makes and enforces the rules for the rest. But the private and social sectors hold public trust too. A pro-chancellor presides over the council of a university, and parents hand over their children on the strength of what that university says about itself. A commentator introduced to the nation as a professor is trusted by viewers on the strength of that title.
If the alleged conduct were established, we would be talking about obtaining by false pretences, false swearing and, where an oath was involved, perjury. Those are not private matters. Too often, our security agencies do not bat an eyelid, as with so much corruption by the high and mighty, including in our tertiary institutions. That is why I welcome and appreciate the involvement of the ICPC team in this case. The Commission deserves our encouragement to follow the evidence wherever it leads, fairly and to a conclusion.
Then comes the cleverest argument of all, the one the Yoruba capture in the proverb about holding on to the one person you are able to catch. Is Kila simply an easy target? Who is next?
My answer is that he is not the first, and he will not be the last. I was an undergraduate at the University of Lagos when the Ọwọshọ scandal broke. It swept many students out of that university. The ICPC has prosecuted cases of fake certificates and unearned titles before. The Ministry of Education is currently trying to stop people from parading honorary degrees, as if they had earned them. If the PREMIUM TIMES reports are upheld, what is alleged here would be more serious than that.
This is why I must also turn to the universities themselves. A newspaper should not be the first body to check a certificate that has already passed through a registry, an appointments committee and a governing council. Nigerian universities, public and private, need to be self-critical. They should thoroughly investigate every credential presented to them before they certify anyone or appoint anyone, whether as a student, a lecturer, a professor or a pro-chancellor. That means writing to the awarding institution, confirming that it exists and is recognised, and keeping the reply in a file. A fine curriculum vitae and a familiar face on television are not enough. Where a false claim has passed through the gate, the gatekeepers also have questions to answer.
We must resist the very Nigerian habit in which a person accused of stealing dares society to first catch every other thief before attending to his case. No country cleans its house that way. We handle each case as it arises, to the best of our individual and collective capacities.
Will one case transform Nigeria? I doubt it. People still present forged results for university admission, decades after the scandal of my student days. But to anyone asking who is next, I say: help to find out. If you know of a similar case, blow the whistle to PREMIUM TIMES , SaharaReporters , the ICPC or anyone else who will do the digging.
We spend a great deal of time lamenting the ills of our dear native land. I often ask whatever became of our Ọmọluabi values. It is true that Ọmọluabi also calls for wisdom in handling human misconduct. Wisdom is always necessary. It means weighing the different sides of an issue against a picture of the society we want to live in.
But wisdom is not the same thing as looking away. The foremost attribute of the Ọmọluabi is integrity. It is the olu-iwa, the head of all characters. To live in society is to be accountable to it. That civic-mindedness is what our brothers and sisters further south call Ubuntu, and it sits comfortably inside Ọmọluabi. A compassion that asks us to drop integrity is not Ọmọluabi.
So here is where I stand. Let his family and friends hold him close. Let PREMIUM TIMES finish its work and correct whatever it got wrong. Let the ICPC do its job without fear or favour. Let our universities look inward and verify before they certify or appoint. Let Mr Kila have his day in court, with every presumption in his favour. And let him, in the meantime, show Nigerians the documents he says will speak for themselves.
If he is vindicated, some of us will owe him an apology, and I will offer mine without hesitation. If he is not, my hope is that this episode becomes a lesson that every Nigerian parent teaches every Nigerian child: a lie may run for many years, but the truth catches up with it in one day.
Babafemi A Badejo is a former Deputy Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Somalia and a former Professor of Political Science and International Relations. He is the author of the best-selling Raila Odinga: An Enigma in Kenyan Politics and of Somalia Just Before Al-Shabaab: Why Peace Was Elusive. He is a recipient of the Mandela Lifetime Achievement Award of the Annual Africa Conference at the University of Texas at Austin, the Medal of the Order of Timor-Leste, and Djibouti’s 27 Juin 1977 Order. He acknowledges the use of AI assistance in preparing this article.

title: Updating Iran defense capabilities changed enemy calculations
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – Iran’s newly-appointed Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi said that updating the defensive capabilities and potentials of the country have altered the enemies’ calculations, especially after 12-day war imposed on Iran.
Speaking in an open session of the Iranian Parliament on Sunday, he emphasized, “Following the 12-day war waged by US and Zionist regime against Iran jointly, the defensive capabilities have been upgraded in such a way that they have altered the enemy’s assessments and calculations, and have created deep doubt among the enemies regarding the continuation of the war.
In the beginning of speech, the newly-elected defense minister commemorated the name and memory of founding father of the Islamic Revolution Imam Khomeini (RA), martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, all martyrs of the Islamic Revolution, martyred defense ministers, especially former Iran’s Minister of Defense Major General Aziz Nasirzadeh.
“We have taken all necessary measures to counter the “Mother of All Bombs” and are confident in our preparations. We are carrying out our duties with complete confidence,” the defense minister emphasized.
Following his approval by parliament, Akhlaghi said the enemy is facing a strategic deadlock because “changes are underway in the nature of threats, the logic of military power, the technological environment and the regional order.”
Iran’s defensive strength depended not only on its operational capabilities but also on its understanding of the strategic environment, He added.
“Since the 12-day war, our defense capabilities have been upgraded and modernized in ways that have changed the enemy’s assessments and calculations,” he noted.
Lashing out at US President Donald Trump for using the sacred term 'mother' for a bomb to threaten Iran, he noted, “If he drops a bomb, he should consider how many of his troops might have to be carried out in body bags. If he follows through on his threats, he will have to face the dire consequences.”
Pointing to the nature of recent conflicts, he stated that modern warfare is "hybrid" in nature—integrating military engagement with economic sanctions and restrictions, cyber warfare, supply chain disruption, information warfare, and the restriction of access to technology.
Consequently, effectively addressing these threats requires a comprehensive understanding of the environment and preparedness to counter the various dimensions of such warfare, he added.
In conclusion, he seized this opportunity to thank President Pezeshkian for trusting him and unwavering support of high-ranking military officials in nominating him for the responsibility of guiding the Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics.
Earlier on Sunday, Iranian lawmakers voted for Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi to appoint him as the Minister of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in an open session on Sunday, after reviewing his plans and qualifications.
He succeeded Major General Aziz Nasirzadeh, the previous defense minister, who was martyred during criminal attacks by the United States and the Zionist regime on February 28.

title: Iran names new defence minister as he warns US over ‘Mother of All Bombs’
body: Iran’s parliament has approved Mehrdad Ketabchi as Defence Minister, the government said. Mr Ketabchi gave Washington a warning that Tehran was prepared to respond to a possible US attack involving the “Mother of All Bombs”. He received 237 votes in favour and 15 against, with no abstentions, following a review of his credentials and proposed programme, said a government statement posted on X. President Masoud Pezeshkian nominated Mr Ketabchi on October 5 and submitted his name to parliament for a vote of confidence. He replaces Brig Gen Aziz Nasirzadeh, who was killed in a US-Israeli air strike at the start of the war in February. Mr Pezeshkian subsequently appointed Brig Gen Majid Ebn Al Reza as caretaker defence minister. Mr Ketabchi is a veteran defence industry official who has headed Iran’s Aerospace Industries Organisation and Defence Industries Organisation, overseeing sectors involved in missile technology and weapons production. The US and UN have imposed sanctions against Mr Ketabchi over his alleged involvement in Iran’s ballistic missile programme. The UN listed him in 2007 in connection with the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, which develops and produces solid-propellant ballistic missiles. In presenting his plans to parliament, Mr Ketabchi pledged to restructure the ministry, accelerate defence technology development and upgrade Iran’s military capabilities. Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of an online parliamentary session on Sunday, he said Iran had taken the necessary measures to counter a possible US attack involving the “Mother of All Bombs”, the semi-official Isna news agency reported. “We have taken the necessary measures for this scenario, and we are at ease. We proceed with our work with full confidence,” he was quoted as saying. Addressing US President Donald Trump , Mr Ketabchi said Washington should focus on ensuring the safe withdrawal of its forces from the region. “He ought to be thinking about how to get his forces out of our region safely. If he drops a single bomb, he will have to consider how many of his troops will end up being carried out of the region in a horizontal position,” he said, in an apparent reference to US military casualties. He said the prospect of retaliation had so far deterred Washington from launching an attack. “Rest assured; it is precisely this fact that has deterred the US from taking such an action thus far,” he said. “Of course, should they move from mere rhetoric to actual threats, they will certainly see the consequences.” CNN reported this week that the US had developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, also known as the Mother of All Bombs, against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if Mr Trump orders renewed combat operations. The weapon is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. Separately, Iranian Army deputy executive co-ordinator Brig Gen Alireza Sheikh said the military’s equipment had been upgraded and its forces were ready to respond to any threat. Speaking on Sunday in response to threats involving the possible use of the bomb against Iran, he said, “The fathers of bombs are the Iranian people, and they can certainly have a more destructive impact than what the enemy expects on its thoughts, psychology, mindset, and strategies.”

title: Sudan’s humanitarian crisis deepens as millions face displacement and aid funding shortages
body: Millions of Sudanese displaced by the country’s war are struggling to rebuild their lives amid worsening humanitarian conditions and a severe shortfall in aid funding, as politicians urge greater international pressure to end the conflict. Mohamed Abdel Hakam, a leader of the Sumoud alliance, which advocates civilian rule in Sudan, described the crisis as one of the world’s largest humanitarian disasters and called for greater attention to the plight of millions seeking safety and a return to normal life. “I believe the catastrophe unfolding in Sudan, which is weighing on millions of Sudanese, is the largest humanitarian disaster in the world at this time,” he told Sky News Arabia. He said the crisis had been described by UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres and other officials of the world body as a “forgotten crisis”, leaving millions struggling to live with dignity amid displacement, harsh conditions in shelters and an uncertain future. “Millions of Sudanese are now living in a state of loss and uncertainty. They want nothing more than to return safely to their homes and places of residence and have normal life restored after enduring immense hardship as a result of this brutal war,” he said. Dr Salah Al Amin, a Sudanese expert in humanitarian affairs, said millions of people had been displaced within Sudan or fled abroad as refugees, many of whom were facing additional hardship because of funding shortages. “Funding has fallen this year compared with previous years, to the point that there is a shortfall of more than 47 per cent in the funding that should reach these refugees,” he told Sky News Arabia. He said international organisations assisting refugees were also struggling financially. “Even Unicef and the UN refugee agency, which is responsible for refugees around the world, are complaining about funding problems, to the extent that many employees who were working to provide services to refugees have been laid off,” he said. The conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces, led by Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan , and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has devastated the country of 50 million people and battered its economy. International efforts aimed at ending the war have struggled to secure a lasting ceasefire. The war, now well into its fourth year, has created one of ​the world's worst humanitarian crises, displacing about 14 million people. Calls for pressure to end the war Mohamed Al Faky, a former civilian member of Sudan’s ruling Sovereignty Council, urged the international community to maintain pressure on army chief Gen Al Burhan to end the war, accusing him of breaking promises and derailing peace initiatives. “This man is, of course, a professional liar and has derailed a number of initiatives,” Mr Al Faky said in an interview with Sky News Arabia. “He had promised regional countries and the United States in September 2024 that he would go to Geneva [for peace talks] but then backed out at the last minute,” he said. “Therefore, the pressure must continue, and the siege must continue. I believe the international community has finally seen through this man’s lies and is now exerting sustained pressure on him.” Mr Al Faky also criticised what he described as attempts by Gen Al Burhan to portray popular support through public appearances, including videos showing him playing cards with soldiers and mingling with crowds. “These are desperate attempts that can only come from a desperate political mind that does not understand what is happening in Sudan or recognise the suffering that Sudanese people are enduring in exile and inside the country,” he said. “It is a mentality that mocks the suffering of Sudanese people and the major issues they face, including displacement, hunger, and the loss of their land, property and memories.” Mr Al Faky said the videos had become a source of ridicule in Sudanese media and on social media. He challenged the army chief to demonstrate his support by organising a public rally rather than appearing unannounced at markets and celebrations. “If you have popular support, organise an event in your own name and deliver a speech in one of the major squares, whether Freedom Square or Martyrs’ Square. Invite people,” Mr Al Faky said. “But showing up uninvited at markets and celebrations is not a measure of popular support. These people are simply walking along the streets and visiting markets to meet their daily needs, only for this man to suddenly confront them.” Mr Al Faky also claimed that Gen Al Burhan’s reported ambition to become president lacked support within the military establishment and the Islamic Movement. He said the three remaining military members of the Sovereignty Council – Shams Al Din Kabbashi, Yasser Al Atta and Ibrahim Jaber – opposed the idea, as did the Islamic Movement, which he said believed Gen Al Burhan could not assume the presidency without an agreement. “No such agreement has been reached,” Mr Al Faky said.

title: 1 Killed, 5 Injured in Ukrainian Drone Attack on St. Petersburg, Governor Says
body:
