title: MoD inks $432-mn deals for IAF satellite and Navy torpedoes
body:
New Delhi, Oct 17. The Ministry of Defence has signed two contracts worth a combined ₹4,106 crore ($432 million) for an indigenous communication satellite for the Indian Air Force (IAF) and Varunastra heavyweight torpedoes for the Indian Navy, bolstering efforts to strengthen domestic defence manufacturing.



The agreements were signed in New Delhi on October 15 in the presence of A Anbarasu, Additional Secretary and Director General (Acquisition), Department of Defence.

Under the first contract, valued at ₹2,563 crore, New Space India Limited (NSIL), Bengaluru, will supply the GSAT-7C communication satellite. Designed, developed and manufactured in India, the satellite is expected to provide the IAF with secure, resilient and seamless communication capabilities, enhancing coordination among its assets and supporting operational effectiveness.

The second agreement, worth ₹1,543 crore, was signed with Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL), Hyderabad, for the procurement of Varunastra heavyweight torpedoes for the Indian Navy.

Developed indigenously by the Naval Science and Technological Laboratory (NSTL), Varunastra is a ship-launched anti-submarine weapon equipped with advanced manoeuvring capabilities. It is designed to engage enemy submarines at long ranges and is expected to strengthen the Navy’s anti-submarine warfare capabilities.

The two procurements reflect the government’s focus on developing indigenous defence technologies and expanding domestic manufacturing under its ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ (Self-reliant India) and ‘Make in India’ initiatives. They are also aimed at strengthening India’s capabilities in critical defence systems and reducing dependence on foreign suppliers.

title: Riyadh airport reopens: Which airlines are still cancelling flights to Saudi Arabia?
body: Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport reopened on Sunday, after it was closed because of attacks by the Houthi rebels in Yemen. However, many airlines have not yet lifted their suspension of flights to the Saudi capital and other destinations in the kingdom. Some carriers have extended cancellations into November and beyond, while others are preparing to resume services. The disruption comes amid wider regional uncertainty, which has already affected airlines’ Middle East operations . Here’s how major airlines have adjusted operations and when flights are expected to resume. Etihad Airways Etihad Airways has cancelled all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until Monday, October 19. Services to Dammam and Jeddah have also been affected, although flight listings show Dammam services and Jeddah flights EY601, EY602, EY603 and EY604 scheduled to operate on Sunday, October 18. Emirates Emirates services from Dubai to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam have been affected by cancellations and schedule changes. Google’s flight listings show six services between Dubai and Riyadh scheduled for October 20. These include outbound flights EK815, EK817 and EK819, along with return services EK816, EK818 and EK820. Flydubai The airline has cancelled flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Abha up to October 19. Air Arabia Air Arabia has cancelled services between Sharjah and several Saudi destinations including Riyadh, Abha, Dammam and Taif. No resumption date has been announced. Qatar Airways The airline has temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam. A resumption date has not yet been announced. Gulf Air Gulf Air has said flights after Sunday, October 18 are currently proceeding as scheduled, following its previously announced Riyadh cancellations. Oman Air Oman Air has announced that all flights to and from Riyadh are suspended until October 22. SalamAir The Omani low-cost airline has cancelled flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until October 31, citing regional security developments. Air France The French airline has extended its suspension of flights to and from Riyadh up to October 24. British Airways British Airways is scheduled to return with a limited service to Riyadh on November 3, operating one flight daily, according to previously announced plans. The airline discontinued flights to Jeddah in April as part of wider changes to its Middle East operations. Air India and Air India Express Air India and Air India Express have suspended flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam until October 24. Akasa Air The Indian low-cost airline has suspended flights to and from Riyadh until October 24 and Jeddah until October 21. Cathay Pacific The Hong Kong airline has extended its suspension of flights to Riyadh up to January 31, 2027. Pakistan International Airlines The airline announced a temporary suspension of flights to Riyadh on October 9, without setting out a resumption date. The Pakistan Airports Authority said at the time that its other Saudi services were continuing as usual. Delta Air Lines The US airline has postponed the launch of flights between Atlanta and Riyadh until March 2027. Services had been scheduled to begin on October 23. IndiGo The Indian airline has cancelled flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah up to October 24. Lufthansa The German airline has suspended flights to Riyadh until November 18, extending its previously announced October 16 deadline. The Lufthansa Group’s advisory also lists Dammam services as suspended through November 30. Eurowings, part of the group, is scheduled to resume flights to Jeddah on November 12. Malaysia Airlines Malaysia Airlines has announced that flights to and from Jeddah and Madinah will resume on October 18 after a safety review. KLM The Dutch airline has extended cancellations of all flights to Riyadh and Dammam up to October 31. Philippine Airlines The Philippine flag carrier has suspended Riyadh flights PR654 and PR655 until November 29, citing the security situation at King Khalid International Airport. Scoot The Singapore Airlines-owned low-cost carrier has cancelled flights between Singapore and Jeddah until December 2.

title: Europe can only cover gas deficit through supplies from Russia — deputy PM
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Europe will not be able to cover the gas deficit without Russian supplies, as the Strait of Hormuz is closed and the Qatari plant was shut down after attacks, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said in an interview with Vesti.
"We are sure that there is currently no way to cover the deficit, given that the Strait of Hormuz is closed and the plant in Qatar was halted as a result of March attacks. This is why, in my view, European politicians are shooting themselves in the foot if they ban supplies, including those from Russia," Novak said.
He said that European consumers would pay the price.
"Accordingly, there will be a shortage. The ban on LNG supplies starting January 1 is very surprising, because today the European market is unbalanced. As we know, the deficit is significant, and the gas storage reserves are much lower--I believe they are 10·% lower than the average reserves for this period in previous years," the deputy prime minister noted.
Novak also said that 12·million tons of LNG were supplied to Europe over the past nine months. "This is even more than last year. It seems that our European partners want to fill up faster and buy more LNG before January·1, 2027," he added.

title: RO 3 million project to strengthen Muttrah coastal road protection
body:
MUSCAT: Muscat Municipality is carrying out a 3 million RO project to repair coastal protection structures along Muttrah’s seafront road, strengthening its protection against waves and erosion. The project covers a 268-metre stretch in zones four and five under the first phase. It is scheduled for completion in April 2027. Mohammed bin Abdullah al Nabhani, a roads engineer at Muscat Municipality, told Oman News Agency that the work aims to improve the road’s protection and reduce future damage. The project includes rehabilitating rock protection structures, constructing concrete piles, installing breakwater units and repairing damaged sections of existing walls. Road and pavement maintenance is also included. Al Nabhani said technical monitoring continues on the anchoring piles and concrete mixes, alongside rock inspections and quality checks on protection units, to ensure compliance with approved specifications. The project has an implementation period of 395 days and is expected to improve the resilience and sustainability of Muttrah’s coastal infrastructure.

title: Iranian nation: The factor behind failure of US calculations
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – A war that was supposed to weaken Iran and place Iranian society against the country's political system has become a factor in strengthening national solidarity and changing Washington's calculations.
A war that was supposed to weaken Iran and place Iranian society against the country's political system has become a factor in strengthening national solidarity and changing Washington's calculations.
The Iranian nation, contrary to the assumption of the architects of maximum pressure, has distinguished between criticism of certain domestic issues and defending the country against foreign aggression; a distinction whose neglect can lead to the failure of strategies that have bet on the erosion of Iran's internal cohesion.
The American publication Foreign Affairs, in an analysis titled "The Theory of Iran's Victory," addresses this very issue and explains that military attacks and economic pressures, contrary to initial expectations, have not been able to realize the strategic objectives of America and the Zionist regime. This analysis states that the Iranian people do not see the war of America and Israel as liberating. Instead, they consider it an unjustified aggression, and the nationalism resulting from it has blurred the boundaries of political factions and reduced the possibility of another political uprising taking shape. This war has strengthened the Islamic Republic.
The importance of this assessment lies in the fact that the outcome of a confrontation cannot be measured solely on the basis of the extent of military damage, the destruction of infrastructure, or economic pressures. In strategic calculations, society and the people's reaction to the crisis also play a determining role. A country may face serious economic difficulties and parts of its infrastructure may be damaged, but this situation does not necessarily mean political defeat or the collapse of its national cohesion. Especially when the people consider the main cause of the crisis to be not internal disputes, but foreign attack and the threat to their country's existence.
The Gap Between Domestic Dissatisfaction and Reaction to Foreign Aggression
One of Washington's miscalculations is ignoring the difference between social and economic dissatisfactions in Iran and society's reaction to a foreign military attack. Dissatisfaction with living conditions, political demands, and criticism of officials' performance are realities that cannot be denied; but from the existence of these demands, one cannot conclude that Iranian society will move in the very direction that the architects of pressure expect in the face of any foreign pressure.
In fact, foreign pressure can change society's priorities. When people feel that their security, independence, or territorial integrity is under threat, they may temporarily marginalize internal disputes and make the defense of the country their common priority. This reaction does not necessarily mean the disappearance of all disputes or the end of criticisms; rather, it shows that national identity and sensitivity toward the country's independence have a capacity independent of political disputes.
From this perspective, the expectation that bombardments and economic pressure will automatically lead to protests against Iran's political structure is based on an incomplete understanding of Iranian society. Such an expectation reduces the people to a variable subordinate to military pressure, as if the more economic and human costs increase, the more likely society is to align with the objectives of the aggressor side. Whereas in many situations, a foreign attack can lead to strengthening the sense of a common threat and increasing the distance between the target society and the aggressors.
Why Does Foreign Pressure Produce the Opposite Result?
Economic and military pressure can lead to the political changes desired by its architects only when there is a reliable relationship between the pressure exerted and the expected political result. But this relationship is neither certain nor does it operate in the same way in all societies. Sanctions may increase people's living costs, disrupt economic activity, and exert pressure on various segments of society; however, whether these pressures lead to the weakening of the government, the strengthening of opponents, or an increase in national solidarity depends on numerous factors.
One of these factors is society's perception of the purpose of the pressures. If people imagine that foreign actions are being carried out with the aim of improving their living conditions, they may show a different reaction than when they consider these actions an attempt to impose political will or weaken their country. When a military attack is accompanied by widespread threats against infrastructure and national capacities, this perception is strengthened that the issue is not merely a dispute with a government, but that the matter is related to the country's security and future.
The Foreign Affairs analysis also emphasizes this same change in the social atmosphere. According to this assessment, foreign attacks, instead of turning existing political fissures into a factor for widespread instability, have at times paved the way for strengthening nationalism and removing factional boundaries. This process shows that external pressure, contrary to the assumption of some American policymakers, does not lead to the weakening of national will and may even increase the motivation to defend the country among groups that had serious disagreements with one another before the crisis.
The Nation: A Determining Variable in the Outcome of the Confrontation
National power is not limited to weapons capability, economic capacities, or the extent of access to advanced technologies. A society's ability to maintain cohesion under crisis conditions is also considered part of a country's power. A country that can preserve social bonds and a sense of national responsibility against external pressure possesses a capacity that purely military calculations are unable to fully explain.
In this context, the role of the Iranian nation must also be examined within the framework of this country's historical experience. Sensitivity toward independence, foreign interference, and attempts to impose the will of great powers has been among the important issues in shaping Iranians' political memory. This background does not mean that all people have the same view on domestic issues or foreign policy; rather, it shows that under conditions in which an external threat becomes prominent, national belonging can become a point of common ground for groups that have many disagreements under normal conditions.
Of course, the strengthening of national solidarity during a crisis should not be taken to mean the permanent elimination of social demands or the resolution of economic problems. Livelihood pressures can still affect people's lives, and after the external threat subsides, domestic demands will again become prominent. However, this very distinction shows that domestic dissatisfactions cannot be used as a definitive tool for advancing foreign military and political objectives. A society that is critical of its officials' performance does not necessarily want foreign military intervention or the weakening of its country.
For American policymakers, the message of this reality is clear: understanding Iranian society without paying attention to national identity, historical experience, and its sensitivity toward independence will lead to incomplete assessments. Relying on the assumption that increased pressure will automatically change the people's political will in the direction desired by Washington can make that very policymaker heedless of the real consequences of his decisions.
Ultimately, assessing the success or failure of a strategy against Iran is not possible merely through the number of attacks, the extent of damages, or the severity of sanctions. One must see what political and social results these measures have produced and whether they have been able to steer society toward the objectives declared by their designers or not. What the Foreign Affairs analysis highlights is the gap between America's expectation and the reaction of Iranian society. Ignoring the role of the nation is considered one of the most important weaknesses of these calculations, because external pressure is not only not a guarantee for the collapse of internal cohesion, but under certain conditions can lead to the opposite result and strengthen the national will to defend the country.

title: White House Defends Russia Sanctions Waiver to Aid Peace Talks
body:
Enforcing new statutory sanctions against Russia at this juncture would impede US diplomatic efforts to negotiate a comprehensive peace settlement between Moscow and Kyiv, according to the White House
Speaking to Axios , White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers defended US President Donald Trump’s decision to indefinitely suspend mandatory sanctions and import tariffs enacted under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Rogers stated that the statute equips the president with critical leverage in ongoing diplomatic consultations rather than serving as an immediate punitive instrument.
“President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the president with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution,” Rogers said in an official statement.
“Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.”
Rogers stressed that the executive waiver does not permanently dismantle the statutory penalties, emphasizing that the administration retains the authority to invoke them whenever national security considerations warrant.
“The president retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests,” Rogers added.
The administration’s defense provides public justification for an executive order signed by Trump on Friday, Oct. 16, which waived sweeping statutory trade duties and secondary penalties just 48 hours before mandatory implementation was scheduled to begin on Sunday, Oct. 18.
In issuing the suspension, Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act, which authorizes presidential waivers upon submitting formal certification to Congress that such actions align with US national interests.
While the formal certification was delivered to Capitol Hill on Friday, the White House had initially withheld specific details regarding the strategic rationale behind the determination.
The waived mechanisms represent some of the most punitive economic measures approved by Congress to date, including a mandatory 500 percent tariff on all Russian imports and 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, such as China and India .
The statute also required retaliatory duties on third countries facilitating petroleum sanctions evasion and established trade actions against Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet” of oil tankers.
The White House statement follows condemnation from President Volodymyr Zelensky , who characterized the executive waiver on Saturday as a grave policy miscalculation that directly aids the Russian military.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I consider the diesel deal to be the first step,” Zelensky told reporters.
“It seems to me that it is impossible to stop [Russian President Vladimir] Putin in this way. On the contrary, he feels joy, happiness that he has such support... It definitely helps only the Russians. It definitely does not stop the war.”
Zelensky warned that pairing demands for Ukrainian military restraint with unilateral economic accommodations to Moscow only encourages the Kremlin to sustain long-range bombardments against Ukraine’s civilian power grid ahead of winter.
The waiver also drew bipartisan criticism on Capitol Hill, where the Graham Act passed with veto-proof margins, including an 86-11 vote in the Senate.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis called the executive order “more than irresponsible,” while Democratic leaders Chuck Schumer and Elizabeth Warren accused the White House of bypassing the statutory will of Congress to offer unwarranted concessions to Putin.

title: IAF Suryakirans to Enthral Dasara Audience in Mysuru on Oct 18-19, 2026
body:
By R Anil Kumar

Bengaluru, Oct 17. The Indian Air Force's (IAF) iconic Suryakiran Aerobatic Team (SKAT) is officially set to perform a spectacular aerial display in Mysuru from October 18 to 20, 2026. The air show is a major highlight of the grand Mysuru Dasara 2026 celebrations.


Event Details
Dates: October 18, 19, and 20, 2026

Time: Performance rehearsals and scheduled slots begin from 10:00 AM onwards.

Venue: Bannimantap Grounds (Torchlight Parade Grounds), Mysuru.


What to Expect
Flying nine British-designed, HAL-manufactured Hawk Mk 132 advanced jet trainers, the elite team will perform highly synchronized close-formation manoeuvres. Spectators can look forward to signature gravity-defying stunts, including:
The Iconic DNA Manoeuvre
Barrel rolls and loops

Inverted (upside-down) flying

Patriotic saffron, white, and green smoke trails painting the Mysuru skies.

The air show was organized following a special request by Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar to Defence Minister Rajnath Singh to inspire and encourage local youth to join the armed forces. Alongside the aerial displays, the 2026 Dasara festival will also feature dedicated military tableaux representing all three wings of the Indian Defence Forces.
THE SURYAKIRAN AEROBATIC TEAM (SKAT) 
The Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team (SKAT) is the premier 9-aircraft aerobatics demonstration team of the Indian Air Force (IAF). Known as "The Sharks", the team operates under the motto "Sadaiva Sarvottama" (Always the Best).
Key Facts
Formation & Base: Formed on May 27, 1996, and based at Air Force Station Bidar in Karnataka as part of the No. 52 Squadron.

Aircraft: Initially flew the HAL HJT-16 Kiran Mk.2 trainer. After a temporary suspension in 2011, the team was re-established in 2015 and currently flies the BAE Hawk Mk.132 jet trainers.

Milestone: Celebrated its 30th Anniversary on May 26, 2026, having completed over 800 displays.

Signature Style: Maintains an ultra-close formation distance of about 5 meters between jets, and features tricolour smoke trails during modern displays.

Recent 2026 Activity: Kicked off its 2026 display season with shows in Meerut (September 2026) and scheduled events for the IAF's 94th Anniversary celebrations.


Prerequisites & Experience
Before being considered for selection, pilots must meet strict professional benchmarks within the combat stream:

Fighter Stream Commission: Must be actively commissioned as a fighter pilot in the IAF.

Seniority: A minimum of 10 years of seniority as a commissioned officer.

Flying Hours: Extensive operational experience, typically requiring around 2,000 hours of fighter flying experience.

Instructional Background: Pilots must be professional-course qualified and serve as Qualified Flying Instructors (QFIs).
Selection Process
Pilots are selected twice a year for a highly competitive three-year tour of duty with the team. The team consists of 13 pilots, though only 9 fly in a live display formation at any given time.

Voluntary Induction: Candidates must actively volunteer out of passion for aerobatics.

Commander's Evaluation: The Commanding Officer (who also serves as the display Formation Leader) puts incoming volunteers through intense flight trials and rigorous tests to judge their reflexes, spatial awareness, and ability to fly in close formation.
The Training Phase
Once a pilot is handpicked to join No. 52 Squadron ("The Sharks"), they a dedicated induction pipeline:

Duration: It takes roughly 6 to 7 months of intensive training to transition an operational fighter pilot into a display-standard aerobatic pilot. This block usually runs from March to September.

Precision Formation Training: Training progresses from simple manoeuvres to ultra-close formation flying, where pilots master keeping a consistent distance of just 3 to 5 meters between the wings of their BAE Hawk Mk.132 jets while pulling high G-forces.

Operational Cycle: A pilot's three-year tenure is strictly divided—dedicating the first six months purely to learning the routines, and the subsequent months to live public air displays.

The primary public schedules and events featuring the nine-aircraft formation include:
Upcoming 2026 Display Schedule
October 18 – 19, 2026 | Mysuru Dasara Air Show

Venue:Bannimantap Grounds, Mysuru, Karnataka.

Details: The team is scheduled to perform its signature loops, barrel rolls, inverted flying, and the crowd-favourite "DNA manoeuvre" over Mysuru beginning at 10:00 AM, utilizing tricolour smoke trails.

October 25, 2026 | "Wings Over Ganges" Air Show (Varanasi)

Venue: Namo Ghat / Assi Ghat, Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh.

Details: Scheduled to headline a massive aerial layout alongside combat jets like the Rafale, Tejas, and Su-30MKI to celebrate the Indian Air Force's 94th Anniversary.

October 31, 2026 | Rashtriya Ekta Diwas

Venue: Statue of Unity, Ekta Nagar, Gujarat.

Details: The team will participate in the Grand Celebration and public flypast marking National Unity Day.

Notable Past 2026 Performances

January 2026: Conducted extensive daily public flying routines at the major Wings India 2026 aviation exhibition at Begumpet Airport, Hyderabad.

May 26, 2026: Celebrated the team’s 30th Anniversary milestone at their home base, Air Force Station Bidar, where the Chief of the Air Staff flew in formation.

September 2026: Delivered a large-scale public demonstration over the skies of Meerut and briefly paused for localized weather adjustments before scheduled runs in Motihari.

October 2026: Participated in aerial manoeuvres at Jodhpur Air Force Station as part of the multinational exercise Tarang Shakti 2026.

title: Paris's cost of living protests spiral into France's worst violence, riots in decades
body: Rioting erupted in cities across France on Saturday as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiraled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze; in Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into city hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city's tourist office.French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year."To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X/Twitter.Some 1,200 people had been arrested during the protests, Lecornu added while visiting the sites in the evening.Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. The CGT union told Reuters it estimated the protesters at 800,000.President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had carried out the attacks."We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," he wrote in a post on X.Protests rage across Europe amid rising living costsBelgium, Portugal, and Italy also saw smaller-scale protests on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, job shortages, and poor education standards.Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president, and the wealthy."We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations.In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks, and goggles to protect against tear gas.Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques, and looted an SFR mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars.In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fueling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.The protests in France began last ‌month at high schools in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending, and living standards.In Paris on Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked Macron's previous term in office.Saturday's protests eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron's pension overhaul.Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.France's efforts to reduce public debt have not reassured investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades.Police tactics criticized after demonstrators injuredPolice tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in Saturday's protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt.Nunez confirmed reports that one person had his hand torn off in clashes with police on Saturday. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade.The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point."Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes," the union said. "Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum."

title: US Navy receives C-130J-30 Super Hercules to become future TACAMO platform, E-130J Phoenix II
body:
MARIETTA, Ga., Oct 16, 2026. A new era of strategic airborne command and control capability for the US Navy has officially begun with Lockheed Martin (NYSE:LMT) delivering a C-130J-30 Super Hercules aircraft destined to become the future of the Take Charge and Move Out (TACAMO) mission, at the company's Marietta, Georgia, facility on Oct. 15.



The C-130J-30 Super Hercules will be modified into the E-130J Phoenix II, the Navy's next-generation TACAMO mission platform, fulfilling an added mission for the Super Hercules. TACAMO is the US Navy's airborne nuclear command-and-control support mission.

The Super Hercules provides the Navy with a domestically produced, reliable, long-endurance, four-engine platform with the proven performance to successfully carry out the TACAMO mission. With advanced avionics, increased power, greater range, fuel efficiency and payload capacity, the C-130J-30 delivers the capabilities and endurance this critical mission demands.

"This delivery marks a historic milestone for the US Navy, Lockheed Martin, and the nation's strategic communications network," said Trish Pagan, Vice President of Lockheed Martin's Air Mobility & Maritime Missions. "The C-130J-30 Super Hercules continues to evolve and adapt to the needs of our customers, carrying the proven reliability of its lineage while transforming into a new, strategic mission set. It is built to deliver the capabilities our joint force demands and built to last through any operational challenge."

The delivery re-establishes the link between the TACAMO mission and the Hercules family. For three decades, the EC-130Q variant served as the Navy's TACAMO platform, flying the mission successfully from 1963 until 1993. The new Super Hercules builds on that legacy while adding advanced avionics, communications and survivability enhancements.

"The C-130J platform has a storied history supporting our strategic communications mission, and accepting this first C-130J-30 marks an exciting new chapter," said US Navy Capt. Roger Davis, Airborne Strategic Command, Control and Communications Program Manager (PMA-271). "Lockheed Martin's delivery of this battle-proven airframe provides the structural and performance backbone our mission requires as we transition into mission systems integration to field the E-130J Phoenix II."

As part of the Super Hercules' transformation, the aircraft will be transferred to Northrop Grumman, the mission systems integrator, where the E-130J TACAMO industry team will complete the conversion that will see the airframe enter service as the E-130J Phoenix II.

title: Emirates to launch daily A380 services to Delhi from Oct 25
body:
New Delhi, Oct 16. Emirates will introduce its refurbished Airbus A380 aircraft on daily flights to Delhi from October 25, bringing its Premium Economy cabin to the national capital and making Delhi the third Indian city to receive the airline’s iconic double-decker aircraft.



The Dubai-based international carrier hosted a preview of the retrofitted A380 at Indira Gandhi International Airport on October 16 for government officials, aviation industry representatives, travel trade partners and the media.

Civil Aviation Minister Kinjarapu Ram Mohan Naidu and Pradeep Panicker, CEO of Delhi International Airport Ltd (DIAL), witnessed the aircraft’s arrival. Abdulaziz Abdulla Al Hashmi, Chargé d’Affaires at the Embassy of the United Arab Emirates, was among the other distinguished guests present at the event.

The visiting dignitaries were given a guided tour of the aircraft’s four-class cabin configuration and its upgraded onboard amenities. The aircraft features Emirates’ Premium Economy cabin, which will be available to passengers travelling from Delhi for the first time.

The tour was hosted by Essa Sulaiman Ahmad, Emirates’ Senior Vice-President of Commercial Operations for West Asia and the Indian Ocean, and Mohammad Sarhan, the airline’s Vice-President for India and Nepal.

From October 25, the A380 will operate daily on flights EK512 and EK513 between Delhi and Dubai. Delhi will join Mumbai and Bengaluru as the third Indian gateway served by the aircraft.

The deployment will complement Emirates’ existing operations using retrofitted Boeing 777 aircraft, which also feature four-class configurations with Premium Economy. The airline said its other three daily flights serving Delhi would also operate with the upgraded B777 aircraft from the same date.

The A380 deployment is part of Emirates’ broader efforts to upgrade its fleet and enhance the passenger experience in India. The airline is expanding the availability of Premium Economy across its Indian network, with the cabin set to be offered at six destinations by October: Delhi, Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Kolkata and Kochi.

Alongside the introduction of the A380 in Delhi, Emirates will deploy its next-generation Airbus A350 aircraft on services to Kolkata from October 25. The A350, the latest aircraft type to join the airline’s fleet, will also feature Premium Economy.

The expansion reflects the airline’s efforts to offer more passengers in India access to upgraded cabin products and improved onboard comfort as it strengthens its services between the country and its Dubai hub.

title: Russia to export diesel to US on Aframax tankers — deputy PM
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Russian diesel will be supplied to the US mainly on Aframax-class tankers with a capacity of about 100,000 tons, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said in an interview with Vesti.
"Traditionally, there are several types of tankers; mainly, when they are used for long·distance transportation, they are Aframax vessels, with a capacity of about 100,000 tons. They can vary. It depends on the commercial terms," Novak said.
He said that after the sanctions are lifted, freight, transportation, and insurance of such transactions are not subject to restrictions.
"If the sanctions are lifted -- and they were lifted for six months, or the US Treasury issued a license allowing supplies to the markets of the United States. This means that both freight and transportation, and consequently insurance, are not subject to sanctions, and these transactions can be carried out," the deputy prime minister explained.
Earlier, Novak said that Russian diesel fuel would enter the US market within 15-20 days after signing the contracts.

title: Russian diesel to enter US market 15-20 days after signing contracts
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Russian diesel fuel will enter the US market within 15-20 days after the signing the contracts, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said in an interview with Vesti.
"The US Department of Energy has identified the companies that will be the counterparties and buyers. Currently, negotiations are underway on commercial terms, in fact, on the signing the contracts. As soon as they are signed, the fuel will be delivered to the markets within 15-20 days -- this refers to the US markets. If we talk about global markets in other, closer countries, the timeframe will be shorter," Novak said.
He said that after a phone talk and an agreement between Presidents Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump the Russian government lifted the restrictions on diesel fuel exports the next day.
"In the future, we will increase production as much as we can, as planned, and as the presidents agreed. This is 500,000 tons in October, 1 million tons in November, and 1 million tons in December. By the end of the year, if the oil refineries operate at full capacity as before, we will be able to supply 3.5 million tons to world markets. This is almost 10% of the entire global market," Novak said.
Novak noted that active work is currently underway between the Russian Energy Ministry and the US Department of Energy, and there is full contact between Russian exporting companies and buyers of Russian diesel.

title: EAEU with 190 million consumers good market for Thailand — Russian deputy PM
body:
BANGKOK, October 18. /TASS/. The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) with its consumer market of 190 million people is an attractive association for Thailand capable of helping to solve economic problems in the current conditions of global unpredictability, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk said in an interview with TASS.
He noted that in today’s "global economic fragmentation, the breakdown of established international supply chains, and unpredictable tariffs, countries are striving for greater stability and consolidation of trade terms, as well as for creating better competitive advantages for their producers."
"One of the possible ways to overcome these problems is a Free Trade Agreement," Overchuk said after an autumn session of the governing bodies of the IMF and the World Bank. "For Thailand, the five EAEU countries with 190 million consumers represent an attractive market."
He added that the trade balance with Thailand, which is also a major market, "is becoming more balanced, so this discussion can be continued together with our EAEU partners.".

title: Drones Hit St. Petersburg Oil Terminals, VK Data Center, and Bridge
body:
A Ukrainian drone attack early Sunday morning, Oct. 18, struck fuel transshipment infrastructure, a major enterprise data center, a logistics warehouse, and a highway bridge across St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region, sparking multiple fires and knocking out power to 20,000 residents.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the municipality came under attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight, resulting in blazes across four city districts.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Beglov acknowledged impacts at the Petersburg Oil Terminal (PNT) alongside damage to additional infrastructure sites, while claiming that emergency responders had been dispatched to contain localized fires.
According to independent Russian outlet Astra, municipal emergency warning systems failed to notify residents ahead of the strikes, with alerts transmitted either after impacts had occurred or with substantial operational delays.
Open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis conducted by Astra verified that fires erupted at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Baltic region’s primary petroleum transshipment hub.
Concurrently in the city’s Krasnogvardeisky district, drone debris ignited a blaze at the “Ruchyi” oil depot. The Ruchyi fuel depot maintains an operational capacity of 3,900 cubic meters, functioning as a bulk storage and loading facility for AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline alongside commercial diesel.
The overnight assault extended across the administrative boundary into the Leningrad region, targeting corporate digital backbones and electrical distribution facilities.
In the village of Novosergievka in the Vsevolozhsk district, strike drones hit a large server data center owned by Russian technology giant VK (VKontakte).
Although VK company representatives claimed corporate services continued operating normally, users across Russia reported widespread connection dropouts and outages affecting the VKontakte social media platform and its integrated ecosystem.
Astra’s OSINT analysts established that an electrical substation located adjacent to the VK data center was also damaged during the strike.
Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed that damage to electrical distribution installations triggered emergency power cuts, leaving approximately 20,000 residents in the area without electricity.
Separately, Russian e-commerce company Ozon confirmed that an aerial impact sparked a fire at its fulfillment center in St. Petersburg’s Kolpino district on Sofiyskaya Street.
Operating as one of Ozon’s busiest logistics facilities in northwestern Russia, the hub spans up to 79,000 square meters.
The company reported that emergency brigades contained the blaze and confirmed no personnel were injured.
Drone impacts were also recorded on municipal transport arteries. According to Astra, a drone struck the cable-stayed bridge spanning the Korabelny fairway in St. Petersburg, located roughly 4.5 kilometers from the Petersburg Oil Terminal.
The bridge forms a critical section of the southern viaduct of the Western High-Speed Diameter (WHSD), a multi-lane toll expressway connecting northern and southern sectors of the metropolis.
Municipal engineering teams were deployed to evaluate structural damage to the suspension cables and road deck.
The multi-site strikes in St. Petersburg and Leningrad region reflect an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign to degrade Russian rear logistics, petroleum transshipment, and corporate digital logistics.
The incident follows consecutive strikes on Russian technology hubs earlier in the month , including attacks that disabled Yandex data centers in Vladimir, Ryazan, and Kaluga regions, alongside reported strikes on a Sberbank data center facility in Saratov region.

title: Samini explains why he avoids X Spaces, TikTok Live sessions
body: Ghanaian dancehall musician Samini says he avoids X Spaces and TikTok Live sessions because they can expose him to disrespect and damage his carefully built brand. The award-winning artiste made this known at the launch of the Samini Xperience 2026, Dansoman Edition, on Friday, 16th October 2026, as he prepares to bring his signature concert to Dansoman during the festive season. Samini explained that although people and businesses must adapt to changing trends, not every new approach to communication is necessarily prudent. “There are always new ways of doing things and we always adapt but you see, not all those ways are prudent,” he said. He recalled a time before social media when fans had fewer opportunities to interact directly with established musicians, explaining that they often had to attend concerts to see their favourite artistes. “Before social media. Before you could tweet at me and say ‘your mother’, the only place you would see me was when they had booked me for show and you have bought your ticket to be in that show and there is a standby photographer that you were hoping to take me and you so that you can say you have been able to [get close to me],” he added. According to Samini, the rise of social media has made it easier for people to approach celebrities online and make comments they might not have made in person. “So for things like Twitter Spaces and TikTok Live, you are live, and some boy in some corner now has the opportunity to say whatever they want to you. And they go overboard to say things to you that if you are not careful as a human being you get derailed and you say things that eventually gonna go detrimental to your hard built brand. So if you have not seen me in those places, these are the reasons,” he noted. He said such interactions could provoke artistes into responding in ways that might ultimately harm their public image and professional reputation. Samini, however, clarified that he had not completely ruled out participating in X Spaces or TikTok Live sessions. He said he could consider joining such discussions if he believed they would contribute to his craft and serve a meaningful professional purpose. The celebrated musician added that his team would carefully assess potential engagements and select participants who could add value to discussions and contribute positively to the projects or initiatives involved.

title: Greece Will Not Transfer Patriot Missiles to Ukraine if It Weakens Its Own Defense — Mitsotakis

title: India, Mongolia review defence ties, discuss expanding military cooperation
body:
Ulaan Baatar, Oct 16. The 14th Joint Working Group meeting between the Defence Ministries of India and Mongolia took place in Ulaanbaatar on October 16. Both sides undertook a comprehensive review of ongoing bilateral defence cooperation activities, assessed the progress of existing initiatives and deliberated on measures to expand cooperation in mutually identified areas, reaffirming the commitment to further strengthen the longstanding partnership through sustained dialogue. They also exchanged perspectives on regional and international developments.

The two sides appreciated the successful conclusion of the Nomadic Elephant exercise showcasing India and Mongolia’s commitment to strengthening bilateral defence cooperation. The Mongolian side acknowledged India’s continued support in capacity building and training of personnel of Mongolian Armed Forces. Joint Secretary Ishita Ganguli Tripathy also held a meeting with Deputy Chief of the General Staff of the Mongolian Armed Forces Major Gen Usukhbayar J, with both sides appreciating the progress of cooperation between the two Defence Forces. They identified avenues to deepen engagement, strengthen defence ties and chart a forward-looking agenda for the India-Mongolia Strategic Partnership.

The Indian delegation also visited National Defence University, where they reviewed the functioning of the Cyber Security Training Centre established with the Indian assistance. The Mongolian side appreciated India’s continued support in language training and cyber security, underscoring the value of capacity building, knowledge-sharing and deeper defence cooperation in strengthening the Strategic Partnership.
India and Mongolia share enduring historical, cultural and civilisational bonds, which provide a strong foundation for their contemporary partnership. The visit highlighted the important role of shared faith and cultural heritage in bringing the two nations closer.

title: JPMorgan’s Dimon: Customers Own the Risk with AI Agents
body: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned that bank customers who let AI agents access their accounts take on the liability themselves. Speaking on the bank’s third-quarter earnings call, Dimon said people must understand the “liability transfer” if they allow agents to use their data or move money. “If data is being misused, they should understand it’s being misused,” he said. He also flagged the danger of “rogue agents,” noting there could be thousands of them. JPMorgan will not allow outside AI agents inside its systems for now. “It’s too risky for the clients and for JPMorgan,” Dimon said. The bank is building its own tools to protect customers and is testing an internal Smart Cash feature that moves money between a customer’s own JPMorgan accounts. The comments come as Meta’s Muse AI assistant has revived industry fears that AI agents could pull deposits from banks in search of better rates. McKinsey has previously warned that such agents could weaken banks’ direct relationships with customers. Dimon added that regulators should prepare for the liquidity risks these tools could create. “It’s a new world,” he said. title: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base
body:
A grass fire killed four Canadian service members and injured 39 other people, 19 of them critically, as it swept through a military training area where soldiers were using live ammunition
WAINWRIGHT, Alberta -- Four Canadian service members were killed and 39 people injured, including 19 critically, when a fast-moving fire overtook soldiers conducting live-fire combat training at a military base in Alberta , officials said Sunday.
Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was sufficiently contained to allow training to continue before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.
“The fire was a kilometer away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometer in 36 seconds,” he said at a news conference in Edmonton.
Rutland said a commander at the scene told him soldiers went from seeing no fire to having flames upon them in less than a minute.
The fire broke out Saturday during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practiced attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.
Rutland said investigators had not determined what ignited the grass fire.
He said the battalion was preparing for rapid deployment to global crises and a mission to reinforce Canadian troops in Latvia next spring.
The military identified those killed as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pvt. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, British Columbia; and Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, British Columbia. All four were serving with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based in Edmonton.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 39 people were receiving medical care. Sayeh Zielke, chief executive of Acute Care Alberta, said 19 were in critical condition, eight were stable and 12 were ambulatory and receiving treatment for less serious injuries.
Smith said some suffered severe burns and could face weeks or months of intensive treatment.
Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil. He ordered flags lowered to half-staff on federal buildings nationwide.
Carney said the families of those killed had been notified. Those affected included regular forces personnel, reservists and soldiers from bases across Canada.
Alberta health officials said patients were transferred from Wainwright to four hospitals — the University of Alberta Hospital and Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton, Foothills Medical Centre in Calgary and Red Deer Regional Hospital.
Alberta officials said they had lifted the “Code Orange” emergency activated at several hospitals Saturday night to mobilize staff and beds for the casualties.
The response involved 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters, with assistance from neighboring Saskatchewan. Smith said all patients had been accounted for and no further patients were awaiting transport.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised local medical personnel.
Rutland confirmed that military search-and-rescue technicians parachuted into Wainwright to reinforce the emergency response. Pugh said their red parachutes were illuminated by flares as they descended shortly before midnight.
Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among those critically injured. “As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta.
Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre, who represents the area in Parliament, visited Wainwright on Sunday and said he had heard accounts of people who ran toward the danger to help others and were now fighting for their lives in hospitals.
Rutland said the fire ignited in the military training area, where multiple exercises were underway, and spread rapidly in unusually strong winds.
He said winds had been within normal operating limits for much of Saturday, generally below 50 kph (31 mph), before intensifying rapidly. Range controllers rely on weather reports to determine whether training can safely continue, he said.
Rutland said investigators would examine whether the wind drove the fire toward the soldiers or whether flames spread unseen through vegetation before suddenly overtaking them.
The fire crossed established firebreaks before being contained with help from municipal firefighters.
The Canadian military said there were no indications of terrorism.
Rutland said military investigators would examine the circumstances, including whether safety protocols needed to change. “If our protocols need to change, then they’ll be updated,” he said.
The military typically convenes a formal board of inquiry after such incidents, Rutland said, cautioning that determining what happened would take time.
Rutland said Charlie Company had been withdrawn from the training area and the rest of the battalion suspended training Sunday.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in the base’s training area.
Large areas of Alberta were hit by a windstorm Saturday, with gusts up to 100 kph (62 mph). The winds toppled trees, sent signs flying and pushed flames beyond the base into surrounding rural areas.
By late Saturday, the Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. No evacuation order was issued for residents.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said the Wainwright Communiplex advance polling location closed early Saturday and election materials were transported securely.

title: Lean Alejandro and climate justice: Why Lidy Nacpil now believes in living for a cause
body: The devastating floods in Thailand and Nepal turned the spotlight on a familiar name for those of us who lived through Martial Law and dictatorship . Lidy Nacpil was one of the leaders who fought the Marcos regime, a cause she and many from our generation were ready to die for. Now she’s a leader in the global battle against climate change, when the romance of dying for a cause has been overshadowed by the pressing need to stick around as long as possible for a struggle for future generations. “Those who contributed the least to global emissions continue to shoulder the heaviest costs without prospects for a resilient future,” she said in an essay co-written with two prominent climate activists from Europe and Africa. For Lidy, the stakes are higher than half a century ago when we faced off with the Marcos regime. We didn’t expect to live long back then. Dying young was possible. We grew up under a dictatorship so brutal and with so little respect for life that many of us from the Martial Law generation believed that if we want to help end it, we would have to give up a lot for the fight — including our lives. The death of Lean For Lidy, that became real on September 19, 1987. What was painfully ironic was that the dictatorship had already been overthrown then. But the fascists were still around and there were still forces who shared the dictator’s disdain for democracy and who targeted those who were fighting to preserve and expand it — like her husband, Lean Alejandro. On that day, Lidy returned home to find the sitter of their 6-month-old daughter Rusan waiting for her at the door. She said Lean had been ambushed. “My first thought was that she said ‘ambush’ So I was really hoping that it did not mean he was dead. So I said, ‘Where was he taken?’ I was so afraid of asking point blank: ‘ Buhay pa ba? Is he still alive?’” But the sitter confirmed her worst fear. Lean was dead. Lean had just led a press conference before the attack to share plans for the upcoming 15th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law. He and several companions were about to drive into their office on Rosal Street in Cubao, when a van pulled up next to the car. Then the assassins opened fire. Rosal Street is about a mile away from our house in Cubao. I actually remember hearing the shots, though I did not think much about it initially. Only an hour later did I realize its significance when a friend called and said she heard a radio report about the ambush. I drove to the office which had been abandoned by the time I arrived. There was blood on the driveway. The staff, including friends of mine, had retreated to a nearby office of a major human rights coalition in New Manila. We were in shock. A brilliant leader, the most inspiring symbol of the Martial Law generation, was gone. Friends and family joined Lidy at the morgue for what she recalls as “a nightmare into the night.” Lean’s face was shattered in the attack. “What I did was not look at where he was badly damaged and just concentrated on looking at parts of his body and his face that were intact,” she said. “My memories of that day are still vivid. I don’t think I’ll ever forget.” I last saw Lidy in person in 2007 when we commemorated Lean’s 20th death anniversary in Quezon City. By then, her activism had expanded in scope, focused not only on social justice and human rights issues in the Philippines, but also on a grim global concern: climate change. In 2012, when I posted a Facebook note celebrating Barack Obama’s reelection despite misgivings about some of his policies, Lidy posted a comment: “Boying, hope he will have a far, far better position on climate change and US cuts on its emissions than he took during his first term.” When we talked four years ago for my series on Martial Law Babies, the urgency of the climate change battle clearly informed her own updated view of activism — and the sacrifices one must be willing to make in the fight for change. (READ: The Martial Law babies’ turn ) We were in our late 20s when Lean was assassinated nearly 40 years ago. Most of us are now in our late 50s or early 60s. When we were younger, being prepared to die for the cause, for the struggle against dictatorship was a given. But things are different now, Lidy told me. “The sacrifices and what we are willing to give up, nag iiba iba iyan (it changes),” Lidy said. “At that time for us, the biggest is you were willing to risk your life.” “The challenge for me today is: you have to live long because there’s so much to do — and to pass on. We cannot recklessly risk our lives today. That’s not what is being asked for. The times are different. The needs are different.” Play Video Lean’s Rado watch Lidy was a high school freshman at UP High when Martial Law was declared in September 1972. After a long break from school after Marcos seized power, she returned to a campus where there were “whispers” of students and teachers who had been arrested. But she had been vaguely aware of the protests and the unrest. She and her schoolmates didn’t have a clear idea of what was going on. “That’s why we were called Martial Law babies. We were just babies, not literally in age but in consciousness.” Although she would later be known as a UP student leader, it was actually through her church and groups like the Student Christian Movement that she became exposed to political activism. In fact, she was initially unimpressed with the first student activists she encountered in Diliman. “I used to see small groups of students marching down the corridors of Palma Hall, sloganeering. I used to think, ‘Ano ba naman iyan, ang babaw. Paano mo mababago ang lipunan kung nagsisigaw ka lang diyan? (It was shallow. How will you change society by just yelling slogans?).” She laughed at the memory, adding, “If that’s all we were going to do as students, do marches and shout slogans, I wasn’t interested. I was looking for something deeper and more profound.” Eventually, she found it. The marches and the slogans turned out to be just one part of a broader and more dynamic activist movement that was at that time starting to push back against the dictatorship. And these efforts, the years of testing the limits and pushing back against the regime — which had led to arrests and even the death of Philippine Collegian editor Ditto Sarmiento — eventually produced victories. By the time Lidy entered UP Diliman, students, after years of struggle, had reclaimed their right to elect their own student councils and other campus rights. It was around that time that she met Lean. They would later share a scary experience — though one that they would later talk about lightheartedly. It happened in 1980 when Lidy and Lean joined a major student demonstration at Liwasang Bonifacio. The rally was violently dispersed. “I fell during the dispersal. I vaguely remember someone helping me get up and then I ran.” She didn’t see and had no idea who helped her up. But Lean later told her that it was him — and he actually paid a price for it. “I was about to get hit with a truncheon when he blocked it with his hand.” Lean was wearing a Rado watch which got smashed in this act of chivalry. “His father had given it to him so it was valuable. Kaya sabi niya, ‘Ikaw ang dahilan kung bakit nabasag. (You’re the reason it got smashed.).” Remembering that made Lidy laugh. I still fondly remember Lean as a brilliant, inspiring activist — intelligent, articulate, charismatic. He was a young leader brimming with confidence who could give a firebrand speech at a rally at Mendiola Bridge and also engage in serious political discussions with established political figures like Lorenzo Tañada and Jose “Pepe” Diokno. He was also a humble, patient young leader who I saw several times up close. During a rally shortly after the Aquino assassination, when he was not yet a nationally known figure, I saw Lean defuse a situation in the crowd where some impatient protesters started throwing little stones at other protesters who decided to stand up to see what was going on at the main stage. “ Huwag po. Magkakainitan lang po tayo niyan. (Sir, please don’t do that. It will just make things worse.),” Lean said calmly, successfully convincing the irritated rallyists to settle down. I also remember Lean for his quirks and unorthodox style. He used to walk around Diliman in faded jeans and flip flops. He was known as a computer geek and an avid fan of chess, The Lord of the Rings , and Fiddler on the Roof . Like many of us back then, he was a chain smoker — perhaps because many of us didn’t expect to lead long lives. So why not smoke our lungs away. We were prepared to go all in so to speak. In fact, Lean famously said: “The line of fire is the place of honor.” The day he was assassinated, Lean was reading Antonio Gramsci, the Italian revolutionary who is also famous for the quote, “The old world is dying and the new world struggles to be born.” For Lidy, it is the first sentence of what Gramsci said that truly resonates more than 30 years later. The world indeed is dying — and there is much to be done. Climate justice Lidy became involved in the climate justice movement about 15 years ago. As one of the leaders of the Asian People’s Movement on Debt and Development, she has emerged as one of Asia’s leading voices in the movement. That fight has become harder. When the UN Climate Change Conference was held in 2021 without the participation of countries in the Global South, she was among those who spoke out. “The conference has long been dominated by wealthy governments and corporate interests, thus it’s always an intense effort to raise the voices, perspectives and calls of people and communities, especially those from the Global South,” she said. When the Nepal tragedy hit, Lidy spoke out in a Bangkok Post op-ed: “Declarations can no longer substitute for action, and excuses can no longer be allowed. Behind every discussion of temperature thresholds, emissions pathways and international obligations are communities losing lives, homes, livelihoods and ecosystems.” It is a different kind of struggle — one that poses a host of unique tougher challenges. “You’re fighting for things not to get worse in terms of the climate. On the other hand, you want to establish systems where there’s more equality and where people will have a better chance of a good livelihood. “ “The real impact of climate change can no longer be reversed. What we’re telling people is we cannot go back to the past. We’re working to prevent things from getting worse.” It would be hard to imagine a time when there are no super typhoons, she said. There is, in a way, the element of making people fearful of what could happen. “That’s not the easiest thing to do. Mas madaling sabihin sa tao, ‘Lumaban tayo dito para mawala iyan’ imbes na ‘Lumaban tayo para hindi lumala .’ (It’s easier to tell people, ‘Let’s fight to make this go away,’ instead of ‘Let’s fight so things don’t get worse.’)” But today’s generation of climate change activists also are “blessed,” she said. Activists from earlier generations had laid the foundation for the fight — similar to the way our generation learned a lot from the experiences of earlier activists and leaders like Tañada and Diokno. Lidy became involved in the climate justice movement a decade after the 1992 international conference which helped make clear the dangers the world faced and establish basic principles on how nations should respond. “I was surprised and wondered how they were able to win progressive provisions and principles, because they are really helping us now.” Her past as a Martial Law baby, and a veteran of the struggle that overthrew the Marcos dictatorship has also helped. A key lesson from our time as Martial Law babies is top of mind for Lidy in the battle for climate justice: You have to keep pushing — even when the odds seem overwhelming. “From our experience in the fight during the dictatorship, you learn to widen and push the edges of these platforms and these opportunities. Hindi ka pwedeng magkasya doon sa ito lang iyong binigay sa iyo. (You must never settle and accept what they say they can offer you.) You push for more so you can have more space to raise your voices. “The discipline we developed as activists in the Philippines was helpful. We were very broad-minded in terms of tactics, strategies, and alliance work… What we experienced during martial law, what we learned about struggle, about strategies and tactics, these are very useful in taking on all these global problems and fights and institutions and arenas.“ For example, she said, with movements in some countries, there is a dichotomy between “those who just believe in mobilizations, mass actions and radical slogans and those who just do policy advocacy and do the nitty gritty of negotiations.” That’s not how she was trained as an activist. In a way, the lesson goes back to her initial reaction to UP activists, those who held loud marches in Diliman — which she subsequently realized were just one part of a broader and deeper movement. Marches and pickets were just as important as other tasks, from studying an issue to formulating a policy and position and engaging negotiations to achieve a goal. “Para sa Pinoy, lahat yan kasama. (For Filipinos, that’s all combined.) Those are all needed.” There’s another lesson Lidy shared and it’s related to how we all remember Lean. “Lean had extraordinary and outstanding traits,” she said. But in honoring his memory, we shouldn’t idealize who he was. “Ang hirap kasing naghohold up tayo ng icons minsan kasi baka ma-frustrate lang . (Holding up people as icons is sometimes not helpful. It may just lead to frustration.) Not everybody can be a Lean Alejandro.” And not everyone has to be a Lean Alejandro, she said. That’s a key lesson from the Martial Law generation. Many of us weren’t. But that didn’t matter. Lean Alejandro’s tsinelas revolution “I think the most important story of our generation is that most of us were just your average youth. The thing that was extraordinary about us is that we rose to the occasion. We weren’t particularly more intelligent. Mas sharper pa nga sila ngayon e. (Young people today are even sharper.) The knowledge base is much larger now. The technology is there. They are faster in dealing with all the technology. “But we rose to the occasion. We realized that we had more than ourselves to live for.” And that’s what she hopes young Filipinos today will keep in mind, she said — that “they realize that they have to live for more than themselves. And that they rise to the occasion, whatever the occasion demands, whatever the times now demand from them. It doesn’t take extraordinary things. It’s your willingness and readiness and there are many ways that you can contribute.” In a way, the idea of “giving your life” for the cause — “ medyo abstract na. (It’s a bit abstract now.),” Lidy said. “That means many different things.” “I want to last as long as it takes until there is a fresh resurgence of movements and struggles so we can pass on whatever knowledge and wisdom we gained from our experiences.” – Rappler.com This essay is based on an article first published in 2022. Benjamin Pimentel is the author of ‘ U.G. An Underground Tale: The Life and Struggle of Edgar Jopson ’ published by Anvil Publishing which just released the 2nd printing of the 3rd edition. He is also a journalist and technology editor based in the San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA. Royalties from ‘U.G.’ are donated to Bantayog ng Mga Bayani.
