title: Drones strike oil facilities, Ozon warehouse and VKontakte data center in St. Petersburg
body:
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the Russian service of the BBC.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov stated that the city was attacked by drones during the night. According to him, the fire broke out at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, as well as at other infrastructure facilities in four districts of the city.
According to the Telegram channel Astra , St. Petersburg residents either did not receive warnings about the drone threat or received them with a significant delay.
According to Astra’s OSINT analysis , the largest fuel terminal in St. Petersburg is on fire following a drone attack. Additionally, the “Strumki” oil depot in the city’s Chervonogvardeisky District has caught fire. According to the channel, the facility has a total capacity of 3,900 cubic meters and is used to store and ship AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline, as well as diesel fuel.
Ozon reported a fire at its warehouse in St. Petersburg following a drone attack. There were no casualties.
In addition, drones attacked a data center belonging to VK (“VKontakte”) in the Leningrad Region. The company states that its services remain available to users as usual.
At the same time, according to OSINT analysis by Astra, following the strike on the data center, users reported widespread disruptions to the “VKontakte” social network and related services. A substation was also hit alongside the data center. The facilities are located in the village of Novosergievka in the Vsevolozhsky District of the Leningrad Region, on the administrative border with St. Petersburg.
In addition, according to Astra, a drone struck a cable-stayed bridge spanning the Korabelny Fairway in St. Petersburg. The bridge is located approximately 4.5 km from the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal. The extent of the damage is being assessed.
This bridge is part of the southern viaduct of the Western High-Speed Diameter—a toll highway connecting the southern and northern parts of the city.
Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenco stated that a drone attack in the region caused an emergency power outage, leaving about 20,000 people without electricity.
As reported by Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed that the “Roboavia” drone development and manufacturing facility in the Rostov Region and a logistics depot belonging to a missile brigade in the Bryansk Region of the Russian Federation had been struck.

title: US Congress Stalled on Response to Trump Russia Waiver – AP
body:
US President Donald Trump’s decision to indefinitely postpone statutory sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia has triggered condemnation from lawmakers across both parties, though formal congressional intervention remains stalled due to the pre-election legislative recess, the Associated Press reported.
Congress previously passed the sanctions package with overwhelming veto-proof majorities, reflecting broad bipartisan backing for Ukraine and international deterrence.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, Trump’s executive order on Friday , Oct. 16, waiving enforcement just 48 hours before statutory enactment ignited pushback among key Republican and Democratic legislators.
Despite the outrage, lawmakers are not positioned to mount an immediate legislative response, as both the Senate and the House of Representatives remain in recess until after the crucial Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Senior Republicans voiced open frustration over the administration’s decision to shield Moscow from statutory trade duties and secondary financial penalties.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis characterized the executive waiver as “more than irresponsible,” pointing out that the Senate enacted the statute by an overwhelming 86-11 margin. Tillis accused the White House of offering unwarranted concessions to Russian President Vladimir Putin while undermining congressional prerogatives.
Tillis further pushed back against the administration’s economic defense, stating that if the White House seeks to reduce domestic energy prices, policymakers must focus on resolving the armed conflict involving Iran rather than enacting commercial steps that subsidize Russia.
Democratic leaders similarly condemned the indefinite suspension, warning that easing economic pressure underwrites the Kremlin’s wartime economy and sustains long-range bombardments against Ukrainian civilian population centers.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of directly propping up the Russian economy at the expense of American allies and democratic norms.
Senator Elizabeth Warren stated that the president is openly defying Congress, asserting that waiving statutory enforcement enables Putin to prolong an aggressive war of conquest.
Warren urged lawmakers to prepare legislative mechanisms to reverse the executive order once Congress reconvenes in Washington following the November vote.
The Associated Press reported that Trump suspended the penalties indefinitely, citing US national security considerations under statutory waiver authorities.
Because members of Congress are dispersed across their home districts campaigning ahead of the Nov. 3 balloting, any formal legislative counter-measures – such as the bipartisan “Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act” introduced by Representative Gregory Meeks or the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act” drafted by Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon – will face procedural delays until post-election sessions commence.
Trump’s executive action waives core enforcement mechanisms codified within the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which the president signed into law on Sept. 18.
The suspended provisions, which were scheduled to take statutory effect on Sunday, Oct. 18, mandated an additional 500 percent tariff on all Russian-origin imports alongside 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, including China and India .
The statute also required trade penalties against third-party nations facilitating petroleum sanctions evasion and established aggressive actions to dismantle Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet.”
In issuing the waiver, Trump invoked Section 115 of the statute, which grants executive discretion upon certifying to Congress that such action serves US national interests.
The suspension aligns with a commercial arrangement unveiled on Oct. 9 between Trump and Putin , under which Moscow consented to export refined diesel onto international markets through 2027 to lower retail fuel costs.
The waiver was met with condemnation from Kyiv, where President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that lifting economic penalties constitutes a grave policy error that provides financial lifelines to the Russian military and signals to Moscow that persistent infrastructure bombardments will carry no economic consequence.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: DeepSeek search and fetch – $0.75 per 1000 successful requests
body:
The Search API and the Fetch API give agents and RAG applications access to live web content:
Both are raw JSON APIs. They use the same bearer authentication as the DeepSeek API.
The base URL is https://api.deepseek.com :
See the Search API Reference and Fetch API Reference for the complete request and response schemas.
Send your API key and the JSON content type in the request headers:
Unknown fields in the request body are ignored.
The query is forwarded with its search syntax intact. The examples below combine operators with a search term; you can combine multiple operators in one query.
A successful request returns HTTP 200 with a results array. A normal search with no matches returns an empty array.
Fetching is subject to the target site's availability and access policies.
Errors follow the OpenAI-compatible error format. The param field is always null .
Search and Fetch are read-only. For HTTP 408, 429, or 5xx errors, wait and retry. For HTTP 402, top up your account before retrying. Do not retry other 4xx errors without changing the request.
Search and Fetch are billed per successful request, not by tokens or by the number of returned results:
A request is billable only when it returns HTTP 200 and produces a result (Search must return a non-empty results array, and Fetch must return page content). Failed requests, empty search results, and timeouts are not billed. count only controls how many results are returned and does not affect the per-request price.
Note: when you use the DeepSeek API through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex, server-side tool calls already hit the Search and Fetch APIs. These calls are currently free of charge; per-request billing starts at 00:00 Beijing time on November 1, 2026.
For each account, Search and Fetch are limited independently, and traffic to one does not consume the other's quota:
The QPS (requests per second) limits are calculated at the account level, regardless of which API key is used, and are separate from the model concurrency limits. Requests above the account-level QPS limit receive HTTP 429. In addition to the account-level limit, Fetch is also subject to a per-domain QPS limit, and requests above that limit also receive HTTP 429.

title: Al Ain stunned by Shabab Al Ahli as historic 38-game unbeaten run comes to an end
body: Vladimir Ivic said he was proud of Al Ain's record UAE Pro League 38-game unbeaten run but was highly critical of his side's defending after a 2-0 loss to title rivals Shabab Al Ahli saw them beaten for the first time in 19 months. Al Ain had not tasted a league defeat since a 3-2 loss to Dibba on March 29, 2025, some 567 days before Saturday's setback. In that time, Ivic had led the team through an unbeaten title-winning season . It was also the first time in 32 matches that Al Ain had failed to score. They sit fourth in the table as part of a four-way tie for the lead, although Al Jazira can go three points clear with victory at Kalba on Sunday. Shabab Al Ahli moved up to second after goals from in-form striker Sardar Azmoun and Kauan Santos gave them victory in Dubai. Ivic said his Al Ain side had been poor at both ends of the pitch but urged his players to get the defeat out of their systems quickly. They have an immediate opportunity to avenge the result when they face Shabab Al Ahli again in the last 16 of the President's Cup on Thursday. “It was a very strange match, but I congratulate Shabab Al Ahli on the win,” said Ivic. “They took their chances and scored two goals from four opportunities, while we created around 10 chances and failed to score a single goal. That was the difference between the two teams. “I don't remember us making these kinds of mistakes since I arrived at Al Ain. What happened was abnormal, especially the way we conceded the two goals. I cannot explain it before watching the match again. End-to-end action from start to finish 🍿⚽️ A look back at Shabab Al Ahli’s impressive win over Al Ain in an entertaining contest! #ADNOCProLeague pic.twitter.com/tkeyrtHYJs — UAE Pro League (@UAEProleague_En) October 18, 2026 “For the first goal, a Shabab Al Ahli player got past two of our defenders easily, as if they were statues standing still on the pitch, before going through on goal and scoring. The second goal came from similar mistakes. These are things that cannot happen. “I am the team's coach and I take responsibility for the defeat. I do not blame the players, but we must return to the basics and correct our mistakes. Even the best teams in the world lose, and I am proud of what our players have delivered over the past period. “We must forget this match quickly because we will face Shabab Al Ahli again in four days, and our objective is to return to winning ways.” كاكو: "صنعنا الكثير من الفرص ولم نستطع التسجيل، وعندما لا تسجل وتستقبل الأهداف يصعب عليك العودة ونعتذر لجماهيرنا على النتيجة" pic.twitter.com/oDyGRmclqs — نادي العين (@alainfcae) October 17, 2026 It was the biggest result so far for Andre Jardine, the Shabab Al Ahli manager, who took over from Paulo Sousa in the summer. He said his players had carried out his game plan to a tee but warned that they would need to maintain their level when they meet Al Ain again in the cup. “For us, beating Al Ain is worth six points because we are talking about a direct clash against a strong rival for the title,” he said. “Almost everything we planned before the match worked, but if I want to speak frankly, taking our chances was the decisive factor in achieving the victory. “Of course, the defeat will give Al Ain extra motivation to come back and win the next match, but our victory today will also give our players a big morale boost. We will face a new match between two teams that have the enthusiasm and desire to win.”

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,565,060 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
body:
Russia has lost 1,565,060 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 18.
The number includes 2,090 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,416 tanks, 25,561 armored combat vehicles, 164,246 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,293 artillery systems, 2,224 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,711 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,968 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Seven killed in explosion at Canada military training base
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – At least seven people have been killed and dozens more injured following an explosion and fire at one of Canada’s busiest military bases.
Authorities were called to the Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta shortly after 4pm local time on Saturday (11pm GMT) following reports of a fire at a training area of the site, according to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).
“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” Canadian defense minister David McGuinty said.
It’s not yet clear what caused the explosion but Mr McGuinty said that the Canadian military and the RCMP were investigating the incident, The Telegraph reported.
“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” he said.
Extreme shifts in wind patterns, with gusts as strong as 100 kilometers (62 miles per hour), moved the fire to the nearby town of Wainwright.
Flames south of the town had been “held”, the municipality said in an update shortly before 11pm local time.

title: Rubio: Ukraine Does Not Have Access to Starshield
body:
Ukraine currently lacks access to the specialized military-grade Starshield satellite network and has requested the technology to conduct deep-interdiction strikes inside Russia , US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
Speaking to journalists in comments released by the US Department of State, Rubio clarified the distinction between SpaceX’s standard commercial Starlink communications framework and the dedicated Starshield architecture operated under contract with the US Department of Defense.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defense product, a military product,” Rubio stated.
“That is something that the United States military uses. It’s not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that’s under conversation. It’s under discussion right now how they would want to use it.”
Responding to questions regarding reports of technological throttling, Rubio directly refuted claims that the Trump administration had mandated bandwidth or velocity caps on terminals operating in Ukrainian combat sectors.
“I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield. They do not have Starshield now. They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” Rubio emphasized.
Rubio pushed back against assertions by President Volodymyr Zelensky that artificial operational constraints imposed on Starlink terminals inside Ukraine were deliberate administrative measures.
“I don’t know what Zelensky said. I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
“Nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored. It’s back to where it was before. That’s Starlink, though. They were using Starlink for their drones.”
Addressing media reports suggesting executive coordination to limit unmanned systems, the secretary of state characterized the allegations as completely unfounded.
“Nothing to do with the White House. I saw a report on that the other day. It’s just categorically false,” Rubio told reporters.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it. But my understanding is it’s back up and running. That’s what I read – that’s what we heard two days ago.”
Rubio’s comments follow detailed disclosures delivered on Saturday, Oct. 17, by President Zelensky, who revealed that Starlink terminals operating inside Ukrainian territory had been subjected to a strict velocity limitation of 161 km/h (100 mph).
According to Zelensky, whenever equipped domestic platforms exceeded the 161 km/h threshold, satellite connections automatically severed , causing operators to lose control of unmanned interceptors in mid-flight.
The velocity cap effectively disabled domestic drone interceptors tasked with neutralizing high-speed, turbojet-powered Russian Shahed loitering munitions, which penetrate sovereign airspace at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (250 mph).
Zelensky highlighted that Ukrainian technical teams conducted cross-border comparative evaluations, sending Starlink-equipped vehicles into EU territory, where the devices operated uninterrupted at velocities of 180 km/h (112 mph). The Ukrainian leader argued that the trials confirmed the restrictions were geographically targeted at Ukrainian airspace rather than stemming from global software glitches.
The technological dispute underscores widening geopolitical friction between Washington and Kyiv over long-range interdiction limits and commercial communications dependencies.
Rubio’s denials echo statements by US President Donald Trump , who told that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered operational caps on Ukraine’s military communications, asserting that “everything is the same as it’s always been.”
However, both official denials contradict reporting by The Telegraph, which cited four sources familiar with the matter stating that Musk directly proposed satellite service limitations to Trump, who approved the measure, clearing the way for the Pentagon to restrict Starshield functionality.
Sources cited in the report claimed Musk sought to shift public accountability onto the White House amid concerns over potential consumer boycotts across European markets following civilian casualties in Kyiv.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: D Cryme calls for museum, podcast studio to honour Dr Duncan
body: Ghanaian musician D Cryme has called on music industry stakeholders to celebrate broadcaster Dr Duncan for his role in projecting several musicians through his Kasahare Level show on Adom FM in the 2000s. Speaking to arts and culture journalist Kwame Dadzie on Joy FM’s Showbiz A-Z , D Cryme outlined several ways the industry could honour Dr Duncan for his contribution to music. “Dr Duncan does not only deserve a statue, but he deserves a super big monumented museum. While he is alive, he deserves all the accolades and appreciation. That is why I mention him wherever I go,” he said. D Cryme said musicians who benefited from the platform Dr Duncan provided should not wait until his death before speaking about his impact on their careers and the music industry. “This is what I want to see him do; if things come and it’s proper, I would rather create a nice podcast for him. Podcast is the way. He still has something in him. It’s just like a solid young but grandpa in the house,” he added. He also noted that others who shared his vision could join forces with him to make the proposed project a reality. “It’s something that I tell my friends and industry colleagues. It’s something I have been trumpeting. I try to let them know that maybe I might have the means but it is not one man fight or one man projection. That clearly tells you that you also have equally something extra to spare. We can pull our resources together. We can make this happen,” D Cryme said. Dr Duncan’s Kasahare Level on Adom FM became a platform for aspiring musicians, particularly rappers, to showcase their lyrical skills and gain exposure in the Ghanaian music industry during the 2000s. The programme helped bring emerging talents before a wider audience at a time when radio airplay was an important route to recognition. Several musicians have been associated with the programme’s influence, including D Cryme and other artistes who built their profiles through radio exposure and the hiplife scene. The programme served as a launchpad for artistes such as Sarkodie, Yaa Pono, Pope Skinny, Shakoma, Stonebwoy, D Cryme, Criss Waddle, Yaw Siki, Edem, Guru, Kwaw Kese, Kofi Korea, and others, several of whom later established themselves in Ghana’s music industry.

title: Saudi Arabia executes five over terrorism-related offences
body: Saudi Arabia has executed five men over terrorism-related offences. The executions were carried out in the Eastern Province on Saturday, the Interior Ministry was quoted by the Saudi Press Agency as saying. It named the five citizens as Mohammed Al Zaher, Ali Al Sheikh, Hassan Al Faraj, Reda Al Abu Abdullah and Ali Al Rabih. The ministry said they joined a foreign terrorist organisation, repeatedly opened fire on security personnel and vehicles with intent to kill, possessed weapons and live ammunition, and provided financial and other support for attacks inside the kingdom. A court found them guilty and sentenced them to death under tazir, a discretionary form of punishment that Saudi judges can impose under Islamic law for offences not carrying fixed penalties. The ministry said the sentences were upheld by the Supreme Court on appeal and a royal order was issued for them to be carried out. The executions reflected the government’s commitment to security, justice and the enforcement of Islamic law against those who threaten public safety, it added.

title: Opinion | The irony of COP17 host Armenia celebrating gold before biodiversity
body: From 19–30 October, Armenia will host the 17th UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) in Yerevan. This year, the official slogan is ‘Taking action for nature’. Yet just nine days before the conference opened, on 10 October, the Armenian government officially launched mining operations at the Amulsar gold mine . Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan himself attended the opening ceremony near the spa town of Jermuk, claiming that the absence of protests around the opening proved that public concerns had been resolved. Civil society organisations and environmental activists, however, have accused the Pashinyan administration of deliberately keeping the ceremony out of public view, arguing that the event had not been announced, so no one could gather to protest. Controversial Amulsar gold mine opens in Armenia after long delay Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan claims they addressed all environmental concerns that prevented the mine from opening earlier OC Media Ani Ghulinyan At the same time, they have criticised the government’s heightened support for the Amulsar project, especially in the run-up to COP17, arguing that promoting mining in a sensitive ecological region contradicts Armenia’s international biodiversity commitments. Indeed, while the government promotes a green agenda globally, local communities and environmental experts warn that the mine threatens endangered wildlife and vital water systems. Removing ‘biodiversity obstacles’ by government decision In March 2020, a coalition of Armenian and international environmental organisations, including Bankwatch, filed a complaint with the Secretariat of the Bern Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats. They argued that the Amuslar mine directly threatened endangered wildlife and affects three candidate sites of the Emerald Network (a network of areas of special conservation interest set up under the Convention): Djermuk Area, Gorhajk Area, and Sevan National Park. The complaint notes that the area affected by the mine is home to a number of species listed as ‘strictly protected fauna’ under the Bern Convention, including the Persian leopard, bezoar goat, brown bear, Eurasian otter, and Eurasian lynx, and that mining would lead to habitat destruction and fragmentation of wildlife populations along the Amulsar mountain corridor. Despite initial promises to abide by the findings of an independent, state-commissioned environmental audit, Pashinyan’s administration has repeatedly and actively promoted the Amulsar mine, disregarding any critical findings which highlighted flawed data on flora and fauna and the lack of biodiversity action and monitoring plans. By late 2024, the government had acquired a 12.5% stake in Lydian Armenia, the company operating the mine, and in early 2025, it approved a $150 million state guarantee for loans from a local bank. In the meantime, Pashinyan’s administration disregarded the results of a government-commissioned international environmental audit . The 13-point document officially drafted in 2019 by the Ministry of Environment outlined instances of non-compliance and gaps in the Amulsar environmental impact assessment. Podcast | The Amulsar mine returns After over a decade of controversy over environmental, labour, and economic concerns, the Armenian government has finally greenlit the operation of the Amulsar gold mine in Jermuk. Since the project’s announcement, local communities in and around Jermuk have expressed concern about the mine’s potential impact on their lives and livelihoods, while environmental activists have warned about the catastrophic environmental effects the mines could have on the region. This week OC Media OC Media Yet the environmental setbacks began over a decade ago. In one of the most important instances, in July 2014, the Armenian government adopted a decision to allow developers to relocate endangered plant species. Some critics have suggested this was designed to clear the way for the Amulsar gold mine by sidestepping domestic biodiversity conservation law. Although the Armenian Mining Code explicitly prohibits mining on land that is home to plant or animal species listed in Armenia’s Red Book, the decision authorised the relocation of Red Book plants such as Potentilla porphyrantha, which grows in the project area. The timing of the decision was highly suspicious: it was adopted less than a month before the public hearing on the project’s environmental impact assessment. Without this legal loophole, the Amulsar mine may not have been able to proceed. By allowing endangered species to be moved to artificial ‘plant zoos’, the government undermined its own domestic laws as well as international treaties such as the Bern Convention, which protect the habitats of threatened species, not just individual plants. Notably, the company itself pointed to the decision as a way around these legal barriers. During a public hearing in the village Gndevaz in August 2014, the company responded to my question about Red Book plant and animal species by stating that the government had adopted a decision the prior month allowing such plants to be relocated from the Amulsar mining zone . As I argued at the time, I believe the decision was passed specifically to help the company bypass environmental protection laws and clear the area for mining infrastructure. Offsetting on paper, not in practice At the same time, both the government and COP’s formal agenda have highlighted biodiversity offsetting and market instruments such as private ‘nature credits’ as a method to protect biodiversity. In reality, however, these efforts risk legitimising efforts by corporations and banks to greenwash the loss of endangered habitats rather than halting ecological destruction at the source. Indeed, Target 19 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Diversity Framework, which calls for more finance from all sources, explicitly encourages ‘innovative schemes’ such as biodiversity offsets and credits. Armenia’s own experience shows how such schemes can play out in practice. In December 2016, Lydian Armenia and the Ministry of Nature Protection signed a Memorandum of Understanding to establish Jermuk National Park as an offset for permanent ecosystem damage on Amulsar mountain, with the company pledging more than $5 million over five years. But the park’s boundaries were later redrawn to exclude the mine. In October 2023, the Armenian government reported to the Bern Convention that the initiative to establish Jermuk National Park had been postponed due to ‘prevailing state priorities and regional instability’. Then there is the Djermuk Area candidate Emerald site, which featured proposals to protect the whole area on the basis of a 2012 World Wildlife Fund-backed feasibility study . Now, once again, the government is proposing to cut Amulsar mountain out of that site too, so that it matches the smaller park. In the case of the Teghut open-pit copper and molybdenum mine in northern Armenia, compensation for lost nature also failed. The mine required the felling of 357 hectares of rich forest, including 128,000 trees. Under the original project terms, the developer, Vallex Group, pledged to plant twice as many trees in adjacent areas to offset the ecological loss. Rather than carrying out the planting and long-term care itself, its subsidiary Teghout CJSC set up a tender committee to outsource the work. Environmental watchdogs and local groups long contended that the afforestation efforts fell short or failed. In 2019, the Prosecutor General’s Office opened a criminal case after state forest monitoring found that most of the trees planted on 132 hectares had not survived, even though officials of the state forestry agency Hayantar (ArmForest), which was contracted to do the work, had recorded it as complete. The case also found that the responsible ministries had failed to supervise the restoration . All of these approaches are at odds with Article 9 of the Bern Convention, which sets out the only exceptions allowed from the protection of species — for example, in the interests of public health and safety, air safety, or other overriding public interests — and only where there is no other satisfactory solution. Offsetting the damage done by a gold mine is not one of them. In April 2025, the Bern Convention’s monitoring committee reiterated its request for a new environmental impact assessment that considers all the species and habitats present in the area and asked the authorities to ‘suspend any permits for the exploitation of subsoil’ until the new assessment had been completed. The Armenian government disregarded the requests, maintaining in its September 2026 report to the Convention that the existing environmental impact assessment’s conclusion and national permits remain legally valid. Notably, it is only now, on the eve of COP17, that the Jermuk National Park concept has been revived, with the government announcing at the mine’s launch that Lydian would put $5 million towards it — the same sum the company pledged a decade ago. Armenian opposition questions state’s $51 million spending on COP17 The opposition is raising concerns about the risk of corruption, while the government says the UN chose the procurement companies. OC Media Ani Ghulinyan In August 2026, Lydian and the government also signed a community development agreement for the Amulsar project. Under it, the company will pay $7 million or $9 million a year to affected communities, depending on the price of gold, through a new foundation. The arrangement goes beyond the social contributions mining companies are legally required to make, and risks becoming a new instrument that makes communities dependent on the company’s money. At COP17, several events in the official negotiation venue will focus on the Bern Convention, bringing together country delegates, the Convention Secretariat, and accredited experts to discuss how to protect wild flora and fauna and their natural habitats. It is worth asking the Armenian representatives how they plan to address their persistent disregard for their Bern Convention commitments while simultaneously ‘taking action’ to protect biodiversity during their two-year COP presidency.

title: SQU to host Italian Language Lectureship
body:
The Italian Language Lectureship presentation will be held at the Sultan Qaboos University (SQU) as part of the ongoing ‘Italian Language Week in the World 2026’, the annual initiative promoted by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation through Italian Embassies and Consulates around the world, on Monday. The event will provide an opportunity to highlight the Italian Language Lectureship as an important linguistic and cultural bridge between Italy and the Sultanate of Oman, and as a platform for strengthening academic, cultural and educational exchanges between the two countries. The first part of the programme will feature a presentation by Prof Silvia Belicchi, Italian Language Lecturer at Sultan Qaboos University, introducing the Lectureship, its activities and its contribution to promoting the study of Italian language and culture among SQU students. This will be followed by a presentation by the Embassy of Italy in Muscat, delivered by Francesca Gimigliano, Commercial Attaché, focusing on language diplomacy as an important component of cultural diplomacy. The 26th edition of the Italian Language Week, held under the theme: Lingua gentile, lingua geniale: ideare, progettare, creare con l’italiano - “A Gracious Language, a Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian” in Oman includes initiatives addressed to both academic audiences and younger generations, reflecting the Embassy’s commitment to promoting Italian language and culture through education, cultural diplomacy and people-to-people exchanges. Through its collaboration with Dar Al Atta’a ‘Let’s Read’ Programme, the Embassy will also bring the Italian Language Week in the World closer to younger audiences with a special children’s event entitled “Pimpa Goes on a Journey Through Italy!” at Let’s Read Library Bus. Children, aged 5 to 9 years, will be given an opportunity to discover Italy and the Italian language in a fun and engaging environment through the beloved Italian cartoon character Pimpa. The programme will include a cartoon screening, puppet show and fun activities. This initiative reflects the Embassy’s commitment to introducing Italian language and culture to younger generations through creative and accessible educational experiences.

title: Russian strikes kill two, injure five in Sumy region in one day
body:
The National Police reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
“In the Sumy community, a 30-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone attack. A 42-year-old man was killed in guided aerial bomb strikes, and women aged 60 and 86 were injured. The enemy attacked a house with a UAV, injuring a 23-year-old woman,” the statement said.
In addition, according to the police, a 34-year-old man was injured in a Russian drone strike in the Shostka community.

title: Occupied Oleshky Turned Into ‘Death Trap’, Sybiha Says
body:
Russian forces have turned the occupied city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region into a “death trap,” leaving approximately 1,700 remaining residents trapped under acute starvation, pervasive mining, and relentless drone surveillance, Ukrainia Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned .
In an official public appeal, Sybiha disclosed that the sole overland exit route from the ruined municipality has been heavily mined and placed under continuous Russian drone targeting, rendering escape attempts potentially lethal for trapped non-combatants.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Those who try to flee risk their lives. The adjacent river is also mined. Residents doubt they will survive this winter. The hospital has run out of medicine. Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in houses, as the Russians forbid residents from burying them,” Sybiha stated.
The foreign minister described extreme shortages of basic sustenance, noting that isolated civilians are struggling to endure on minimal rations while confronting harassment from occupation troops.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Sybiha added.
Reiterating that Kyiv has repeatedly pressed for safe civilian evacuations and unhindered humanitarian access, Sybiha issued an urgent appeal to the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and international partners to mobilize every diplomatic and operational conduit to deliver emergency supplies and evacuate those seeking to depart.
“People cannot survive on statements of concern. They need action. They need a way out. And they need it now,” Sybiha emphasized.
Oleshky, situated on the east (left) bank of the Dnipro River approximately five kilometers southeast of the regional capital of Kherson, has been under Russian military occupation since the initial weeks of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The city has been completely cut off from authorized commercial freight convoys and organized institutional aid since late May.
While earlier demographic assessments by Ukrainian authorities indicated several thousand residents remained scattered across the wider river basin, civilian numbers within the municipal core have contracted to roughly 1,700 as conditions have deteriorated ahead of sub-zero winter temperatures.
Local municipal officials have confirmed that central utility grids – including drinking water supply, electrical networks, and municipal gas heating – have suffered significant damage.
With ground logistics paralyzed by dense minefields, destroyed bridge spans, and persistent Russian first-person view (FPV) drone patrols along the riverfront, Ukrainian defense units have intermittently deployed heavy multi-rotor transport drones to air-drop food and medical packages directly into residential yards .
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets previously reported that his office had documented hundreds of verified appeals from civilians trapped in the enclave, noting that residents desperate to flee have attempted to navigate active minefields on foot due to the absence of negotiated humanitarian corridors.
The escalating emergency in Oleshky has attracted top-level international diplomatic intervention.
On Friday, Oct. 16, Pope Leo XIV held a telephone consultation with Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge an immediate localized ceasefire in Oleshky , calling for verified arrangements to permit emergency food and medical deliveries alongside the safe, voluntary evacuation of non-combatants.
The Vatican confirmed that the pope expressed deep concern over the grave humanitarian collapse in the municipality and pressed Moscow to facilitate unhindered relief operations.
In its official readout of the discussion, the Kremlin claimed that Putin offered what it described as a “detailed explanation” attributing responsibility for the municipal situation to Ukrainian authorities, while expressing general willingness to coordinate with Vatican initiatives.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has similarly characterized the humanitarian situation in Oleshky as desperate, appealing directly to the Russian Federation to fulfill its legal obligations under international humanitarian law as an occupying power by permitting the immediate evacuation of civilians and allowing international aid agencies unfettered access.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: New Road Opens Gateway to East Kazakhstan’s Altai Wonders
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA — Glacier-covered peaks, alpine lakes, thermal springs and ancient burial grounds lie scattered across the East Kazakhstan Region’s Altai Mountains, where reaching some of the most remarkable destinations has long been an adventure in itself. A newly repaired 13-kilometer road section leading to Rakhmanov Springs is easing access to the region’s mountain landscapes and opening new possibilities for travelers. Altai Mountains. Photo credit: Depositphotos. Click to see the map in full size. The map is designed by The Astana Times. According to the Kazakh Ministry of Tourism and Sports, approximately 446,000 tourists visited the East Kazakhstan Region in 2025, including more than 26,000 visitors to Katon-Karagai State National Nature Park. Yet exploring the region still requires careful planning, with long distances, mountainous terrain and seasonal conditions shaping the travel experience, local tour operators said. Katon-Karagai: from Rakhmanov Springs to Muztau Stretching across more than 643,000 hectares near Kazakhstan’s borders with Russia and China, Katon-Karagai State National Nature Park encompasses forests, alpine meadows, mountain rivers and glacial landscapes. Its attractions range from nature trails and cultural sites to remote locations requiring multi-day expeditions. Alexander Myakinin of Altai Travel described the district as a suitable starting point for exploring the region, particularly for visitors with limited time. “A three- to five-day itinerary allows visitors to discover the nature of the Altai , visit the national park, see mountain rivers, waterfalls and lakes, explore maral deer farms and cultural sites, and learn about the region’s history. There are numerous hiking trails of varying difficulty, so travelers can choose a route suited to their abilities,” Myakinin told The Astana Times. Katon-Karagai State National Nature Park. Photo credit: toor.kz Among the district’s principal attractions are Rakhmanov Springs, known for their naturally occurring radon-containing thermal waters. Located near Rakhmanov Lake, the destination attracts visitors interested in wellness retreats, hiking and mountain recreation. The surrounding area offers waterfalls, forest trails and viewpoints overlooking the Altai Mountains. Access to the springs improved following the completion of repairs on a 13-kilometer section of the Oskemen -Altai-Ulken Naryn-Katon-Karagai-Rakhmanov Springs highway, which opened Oct. 4. According to the ministry, the previously unpaved mountain stretch could take motorists up to 2.5 to three hours to cross. The new road surface has eased travel along the section, which now includes designated stopping areas with mountain views. For a shorter visit, local tour operator Svetlana Chakileva suggested a three-day route through Katon-Karagai, allowing time to explore Rakhmanov Lake and the springs. She also mentioned local apiaries and maral deer farms, where travelers can learn about beekeeping and deer breeding, two activities closely associated with the region’s rural economy. More demanding adventures lead toward Muztau , also known as Mount Belukha, the highest peak in the Altai Mountains at approximately 4,506 meters above sea level. Surrounded by glaciers and mountain valleys, it attracts experienced trekkers and mountaineers. Nearby Yazevoe Lake offers views of the peak in clear weather, and longer expeditions lead toward remote waterfalls and glacial areas. Muztau. Photo credit: visiteast.kz. Myakinin said reaching Muztau’s foothills overland typically requires an eight- to 10-day expedition involving horseback travel. Helicopter excursions offer an alternative for seeing the mountain within a single day, subject to weather conditions and availability. A new tourist route could also make the area more accessible to hikers. In September, Katon-Karagai National Park introduced the Altai Trails route, which begins near Rakhmanov Springs and continues through the Sarsembay tract toward the foot of Muztau. The route is intended to provide an alternative to existing trails affected by difficult terrain and border-zone restrictions. The district’s appeal also extends to its archaeological heritage. Near the village of Berel, excavations have uncovered Saka-era burial mounds containing preserved horse remains, textiles, wooden objects and ceremonial artifacts dating back more than 2,000 years. The Berel State Historical and Cultural Museum Reserve introduces visitors to these discoveries and the burial traditions of ancient nomadic communities. Beyond Katon-Karagai: mountain lakes, historic routes and winter trails Travelers with more time can explore other parts of the East Kazakhstan Region, where high-altitude lakes, rugged mountain roads and recreational areas offer experiences distinct from those found in Katon-Karagai. For a weeklong itinerary, Myakinin suggested visiting Lake Markakol , the Old Austrian Road and the Bukhtarma shoreline, with additional time in Oskemen, the regional capital. These destinations cover considerable distances, making transportation and the choice of route important considerations. Lake Markakol. Photo credit: visiteast.kz Situated approximately 1,447 meters above sea level between the Kurchum and Azutau mountain ranges, Lake Markakol stretches nearly 38 kilometers in length. Surrounded by forests and mountain slopes, the freshwater lake is known for its cold waters and uskuch, a fish found in the lake. The nearby Markakol State Nature Reserve protects wildlife and plant species, attracting visitors interested in hiking, photography and nature-based travel. The lake can be incorporated into an expedition along the Old Austrian Road, a historic mountain route connecting the Katon-Karagai and Markakol areas. Built in the early 20th century by Austro-Hungarian prisoners of war, the road winds through remote mountain terrain and is now popular among travelers seeking off-road adventures. Chakileva suggested allowing five days for an itinerary incorporating this route, with the usual travel season extending from mid-June through late August, depending on weather and road conditions. Elsewhere in the region, the Kiin-Kerish tract in Kurchum District offers an entirely different landscape. Its red, orange and pale-colored clay formations, shaped by erosion into hills and ridges, resemble a desert, contrasting with the forests and alpine lakes of the Altai. Kiin-Kerish Valley. Photo credit: travelbook.kz. For a more relaxed holiday, the Bukhtarma Reservoir along the Yertis River remains a popular summer destination, with beaches, boating, fishing and holiday accommodation along its shoreline, including the Samar area. According to Chakileva, lakeside recreation continues to attract visitors, and interest in more active experiences, particularly jeep tours, trekking and helicopter excursions, has also increased. The waterfall on the Bolshoi Kok-Kol River (Big Blue Lake River). Photo credit: Live Journal’s website The choice of destination also depends on the season. Summer is particularly suited to mountain expeditions and water-based recreation, and September brings autumn colors to the forests and valleys. During winter, skiers, freeride enthusiasts and snowmobilers head to Ridder , a mountain town near the West Altai State Nature Reserve, as well as ski resorts near Oskemen, including Altai Alps and Nurtau. Despite the popularity of Katon-Karagai, Myakinin highlighted that travelers should also pay closer attention to the western part of the Altai. “The West Altai, especially the surroundings of Ridder, remains undeservedly overlooked. I consider it a compact version of Katon-Karagai. This destination has enormous tourism potential, with dense taiga forests, clear rivers, high-altitude lakes and established routes for hiking and winter recreation. I am sure that interest in this area will continue to grow in the coming years,” he said. Easier access, but planning remains essential Improving transportation remains an important part of tourism development in the East Kazakhstan Region, where some destinations are separated by 400-500 kilometers and mountain routes can be difficult to navigate. Alongside road improvements, a new airport is under construction in Katon-Karagai District, with completion scheduled for the end of 2026. The project includes a 2,200-meter runway and a passenger terminal designed to accommodate up to 150 travelers per hour. The airport is intended to improve connections with Kazakhstan’s major cities and reduce travel time to the district. However, scheduled passenger services have yet to be announced, and reaching individual attractions will still require ground transportation. Local tour operators said advance arrangements remain essential, particularly during the peak summer season, when demand for accommodation, transportation and qualified guides can exceed availability. “The biggest mistake when planning a trip is not planning it at all. People arrive and start looking for guides and vehicles on the spot. You need to research everything in advance, find a guide and book accommodation beforehand, because demand has grown significantly, while accommodation options are limited and there are not enough guides,” said Chakileva. She added that traveling without a knowledgeable guide can affect both safety and the overall experience, particularly when visitors reach natural or historical attractions without understanding their significance. Kiin-Kerish-tract. Photo credit: visiteast.kz Although Rakhmanov Springs can be reached by an ordinary passenger vehicle under suitable conditions, more demanding mountain routes may require four-wheel-drive transportation and experienced local drivers. Travelers should also prepare for rapidly changing weather, limited fuel availability and unreliable mobile coverage in remote areas. Myakinin said temperatures can fluctuate sharply even in summer, making warm clothing and appropriate equipment essential. Some protected areas and border territories also require registration or advance permits, depending on the destination. The cost of travel varies according to the itinerary and level of service. Myakinin estimated that one-day excursions and hiking trips start at approximately 20,000-30,000 tenge (US$45-65), while individual premium programs involving complex logistics or helicopter flights can cost 500,000 to one million tenge (US$1,100-2,200) or more. Chakileva said organized multi-day tours generally range from 50,000 to 100,000 tenge (US$110-220) per person per day, depending on accommodation, transportation and guide services. As road improvements and new transport connections make the East Kazakhstan Region’s remote destinations more accessible, growing tourism also raises questions about preserving the natural environment. Asked which lesser-known attractions deserve greater attention, Chakileva offered a different perspective. “I actually try not to talk publicly about such places because I believe some locations should remain undiscovered. Let people visit the places they already know about. As for the places they don’t know, I would rather keep it that way for now, because some areas should remain wild,” she said. The post New Road Opens Gateway to East Kazakhstan’s Altai Wonders appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Moscow’s other front: Why Ukraine’s churches are a security issue
body:
The CIA director and the Vatican’s foreign minister were in Moscow in August. The spy chief drew the coverage; the Archbishop’s visit showed religion belongs in any analysis and resolution of Russia’s war.
On 25 August 2026, two very different representatives of Western power were doing business in Moscow. CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew in unannounced aboard a US military transport for talks with Russian intelligence officials, delivering a bleak assessment of the war and warning against any attack on the Baltic states . He did not meet President Putin, and President Trump dismissed the trip as “semi-routine” . That same day, Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican’s British-born Foreign Secretary , met Sergei Lavrov and declared that the war in Ukraine must end . His five-day programme also took in meeting the Moscow Patriarchate and the small Catholic community.
The visits were not coordinated. Ratcliffe embodied raw US power; Archbishop Gallagher embodied soft Vatican influence exercised through access, historical memory and communion with believers across frontiers. The timing inevitably invited a “Bad-cop (Ratcliffe)/Good-cop (Gallagher)” reading. Lavrov dismissed this, saying both visitors merely wanted to “come and talk” .
Strategic culture shaped the two missions differently. Western institutions tend to separate intelligence, diplomacy, military power and religion; Moscow treats them as mutually reinforcing. The Kremlin and the Moscow Patriarchate narratives combine territorial, historical, civilisational and spiritual claims, presenting NATO enlargement and Catholic pastoral activity as two expressions of the same Western encroachment. The war is therefore being fought not only over territory, but over the spiritual inheritance of contested lands.
Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy both claim catholicity – universality and fullness – but organise it differently. Catholic local churches are united through their bishops under the Pope’s supreme authority. Orthodoxy is a communion of self-governing, or autocephalous , churches ordered by patriarchal precedence rather than a single leader. Each normally claims exclusive jurisdiction within its “canonical territory”, while authority to actually recognise a new autocephalous church remains disputed.
Russian usage has moved from administrative boundary to civilisational concept. Moscow measures canonical territory not by Russia’s borders, but by where the 988-AD Baptism of Rus is believed to have reached. Despite the fall of the Soviet Union, the Patriarchate still claims jurisdiction across the former territory – including Ukraine.
To secular strategic audiences, this may appear an obscure ecclesiastical quarrel. It is not. Ecclesiology – how the Church is constituted and governed – raises a question of sovereignty: can an independent Ukraine possess a church independent of Moscow? Constantinople’s 2019 grant of autocephaly to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine aligned ecclesiastical jurisdiction with Ukraine’s borders. Moscow continues to viscerally reject this as spiritual theft.
Ukraine’s ecclesiastical landscape is divided among three principal Eastern Churches: the independent Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), supported by most Ukrainians identifying as Orthodox; the minority Ukrainian Orthodox Church (UOC), historically linked to Moscow but claiming independence since 2022; and the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church (UGCC) in communion with Rome. Their competing allegiances make church governance a question of sovereignty and geopolitical orientation as much as theology.
Under Ukraine’s 2024 law on religious organisations linked to Russia , the state concluded in 2025 that the UOC’s Kyiv governing body – the Metropolia – remained affiliated with the Russian Orthodox Church. It then opened proceedings to dissolve it and transfer its non-religious assets to the state . Pressure has also moved to the diocesan level: on 30 August 2026, the Zaporizhzhia eparchy was reportedly ordered to sever ties with the Metropolia , according to the Union of Orthodox Journalists , whose coverage reflects the UOC’s position.
A separate judgment shows why Kyiv must proceed carefully. On 6 April 2026, the Sixth Administrative Court of Appeal found that officials had failed to consider the Metropolia’s objections to allegedly biased members of a panel conducting an earlier, 2023 review of its charter. The court neither found the UOC independent of Moscow nor overturned the separate 2025 investigation underpinning the dissolution case. It cancelled only the order approving the earlier review and required reconsideration .
This distinction is legally important but strategically uncomfortable. Each procedural failure gives Moscow evidence from a Ukrainian court that the state failed to act fairly. Combined with Human Rights Watch’s warning that the law is overly broad, it enables Russia to recast a legitimate Ukrainian security concern as religious persecution.
Yet legal precision does not require moral neutrality. Ukraine must uphold due process because it is fighting for government under law, as this ruling itself demonstrates. But expecting a population under bombardment to view structures linked to a Patriarchate that calls the war “Holy” solely through the abstract language of religious liberty is politically unrealistic and humanly unreasonable.
After the Soviet collapse, Orthodoxy offered Russia what a discredited communism no longer could: continuity, sacrifice, moral order and national destiny. Under Putin and Patriarch Kirill, these themes converged on the Russkiy Mir, or “Russian World” – a civilisation bound by language, memory and Orthodox inheritance. Under this concept, Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia form a single spiritual and territorial space, with Ukraine as its central religious pillar. The 988-AD Baptism of Rus under Prince Volodymyr – Vladimir, in Moscow’s telling – supplies the foundational story. Without Kyiv, Russia can still hold an empire, but not the account of where that empire began, nor the spiritual legitimacy that this confers.
Putin’s 2021 essay “On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians” called them “one people”. Theology and territory were fused explicitly in March 2024, when a decree of the World Russian People’s Council , chaired by Kirill, described the invasion as a “Holy War” defending “the single spiritual space of Holy Russia” and declared that “the entire territory of modern Ukraine should enter Russia’s exclusive zone of influence” .
In July 2026, the Patriarchate published Kirill’s War: Beyond Visible Causes and Consequences , which casts the war as a metaphysical conflict, describes a soldier’s death as “co-crucifixion” and insists that “first and foremost the Church must be mobilised” . Regular religious practice in Russia remains weak , but observance is the wrong metric. The Patriarchate’s power is institutional, not parochial: it works through military chaplaincy, state media and national commemoration, not local attendance.
Imperial ambition, not theology, defined the invasion. Putin does not conduct foreign policy from a catechism. Religion is not the cause of this war; it is a resource for propagating, justifying and consolidating Russia’s invasion . Russkiy Mir causes Ukraine’s separation to be perceived as an amputation from Russia’s national soul rather than as a geopolitical territorial loss. A ceasefire can determine where Russian soldiers stop fighting without determining where Moscow genuinely believes Russia ends.
Nothing embodies Moscow’s fear of religious encroachment more sharply than the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. It originates in the 1596 Union of Brest, when a number of Orthodox bishops in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth entered communion with Rome whilst keeping their Byzantine rite and traditions: Rome saw proof that Eastern Christians could retain their identity under papal authority; Moscow saw Polish-inspired Catholic expansion in Orthodox vestments. In western Ukraine, it became guardian of Ukrainian language and national memory; thus, Soviet authorities used the 1946 Lviv assembly to liquidate the union . Its re-emergence – after surviving underground for four decades – fused Russia’s worst fears: Polish influence, Vatican infiltration and Ukrainian nationalism.
For Moscow, John Paul II’s 1979 visit to Poland supplied the contemporary warning: religious authority could strengthen national identity outside state control. The Catholic-inspired workers’ trade union movement Solidarność mobilised within fifteen months and would influence Communism’s downfall in a way Moscow could neither control nor suppress, belatedly answering Stalin’s purported question about how many divisions the Pope actually commanded.
That history explains both Moscow’s suspicion of Rome and Rome’s value as an intermediary, and why Archbishop Gallagher’s meetings with the Patriarchate mattered as much as his meeting with Lavrov. By condemning Russia’s aggression without echoing Western policy, the Vatican can mediate across religious channels and pursue humanitarian missions – though it risks enabling Moscow to manipulate any contact for propaganda purposes.
Four practical steps follow. They require attention more than additional funding.
Treat the Moscow Patriarchate as a warning indicator. Synodal decrees and episcopal appointments in occupied dioceses are open, cheap to monitor and rarely noticed strategically. One example is Moscow’s July 2026 appointment of a former Soviet military officer to a Ukrainian diocese carved from the UOC’s Kherson eparchy , renaming its seat from Ukrainian Oleshky to its old Russian Imperial name Aleshki and classifying the territory as “Donbas and Novorossiya” – effectively annexation through church boundaries, personnel and place names. Agencies should also track how death framed as religious duty enters preaching, military chaplaincy and memorial ritual. September’s frontline tour of Prince Dmitry Donskoy’s relics is one example: not conclusive alone, but evidence of sacred sacrifice being used to sustain soldiers and society through a longer or escalating war.
Draft the religious annex now, not in the last fortnight of talks. Negotiations must address contested churches, Moscow-linked parishes, clergy and property alongside territory and security guarantees. Despite institutional complexities, this area requires ownership and access to relevant expertise, especially given Moscow’s propensity for weaponising negotiations. Allies should establish both now, before Russia frames ecclesiastical jurisdiction as an internal civilisational matter.
Help Kyiv make its legal process unimpeachable. Ukraine faces a genuine security problem, and no state at war is obliged to tolerate ecclesiastical structures acting on behalf of its invader. But a broad-brush ban is self-defeating. Russia already publishes reports alleging the “persecution” of the Moscow-aligned church , while UN special rapporteurs have raised concerns that the law targets presumed affiliation rather than proven threats. Links to Moscow may be real but should be demonstrated case by case. Western assistance should thus support evidence-based adjudication and genuine appeal rights, denying Moscow the victimhood narrative it promotes among its Western and Global South fellow travellers.
Disaggregate Orthodoxy and protect the Vatican channel. Orthodoxy is not the Moscow Patriarchate. The Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople – first among equals within Orthodoxy – the Orthodox Church of Ukraine and other autocephalous churches require sustained engagement rather than occasional courtesy. Treating Orthodoxy as a single bloc concedes Moscow’s usurping claim to speak for it. Equally, the Holy See is not an arm of Western foreign policy, and its usefulness depends on not becoming one. Its channel – which has delivered where state diplomacy could not, including on prisoner exchanges and the return of deported children – should be protected from allied pressure to align its public messaging.
Western policymakers seek to resolve wars through borders, treaties and security guarantees: the familiar architecture of the Westphalian order . Yet Moscow views Ukraine not simply as a sovereign state, but as part of a “single spiritual space” rooted in “the Baptism of Rus.” A territorial settlement may stop the fighting while preserving the religious claim that helped legitimise it – and with it, an ideological basis for renewed conflict. The West cannot negotiate Russia out of its theology, but it must understand its strategic consequences. A settlement may determine where the border lies; the harder question is whether Moscow accepts that the border settles anything. In Ukraine, control of church history supports claims to political authority; thus, Moscow’s claim to Ukraine’s past becomes a claim over its future.

title: How to Make Zero-Training Tabular Predictions with NVIDIA Structured Data Models
body:
In this tutorial, we implement Structured Data Models , NVIDIA’s new library that puts several pretrained foundation models for tables behind one PyTorch interface, and use it to make predictions without training. The library wraps TabICLv2 and KumoTabular for single tables and KumoRelational for whole relational databases, and each of them answers by in-context learning: we hand the model a set of labeled rows and the rows we want predicted, and it returns probabilities or a full predictive distribution in one forward pass. We start with the library’s typed table tensors, compare the two tabular models against trained scikit-learn baselines, reuse an encoded context across many queries, read calibrated prediction intervals off a regression, and scale to twenty classes. We then look at the places where the defaults quietly do the wrong thing: a preprocessing recipe that drops timestamp and text columns and an explainer with two traps in it, before building a small three-table shop database and predicting customer activity from it directly, including the one argument that separates an honest relational model from a leaky one. Both would reach the model as features. Override, or ask: text='infer', id='infer'.") table = sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(df, sdm.infer_stypes(df, text="infer", id="infer")) print("

Numbers come back float32") print(" (the numerical block is one float tensor), nullable Int64 becomes float with NaN, and strings") print(" marked categorical come back as a pandas category.") base = pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01 08:00:00"] * 3).as_unit("ns") whole = pd.DataFrame({"t": base}) nanos = pd.DataFrame({"t": base + pd.to_timedelta([0, 0, 1], unit="ns")}) print(f"
 datetime64[ns], whole seconds: {sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(whole, {'t': 'datetime'}).size()} OK") try: sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(nanos, {"t": "datetime"}) except Exception as e: print(f" same column, one value 1 ns later: {type(e).__name__}: {str(e).split(':')[0]}") ok = sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(nanos.assign(t=nanos.t.dt.floor("us")), {"t": "datetime"}) print(f" floor('us') first: {ok.size()} OK") print(" SDM stores datetimes as int64 microseconds and Arrow refuses any cast that drops a digit. The") print(" unit is not the problem; a single value with nanosecond digits fails the whole column.") return "6 columns -> 5 typed blocks; text and id need opting in" typed_tables() Everything in the library flows through TableTensor, a PyTorch tensor subclass that keeps one typed block per semantic type: numerical, categorical, datetime, text and id. infer_stypes decides the types, and with its defaults it gets two things wrong on a realistic support-ticket frame: the free-text comment becomes a categorical with four hundred levels and the ticket id becomes a number, so both would reach a model as features. Passing text and id inference flags fixes that. The round trip back to pandas preserves every value, missing ones included, but not every dtype: numbers return as float32 because the numerical block is a single float tensor, nullable integers become floats with NaN, and categorical strings return as a pandas category. On pandas 2.x the string columns print as object rather than str and the timestamp goes in at nanosecond resolution; the same values come back either way. One more trap is worth knowing before you load a real event log: the library stores datetimes as integer microseconds, and Arrow refuses any cast that would drop a digit. A nanosecond column of whole seconds converts fine, but a single value with nanosecond digits fails the whole column, so we floor timestamps to microseconds first. Check out the Full CODES here . Zero-training classification: two foundation models vs. two trained baselines") def zero_training(): df = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True).frame.sample(frac=1, random_state=0).reset_index(drop=True) table = as_table(df, "target") n_ctx = 300 x_ctx, y_ctx = table[:n_ctx].drop_columns("target"), table[:n_ctx, "target"] x_q, y_q = table[n_ctx:].drop_columns("target"), df.target.to_numpy()[n_ctx:] rows = [] for name, make in [("TabICLv2", lambda: sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE)), ("KumoTabular (small)", lambda: sdm.models.KumoTabular(size="small", device=DEVICE))]: model = make() torch.manual_seed(0) proba = model(x_context=x_ctx, y_context=y_ctx, x_query=x_q, num_estimators=4).to_pandas() rows.append((name, "none", proba.idxmax(axis=1).astype(int).to_numpy(), proba["1"].to_numpy())) X, y = df.drop(columns="target"), df.target for name, est in [("LogisticRegression", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))), ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0))]: est.fit(X[:n_ctx], y[:n_ctx]) rows.append((name, "fit on 300 rows", est.predict(X[n_ctx:]), est.predict_proba(X[n_ctx:])[:, 1])) print(f" breast cancer: {n_ctx} labelled rows, {len(y_q)} to predict, 30 numeric features
") print(f" {'model':22s} {'training':16s} {'accuracy':>9s} {'AUC':>7s}") for name, training, pred, score in rows: print(f" {name:22s} {training:16s} {np.mean(pred == y_q):9.3f} {roc_auc_score(y_q, score):7.3f}") print("
 The output is itself a TableTensor: one probability column per class, named by label.") best = max(rows[:2], key=lambda r: np.mean(r[2] == y_q)) return f"{best[0]} {np.mean(best[2] == y_q):.3f} accuracy with no training" zero_training() The tabular models take labelled context rows and unlabelled query rows and return a TableTensor with one probability column per class, named by label, so there is no fit step and no hyperparameters. On the breast cancer dataset, with three hundred labelled rows and two hundred and sixty-nine to predict, TabICLv2 and KumoTabular reach 0.970 accuracy and AUCs of 0.996 and 0.995 with no training, against 0.970 and 0.993 for a logistic regression and 0.967 and 0.992 for gradient boosting, both fitted on the same three hundred rows. num_estimators sets how many differently preprocessed views of the data the model averages over, which is the library’s built-in ensembling.  fit() encodes the context once into a key/value cache; predict() only runs the queries.") print(" clear() frees it. Nothing is learned: fit() here means 'remember these examples'.") return f"{t_forward / (t_fit + t_predict):.1f}x faster for five batches" kv_cache() Calling the model directly re-encodes the context on every call. When the same labelled rows will answer many batches of queries, fit encodes the context once into a key and value cache and predict then runs only the query rows; clear frees the cache. Nothing is learned in fit, which here means remember these examples. Answering five batches of thirty rows against the same four hundred context rows finished several times faster this way on our CPU, and once the context was cached, each further batch cost a small fraction of a full forward pass. The exact ratio depends on the machine, which is why the cell measures it rather than assuming it. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser @section("5. Regression returns a distribution: 999 quantiles, and how honest they are") def quantile_regression(): df = load_diabetes(as_frame=True).frame.sample(frac=1, random_state=0).reset_index(drop=True) table = sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(df, sdm.infer_stypes(df), device=DEVICE) model = sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE) torch.manual_seed(0) q = model(x_context=table[:300].drop_columns("target"), y_context=table[:300, "target"], x_query=table[300:].drop_columns("target"), num_estimators=4).to_pandas() y = df.target.to_numpy()[300:] print(f" output: {q.shape[1]} columns {list(q.columns[:3])} ... {list(q.columns[-2:])} per query row") X, Y = df.drop(columns="target"), df.target rmse = lambda p: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(p) - y) ** 2))) print(f"
 {'point prediction':34s} {'RMSE':>7s}") print(f" {'TabICLv2 median (q500), no training':34s} {rmse(q['q500']):7.2f}") print(f" {'RidgeCV, fit on 300 rows':34s} {rmse(RidgeCV().fit(X[:300], Y[:300]).predict(X[300:])):7.2f}") print(f" {'HistGradientBoosting, fit on 300':34s} " f"{rmse(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X[:300], Y[:300]).predict(X[300:])):7.2f}") print(f"
 {'interval':12s} {'nominal':>8s} {'empirical coverage':>19s} {'mean width':>11s}") coverage = {} for lo, hi in [("q250", "q750"), ("q100", "q900"), ("q050", "q950")]: nominal = (int(hi[1:]) - int(lo[1:])) / 1000 coverage[nominal] = float(np.mean((y >= q[lo]) & (y <= q[hi]))) print(f" {lo}-{hi:6s} {nominal:8.0%} {coverage[nominal]:19.3f} {np.mean(q[hi] - q[lo]):11.1f}") print("
 The quantiles come from one forward pass over 300 examples, yet the 80% and 90% intervals") print(" cover close to 80% and 90% of held-out targets. The 50% band runs a little narrow.") return f"median RMSE {rmse(q['q500']):.1f}; 80% interval covers {coverage[0.8]:.1%}" quantile_regression() For regression, the model does not return a single number. It returns 999 quantiles per query row, a full predictive distribution read off one forward pass. On the diabetes dataset with three hundred labelled rows, the median of that distribution has an RMSE of 53.6, slightly better than RidgeCV at 54.3 and clearly better than gradient boosting at 64.7, both trained on the same rows. The more useful property is calibration: the interval between the 10th and 90th percentiles contains 81.0 percent of the held-out targets and the 5th to 95th percentile interval 91.5 percent, close to their nominal 80 and 90 percent, while the 50 percent band runs somewhat narrow at 43.7 percent.
