Twenty classes from one forward pass") def many_classes(): X, y = make_classification(n_samples=800, n_features=12, n_informative=8, n_redundant=2, n_classes=20, n_clusters_per_class=1, class_sep=1.5, random_state=0) df = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=[f"f{i}" for i in range(12)]) df["label"] = [f"c{v:02d}" for v in y] table = as_table(df, "label") model = sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE) torch.manual_seed(0) t0 = time.time() proba = model(x_context=table[:600].drop_columns("label"), y_context=table[:600, "label"], x_query=table[600:].drop_columns("label"), num_estimators=1).to_pandas() secs = time.time() - t0 acc = float(np.mean(proba.idxmax(axis=1).to_numpy() == df.label.to_numpy()[600:])) hgb = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X[:600], y[:600]) acc_hgb = float(np.mean(hgb.predict(X[600:]) == y[600:])) print(f" 20 balanced classes, 600 labelled rows (30 per class), 200 queries") print(f" TabICLv2, no training {proba.shape[1]} probability columns, accuracy {acc:.3f} ({secs:.1f}s)") print(f" HistGradientBoosting, trained accuracy {acc_hgb:.3f}") print("
 The pretrained head has a fixed number of class slots. Past that, SDM splits the problem") print(" into error-correcting output codes (sdm.models.ecoc) and recombines the log-probabilities,") print(" so the caller still gets one column per label without doing anything.") return f"20 classes: {acc:.3f} vs {acc_hgb:.3f} for gradient boosting" many_classes() The pretrained classification head has a fixed number of class slots, and the library handles problems with more classes than that through error-correcting output codes, splitting the problem into smaller coded subproblems and recombining the log-probabilities. The caller never sees this: on a balanced twenty-class synthetic problem with thirty labelled rows per class, TabICLv2 returns twenty probability columns and reaches 0.760 accuracy in a single forward pass, against 0.615 for gradient boosting trained on the same rows. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser def make_tickets(n=1600, seed=1): """Support tickets whose escalation depends on WHEN they were opened and WHAT they say.""" rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) opened = pd.Timestamp("2026-03-02") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 86_400 * 56, n), unit="s") neutral = ["order", "item", "delivery", "account", "app", "invoice", "question", "help", "update", "status"] hot = ["refund", "broken", "charged", "twice"] comments, has_hot = [], [] for _ in range(n): words = list(rng.choice(neutral, rng.integers(4, 9))) flag = rng.random() < 0.3 if flag: words.insert(rng.integers(len(words)), rng.choice(hot)) comments.append(" ".join(words)) has_hot.append(flag) hour, weekend = np.asarray(opened.hour), np.asarray(opened.dayofweek >= 5) amount = rng.gamma(2, 40, n).round(2) logit = (-1.6 + 2.2 * np.array(has_hot) + 1.4 * ((hour >= 22) | (hour < 6)) + 1.0 * weekend + 0.004 * (amount - 80)) escalated = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int) return pd.DataFrame({"amount": amount, "channel": rng.choice(["web", "app", "phone"], n), "opened_at": opened, "comment": comments, "escalated": escalated}) @section("7. Recipes: the default one drops your timestamps and your text, and says so once") def recipes(): df = make_tickets() stypes = sdm.infer_stypes(df, overrides={"escalated": "categorical"}, text="infer") table = sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(df, stypes, device=DEVICE) x_ctx, y_ctx = table[:1000].drop_columns("escalated"), table[:1000, "escalated"] x_q, y_q = table[1000:].drop_columns("escalated"), df.escalated.to_numpy()[1000:] print(f" columns: {', '.join(f'{c}={s}' for c, s in stypes.items())}") print(" escalation is driven by night-time / weekend opening and by words like 'refund'
") default = sdm.models.TabICLv2.default_recipe() with_calendar = sdm.models.TabICLv2.default_recipe() with_calendar.prepend_features(sp.StypeDispatch( datetime=sp.AddCalendarFields(["hour", "weekday"], encoding="cyclic"))) calendar_and_text = sp.StypeDispatch( datetime=sp.AddCalendarFields(["hour", "weekday"], encoding="cyclic"), text=sp.TFIDF(ngram_range=(1, 1), max_features=64)) with_both = sdm.models.TabICLv2.default_recipe() with_both.prepend_features(calendar_and_text) model = sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE) aucs = {} for label, recipe in [("default recipe", default), ("+ AddCalendarFields(hour, weekday)", with_calendar), ("+ AddCalendarFields + TFIDF(64 terms)", with_both)]: torch.manual_seed(0) proba = model(x_context=x_ctx, y_context=y_ctx, x_query=x_q, num_estimators=4, recipe=recipe).to_pandas() aucs[label] = roc_auc_score(y_q, proba["1"]) print(f" {label:40s} AUC {aucs[label]:.3f}") print("
 The default TabICLv2 recipe dispatches on stype and only has branches for categorical and") print(" numerical columns, so datetime and text columns never become features. SDM does say so, in") print(" the RuntimeWarning above, but it is a warn-once: it fires the first time and is suppressed for") print(" the rest of the process. Every later model in the same notebook or service drops those columns") print(" in silence. The fix is two processors, prepended to the features:") print(textwrap.indent(repr(calendar_and_text), " ")) return " -> ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in aucs.values()) + " AUC" recipes() Preprocessing in the library is a Recipe of composable processors, and the default TabICLv2 recipe dispatches on semantic type with branches only for categorical and numerical columns. Timestamp and text columns therefore never become features. On support tickets whose escalation depends on when they were opened and on words such as refund, the default recipe scores an AUC of 0.525, close to chance. The library does emit a RuntimeWarning naming the ignored column types. Still, it is a warn-once: it fires the first time and is suppressed for the rest of the process, so every later model in the same notebook or service drops those columns in silence. Prepending two processors fixes it: AddCalendarFields turns the timestamp into cyclic hour and weekday features, lifting the AUC to 0.634, and TFIDF adds the comment’s terms, lifting it to 0.789. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser @section("8. Explaining a prediction: two traps inside the explainer") def explain(): rng = np.random.default_rng(2) X = rng.normal(size=(500, 8)) true = {"x0": 2.0, "x3": -1.5, "x5": 1.0} logit = sum(w * X[:, int(c[1:])] for c, w in true.items()) df = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=[f"x{i}" for i in range(8)]) df["y"] = (rng.random(500) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int) table = as_table(df, "y") model = sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE) ctx = dict(x_context=table[:400].drop_columns("y"), y_context=table[:400, "y"]) x_q = table[400:].drop_columns("y") p1 = lambda pred: pred.numerical[..., pred.columns[sdm.Stype.numerical].index("1")] # P(y=1), by NAME seen = [] def peek(pred): seen.append(pred.columns[sdm.Stype.numerical]) return pred.numerical.sum() * 0 torch.manual_seed(0) sdm.explain.GradientExplainer(output=peek).explain(model, x_q, num_estimators=4, **ctx) print(f" num_estimators=4: the output function is called {len(seen)} times, class order per call:") print(f" {seen}") def only_call(n): calls = {"i": 0} def f(pred): calls["i"] += 1 return p1(pred) if calls["i"] == n else p1(pred) * 0 return f sizes = {} for n in (1, len(seen)): torch.manual_seed(0) g = sdm.explain.GradientExplainer(output=only_call(n)).explain(model, x_q, num_estimators=4, **ctx) sizes[n] = float(g.x.to_pandas().abs().mean().mean()) print(f"
 Trap 1 - only the LAST estimator is explained. Output function live only on call 1:" f" mean |grad| {sizes[1]:.4f};") print(f" live only on call {len(seen)}: {sizes[len(seen)]:.4f}. Each call overwrites the previous result, so") print(" with several estimators you get one of them, not their average. Explain with num_estimators=1.") print("
 Trap 2 - class order differs per estimator. num_estimators=1, six seeds, P(y=1) selected two ways:") print(f" {'seed':>6s} {'order':>12s} " + "".join(f"{c + f' ({true[c]:+.1f})':>20s}" for c in true)) print(f" {'':6s} {'':12s} " + "".join(f"{'position / name':>20s}" for _ in true)) by_name = [] flipped = name_ok = 0 for seed in range(6): order = [] def note(pred): order.append(pred.columns[sdm.Stype.numerical]) return pred.numerical.sum() * 0 torch.manual_seed(seed) sdm.explain.GradientExplainer(output=note).explain(model, x_q, num_estimators=1, **ctx) res = {} for label, fn in (("position", lambda pred: pred.numerical[..., 1]), ("name", p1)): torch.manual_seed(seed) res[label] = sdm.explain.GradientExplainer(output=fn).explain( model, x_q, num_estimators=1, **ctx).x.to_pandas().mean() by_name.append(res["name"]) flipped += any(np.sign(res["position"][c]) != np.sign(w) for c, w in true.items()) name_ok += all(np.sign(res["name"][c]) == np.sign(w) for c, w in true.items()) print(f" {seed:>6d} {str(order[0]):>12s} " + "".join(f"{res['position'][c]:>10.2f} /{res['name'][c]:>7.2f}" for c in true)) avg = pd.concat(by_name, axis=1).mean(axis=1) noise = float(avg.drop(list(true)).abs().max()) print(f"
 When the shuffle puts class '1' first, column 1 is P(y=0) and every sign flips. Selecting by") print(f" name gives the right sign on {name_ok}/6 seeds. Averaged over the seeds, by name: " + ", ".join(f"{c} {avg[c]:+.2f}" for c in true) + f"; largest noise feature {noise:.2f}.") print(" Gradients are with respect to the PREPROCESSED, i.e. standardized, inputs.") return f"position flipped signs on {flipped}/6 seeds; name correct on {name_ok}/6; last estimator only" explain() The library’s GradientExplainer returns the gradient of a chosen output with respect to the preprocessed query inputs, and we test it on synthetic data where only three of eight features matter, with known signs. It has two traps, both visible only by looking at what the output function receives. First, the function is called once per estimator and each call overwrites the previous result, so with four estimators an output function that is live only on the first call yields an all-zero explanation, and the explanation you get is only the last estimator’s. Second, each estimator’s raw output has its own class order, because the default recipe shuffles class labels per estimator. Explaining with a single estimator across six seeds, selecting the probability of class one by column position flips the sign of every feature on the two seeds whose order is reversed, while selecting it by column name gives the right sign on all six, and averaging over the seeds recovers the three real features with the noise features near zero. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser def make_shop(seed=0, n_customers=800, n_products=60): """Customers, products and a year of orders. Some customers' activity collapses at a random date.""" rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) plans = rng.choice(["basic", "pro"], n_customers, p=[0.7, 0.3]) customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": np.arange(n_customers), "region": rng.choice(["NA", "EU", "APAC", "LATAM"], n_customers), "plan": plans}) products = pd.DataFrame({"product_id": np.arange(n_products), "category": rng.choice(["books", "tech", "home", "toys"], n_products), "price": rng.gamma(2.0, 20.0, n_products).round(2)}) weekly_rate = rng.gamma(1.5, 0.6, n_customers) * np.where(plans == "pro", 1.6, 1.0) fade_day = rng.uniform(60, 500, n_customers) rows, start = [], pd.Timestamp("2025-01-01") for c in range(n_customers): t = 0.0 while True: rate = weekly_rate[c] / 7 * (1.0 if t < fade_day[c] else 0.08) t += rng.exponential(1 / max(rate, 1e-6)) if t > 364: break p = int(rng.integers(n_products)) rows.append((c, p, start + pd.Timedelta(float(t), unit="D"), float(products.price[p] * rng.integers(1, 4)))) orders = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["customer_id", "product_id", "order_date", "amount"]) orders.insert(0, "order_id", np.arange(len(orders))) orders["order_date"] = orders["order_date"].dt.floor("s") return customers, products, orders def task_rows(customers, orders, cutoff, horizon_days=30): """Label: does the customer order again within 30 days of the cutoff?""" window = orders[(orders.order_date > cutoff) & (orders.order_date <= cutoff + pd.Timedelta(horizon_days, unit="D"))] active = set(window.customer_id) return pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": customers.customer_id, "timestamp": cutoff, "label": [int(c in active) for c in customers.customer_id]}) @section("9. A relational database as input: tables, keys, and a time-aware sampler") def relational_setup(): customers, products, orders = make_shop() data = sdm.RelationalData( tables={ "customers": sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(customers, {"customer_id": "id", "region": "categorical", "plan": "categorical"}), "products": sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(products, {"product_id": "id", "category": "categorical", "price": "numerical"}), "orders": sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(orders, {"order_id": "id", "customer_id": "id", "product_id": "id", "order_date": "datetime", "amount": "numerical"}), }, relationships=[ dict(left_table="orders", left_column="customer_id", right_table="customers", right_column="customer_id"), dict(left_table="orders", left_column="product_id", right_table="products", right_column="product_id"), ], ) cutoffs_ctx = [pd.Timestamp(d) for d in ("2025-06-01", "2025-07-01", "2025-08-01")] cutoff_q = pd.Timestamp("2025-09-15") task_df = pd.concat([task_rows(customers, orders, c) for c in cutoffs_ctx + [cutoff_q]], ignore_index=True) task = sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(task_df, {"customer_id": "id", "timestamp": "datetime", "label": "categorical"}) n_ctx = len(cutoffs_ctx) * len(customers) link = dict(task_link={"task_column": "customer_id", "table": "customers", "table_column": "customer_id"}, num_neighbors=[16, 16], task_time_column="timestamp") print(f" {len(customers)} customers, {len(products)} products, {len(orders):,} orders over 2025") print(" relationships: orders.customer_id -> customers, orders.product_id -> products") print(f" task: will the customer order in the 30 days after a cutoff? positive rate {task_df.label.mean():.2f}") print(f" context: cutoffs {[str(c.date()) for c in cutoffs_ctx]} ({n_ctx:,} rows); query: {cutoff_q.date()}") sampler = data.sampler(time_columns={"orders": "order_date"}) sample, related = sampler(task[:3].drop_columns("label"), **link) print("
 what the sampler hands the model for the first 3 task rows (16 neighbours, then 16 more):") for name, tbl in related.tables.items(): print(f" {name:10s} {tuple(tbl.size())}") latest = related.tables["orders"].to_pandas()["order_date"].max() print(f" latest order the sampler returned: {latest} task timestamp: {cutoffs_ctx[0]}") print(" The sampler walks the foreign keys backwards in time: no order dated after the task row's") print(" own timestamp is eligible, so the rows that define the label cannot leak in.") globals().update(SHOP=dict(customers=customers, orders=orders, data=data, task=task, task_df=task_df, n_ctx=n_ctx, link=link, cutoffs=cutoffs_ctx + [cutoff_q])) return f"{len(orders):,} orders across 3 linked tables" relational_setup() KumoRelational takes a relational database instead of a single table. We generate a small shop with eight hundred customers, sixty products and a year of orders, in which some customers’ activity collapses at a random date, and ask whether each customer will order again within thirty days of a cutoff. RelationalData holds the tables and the foreign keys between them, and its sampler walks those keys outwards from each task row, collecting up to sixteen neighbours per hop. Declaring the order date as a time column makes the walk temporal: we check that the latest order the sampler returns for a task row dated the first of June was placed on the thirty-first of May, so the rows that define the label are out of reach. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser def relational_auc(time_columns): s = SHOP sampler = s["data"].sampler(time_columns=time_columns) model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device=DEVICE) torch.manual_seed(0) context, related = sampler(s["task"][:s["n_ctx"]], **s["link"]) model.fit(x=context.drop_columns("label"), y=context["label"], related_tables=related, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)) query = s["task"][s["n_ctx"]:].drop_columns("label") proba = model.predict(*sampler(query, **s["link"])).to_pandas() return roc_auc_score(s["task_df"].label.to_numpy()[s["n_ctx"]:], proba["1"]) def history_features(customers, orders, cutoff): """The feature engineering a data scientist would write by hand, strictly before the cutoff.""" past = orders[orders.order_date <= cutoff] by_customer = past.groupby("customer_id") f = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": customers.customer_id}) for days in (30, 90): recent = past[past.order_date > cutoff - pd.Timedelta(days, unit="D")].groupby("customer_id") f[f"orders_{days}d"] = f.customer_id.map(recent.size()).fillna(0) f[f"spend_{days}d"] = f.customer_id.map(recent.amount.sum()).fillna(0) f["days_since_last"] = f.customer_id.map((cutoff - by_customer.order_date.max()).dt.days).fillna(999) f["orders_total"] = f.customer_id.map(by_customer.size()).fillna(0) return f.merge(customers, on="customer_id").drop(columns="customer_id") def flat_auc(frame_fn): s = SHOP X = pd.concat([frame_fn(c) for c in s["cutoffs"]], ignore_index=True) X["label"] = s["task_df"].label.values table = as_table(X, "label") model = sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE) torch.manual_seed(0) proba = model(x_context=table[:s["n_ctx"]].drop_columns("label"), y_context=table[:s["n_ctx"], "label"], x_query=table[s["n_ctx"]:].drop_columns("label"), num_estimators=4).to_pandas() return roc_auc_score(s["task_df"].label.to_numpy()[s["n_ctx"]:], proba["1"]), list(X.columns[:-1]) @section("10. KumoRelational vs. hand-built features: the same question, three ways") def relational_vs_features(): s = SHOP results = [] t0 = time.time() auc, cols = flat_auc(lambda c: s["customers"].drop(columns="customer_id")) results.append(("TabICLv2 on the customers table only", auc, f"{len(cols)} raw columns", time.time() - t0)) t0 = time.time() auc, cols = flat_auc(lambda c: history_features(s["customers"], s["orders"], c)) results.append(("TabICLv2 on hand-engineered features", auc, f"{len(cols) - 2} engineered + 2 raw", time.time() - t0)) t0 = time.time() results.append(("KumoRelational on the raw tables", relational_auc({"orders": "order_date"}), "3 raw tables", time.time() - t0)) print(f" {'approach':40s} {'AUC':>6s} {'inputs':22s} {'seconds':>7s}") for label, auc, inputs, secs in results: print(f" {label:40s} {auc:6.3f} {inputs:22s} {secs:7.1f}") print("
 Demographics alone barely beat a coin. Purchase history is where the signal is, and the") print(" relational model reaches it without anyone writing orders_30d, spend_90d or days_since_last:") print(" it reads the order rows themselves through the keys, as of each task row's timestamp.") globals()["REL_AUC"] = results[2][1] return (f"customers only {results[0][1]:.3f} / hand-built {results[1][1]:.3f}" f" / KumoRelational {results[2][1]:.3f} AUC") relational_vs_features() We then answer the same question three ways. TabICLv2 on the customers table alone, with only region and plan to go on, reaches an AUC of 0.556. TabICLv2 on six engineered history features, orders and spend in the last thirty and ninety days, days since the last order and lifetime order count, computed strictly before each cutoff, reaches 0.828. KumoRelational on the raw tables, with no features written by anyone, reaches 0.823. The relational model gets within a rounding error of the hand-built pipeline by reading the order rows themselves through the keys, as of each task row’s timestamp. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser @section("11. The one argument that keeps a relational model honest") def leakage(): leaky = relational_auc(None) print(f" KumoRelational with time_columns={{'orders': 'order_date'}} AUC {REL_AUC:.3f}") print(f" KumoRelational with time_columns=None AUC {leaky:.3f}") print("
 Without a time column the sampler is free to return orders placed AFTER the cutoff, which") print(" are exactly the orders that define the label. The model is not predicting anymore, it is") print(" reading the answer. Nothing errors and the number looks like a breakthrough. On a real") print(" database, a relational model that is suspiciously better than your hand-built baseline") print(" should be the first thing you re-run with every time column declared.") return f"{REL_AUC:.3f} honest vs {leaky:.3f} with future rows visible" leakage() Finally we run the same relational model without declaring the time column. The AUC rises to 0.940. Without a time column the sampler is free to return orders placed after the cutoff, which are exactly the orders that define the label, so the model is no longer predicting but reading the answer, and nothing errors. On a real database, a relational model that is suspiciously better than the hand-built baseline is the first thing to re-run with every time column declared. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser banner("SUMMARY") for name, res in RESULTS.items(): print(f" {name:<76s} {res}") print(""" What to carry over - Declare stypes deliberately: text and id columns are not detected unless you ask, and the default TabICLv2 recipe drops datetime and text columns with a warning that fires once. - In an explainer output function, select classes by name, never by position. - Every table with a time column goes in time_columns. A relational model that is not time-aware is a leakage detector, not a forecaster. Where to go next - Fine-tuning: examples/tabular/finetune.py disables the output recipe and trains on raw logits. - Real relational benchmarks: examples/relational/rel_bench.py runs KumoRelational on RelBench. - On a T4 runtime, set DEVICE = "cuda" for the tabular models; cudf keeps dataframe work on GPU. - Docs: nvidia.github.io/structured-data-models Code: github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models """) The summary prints the one-line result each section returned and the three habits worth carrying over: declare semantic types and recipes deliberately, select classes by name inside an explainer and explain with one estimator, and put every table with a time column into time_columns. It then points at fine-tuning, the RelBench example, and GPU execution. In conclusion, NVIDIA’s Structured Data Models delivers on its central promise: across classification, regression, a twenty-class problem, and a three-table database, its pretrained models matched or beat scikit-learn baselines trained on the same rows without being trained themselves, returned calibrated predictive distributions for free, and in the relational case reached the accuracy of a hand-built feature pipeline from the raw tables. The defaults deserve more scrutiny than the models. Free text and IDs are not detected unless requested, the default recipe drops timestamp and text columns and warns only once per process, the explainer reports only the last estimator and needs classes selected by name, the pyg-lib URL in the library’s own error message points to an empty page, and a relational model without its time column produces an impressive and meaningless number. Each of these has a one-line fix, and each would otherwise pass silently, which is the practical lesson to carry into real data: check what reaches the model before trusting what comes out of it. title: UKMTO reported an incident northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operation (UKMTO) on Sunday announced that a southbound tugboat was struck by two unidentified projectiles northeast of Khor Fakkan, the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
The UKMTO has received a report of an incident northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE.
A tug travelling southbound has reported being struck by 2 unknown projectiles.
The tug has sustained damage but is continuing on its route. One minor casualty has been reported.
Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO, whilst authorities investigate.

title: Russian forces attack Dnipropetrovsk region over 10 times overnight, injuring three
body:
Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
“Three people were injured. The enemy attacked three districts more than 10 times using drones and artillery,” he said.
Hanzha specified that infrastructure and vehicles were damaged in Dnipro.
In the Synelnykove district, Russian forces struck the Shakhtarske and Petropavlivka communities.
“A truck and private houses were damaged. A 44-year-old man and women aged 75 and 90 were taken to hospital in moderate condition,” he said.
In the Nikopol district, Russian forces targeted the Chervonohryhorivka community.
As reported, on October 17, Russian forces attacked Dnipropetrovsk region more than 30 times, injuring three people.

title: Super Typhoon Champi to enter PAR on October 20
body: MANILA, Philippines – A tropical cyclone with the international name Champi is expected to enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) on Tuesday, October 20. Champi had intensified from a typhoon into a super typhoon as of 2 am on Sunday, October 18, and it is projected to enter PAR as a super typhoon. The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in an advisory that Champi was located 2,090 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon as of 10 am on Sunday. The super typhoon is moving west at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h), while over the sea near the United States island territory of Guam. Champi did not make landfall in Guam, but still lashed the island with heavy rain and damaging winds during its closest point of approach in the early hours of Sunday, according to Guam Homeland Security . Guam is just two hours ahead of Manila. So far, Champi has maximum sustained winds of 185 km/h — the minimum threshold for classification as a super typhoon by PAGASA — and gustiness of up to 230 km/h. The weather bureau sees Champi strengthening further and possibly reaching a peak intensity of 205 km/h before its entry into PAR, but it may start gradually weakening on Tuesday. Once it enters PAR on Tuesday morning or afternoon, Champi will be given the local name Rosal . It would be the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. Champi only has a slim chance of making landfall in the Philippines, as it is more likely to head for Taiwan. Taiwan, located above the northernmost province of Batanes, is within PAR. Although landfall is less likely in the country, PAGASA warned the public that Champi may still bring heavy rain to extreme Northern Luzon, or the Batanes-Babuyan Islands area. The weather bureau might also raise tropical cyclone wind signals for the northern and eastern portions of Northern Luzon and even parts of Bicol as early as Monday evening, October 19, or by Tuesday morning, since winds from Champi could reach these areas. The highest wind signal may be Signal No. 3 or 4. PAGASA added that most parts of Luzon and the Visayas, as well as portions of Mindanao, are likely to experience gusty conditions beginning Tuesday or Wednesday, October 21. Also on Tuesday, moderate to rough waters are expected in the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon and the eastern seaboards of the Visayas and Mindanao. Starting Wednesday, very rough, high, or very high waters may affect the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon. ALSO ON RAPPLER Part 1: No kids, no apologies: Why Filipino women are opting out of motherhood | Part 2: As Asia grays, can an aging Philippines avoid its neighbors’ fate? How world No. 1 Anna Leigh Waters balances life and pickleball [Vantage Point] When a paycheck runs out before payday For now, the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) and the easterlies are the weather systems affecting the country on Sunday. The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet, while the easterlies are warm winds from the Pacific Ocean. The ITCZ is causing scattered rain and thunderstorms in the Zamboanga Peninsula, Basilan, Lanao del Sur, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, and Palawan, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms in the rest of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and Soccsksargen. Meanwhile, the easterlies are bringing scattered rain and thunderstorms to Quezon and Camarines Norte, and isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of the country. The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat , which was announced last October 5. The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

title: Pete Fry projected to be next mayor of Vancouver, beating out Ken Sim
body:
It appears that Vancouver is going to have a new mayor.
Pete Fry is projected to be the next Vancouver mayor, beating out incumbent Ken Sim.
In a speech to his supporters, Fry said it was a bit overwhelming to receive the news.
“Putting your trust in me and my team here, we’re not going to let you down,” Fry said.
“We love the city a lot, and we’re here to work for the city, to fight for the city.”
Fry said he has a great team, some great ideas and they are going to get started right away.
Sim acknowledged that politics is a hard job and it can take a toll on families.
“You know, public life does ask a lot of the people that are closest to us,” he said.
Sim said that voters obviously wanted to go in a different direction and it is important that is acknowledged.
“Tonight marks the end of my time as mayor. Actually, that’s not true. I think I have a couple more weeks left, so yeah, all right, let’s make some changes now,” Sim said.
“Anyways, I just want to say thank you for being elected to the office of mayor. You know, it’s been the highlight of my life.”
Colleen Hardwick came in third, with Kareem Allam coming in fourth.

title: Tanker attacked off Yemen’s coast: UKMTO
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – The UK’s Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency says an LNG tanker has been attacked by several people on a skiff off the Yemeni city of al-Mukalla.

title: I’m a Russian Fashion Designer – Vladimir Putin Is Terrified of Me
body:
Less than five years ago, her life could hardly have been more glamorous or safer. Anastasia Vistorobska worked in Paris for two of the world’s best-known fashion houses. Today her life could hardly be more challenging or dangerous: working as a combat medic for Ukraine’s armed forces on the front line of its brutal all-out war with Russia.
Anastasia’s story is all-the-more remarkable because of her nationality – she is Russian, which means she has volunteered to risk her life fighting against her homeland. For more than two-and-a-half years, she has worked as a combat medic, treating her comrades close to the front line, while also seeing countless others die on the battlefield.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
It is physically and mentally exhausting work. Typically, Anastasia’s days are full of both good and bad news. She fought back tears as she talked about the recent death of a close comrade. “The constant death is terrible. It builds up and it makes me sad and angry. I have seen 42 comrades go on a mission but only 38 came back,” she reflects.
However, there are rewarding days too. “On one occasion, a wounded soldier passed on a message through a comrade: ‘Thank you for saving my life.’ That was very inspiring. I am fortunate, too, that I have never had anyone die in my arms.”
On Feb. 24, 2022, when Russia began its all-out invasion, Anastasia was sleeping in a beautiful house in rural France, when suddenly friends started messaging her that the war had started. “They all said the same: that Ukraine was under bombardment. My immediate reaction was: ‘this cannot be happening!’”
At that time, Anastasia, then aged 36, had lived in France for 15 years, for the last seven working in the fashion industry for Chanel and Givenchy as an embroidery designer. With friends and relatives in Ukraine, she typically visited the country twice a year. “After the all-out invasion, I wanted to join the Ukrainian army straightaway but I felt helpless. I was conscious that I had a Russian passport and no previous military experiences. I feared that I would be useless and that no one would take me seriously. But I do have an ability to act decisively. I wanted to go and start killing these invaders.”
As she pondered how to get involved, the Russian massacre of some 500 people at Bucha, near Kyiv, in March 2022, was the final straw. “For me, this was the most horrific moment of the whole war,” she said. Anastasia initially wrote a letter to a military committee in Ukraine explaining: “I know I am Russian but I want to go and defend Ukrainian children. Can you please accept me?”
Her offer was rejected but friends advised her to look into the Freedom of Russian Legion, Russians fighting against their homeland. “I looked at their videos and documentaries and I was astounded by the way they thought and spoke. They seemed to be the best of people and, four years on, having met them, I still feel the same.”
Fearing she was too old and too weak, Anastasia first got herself fitter and stronger over six months before going to Texas, in the US, for a two-month military training course. Eventually, she passed a long vetting procedure and was successful in joining the legion. “The process is strict: Every potential recruit’s background is scrutinized down to the smallest detail to completely eliminate any possibility of FSB [Russian security] infiltration,” she said.
It was not until February 2024, on the second anniversary of the full-scale invasion, that she finally arrived in Ukraine and started undergoing four months of training at a secret location. “It was horrible – really, really hard – but at the end of it I could shoot five different weapons and I learned a lot about the battlefield and communications. I also learned medical skills and evacuation techniques.”
At the end of her training, she chose to work as a combat medic and is now head of a tactical evacuation team. Typically, she operates some six miles from the front line. The aim is that an injured soldier is given basic first aid and evacuated by his comrades, so he or she can receive fuller medical attention from combat medics in slightly safer locations.
I asked Anastasia, who is 5 feet 8 inches (173 cm) tall and of slim build, how she felt fighting a war against her homeland. “I prefer to judge people on their actions rather than their passport. People either do good things or bad things and I want to be on the side of right versus wrong. Stealing land, killing civilians, harming children – they are all wrong.” Strangely perhaps, Anastasia considers it more dangerous to be in Kyiv on leave than she does working close to the front line. The capital is hit almost daily by ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“In the war zone, I am wearing body armor, I am surrounded by comrades, I am always on alert and I trust my commanders to keep me safe. But in Kyiv this summer I was sleeping in my pajamas on the 14th floor of an apartment building when the area was being hit by missiles and drones. That was terrifying.”
Her worst times have come when comrades are being killed or wounded on the front line. “When you hear someone screaming [for help] on the radio that’s probably one of the hardest moments,” she said.
Anastasia, who left Russia aged 23, has signed a three-year contract with the legion. She does not know yet if she will stay in the army longer because she also has a yearning to go back to her artistic roots. Even now, she applies her talents by creating artistic projects, including making art works from the uniforms of dead soldiers and their belongings. It is intended as a memorial to their sacrifice and, in time, she hopes to exhibit her work. Hundreds of Russians are currently fighting for Ukraine and Anastasia admires them all.
“I am soaked in the stories of my comrades, their chivalry and bravery,” she said. “But what upsets me is that after they die in battle and are cremated, no one [from their family] will come and visit their grave. So I hope my work will commemorate their death, their memory. The huge power of war and art often go hand in hand.”
For security reasons, Anastasia prefers not to discuss details of her family. However, she says all her family members, including her mother, now live outside Russia, which is why she is willing to be identified by name, without fear of reprisals in her homeland.
“I am not scared by the reality that I might get killed. I am just proud to have done a little bit to make the situation better for Ukrainians. Putin is scared of the Legion of Russia which means he is scared of me.”
Her hatred of the Russian president has no limits. She says: “He is one of the biggest war criminals in history. He has been compared to Hitler but he is much worse than Hitler. Putin is destroying Russia even more horribly than he is Ukraine. He stole my pride and my joy at being Russian. He has stolen the right of the Russian language to be the beautiful language it once was.”
She hopes that, once the war ends well for Ukraine, she will be able to divide her time between France and Ukraine. Now aged 41 years old, she is engaged to a Russian man who also serves in the legion. Anastasia says Ukrainians have been largely supportive, rather than suspicious, of her and other Russians fighting for their cause, but she added: “If a Ukrainian was to spit in my face, I would not say a word because I would understand the anger. The reality is that Russia owes a huge debt to Ukraine.”
Lord Ashcroft KCMG PC is an international businessman, philanthropist, author and pollster. For more information on his work, visit lordashcroft.com. Follow him on X/Facebook @LordAshcroft.

title: Drone attack on Leningrad Region one of largest in four years
body:
SAINT PETERSBURG, October 18. /TASS/. The Ukrainian drone attack on the Leningrad Region has become one of the largest in the last four years, according to TASS calculations based on the data released by the region’s Governor Alexander Drozdenko.
According to his information, 135 drones were intercepted over the Leningrad Region. The largest attack was repelled on June 6, 2026, when 144 drones were shot down.

title: Drone debris falls on residential building in Leningrad Region
body:
SAINT PETERSBURG, October 18. /TASS/. Drone debris has fallen on an apartment building in Gatchina in the Leningrad Region, and 55 parked cars have been damaged in the village of Novoselye, Governor Alexander Drozdenko said.
"The fall of drone debris onto an apartment building in Gatchina was recorded. In Novoselye, Lomonosovsky District, 55 parked cars were damaged," he said.
Drozdenko added that there were no casualties.

title: ADF down 152 out of 180 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine
body:
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram .
Starting at 18:00 on Saturday, October 17, the enemy attacked Ukraine with one Iskander-M ballistic missile launched from Russia’s Voronezh region, as well as 180 Shahed-type attack UAVs, 26 of them jet-powered, S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from the directions of Oryol, Bryansk, Kursk, Shatalovo and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by Ukrainian Air Defense Forces, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 on Sunday, October 18, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 152 enemy UAVs.
Hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 20 locations, while downed drones and their debris fell at four locations.
The attack is ongoing. About 10 enemy UAVs remain in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Starlink operations in Ukraine are restricted to speeds of up to 161 km/h, making it impossible to use the system on interceptors designed to counter jet-powered Shahed drones.

title: Kazakhstan Cannot Wait 202 Years For Gender Parity
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. Editor’s note: The Astana Times continues a section featuring articles by our readers. As a platform that values diverse perspectives and meaningful conversations, we believe that this section provides space for readers to share their thoughts and insights on various topics that matter to them and the AT audience. Adilya Tugel. Photo credit: Adilya Tugel’s personal archive A girl born today in Central Asia will not live long enough to witness gender parity if progress continues at its historical pace. The World Economic Forum (WEF) released a 2026 Global Gender Gap Report, stating that closing the region’s gender gap could take 202 years. On its current trajectory, Central Asia would be the last region in the world to reach parity. The index is based on an established reasoning: economies are less competitive when they fail to develop and use the talents of their entire population. Kazakhstan presents a striking paradox, ranking fourth out of five countries of the region. Since the WEF began measuring gender gaps in 2006, the country has experienced substantial economic growth, rapid digitalisation and deeper integration into the global economy. It has nearly closed its gender gaps in education and health. Yet in political empowerment, only 12.3% of the gap has been closed. More strikingly, Kazakhstan’s overall gender-parity score remains within one percentage point of where it stood in 2006. The paradox is not that Kazakh women have been left outside the country’s development. Quite the opposite. Women are economically active and deeply embedded in the institutions of the state. The problem is: representation did not automatically translate into authority and power. The bottleneck is visible in the statistics. While women make up a majority of Kazakh civil servants, their representation declines sharply as authority increases. As of January 2024, women accounted for 56% of Corps B administrative civil servants, but only around 12.9% of Corps A and around 8.3% of political civil servants. Women increasingly disappear on the way up. The reasons are clear and well known: gender stereotypes, unpaid care work and expectations about women’s roles. Artificial intelligence could reinforce existing gender inequalities. The International Labor Organization has found that female-dominated occupations are almost twice as likely to be exposed to generative AI, partly because of women’s greater concentration in administrative roles. These findings matter for a public sector in which women constitute the majority. Kazakhstan needs to ensure that traditional rungs of the career ladder are not eliminated without creating stronger pathways for women towards leadership roles. The government has already laid the foundations for the solution. It has invested considerably in e-Qyzmet to digitize significant parts of recruitment and personnel administration to make HR processes more transparent and standardized. However, while women enter the civil service in large numbers, they still progressively disappear as positions become more powerful. The next task is to make that leadership pipeline visible. Among civil servants with comparable qualifications, competencies, and performance, do women and men progress at similar rates? If not, at what point do their careers begin to diverge? Technology can help institutions ask these questions systematically. HR analytics could identify where promising employees stall, who receives the assignments and experience that prepare officials for senior leadership. This is not to say that gender should become a criterion for promotion, but rather an audit variable. AI could eventually strengthen this process by identifying capabilities that conventional career paths or solely human judgement may overlook. The purpose of technology should therefore not be to decide who deserves to lead, but to make the evidence behind human decisions more visible and accountable. One may argue that the government cannot solve a problem that ultimately lies in society. Assumptions about leadership, family obligations and informal professional networks do not disappear because recruitment rules are formally neutral. Culture became a convenient explanation for institutional inertia. However, Kazakhstan cannot wait for social attitudes to evolve over generations. The right policies and strong institutions can potentially shape and change the culture to drive further progress. Closing the gender gap is not only about justice. The government has invested heavily in women’s human capital. The economic question is whether the country is receiving the full return on that investment. A country that educates women, brings them into professional life and employs them throughout the machinery of government, but loses much of that talent before the highest levels of decision-making, is not only facing a gender-equality problem. It is facing a human-capital allocation problem. For Kazakhstan, the next phase of gender equality is therefore not primarily about getting women through the door. It is about turning existing representation into influence. The 202-year projection is not destiny. It is an extrapolation from the past. Whether Kazakhstan follows that trajectory will depend, in part, on the policies and institutions it designs now. The author is Adilya Tugel, a graduate student at the Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Public Policy. Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times. The post Kazakhstan Cannot Wait 202 Years For Gender Parity appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Joyce Bawah Mogtari shares O-Level setback and success story at Assisi Girls SHS anniversary
body: Joyce Bawah Mogtari arrived at St Francis of Assisi Girls’ Senior High School in Jirapa to resit her O-Level examinations after an unsuccessful attempt. The school gave her a second chance. Today, she returned as a senior lawyer, Senior Presidential Advisor and Special Aide to President John Dramani Mahama. Her return as Special Guest of Honour for the school’s 67th anniversary and FOGA Homecoming was also the homecoming of a daughter who found her path in Jirapa. Delivering the keynote address on Saturday, October 17, on the theme, “67 Years of Nurturing Leaders and Inspiring Excellence: Time to Retrace Our Steps”, she shared an emotional account of how she came to Assisi. “There is something profoundly satisfying about returning to a place that once offered you your dreams,” she began. “I came here to resit my O-Levels because it was an exam that literally eluded me.” Her uncle, who had been transferred to Wa as the Inspector-General of Police’s representative, recommended Assisi as “quiet and just the kind of place that I needed”. “The rest, as they say, is history,” she said. The records, she said, would show that she obtained a distinction and won WAEC awards for Best Student in English Language and Home Economics. “Let me tell you something else, the Home Economics and typing – not French and Maths – gave me the best possible results,” she said to cheers. She paid tribute to the then headmistress, Mrs Gyader, and Madam Dakurah, a former student of her mother. “The sense of Catholicism I developed came from here – my independence and spirit of competition was likewise borne from here. Some of the best friends that I have I met them here too. And finally the man I eventually married also hails from this region. They say that the best comes from the West.” Reflecting on her journey, she asked: “Who would have imagined, all those years ago, that one day I would return to this school as a very Senior Lawyer, Maritime Lawyer, founder of a Law Firm, an entrepreneur and Senior Presidential Advisor and Special Aide to the President?” Mahama’s message Mrs Mogtari also conveyed President Mahama’s greetings to the school community. “I bring you greetings and warm wishes from the President. His Excellency remains deeply committed to expanding educational opportunities for all Ghanaians, particularly girls and young women,” she said. “The President recognises that when we invest in the education of girls, we invest not only in their individual futures, but also in the prosperity and progress of our nation.” ‘Marry your books’ To the current students, she offered a clear piece of advice: “Marry your books!” “For now, let your textbooks be your closest companions. Let your assignments command your attention,” she said. “Do not spend so much time on social media that you neglect your studies. Failure in one examination is not failure in life.” Citing Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang’s achievement as Ghana’s first female Vice-President, she said the next barrier to overcome was electing a female President. “Perhaps she is sitting in a classroom somewhere in Ghana today. Perhaps she is sitting right here at St. Francis of Assisi Girls’ Senior High School. Why should that not be possible?” She praised President Mahama for choosing Prof Opoku-Agyemang as his running mate in the 2020 and 2024 elections. Acta Non Verba – deeds, not words The presidential aide, who often signs off on Facebook with the phrase Acta Non Verba , joked about its similarity to Holy Child School’s motto, Facta Non Verba . “I did not attend Holy Child. Neither did I borrow my personal creed from the school,” she said with a laugh. “Acta Non Verba reflects something I believe very strongly. Our words must be supported by our actions.” She challenged the old students to reflect on the opportunities the school had given them and how they could improve the experience for the next generation. “What opportunities did this school give us? What are we prepared to do to make the experience even better?” she asked. “The measure of our gratitude is not simply how proudly we speak about St. Francis. It is what we are prepared to do for St. Francis.” She urged FOGA to ensure that “every homecoming leaves behind more than photographs and pleasant memories”. Her final charge to the students was: “Dream boldly. Study diligently. Conduct yourselves with integrity.”

title: Iran freestyle wrestlers win gold at World U23 C’ships in US
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – Iranian freestyle wrestlers “Abolfazl Mohammadnejad” (125kg) and “Abolfazl Rahmani” (92kg) claimed gold at the World U23 Championships in the United States.
The medal matches and finals for the 61kg, 74kg, 86kg, 92kg, and 125kg weight classes at the U23 World Freestyle Wrestling Championships took place early this morning in Las Vegas, the United States. In 125kg category, Abolfazl Mohammadnejad defeated Kochanov of Ukraine 10–0 to advance to the quarterfinals.
Mohammadnejad defeated Bestayev from Russia 11–0 and advanced to the semifinals. At that stage, Mohammadnejad overcame Khetag Karsanov of Azerbaijan 5–0 to reach the final. In the final, Mohammadnejad secured a 10–0 victory over Abramishvili from Georgia, clinching Iran’s second gold medal.

title: Iran's Araghchi, OIC chief discuss Islamic world issues
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Organisation of Islamic Cooperation Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed in Baghdad, discussing issues facing the Islamic world and the organization's agenda.
Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi, in Iraq to attend the annual session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, met Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed on Saturday afternoon.
The two exchanged views on issues facing the Islamic world and items on the organization's agenda.
Araghchi congratulated the new secretary-general and stressed the importance of the OIC playing an effective role in strengthening solidarity among Islamic countries and confronting common challenges and threats against the Islamic world, particularly regarding occupied Palestine.
Pointing to Iran's status as a founding member of the OIC, Araghchi said the Islamic Republic expects the secretariat to act with a professional and impartial approach to strengthen Islamic understanding and solidarity, and to prevent any impression of bias by the secretariat for or against any member state.
The meeting also covered developments in the Arabian Peninsula and the escalation of conflicts, with Araghchi stressing Iran's readiness to help facilitate dialogue and engagement between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The OIC secretary-general, for his part, thanked the Iranian foreign minister for attending the summit and said the secretariat is keen to draw on Iran's experience and capacities to design and advance new initiatives on mediation and the settlement of disputes among Islamic countries.
