title: Republic Bank–JoyNews Habitat Fair draws patrons with discounts of up to 30% as event enters final day in Ho
body: Exhibitors at the Republic Bank–JoyNews Habitat Fair in Ho are offering discounts of up to 30% on selected products and services as the event enters its final day. JoyNews reporter Maxwell Agbagba, reporting from the Ho Sports Stadium, says the offers are attracting prospective homeowners and other patrons seeking affordable housing solutions. The discounts have added to activity at the venue, where exhibitors are showcasing products and services covering various aspects of homeownership, construction and property development. The offerings range from building materials and home appliances to real estate financing options and property development services. Patrons have also expressed satisfaction with the range of housing and real estate solutions available at the fair. The fair remains open until 8 p.m. today, giving visitors a final opportunity to explore the available offers, compare products and engage directly with exhibitors. The Republic Bank–JoyNews Habitat Fair brings together businesses and other stakeholders in Ghana’s housing and real estate sector, connecting consumers with products, services and information to support their homeownership plans. This year’s edition in Ho forms part of efforts to extend the fair’s reach beyond Accra and other major urban centres, bringing housing-related products and services closer to prospective buyers in the Volta Region and surrounding areas. Organised by JoyNews and sponsored by Republic Bank, the event provides a platform for exhibitors to engage potential customers while allowing patrons to explore available options in the housing market. With the fair closing at 8 p.m., interested patrons have until this evening to visit the Ho Sports Stadium and take advantage of the offers available.

title: Doug McCallum projected to reclaim Surrey mayor’s office as Brenda Locke concedes
body:
Doug McCallum is projected to be the next mayor of Surrey again.
“Tonight Surrey has become a global city,” McCallum said.
“We will address your affordability, we will address your safety, and we will address your infrastructure.”
McCallum told his room of supporters that he loves Surrey; that’s why he ran.
“Together we’re going to build a great city that our families will live in, have jobs and go to sports, enjoy each other, work together to make one of the best global cities in the world! Go, go, Surrey!”
Incumbent mayor Brenda Locke conceded to McCallum in a speech before the polls had closed.
“The voters have truly spoken,” she said.
“I want to wish them every success as they take on the responsibility of leading our most incredible city of Surrey. Surrey deserves our full support; there is no doubt.”
Locke thanked her team for how much they cared.
“Four years ago, the people of Surrey gave me an honor of serving as mayor,” she said.
“It has been the privilege of a lifetime. We did make progress in Surrey, great progress, on housing, on infrastructure, on public safety, and the facilities that are growing in our city today. To every resident who put their faith in me, I am so deeply grateful.”
McCallum led the City of Surrey as mayor for 13 years and lost to Locke in 2022.
He ran this election again under the banner ‘Doug Gets it Done,’ and it appears he has done that again.

title: China’s Rise and Central Asia: What Will Next Ten Years Look Like?
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. For much of my time as a journalist, the story of China’s rise has come with a familiar undertone of alarm. China is either becoming the next great global power, challenging the West, rewriting the rules of international politics or quietly building a parallel system that the rest of the world will eventually have to adapt to. All of these arguments have some basis. But I sometimes wonder whether we make the China story too simple, especially from Central Asia, where China is not some distant geopolitical competitor, but a country next door, a major trading partner and an increasingly visible part of our economic landscape. Jiyang Dong. Photo credit: Nazarbayev University So I wanted to ask a broader question: if China continues to gain economic and geopolitical weight over the next 10 years, what will that power actually look like by 2035, and what will it mean for Central Asia? I spoke to several experts and their answers were more nuanced than the usual China-versus-the-West narrative. The most interesting conclusion was not that China will necessarily replace the existing international order. It may not have to. China may reshape the order without replacing it Jiyang Dong, assistant professor at Nazarbayev University’s Graduate School of Business, made a point that immediately shifted the question for me. “Ironically, the key variables impacting China’s future role in the international system are not necessarily within China,” he said. China’s policies, he said, are already laid out in successive five-year plans and implemented with consistency. What matters just as much is what happens elsewhere: whether the United States (U.S.) continues to retreat from multilateralism and whether institutions such as the World Bank and IMF continue to meet the development needs of the Global South. If they do not, Dong believes, institutions in which China plays a central role could gradually become more important. He points to the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank as one example. That means China’s rise may not depend entirely on Beijing building a new system from scratch. It may also depend on whether existing institutions leave enough space for China and other emerging powers to build something alongside them. Gulnar Shaimergenova, director of the China Studies Center in Kazakhstan, sees the process in similar terms. “I would rather speak not about the creation by China of a completely alternative world order, but about an attempt to change the balance and rules within the existing international system,” she said. By 2035, she expects a more polycentric system in which China becomes one of the key centers of economic, technological and political influence. The real question, she said, is not whether one world order will simply replace another, but which institutions and norms will adapt to the new balance of power. Ken-Moriyasu-Hudson. Photo credit: nationalinterest.org Deputy Chairman of the Institute of Foreign Policy Studies under Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs Amangeldy Tazhenov reaches a similar conclusion. China, he said, is not trying to “break” the existing system. It is pushing for its transformation and reform so that it better reflects current realities and the changing distribution of power. But Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at Hudson Institute, offered a sharper interpretation of the same trend. For much of the post-Deng Xiaoping era, he noted, China largely adapted to an international system shaped by Western powers. Under Xi Jinping, the ambition is different. “It is less about reforming China to fit the existing order and more about changing the order to fit China,” Moriyasu said. At the same time, he cautions against assuming Beijing is confident it can simply build the order it wants. China also knows that its rise generates resistance and suspicion. That, he said, helps explain why Beijing continues to emphasize the UN and existing institutions while simultaneously promoting BRICS, the SCO and a more multipolar system. “Beijing will preserve institutions that reinforce China’s status, seek to reshape institutions where Western influence remains predominant, and simultaneously build organizations, relationships and economic networks that give Beijing alternatives,” he said. I find that distinction more useful than the familiar question of whether China is trying to become “the next U.S.” Perhaps China does not need to replace the system. It may simply need to become powerful enough to change the way the system works around it. Central Asia is becoming more important for a different reason Amangeldy Tazhenov. Photo credit: sszi.kz This is where the discussion becomes more interesting for Central Asia. For years, China’s relationship with the region was discussed largely through the familiar vocabulary of trade, energy, resources and transport corridors. Those things still matter. But the strategic logic appears to be changing. Moriyasu calls the emerging logic “strategic resilience.” Much of China’s trade and energy still moves through maritime routes exposed to American naval power. Central Asia gives Beijing something the South China Sea cannot: a vast continental hinterland connecting China westward across Eurasia. “Central Asia matters to Beijing not only because of the energy, minerals and markets within Central Asia, but increasingly because of what lies beyond it. It connects China westward across the Eurasian landmass,” he said. His forecast is striking: “I would expect Central Asia to move from China’s economic periphery toward the strategic center of China’s relationship with Eurasia.” That changes the question because Central Asia’s value for China is no longer simply what Beijing can obtain from the region. It is also what the region allows China to reach. Jiyang Dong approaches this from a more economic perspective. “Central Asia’s greatest strategic significance hinges on its potential as a connectivity hub in the heart of Eurasia,” he said. Without sufficient connectivity infrastructure, he notes, trade volumes remain limited, and resources remain effectively locked in the region. That is why projects such as the expansion of the Aktau container hub and the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway matter beyond their immediate economic purpose. They are helping turn Central Asia’s geography into an asset. Perhaps this is where we should stop thinking of infrastructure simply as infrastructure. Infrastructure may be the new geopolitics Moriyasu said something that stayed with me: “Infrastructure becomes the new hinge of geopolitics.” “Once trade routes, pipelines, power grids and supply chains are built around particular networks, they begin to shape the economic choices available to countries using them,” Moriyasu said. That is a much more subtle form of power than the geopolitics I grew up reading about. There is no flag going up. No alliance is announced. No military base appears. But the network changes. And once a country’s trade, logistics, power systems, digital infrastructure or industrial supply chains are deeply embedded in a particular network, those connections can begin shaping the choices available to it. This is also where my own perception of China has changed. It is difficult to ignore the efficiency of some of the infrastructure projects I see around me. The LRT in Astana is a very concrete example. Whatever one’s broader political view of China may be, a functioning project creates a different impression than a political speech or diplomatic statement. This is where infrastructure can begin to operate as soft power. Not necessarily because Beijing tells people to admire China, but because people encounter its capabilities in practical ways: a railway, a road or a technology. Over time, that can produce something harder to measure but politically significant: familiarity, respect and, potentially, a certain degree of loyalty. Tazhenov described China’s approach in similarly long-term terms, noting that Beijing tends to think in much longer horizons than many other countries. He also pointed to the growing visibility of Chinese economic activity in Kazakhstan: from infrastructure and roads to new enterprises and resource projects. That matters because soft power is usually discussed in terms of culture, education or films. Perhaps in the next decade, we will have to add infrastructure to that list. The next phase may be about technology, not concrete This is where the forecasts become even more interesting. Shaimergenova believes the development most underestimated today is the transition from physical infrastructure connectivity to technological and institutional connectivity. A few years ago, the China conversation in Central Asia focused on roads, railways, pipelines and energy. Today, she notes, the agenda increasingly includes AI, digital infrastructure, green technologies and critical minerals. “Central Asia will be not only a territory through which flows between China and Europe pass, but increasingly a space where different technological, production and regulatory systems will intersect,” she said. That is probably the part of the China story that deserves more attention. Dong sees another underestimated area: cooperation in non-fossil energy. Solar panels, wind turbines, energy storage, flexible grids and nuclear power could all become increasingly important as Central Asian economies grow and demand more electricity. In other words, China’s future role in Central Asia may be less about simply connecting the region to China and more about helping shape the systems through which the region itself develops. More China: more choices, or fewer? This is where the experts stop agreeing. Dong sees growing competition among major powers as potentially useful for Kazakhstan because it creates more room to advance national interests through different partners and financial systems. Shaimergenova is more cautious. “The strengthening of competition among major powers provides Kazakhstan with additional opportunities for investment, technology, transport projects and access to different markets. But at the same time, the risk increases that economic, technological and even logistical decisions will increasingly be viewed through the prism of geopolitical choice,” she said. Tazhenov is even more direct: “My opinion is that an aggravation of geopolitical rivalry is certainly unfavorable for Kazakhstan. It actually narrows the field for foreign policy maneuver.” This may be the real paradox of the next decade. China’s rise can give Kazakhstan access to more capital, infrastructure, technology and markets. But if rivalry between China and the U.S. continues to harden, those same economic choices may increasingly be interpreted as political choices. The more interconnected Kazakhstan becomes with major external powers, the more important it is to remain capable of deciding where each connection leads. What we may be underestimating One idea kept returning throughout these conversations, even when the experts approached it from very different directions. It is not simply that China is becoming more present in Central Asia. The region and China are becoming more mutually interested in one another. Tazhenov believes this growing mutual interest, connectivity and economic complementarity is one of the least appreciated trends. For China, Central Asia offers transport routes, resources, energy and stability. For Kazakhstan and its neighbors, China increasingly offers markets, investment and technology. The relationship is therefore becoming more complicated than a simple story of a rising power expanding into a neighboring region. It is also becoming a story of mutual dependence which is not automatically good or bad. Its consequences depend on who has the capacity to negotiate, diversify and create value of their own. That may be the most important question for Kazakhstan as we look toward 2035. Not whether China will become stronger or have more influence in Central Asia. It is already deeply embedded in the region’s economic geography. The more interesting question is what kind of region Central Asia becomes as that influence grows. If the next phase is about technology, industrial capacity, energy systems, and digital infrastructure as much as railways and ports, then Central Asian countries will have to think beyond attracting projects. They will have to think about what they build themselves. Because by 2035, I suspect the China story in Central Asia will no longer be mainly about a powerful country coming into the region. It will be about systems becoming intertwined: railways with ports, energy with technology, trade with digital payments, industrial projects with skills and education. There may be no dramatic moment when the old order ends, and a new one begins. The balance may simply look different one day because the underlying architecture has changed. And perhaps that is the real foresight question: not whether China will reshape the world, but how much of Central Asia’s future architecture will be shaped by China, and how much Central Asia will be capable of shaping itself. The post China’s Rise and Central Asia: What Will Next Ten Years Look Like? appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: What makes a story film festival-worthy?
body: The lights come up slowly inside Gateway Cineplex 18, and nobody moves right away. Outside, the Cubao mall hums with its usual Wednesday noise, the escalators, the food court, the smell of butter popcorn drifting in from the concession stand. This festival season, the noise is shut out, and the dark cinema becomes the loudest room. Inside it, Puregold CinePanalo films are doing the thing local movies do best: to make audiences laugh, grieve, remember, and feel. The selected full-length films each received a P5-million production grant, while student short films secured P200,000. The festival’s support extended well past the cash awards: sponsors supplied free equipment worth P1.2 million, alongside post-production discounts and grocery packages to help cover production costs. As the festival ends, a consultant helps bring the films to international festivals, with the Film Development Council of the Philippines (FDCP) partnership widening their reach. From 203 full-length submissions and 267 shorts, seven full-length films and 19 shorts made the cut. As the festival rolled into its screening dates, early moviegoers were already weighing in on the full-length film slate. For longtime festival-goer Raymond Reynosa, the festival improved in several areas this year: more venues, more ticket booths, an arranged queue, and a published screening schedule. Raymond Reynosa updates his followers on the turnout of events during the Cinepanalo screenings. Jade Tan/Rappler Between the living and the dead One of CinePanalo’s picks this year features Carl Joseph Papa and Ian Pangilinan’s Patay Gutom . The film follows a grumpy delivery driver, Tristan, whose third eye is opened after eating an offering meant for a charming but lonely ghost, Arthuro “Art” Aquino. The directors of Patay Gutom together with the cast. Photo courtesy of Cinepanalo Press Bound together, they uncover family secrets, boys’ love (BL) heartaches, and a love that blurs the line between life and the afterlife. Papa, who has made a name for himself with his distinct use of rotoscoping in his work, created two different worlds rendered in two different textures, making Patay Gutom visually unique. Play Video Reynosa admitted some of the drifting between worlds confused him at first, until the film revealed that the past and the present were interrelated all along. Another viewer, Janice, connected most with the character of Tristan and one scene involving pag-aatang , a traditional Filipino food offering that connects the living with the dead to honor departed loved ones. “‘Yung binibigyan pa rin ng food yung mga namatay na, kasi ‘di ba tayong mga Pilipino meron tayong mga paniwala na kinakain nila ‘yun,” she said, adding that the film brought her back to the days she failed to bring food to her departed loved ones. (The way we still offer food to those who have died, because us Filipinos believe that they actually eat it.) If Patay Gutom grieves what was left unsaid to the dead, Multwoh centers on a confession that never happened at all. Written and directed by queer artist Rodina Singh, the film follows a college queer student who dies suddenly and returns as a ghost, not to seek revenge, but to say the one thing they never found the courage to say in life: “I love you.” Director Rodina Singh (left) with leading lady, Sassa Gurl. Photo courtesy of Cinepanalo Press The film bills itself as haunting, hilarious, and tender, a story about fear, desire, and the kind of love that refuses to die. In the cinema, that mix is physical. The prosthetics on the film’s ghosts, the pantheon of departed souls played by the likes of Inah Evans and Joao Constancia’s allies-in-death, are startling enough that one first-time festivalgoer leaned over mid-film just to whisper how scary the makeup was. Director Rod Singh of Multwoh (Patay na Patay Sa’yo) together with the cast. Photo courtesy of Cinepanalo Press “Death may end a life, but love remembers how it will,” Singh said, adding that a huge part of the discussion goes missing when queer deaths reach the news only as “victims of murders, crimes, and accidents.” “We want to normalize queer love, because this is like a Disney film for queer kids,” Sassa Gurl said in a mix of English and Filipino. For Luis Mercado, 21, who watched Multwoh for the first time at the festival, the film felt personal. Luis Mercado shows up to watch both Patay Gutom and Multwoh. Jade Tan/Rappler It was Sassa Gurl’s character, Marcel, whom he saw himself in — a role that captured the anxiety of harboring a secret crush on a classmate and the fear that speaking the truth aloud would change everything between them. ”Huwag kang matakot mag-confess, kasi although hindi ‘yun yung gusto mong outcome, at least naexpress mo lang before mag-end ‘yung life mo,” Mercado said. (Don’t be afraid to confess, because even if you don’t get your desired outcome, at least you expressed yourself before your life ended.) Four confessions, one festival These are just two of the four films that feature four kinds of unsaid: a ghost’s love for the living, a family’s words to its dead loved one, a boy’s first attempt to understand love for a teacher, and a father’s indebtedness dressed up as a gratitude. But the festival stories do not stop with its full-length films. Cahilig also shared that 19 submissions for the short films lean heavily toward social commentary, with themes on abortion, mental health, socio-political issues, and complicated family setups. He said Puregold had specifically searched for stories that weren’t commonly told on screen. Play Video Among the shorts presented as part of this year’s lineup is Alumahan , a story about a grieving 13-year-old seeking to join a violent gang. There’s also Ang Huling Banlaw ni Susan, which follows a Filipina labandera (laundry woman) whose fantasies begin to overtake her reality. No Mad Is An Island, meanwhile, is about a young dancer in a fishing town whose dreams keep meeting the limits placed around him. Play Video For Keith Ian Serfino of the short film Limlim , the festival’s effect was almost physical. After staying away from cinemas since watching Oppenheimer , returning to the theater felt like something inside him had been switched back on. As a self-confessed lola ’s boy, Serfino felt that the nostalgia-packed Alumhan struck a chord with him most out of all the short films — the kind of story that unexpectedly stays with viewers long after they’ve left the cinema. Outside Gateway Cineplex 18, the mall is still bustling. But for two hours at every Cinepanalo film, the carefully handpicked stories all come to life on the big screen. – Rappler.com Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

title: 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police
body:
Police said the driver of the truck is a 34-year-old mother.
Two people, including a 6-year-old boy, were killed and 11 others injured after a truck drove through a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday afternoon, police said, in what officials called a "heartbreaking" incident that authorities are still investigating.
Among those injured were five children, ages 5 to 9, and five adults, ranging from a 28-year-old woman to a 68-year-old man, the Wichita Police Department said on Sunday. The injuries ranged from bruises to "extremely severe injuries."
A 61-year-old woman also experienced medical complications unrelated to traumatic injuries caused by the truck, bringing the total number of people sent to local hospitals to 11, police said.
First responders rushed to Stryker Soccer Complex after receiving multiple 911 calls around 3:25 p.m. CT, Capt. Aaron Moses of the Wichita Police Department told reporters at a press conference Saturday evening.
Police said the driver, who they identified only as a 34-year-old woman of Garden City, Kansas, stayed with the truck after the incident.
As of Sunday afternoon, no charges had been filed in the incident, according to police. The driver of the Chevrolet pickup truck involved in the incident was released from custody pending the results of toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of the vehicle.
"She has been cooperative to this point in the investigation," Moses said.
The two people killed in the incident were pronounced dead at the scene, police said. They were identified on Sunday by police as 6-year-old Cole Adrian and 35-year-old Nicholas Schafer, both of McPherson, Kansas.
These families "face an unimaginable loss ... what should have been a day of children playing soccer and families spending time together ended in tragedy," Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan said in a statement.
Investigators interviewed more than 30 witnesses, including the two juveniles who were inside the pickup at the time of the crash, police said on Sunday.
Moses told reporters on Saturday that one of the driver's children was playing soccer at the complex on Saturday but was not on that field at the time the incident occurred.
When police arrived at the scene, the truck was located on the west end of the field, and bystanders were helping to render aid to the injured people on the field, Moses said.
Police stressed they are still investigating and asked the public for patience.
"We know what happened, but now we're working very hard to find out why it happened, and we're not there yet," Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan told reporters.
Police said they have interviewed over 30 witnesses at the scene and are asking anyone with pictures or video of the incident to share them with investigators.
Police also credited bystanders who the police chief said "sprang into action so quickly and gave life-saving assistance until the arrival of first responders." Sullivan added, "It was truly amazing, but I think it's indicative of the of the Wichita community."
Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said "Tonight, Wichita grieves together."
"Today is a heartbreaking day for Wichita," Mayor Lily Wu told reporters. "Families came to Stryker Sports Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon watching their children play soccer. No one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold."
The city of Wichita said in a Facebook post Saturday afternoon that all events at the sports complex have been canceled until further notice.
"We ask that you keep all individuals and families affected in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time," the city said in a statement.
Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly said in a statement she was monitoring the situation and in touch with the mayor.
"My condolences go out to the families of the victims, the survivors, and all those impacted by this event," Kelly said in a statement.
In a statement, the Stryker Soccer Complex said it was praying for those affected.
"Our hearts are heavy as we process the tragic events at Stryker today," the statement said. "We are holding everyone impacted, the injured, their families, and all those who witnessed this heartbreaking event close in our thoughts and prayers."
ABC News' Chris Barry, Brianna Sanchez and Michael Pappano contributed to this report.

title: Samuel Jinapor questions expected economic benefits of Ghana’s proposed BRICS partnership
body: The Ranking Member of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, has questioned the benefits outlined by the government for Ghana’s proposed partnership with BRICS, describing the expectations as unrealistic. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 17, 2026, the Damongo MP argued that Ghana would still require clearance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to access certain forms of financial assistance. In his view, this would limit the opportunities Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa had suggested the partnership would offer. “It is comforting that we have been told now, that we are not going for full membership, but that we are starting with partnership. That is all well and good, but the point we (the minority in parliament) made, which I want to reiterate, is that in taking this decision- in other words, making a move to join BRICS, to join G20, even the New Development Bank- the point is that for you to access funding from the New Development Bank, you need IMF approval, and so the argument that this is going to help us move away from the dollar, that this is going to help us broaden our opportunities and to stabilise our currency, I am afraid, is a bit simplistic because you need IMF approval,” he said. Mr Jinapor nevertheless welcomed the government’s decision to pursue the relationship, acknowledging that initial steps towards engagement with BRICS began under the administration of former President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo. He said it was positive that the current administration was continuing that process, but maintained that the anticipated benefits needed to be assessed realistically. His comments followed Mr Ablakwa’s explanation that Ghana was seeking partner status with BRICS rather than full membership, as part of efforts to broaden its international cooperation.

title: Day two of Republic Bank- JoyNews Habitat Fair ends with massive turnout, Borborbor performances
body: The second day of the Republic Bank–JoyNews Habitat Fair in Ho ended with a cultural performance by the Woelinam Borborbor Group, as massive crowds continued to troop to the venue. The group from Ho entertained visitors at the Ho Sports Stadium with Borborbor music, songs and traditional dance, adding a cultural touch to the three-day housing exhibition. The performance drew attention to the Volta Region’s rich cultural heritage while providing entertainment for visitors exploring the exhibition stands. Children also had their share of the fun, with a bouncy castle providing a space for them to play as parents and other visitors engaged exhibitors. As the day drew to a close on Saturday, October 17, large numbers of visitors continued to arrive at the venue, adding to the lively atmosphere and creating opportunities for businesses to interact with potential customers. Exhibitors have been presenting a range of offerings, including building materials, property development, roofing systems, water storage solutions and home security services. The event continues to provide a platform for visitors to explore housing and home improvement options while engaging directly with participating companies. The three-day Republic Bank–JoyNews Habitat Fair continues on Sunday, October 18, at the Ho Sports Stadium, giving members of the public another opportunity to visit the exhibition stands and explore the products and services on display. title: By sending footage to enemy, people become tool in hands of invaders – CCD
body:
This was stated by the Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD), according to Ukrinform.
The Center stressed that by sending such materials to the enemy, people become a tool in the hands of the invaders, helping them conduct additional reconnaissance of targets and adjust subsequent strikes on Ukrainian cities.
“Transmitting information to the enemy about the movement of drones or missiles, the operation of air defense systems, and the aftermath of strikes in Ukraine is a criminal offense punishable by a lengthy prison term, up to life imprisonment,” the statement said.
The Center urged people not to interact with enemy chatbots and not to film or share photos and videos of air defense operations or the aftermath of attacks.
As reported, according to Serhii Beskrestnov (Flash), an adviser to the President on a non-staff basis, Russia is collecting footage of strikes by Geran attack drones, apparently to test the performance of optical recognition and target-guidance algorithms under combat conditions.

title: Daniel Dubois' five options after Fabio Wardley knockout - from Filip Hrgovic to Tyson Fury
body: Daniel Dubois ​retained his WBO heavyweight ​belt with a one-sided and devastating second-round stoppage of ⁠fellow Briton Fabio Wardley in their world title rematch on Saturday. The 29-year-old ⁠champion made a storming start at London's O2 Arena and ​Wardley's legs went from under him for a count within 17 seconds of the opening bell as Dubois floored him ⁠with a straight right. Wardley, 31, beat the count and could have been stopped at the end of the first round when he took a further brutal pounding on the ropes but was saved by the bell. There was no escape from the onslaught of ⁠blows in the second with Dubois picking up where he left off and Wardley taking punch after punch ​until the ⁠towel was thrown in and referee Steve ‌Gray brought the fight to a close. "Fabio is a great warrior, coming in for a second time, but it ​was my time and my era," said Dubois, never a man for long speeches. "I had my intentions, bad intentions, from the beginning. "Our back was against the wall the first time, this time we just had to go out there and show that we mean business and that's what we did tonight." Dubois dealt Wardley his first defeat as a professional when he came back from two knockdowns, the first after 16 seconds, to take the title in the 11th round of a thunderous and bloody clash in Manchester last May. Wardley, promoted to WBO champion last November after Ukraine's Oleksandr Usyk vacated the title, was acclaimed for his courage and refusal to give in first time around but on Saturday he looked a shell of the man seen in Manchester. He now has a 20-2-1 record with Dubois on 24 wins with three defeats. "I've always thrown myself in with the best competitors out there, ​the toughest, the biggest, hardest, meanest guys around. There's no shame in testing yourself ‌against the best," he said. "Daniel's a testament to ⁠coming up short and coming again, I'll be looking ​to do the exact same thing. "Boxing is a game of fine margins. It can be done ​and over in a ‌round or two or it can go into a big old war like it was last time." Here are five options for his Dubois's next opponent: 1 Filip Hrgovic The Croatian holds the IBF title after his win over Moses Itauma. In theory he must first defend it against Frank Sanchez, his mandatory challenger. Hrgovic lost to Dubois in 2024, but his appetite for a rematch was clear as he climbed into the ring at the O2 Arena on Saturday night. Hrgovic wants revenge 💥 #DuboisWardley2 ▪️ pic.twitter.com/9ZtJ2Fo6jk — DAZN Boxing (@DAZNBoxing) October 17, 2026 2 Agit Kabayel Kabayel holds the WBC title and is set to defend against Nelson Hysa next month. A unification against the Kurdish-German champion would make a lot of sense. 3 Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury winner Fury and Joshua will finally fight in December, with the WBA title reported to be on the line. Whether the winner would have the hunger to fight again and face Dubois is another question. 4 Frank Sanchez Should the Cuban beat Hrgovic then there's a strong chance he'd be lined up for Dubois. 5 Oleksandr Usyk The Ukrainian has beaten Dubois twice, but why not have another crack at the number one guy in the division?

title: Marco Rubio says Trump's Russian oil sanctions waiver is a '60-day pause,' denies restricting Starlink access
body:
Speaking with reporters on Oct. 18, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio detailed U.S. President Donald Trump waiving sanctions on the sale of Russian oil and addressed issues surrounding Ukraine's access to Starlink services.
When asked to respond to criticisms of Trump waiving sanctions that restrict the sale of Russian oil , Rubio said the waiver was a temporary measure to study the policy's impact on the global economy.
"I think the President wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," said Rubio.
Noting high energy prices around the world as a result of the U.S's war with Iran and the global need for oil, Rubio said that "we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is."
The Secretary's comments come following widespread outcries that Trump's move will create a windfall for Moscow, helping it continue attacking and killing Ukrainians.
"Unfortunately, I don't think this is a way to stop (Russian President Vladimir) Putin. On the contrary, he feels joy that he has such support," President Volodymyr Zelensky said about Trump's actions amid a falling out between the two leaders .
Rubio also addressed rumors that the U.S. had a role in limiting Ukrainian access to vital Starlink systems.
"No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it," Rubio said.
Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink, a satellite internet network operated by SpaceX, for battlefield communications and drone operations, including its campaign against Russian forces and logistics, and interceptor drones used against Russian long-range attack drones.
Ukraine first experienced malfunctions with Starlink systems on Oct. 14, when they began losing connectivity as they approached a certain speed.
While Ukraine reported that connectivity was restored by the next day, Zelensky claimed that a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour remains in place.
"Some of our interceptor drones use Starlink to intercept the enemy's fast-moving jet-powered drones," Zelensky said.
Multiple media reports have alleged that the issues with Starlink stem from U.S. leadership.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk approached U.S. President Donald Trump with the idea of restricting Starlink speeds for Ukrainian forces, the Telegraph reported on Oct. 16, citing four sources familiar with the matter.
Conflicting reports about the reason for the cutoff — and who was responsible — have left Ukraine with questions even after Starlink service stabilized on the front lines.
"I don’t know what their theory is, but nothing to do with the White House," said Rubio. "I saw a report on that the other day. It’s just categorically false."
When asked to respond to Zelensky's comments, Rubio pushed back.
"I don’t know what Zelenskyy said," said Rubio. "I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that."

title: SSU charges five more Russian soldiers over killing of Ukrainian POWs
body:
As reported by Ukrinform, the SSU said this in a statement.
The SSU recalled that Russian troops shot unarmed Ukrainian defenders on the premises of a local aggregate plant at the time.
Earlier, based on SSU evidence, one of the perpetrators, Russian national Sergey Tuzhilov (call sign “Altay”), was sentenced to life imprisonment. He personally killed one Ukrainian serviceman with an automatic weapon and helped organize the executions of two others.
The crimes of five more of his accomplices have now been documented. All of them served in the 82nd Motor Rifle Regiment of Russia’s 69th Motor Rifle Division. They are:
Privates Ruslan Kabanov (call sign “Koba”) and Vladislav Bortsov (call sign “Vudu”), who provided cover for the perpetrators during the execution of two prisoners.
The investigation established that in June 2024, on the territory of the plant temporarily occupied by Russian forces, the Russians first interrogated and then killed a Ukrainian prisoner of war.
“The Ukrainian serviceman was taken to a checkpoint near the administrative building of the facility, where he was shot in the head,” the SSU said.
Two weeks later, Russian troops captured two more Ukrainian defenders. They were taken to the plant, interrogated and tied to posts inside the administrative building.
“On July 3, 2024, the bound servicemen were taken to a utility room and shot in the back of the head,” the SSU said.
SSU investigators have now formally notified all five suspects in absentia that they are suspected of violating the laws and customs of war, combined with intentional murder, under Part 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
The actions of two of them have been classified as aiding and abetting a crime committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy.
Comprehensive measures are underway to bring those responsible to justice.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Book of Executioners of the Ukrainian People project published the names of 49 Russian judges allegedly involved in fabricating convictions against Ukrainian prisoners.

title: Hormuz insecurity result of US, Israeli aggression: Araghchi
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – Iran's foreign minister said insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is a direct result of US and Israeli aggression that began on February 28.
Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi said insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is a direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Zionist regime, which began on Feb. 28, 2026, and has continued in various forms since.
Araghchi made the remarks in a meeting with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty on the sidelines of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation's Council of Foreign Ministers summit in Baghdad, where they discussed bilateral relations and regional and international developments.
Araghchi described Palestine as still the most important issue of the Islamic world and, citing the genocide of Palestinians and crimes committed in occupied Palestine, stressed the need for urgent and joint action by the Islamic ummah to end the occupation and genocide and to stop the Israeli regime's impunity.
He pointed to Iran's commitment to diplomacy and peace in the region, saying the Islamic Republic has always adhered to diplomacy with a responsible approach to reducing tensions, but the US side repeatedly broke its commitments, most recently violating its pledge just two weeks after signing an MoU to end the war.
Araghchi also briefed his Egyptian counterpart on the latest diplomatic consultations through mediators.

title: Dubai's economy reaches Dh473 billion in first half of 2026 as key sectors expand
body: Dubai's economy reached Dh473 billion in the first half of 2026, down 2.3 per cent from a year earlier, as growth in financial services, healthcare and construction helped offset weakness in other sectors. The emirate's real gross domestic product declined from Dh484 billion in the same period last year, according to figures released on Sunday by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment at Digital Dubai. The slowdown came as the Iran war, which began on February 28, disrupted regional travel and trade, weighing on Dubai's tourism and transport sectors and dampening economic activity during the first half of the year. GDP at current prices, however, increased by 0.2 per cent to Dh505 billion, reflecting growth across several key sectors. Helal Almarri, director general of the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, said the figures demonstrated the emirate's ability to navigate global uncertainty. "Dubai’s H1 2026 GDP performance reflects the strength and adaptability of an economy built to navigate periods of significant global uncertainty," he said. The first-half numbers, however, mark a reversal from the 2.4 per cent annual growth recorded in the first quarter , when Dubai's economy reached Dh232 billion despite regional economic challenges. Financial and insurance activities were among the strongest performers in the first half, expanding 8.8 per cent in real terms to Dh65.9 billion, compared with Dh60.6 billion a year earlier. The sector's contribution to GDP increased to 14 per cent from 12.5 per cent, highlighting its growing importance to the emirate's economy. The expansion comes as the Dubai International Financial Centre continues to attract international financial institutions , with the number of companies operating at the financial hub exceeding 10,000 in the first half of the year. Healthcare and social work activities recorded the fastest growth, expanding 14.3 per cent, while information and communication activities increased 2.7 per cent. Construction grew 2.4 per cent in real terms, generating Dh33.2 billion in value added, while government services expanded 2.9 per cent. However, several major sectors contracted during the period. Dubai's GDP reaches AED473 billion in H1 2026 #WamNews https://t.co/x6Y1agL9wD https://t.co/G8rxQVRfZ9 — WAM English (@WAMNEWS_ENG) October 17, 2026 Wholesale and retail trade, Dubai's largest economic activity, declined 6 per cent in real terms, although it continued to account for 20.5 per cent of GDP. Transport and storage fell 7.4 per cent, while real estate activity contracted 2.5 per cent in constant prices, despite growing 5.4 per cent at current prices. Manufacturing also declined 0.9 per cent in real terms. The slowdown reflects wider economic challenges across the region, with the UAE's economy expanding just 0.4 per cent in the first half amid disruption caused by the Iran war. Free zone boost However, despite the geopolitical headwinds, trade in the first six months of this year through Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (Diez) free zones achieved another record. The total value of trade across its three economic zones climbed 17 per cent annually to Dh246 billion, Dubai Media Office said on Sunday. The results marked Diez's sixth consecutive year of record first-half trade performance, reflecting the confidence of investors and international trade stakeholders in Dubai's and the UAE's position at the heart of global trade. The value of imports during the first half rose to Dh134.8 billion, a 14 per cent increase compared to the same period last year. Re-exports grew by 22 per cent to about Dh109 billion. Trade volumes reached approximately 270,000 tonnes during the first half of the year, compared to approximately 298,000 tonnes during the same period in 2025, the media office said. Projects continue Dubai is moving ahead with Dh2.1 trillion in projects covering housing, aviation and transport, including the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport, as part of efforts to support long-term economic growth. Meanwhile, Dubai CommerCity announced a Dh1.8 billion expansion this month to boost its digital commerce sector and attract more technology investment. Mr Almarri said that continued growth across strategic sectors highlighted the strength of Dubai's economic fundamentals and its focus on long-term development. Dubai is pressing ahead with its D33 economic agenda, which aims to strengthen its position as a global business and investment centre. The emirate has also introduced measures to support businesses, including a Dh1.5 billion economic relief package announced in May to help sectors affected by regional uncertainty.

title: IPL 2027: Yuvraj Singh, Sourav Ganguly and Zaheer Khan lead coaching shake-up
body: IPL 2027 will be the 20th edition of the T20 league, with the Indian cricket board planning to celebrate the milestone moment on a big scale. The teams are also busy. A number of sides have already made changes ahead of the new season, with most developments taking place at the management level. Here is the story so far ahead of IPL 2027. Yuvraj Singh One of the bigger developments ahead of IPL 2027 is the recruitment of India’s multiple World Cup winner Yuvraj Singh as coach. Former India all-rounder Yuvraj was unveiled as Delhi Capitals' assistant and batting coach. It will be Yuvraj’s first official stint as coach, having earlier mentored young batters like Abhishek Sharma in his personal capacity. “I am excited to begin a new chapter in my life with the Delhi Capitals,” Yuvraj said in a statement. “I have an old association with the franchise and know the owners well, which makes this a special opportunity for me.” Delhi Capitals have once again undergone a major personnel change, coinciding with change of management control; the franchise’s co-owners exchange management control every two years. "𝘐𝘵 𝘩𝘢𝘴𝘯'𝘵 𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘢𝘴𝘵, 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴𝘯'𝘵 𝘮𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘯'𝘵 𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘯 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘶𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦." 💪 pic.twitter.com/7aEUdBspNF — Delhi Capitals (@DelhiCapitals) October 13, 2026 Sourav Ganguly Former India captain Sourav Ganguly will be in charge of Delhi Capitals franchise after being appointed ⁠as head coach for the 2027 season. Ganguly will have his protege Yuvraj in the dugout as he embarks upon another stint with the franchise that is yet to the win the league title. Ganguly joined the Delhi franchise as an adviser in 2019 and also was the ⁠team's director of cricket in 2023/24. The former opener took over from Hemang Badani. Stephen Fleming The biggest move in the IPL happened at Chennai as Stephen Fleming stepped down as head coach of the highly successful Super Kings after 18 years in charge. Fleming had formed a wildly successful partnership with Chennai icon MS Dhoni, which brought in five IPL and two (defunct) Champions League T20 titles. However, with Dhoni largely out of the picture and the Super Kings struggling over the last three seasons, Fleming’s tenure came to an end. The former New Zealand captain quickly moved to a set-up that should suit his cricket philosophy – the England Test squad. Fleming took over from Brendon McCullum , who remains England’s white-ball coach, after a tumultuous year which was riddled with questionable player and team behaviour. Fleming’s former Chennai associate Eric Simons has joined him as Test bowling coach. Rishabh Pant The wicketkeeper batter returned to Delhi Capitals for the 2027 season after completing his trade from Lucknow Super Giants. Pant had become the most expensive Indian player in IPL history when he was acquired by Lucknow for a record $3.2 million in 2025 . But that price tag weighed him down as he failed to turn things around at the Super Giants, resulting in a trade that has seen Pant take a substantial pay cut. In return, Lucknow got the services of left-arm spinner Kuldeep Yadav. Both players returned to the cities where they played at the domestic level. For Pant, it will be a critical season as he seems to be slipping down the pecking order in Indian cricket, being frozen out of the T20 side and not considered in ODIs as well. A good IPL 2027 could see him force his way into the team for the ODI World Cup in southern Africa next year. Zaheer Khan The 2011 World Cup winner has been appointed as the new Chennai coach, taking over from Fleming, and reuniting with his former captain Dhoni who remains an active player on paper. Zaheer was with Mumbai Indians management from 2018 until 2022, before being named as mentor of Lucknow. Now, he takes over as head coach of the most successful franchise in IPL history, with the aim of forming a clear path ahead with the talismanic Dhoni expected to move further away from the playing side of the team. A new chapter Ungal Anbuden, Zaheer! 🦁💛 #WhistlePodu #Yellove pic.twitter.com/zpoP0HVMOU — Chennai Super Kings (@ChennaiIPL) September 24, 2026 Hardik Pandya This seems like a never ending saga. India all-rounder Hardik Pandya left the Mumbai Indians franchise, enjoyed a wildly successful two seasons at Gujarat Titans, was brought back to Mumbai in a hugely controversial move and has been struggling there since, with Rohit Sharma, Suryakumar Yadav and Jasprit Bumrah also in leadership positions. Now, there is a strong possibility that Rohit is handed the captaincy once again, with the India opener having hit form at the international level in ODIs. Pandya, meanwhile, is struggling with fitness with multiple injuries this season and doubts over his long-term availability. Pandya, however, remains an attractive option for many franchises as he is one of the few quality all-rounders in the country with a proven record with title winning sides. The seam-bowling all-rounder could be traded ahead of IPL 2027. Elsewhere, Sunrisers Hyderabad brought left-arm seamer T. Natarajan back into the team, trading him from Delhi Capitals who got leg-spinner Zeeshan Ansari in return. Mahela Jayawardene Big changes are taking place at Mumbai Indians. The franchise parted ways with head coach Mahela Jayawardene . The Sri Lankan great was Mumbai's head coach for the last two seasons - his second stint with the franchise - and coincided with a leadership crisis where Pandya was brought in as captain despite the presence of MI veterans Rohit, Suryakumar and Bumrah. "Mumbai Indians has been a very special part of my journey for over a decade now," Jayawardene said in an statement. "The players, coaching team, and above all the fans have made this an experience I will always treasure."

title: Melitzanosalata: A Smoky Greek Eggplant Salad With Feta
body: This chunky melitzanosalata mixes smoky grilled eggplant with feta, tomato and onion, and it scores 4.7 out of 5 from 17 ratings on Allrecipes. Melitzanosalata with feta, tomato and parsley. Photo: Allrecipes Melitzanosalata, the smoky taste of the meze table Melitzanosalata is one of the best-loved dips in Greece. In fact, Greek City Times listed it among five Greek dips in TasteAtlas’s top 50 , praising its smoky depth. Most versions are smooth, made by mashing charred eggplant with garlic, lemon and olive oil. According to TasteAtlas , cooks often add cheese, nuts, other vegetables or fresh herbs. This recipe takes the chunky road instead. Allrecipes member constantina calls it melitzanosalata agioritiki and translates it as Athenian eggplant salad. However, agioritiki usually points to Agion Oros, the monastic community of Mount Athos in northern Greece. Either way, the result is a fresh, diced salad rather than a purée. It also needs no garlic and no lemon, since vinegar brings the sharpness. Ingredients for Greek eggplant salad This Greek eggplant salad makes about four cups, or eight serves. Allrecipes lists roughly 99 calories per serve. You will need: 1 large eggplant, washed 1 small onion, diced 1 tomato, seeded and chopped 1/2 cup crumbled feta cheese 2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil 2 tablespoons distilled white vinegar Salt, to taste Leave out the feta and this Greek eggplant salad suits the fasting table, too. Greek City Times has noted that the smoky dip is a popular Lenten dish , alongside taramosalata and halva. How to make it Allrecipes lists 20 minutes of preparation and about 15 minutes on the grill. As a result, with an hour of chilling, allow just under two hours for this melitzanosalata. Heat an outdoor grill to medium-high and lightly oil the grate. Prick the eggplant a few times with a small knife or fork. Grill it, turning often, for about 15 minutes, until the skin is charred and the flesh is soft. Let it cool until you can handle it, then peel off and discard the skin. Dice the flesh and tip it into a bowl. Add the onion, tomato, feta, parsley, olive oil and vinegar, then mix well. Chill the melitzanosalata for one hour, then season with salt just before serving. Serve it as part of a meze spread with bread, olives and tzatziki . For another way to enjoy the same vegetable, try Greek City Times’ recipe for papoutsakia , baked stuffed eggplant. What home cooks say Home cooks have rated this Greek eggplant salad highly. Of the 12 reviews shown with the recipe, all give it five stars. One reviewer, veka, wrote that it tasted “just like we eat in Thassos this summer.” Another, KVarn, called it a go-to summer eggplant recipe and only added some pepper. Several cooks made the melitzanosalata exactly as written. For instance, cldebbie called it a very refreshing dish, while pizzacake made it a second time within three days. Imanewme also noted that the eggplant was not bitter at all. In addition, Jezebelina doubled the eggplant and tomatoes and still called the result excellent. Others changed the mix itself. Lyn Galiote added peppers and yellow squash from the garden. By comparison, pricefamilyx6 stirred in chickpeas and left out the feta and tomato. There is one warning, though. As sloandeasy put it, if you don’t like raw onion, this is not the dish for you. Tips for a smoky melitzanosalata without a grill Not everyone owns an outdoor grill, so reviewers shared other ways to cook the eggplant for this melitzanosalata. Imanewme roasted it in the oven instead, while sloandeasy suggested wrapping it in foil first. Similarly, Deborah Ward Hill used an indoor electric grill and sliced the eggplant beforehand to speed things up. When dochele’s grill failed, the eggplant came off half cooked. So that cook diced it and finished it in a pan with the olive oil and a little garlic. Then, while it was still hot, the rest of the ingredients went in. Whatever the method, the aim of a good Greek eggplant salad stays the same: soft flesh and a hint of char. Also, seed the tomato as the recipe asks, so the salad does not turn watery in the fridge. Overall, this melitzanosalata is simple, cheap and easy to scale up for a crowd. The original recipe on Allrecipes also includes four photos from home cooks. Source: Allrecipes The post Melitzanosalata: A Smoky Greek Eggplant Salad With Feta appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Meet Voxel51 3.0: A Unified Multimodal Data Platform for Physical AI
body: Voxel51 has released Voxel51 3.0 , a very important update to its data platform. Voxel51 3.0 is an end-to-end multimodal data platform that puts search, curation, annotation and evaluation in one system. It targets teams training models on sensor data from robots, vehicles and factories. The release adds Voxel51 Agent, a data provenance layer and free self-service access . TL;DR Scale: Voxel51 Agent ships with 45+ MCP tools, 80+ operators and 18 open-source skills. Runs on: Hosted web app at app.voxel51.com, or self-hosted in cloud, hybrid, on-prem and air-gapped setups. No local GPU requirement disclosed. Performance: No product benchmarks published. Voxel51 cites its own survey data instead. Best: Free tier includes Voxel51 Agent, 30,000 inference requests and 30 compute hours per month. Worst: Free tier caps at 3 datasets of 10,000 samples each and 20 GB of storage. What is new in Voxel51 3.0? Voxel51 3.0 expands the platform beyond its roots in visual data with 3 core additions. Time-series multimodal support : Teams can view multiple sensor streams on 1 timeline. Segment-level embeddings find specific moments inside long recordings. Unified annotation : Labeling covers 2D, 3D, video and multimodal data. It includes automated QA, annotator metrics and human-in-the-loop review. Agentic Labeling : Vision-language models generate labels from natural-language instructions and examples. Supported modalities include MCAP, images, video, 3D point clouds, meshes, DICOM, NIfTI, geospatial data and audio. How does Voxel51 Search work? Voxel51 Search is a persistent hybrid index. It indexes datasets and computes embeddings automatically, so search works from day 1. Semantic retrieval finds visually or semantically similar moments, even without shared labels. Lexical and structured queries handle exact terms, timestamps, sensor fields and metadata. Embeddings and structured fields stay in native form and are combined at retrieval time. Vector retrieval runs on LanceDB. It supports vector, scalar and full-text indexes, and separates storage from compute. Teams choose what to embed, which model and compute to use, and when. Incremental updates avoid full rebuilds when samples arrive or schemas change. What can Voxel51 Agent do? Voxel51 Agent chains search, curation, annotation and evaluation into repeatable workflows. Example workflows: A robotics team searches behaviors across thousands of episodes, then curates balanced training sets. A perception team starts from a model failure and pulls similar long-tail scenarios for labeling. The agent can also write code to build custom plugins. All workflows inherit the organization’s permissions and governance controls. How does data provenance work in Voxel51 3.0? Voxel51 3.0 adds 4 provenance layers : Deployment-level activity log: who did what, and when, across the deployment. Dataset-level activity log: how a single dataset evolved. Sample-level edit history: label, metadata and property changes per sample. Dataset versioning: immutable snapshots to reproduce training and evaluation runs. Events flow through fiftyone-mq for job scheduling and Activity Core for event tracking. Can teams bring their own models? Yes. The platform is model-agnostic across embeddings, auto-labeling, inference and evaluation. A team can bootstrap with a foundation model, then swap in its own domain model. Why does Voxel51 argue data work decides outcomes? Voxel51 cites its 2026 State of Physical AI survey . 58% of “exceptional” teams spend more than half their project time on data work. Only 21% of struggling teams do the same. This is vendor-run research, so read it as directional. #v51x-embed iframe{width:100%!important;border:0!important;display:block;background:transparent!important;}#v51x-embed p:empty,#v51x-embed hr{display:none!important;} (function(){var f=document.getElementById('v51x-frame');window.addEventListener('message',function(e){if(e.source!==f.contentWindow)return;var d=e.data;if(d&&typeof d.v51h==='number'&&d.v51h>100){f.style.height=d.v51h+'px';}});})(); How does Voxel51 3.0 compare with Encord and Foxglove? Feature Voxel51 3.0 Encord Foxglove Core focus Search, curate, annotate, evaluate multimodal data Annotation, curation and data management Robotics visualization, observability and data management Free tier 3 datasets, 10,000 samples each, 20 GB Not disclosed 10 GB storage, 3 users, 5 devices Paid entry Team: 8 seats, 2,800 compute hrs/mo (price not disclosed) Starter (price not disclosed) Pro: $20/mo + usage, 1 TB storage Built-in agent Voxel51 Agent Data agents (Team plan) Agent sidebar MCP 45+ MCP tools Not disclosed Foxglove MCP (local MCP on paid plans) Search Hybrid semantic, lexical and metadata Multi-modal search, querying, filtering Semantic Search (beta) plus structured search Annotation 2D, 3D, video, multimodal, Agentic Labeling Image, video, audio, documents; 3D and LiDAR add-on Events on time segments Time-series sensor data MCAP, synced streams, segment embeddings Sensor streams (see note) MCAP, ROS 1, ROS 2 native Provenance Activity logs, edit history, versioning Not disclosed Audit logs (not on Free) Self-hosted On-prem and air-gapped available VPC and on-prem (add-on or Enterprise) Self-hosted data on Enterprise; BYO storage on Pro Encord’s sensor-stream support is stated in its Series C release . Prices verified October 17, 2026. Key Takeaways Voxel51 3.0 merges search, curation, annotation and evaluation in 1 platform. Voxel51 Agent ships with 45+ MCP tools, 80+ operators and 18 skills. Activity logs, edit history and versioning make training data traceable. Free tier: 3 datasets, 10,000 samples each, no credit card. Check out the official blog post , the press release and the Voxel51 docs , or try it at app.voxel51.com . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: PMA’s first female summa cum laude takes command of cadets
body: BAGUIO CITY – Leah Lorenzo entered the Philippine Military Academy (PMA) in 1993 as one of its first 17 female cadets, stepping into an institution that had never admitted women in its decades of military training . Only seven would graduate four years later. Lorenzo was among them, finishing third in her class and becoming the Academy’s first female summa cum laude. On Saturday, October 17, nearly three decades after her graduation, she returned to PMA to make history again. Now a colonel in the Philippine Army , Leah Lorenzo Santiago became PMA’s first female commandant of cadets, overseeing the military training, discipline, and leadership development of future Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) officers. As a former member of Charlie Company, Santiago belonged to a generation of women who had to prove they deserved a place at PMA. She will now help shape the next generation of military leaders. Santiago, a member of the Kalasaglahi Class of 1997, formally assumed her post during a change of command ceremony at Yap Hall, Fort General Gregorio H. del Pilar, in Baguio City. She succeeded Colonel Eugene Henry Cabusao, who served as acting commandant following the retirement of Brigadier General Nelson Aluad on September 26. YOUNG. Colonel Leah L. Santiago during her days as a cadet at the Philippine Military Academy. Photo courtesy of PMA One of the Magnificent Seven Santiago’s journey at PMA began on April 1, 1993, when the Academy admitted its first female cadets following the passage of Republic Act No. 7192, or the Women in Development and Nation Building Act. The law opened the Academy’s doors to women, ending its long-standing male-only admission policy. Of the 17 female cadets who entered, only seven completed the demanding four-year program. They became known as the Magnificent Seven, the first women to graduate from PMA. Three ranked among the top 10 in the 136-member graduating class. Santiago placed third overall. Her achievement drew international attention. In an Associated Press report published on March 17, 1997, Santiago described the resistance some female cadets initially faced from their male counterparts. “It’s been a learning process for both us and our male counterparts,” she said at the time. The report also recounted how she persevered through physically demanding training, including an incident in which she fainted during an exercise. Rather than abandon the course, she stayed and completed it, eventually graduating with one of the Academy’s highest academic distinctions. A career beyond academic honors After graduating in 1997, Santiago was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the Philippine Army. She began her military career with the 30th Infantry Battalion of the 4th Infantry Division, serving as a platoon leader and executive officer of Bravo Company before becoming its commander. Her subsequent assignments spanned military administration, field artillery, personnel management, and cadet training. From 2016 to 2019, she returned to PMA as its first female Senior Tactical Officer, overseeing aspects of the Cadet Corps’ military training and development. She later commanded the 9th Field Artillery Battery (Provisional) of the Army Artillery Regiment in Sulu before taking on senior personnel management responsibilities at Army headquarters. Her assignments included serving as executive officer and deputy of the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff for Personnel (G1), as well as director of the Philippine Army’s Personnel Management Center. Before her appointment as Commandant of Cadets, she served as the Army’s Assistant Chief of Staff for Personnel, G1. Santiago also pursued advanced military and civilian education, earning master’s degrees from the Development Academy of the Philippines, the Australian National University, and the Ateneo Graduate School of Business. She completed additional military courses in the Philippines and Australia, along with training in gender and development planning and budgeting at Miriam College. ARRIVAL. The Philippine Military Academy renders foyer honors to incoming Commandant of Cadets Colonel Leah Santiago in front of Lim Hall. Photo courtesy of PMA Shaping the next generation Santiago’s appointment places her in charge of a central part of PMA’s mission, preparing cadets to become officers capable of leading soldiers, exercising sound judgment, and fulfilling their responsibilities to the country. PMA Superintendent Lieutenant General Michael Logico, who presided over the ceremony, expressed confidence in her ability to take on the role, citing the demands that future military leaders will face. “As Commandant of Cadets, she will have the responsibility of helping shape the character, competence, and leadership of the next generation of officers,” he said. “She will help prepare them not only to meet the demands of today’s operational environment, but also face the challenges of a future we cannot fully predict. That is tremendous responsibility. And I have every confidence that she is prepared to meet it.” For Santiago, the assignment brings her back to an institution where she once endured the rigorous training and pressures now facing the cadets under her command. In her remarks, Santiago committed to developing officers guided by integrity, professional competence, and dedication to duty. “Remember, you are not here merely to earn a degree or a commission. You are here to prepare yourselves for the responsibility of leading soldiers and defending our Republic,” she told the cadets. She also stressed that military leaders are not expected to be perfect. “I do not expect you to be perfect. I expect you to be honest about your weaknesses, receptive to correction, and determined to improve.” She reminded the cadets that, despite her rank, accomplishments, and years of military service, she had once stood where they stand today. – Rappler.com

title: Critical infrastructure damaged in Russian air attack on Vinnytsia region
body:
This was reported by Natalia Zabolotna, Head of the Vinnytsia Regional Military Administration, on her Telegram channel, according to Ukrinform.
“The enemy’s air attack caused damage to critical infrastructure. Emergency power outages are currently in effect across the region. Where necessary, critical infrastructure facilities are switching to backup power sources,” the post said.
According to Zabolotna, energy workers are already working to restore power supplies, but the electricity situation is expected to remain unstable in the near future.
Residents of the Vinnytsia region are urged not to switch on all electrical appliances at the same time in order to avoid artificially overloading the grid.
