title: Dems lead GOP in House vote choice as Trump's approval rating hits record low: Poll
body:
Half or more Americans call every household purchase measured "unaffordable."
Just over two-weeks out from consequential midterm elections, a record share of Americans disapprove of President Donald Trump, about 7 in 10 say gasoline is unaffordable and that the country is headed in the wrong direction, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted using Ipsos’ KnowledgePanel .
By an 8-percentage point margin, likely voters support the Democratic candidate in congressional district elections over the Republican candidate, 52% to 44%. That margin remains 8 points among registered voters overall, 50% to 42%, an improvement from a July Washington Post-Ipsos poll for Democrats, when just 3 points separated the Democrats from the Republicans.
Although control of the House will ultimately be determined in votes for individual candidates in individual congressional districts across the county, the generic House question is a useful barometer. For example, before the last midterms, a fall 2022 ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll found registered voters nearly split and Republicans went on to win Congress. In a fall 2018 poll , Democrats had an 11-point lead over Republicans among registered voters and Democrats went on to win the House that year.
Overwhelming shares of partisans support their party’s candidates – 98% of Democratic likely voters and 96% of Republican likely voters each support their party candidates.
Democrats are bolstering their lead among independent likely voters, who support Democratic candidates by a 21-point margin, 56% to 35%.
Democrats are also benefiting from the fact that there’s more enthusiasm from their supporters. More Democratic voters (72%) than Republican voters (65%) say they are absolutely certain to vote and more Democratic voters are following the midterms “extremely” or “very” closely than Republican voters – 44% to 31%.
About 9 in 10 of the roughly half of likely voters who strongly disapprove of Trump plan to vote for the Democratic candidate in their congressional district. And over 9 in 10 of the likely voters who approve of Trump plan to vote for Republicans. But the roughly 1 in 10 voters who somewhat disapprove of Trump support the Republican candidate over the Democratic one by a double-digit margin, 58% to 34%.
Half or more Americans call every household purchase category measured “unaffordable” in the latest poll, including 71% who now call gasoline unaffordable, up from 28% who said the same in February , before the war in Iran drove up fuel costs. The national average gas price has topped $4 a gallon for a record 158 days in 2026 so far.
An increasing share of Americans also call healthcare unaffordable (65%, up from 56% in February) along with home energy and utility costs (57%, up from 45%) and rent or mortgage (50%, up from 37%).
And 60% call groceries unaffordable, also up from February (45%) but less than July (66%).
Growing shares of Americans call relative luxuries unaffordable, too. A 61% majority of Americans call going out to dinner unaffordable, up from 49% in February. Even more, 69%, say a weeklong vacation is unaffordable, up from 60%. And 80% call a new car unaffordable, up from 74% in February.
In all, 75% of Americans rate the nation’s economy negatively, including 35% who call it poor. Roughly half, 48%, say they are “not as well off” as they were when Trump became president, a high over both of his presidential terms.
Likely voters who rate the economy poorly support Democrats over Republicans in the generic ballot by 72 points. Likely voters who say they are not as well off support Democrats over Republicans by 60 points.
Beyond just the economy, Americans are unhappy with the direction the country is moving in: 72% say things in the country are headed in the wrong direction; just 26% say things are heading in the right direction.
Trump’s weak approval ratings do not bode well for his party given that midterms are often a referendum vote on the president. And Trump’s approval rating has reached a record personal low of 33% percent in the ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, lower even than after the Jan. 6, 2021, attacks on the U.S. Capitol when 38% approved. Today, 66% of Americans disapprove, a record high over both terms.
Just over half of Americans, 52%, strongly disapprove of Trump, matching his strong disapproval rating after the Jan. 6 attack, and a record high for his second term, according to the poll.
Over both of his terms, a record-low 22% of independents approve of Trump and a record-high 76% disapprove, including 58% who strongly disapprove – another record high over both of Trump’s terms.
Among Republicans, 79% approve, down just slightly from a July Post-Ipsos poll but down significantly from 88% near the beginning of his second term. And a record-low 39% strongly approve of Trump, down from 63% in February 2025 . Today, 21% of Republicans disapprove, up from 12% in February 2025. That includes nearly half of non-MAGA Republicans (47%) who disapprove today.
A majority of MAGA Republicans strongly approve of the president, 55%, but that’s down from 65% in February. About 6 in 10 Republicans consider themselves supporters of the MAGA movement, both now and in February.
Among registered voters overall, Trump’s overall approval rating is slightly better: 37% approve and 63% disapprove.
Majorities of Americans also disapprove of how Trump is handling every issue measured, and for many issues, Trump is at or near record-low approvals.
His worst issue is handling the cost of living in the U.S. -- perhaps the defining issue for the 2026 midterms -- and his ratings are similarly low to what they were in the ABC/Post/Ipsos poll in April . Now, just 21% approve while 77% disapprove.
Trump has similarly low ratings on handling inflation: 23% approve and 75% disapprove, a worse margin than in April when 27% approved and 72% disapproved.
On the economy overall, 28% approve of how Trump is handling things and 70% disapprove, a record-low approval and a record-high disapproval over both of Trump’s terms. In a July Post-Ipsos poll, 33% approved and 65% disapproved. His approval rating on the economy peaked at 56% in January 2020.
On Iran, 27% approve of how Trump is handling the situation and 70% disapprove, virtually the same as in a July Post-Ipsos poll. A 65% majority of Americans say it was a mistake for the U.S. to use military force against Iran.
On relations with U.S. allies, 30% approve of how Trump is handling things and 68% disapprove. A 58% majority of Americans say the U.S. should either reduce military support to Israel (25%) or end it completely (33%).
Trump’s best issue is immigration, where 38% approve and 61% disapprove, slightly down from his July approval ratings on the issue. A 56% majority of Americans say Trump is “going too far” in deporting undocumented immigrants while 15% say he is “not going far enough” and 28% say he’s handling it about right.
On how Trump is managing the military, 35% approve and 63% disapprove.
About two-thirds of Americans say since taking office, Trump has “gone beyond his authority as president;” about a third say he has acted within his authority.
Majorities of Americans say Trump is “not committed” to respecting the authority of Congress (68%), protecting freedom of the press (67%), respecting the authority of the courts (66%), free and fair elections (61%) or protecting freedom of speech (61%). Shares of Americans saying that Trump is not committed to protecting freedom of the press, free and fair elections and freedom of speech are all up from last October.
A record-high 66% of Americans say Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, up from 62% in February and 56% in September 2025. Majorities of Democrats (94%) and independents (73%) along with just over a quarter of Republicans (27%) say Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself.
Wide majorities of Americans also say that it is “inappropriate” for Trump to push to have his name put on the Kennedy Center (80%, including 59% who say it is “totally inappropriate”), including majorities across partisan groups. Even 57% of Republicans say it is inappropriate.
And when it comes to the federal government paying for TV ads promoting Trump and his policies , 74% say it is inappropriate, including 55% who say it is totally inappropriate. Trump has said he would pay for the ads from political fundraising coffers, but the ads continued to air with a line saying they were "paid for by the U.S. government." A federal judge has ordered the government-funded ads to stop running.
About 6 in 10 Americans say Trump is focused too much on building projects in D.C. (59%); just 11% said he’s focused too little and 27% say he’s focused “the right amount” on building projects.
Most Republicans and Republican-leaning independents say the party should follow Trump’s leadership going forward (61%), with 37% saying the party should go in a different direction.
By a wide margin, Americans prefer that the next Congress be controlled by Democrats, to act as a check on Trump (59%) than by Republicans, to support Trump’s agenda (35%).
Americans trust Democrats over Republicans to handle 10 out of 12 issues measured in this poll.
U.S. adults trust Democrats over Republicans by 23 points to handle healthcare and by 14 points to handle education, the cost of living and inflation – all by wider margins than they have recently. Americans trust Democrats over Republicans by 11 points to handle the situation with Iran, by 9 points to handle reducing corruption in the government and transgender issues. Americans trust Democrats by 9 points to better handle the economy, the largest margin they’ve had on the issue since 2022 – previously they’ve been about tied with Republicans or were at a deficit to them. Adults trust Democrats over Republicans by 7 points to handle taxes along with the situation with Israel and Gaza.
The public is roughly divided on whether they trust Democrats or Republicans to do a better job handling immigration.
Americans trust Republicans more than Democrats to handle just one issue, crime, for which they prefer Republicans by a 5-point margin. Still, that’s a recent high mark for Democrats, who have trailed Republicans on the issue by double digits dating back four years.
Americans feel negative toward both the Democratic and Republican parties, but while the Democratic Party is just 10 points underwater on favorability (44% favorable and 54% unfavorable), the Republican Party is worse at 28 points underwater (35% favorable and 63% unfavorable).
Double haters, those who are unfavorable toward both parties, who make up about 2 in 10 voters, favor the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate in the generic ballot by 26 percentage points, 58% to 32%. This has been a key swing group in previous elections dating back to 2016.
More Americans call Trump and the Republican Party “too extreme” – 66% and 55%, respectively – than the Democratic Party (36%).
The MAGA movement is underwater by 41 percentage points, with 28% favorable and 69% unfavorable. Among Republicans, 70% are favorable and 28% are unfavorable.
Democratic socialism is underwater by 22 points, 37% of Americans are favorable and 59% are unfavorable. Among Democrats, 70% have a favorable view of democratic socialism and 27% are unfavorable.
Likely voters who plan to vote in different ways have different vote preferences. Voters who plan to vote in person on Election Day make up about 4 in 10 voters and support Republicans over Democrats by 11 points.
But the other ways voters plan to vote have a Democratic advantage: Those who plan to – or who have already voted early by mail – who make up just under 3 in 10 voters, support Democrats over Republicans by 26 points. About a quarter of likely voters plan to vote early at a polling place or already have, and they favor Democrats by 14 points. And about 1 in 10 voters plan to or have dropped off a ballot before Election Day and they support Democrats over Republicans by a wide 50-point margin.
See PDF for full results and detailed methodology.
Methodology: This ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll was conducted via the probability-based Ipsos KnowledgePanel Oct. 9-13, 2026, among 2,545 U.S. adults including 2,032 registered and likely voters and has an error margin of +/- 2 percentage points overall and +/- 2.2 points among registered and likely voters. All registered voters were assigned a probability of voting to produce likely voter results. Error margins among most other subgroups are larger.
ABC News’ Liz Schreier contributed to this report.
Email ABCNEWS.Polls@abc.com to be added to ABC News’ polling distribution list.
More ABC News polls can be found at abcnews.com . Media contacts: Jeannie Kedas and Van Scott.

title: 7 highlights from JD Vance's CBS News town hall
body: In an hour-long town hall hosted by CBS News, Vice President JD Vance argued the Trump administration's handling of the economy and Iran strategy will pay dividends in the future.He was also pressed on the Trump administration's controversial immigration tactics, widespread discontent about the cost of living and his own political future during "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance," which aired Saturday evening and was hosted by "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil.Vance took questions from voters in Michigan, a swing state that helped propel Vance and President Trump to victory in 2024 — and is the host of a tight Senate race that could help determine which party wins control of the upper chamber in next month's midterm elections.Vance says he hasn't decided if he'll run for presidentIf he decides to run for president in 2028, the vice president is widely viewed as an early frontrunner in the Republican primaries and a possible heir to Mr. Trump's political movement. Mr. Trump has called Vance his "most likely" GOP successor and has joked about a potential contest between Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.Asked by Dokoupil if there's any chance he won't run, Vance said: "Of course there's a chance.""The way that I think about life, big life decisions — my wife will tell you this — is I'm a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it," said Vance, adding that he'll "have to think about it."He also noted that he and his wife, Usha Vance, have four young children, and the second lady "has never loved politics," though "she loves public service."On economy, Vance says "we're turning the ship around" but it will take timeSeveral town hall attendees asked Vance about cost-of-living issues. The topic weighs heavily in the midterms, and has demonstrated it's a liability for Republicans based on CBS News polling. Voter dissatisfaction with inflation and the state of the economy under the Biden administration helped bring Mr. Trump and Vance to power, but polls indicate that most voters are still unhappy with the economy and hold the Trump administration responsible.Sandy Johnson said the family entertainment center she owns is "barely making ends meet," and asked when she can expect changes "so that the normal American has money to spend on small businesses."The vice president argued it could take some time. "What broke the United States, as much as I might like to criticize Joe Biden, but it was a bipartisan, multi-generational failure to under-invest in American workers, to under-invest in American manufacturing, to ship all of our good jobs overseas," Vance said. "If all the good jobs are overseas, then people here in Michigan can't spend money at your family business."He pointed to promises of new foreign investment in the United States, and growth plans by the three major Detroit-area automakers, General Motors, Ford and Chrysler parent Stellantis."We are turning the tide on this," Vance said, referring to the decline in U.S. manufacturing. "And I think there are all these things I pointed to that show signs of progress. But Sandy, I'll be the first person to tell you that, just as this country wasn't broken in one presidential term, it's gonna take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around."Since Mr. Trump returned to office last year, the unemployment rate has remained low, but inflation has remained stubbornly higher than the Federal Reserve's 2%-per-year target, eating into Americans' wages. The number of manufacturing jobs has also remained roughly flat.Asked by Dokoupil about Mr. Trump's assessment of an "A+" economy, Vance said the president was referring to new investments, "but he would be the first person to tell you that you gotta build the factories first before you can employ the workers working in those factories."Vance later said: "I think what we're doing is, we're turning the ship around."Iran and energy: "I recognize that gas prices are too high right now"One of the biggest pressure points on Americans' wallets is the Iran war, which has kept oil prices high even as the U.S. and Iran have refrained from active fighting in recent weeks.Keshon Wheatley, a barber from Detroit, told Vance that he voted for Mr. Trump in 2020 and 2024, in large part because he gave the president credit for low gas prices during his first term. Now, gas prices are far higher — and he said he plans to vote for Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, not Republican Mike Rogers.Vance pointed to Iran's attacks on oil tankers."We've never had a situation like this, where you have effectively the largest state sponsor of terrorism that's trying to completely choke off world energy supply," the vice president said, arguing that "if we just … left, and we let the Iranians control shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz, what that would mean is you would pay a lot more for gasoline."Asked how long it will take for prices to ease, Vance said, "When this conflict is over, we are going to see gas prices come down." He said oil is still being exported from the Middle East because of efforts by the U.S. military to allow ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.On the competitive Michigan Senate race, he argued El-Sayed — a frequent critic of the Iran war — has not offered a solution to the problem, and gave Rogers credit for calling for the war to end. "He's been remarkably independent about this," Vance said of Rogers.Dokoupil asked Vance why the U.S. hasn't decisively won the Iran war, which has dragged on for longer than Mr. Trump initially expected.Vance argued that "in some ways we have won decisively," but "the enemy gets a vote here."The vice president — who participated in negotiations with Iran over the summer — defended the president's Iran strategy, and said the Trump administration is looking for a "final firm commitment from the Iranians that they're not going to rebuild their nuclear program."Man whose wife died in Iranian strike decries "fundamental failures"The Iran war has also imposed human costs, with 21 U.S. service members killed and hundreds injured since the conflict began in late February. In the war's early hours, six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed in an Iranian strike on a site in Kuwait, including Master Sgt. Nicole Amor. Her husband, Joey Amor, asked Vance about reports that the facility in Kuwait was not adequately secured."Though the Iranian drone was the weapon that killed my wife, there were a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures that led up to that," Amor said, asking Vance "how this administration is gonna start holding those leaders accountable."Vance said he didn't doubt there were failures, but "sometimes information doesn't filter up to me." He vowed to "take every single failure extremely seriously."He also noted that cheap drones have changed warfare, and "we have changed a lot of our tactics to try to suppress that drone fire, to try to protect our troops to make it so that more people don't have to pay the ultimate sacrifice."Vance also said: "I know that there are some issues with, for example … where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake and that we could do better on. And we have changed that."Nun presses Vance on immigration tacticsSister Nancy Sylvester, a member of the Sister Servants of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, asked Vance about the Trump administration's approach to immigration enforcement.She asked Vance, a fellow Catholic, "how you would justify [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactics] to people of faith," and "what policies would you advocate to try to promote more compassionate and [respectful] behavior toward our immigrant sisters and brothers."Vance responded, "We're trying to strike a balance between: How do we do law enforcement, but how do we also do it humanely, and how do we not do so little law enforcement that you actually empower some of the worst people in the world."Vance later said most ICE agents are "amazing people who are patriots," but some of them "make mistakes" or "really screw up." He added that "obviously, we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up."Asked if any major mistakes by ICE come to mind, Vance responded that "there are a number of cases where we've investigated and either provided further training, or sometimes even provided disciplinary situations within ICE."Another town hall attendee pressed Vance on some of the administration's rhetoric around immigration, including Vance's own comments that likened some holders of employment-based H-1B visas to "foreign indentured servants."Vance responded, "To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me."He said his comments were "not a criticism of the H-1B holder.""That's a criticism of a company who brings a person in, who sometimes will literally lay off an American worker, bring somebody else in, and knows that person, if they complain, if they get too uppity at work, if they have a disagreement with their boss, they couldn't just lose their job, … they can be shipped back to their country of origin," Vance said. "And I think that gives employers way too much power."He said, "My goal here is not to dehumanize any immigrant." But he said he is seeking "to make it so that we can have a country with some baseline of social cohesion and sense of community, because what happens when too many people come to the United States, even if they're very good people, … [is] it changes the country in very profound ways.""D.C. is a corrupt town," but Vance says no evidence Trump is participating in itDokoupil asked Vance about polling that indicates many voters are concerned about corruption and believe Mr. Trump is prioritizing his own personal business interests while in office. Vance said, "I've never seen anything like that from the president.""Yes, D.C. is a corrupt town," Vance said, but "I have not seen a single shred of evidence that he participates or sanctions in that corruption."Dokoupil also asked about a string of recent reports, including Mr. Trump's cryptocurrency earnings and U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's ouster over allegations that she asked a person seeking help from the Trump administration to wire her $100,000. Guilfoyle has denied all wrongdoing. Mr. Trump has denied any conflicts of interest.Vance responded: "If somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable and they should suffer consequences."The vice president also said he will "follow the law" if a Democratic Congress launches investigations and subpoenas the Trump administration.Data centers need to be "good community citizens"A major point of tension in many communities across the country is the explosion in data center development, as the artificial intelligence boom leads to insatiable demand for computing power.Mr. Trump has enthusiastically backed the AI industry, casting it as an engine of economic growth and a key area of competition with China. He has also argued data center construction can be beneficial to local communities, bringing jobs and investments in crucial technology. But many voters have raised concerns about noise, disruption and pressure on the electrical grid, leading to calls for development to slow down.Vance took a question from one Michigan resident who lives across the street from a data center and said the constant buzzing has made "opening our windows to let in a breeze … a luxury that we could no longer enjoy."The vice president said "data centers can be good" and can also "cause real problems." He said his view is that data centers should be "good community citizens," offering more tax revenue to local governments. The data centers should also not lead to higher residential utility bills, Vance said."Some of the economic benefits they're generating, they can't just go to a few tech billionaires," he said. "It has to go to the community writ large."Watch the full episode of "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" streaming on Paramount+, YouTube, CBS News 24/7 and CBSNews.com.

title: Iran FM affirms support for Lebanon's sovereignty
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – Iran's foreign minister voiced support for Lebanon's right to defend its sovereignty and national security against Israeli aggression during a meeting with his Lebanese counterpart in Baghdad.
Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi and Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji met on Saturday evening on the sidelines of the 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad.
The two sides exchanged views on bilateral relations between Tehran and Beirut and discussed ways to strengthen ties.
Araghchi reaffirmed Iran's principled position on the need to preserve Lebanon's territorial integrity and sovereignty, stressing Iran's support for Lebanon in defending its sovereignty and national security against the aggression and expansionism of the Zionist regime.

title: UAE Property: 'Can I stay in my company-rented apartment after resigning?'
body: Question: I recently relocated to Dubai for work and my employer has rented an apartment for me as part of my package. The tenancy contract is in the company's name and the company pays the rent directly to the landlord, although I'm the person living there with my family. I'm considering leaving the company for another job. The HR department has told me that if I resign, I may have to leave the apartment almost immediately because the company is technically the tenant. I assumed that because this is our family home and there is still plenty of time remaining on the tenancy contract, we'd be entitled to stay until it expires. Who actually has the rights in this situation – me or my employer? Michael, Dubai Answer: This is one of those situations where the person living in a property and the legal tenant aren't necessarily the same person. If your employer is named as the tenant on both the tenancy agreement and Ejari, then the contractual relationship with the landlord is primarily with the company, not you personally. Your right to occupy the apartment may therefore come from your employment package rather than from having an independent tenancy relationship with the landlord. I'd check three things before making any assumptions: the tenancy agreement, the Ejari registration and your employment contract or company housing policy. There may be specific provisions explaining what happens to company-provided accommodation when employment ends. I wouldn't assume that the remaining term of the tenancy automatically gives your family the right to remain. Equally, however, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll have to move. If you like the apartment, approach the landlord early. They may be happy to replace the corporate tenancy with a new agreement in your name once the company's obligations have been dealt with. You're already living in the property and presumably you've looked after it. From the landlord's perspective, retaining a known occupant may be preferable to remarketing the apartment and accepting the risk of a vacancy period. Just make sure any new arrangement is formally documented. Don't rely on an informal understanding that you can simply “take over” the company's tenancy. Q: I'm considering buying an off-plan apartment in Dubai and the developer is advertising a “guaranteed 10 per cent return for three years after handover”. On paper, it looks fantastic. The projected return is considerably higher than I could achieve from a normal long-term rental, and the broker says I don't need to worry about finding tenants because everything will be managed for me. What I'm struggling to understand is where the 10 per cent actually comes from. If the apartment doesn't generate enough rental income, is the developer legally required to make up the difference? And should I be suspicious when a guaranteed return looks much higher than normal market rent? Daniel, Manchester A: Whenever somebody uses the word “guaranteed” in an investment proposition, my next question is always: guaranteed by whom, and where exactly is that guarantee written down? Don't assess the investment on the headline percentage alone. Ask for the actual rental guarantee agreement and establish which legal entity is responsible for paying you. Is it the developer, management company or another company entirely? A guarantee is ultimately only as strong as the entity standing behind it. Then establish exactly how the 10 per cent is calculated. Is it based on the original purchase price, the amount you've paid, or another figure? Are service charges, furnishing costs, management fees and maintenance deducted before or after your guaranteed payment? I'd also want to know whether you're free to occupy or sell the apartment during the guarantee period and what happens to the arrangement if you do. There may be restrictions that aren't obvious from the headline advertisement. Most importantly, compare the promised income with the property's realistic open-market rental value. If a Dh2 million apartment would ordinarily rent for Dh120,000 a year, that's a 6 per cent gross yield. Someone promising Dh200,000 every year isn't creating the additional Dh80,000 through magic. There is an economic reason for it somewhere, and you need to understand where the money is coming from. Sometimes, these schemes are perfectly legitimate and genuinely useful to an investor. In other cases, part of the promised return may effectively have been incorporated into a higher purchase price. So I'd judge the property first and the guarantee second. Look at comparable prices, realistic rent, location, developer track record and likely resale demand without including the incentive. Then, ask yourself one simple question: if the guarantee disappeared tomorrow, would I still be happy owning this apartment at the price I'm paying? If the answer is no, I'd think very carefully before signing anything. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. Please send any questions to mario@evadxb.com

title: Oyedele: World Markets Have Written Off Opposition, Eyeing Tinubu’s 2nd Term
body: •Rules out return to fuel subsidy, warns of risks to naira •CBN seeks Chinese capital, deeper financial ties to boost investment in Nigeria • World Bank report: ADC asks Tinubu to explain ‘missing’ $12.4bn Nume Ekeghe in Bangkok, Thailand and Chuks Okocha in Abuja The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has said financial markets and the international community have largely written off Nigeria’s opposition political parties as unserious, with investors already pricing in the prospects of President Bola Tinubu securing a second term and expecting continuity in his economic reforms. This is just as the Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Olayemi Cardoso, also said policy consistency and transparency were essential to sustaining investor confidence, as improvements in economic and foreign exchange stability created better conditions for long-term investment. Meanwhile, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) has called on President Tinubu to explain the $12.4 billion gap, an equivalent of about N16.5 trillion, in Nigeria’s external accounts identified in the World Bank’s October 2026 Nigeria Development Update. Oyedele and Cardoso spoke at the closing press briefing of the IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, where the CBN governor said policy consistency would be critical to attracting long-term capital, sustaining economic stability and accelerating growth. On his part, Oyedele argued that investors’ expectations of continuity under Tinubu had influenced their assessment of Nigeria’s economic outlook, including their response to opposition proposals to restore fuel subsidies. “In all the meetings I have had, I came to a conclusion that the markets, including the domestic market, which you can read from the capital market, and the international market, have largely written off the opposition in Nigeria as being unserious. That is why they have not priced in the proposed return of subsidy,” he said. He added that any indication that the president intended to restore the subsidy would immediately be reflected in market prices. “So, maybe the international and domestic markets are aware about who is sincere about Nigeria and what direction they should travel,” he said. “As I said, the markets and the international community have been pricing in the prospect of a second term for the President, and they expect continuity in the reforms.” The minister’s comments followed repeated questions from investors about whether the government would sustain its policies as Nigeria approaches another election cycle. He said concerns about possible policy reversals had featured prominently in his engagements with investors in Thailand and during two visits to London, particularly over whether electoral pressures could force the administration to abandon its reform agenda. “Throughout the meetings we have had this week, as well as those I attended before now, including two visits to London to meet investors, one question has repeatedly come up: Are you going to reverse your reforms? Are you under pressure because of elections?” he said. According to Oyedele, the government remained committed to the reforms, which he described as necessary to restore macroeconomic stability and lay the foundation for sustainable growth. He said the next phase of the economic programme would focus on translating the gains in stability into stronger investment, lower financing costs, job creation and improved economic opportunities for Nigerians. Oyedele said private investment had increased twentyfold since the reforms began, rising from about $300 million in 2023 to $6 billion in 2026. He also highlighted improvements in Nigeria’s external position, saying net reserves had risen from barely $3 billion to more than $45 billion, representing a fifteen-fold increase. Oyedele ruled out a return to fuel subsidies and multiple exchange rates, warning that reversing the reforms could undermine investor confidence, trigger capital flight and put renewed pressure on the naira. “Let me be clear: there will be no return to fuel subsidies or multiple exchange rates,” he said. “If, for any reason, Mr President were to say today that we were considering bringing back fuel subsidies, what happened in Indonesia would be child’s play in comparison,” he said. “At the end of the day, capital would leave because investors understand what such a decision means.” He argued that capital flight could intensify pressure on the foreign exchange market and weaken the naira, with the consequences ultimately borne by ordinary Nigerians. “When capital leaves, the foreign-exchange market will come under pressure, and the naira will crash. The exchange rate could move to N3,000, N3,500 or N4,000 to the dollar,” he said. Oyedele said such a development would worsen the economic pressures facing households. The minister also defended the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited’s recent temporary reduction in petrol retail margins, insisting that it was a commercial decision rather than a subsidy financed with public funds. “The recent temporary reduction in the retail margin on fuel was a time-bound commercial decision by the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited to reduce margins and support Nigerians,” he said. “It is not a subsidy paid for with public funds.” He explained that a company’s decision to reduce its profit margin to lower prices should not automatically be classified as a subsidy. “If you offer a discount by reducing that profit margin, how does that become a subsidy?” he asked. Cardoso: Policy Consistency, Transparency Critical to Investor Confidence Meanwhile, Cardoso has stressed that policy consistency and transparency were essential to sustaining investor confidence, as improvements in economic and foreign exchange stability created better conditions for long-term investment. Cardoso said Nigeria was seeking to deepen financial cooperation with China to attract more Asian investment into its markets and improve cross-border payments, settlement arrangements and trade finance. He disclosed that discussions with the Governor of the People’s Bank of China, Pan Gongsheng, had focused on practical ways to strengthen cooperation among financial institutions in both countries. Cardoso said China’s developed payments infrastructure offered lessons for Nigeria, while stronger financial links could facilitate trade and investment between the two economies. He said the discussions would be followed by technical engagements during his forthcoming visit to Beijing, where officials would examine specific areas of cooperation and identify initiatives capable of delivering practical results. The CBN governor said Nigeria was particularly interested in attracting Chinese capital into its financial markets, noting that investment in Nigerian financial instruments had remained limited despite the substantial liquidity available in China. “Finally, bear in mind that, despite the considerable liquidity available in China, there has not been much investment in Nigerian financial instruments over time,” he said. “This could be an opportunity to change that trajectory and generate greater interest from Asian markets in Nigerian instruments and African instruments generally.” Cardoso said the initiative formed part of a broader effort to strengthen Nigeria’s financial relationships with Asian economies and expand the pool of capital available to domestic markets. World Bank Report: ADC Asks Tinubu-led Govt to Explain ‘Missing’ $12.4bn Meanwhile, the ADC has called on President Tinubu to explain the $12.4 billion gap, equivalent to about N16.5 trillion, in Nigeria’s external accounts identified in the World Bank’s October 2026 Nigeria Development Update. In a statement issued yesterday by its National Publicity Secretary, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the party said Tinubu owed Nigerians a clear account of the discrepancy, especially as families struggling with the cost-of-living crisis were forced to account for every naira. Citing the report, the ADC said Nigeria recorded a $12 billion current-account surplus and $6.2 billion in net financial inflows in the first half of 2026. The party said these inflows should have strengthened the country’s reserves, but the report instead identified a $12.4 billion gap. Abdullahi said the World Bank attributed the gap, in part, to oil export earnings that were not repatriated. He added that the report noted that the repatriation of export proceeds remained limited, partly because Nigerian oil had been pledged against several long-term loans. “The scale is staggering,” the ADC said. “This unexplained gap is larger than the entire current-account surplus for the same period. It is about 5.6 times the $2.2 billion Nigeria attracted in foreign direct investment. In naira terms, it is almost a quarter of the N68.32 trillion 2026 federal budget. “This cannot be dismissed as a minor accounting discrepancy. President Tinubu welcomed this report. He cannot celebrate one part of the report and stay silent on a gap bigger than the surplus that he and his government are celebrating. “Due to President Tinubu’s failed policies, families across Nigeria are forced to skip meals and account for every naira just to survive. Meanwhile, money that could have eased their hardship is currently unaccounted for. Tinubu owes Nigerians an explanation. “Sacrifice cannot be compulsory for everyday citizens while accountability remains optional for the government that is in charge of our collective resources.” The ADC called on the federal government to publish a full public reconciliation of the $12.4 billion gap and disclose all oil-backed loans and pledged crude commitments. It also demanded updated net reserve figures and clear evidence that higher revenues were improving essential services such as health, education and power. “President Tinubu must open the books. Nigerians have sacrificed enough. We deserve answers,” the party said.

title: Russian strikes destroy half of nearly 500 Ukrainian drone crews near Dobropolye
body:
DONETSK, October 18. /TASS/. Russian forces have destroyed half of nearly 500 Ukrainian drone crews stationed in and around Dobropolye, the reconnaissance chief of the 110th Brigade of Russia's Battlegroup Center, who goes by the call sign "Udav" (Boa), told TASS on Sunday.
"Initially, they had 325 crews, but then they began reinforcing them. The peak figure they reached during this period was 460 [drone] crews. This covers the town of Dobropolye, the village of Annovka - essentially, the town itself and its surrounding areas," the reconnaissance chief said.
He added that while Russian forces destroyed half of the crews, the remaining personnel fled. Drones and aircraft, including those deploying FAB high-explosive bombs, carried out the strikes against the Ukrainian positions.

title: North Will Give Tinubu Over 70% of Votes in 2027, Says Yilwatda
body: • Shettima: Region will re-elect president • Makinde will defeat Tinubu in his 12 battleground states, others, says campaign council Deji Elumoye, Chuks Okocha and Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja The National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Professor Nentawe Yilwatda, has predicted that the North will give President Bola Tinubu more than 70 per cent of its votes in the 2027 presidential election. Vice President Kashim Shettima has also said the North will re-elect Tinubu, stressing that the region had spoken with a resounding voice and unmistakable conviction for Tinubu’s re-election. But the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) declared that its presidential candidate on the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Governor Seyi Makinde of Oyo State, will defeat Tinubu in the 12 battleground states identified by the president, as well as in other states across the federation. Speaking yesterday in Abuja when Shettima unveiled the Arewa for Asiwaju Campaign Head Office and formally inaugurated the campaign structure of the northern think tank, Yilwatda urged people in the North to support Tinubu’s re-election bid, citing infrastructure projects, appointments and other initiatives of the President’s administration. The APC chairman listed road projects across northern states, the Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano gas pipeline, irrigation dams, railway projects, healthcare initiatives and the Nigerian Education Loan Fund among the interventions he said should encourage the North to support Tinubu for a second term. “I can’t mention all of them, but President Bola Tinubu has done wonderfully. He has covered all the geopolitical zones in the North in terms of road projects,” he added. He moved a motion for the northern region to support the re-election of the Tinubu/Shettima ticket, outlining reasons why the region should mobilize massively for the president. He noted that the region’s strong backing stems from the Vice President’s inclusive leadership and progressive mindset over the past three years. Shettima: Region Will Re-elect President in 2027 Also speaking, Shettima declared that the North will re-elect Tinubu, adding however, that the growing northern support for president’s re-election was not a blank check. According to him, Tinubu’s administration will earn it through facts, radical transparency and measurable results. He maintained that expanding loyalty in the region would demand greater accountability and an honest dialogue with citizens about ongoing reforms undertaken by the administration. Shettima said the North had spoken with a resounding voice and unmistakable conviction in its support for the President. According to him, renewed political confidence should never be taken for granted, adding that the government and its supporters must continue to engage Nigerians with facts and show how the ongoing reforms are improving security, livelihoods, and economic opportunity. “By now, I believe the North has spoken. We have spoken with a resounding voice and unmistakable conviction. From Adamawa to Zamfara, from Borno to Niger, we have spoken. Such confidence places an obligation upon us that no officeholder should ever underestimate,” he stated. The Vice President noted that President Tinubu’s bid for a renewed mandate must rest on the administration’s record and a clear account of how another term would advance Nigerians’ interests. He restated that the North had nothing to fear in President Tinubu’s second term as Nigeria’s leader. Shettima acknowledged that Nigerians had endured difficult economic adjustments, warning campaigners against dismissing genuine concerns or relying on political slogans to defend government policies. “Our citizens have endured difficult adjustments. We cannot pretend otherwise. What we owe them is an honest account of the decisions taken, the gains achieved and the difficulties that persist. We lose our hearing when applause becomes our only source of information,” he added. The Vice President said the concerns of traders facing higher costs, graduates searching for work and families struggling with daily expenses must remain central to government decision-making. “A failed policy enters somebody’s home as a missed meal, an unpaid school fee or an opportunity lost,” he said. He also defended criticism as essential to democratic governance, saying the administration must remain open to useful ideas irrespective of political affiliation, ethnicity, religion or region. “There is no democracy without critics. Progress demands that our assumptions endure the examination of those who disagree with us,” Shettima said. The Vice President said the administration’s priorities remain security, economic opportunity, poverty reduction, education and stronger public institutions. “The farmer should be able to cultivate in safety. A child’s education should prepare that child for a productive life. Public institutions should give citizens confidence that effort can yield opportunity,” he said. Earlier, Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin said the inauguration of the A4A structure for the 2027 presidential elections came at a time when the region needed a strong, trusted platform to mobilise support for Tinubu. Similarly, Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Senator George Akume, said history was beckoning the North to act with wisdom and evidence, not sentiment, in its decision to support the Tinubu administration in the 2027 elections. On his part, Kano State Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, speaking on behalf of all the governors of the North, said the northern region’s support for the President in the forthcoming elections would be based on its conviction to uphold fairness, equity, unity and the progress of the country. In his welcome address, the Director General of A4A and former Jigawa State governor, Abubakar Mohammed Badaru, said the group’s emergence was not accidental, but born of the conviction that President Tinubu and his deputy have performed well and deserve re-election. Makinde Will Defeat Tinubu in His 12 Battleground States, Others, Says Campaign Council Meanwhile, the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) has declared that its presidential candidate on the platform of the APM, Governor Makinde will defeat Tinubu in the 12 battleground states identified by the president, as well as in other states across the federation. Makinde also declared that Nigeria’s biggest problem is grinding poverty, not religion, urging Christians to stop shunning politics and take an active role in transforming the country. The MDPCO, in a statement by its Director of Strategic Communications, Hon. Richard Nnanna Ihediwa, asserted that Makinde would decisively defeat Tinubu and his APC Presidential Campaign Council in Rivers State and the FCT, insisting that no amount of political manoeuvring, intimidation or abuse of incumbency by the President’s henchmen can reverse the growing tide of opposition to his re-election. The organisation said the arrogance and political overreach of Tinubu’s inner circle had deepened public resentment and further weakened his electoral prospects. It added that President Tinubu’s decision to personally visit and campaign in only 12 states — Oyo, Kaduna, Rivers, Plateau, Borno, Enugu, Bauchi, Sokoto, Delta, Kano, Adamawa and Lagos — further confirmed his apprehension over the mileage and foothold already achieved by Makinde with his RESET NIGERIA Agenda message in the aforementioned and other states of the federation. “Mr President should know that his visit to these states, if he eventually does, will not in any way change the direction or the determination of the people to vote him out, given his unpardonable failures in office which have brought unprecedented hardship across the country,” the organisation said. “President Tinubu has no meaningful achievement he can boast of in these and other states of the federation where Nigerians now refer to his government as ‘T-Pain’ following the suffering they have been subjected to by the policies of the Tinubu administration in the last three and a half years.” The MDPCO challenged President Tinubu not to have a change of mind but to visit the states to face the people. “We challenge President Tinubu to travel around the country by road and witness the decrepit state of federal highways, the squalor in which Nigerians live and the level of infrastructural decay across the country, while his government squanders trillions of Naira on white elephant projects and wasteful programmes. “If President Tinubu believes he is popular as he claims, he should not stop at the rally ground or at the airport when he gets to any of the states. He should go beyond waving to a gathering of APC rented crowd and be bold enough to directly engage the people in the communities and towns to seek their votes, as the APM candidate, Makinde, has been doing since he started his campaign,” it said. “Nigerians are gravitating towards the core campaign pillars and proposals in Makinde’s RESET NIGERIA Agenda, which include the establishment of an all-inclusive, four-year transitional government of national unity with four priority pillars of education, economy, security and socio-political policies. “Unlike President Tinubu’s visionless, thoughtless and rudderless rule characterised by crass arbitrariness, Makinde’s RESET NIGERIA Agenda offers data-driven strategies that revolve around tackling poverty through massive production; a security plan that prioritises intelligence gathering, social reorientation and decisive kinetic and non-kinetic actions; an education plan that focuses on expanding access to quality functional education; and institutional reform that emphasises inclusive governance and sincere public leadership.” The campaign urged Tinubu “not to waste the nation’s resources on his ‘Nebuchadnezzar’ Campaign Council of failed politicians who, like the president himself, cannot attract votes from Nigerians.” In another development, Makinde has declared that Nigeria’s biggest problem was grinding poverty, not religion, urging Christians to stop shunning politics and take an active role in transforming the country. He said Christians could not afford to stand aloof from politics because it was dirty or because they should not serve under leaders who did not share their faith, stressing that national transformation required their active participation. Makinde spoke yesterday in Abuja after receiving a Christian Icon Award at the Christian Association of Nigeria’s (CAN) 50th anniversary celebration. The governor said Christians should draw lessons from biblical figures who accepted difficult assignments in pursuit of a greater purpose. Makinde cited David, who, despite having been anointed king, served in the palace of Saul, from whom God had departed.

title: Tinubu Mourns as Journalist, Ex-Nigerian Ambassador, Dele Cole, Dies in London at 86
body: Deji Elumoye in Abuja President Bola Tinubu last night expressed profound sadness at the news of the passing of a distinguished diplomat, journalist, politician, historian and elder statesman, Ambassador Patrick Dele Cole, who died in London at 86. Cole’s death was confirmed yesterday by a family source, who disclosed that the former Nigerian ambassador died earlier in the morning following weeks of deteriorating health. The source revealed that Cole had recently been discharged from the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), but his health had continued to decline. “He left ICU a few days ago. He had been doing poorly in recent weeks leading to this end,” the family source said. Born on August 4, 1940, Cole turned 86 in August, barely two months before his death. He was widely known for his contributions to Nigeria’s diplomatic service, journalism, and historical scholarship, having held several prominent positions throughout his career. Before entering diplomatic service, Cole established himself in Nigeria’s media industry, serving on the editorial board of The Guardian newspaper and subsequently as Managing Director of Daily Times, one of the country’s most influential newspapers. He later represented Nigeria as Ambassador to Argentina and Brazil, extending his public service career into international diplomacy. He served as Special Adviser on International Relations under President Obasanjo from 1999 to 2007. He was also appointed Nigeria’s ambassador to Brazil and Argentina. He also ventured into politics and was associated with the Social Democratic Party (SDP) in the 1990s. Beyond his diplomatic assignments, Cole was recognised for his involvement in national discourse, particularly on governance, politics, and Nigeria’s historical development. His career spanned journalism, public administration, and diplomacy, placing him among a generation of Nigerian public figures who contributed to the country’s political and institutional development. In a statement he personally signed, President Tinubu said Ambassador Cole devoted his life to national service, bringing distinction to his work in diplomacy, journalism and politics. Tinubu noted that Cole’s career reflected the enduring value of dialogue, tact, mutual respect and the pursuit of shared interests in advancing national development and international cooperation. “His contributions to Nigeria’s media landscape were particularly notable. As Managing Director of the Daily Times, he upheld the vital role of the press in holding public officials accountable, speaking truth to power, and strengthening democratic governance. His legacy in journalism and public life remains an enduring part of our national story,” Tinubu explained. The president added that at 86, the deceased witnessed defining moments in Nigeria’s history and contributed to the nation’s development through his work in the media, diplomacy and public service. According to Tinubu, his life stood as a testament to the value of experience, principled engagement and commitment to the public good. “As we mourn his passing, I extend my heartfelt condolences to his family, friends, professional associates and all whose lives he touched. I pray that memories of his remarkable life will bring them comfort and strength at this difficult time. May Almighty God grant Ambassador Cole eternal rest and give his family and all who mourn him the fortitude to bear this profound loss,” the statement added.

title: Over 40 Companies Raise N2.45 Trillion from Stock Market in Nine Months
body: Kayode Tokede Over 40 companies raised N2.45 trillion from the Nigerian capital market between January and September 2026, as businesses positioned themselves for growth amid persistent economic pressures, according to data on corporate listings on the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX). The capital-raising surge underscores the NGX’s growing importance as a source of long-term financing for businesses seeking alternatives to expensive bank loans. Data on corporate listings on the NGX show total corporate capital raising hit about N2.45 trillion in nine months of 2026, covering public offers, private placements and supplementary listings. The surge came as the Nigerian Exchange Limited All-Share Index gained 61.43 per cent year-to-date (YtD) as of September 2026 to 251,211.67 basis points, making Nigeria one of Africa’s best-performing exchanges. Among the over 40 companies are: Dangote Sugar Refinery, which raised N485.88 billion through a rights issue; Abbey Bank raised N64.547 billion; Guinea Insurance listed 12.673 billion new shares; Regency Alliance Insurance raised N6.051 billion; Sunu Assurance raised N9.339 billion; Sovereign Trust Insurance raised N5.022 billion; Neimeth International Pharmaceuticals raised N2.442 billion; Critical Minerals Financing Corporation raised N1.807 billion and Eunisell Interlinked raised N200 million, among others. Of the corporate listings, Fidelity Bank Plc, United Bank for Africa Plc (UBA), FCMB Group Plc, First HoldCo Plc, Access Holdings Plc, Sterling Financial Holdings Company Plc and Guaranty Trust Holding Company Plc led the listed firms, with listings of N883.8 billion in the period under review. The N883.8 billion listing on the NGX by these four financial institutions came against the backdrop of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) policy mandating that firms raise fresh equity to meet paid-up capital thresholds. As GTCO listed N10 billion after a successful private placement of 125,000,000 ordinary shares of 50 kobo each at N80.00 per share, NGX admitted UBA’s and First Holdco’s N157.8 billion and N128.7 billion rights issue and private placement in early January 2026, respectively. Access Holdings, N21.4 billion; FCMB Group, N231.83 billion; Sterling Financial Holding Company, N106.978 billion; and Fidelity Bank, N227.05 billion, were new listings on NGX. The Managing Director of Globalview Capital Limited, Mr. Aruna Kebira, said the recent surge reflected rising investor confidence in the Nigerian Exchange, not apathy, and that confidence is key to capacity building. Speaking on market participation, Kebira said innovations, improved transparency and the T+1 settlement cycle, where investors get proceeds a day after selling, have deepened retail participation and awareness. Kebira cited the Dangote Refinery offer, where platforms like OPay and banks actively mobilised investors, as a driver of serious market awareness. He said the market had evolved significantly since 2011 and was aligning with global standards, moving away from the speculative ‘kalokalo’ approach seen in 2004. On funding options, Kebira said equity remained the cheapest way to run and expand a manufacturing organisation, as interest on bank loans must be paid regardless of profitability, while equity allowed profits to be ploughed back into the company to do more for shareholders. He added that the funds had a multiplier effect on capacity expansion, technology adoption and job creation. He said boards would be under pressure to deliver value, increase production, pay good dividends and put square pegs in square holes because reputation was at stake, adding that the recapitalisation in insurance was necessary to restore the ability to pay claims and rebuild public confidence in the sector. On his part, the National Chairman of New Dimension Shareholders Association, Mr. Patrick Ajudua, however, stated that fresh capital raising did not automatically translate to higher dividends or immediate job creation. “You need to know that investment has a risk element. Not all companies that raise fresh capital deliver better dividends,” Ajudua said. He noted that, in fairness, many companies had delivered dividends, particularly since this administration came to power, which stabilised the economy, especially the foreign exchange market.

title: From Liverpool to Sultana: Testimonies to centuries-old Omani-British friendship
body:
Omani-British relations draw their historical roots from the convergence of two maritime powers in the Indian Ocean, a beginning embodied in the Treaty of 1800 that enshrined a framework of "permanent friendship" between the two countries. On January 18 of that year, Sayyid Sultan bin Ahmed and Captain John Malcolm, envoy of the British Governor-General in India, signed a supplementary agreement affirming the Treaty of 1798 and stipulating that " the friendship of the two States may remain unshook till the end of time, and till the sun and moon have finished their revolving career." The first half of the nineteenth century is regarded as the golden age of this relationship. During the reign of Sayyid Said bin Sultan (1806–1856), the Omani fleet possessed major vessels, among them the ship "Liverpool," built in Bombay in 1826 and armed with seventy-four cannons—specifications rivalling those of the great European powers of the time. Sayyid Said later presented it to King William IV, and it was incorporated into the Royal Navy. This parity reflects the depth of Oman's maritime tradition, for the Omanis, after expelling the Portuguese from Muscat in 1650, had come to dominate the trade routes of the western Indian Ocean. Dr. Nasser bin Abdullah al Saqri, Assistant Professor of Modern and Contemporary History at Sultan Qaboos University (SQU), said that the anticipated state visit by His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik to the United Kingdom acquires exceptional historical and civilizational significance. It comes as an extension of relations whose roots reach back to the late eighteenth century, evoking a long legacy of political communication and civilizational interaction between the two countries, and carries profound symbolic meaning as the first state visit to the United Kingdom since 1982, embodying the continuity and renewal of relations across generations and eras. He explained that Omani-British relations are read as a unique or exceptional model within the context of Britain's relations with the countries of the region—a distinction owed not merely to their antiquity, but to the historical and diplomatic characteristics that set them apart in both quantity and quality. He added: "At a time when Britain's relations with a number of countries in the region crystallized during the twentieth century, the official roots of relations between Oman and Britain extend back to 1798, reflecting more than two centuries of continuous communication and interaction. This historical extension was not merely a chronological succession of events and interests; across multiple phases it contributed to the formation of what can be described as a historical-diplomatic balance in which mutual expertise, interests, and a level of trust and political understanding accumulated, granting this relationship a degree of particularity, flexibility, and continuity not equally available in many other regional relationships." He indicated that the continuity of Omani-British relations across disparate historical periods is explained as the product of conscious diplomatic engineering, having succeeded in transcending historical phases marked by tensions and major events that swept the region—from the Cold War and the post-colonial era, to the emergence of oil and the transformations it wrought, to globalization and the rise of new powers, and on to the crises the region currently witnesses. At every stage, the relationship between the two countries was redefined in keeping with the context. He pointed to several factors that contributed to the relationship's endurance across decades, foremost among them the intersection of deep interests between the two sides in security, trade, and energy; the accumulation of trust and understandings; and the strategic flexibility that made the relationship adaptable to change without rigidity or binding dependency, in addition to the human dimension embodied in deeply rooted personal and institutional ties that gave the relationship another dimension lacking in many alliances and relationships. He noted that a clear Omani influence on British policy toward the region can be observed, as the Sultanate of Oman has remained a trusted partner, a channel of communication on sensitive files, a mediator in complex regional issues, and a source of stability in a turbulent region. Britain, in turn, benefited from Oman's geostrategic location in securing international navigation corridors, and from cultural and educational cooperation that reinforced the British presence in the region. He explained that this mutual influence reflects the nature of a relationship that has never been one-directional but rather mutually beneficial, making it a rich case study for understanding the dynamics of mutual influence in asymmetrical international relations. He pointed out that this relationship offers an important lesson: that history, as strategic memory, helps in understanding the present and envisioning the future. Hence the value of the Omani-British experience lies not only in its longevity, but in its ability to move across different historical phases while retaining an essence of communication, dialogue, and mutual interests. In a related context, Dr. Badriya Mohammed al Nabhani, a researcher in history, affirmed that the nineteenth century constitutes a pivotal phase in the history of Omani-British relations, noting that she tends to read this century in three stages. She explained that the first stage began in an international context, as on 12 October 1798, the first cooperation agreement between the Sultanate of Oman and Britain was signed by Sayyid Sultan bin Ahmed and the envoy of the East India Company, Mehdi Ali Khan. On 18 January 1800, Captain John Malcolm affirmed this agreement, under which the presence of an agent of the Company in Muscat was approved. She noted that the second stage is the era of Sayyid Said bin Sultan (1806–1856), which in her view was the most mature phase of Omani diplomacy in that century. She explained that the third stage began with the death of Sayyid Said, and noted that during the reign of Sultan Faisal bin Turki, the Treaty of Friendship, Commerce, and Navigation was signed on 19 March 1891. She explained that the milestones of cooperation between Oman and Britain can be summarized in four: first, the security of navigation in the Gulf, where Omani forces participated in the campaigns of 1809 and 1819–1820 that culminated in the General Treaty of 1820; second, cartography, where the Indian Navy conducted precise surveys of the Omani coasts in the 1830s, accompanied by travellers such as Lieutenant James Wellsted, who published his book on his travels in Oman in 1838, and these maps served commercial navigation for long decades. Third, communications, where a telegraph station was established in 1864 on the island of Maqlab in Khasab, Musandam, as part of the line linking India to Europe. Fourth, steamships, where vessels of the British India Steam Navigation Company began calling regularly at Muscat from the 1860s, connecting it to Bombay and Basra. She noted that under the Renewed Renaissance led by His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik, the relationship has acquired a clear economic dimension consistent with Oman Vision 2040, as the United Kingdom was in 2025 the largest foreign investor in the Sultanate of Oman, with its direct investments amounting to nearly $42 billion, an increase of 11 percent over the previous year. In January 2022, a Sovereign Investment Partnership was signed between Oman Investment Authority and the British Office for Investment, targeting clean energy and technology. On 20 May 2026, negotiations for a free trade agreement between the United Kingdom and the GCC countries, which began in June 2022, were concluded. For her part, Dr. Bahiya Said Al Athobi, a researcher in Omani military history, explained that when speaking of Omani-British military relations, it is necessary to distinguish between the early beginnings of political and maritime relations between the two countries and the phase in which military cooperation took on a direct character in organizing forces and establishing military units. She added that the most prominent shift in the nature of military relations began in the second decade of the twentieth century, specifically from 1913, when Oman witnessed internal political developments that necessitated a reconsideration of the organization of forces in Muscat. She noted that British documents revealed the role played by the British Political Resident in the Gulf, Percy Cox, who in 1913 presented a conception for forming a military force in Muscat. This was followed by the Omani military statement issued by Sultan Taimur bin Faisal in 1914, and then the Political Agent and British Consul in Muscat, Robert Benn, advanced a plan for the formation of the Muscat Levy Corps, encompassing the organizational and financial aspects necessary for its establishment. She explained that these plans reveal the beginning of the transition from reliance on traditional military formations and auxiliary forces to thinking about establishing a more regular force subject to a defined military organization. She pointed out that among the most prominent milestones worth pausing at is the Battle of Bayt Al-Falaj in 1915, which represented an early model of joint military operations between the forces of the Sultanate of Oman and British forces within the framework of the internal military conflict in Oman. She explained that the phase of establishing the Muscat Levy Corps in 1921 came to form a foundational milestone in the history of modern military organization in the Sultanate of Oman, after a series of military plans and proposals put forward during the preceding years. She said that the relationship between the two countries was not based on entirely identical motives: Oman sought to enhance its security and stability and build forces capable of confronting internal challenges, while the British position was also linked to protecting its strategic interests in the Gulf and securing the position of Muscat. Therefore, she believes that 1913 marked the beginning of a new phase in Omani-British military relations, while 1921 constituted an important milestone in the transformation of this relationship into institutional cooperation linked to the building of regular forces in the Sultanate of Oman. She noted that documents relating to joint military exercises in the 1960s acquire particular importance because they provide precise details about the nature of training cooperation between the two countries. Among the important examples of this are British reports relating to the series of field exercises known as (OMEX), carried out during 1961 and 1962, in which British units participated in cooperation with units of the Sultan's Armed Forces, including the Muscat Battalion, the Northern Frontier Battalion, and the Air Force. She explained that the role of British expertise and experience contributed to accelerating certain aspects of modernization, particularly in the fields of leadership, training, and technical specializations, but it is important to emphasize that this development came within the framework of specific Omani needs imposed by security and military circumstances, and was then reinforced by the national orientation toward building modern armed forces. She revealed that training cooperation between the two friendly countries preceded Al Saif Al Sareea "Swift Sword" maneuvers by decades, and that Omani and British forces had been conducting joint field exercises since the early 1960s. She believed that the Omani experience in military training was not merely a direct transfer of British expertise, but was based on benefiting from this expertise and re-employing it in a local environment of a different geographical and military nature, for Oman possesses diverse terrain from towering mountains to vast deserts and coastal areas, which necessitated the development of skills and training methods suited to these environments. She noted that these maneuvers reflected an advanced level of coordination between the armed forces of the two countries, especially in the areas of operational planning, logistical support and joint command. They also highlighted the importance of benefiting from Oman's diverse geographical environment in conducting military exercises. She explained that among the important milestones that followed these maneuvers was the signing of the joint defence agreement between the Sultanate of Oman and the United Kingdom in 2019, which reinforced the institutional framework for defence cooperation between the two countries. She added that under the Renewed Renaissance led by His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik, Omani-British military relations have continued to develop, among the most prominent manifestations of which is the joint military exercise "Khanjar Oman," which included joint field exercises aimed at developing combat and training efficiency and enhancing the ability to coordinate and carry out joint military tasks. She concluded by affirming that the study of Omani-British military relations reveals a long historical trajectory of transformations, beginning with understandings linked to maritime security and commercial interests, then developing into direct cooperation in organizing, training, and arming military forces, and culminating in modern defence partnership. Historical documents have shown that this cooperation was not constant in its nature or objectives, but was influenced by the political and military circumstances through which Oman and the region passed, and by the strategic interests of each party. For his part, Dr. Younis bin Jamil Al Nu’amani, a researcher in historical affairs, said that trade played a pivotal role in Omani-British rapprochement, particularly given Oman's strategic location on global trade routes, and that the economic aspect, especially commercial exchange, was the gateway to the convergence of the two countries. He added that the agreement signed by Britain with Oman in 1798 is among the most prominent and earliest agreements that paved the way for Omani-British rapprochement, as dangers were closing in on Oman both internally and externally. Sayyid Sultan bin Ahmed therefore renewed the treaty with Britain in 1800, with new clauses added, and commercial agreements between the two countries followed thereafter in what later became known as the Treaty of Friendship and Commerce. He explained that with regard to missions and diplomatic representation, Sayyid Said bin Sultan bin Ahmed Al Busaidi signed the Treaty of Friendship and Commerce with Britain in 1839, whose third clause stipulated the exchange of consular representation between the two countries. After this treaty, Omani-British relations became alliance relations. He noted that the voyage of the Omani ship "Sultana" to London in 1842, carrying the envoy and ambassador Ali bin Nasser, is among the most important stages of diplomatic representation between Oman and Britain, as he carried with him letters and lavish gifts addressed to Queen Victoria. He said: "The relationship between Britain and Oman can be described as one of mutual respect, for neither imposed its culture on the other; rather, each respected and came to know the other, unlike some countries that imposed their policies and culture at the same time." He noted that there are indicators pointing to the depth of cultural relations, among them the Omani-British Friendship Association, the British Council, and partnerships between educational institutions, such as the adoption of curricula like the Cambridge curriculum, as well as the cooperation of Sultan Qaboos University with several British universities, and the scholarships offered by both countries. He noted that museums play a prominent cultural and educational role, and that there is cooperation between the National Museum of Oman and British museums (such as the British Museum and the Victoria and Albert Museum) in many respects. He believes that this civilizational acculturation is important and serves the interests of the two countries, which are bound by historical relations extending over four centuries. Dr. Younis believes that political and economic interests were—and still are—the main driver in relations between the two countries. Accordingly, these relations must be invested in light of the existence of great opportunities for economic, cultural, and scientific exchange; other aspects must also be developed, and partnerships built in diversifying income sources, environmental protection, net zero, and benefiting from all expertise in both countries.
