title: US ambassador condemns Israeli settler attack on Washington Post journalist
body: US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has condemned an Israeli settler attack on an American photojournalist in the occupied West Bank , demanding a full investigation, arrests and the prosecution of those responsible. Heidi Levine of The Washington Post suffered serious injuries when she was attacked by Israeli settlers on Friday morning, the newspaper’s executive editor, Matt Murray, said. “Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Mr Huckabee said in a post on X early on Sunday. “Dishonourable act of senseless violence.” The US envoy said Ms Levine had been clearly identified as a journalist and was unarmed. He called for those involved to spend years in prison and demanded prosecution “to the fullest extent of the law”. The Washington Post said Ms Levine was attacked when "dozens of masked settlers” set fire to shrubs and threw rocks in a “co-ordinated assault” on Palestinian olive harvesters. “She was knocked to the ground, kicked repeatedly and stripped of her cameras and phone,” the paper said. Ms Levine was later taken to hospital in Ramallah. Photos showed her lying on a trolley with a wound dressing on the left leg and a gash on her right knee, among other injuries. Heidi Levine, photojournalist for @wapo suffered serious injuries from vicious & cowardly attack. Heidi is US Citizen, clear ID as journalist. Details of who under investigation, but those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison. We have called for a full… — Ambassador Mike Huckabee (@GovMikeHuckabee) October 17, 2026 On Sunday, the Post welcomed the support of the US ambassador. "We appreciate the support we’ve gotten today for our photographer, Heidi Levine, after the brutal and unwarranted attack on her. We reiterate the call for action from the government. Press freedoms are a cornerstone for democracies," Mr Murray wrote on X. The attack comes amid renewed international concern over Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, after European diplomats and a French mayor were assaulted by masked people in a separate incident on Saturday. Belgium criticised the attack on its consul general and the other diplomats and urged Israel to bring those responsible to justice. Poland’s Foreign Ministry said preliminary evidence indicated Israeli settlers were responsible for the assault. Polish diplomats travelling in the convoy were unharmed, the ministry said. “We expect the Israeli authorities to provide urgent and detailed explanations, identify those responsible and ensure that they are held accountable,” it added. “We also expect effective measures to be taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the mayor of a French town had also been assaulted by what he described as “extremist settlers” during Saturday’s incident. He called on Israeli authorities to stop the violence. Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Ms Levine to apologise for the attack and urged an investigation. The Israeli military described the violence as intolerable and said the incidents would be investigated. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said the circumstances remained unclear and more evidence was needed before responsibility could be established. It also noted that the diplomats’ visit had not been coordinated with Israeli security officials. Britain, France, Canada and other countries announced sanctions focused on Israeli settlements last month, while the US said it would not join those measures.

title: FACTBOX: What is known about drone attacks in Leningrad Region, St. Petersburg
body:
MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Ukrainian forces launched a massive drone attack on St. Petersburg and the Leningrad Region, with Russian air defense forces downing 126 UAVs over the region, Governor Alexander Drozdenko reported on his Telegram channel.
Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsia, said Pulkovo Airport imposed temporary operational restrictions. Airport officials added that they moved passengers and staff to safe locations.
In St. Petersburg, drones targeted the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal and civilian infrastructure across four city districts, causing no casualties, Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed.
Debris hit a private house near the town of Kirovsk and an apartment building in Vsevolozhsk, in the Leningrad Region.
In the meantime, Russian tech giant VK confirmed a drone attack on its data center, noting that all services continue to operate normally.
TASS has compiled the key details regarding the aftermath.
- Air defenses shot down 126 drones over the Leningrad Region, Drozdenko reported.
- In the region, the attack targeted Nizino in the Lomonosovsky District, the area near the town of Kirovsk, and Vsevolozhsk.
- St. Petersburg faced an overnight attack by military-grade drones, Beglov stated.
- Impact and debris fallout were recorded across the Nevsky, Krasnoselsky, Krasnogvardeysky, and Moskovsky districts of St. Petersburg.
- Pulkovo Airport suspended all arrivals and departures, according to Rosaviatsia.
- Airport authorities moved passengers and staff to safe locations.
- Drone debris damaged a private house near Kirovsk and an apartment building in Vsevolozhsk, Drozdenko stated.
- In Nizino, falling debris damaged four parked vehicles and ignited a fire.
- Drone debris striking power lines caused localized power outages.
- Drones targeted a VK data center, though the company stated all services remain fully operational.
- A fire broke out at the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, Beglov reported.
- Emergency services (EMERCOM) are extinguishing fires at civilian infrastructure sites across four St. Petersburg districts.
- Mobile internet services in St. Petersburg may experience disruptions.
- An operational headquarters led by Beglov is coordinating the emergency response and interagency efforts.

title: Japanese Diplomat Takaaki Nemoto Farewells Greece With Cavafy Verse in Greek
body: ATHENS, October 2026 — Takaaki Nemoto, Deputy Head of Mission at the Embassy of Japan in Greece, has farewelled the country in a moving message in Greek, quoting Constantine Cavafy in a video the embassy posted on Friday. Nemoto, who also holds the rank of Counsellor, said he was leaving after four years at the embassy. He made the remarks in a 71-second Reel on the embassy’s official Instagram account, @japan_in_greece. Coverage in Greece widely described the message as particularly moving and heartfelt. Headlines highlighted his fluent Greek and his recitation of Cavafy, as well as his thanks for Greek hospitality, kindness and courtesy. Reports also noted the graceful way he handed over to his successor. Some coverage contrasted its tone with other recent diplomatic noise, holding it up as a model of politeness and cultural sensitivity. In the video, Nemoto first thanked the people who had welcomed him during his posting. “During this period, many Greek friends and colleagues welcomed me warmly. I would like to thank them from the heart for their kindness, courtesy and hospitality.” Takaaki Nemoto The Embassy of Japan in Greece shared Takaaki Nemoto’s farewell video on Instagram. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Embassy of Japan in Greece (@japan_in_greece) Takaaki Nemoto names successor Nemoto then named Yoko Maejima as his successor. He described her as “an excellent and gracious colleague of mine, with a deep knowledge of the Greek language.” Before signing off, he made one request of his Greek audience. “I would like to ask you to give her the same support and trust with which you honoured me all these years. Be well, all of you. Until we meet again.” Takaaki Nemoto His closing words in Greek were “Να είστε όλοι καλά. Καλή αντάμωση.” In its caption, the embassy said Takaaki Nemoto had worked to further strengthen ties between Japan and Greece during his posting. It described a friendship based on mutual respect, shared experiences and lasting bonds between the two peoples. As he completes his term, he leaves with deep appreciation for the relationships he built, the embassy said. He is also confident that close ties between the two countries will continue to grow, it said. Earlier, in March, Takaaki Nemoto represented the embassy at a TIF-Helexpo press conference on Japan’s role as honoured country. Japan later exhibited in Pavilion 13 when the 90th Thessaloniki International Fair opened in September. Lines from a 1911 poem The lines Nemoto recited come from Cavafy’s poem “The God Abandons Antony” (“Απολείπειν ο θεός Αντώνιον”), first published in 1911. The Onassis Cavafy Archive holds manuscripts and early editions of the poem. Cavafy’s original Greek lines, followed by an English translation, read: “Σαν έτοιμος από καιρό, σα θαρραλέος, αποχαιρέτα την, την Αλεξάνδρεια που φεύγει.” (“As one long prepared, as one full of courage, say goodbye to her, to Alexandria that is leaving.”) C.P. Cavafy, The God Abandons Antony (1911) “With Cavafy’s verses engraved in my heart, I return to my homeland, Japan,” Takaaki Nemoto said. The poem takes its title from Plutarch’s life of Mark Antony. In that account, Antony hears an unseen procession leave Alexandria at midnight before his defeat. The procession, Plutarch wrote, signalled that the god Dionysus was abandoning him. In April, the Onassis Foundation also donated a sculpture of the poet to the Municipality of Athens, Greek City Times reported. The embassy’s caption also told followers to stay tuned to meet the new members of its team. title: Woman killed, two injured in Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia
body:
This was reported by Ukrinform, citing the Telegram channel of Mykhailo Semikin, Acting Head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration.
“A residential building in Zaporizhzhia was hit. Unfortunately, a 27-year-old woman was killed in the enemy attack,” the statement said.
Later, Semikin updated the information on the casualties.
“Two more people were injured – a 58-year-old woman and a six-year-old girl. The attack damaged two apartment buildings, 18 vehicles and a building of an educational institution,” he added.
Municipal services are working at the sites of the strikes, clearing debris and assisting residents.

title: Yemeni army downs Saudi drone
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – Yemen's armed forces spokesman Yahya Saree said the military downed an armed Saudi Karayel reconnaissance drone over Hajjah province, the fourth of its kind in recent tensions.
Yemen's armed forces downed an armed Saudi Karayel reconnaissance drone over Hajjah province, spokesman Yahya Saree said.
Saree said it was the fourth drone of the same model since the start of recent tensions and the seventh since this type of drone entered Yemen's airspace.
On Saturday night, the spokesman said Yemeni forces downed a Saudi Apache helicopter in the Najran border area with Yemen.

title: Preparations underway to welcome His Majesty in UK
body:
Windsor: Preparations are underway in the friendly United Kingdom to welcome His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik, who is paying a state visit in response to a invitation extended by His Majesty King Charles III, King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and Head of the Commonwealth. The streets of Windsor have been adorned with the flags of the Sultanate of Oman and the United Kingdom—a display that reflects the deep-rooted bonds of friendship and the historical relations between the two nations. It also signifies a warm welcome for this royal visit, which marks a significant milestone in the trajectory of Omani-British relations. The visit aims to bolster bilateral cooperation across various sectors, serving mutual interests and supporting the aspirations of both countries toward broader horizons of partnership and collaboration.

title: Rarely seen on screen, Nagaland is now in the Oscars race thanks to Angh
body: When Angh , a film set in a remote corner of north-east India rarely depicted on screen, won the Platform Prize at the Toronto International Film Festival in September, it made history in more ways than one. The debut feature by 31-year-old Naga filmmaker Theja Rio became the first Indian film to win the prestigious award, earning a place in the race for Best International Feature Film at the 2027 Academy Awards. Thanks to a change in Oscar eligibility rules, the victory means Angh can compete for consideration independently of India's official submission, the Marathi-language film Gondhal . Told primarily in Konyak , the language of one of Nagaland 's many indigenous Naga tribes, the film explores the tension between ancestral traditions and the arrival of Christianity in the region in the 1960s. For Rio, the international recognition is particularly meaningful. “Growing up, I've never seen Nagaland in a film before or in a series before,” he tells The National . “And very often, every time you introduce yourself, you're getting into the backdrops of where you come from and then you're having to describe geographically where exactly it is.” Rio first explored the story in a short film in 2019, inspired by a visit to Nagaland's Mon district three years earlier. But he soon realised that the characters and the cultural transformations he wanted to explore needed more room to develop, prompting him to expand the story into his first feature. The response since the Toronto victory has exceeded his expectations, he says. Rio returned to Nagaland last month to celebrations and messages of pride, while the film has attracted attention from across India and beyond. “It's been a fever dream,” he says. “It's just my debut feature and it's yet to release, but to receive the reactions we have received and the fact that anyone is interested in having to hear what I have to say is completely baffling, but something that I'm very grateful about. “And just being able to make our people feel represented is by far the most heartwarming thing.” It is a fitting response to a film concerned with identity and belonging, and with what happens when the world around a community changes faster than its people can adapt. Between the past and present Set in Nagaland in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba (played by Anghlong Konyak), an ageing Konyak village chief, and his son as they confront the arrival of a Christian missionary and the changes it brings to their traditional way of life. The story is not simply about the clash between two belief systems. It explores the uncertainty of people caught between generations, as familiar customs begin to disappear and new ideas reshape their understanding of the world. During his journey to Mon, a district in eastern Nagaland bordering Myanmar, Rio encountered elderly Konyak men with traditional facial tattoos whose appearances reflected a way of life that had largely disappeared. “Mon is a very interesting place in the sense that they still have a lot of the practices and a lot of the structures from their older traditions that is still exist, while at the same time, like the rest of Nagaland, it has also become very modern in a sense,” he explains. “There were a lot of the tattooed faces but they were all dressed in modern clothes.” The contrast fascinated him. Here were people whose faces carried the visible history of an earlier generation, yet who were living in a world transformed by religion, education and modernity. The encounter also connected with Rio's long-standing fascination with characters whose lives have been overtaken by history. “I wanted to make a film about those people who have gone through that phase of rapid transition in the 60s and the 70s,” he says. “I'm very interested and very passionate about characters that have been sort of left behind by time. There's something very tragic and melancholic about characters like that.” It was the combination of these two ideas – a community experiencing profound change and a character struggling to hold on to an older world – that eventually became Angh . The complexities of change The relationship between Christianity and indigenous Naga traditions is not merely a subject from the past, it's a question that touches Rio's own identity. Christianity is now deeply embedded in much of Nagaland's society, but its spread also coincided with the decline of ancestral beliefs and practices. Exploring that history can be sensitive, particularly when it involves examining the consequences of missionary activity. Rio, who is Christian, was determined not to portray either side as entirely right or wrong. “It was very important to not antagonise any side,” he says. “I see both sides of it, and that's why I feel all my characters have a lot of depth. They're not one-dimensional characters who are almost caricature like. They're not there to play a villain or there just to be the opposition of the other.” That approach shapes the relationship between the village chief and the missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall. “When you watch the film, you'll realise that the white priest comes with the best intention, but from Anghba's perspective, he poses a threat to the community and to the culture that he is trying to hold on to. “That's one of the reasons why I like to make films about things that I'm conflicted about rather than make films about things that I'm sure about, which is dangerously treading the propaganda line.” But how did a story so deeply rooted in Nagaland's history and culture strike a chord with an international jury at one of the world's biggest film festivals? At the Toronto International Film Festival, jury members praised Angh “for its refreshing perspective, strength of filmmaking and deeply resonant portrait of a world”. “We praise the filmmaker’s vision, audacity and courage,” they said. For Rio, the film's universal appeal lies in its themes of rapid change and cultural preservation. “The film is something that is obviously very culturally specific, but thematically something that is very universal,” he says. “We're living in a time where we're dealing with great change happening at a rapid speed than it's ever been. So in that sense, it's quite topical as well. “There's also so much conversation about conservation of, not just the environment, but of culture. So I think the film is very topical in that sense.” Bringing Angh to life When Rio was developing Angh as a short film in 2019, he had already realised the characters and their conflicts required a larger canvas. “I was struggling to compress the entire thing into a short film, and I knew it was always meant to be a feature. The characters, the conflict, it's just too big to be restricted into a short film format,” he says. At the time, however, he lacked the experience and resources to make a full-length production. The short film's positive reception on the festival circuit encouraged him to expand the screenplay. He subsequently studied at the National Film and Television School in the UK, where working on other projects gave him time away from the story. When he returned to it, he had gained experience and a new perspective on the material. Supporting him through much of that journey has been Nancy Nisa Beso, a long-time film producer whose career spans more than two decades across documentary, commercial and independent filmmaking. Beso has known Rio since childhood and has worked with him on several projects, including the original short film. The success of Angh is the culmination of years of dedication rather than an overnight breakthrough, she says. “Technically, while this is his first feature film, he has been working on films for the last 11 years of his life,” she says. “This is a product of 11 years of just working towards your skill and expanding what you built.” The feature presented numerous challenges, particularly when it came to casting. With few professional actors available locally, Rio and his team travelled through villages in the Mon region searching for people who could convincingly portray the characters. “We had no option but to cast non-actors because we don't have professional actors where we come from, so it wasn't necessarily a choice,” Rio says. The lead role eventually went to Konyak, a stand-up comedian Rio discovered on YouTube after struggling to find someone with the necessary screen presence. Rio's decision to shoot on 16mm film, despite its many logistical challenges, was equally deliberate. He had been influenced by archival photographs and footage of the region taken during the early years of missionary activity. “There's something about film that is so filled with nostalgia. Obviously, I wasn't around in the 60s. But it's something that has a texture that's so atmospheric and so mystique,” he says. The project also received backing from the Red Sea Fund, an initiative of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea International Film Festival supporting filmmakers from the Arab world, Africa and Asia. Road to the Oscars But making history at Toronto was one thing. Now comes the challenge of turning that victory into an Oscar nomination. For Rio and his team, the coming months will be a whirlwind of screenings, meetings with Academy voters, networking and fund-raising. The film's Platform Prize win has opened the door to consideration for Best International Feature Film, but securing a place on the shortlist, let alone among the final five nominees, will require an entirely different kind of effort. Preliminary voting for the Oscars' Best International Feature Film will take place from December 7 to 11, with the shortlist announced on December 15. Nominations voting will run from January 11 to 15, with the final five nominees for the category announced alongside the other Oscar nominations on January 21. Producer Beso is preparing for a campaign that will take the filmmakers from India to Britain and the US, with Los Angeles and New York becoming key stops. “The plan is to move to LA very soon, but we are also in the meantime trying to get all the Academy members to watch the film, whether it's in India or in the UK and in the US,” she says. “The next few months are very exciting, but it's also like a marathon. “Every day there is lobbying and interviews. I usually say a producer's job is to beg, borrow and steal. So right now I'm in the begging stage. “It's expensive to make a film, but it's even more expensive to do that entire campaign.” For Rio, who has already experienced a remarkable few weeks since Toronto, the prospect of navigating Hollywood's awards circuit is another unfamiliar chapter. “I don't know what I'm getting into, but I'm looking forward to it,” he says.

title: Oman hosts 6th session of International Date Council
body:
Muscat: The Sultanate of Oman, represented by the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources, is hosting the 6th Session of the International Date Council, with participation from several member states at the St Regis Hotel on Sunday. The session aims to address key topics related to the development of the date palm and date sector and to enhance international cooperation in this vital field. The meeting is featuring a review of the Council’s annual report for 2026 and discussions on various organisational and technical matters. Participants will examine key achievements from the preceding period, alongside the Council’s future plans, programmes and initiatives designed to support and advance the date palm and date sector at both regional and international levels. The Council will also deliberate on ways to strengthen cooperation among member states, including the exchange of expertise, knowledge, research, studies, technologies and best practices in areas such as production, quality control, processing, marketing and international trade — all of which contribute to increasing the competitiveness of date products and bolstering their presence in global markets. "The meeting, organised by the Inrernational Date Council, highlights the Council’s vital role in providing data and indicators concerning production, trade and markets, besides exploring ways to support member states in developing joint projects and forging partnerships with the private sector, universities, research centres and other relevant institutions," said Saud bin Hamoud al Habsi, the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Qater Resources. He further said that the session will focus on building national capacities and facilitating the exchange of expertise in innovation, sustainability and value chains. The Council will also review the matter of state membership, examining the opportunities it provides for member states to participate in shaping directions, strategies and initiatives concerning the future of the date palm and date sector. It will additionally address the enhancement of cooperation in areas such as standards, quality, food safety and access to international markets. During its sixth session, the Council of Members will adopt several resolutions, including the approval of the Council’s annual report on its activities for 2026. It will also address various organisational and financial matters in accordance with established rules and regulations, and oversee the implementation of programmes and activities for the coming period. The Sultanate of Oman’s hosting of this meeting underscores its role in supporting international cooperation within the agricultural sector and strengthening joint efforts to develop the date palm and date industry — aligning with broader objectives to achieve sustainable development and enhance the economic value of this sector.

title: Iraq’s dinar devaluation tests efforts to protect consumers from rising prices
body: Iraq’s decision to devalue its currency has exposed the competing interests of households and the state, as residents warn of rising living costs while economists argue the move could help protect public finances amid a sharp fall in oil revenue. The Central Bank of Iraq raised the official dollar selling rate from 1,320 to 1,520 dinars on October 7, a devaluation of about 15 per cent. The move came as disruption to oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz exerted additional pressure on government revenue and its capacity to finance public spending. “The situation is very bad,” one market owner in Erbil lamented. He said the price of goods has been rising since the Iran war broke out in February, particularly due to higher transport costs as most items come from Turkey and Iran. Iraq imports a substantial share of the products it uses, including food, medicine and consumer goods. For Iraqis paid in dinars, the weaker currency threatens to erode purchasing power. But the effects are not uniform, as those earning in dollars may receive more dinars when converting their salaries, while people with dollar-denominated expenses face a different calculation. In Erbil, where rent is often set in dollars, the exchange-rate change can have a direct effect on tenants paid in dinars. The measure places economic pressure on tenants who need to buy dollars with their dinar salaries, although the actual cost depends on the exchange rate available to them and how rent is paid. The gap between the official and parallel-market rates adds another layer to the pressure on households. While the official public rate is 1,520 dinars to the dollar, people and businesses seeking cash dollars often turn to exchange shops, where the price fluctuates according to supply and demand. In Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Iraqi Kurdistan region, the dollar was selling for about 166,350 dinars per $100 this week, around nine per cent above the official rate. The parallel-market rate rose sharply after the devaluation was announced on October 7, when exchange shops in the city quoted selling prices as high as 180,000 dinars per $100. The rate subsequently eased, although it remained above the official figure. The National visited several exchange shops in the Eskan neighbourhood of Erbil, where many dollar shops can be found, but employees declined to comment on the fluctuations. Dollar-denominated rents are part of a wider pattern in Iraq, where the dollar plays a prominent role in parts of the property market and some business dealings, even though most salaries and everyday purchases are made in dinars . The result is that households can be exposed on several fronts – rent may become more expensive in the national currency, while imported food, household goods and other products may also rise in price as businesses face higher costs for dollars. The use of the US dollar for some expenses while the majority of salaries are in Iraqi dinar “is what is fundamentally wrong with us”, Ahmed Tabaqchali, non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told The National . Those paid in dollars may benefit from converting their income into more dinars to cover expenses. But the advantage is less straightforward for people who also pay rent or other bills in dollars, since those costs do not become cheaper simply because the exchange rate changes. Ahmad Abbas, who receives his income in dollars, said: “It’s safer to be paid in dollars because it’s unstable when it comes to the currency here. My rent is in dollars and my bills are in Iraqi dinars but I expect prices to go higher, so at the end of the day it will kind of be the same.” He had observed prices rising during the war earlier this year but said they were “even higher now”. “I went to the market the other day and bought the same detergent for 20,000 Iraqi dinar and before it used to cost 9,000,” he said. The decision has prompted criticism from residents and political factions, with legislators demanding explanations from the government and proposing measures to contain price increases. Others argue the adjustment was necessary to help Baghdad meet its financial obligations. “There is no denying the affect is there but it’s not as dramatic as people make it out to be,” Mr Tabaqchali said. “The country had to do something,” he said, before adding he was “surprised it was proactive”. “In the past we didn’t act but we acted while the reserves are still healthy,” he added. At the Meri Forum in Erbil on Tuesday, Samir Fakhri, director general of the Statistics and Research Directorate at the Central Bank, defended the devaluation, arguing it was necessary to protect the country's foreign currency reserves following the decline in oil revenue. He highlighted Iraq's dependence on oil , which accounts for more than 90 per cent of government revenue, leaving public finances particularly vulnerable to disruptions in exports. He explained the scale of government spending and the pressure it places on the Central Bank of Iraq to supply dollars, arguing the exchange-rate adjustment must be considered alongside the country's wider financial difficulties. The argument in favour of devaluation is that Baghdad receives more dinars for every dollar earned from oil exports, helping it finance salaries and other domestic spending even as oil income comes under pressure. But that fiscal benefit does not necessarily translate into greater purchasing power for households. The government led by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has said it needs to maintain public spending and ensure salaries can be paid despite the loss of oil income. But opposition has grown within parliament, with politicians questioning why the measure was adopted and whether alternative options were adequately considered. The Co-ordination Framework , the main alliance of Shiite political parties that backs the government in Baghdad, has called for measures to limit the burden on citizens. “We can’t catch a break from them,” said Rizgar Ali, a taxi driver in Erbil, referring to the Iraqi government. “I have relatives who are public servants and their salaries are always delayed because Baghdad doesn’t send us our budget and now they’re weakening the money.” The recurring delays, amid disputes between Baghdad and Erbil over oil revenue and budget allocations, leave many households with limited financial flexibility to absorb higher prices and currency costs. Mr Ali complained about the rise in petrol prices and said he has to refuel his car frequently, making driving passengers around the city a much more difficult source of income – he turns the engine off at most traffic lights. Devaluation precedence Mr Tabaqchali said the current situation reminds him of the devaluation in 2020 when Iraq faced a similar dilemma during the Covid-19 pandemic, when a collapse in oil prices and a decline in revenue left the government struggling to finance its budget. The adjustment was intended to generate more dinar revenue from oil sales, ease the budget deficit and help the government meet its spending obligations. In January 2023, the government of prime minister at the time, Mohammed Shia Al Sudani, moved in the opposite direction, strengthening the dinar and setting the public exchange rate at 1,320 per dollar after the currency weakened on the parallel market amid tighter US restrictions on dollar transfers and increased scrutiny of Iraqi banks. That decision, too, was met with concern by residents because the dollar continued to trade at a higher value on the parallel market. The latest devaluation reverses that strengthening. Whether the devaluation achieves its intended financial objectives will depend not only on oil revenue and foreign currency reserves, but also on the government's ability to prevent unjustified price increases, protect lower-income families and pursue reforms that reduce Iraq's reliance on oil. Mr Tabaqchali also highlighted government subsidies as a means of cushioning the impact on lower-income Iraqis. Subsidies on fuel and some basic services, alongside the public distribution system that provides subsidised staple foods, can help shield poorer households from some of the immediate effects of a weaker currency. The government has also pledged to maintain fuel and basic-service subsidies following the latest devaluation, while considering customs relief for food and essential goods. However, subsidies do not cover all household expenses, such as rent, and imported goods can still become more expensive. “The worst is over for us as long as we continue shipping through the [Strait of] Hormuz,” Mr Tabaqchali said. “This doesn’t mean we have passed the crisis because the damage has been done and we have to adjust. The devaluation is part of a bigger thing, like structural changes to our budget services.”

title: Rioters attack police station in central Paris — mayor
body:
PARIS, October 18. /TASS/. Radicals have attacked a police station in central Paris amid nationwide riots triggered by protests against inflation and declining purchasing power, Ariel Weil, the mayor of central Paris, told BFMTV.
"Some law enforcement forces in central Paris were forced to defend the precinct. It was difficult for the police commissioner to deploy personnel across all fronts because they also had to protect their own station," Weil said.
Weil noted that small organized groups carried out a series of attacks on commercial and government properties throughout the day, including the 10th arrondissement town hall. Earlier, Paris Deputy Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire stated that radicals had "trashed entire streets" and looted numerous shops.
On October 17, mass demonstrations took place across France against soaring fuel prices and a drop in living standards. The Interior Ministry estimated that 550,000 people protested nationwide, including 110,000 in Paris. In several cities, the rallies escalated into clashes with police. On Saturday evening, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced 400 detentions nationwide and vowed that authorities would continue to pursue everyone involved in the rioting and looting.

title: Sanctions strangle Iranian economy as IRGC goes on high alert over civil unrest risks - analysis
body: Senior Israeli defense officials estimate that economic sanctions are choking the Iranian regime, forcing internal security apparatuses onto high alert to preempt widespread civil unrest.According to assessments, the Iranian street is simmering, and the next boiling point, driven by American leverage, could arrive within months, though public reaction remains unpredictable.Simultaneously, the regime is pursuing diplomatic and military maneuvers to break its isolation, conveying threats and engaging in provocative actions across the region. Officials note that Tehran deeply fears an American or Israeli surprise strike and is preparing for extreme scenarios.Following new US sanctions that took effect on September 23 and targeted flights from Iran, many countries suspended Iranian flights.While China rejected the sanctions and Turkey reduced flight volumes without fully canceling them, Armenia, Russia, Afghanistan, and Pakistan continue to allow Iranian flights following diplomatic outreach. Pressure on Iraq also secured designated flight corridors (excluding Baghdad).Iran maintaining proxy network, transfers millions of dollarsConcurrently, Tehran works around the clock to maintain its regional proxy network. Reports from Beirut indicate that approximately $200 million was recently transferred to Hezbollah. Iran also continues providing advice, training, production support, and weapons transfers to the Houthis in Yemen, while preserving ties with pro-Iranian Shia militias in Iraq and seeking new anti-Western partnerships. The objective is to ensure proxy alignment in any future conflict.To establish deterrence against Gulf states and pressure Washington through them, Tehran has issued threats over the past week indicating a capacity for ground invasions into neighboring countries - a scenario Israel warns could dramatically escalate regional turmoil. These threats accompany reports of naval mine incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and damage to maritime vessels.Iran resumes ballistic missile production, restores damaged weaponryAccording to Israeli sources, Iran has resumed ballistic missile production and is working to restore damaged weaponry alongside completing manufacturing processes initiated before Operation Roaring Lion. "The process is slow and constrained by knowledge gaps and production limits, but they are actively moving in that direction," a defense official noted.Politically, Tehran is attempting to open diplomatic channels to buy time, restrict American operational flexibility, and prevent further strikes on its territory.In response, Israel conveyed messages to the US, Gulf nations, and regional mediators stressing that any Iranian surprise offensive will trigger an exceptionally severe military response.Jerusalem clarified that its objectives regarding Iran's nuclear project, missile array, and defense industry infrastructure are not yet complete. Should Iran initiate an attack, Israel may act with greater force than during Operation Lion's Roar, including strikes on national infrastructure previously limited by Washington to shorten conflict duration.Defense officials emphasize extremely high operational coordination between the IDF and US Central Command (CENTCOM). Sources in daily contact with American counterparts say that US President Donald Trump has placed the military on high alert, keeping the option of strikes open until the last minute.However, officials assess that an American strike prior to the US midterm elections remains unlikely unless Iran initiates offensive actions or signals imminent regional aggression.Consequently, the IDF maintains heightened vigilance, closely monitoring developments in Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq, and the maritime domain against unexpected aggression from Tehran or its proxies.

title: Lavrov to discuss escalation in Persian Gulf with GCC counterparts in Manama
body:
MANAMA /Kingdom of Bahrain/, October 18. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will discuss regional tensions with his counterparts from the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) member states. The Russian Foreign Minister is set to participate in the ninth Russia-GCC Strategic Dialogue in Manama.
Bahrain will be the first stop on the minister’s Middle East tour, which aims to promote de-escalation in the region. The trip will conclude with a visit to Tehran for talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
Tensions in the Persian Gulf are mounting due to actions taken by the United States and Israel against Iran, as well as the ongoing conflict between the Yemeni Houthis and Saudi Arabia. This has led to a spike in oil prices and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
According to IMF estimates, the crisis threatens to cause a 4.8% economic contraction in GCC countries this year. In the event of a large-scale war and the complete closure of these straits, experts predict that oil prices could surge above $200 per barrel, potentially triggering a global food crisis. Against this backdrop, Russia seeks to facilitate de-escalation while reaffirming its status as a reliable supplier of energy resources.
The crisis has led to a breakdown in political ties between the region and the West. Brussels has indefinitely postponed the EU-GCC summit, which was scheduled to take place in Riyadh on October 24. This decision follows a recent attack by the Houthis on Riyadh’s airport, which resulted in at least 17 deaths.
The GCC comprises six countries in the region: Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, Oman, and Saudi Arabia.

title: Mining Marshals deny involvement in operation linked to miners’ deaths
body: The Commander of the Mining Marshals, Assistant Commandant of Corps, John Onoja Attah, has rejected claims linking the specialised NSCDC unit to the September 16 operation at M.I. Wushishi Housing Estate in Minna, Niger State, declaring that the suspended Niger State Commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, lacked the authority to deploy its operatives. Onoja Attah, in a statement issued by his office at the NSCDC National Headquarters in Abuja, described the claim attributed to Aniviye in a publication on October 16, 2026, as false and misleading, insisting that no Mining Marshals personnel participated in the operation now under investigation by the Justice Mohammed Mohammed Commission of Inquiry. The suspended commandant was quoted as saying that he visited the mining site on September 15 before deploying Mining Marshals to the area. But Attah dismissed the assertion, arguing that it misrepresented the command structure and operational jurisdiction of the specialised unit. Bauchi agency CEO, 4 chidren die in road accident Nigerian courts must stop becoming ‘market stalls’ – Retired Justice Augie “No Mining Marshals operative is attached to the Niger State Command or to any State Command of the Corps for that matter,” he stated, stressing that the unit operates exclusively from the National Headquarters under the direct command, control and operational directives of the Commandant-General, in collaboration with the ministry of Solid Minerals Development. He added that a state commandant had no authority to deploy Mining Marshals for any operation. “Our operational records confirm that at no time were Mining Marshals personnel deployed or involved in the said operation,” Onoja Attah said, warning against attempts to associate the unit with the custodial deaths currently being investigated. The commander also defended the operational record of the Mining Marshals, describing its enforcement activities under the Nigerian Minerals and Mining Act, 2007, as professional, civil and guided by the law. According to him, the unit has maintained strict adherence to its rules of engagement since its establishment, with no record of human rights violations in its operations across the country and no pending Fundamental Human Rights Enforcement suit against it in any Nigerian court. The Mining Marshals, he said, remained committed to sanitising Nigeria’s solid minerals sector and would not allow what he described as erroneous publications to distract it from its statutory responsibilities.

title: Kwara APC: Ex-VC Leads High-profile Group to Resolve Disputes, Reconcile Aggrieved Members
body: Elder statesman and former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ilorin, Prof. Oba AbdulRaheem, is leading a group of prominent Kwara indigenes to reconcile aggrieved members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and mobilise support for the party ahead of the 2027 general election. The group, which held its inaugural meeting at Abdulraheem’s Ilorin residence on September 17, said it is committed to resolving all disagreements that trailed the outcome of the APC’s primaries. Abdulraheem, also a former Chairman of the Federal Character Commission (FCC), chairs the group, the Kwara APC Peace Committee. Apart from Abdulraheem, eminent indigenes of Kwara in the group include Dr. Johnson Adewumi, a foremost educationist/ entrepreneur and founder of the Thomas Adewumi University, Oko; former Minister and former Speaker, Kwara State House of Assembly, Hon. Issa Bio Ibrahim; and former Secretary to Kwara State Government and former Member, Federal House of Representatives, Hon. AbdulGaniyu Cook Olododo. Other members include Oloriewe Raheem Adedoyin, a veteran journalist and member representing Africa in the Executive Board of the International Press Institute; elder statesman and former Speaker, Kwara State House of Assembly, Hon. Benjamin Ezekiel Issa; elder statesman and Member of Tinubu Shettina PCC, Pastor John Dara; and former Commissioner, Federal Character Commission, Hon. James Jiya Kolo. According to the statement, the committee intends to serve as a voice of conscience among APC leaders by addressing internal grievances and promoting the achievements of the administrations of President Bola Tinubu and Kwara State Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq. It said the group had reached out to some aggrieved political leaders and influential stakeholders to encourage reconciliation and forge a common front ahead of the elections. The committee is also canvassing support for the APC’s governorship candidate, Hon. Yakubu Danladi, and other party candidates in the state. The statement said the initiative aimed to secure the backing of party stakeholders for the candidates and strengthen cohesion within the APC ahead of the general election.

title: Makinde: Nigeria’s main challenge Is Poverty, not Religion
body: Presidential Candidate of Allied Peoples Movement (APM) and Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, says the country’s biggest problem is poverty. Makinde said this while reacting to his recognition as Christian Icon of the Year, by the Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN) in Abuja, on Saturday. He said the honour presented an opportunity to encourage Christians to take active role in politics where they can shape the country’s political and economic future. He cautioned against the tendency among many Christians to avoid politics because of the notion that it is a dirty game or at variance with their religious beliefs. Nigerian courts must stop becoming ‘market stalls’ – Retired Justice Augie Bagudu: Tinubu’s reforms yielding results Makinde said Christians must move beyond such perceptions and recognise politics as an important platform for contributing to national development and addressing the challenges confronting the people. He urged them to draw inspiration from biblical examples of individuals who served in difficult circumstances in order to advance the work of God and the people. The governor said the biblical account offered an important lesson for Christians who might be reluctant to serve in political environments because of the religious beliefs of those in authority. He argued that religious considerations should not prevent them from participating in governance or contributing their expertise and values to the transformation of society. “I will use this opportunity to encourage our Christian brothers and sisters across the country to rise and participate in the agenda to transform Nigeria and reset our country,” Makinde said. He maintained that Nigeria’s most pressing challenge was the widespread poverty confronting millions of people, stressing that national attention should focus on addressing the economic difficulties affecting the population. “Our problem is not primarily a religious one. Our problem in this country is poverty, grinding poverty,” he said. Makinde said the country could not afford to lose sight of the urgent socioeconomic issues requiring attention by allowing religious differences to dominate national conversations. The governor stressed that the task of national transformation required collective participation, irrespective of religious affiliations, political differences or personal convictions.

title: Elumelu Backs $15bn Infrastructure Investment Drive Across West Africa
body: Festus Akanbi Heirs Holdings Chairman Mr Tony Elumelu is backing efforts to assemble a $15 billion portfolio of infrastructure projects across West Africa, as regional leaders and investors seek to turn economic integration ambitions into bankable investments. The initiative, being developed ahead of the inaugural West Africa Integration and Investment Summit (WAIIS) in Sierra Leone next month, will bring selected projects before prospective financiers to mobilise capital for infrastructure and productive enterprises. Elumelu, who co-chairs the summit, disclosed the plans in an emailed response to questions from Bloomberg, which reported the development on Thursday. Potential financiers include United Bank for Africa (UBA), the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), Africa Finance Corporation (AFC) and Africa50. Priority sectors comprise energy, trade, industrialisation, strategic minerals, agriculture and digital infrastructure. The proposed $15 billion represents the anticipated value of the investment pipeline, rather than funding already committed by Elumelu or the participating financial institutions. Organisers have so far shortlisted 26 projects worth more than $10 billion from 170 submissions spanning more than 10 countries, with expectations that the portfolio will expand before the November gathering. Special Envoy for WAIIS, Dr Kandeh Kolleh Yumkella, said the selection reflected progress towards presenting investors with concrete opportunities across the region. “We received 170 project submissions and have selected 26 real projects worth more than $10 billion from over ten countries,” Yumkella said in a statement issued by the organisers. “We expect that portfolio to reach $15 billion or more,” he added. Convened by Sierra Leone’s President, Julius Maada Bio, the summit is scheduled for November 17 and 18 at the Julius Maada Bio International Conference Centre in Lungi. It will bring together governments, business leaders, project developers and development finance institutions to advance strategic regional investments. The investment drive places project preparation and access to finance at the centre of West Africa’s integration agenda. Its immediate task is to connect viable proposals with institutions capable of financing their development, while aligning commercial opportunities with national and regional priorities. Energy and transport connections, agricultural investment and digital networks are central to that ambition, offering opportunities to strengthen trade, expand production and improve access to markets. The initiative also comes against the backdrop of efforts to develop major cross-border infrastructure, including the proposed $25 billion Nigeria–Morocco Gas Pipeline, also known as the African Atlantic Gas Pipeline. Backed by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), the project is intended to carry Nigerian natural gas through several West African countries to Morocco, with potential connections to European markets. The proposed gas link illustrates the scale of the region’s infrastructure ambitions and the importance of coordinating governments, project sponsors and financiers across national boundaries. It is a separate undertaking from the investment portfolio being assembled for the summit. Elumelu’s involvement in the regional financing initiative coincides with the expansion of his interests in Nigeria’s energy sector. According to Nairametrics, Heirs Energies Limited acquired an additional six million shares in Seplat Energy Plc on September 30, increasing the combined holdings of Heirs Energies and Heirs Holdings from 120.4 million to 126.4 million shares. The acquisition raised their combined voting interest from 20.07 per cent to 21.07 per cent. A separate analysis by the publication estimated that the combined market value of Elumelu’s holdings in Seplat, UBA and Transnational Corporation Plc rose by N684.59 billion between June and September, reaching approximately N2.43 trillion. For the West African initiative, the next milestone is presenting the shortlisted projects to prospective financiers in Sierra Leone, where the proposed portfolio will be tested against investors’ financing requirements.

title: Makinde Will Defeat Tinubu in His 12 Battleground States, Others, Says Campaign Council
body: • Challenges president to travel to Kaduna, Kano, Plateau, other s by road •Insists Nigeria’s biggest problem is grinding poverty, not religion Chuks Okocha in Abuja The Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) has declared that its presidential candidate on the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Governor Seyi Makinde of Oyo State, will defeat President Bola Tinubu in the 12 battleground states identified by the president, as well as in other states across the federation, in the January 2027 presidential election. This is as Makinde declared that Nigeria’s biggest problem is grinding poverty, not religion, urging Christians to stop shunning politics and take an active role in transforming the country. The MDPCO, in a statement by its Director of Strategic Communications, Hon. Richard Nnanna Ihediwa, asserted that Makinde would decisively defeat Tinubu and his All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council in Rivers State and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, insisting that no amount of political manoeuvring, intimidation or abuse of incumbency by the President’s henchmen can reverse the growing tide of opposition to his re-election. The organisation said the arrogance and political overreach of President Tinubu’s inner circle had deepened public resentment and further weakened his electoral prospects. It added that President Tinubu’s decision to personally visit and campaign in only 12 states — Oyo, Kaduna, Rivers, Plateau, Borno, Enugu, Bauchi, Sokoto, Delta, Kano, Adamawa and Lagos — further confirmed his apprehension over the mileage and foothold already achieved by Makinde with his RESET NIGERIA Agenda message in the aforementioned and other states of the federation. “Mr President should know that his visit to these states, if he eventually does, will not in any way change the direction or the determination of the people to vote him out, given his unpardonable failures in office which have brought unprecedented hardship across the country,” the organisation said. “President Tinubu has no meaningful achievement he can boast of in these and other states of the federation where Nigerians now refer to his government as ‘T-Pain’ following the suffering they have been subjected to by the policies of the Tinubu administration in the last three and a half years.” The MDPCO challenged President Tinubu not to have a change of mind but to visit the states to face the people. “We challenge President Tinubu to travel around the country by road and witness the decrepit state of federal highways, the squalor in which Nigerians live and the level of infrastructural decay across the country, while his government squanders trillions of Naira on white elephant projects and wasteful programmes. “If President Tinubu believes he is popular as he claims, he should not stop at the rally ground or at the airport when he gets to any of the states. He should go beyond waving to a gathering of APC rented crowd and be bold enough to directly engage the people in the communities and towns to seek their votes, as the APM candidate, Makinde, has been doing since he started his campaign,” it said. The organisation said the APM candidate had been engaging Nigerians with his clear-cut RESET NIGERIA message, focused on rebuilding systems and institutions that produce excellent outcomes rather than relying on sloganeering like President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda. “Nigerians are gravitating towards the core campaign pillars and proposals in Makinde’s RESET NIGERIA Agenda, which include the establishment of an all-inclusive, four-year transitional government of national unity with four priority pillars of education, economy, security and socio-political policies. “Unlike President Tinubu’s visionless, thoughtless and rudderless rule characterised by crass arbitrariness, Makinde’s RESET NIGERIA Agenda offers data-driven strategies that revolve around tackling poverty through massive production; a security plan that prioritises intelligence gathering, social reorientation and decisive kinetic and non-kinetic actions; an education plan that focuses on expanding access to quality functional education; and institutional reform that emphasises inclusive governance and sincere public leadership.” The campaign added: “Our campaign is proud to acknowledge that feedback from the field indicates that Seyi Makinde’s RESET NIGERIA Agenda is resonating with Nigerians, especially the youths, who not only see light at the end of the tunnel, but a bright sunny day under a Makinde-Daura presidency. “President Tinubu is for the umpteenth time urged not to waste the nation’s resources on his ‘Nebuchadnezzar’ Campaign Council of failed politicians who, like the president himself, cannot attract votes from Nigerians,” the campaign said. In a development, Makinde has declared that Nigeria’s biggest problem is grinding poverty, not religion, urging Christians to stop shunning politics and take an active role in transforming the country. He said Christians could not afford to stand aloof from politics because it was dirty or because they should not serve under leaders who did not share their faith, stressing that national transformation required their active participation. Makinde spoke yesterday in Abuja after receiving a Christian Icon Award at the Christian Association of Nigeria’s (CAN) 50th anniversary celebration. The governor, the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential candidate, said Christians should draw lessons from biblical figures who accepted difficult assignments in pursuit of a greater purpose. “It is typical for us to say, ‘Politics is dirty. I don’t want to be yoked with unbelievers’, and things like that. But we must look at biblical examples,” he said. Makinde cited David, who, despite having been anointed king, served in the palace of Saul, from whom God had departed. He said the biblical account should challenge Christians who believe they cannot serve under leaders of different religious persuasions. “I will use this opportunity to encourage our Christian brothers and sisters across the country to rise and participate in the agenda to transform Nigeria and reset our country,” he said. Makinde urged Christians to focus on the hardship confronting Nigerians rather than allowing religious differences to define their engagement with national affairs. “Our problem is not primarily a religious one. Our problem in this country is poverty — grinding poverty,” he said. “At this stage, we must focus on addressing the issues currently confronting us. Those are the challenges we need to tackle.”

title: Okonjo-Iweala: $2.4bn Subsidy Fraud Probe Triggered My Mother’s Kidnap
body: Francis Ndubuisi in Abuja The Director-General of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, has recounted how her efforts to uncover an alleged $2.4billion fuel subsidy fraud in Nigeria led to threats against her and the kidnapping of her mother. Okonjo-Iweala said the abductors demanded that she resign as finance minister and leave the country in exchange for her mother’s release. She recounted the ordeal during an interview with Bloomberg’s Francine Lacqua on the Leaders programme, published earlier this week. The former finance minister said the investigation began after officials noticed that claims submitted by fuel importers under Nigeria’s subsidy programme were increasing sharply. Nigeria, despite being an oil-producing country, relied on imported refined petroleum products to meet domestic demand at the time. Under the subsidy arrangement, importers received government payments that enabled them to sell petrol at regulated prices. However, Okonjo-Iweala said the amounts being claimed had risen to levels that raised suspicion. “So, I went to the president and said, look, something is going on here. Could we audit the accounts? And he said, ‘yes, go ahead.’ And we found about $2.4 billion worth of fraud. So, we refused to pay,” she said. She said the decision triggered threats against her before her mother was abducted. “I was told that for her to be released, I should resign and leave the country,” she said. Describing the experience, Okonjo-Iweala said the five-day ordeal was among the most painful periods of her life because she feared that her actions could lead to her mother’s death. “It was a terrible, terrible five-day ordeal. I think it’s the worst in my life,” she said. She disclosed that her mother was held in a forest before escaping one night. “She was held in the middle of a forest, and one night she escaped. She’s still alive. She’s 96 now,” she said, adding that her mother still becomes distressed whenever the incident is mentioned. Asked whether she had considered quitting her job during the crisis, Okonjo-Iweala said she would have prioritised her mother’s life over remaining in office. “Between my mother, having my mother alive and staying in a job, I would pick my mother any day,” she said. However, she recalled that her father urged her not to surrender to the kidnappers’ demands. “He said, ‘we don’t give in to blackmail.’ And he said, ‘you’ve got to carry on. You’ve got to go to work,” she recounted. Okonjo-Iweala said she initially felt paralysed by fear and considered resigning to secure her mother’s release, adding that the experience left her with a sense of guilt that she still felt today. “I never dreamt my parents could ever be touched in this way – that people would be that evil,” she said. She added that her experiences over the years had made her more patient and helped her focus on finding solutions when confronted with difficult situations. “I feel that this is a real fight that has to be waged. If you are a country that is not that rich, every single penny counts,” she said. Okonjo-Iweala served as Nigeria’s finance minister under former President Goodluck Jonathan before becoming director-general of the WTO in March 2021. Her mother, Kamene Okonjo, was kidnapped from her home in Ogwashi-Uku, Delta State, in December 2012. The incident drew national attention amid concerns over the safety of the finance minister’s family.

title: World Bank Report: ADC Asks Tinubu-led Govt to Explain ‘Missing’ $12.4bn
body: • Says gap equivalent to almost a quarter of 2026 budget Chuks Okocha in Abuja The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has called on President Bola Tinubu to explain the $12.4 billion gap, equivalent to about N16.5 trillion, in Nigeria’s external accounts identified in the World Bank’s October 2026 Nigeria Development Update. In a statement signed by its National Publicity Secretary, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the party said Tinubu owed Nigerians a clear account of the discrepancy, especially as families struggling with the cost-of-living crisis were forced to account for every naira. Citing the report, the ADC said Nigeria recorded a $12 billion current-account surplus and $6.2 billion in net financial inflows in the first half of 2026. The party said these inflows should have strengthened the country’s reserves, but the report instead identified a $12.4 billion gap. Abdullahi said the World Bank attributed the gap, in part, to oil export earnings that were not repatriated. He added that the report noted that the repatriation of export proceeds remained limited, partly because Nigerian oil had been pledged against several long-term loans. “The scale is staggering,” the ADC said. “This unexplained gap is larger than the entire current-account surplus for the same period. It is about 5.6 times the $2.2 billion Nigeria attracted in foreign direct investment. In naira terms, it is almost a quarter of the N68.32 trillion 2026 federal budget. “This cannot be dismissed as a minor accounting discrepancy. President Tinubu welcomed this report. He cannot celebrate one part of the report and stay silent on a gap bigger than the surplus that he and his government are celebrating. “Due to President Tinubu’s failed policies, families across Nigeria are forced to skip meals and account for every naira just to survive. Meanwhile, money that could have eased their hardship is currently unaccounted for. Tinubu owes Nigerians an explanation. “Sacrifice cannot be compulsory for everyday citizens while accountability remains optional for the government that is in charge of our collective resources.” The ADC called on the federal government to publish a full public reconciliation of the $12.4 billion gap and disclose all oil-backed loans and pledged crude commitments. It also demanded updated net reserve figures and clear evidence that higher revenues were improving essential services such as health, education and power. “President Tinubu must open the books. Nigerians have sacrificed enough. We deserve answers,” the party said.

title: Jonathan: My Administration Built Almajiri Schools to Counter Extremism, Empower Northern Youths
body: Linus Aleke in Abuja Former President Goodluck Jonathan has said that his administration established Almajiri schools across northern Nigeria to deny extremist groups access to potential recruits and provide young people with technical education that would empower them economically beyond religious instruction. Jonathan made this revelation yesterday during the public presentation and formal launch of ‘Beyond the Bullets: Policing Terrorism in a Democratic System,’ a book authored by former Inspector-General of Police (IG), Mohammed Dikko Abubakar (rtd.). President Jonathan’s administration built no fewer than 121 Almajiri schools across northern Nigeria. However, the schools have become shadows of their former selves, as successive administrations have abandoned the project despite its laudable aims and objectives. Speaking as the chairman of the occasion, Jonathan said successive administrations since the beginning of the Fourth Republic had been confronted with terrorism and other forms of violent insecurity. Represented by his former Chief of Staff, Mike Oghiadomhe, Jonathan said: “Since the beginning of the Fourth Republic, successive administrations have had to confront terrorism and other forms of violent insecurity in our country. Each administration has faced its own circumstances and challenges and has, in different ways, sought to protect the lives and property of Nigerians and preserve the territorial integrity of our nation. “As President, working with the author and other key security heads, I also confronted this scourge and made every effort, within the circumstances and resources available to my administration, to strengthen our security response and protect our citizens. “I believe the author has pointed out the fact that the fight against terrorism is not the responsibility of one administration or another. It is a continuing national and global challenge that requires sustained commitment, institutional learning and co-operation across successive governments and generations. “This is what makes Beyond the Bullets particularly valuable. The title itself suggests that the response to terrorism must go beyond the use of kinetic force, which I fully believe in. “In furtherance of this, my administration established Almajiri schools aimed at providing skills to millions of young people beyond religious education alone. This was intended to enable them to earn a living and contribute meaningfully to national development, while reducing the number of young people available for recruitment into violent crime. “We also engaged in the Great Green Wall Project, which, apart from helping to combat desertification and making more fertile land available for crop farming and animal husbandry, had the potential to provide employment for hundreds of thousands of people. I therefore use this opportunity to call on the government to revisit and review these programmes,” Jonathan explained. On his part, a former Senate President, Dr Bukola Saraki urged Nigerians not to leave the fight against insurgency and other forms of violent extremism to the military and police alone. He described the author as not only a professional police officer but also an incorruptible one. Saraki recalled that, while serving as Governor of Kwara State, he travelled to Abuja with his late father to lobby behind the scenes for Abubakar not to be redeployed from the state, where he served as Commissioner of Police, because of his efforts to maintain peace and security. According to Saraki: “He should have left Kwara much earlier. Every time they wanted to post him out, my father, of blessed memory, and I would go behind the scenes and make sure they retained him because he was so important to maintaining the stability and security of the state. Eventually, of course, he had to leave to further his career and become an IG.” Also speaking, the IG, Olatunji Disu, said the book was a profound reminder that the true power of policing did not lie in the barrels of guns, “but in the strength of our values, the rule of law and the trust of the people we serve”. Disu said the book offered policymakers, security practitioners, scholars and the general public a valuable insight into the dilemmas, decisions and discipline that define leadership at the highest level of policing. The chief launcher, Alhaji Aliko Dangote, said the former IG had made remarkable contributions to the fight against terrorism in Nigeria. In his remarks, the author, Abubakar, charged the military and other security agencies to remain professional in carrying out their constitutional mandates. He warned security personnel against succumbing to the temptation to replicate the very practices they were trained to prevent.

title: Niger Miners’ Deaths: Suspended Niger NSCDC Commandant Admits ‘Costly Mistake’, Apologises
body: The suspended Commandant of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger State, Siaka Zubeiru Anirive, has admitted that the deaths of suspected illegal miners in the corps’ custody could have been avoided, tendering an apology to their bereaved families and the Niger State Government. This came as it was revealed that his legal officer had advised him to release minors arrested during the operation. Anirive, who described the incident as a “costly mistake,” apologised while testifying before the Justice Mohammed Mohammed Commission of Inquiry in Minna, which was investigating the circumstances surrounding the deaths of the detainees. “A mistake has been made, but a very costly one. My apology to the parents of the deceased and to the people and government of Niger State,” he told the commission. The former commandant also expressed regret that the deaths occurred during his tenure, acknowledging that the incident could have been prevented. The apology, however, came amid troubling testimony about the handling of the detainees, including allegations that the advice to release minors on bail was ignored and evidence from a medical worker who said one suspect was coughing severely around the time the bodies were being removed from the detention cell. Testifying before the commission, Anirive said he assumed duty as Niger State NSCDC Commandant on August 25, 2025, and remained in office until September 18, 2026, explaining that the operation at a mining site along the M.I. Wushishi Housing Estate in Minna followed written and oral complaints from residents who alleged that the miners’ activities were disturbing their community. He said he visited the site on September 15, 2026, and then directed the command’s head of operations, Assistant Commandant of Corps Joha Achagwa, to act on the complaints. He said the Mining Marshal unit was deployed, leading to the arrest of suspected illegal miners during an operation conducted on the evening of September 16. However, the following day, detainees in NSCDC custody died. Anirive told the commission that he received a telephone call informing him that some suspects had died while in detention, adding that he immediately rushed to the command headquarters, where he found several bodies lying on the floor of the cell. He said he contacted Niger State Governor Mohammed Umar Bago and was directed to arrange for the bodies to be taken to the hospital, disclosing that he also informed the Commissioner of Police and the Director of the Department of State Services about the incident. The former commandant further told the commission that arrangements were underway to arraign the suspects in court on September 17 before their deaths. The testimony of the suspended head of the command’s Legal Unit, Assistant Commandant of Corps Stephen Tsado, raised further questions about how the detainees were handled. Tsado said his responsibilities included preparing case files, forwarding cases for prosecution and advising the commandant on legal matters. He told the commission that after noticing minors among the arrested suspects, he advised Anirive to release them to their parents on bail to protect their rights. The legal officer said he personally urged the commandant to act on that advice but did not know why he did not follow it. “I advised him to grant them bail to their parents,” he said, adding that the minors’ rights should not be violated. The commission also heard testimony from Nurse Maryam Etang of the NSCDC medical unit, who said she visited the detention cell as part of her routine duties on September 16 and 17. She disclosed that one of the suspects was coughing severely on September 17, while the bodies were being brought out of the cell. She also told the commission that she was shocked to find the body of Emeka Emmanuel among those removed, saying he was not among the miners arrested during the operation. The circumstances surrounding Emmanuel’s presence among the bodies raised further questions about the identities of those who died and the events leading to their detention. The inquiry is also expected to establish the circumstances of the deaths, examine the treatment of detainees and determine whether there were lapses in the handling of those held by the NSCDC. It would be recalled that in earlier proceedings, a mortician at Minna General Hospital had told the commission that 33 bodies were delivered to the hospital’s mortuary, against the 37 deaths widely reported by the state government and other authorities.

title: Ribadu: Military Operations Alone Cannot End Banditry
body: Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto The National Security Adviser (NSA), Malam Nuhu Ribadu, has said military operations alone cannot end banditry, calling for stronger intelligence-sharing, border security and community participation to tackle insecurity. Ribadu said banditry had evolved beyond cattle rustling, highway robbery and kidnapping to include territorial control, illegal taxation of rural communities and disruption of economic activities. He spoke through the Director of Legal Services in the Office of the National Security Adviser, Zakari Mijinyawa, at a brainstorming session on coping with banditry organised yesterday by the Sokoto Advancement Forum in collaboration with the Centre for Peace Studies, Usmanu Danfodiyo University, Sokoto. The NSA said Sokoto’s proximity to Niger Republic and the wider Sahel had given the crisis a cross-border dimension, with armed groups exploiting porous borders and security gaps to sustain their activities. “Sokoto’s proximity to the Republic of Niger and the wider Sahel adds a significant cross-border dimension to this challenge. “We must therefore combine intelligence-led operations, effective border management, regional cooperation and sustained action against the supply of illicit weapons and other logistical support,” he said. Ribadu also called for measures to address the socioeconomic conditions that made the young people vulnerable to recruitment by criminal groups, alongside lawful rehabilitation programmes for eligible individuals willing to abandon violence. “Reintegration must never replace justice or reward violence,” he said. The NSA outlined five priority areas for improving security in Sokoto: Denying armed groups safe havens, strengthening intelligence and early-warning systems, building community trust, protecting agriculture and rural livelihoods, and preventing youth recruitment into criminal networks. He urged security agencies to improve coordination and information-sharing, adding that communities would be more willing to provide intelligence if they trusted authorities to respond effectively and protect sensitive information. Ribadu identified Sabon Birni, Isa, Tangaza and Goronyo as areas where early-warning arrangements should be strengthened to ensure that reports of suspicious movements and emerging threats reached security agencies promptly. He warned that insecurity was disrupting farming, commerce and children’s education, with consequences for food production and the wider economy. The NSA said security operations should be assessed not only by arrests, weapons recovered or territory cleared, but also by whether displaced residents could return home and resume their livelihoods. He said, “We must measure progress by more than arrests, weapons recovered or territory cleared,” he said. “Success must also mean safer communities, returning families, productive farms, reopened schools, functioning markets and the restoration of public confidence.” Earlier, the Chairman of the Sokoto Advancement Forum, Prof. Muhammad Ahmad Wali, said security incidents had been recorded in 21 of the state’s 23 local government areas. Wali added that more than 1,100 people were reportedly kidnapped in Sokoto in the 12 months leading to June 2026, describing the crisis as a threat to residents’ lives, livelihoods and the authority of government. He called for stronger intelligence gathering, effective border control, swift justice, community involvement and economic opportunities for young people. The Vice Chairman of the forum, Prof. Riskuwa Arabu Shehu, urged participants to produce measurable recommendations, saying the organisation would compile the outcome of the discussions into a report and communiqué for presentation to government, security agencies and community stakeholders.

title: JAMB Moves to Rescue Graduates Stuck for Years over NIN Data Mismatch, Unveils New Service
