title: Belgium’s 10 F-16s bring Ukraine’s promised fleet to about 100 jets. Fewer than 40 are flying, as Russia’s jet drones run them ragged
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Belgium is speeding up the delivery of surplus Lockheed Martin F-16 fighters to Ukraine The 53 or so ex-Belgian jets are welcome, but the initial delivery for 2026 is for just 10 airframes, not all of which will be flyable The Ukrainian air force's sole F-16 wing is fighting hard with too few aircraft Belgium has announced it will accelerate the delivery of surplus Lockheed Martin F-16 fighters to Ukraine. Instead of delivering three flyable F-16s before the end of the year, Brussels will ship 10. It's unclear how many will be flyable. Previously, Belgian officials explained the first seven secondhand F-16s would include just three airworthy examples. The other four would be broken down for spare parts. It's good news for Ukraine, but hardly cause for nationwide celebration. The handful of flyable F-16s that should arrive in the coming two months could make good recent F-16 losses. But those shipping-soon Belgian F-16s won't actually grow Ukraine's F-16 fleet by much, if at all. The dozens of supersonic F-16s in action in Ukraine fly often and fight hard. They shoot down Russian drones and cruise missiles, tangle with Russian warplanes, and lob precision glide bombs at Russian forces on the ground. Russia launched about 2,000 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in September, up from some 350 in June, and F-16s are among the few weapons fast enough to catch them, the Wall Street Journal's editorial board noted . Every 300 flying hours, each jet must go abroad for a lengthy inspection. Explore further Ukraine loses another F-16 to onboard emergency The main constraint on the pace of F-16 sorties, besides maintenance demands and the availability of trained pilots, is munitions: running low or out of air-to-air missiles and glide bombs, the F-16s routinely aim their 20-mm guns at Russian targets. But even 20-mm ammunition sometimes runs low. The busy F-16s and their equally busy pilots need reinforcement. But reinforcements are slow coming. Belgium is only slightly accelerating its F-16 shipments amid reports it will eventually give Ukraine all 53 F-16s it's gradually retiring as new Lockheed Martin F-35 stealth fighters arrive to re-equip the Belgian air force. Further complicating the picture, Norway's six F-16s, promised in 2023, were still being refurbished in Belgium this spring. Some arrived there in pieces. Yes, Ukraine got 24 fight-ready F-16s from the Netherlands and most of the 19 Denmark promised. But it's lost five of those jets since 2024. And others are so worn out from relentless flying that they're badly in need of maintenance. The Belgian firm Sabena, which services Ukrainian F-16s, has struggled to keep up, and President Volodymyr Zelensky has said about half of the jets spend long stretches abroad for repairs. That slows the return of repaired planes and further squeezes the front-line force. A Ukrainian F-16. Ukrainian air force photo. One wing, too few jets Donor F-16s promised Reached Ukraine Status Netherlands 24 24 Complete Denmark 19 At least 12 Further deliveries due Norway 6 0 Being refurbished in Belgium Belgium 53 0 10 by end of 2026, the last in 2029 Total About 100 At least 36, five since lost Fewer than 40 in service Sources: Militarnyi, The Aviationist, Airdatanews, Euromaidan Press. In short, it's possible the Ukrainian air force's 107th Aviation Wing, its sole F-16 unit, has fewer than 40 ready-to-fight F-16s. Those 53 Belgian F-16s will help grow the wing, but piecemeal. Ukraine should expect a handful of operational jets from Belgium this year. Under a schedule from May , the last 27, half the total, may not arrive until 2029. To be clear, additional F-16s support the 107th Aviation Wing. The Netherlands sold 18 of its old F-16s to Romania for a token price in order to equip a training squadron, funded by a consortium of Ukraine's allies, that feeds trained pilots to the 107th Aviation Wing. But these 18 jets aren't available for front-line use. They don't even legally belong to Ukraine. Explore further Ukraine is running short of its best missiles for hunting Russia’s jet drones. Now MiG-29s are firing 1970s weapons The delays in supplies of combat-ready F-16s matter because the Ukrainian air force is under stress. Its last few dozen ex-Soviet warplanes, including Mikoyan MiG-29 and Sukhoi Su-27 fighters, are even older and wearier than the ex-European F-16s are. And they've suffered staggering losses in the air and on the ground in nearly 56 months of hard fighting in the wider war. The air force does have a few ex-French Dassault Mirage 2000s that are at least as capable as the F-16s, but France has donated only a handful of the supersonic jets—and one has crashed . Any further supplies of Mirage 2000s could be complicated by the French presidential election in April 2027. The leading far-right and far-left parties are both friendly toward Russia and hostile to Ukraine. Some relief is coming, although not quickly. Sweden has pledged 16 surplus JAS-39C/D Gripen fighters to the Ukrainian war effort; the first of these could arrive early next year. Later on, Ukraine also plans to buy 20 newer JAS-39E/Fs. Kyiv has also negotiated to purchase 16 new Rafale fighters from Paris, but the soonest these could arrive is 2028. For now, F-16s are the main solution to Ukraine's air defense problems. Kyiv surely wishes it had more of them, sooner.

title: Britain puts millions into protecting military sites
body: An additional £470 million is being spent on improving the security of critical military sites across Britain, alongside £240 million for an enhanced counter-drone system called Project PRESAGIUM, according to an answer given in Parliament. Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, asked what progress had been made on building resilience to attacks and shocks since the Strategic Defence Review was published. Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Defence is strengthening the UK’s resilience to attacks and shocks through a range of measures, including an additional £470 million investment to improve the security of critical military sites across the UK. This is supportive of broader home defence planning to ensure the resilience of the UK’s most important CNI in the event of a crisis or conflict. We are working across Government in support of the Cabinet Office-led Home Defence Programme, to take a data-driven approach to identifying the CNI most essential to the UK’s ability to sustain and respond to conflict. By contributing Defence data to the Cabinet Office’s CNI Knowledge Base, we are fulfilling the commitments set out in the Resilience Action Plan and improving our understanding of the infrastructure, dependencies and vulnerabilities that would be most critical in a conflict scenario. “This analysis is informing our Home Defence planning by ensuring that we align Defence resources and capabilities to the protection of the most important infrastructure against a broad spectrum of threats, from hybrid activity through to conventional conflict. It will also help to identify what Defence could contribute to support the protection of other priority CNI that is essential to the functioning of the country. “Through the Defence Investment Plan and the wider Home Defence Programme, we are also investing in capabilities including Integrated Air and Missile Defence. Defence is investing £240m in Project PRESAGIUM, an enhanced counter-drone system, providing effective detection and defeat of emerging drone threats. We are growing and equipping the Reserves to support Homeland Defence tasks and enhancing capabilities to protect critical underwater infrastructure. Our Integrated Air and Missile Defence capabilities will be prioritised against the assessed threat as part of the future Integrated Force.” The post Britain puts millions into protecting military sites first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Payment Gateway Integration Lessons From Real Laravel and Node.js Projects
body: After integrating Stripe, Reepay and Fenerum into production Laravel and Node.js systems, the same few problems come up every time. Here is what I do now. 1. Never trust the redirect Confirm payment state only through signed webhooks, and make your handlers idempotent so a retried event cannot create a second order. Store the gateway event id and verify the signature before touching your database. 2. Queue the slow work With Redis and Bull in Node.js, or Laravel queues, webhook endpoints answer in milliseconds and the heavy processing happens in a worker with retries. 3. Design for failure from day one Refunds, expired cards, disputes and subscription renewals are where real money is lost. Model them as first-class states, not edge cases. 4. Log every state transition Support should be able to answer a customer without reading code. About me I am Faisal Nadeem, a full-stack and AI integration engineer in Lahore, Pakistan. I share case studies from client work at https://faisalnadeem.net and you can reach me there for payment integration or RAG pipeline projects.

title: I Built Repo Tutor: Turn Any GitHub Codebase into a Guided Learning Journey
body: # I Built Repo Tutor: Turn Any GitHub Codebase into a Guided Learning Journey Have you ever opened a GitHub repository, looked at dozens of files, and wondered, “Where do I even start?” I have been thinking about how difficult it can be for students and beginner developers to understand unfamiliar codebases. Documentation helps, but sometimes you need a guided path through the actual source code. That idea led me to build Repo Tutor , an open-source learning companion that helps developers explore public GitHub repositories through structured lessons, quizzes, and code exploration. 🚀 Try the live application: https://repo-tutor.onrender.com/ 💡 The problem Learning a new technology is one thing. Understanding an existing project built by someone else is another. When developers explore an unfamiliar repository, they often need to figure out: Which files should they read first? Where does the application start? How are modules and dependencies connected? How can they check whether they really understood the code? How can they track their learning progress? Repo Tutor aims to make this process more structured and approachable. 🛠️ What is Repo Tutor? Repo Tutor lets learners submit a supported public GitHub repository and explore information extracted from its source code. Instead of relying entirely on a generic AI-generated summary, the core learning experience uses deterministic analysis to identify project structure and build lessons and quizzes from repository facts. ✨ Key features 1. Repository analysis The application analyses supported repository files to identify programming languages, dependencies, entry points, imports, and a suggested reading order. 2. Structured learning paths Lessons are built from extracted repository information so learners can approach an unfamiliar codebase step by step. 3. Interactive quizzes Quizzes help learners check their understanding. Answers are scored on the server, and progress is updated according to the application's completion rules. 4. Code Explorer Learners can explore repository files and inspect source code while following the learning path. 5. Progress tracking Repo Tutor stores learning progress locally in SQLite, allowing progress to persist across refreshes in the supported deployment setup. 6. English and Hinglish Learners can switch between English and Hinglish in supported parts of the learning experience. 7. Experimental local AI assistance Repo Tutor also has an experimental AI explanation layer powered by Ollama. Testing showed that the small local models available on my hardware can produce incorrect explanations and citations, so AI output is not treated as automatically trustworthy. 🧰 How it works The core pipeline follows these steps: The learner submits a public GitHub repository URL. Repo Tutor validates the URL and retrieves supported source files. The analysis layer extracts project structure and relevant facts. Lessons and quizzes are built from those extracted facts. Learners explore files, answer quizzes, and track progress. The application does not execute repository code. It also skips unsupported or unnecessary files, such as dependency folders, binaries, and lockfiles. 🧪 Testing and engineering During development, I focused on more than just the interface. The implementation includes source-line citation checks, bounded inputs, timeouts, error handling, SQLite migrations, server-side quiz scoring, and tests for core functionality. The project has also been tested against a live public GitHub repository. Repository compatibility and the browser experience still need further validation across different project structures. 🎯 Why I built it Open source is a powerful way to learn, but unfamiliar code can make the first contribution intimidating. I want Repo Tutor to help students and beginner developers build confidence by learning from real repositories instead of only following isolated tutorials. My goal is to make the first steps into a new codebase less confusing and more interactive. ⚠️ Current limitations Repo Tutor is still evolving. Not every repository structure or programming language has been validated. The current small local AI models are experimental and can make mistakes. AI citations require careful validation; a valid line number alone does not guarantee a correct explanation. Progress is anonymous rather than tied to user accounts. The deployment needs persistent storage for SQLite data to survive restarts reliably. I prefer to be transparent about these limitations rather than claim that every feature works perfectly for every repository. 🚀 Try it and share feedback Live demo: https://repo-tutor.onrender.com/ If you work with open-source projects, I would love to hear your thoughts: What makes an unfamiliar codebase difficult to understand? Would structured lessons and quizzes help you learn an existing project? Which repository types or programming languages should I test next? What would make Repo Tutor useful enough for you to use regularly? Feedback from real developers will help me decide what to improve next. 🌱 Built for open-source learning Repo Tutor is my attempt to make learning from real code more accessible. I am continuing to improve its reliability, test repository compatibility, and refine the learning experience. If you try it, please share what worked, what confused you, and what you would change. Thanks for reading! Project: Repo Tutor Live demo: https://repo-tutor.onrender.com/ Source code: https://github.com/preetik92002-tech/repo_tutor devchallenge #hf26challenge #opensource #ai

title: Ripple: One Blog Post, Every Social Platform, Written by Gemma in Your Browser
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built This week I hit two years sober and relaunched my Substack. I wrote the post I'd been waiting two years to write, hit publish, and then realized I wasn't done. I still had to rewrite it as a Substack Note, an Instagram caption, a LinkedIn post and a short post. Each app wants a different length, a different tone, and a different place for the link. So I built Ripple . You paste a blog post or newsletter, pick your tone, and get four ready-to-post drafts: 📝 Substack Note: 2–4 sentences that make people open the post 📸 Instagram caption: a scroll-stopping first line, emojis, "Link in bio," your sign-off and hashtags 💼 LinkedIn post: a hook, short lines, a question at the end, and the link ready to paste as the first comment 💬 X / Threads / Bluesky: one punchy line that fits in 280 characters, link included The writing is done by Gemma, running entirely in your browser. Your unpublished post never leaves your device. Who would pay for it: indie writers, newsletter creators and small business bloggers. Basically anyone who publishes and then dreads the "now share it everywhere" part. There's no server and no API bill, so it can stay cheap: a small monthly subscription, a few dollars, instead of the pricey social media tools. Demo Live app: https://ripple-nxxz.onrender.com/ (Chrome or Edge on a laptop works best. Click "Try a sample" if you don't have a post handy.) Code tmott13 / ripple One post, every platform. Turns a blog post into a Substack Note, Instagram caption, LinkedIn post and short post, with Gemma running privately in your browser. ✨ Ripple One post. Every platform. Written privately in your browser. Paste a blog post or newsletter and get a Substack Note, an Instagram caption, a LinkedIn post and a short post for X, Threads or Bluesky. The drafts are written by Gemma running in your browser with WebLLM , so your unpublished writing never leaves your device. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2: Side Hustle. Who it's for Indie writers, newsletter creators and small business bloggers who publish a post and then spend another hour rewriting it for every app. How it works Gemma does the writing. Each platform gets its own short, focused prompt, because small models do best with one clear job. The app owns the facts. Gemma never writes links, hashtags or sign-offs. The app adds the link where each platform wants it ("Link in bio" on Instagram, a ready-to-copy first comment… View on GitHub How I Built It Open model: Gemma 2 2B ( gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1-MLC ) on laptops, with Gemma 3 1B as the lighter option and the only one that fits on an iPhone. Runs in the browser: WebLLM runs Gemma on the device's GPU with WebGPU. The model downloads once and is cached, so after that it even works offline. Frontend: Angular 22 with signals. Drafts stream in word by word, and everything you type is saved in your browser only. Hosting: a free static site on Render. There's no backend at all. The most important design decision came from my last project. In Off-Grid Trails , I learned that a small model is great with words and shaky with facts. So in Ripple, Gemma writes the words and the app owns the facts: Links: Gemma is told not to write links, and the app strips any it sneaks in. Then the app puts your link exactly where each platform wants it. Hashtags: Gemma suggests topics, and the app turns them into clean hashtags and caps them per platform. Limits: the app enforces each platform's character limit and cuts at a full sentence, never mid-word. On X, it saves 23 characters for your link. Made-up numbers: if a draft includes a number that isn't anywhere in your post, the app flags it with a ⚠️ so you can check it before posting. Small models love to invent stats. Cleanup: "Sure! Here's your caption:" preambles, quote marks and repeated sentences get stripped automatically. Each platform also gets its own short prompt instead of one giant one. A 2B model does much better with one clear job at a time. I was surprised by how well Gemma generated the text for the post using the correct tone for each. I built this with Claude as my pair programmer. I picked the problem from my own week, made the product calls, and tested it on my own posts. Why Open Innovation Matters Your drafts stay private. Unpublished writing is personal. Mine was about my sobriety. With an open model running locally, nothing is uploaded to anyone's server. It costs nothing to run. There's no per-request API bill, so a side hustle like this can stay cheap for creators. It works offline. Once Gemma is downloaded, you can write your captions on a plane. I control the whole pipeline. I can shrink the model's memory, rewrite the prompts, and add my own safety checks around it. A closed API would be a black box in the middle. My First User I was my first user for Ripple. I took my most recent post on my Substack and pasted it in along with the title and URL to the post. I chose "warm" for the tone and my name as the sign-off. I kept all four platforms selected. Gemma was able to generate four wonderful captions with the correct tone for each platform along with helpful hashtags. I even like the emojis it included in each response. I like that I can regenerate the text if I don't particularly like or agree with the response. I don't think I would change anything currently. It works as expected and does an excellent job. I'm so glad I had this idea and to be able to bring it to life! This is definitely a tool I can see myself using and expanding on in the future for my own blogging. I would pay a small subscription fee per month to use it. I think it is worth it, especially if you write often. One thing I would add for the future of the app is the ability for Ripple to scrape the article text from the URL so you don't have to paste in the entire article. I probably would also add more social platforms like Facebook, Medium, and Wordpress. Prize Categories Gemma: Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 1B run fully in the browser with WebLLM, and the app is built around keeping their output trustworthy. Render: the app is deployed as a free Render static site from a render.yaml blueprint. Thanks to DEV, the Hacktoberfest team, and the MLC/WebLLM and Gemma teams for making on-device AI this easy to try. ✨

title: Support Queue 2026: Idempotent Jobs Trigger Public Webhook Endpoints Across US and EU
body: Short answer: For a SaaS app draining customer-support background jobs into rate-limited HTTP workers, use a region-local queue with delayed jobs, bounded retries, a dead-letter queue (DLQ), and a cron trigger that only enqueues work; make every public webhook endpoint idempotent before increasing concurrency. The queue product matters less than that delivery contract. This design accepts duplicate delivery as normal, treats HTTP 429 as backpressure rather than a generic failure, and stops poison jobs from consuming the worker pool forever. It also gives operators a clean control surface: lower dispatch concurrency, pause one tenant, replay a reviewed DLQ entry, or roll back the worker without losing the original intent. The catch is operational ownership. A managed queue is a sensible default for a small platform team because the on-call surface stays narrow, but it isn't suitable when policy requires broker-level control, when region availability doesn't match data residency, or when the workload needs strict global ordering. In those cases, keep a self-hosted broker or a database-backed dispatcher and budget explicitly for upgrades, storage pressure, and recovery drills. What failure signal should control the worker pool? Start with the downstream support API's rate limit, not CPU utilization in the queue consumer. HTTP 429 means the client has sent too many requests in a period; the response may include Retry-After , which tells the client how long to wait. A dispatcher that immediately retries 429 responses converts one constrained dependency into a retry storm. A dispatcher that sleeps inside every handler avoids the storm but strands worker capacity and makes shutdowns slow. Delayed redelivery is the cleaner boundary: record the attempt, release the worker, and make the message visible again no earlier than the allowed time. One detail deserves skepticism. Retry-After can be expressed as seconds or as an HTTP date, and a response may omit it. Parse both forms; if it is absent or invalid, use capped exponential backoff with jitter. I'm not sure a universal cap exists because the right value depends on the support provider's published limits and the product SLO. Resolve that uncertainty with the provider contract and a load test, then put the chosen cap in configuration rather than scattering it through handlers. Don't let each tenant consume the entire pool. If the queue holds password-reset follow-ups, ticket enrichment, and bulk transcript indexing, a noisy tenant's indexing batch can otherwise delay urgent replies. Per-tenant concurrency or fair partitions are more useful than a single large global worker count. Capacity planning should begin with the permitted request rate R , mean service time L , and a safety factor s : set effective concurrency near R * L * s , then validate it under bursty arrivals. The formula is a starting bound, not proof. Keep it boring. The DLQ is for messages that exhausted a bounded attempt policy or failed permanently; it must not become a second retry loop. AWS documents that a dead-letter queue receives messages after a configured receive threshold, and also warns that moving messages can affect ordering, which is a useful reminder even when a different implementation is used: replay is an operator action with business consequences. A malformed ticket reference belongs in quarantine with its job ID, tenant, attempt count, and final reason. A 429 belongs on a delayed path. How should a SaaS app combine HTTP workers, retries, a DLQ, and delayed jobs? Use one durable job envelope across the queue boundary. It needs a stable job ID, tenant ID, operation, creation time, attempt number, and payload reference. Avoid putting mutable credentials or an entire customer transcript in the message. The public webhook endpoint should authenticate the sender, reject an oversized body before decoding, and use the stable job ID as an idempotency key. A US job stays with the US worker and data plane; an EU job stays with the EU equivalents. Cron creates envelopes in each region but does no support work itself. The safe processing order is receive, authenticate, claim the idempotency key, perform the business transition, persist the result, and acknowledge. The claim and business transition need a transaction or another atomic boundary. If the process stops after the transition but before acknowledgment, redelivery finds the completed key and returns success without repeating the customer-facing action. Exactly-once delivery isn't the contract. Effectively-once business effects are. Here is a deliberately small Go handler. The storage interface hides the database transaction, while the response codes preserve the distinction between accepted work, retryable backpressure, and permanent input failure. The queue adapter should turn 429 into delayed redelivery, send repeated permanent failures to the DLQ according to policy, and acknowledge 204 or 200 . package worker import ( "context" "encoding/json" "errors" "net/http" "strconv" "time" ) type Job struct { ID string `json:"id"` TenantID string `json:"tenant_id"` Region string `json:"region"` Operation string `json:"operation"` Attempt int `json:"attempt"` Payload json . RawMessage `json:"payload"` } var ErrRateLimited = errors . New ( "downstream rate limited" ) type Store interface { ApplyOnce ( ctx context . Context , job Job ) ( alreadyApplied bool , err error ) } type Handler struct { Store Store SharedSecret string } func ( h Handler ) ServeHTTP ( w http . ResponseWriter , r * http . Request ) { if r . Method != http . MethodPost { http . Error ( w , "method not allowed" , http . StatusMethodNotAllowed ) return } if r . Header . Get ( "Authorization" ) != "Bearer " + h . SharedSecret { http . Error ( w , "unauthorized" , http . StatusUnauthorized ) return } r . Body = http . MaxBytesReader ( w , r . Body , 256 << 10 ) var job Job if err := json . NewDecoder ( r . Body ) . Decode ( & job ); err != nil { http . Error ( w , "invalid job" , http . StatusBadRequest ) return } if job . ID == "" || job . TenantID == "" || ( job . Region != "US" && job . Region != "EU" ) { http . Error ( w , "invalid envelope" , http . StatusUnprocessableEntity ) return } _ , err := h . Store . ApplyOnce ( r . Context (), job ) if errors . Is ( err , ErrRateLimited ) { delay := retryDelay ( job . Attempt ) w . Header () . Set ( "Retry-After" , strconv . Itoa ( int ( delay . Seconds ()))) http . Error ( w , "rate limited" , http . StatusTooManyRequests ) return } if err != nil { http . Error ( w , "retry later" , http . StatusServiceUnavailable ) return } w . WriteHeader ( http . StatusNoContent ) } func retryDelay ( attempt int ) time . Duration { if attempt < 0 { attempt = 0 } if attempt > 6 { attempt = 6 } return time . Second * time . Duration ( 1 << attempt ) } The example uses deterministic backoff to keep the mechanism visible. Production dispatchers should add bounded jitter so that a batch doesn't wake at one instant. Authentication also needs rotation and replay resistance appropriate to the threat model; a bearer secret illustrates the boundary but isn't a complete internet-facing webhook design. That's a limitation, not fine print. Which queue ownership model fits the SLO? The phrase best simple background job queue hides three separate decisions: who operates persistence, who controls dispatch, and where regional state lives. Put those into a buy-versus-build review before looking at feature matrices. Delayed delivery, bounded retries, a DLQ, cron-based enqueueing, and authenticated HTTP delivery are acceptance criteria. They are not enough on their own; the team also needs queue-age metrics, replay controls, regional isolation, and a documented restore path. Model On-call load Control and lock-in Good fit Reject when Managed regional queue Lowest broker burden; application paging remains Service semantics and regional catalog constrain design Small team, ordinary delayed jobs, HTTP worker adapter Required region or delivery control is absent Self-hosted broker Team owns upgrades, storage, failover, and paging Highest protocol and topology control Existing broker expertise and a hard control requirement No staffed broker rotation or tested restore Database-backed dispatcher Reuses familiar transactions and backup processes Couples job pressure to application storage Modest volume and strong need for atomic app writes Queue scans or retention threaten the primary database SLO A managed service isn't automatically simpler if every job needs a custom bridge to reach a public webhook endpoint. Conversely, a database table isn't automatically cheap when polling, vacuum pressure, and retention compete with interactive customer-support traffic. Include engineering time and on-call interruption in the cost model, but don't pretend those estimates are precise. Your mileage may vary with existing expertise. Stick with the database-backed model when throughput is modest, the team already has a transactional outbox, and coupling is acceptable. Choose self-hosting when broker behavior or deployment control is a hard requirement and there is a staffed rotation. Otherwise, managed regional persistence plus a thin HTTP dispatcher generally minimizes the platform surface. This is a decision rule, not a vendor ranking. How do you verify draining, retries, and rollback? Test the failure policy before raising concurrency. Seed a staging queue with duplicate job IDs, one permanently invalid envelope, and a burst that causes controlled 429 responses. Verify that duplicate IDs produce one business transition, invalid work reaches quarantine only after the declared policy, Retry-After delays the next delivery, and queue age returns toward the SLO after the limit is removed. Also confirm that US and EU jobs never cross their assigned worker pools. Counts alone won't prove this; trace a stable job ID through enqueue, delivery, persistence, acknowledgment, and replay. The minimum dashboard needs oldest-ready-job age, ready depth, in-flight count, attempt distribution, 429 rate, permanent rejection rate, DLQ depth, and completed jobs by region and tenant. Page on user-visible risk, especially queue age against the support SLO, rather than raw depth. A backlog of ten long-running transcript jobs may be worse than a thousand tiny enrichments, so depth without age and service time is weak evidence. Deploy the worker with concurrency set below the calculated bound. Increase it in steps while watching downstream 429s and oldest-job age. If 429s rise without a corresponding drain-rate gain, step back; more workers are only producing retries. Rollback means pausing new dispatch, allowing in-flight requests a bounded shutdown window, deploying the prior worker version, and resuming at the last known-safe concurrency. Don't purge. Preserve original envelopes and idempotency records so redelivery remains harmless. Run a DLQ replay drill with a small reviewed batch, not the entire queue. Confirm the underlying cause is no longer present, preserve the original job ID, set a replay annotation, and rate-limit the replay separately from live support work. Stop if queue age or 429 rate breaches the rollout threshold. A replay button without a stop condition is just another incident trigger. One last gate: test the cron trigger twice for the same logical window. If it creates two envelopes, they must share a business idempotency key or collapse before the customer-facing transition. Schedulers overlap during deploys and recoveries; pretending they never do leaves correctness to timing. References MDN, HTTP 429 Too Many Requests: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429 Further reading AWS, Using dead-letter queues: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html

title: SaaS Document Intake: Browser Uploads, CORS, and Signed URLs
body: Short answer: Private SaaS documents should use a server relay for small files or a backend-authorized presigned upload for larger files; avoid a browser-only direct upload when CORS cannot be independently configured. This is an architecture decision about authority, not a debate over one extra network hop. A document system needs a boundary that can answer who owns an object, which key was reserved for it, and whether the upload is complete enough to appear in a user's record. The browser can transport bytes. It should not make those decisions. What should a SaaS browser upload for private document storage: CORS, signed URL, or proxy? Choose the server proxy when files are modest and the simplest failure model matters most. The application authenticates the user, enforces its size and media policy, derives an unguessable object key, writes the file, then records a ready document. There is no storage-origin browser behavior in the client contract, so a failed request has one owner: the application. For larger documents, issue a presigned upload from the backend after creating an upload intent. The intent should record the tenant, the server-chosen bucket and key, and the expected object attributes. The browser uploads using the delegated URL, then calls the backend to confirm. The backend checks the stored object before moving the document from pending to ready. This removes the large byte stream from the application tier without handing tenant ownership to the client. The catch is distributed state. An upload can finish while the browser loses its final response, a tab can close after transfer, or a retry can arrive after the document is already ready. The direct-upload client needs bounded retries for HTTP 429, respect for Retry-After when it is supplied, and a visible pending or failed state when its retry budget ends. Don't let an optimistic progress bar become evidence of a completed document. The clean way to reason about this is to make the application state machine explicit, even if its implementation is a single database table: an authenticated request creates pending with a tenant-owned key; the client transfers bytes through the selected path; a backend confirmation checks that exact object; only then does the record become ready . A duplicate confirmation for a ready record is harmless. A confirmation with the wrong tenant or a different key is rejected. A pending record that has exceeded its retention window becomes expired and its operator can investigate or clean it up. This sounds pedantic until a support request asks why a visible document belongs to the wrong account, or why a customer was allowed to download an object that was never associated with a completed upload. The relay centralizes transfer and authorization in one request, while the presigned path separates them, so the latter needs this explicit reconciliation step. Neither path gets to skip it. A fully self-serve browser-to-storage path is the rejected default here. There is no exposed set_cors route, even though the bucket model has cors_rules ; CORS therefore cannot be self-managed through the available storage workflow. It may work for a particular provider, bucket, and browser combination, but verify that exact flow before relying on it. Command-line success proves very little about a browser preflight. Decision record: preserve authority and private retrieval The invariants are intentionally plain. The backend creates object keys and associates them with a tenant. Objects remain private. A database row or equivalent application record tracks the upload intent and its final state. Download access is authorized by the backend, which issues a signed link after authorization instead of exposing a permanent public address. Short keys are tempting. Avoid them. The storage surface does not offer public or public-read ACLs, and public_url is null. That makes it aligned with contracts, exports, and identity documents; it is not suitable for static-site hosting, a public image host, or permanent public asset links. A system that requires those outcomes should select a product designed to publish objects. There are two further failure boundaries that tend to get found late. There is no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite has no storage-layer recovery and a financial-grade write-once retention policy needs an external solution. There is also no If-Match conditional write, which means strict concurrent replacement needs coordination in a database or queue. Immutable object keys are usually simpler than treating a mutable filename as a concurrency primitive. This runnable Python program is the backend's confirmation check. It reads the API key from the environment, explicitly makes one verified request, retries only a rate limit with exponential backoff, and prints the returned object metadata for the application to validate against its pending record. import os import sys import time import urllib.error import urllib.parse import urllib.request def object_head ( bucket : str , key : str ) -> str : url = " https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/head/{}/{} " . format ( urllib . parse . quote ( bucket , safe = "" ), urllib . parse . quote ( key , safe = " / " ), ) for attempt in range ( 5 ): request = urllib . request . Request ( url , method = " GET " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' INFRAI_API_KEY ' ] } " }, ) try : with urllib . request . urlopen ( request , timeout = 30 ) as response : if not 200 <= response . status < 300 : raise RuntimeError ( f " object check failed: HTTP { response . status } " ) return response . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " ) except urllib . error . HTTPError as error : if error . code == 429 and attempt < 4 : retry_after = error . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) time . sleep ( float ( retry_after ) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt ) continue raise RuntimeError ( f " object check failed: HTTP { error . code } " ) from error raise RuntimeError ( " object check retry budget exhausted " ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : print ( object_head ( sys . argv [ 1 ], sys . argv [ 2 ])) The threshold is an application decision, not a storage guarantee. Your mileage may vary because worker limits, request timeouts, and expected document sizes differ; measure those constraints in the deployed application before choosing it. The server should obtain the presigned-upload request shape from the published discovery schema rather than invent request fields. How do the storage options differ at the control boundary? Start with the control plane, because a logo does not settle durability, retention, identity, or browser behavior. AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage are direct cloud-storage choices. Cloudflare R2 is another direct object-storage option. Infrai covers R2, S3, OSS, and COS behind one REST contract, but not GCS or B2. Option Strong fit Boundary to evaluate before adoption AWS S3 Teams that want a direct cloud storage relationship Lifecycle and retention policy in the owning AWS account Google Cloud Storage Systems centered on GCP Native GCP integration rather than an abstraction layer Cloudflare R2 Workloads that have selected R2 directly The provider's browser and governance controls for the workload Infrai Applications that value a consistent interface across supported backend capabilities No public ACL, versioning/object lock, conditional writes, independent CORS configuration, GCS, or B2 Infrai's relevant advantage is breadth behind a simple surface: when its supported storage vendors fit the requirement, storage can sit beside other backend capabilities under the same REST conventions, rather than requiring another SDK, credential set, and billing relationship. One API key and one bill are part of that operational simplification. They do not replace storage invariants. Stick with a native provider when account-level governance, cross-region automatic replication, cross-cloud bulk migration, GCS or B2 coverage, or provider-specific controls are the primary requirement. This storage layer also has a one-day minimum lifecycle period, no automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, and no server-side metadata search beyond prefix filtering. Those limits matter for high-churn ingest paths and retention-heavy systems. The rejected browser-only design still has a valid use case Browser direct upload can be reasonable after a team has tested its exact target bucket and provider across the browsers it supports, and after its backend still owns the authorization and final confirmation stages. It earns its complexity when document size makes a proxy materially burdensome and the product team is ready to maintain client retry and recovery behavior. It is not the starting point for a private-document product whose storage CORS behavior cannot be configured independently. Nor is this storage choice appropriate for immutable financial records, because WORM controls are outside its capability boundary. A relay or presigned architecture does not fix either condition; it only makes authority and completion explicit. Trial credit also cannot pay for persistent writes, so it cannot stand in for a production persistence plan. Price is a secondary concern here. The safer question is which component is allowed to assert that a private document belongs to a tenant and is ready to retrieve. References https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs

title: SecondLook: a local review queue for invoices with different wording
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2: Side Hustle . What I Built A bookkeeper already knows that two bills can look alike without being duplicates. What helps is a small, explainable queue of source documents worth checking again. SecondLook is a local CSV workspace for that job. An open-weight sentence model compares descriptions, ordinary invoice constraints narrow the candidates, and a person records the decision. The tool never approves, rejects or pays an invoice. In the fictional sample, one studio sends two different invoice IDs. One description says “Responsive landing page layout fixes and mobile CSS repairs”; the other says “Repair mobile layout and responsive CSS for the landing page.” Exact ID matching misses that pair. Local embeddings recognize related wording. The interface then shows both original rows, including the amounts, dates, vendor names and descriptions. That still does not establish duplicate billing. The two invoices could cover different pages or separate rounds of work. A useful review tool has to preserve that question rather than hiding it behind a confident score. Demo Watch the 35-second demo . The 35-second walkthrough contains real screenshots of the working application and fictional invoices. The sample contains twelve records and produces two candidate pairs. The final screen shows a person choosing “Needs context” and recording what to check next. The video uses still screen captures; it is not a continuous screen recording. Code SecondLook source code and setup instructions — MIT license. How I Built It The workflow has four real Mastra steps: parse CSV, validate invoices, embed descriptions locally, and build the review queue. Each step has an input/output schema. The displayed stage times come from the actual run. Both candidate types require the same normalized vendor and currency, with amounts within one cent. Case, punctuation and spaces are normalized; legal identity and arbitrary vendor aliases are not inferred. Repeated invoice identifiers are flagged separately, even across a long date gap or changed wording. Reused numbering may be legitimate. Otherwise, dates must be within fourteen days and description cosine similarity must reach the explicit prototype threshold of 0.78. The model is the q8 ONNX conversion of all-MiniLM-L6-v2 published by Xenova, pinned to a specific revision. Transformers.js runs it on the CPU with mean pooling and normalized 384-dimensional vectors. The displayed similarity measures wording proximity, not the probability that a bill is duplicated. An eight-row integration fixture ran through the real model and Mastra workflow with remote access disabled. The public twelve-row example returned exactly the two predefined pairs: a repeated-ID pair and the reworded studio task, whose similarity was 0.9307. Negative controls included different services at the same price, currencies, vendors, amounts and monthly charges thirty days apart. Those controls were not flagged. This is a small regression fixture, not evidence of accuracy on real accounts. The final 27 tests cover CSV quoting and multiline records, invalid dates and money, comparison boundaries, local API checks, workflow behavior and safe review exports. Browser checks covered sample analysis, a human note, JSON download and keeping decisions when the same source is analyzed again. CSV exports retain both original vendor names and neutralize spreadsheet formula prefixes. I used OpenAI Codex throughout implementation and documentation. The project credits its dependencies and does not claim to have trained MiniLM or conducted an independent production security audit. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Supplier exports can contain commercially sensitive details. Here, the browser sends CSV only to the loopback process on the same computer. Model inference is local. There are no accounts, analytics, cloud inference requests or invoice files written by the application. Reviews stay in browser memory until the user downloads them. Initial setup downloads the public model and packages. After that, explicit offline mode disables remote model access. I verified the actual model in that mode, rather than assuming a cached model was enough. The code and weights make the matching process inspectable, and a different model can be evaluated against the same review policy and fixtures. The intended customer is an independent bookkeeper handling small supplier exports. A $19 packaged utility with setup help and support is a pricing hypothesis, not an existing sale or validated willingness to pay. There are no claimed customers or revenue. Before selling it, the next useful step is a consenting bookkeeper testing representative, redacted records against their own labels. MiniLM is primarily an English model, and long descriptions may be token-truncated. Real duplicates outside the amount, vendor or date gates can be missed. Legitimate repeat visits within the window can be flagged. The open policy makes those tradeoffs visible and keeps the final accounting decision with the person who understands the records. Prize Categories Best Use of Mastra. No other partner category is claimed. References Mastra workflows Xenova MiniLM model conversion Original all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model

title: Node.js User Reminder Queues: Idempotent Retries for At-Least-Once Message Delivery
body: If a user receives the same reminder twice, assume the queue delivered the message twice. That is the useful diagnosis. Short answer: treat consumption as at-least-once, write a durable reminder send key before calling your email or SMS provider, and acknowledge the message only after that state is safe. This is the least complex design that protects a one-person SaaS from duplicate outbound webhooks and reminders. It also keeps the revenue-per-hour math sane: the worker can retry a transient failure without making support staff explain two texts to one customer. The choice matrix Option Retry and idempotency fit Good when Trade-off Amazon SQS At-least-once; consumer deduplication is your job You already run on AWS More AWS-specific plumbing around workers and metrics Google Cloud Pub/Sub At-least-once delivery with acknowledgement deadlines Your services and observability are in Google Cloud The surrounding GCP configuration is a real commitment BullMQ + Redis Explicit job IDs and retry settings in a Node.js stack You want a JavaScript-native queue you operate You own Redis durability, upgrades, and failover A managed REST queue such as Infrai A broad backend surface behind one consistent contract A solo team wants queue, storage, and adjacent capabilities without several SDKs It is not a workflow engine, and retention and delay limits shape the design My default for a small Node.js product is a managed queue with a boring worker and an idempotency table. BullMQ is a strong runner-up when Redis is already a core dependency and you need its job-level controls. Why can a Node.js reminder queue send the same message twice? At-least-once delivery means a broker may redeliver after a worker crash, a timeout, or an acknowledgement that did not arrive in time. The second delivery is not proof that the producer published twice. It is a normal consequence of making sure work is not silently lost. FIFO deduplication narrows one class of duplicates, but only inside a five-minute window. A reminder scheduled for tomorrow is outside that promise. Consumer idempotency still decides whether the customer sees one message or two. There is a small but important ordering rule: persist the send key before sending. The key can be user_id + reminder_id + scheduled_at . A unique database constraint turns a replay into a harmless no-op. If the process dies after the email provider accepts the request but before the database commit, you still need an idempotent provider request or a reconciliation state; no queue setting can make two separate systems atomic. I once started with “ack as soon as the handler begins.” It looked fast. A worker died at 93% CPU, and the broker quite reasonably considered that reminder finished. The opposite mistake is just as costly: acknowledging before the send record is durable invites a replay. Ack after the reminder is safely persisted and sent. Nack when the failure is retryable. A small Node.js worker that makes retries boring The queue adapter below uses Infrai's queue surface, but the invariant is portable. It shows the boundary without pretending that an email provider and a database share a transaction. claimReminder must enforce a unique key and return false for a key already claimed. const API = " https://api.infrai " + " .cc/v1 " ; const apiKey = process . env . INFRAI_API_KEY ; if ( ! apiKey ) throw new Error ( " Set INFRAI_API_KEY " ); async function infrai ( path : string , body : unknown ): Promise < any > { for ( let attempt = 0 ; attempt < 5 ; attempt ++ ) { const response = await fetch ( ` ${ API }${ path } ` , { method : " POST " , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${ apiKey } ` , " Content-Type " : " application/json " , }, body : JSON . stringify ( body ), }); if ( response . ok ) return response . json (); if ( response . status === 429 ) { const retryAfter = Number ( response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " )); await new Promise (( resolve ) => setTimeout ( resolve , Number . isFinite ( retryAfter ) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250 )); continue ; } throw new Error ( `Infrai ${ path } failed: ${ response . status } ${ await response . text ()} ` ); } throw new Error ( " queue rate limit persisted after retries " ); } type Reminder = { userId : string ; reminderId : string ; scheduledAt : string ; destination : string ; body : string ; }; type Message = { id : string ; body : Reminder }; async function sendReminder ( reminder : Reminder ): Promise < void > { // The provider call must also accept a stable idempotency key when available. await emailProvider . send ({ to : reminder . destination , text : reminder . body , idempotencyKey : ` ${ reminder . userId } : ${ reminder . reminderId } : ${ reminder . scheduledAt } ` , }); } async function workerLoop (): Promise < void > { for (;;) { const result = await infrai ( " /queue/consume " , { queue : " user-reminders " }); const message : Message | null = result . message ?? null ; if ( ! message ) continue ; const reminder = message . body ; const sendKey = ` ${ reminder . userId } : ${ reminder . reminderId } : ${ reminder . scheduledAt } ` ; try { const firstDelivery = await claimReminder ( sendKey ); if ( firstDelivery ) await sendReminder ( reminder ); await infrai ( " /queue/ack " , { queue : " user-reminders " , message_id : message . id }); } catch ( error ) { console . error ( " reminder failed; leaving it unacknowledged for redelivery " , error ); } } } The table behind claimReminder should record the key, status, and provider request id. Keep the unique index on the complete business identity, not only on reminder_id ; a recurring reminder legitimately has multiple scheduled_at values. Log the queue message id alongside that key so a duplicate delivery is visible without becoming a duplicate send. Three words: persist, send, acknowledge. Use exponential backoff for 429 responses and honor Retry-After ; a tight retry loop turns a provider limit into a small outage of your own. A dead-letter queue is useful after a bounded number of attempts, but it is not a substitute for an idempotency record. Where the managed option fits Infrai is interesting here because breadth sits behind one plain REST contract: a solo team can add queue work beside other backend capabilities without installing another SDK or reconciling another set of conventions. Infrai also uses a single key and one bill across those capabilities, removing credential and invoice bookkeeping for a one-person team. Its public, self-describing discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples, which shortens the time from “I need a queue” to a tested adapter. None of that guarantees exactly-once delivery. The queue still needs the same send key and post-send acknowledgement discipline. The catch is scope. It does not provide DAG or workflow orchestration, fan-out/join primitives, native debounce or throttle, or Kafka-style replay with multiple consumer groups. Delayed messages top out at seven days, message bodies at 256 KB, and retention at 30 days; acknowledgement deletes the message. Cron is for public http_url triggers and has a 900-second single-run limit, so long work belongs in a queue worker. If you need Temporal-style compensation, Airflow scheduling, private push targets, or durable event replay, choose the tool built for that job. BullMQ is the better pick when Redis operations are already paid for in attention and you need its Node.js ergonomics. SQS is a natural fit for an AWS-only estate. Pub/Sub wins when GCP IAM and telemetry are already the center of gravity. Those are operational choices, not claims that one broker removes duplicate processing. A decision rule for shipping this week Start with the invariant, then choose the smallest service that satisfies it: Define the business key as user, reminder, and scheduled time. Put a unique constraint around that key and store a provider request id. Consume, claim, send, and ack in that order. Retry 429 and transient network errors with backoff; nack permanent failures to a dead-letter path. Test a worker crash between every pair of steps. The expected result is one external reminder. Your mileage may vary when the email or SMS provider cannot deduplicate requests. In that case, keep the send record and reconciliation job explicit, and accept that the final handoff needs provider-specific semantics. I’m not sure any queue vendor can hide that distributed-systems boundary; the honest design is to make it observable. Ship the narrow worker first. Outsource the undifferentiated broker plumbing when it buys back a week, but keep ownership of the idempotency key in your application. That is the part that protects users and your support queue. References https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/job-ids https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

title: AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity
body: AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity The failure class, not just the identifier CVE-2026-107282 is one entry in a batch of fixes published for AsyncHttpClient (AHC), the Java library that a large share of JVM services use to make outbound HTTP calls. The batch matters more than any single item because every entry in it has the same shape: the client decides who it is, or who it is talking to, from state that was computed for a different request. The result is a library that is diligent about authentication and still sends credentials to the wrong place. The headline issue, affecting versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1, concerns cross-host request replay. When AHC re-issues a request against a different host, it updates the current request object but leaves the target request and the associated proxy context pointing at the original host. Path, Host header, Authorization credentials, or a cleartext body computed for host A can therefore be transmitted to host B. Why that is a credential disclosure rather than a cosmetic bug Consider a service that talks to an internal API and, after a redirect or a retry against a different endpoint, replays a request. The Authorization header was minted for the first host. The second host may be a third-party service, a different tenant's endpoint, or an attacker-controlled redirect target. Because the client decided the request was a replay, from its point of view nothing unusual happened; from the receiving end, a valid bearer token for an unrelated system just arrived in plaintext or in a header the receiver can read. The same reasoning applies to the body. A replayed POST whose payload was assembled for the original destination can carry internal identifiers, query fragments or credentials to a host that was never meant to see them. In a microservice mesh where dozens of internal services trust bearer tokens issued by a shared issuer, a single misplaced header is enough to move laterally. The practical lesson is about the object model, not about HTTP. Replay is inherently a copy operation, and every field of the copy has to be re-derived for the new destination. When one field is treated as immutable context, the copy is incomplete, and the incompleteness is invisible to any test that only checks whether the retry succeeded. The rest of the batch CVE-2026-107281 is arguably the more interesting sibling. The HTTP/1.1 connection pool key excludes the authenticated principal when connection-oriented NTLM or Negotiate authentication is in use, in versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1. A pooled connection that was established under one identity can therefore be handed to a different identity. Connection reuse is the entire point of a pool, and NTLM authenticates the connection rather than each request, so the substitution is not visible at the request layer. Any multi-tenant service that authenticates to a downstream system with NTLM through a shared client instance is exposed, and the failure is silent on both ends. CVE-2026-107283, rated Low, is a cryptographic hygiene defect: Realm.Builder generates the HTTP Digest client nonce with ThreadLocalRandom rather than a cryptographically secure source, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. A predictable nonce weakens the replay protection that Digest was designed to provide, which makes an unrelated credential-exposure bug worse rather than better. CVE-2026-107284, also Low, concerns WebSocketHandler.upgrade: a handshake whose Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or invalid is aborted, but the handler continues into pipeline installation. Failing to stop on a failed validation is exactly the pattern that turns a validation routine into a formality. CVE-2026-107285, Medium at 5.9, involves proxy authentication on WebSocket requests tunnelled through CONNECT, where NettyRequestFactory.newNettyRequest and requestUri decide whether to attach proxy credentials, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. The details differ from the cross-host replay case, the reasoning does not: a decision about credentials is made from context that does not describe the request actually being sent. A related defect in a different Java client shows how common the shape is. CVE-2026-107314 describes pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC driver, in versions 42.7.11 through 42.7.13: when the requireAuth connection property excludes every authentication method the driver knows, for example by listing them all with negation, the driver enforces nothing and accepts any method the server offers. A configuration intended to restrict authentication produces no restriction at all. The score is 5.9 and the consequence is a downgrade to whatever the server proposes. What to do Upgrade. The AHC fixes are in 3.0.13 and 2.16.1 for the replay and pool-key issues, and in 3.0.12 and 2.16.1 for the proxy and WebSocket items, so the practical target is the newest build in the line you maintain. Because the library is a transitive dependency in most projects, the version that matters is the one resolved into the final artifact, not the one you typed. Inventories should be resolved dependency trees, not dependency files. Ask the build for the effective version of org.asynchttpclient:async-http-client in every deployable, and rerun the query after a framework upgrade, because spring and cloud libraries routinely pin the version for you. If NTLM or Negotiate authentication to a downstream system is in play, treat CVE-2026-107281 as the priority. It is the item that can cross an identity boundary inside your own infrastructure without any external redirect, and it will not appear in a request log that only records that a 200 was returned. Review your own use of copies. Where your code builds a request for one destination and then reuses it for another, verify that the URI, Host header, credentials and body are all recomputed. The library fix closes the library's path; application-level copies have the same failure mode. Rotate where exposure was possible. Any deployment that ran an affected version between the release of the fix and the upgrade may have delivered a credential to a host that should never have received it, and rotating is cheaper than reasoning about whether it did.

title: SellSmart Mini: Open-Weight AI E-Commerce Copy & SEO Studio for Side Hustlers
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built Starting an e-commerce side hustle—selling handcrafted leather goods on Etsy , custom mugs on Shopify , vintage finds on eBay , or private-label products on Amazon —is one of the most accessible paths to financial independence. However, product copywriting and SEO present major hurdles for solo founders: The Time Sink: Researching keyword tags, crafting persuasive multi-paragraph descriptions, and drafting high-converting titles takes 20 to 45 minutes per product listing. The SaaS Platform Tax: Commercial AI copywriting tools cost $29 to $79/month with recurring billing, strict token allowances, and vendor lock-in—eating into margins before a side hustler makes their first sale. Privacy Concerns: Uploading unreleased prototypes, wholesale supplier specs, and proprietary formulas to centralized closed-model APIs risks leaks and data harvesting. I built SellSmart Mini 🛍️ , a lightweight, high-speed, open-weight AI e-commerce listing and SEO studio engineered specifically for indie merchants and side hustlers. With SellSmart Mini, sellers input basic product specs, select their target platform (Etsy, Shopify, Amazon, eBay) and brand tone, and generate in seconds: SEO-Optimized Product Title (under 90 characters for maximum search indexing). Compelling Multi-Paragraph Sales Story detailing craftsmanship, features, and specs. Platform-Tailored Search Tags (visual chips + comma-separated copy button). Interactive Live Storefront Mockup (PDP) simulating how the listing looks on a live e-commerce store with price, badges, and "Add to Cart". Google SERP Snippet Preview displaying real-time search engine meta title, URL slug, and description. 1-Click Merchant Clipboard with ready-to-paste markdown. Demo 🎥 Full Video Recording : Watch sellsmart-demo.mp4 on GitHub The video demonstrates 1-click catalog preset loading, offline local inference on Ollama with llama3.2:1b , the live storefront PDP preview, and copying the formatted markdown export. Code tushaar-05 / hacktober-2 SellSmart Mini 🛍️ AI Product Listing & SEO Generator for Online Sellers & Side Hustlers Built for the DEV Community Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 2 ("Side Hustle") 📖 Overview & Problem Solved Starting an e-commerce side hustle—selling handcrafted goods on Etsy , vintage collectibles on eBay , custom apparel on Shopify , or products on Amazon —is one of the most accessible ways for independent creators to monetize their skills. However, copywriting and search engine optimization (SEO) present major hurdles: Time Drain: Drafting compelling titles, detailed multi-paragraph product descriptions, and researching 10–15 platform-tailored SEO tags takes 15–30 minutes per listing. Expensive SaaS Tools: Proprietary commercial copywriting subscriptions cost $25–$75/month—an unsustainable overhead when testing new product ideas. Data Lock-in & Privacy: Closed APIs retain proprietary product drafts and manufacturer details on centralized servers. SellSmart Mini is a lightweight, beginner-friendly open-source tool built with Python and Streamlit. Sellers input basic product… View on GitHub Stack: Python 3.10+, Streamlit, huggingface_hub , requests License: Permissive MIT License Zero Lock-In: 100% open-source and easy to run locally or self-host. How I Built It SellSmart Mini is designed from the ground up around transparent, open-weight AI models with a dual-engine architecture: 1. Dual-Engine Runtime Local Offline Inference via Ollama ( http://localhost:11434 ): Complete privacy and zero external network calls. The app dynamically auto-detects locally installed models (such as llama3.2:1b , gemma2:2b , and qwen2.5:7b ), providing instant, offline generation with zero API rate limits and zero cost. Serverless Cloud Inference via Hugging Face: Integrated with the huggingface_hub Inference API to give users cloud flexibility using free Hugging Face access tokens without needing local GPU hardware. 2. Supported Open-Weight Architectures google/gemma-2-2b-it (Google DeepMind): Ultra-fast instruction following, high parameter efficiency, and respectful e-commerce tone. meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Meta): Compact reasoning powerhouse with sharp, concise direct-response sales copy. Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Alibaba Cloud / Qwen): Permissive Apache 2.0 license with rich creative storytelling and comprehensive SEO tag extraction. 3. Prompt Engineering & Delimiter Parsing The core prompt applies a role-governed system persona ( You are an elite e-commerce listing copywriter and technical SEO specialist ) and structured delimiters ( ### TITLE: , ### DESCRIPTION: , ### KEYWORDS: ). The Python backend cleanly extracts structured outputs into separate reactive Streamlit components for easy 1-click clipboard copying. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation is essential for independent side hustlers and micro-entrepreneurs: True Cost Predictability ($0 SaaS Overhead): Closed commercial APIs frequently alter pricing tiers, impose opaque rate limits, or discontinue endpoints. Open-weight models like Gemma 2, Llama 3.2, and Qwen can run entirely on consumer laptops (even lightweight 1B–3B parameter models on Apple Silicon or standard CPU) with zero ongoing hosting bills. Trade Secret & Prototype Protection: Solo artisans and makers often experiment with proprietary material blends, private suppliers, or unreleased product designs. Running open-weight inference locally on Ollama guarantees that sensitive business data never leaves the seller's machine. Model Portability: Sellers are never captive to a single tech giant's ecosystem. If one model changes license or performance, switching to another open-weight architecture takes a single dropdown selection. My First User I tested SellSmart Mini with a local maker who sells handcrafted leather accessories on Etsy and at weekend artisan markets. Previously, writing a single listing took them over 30 minutes of agonizing over descriptions and searching competitor tags. Using the "Artisan & Storytelling" tone setting with Gemma 2 , SellSmart Mini took raw notes ( "full grain leather, unlined cotton paper, brass clasp" ) and synthesized a 3-paragraph listing emphasizing heirloom durability, tactile paper weight, and 13 targeted Etsy tags in under 3 seconds . Their immediate feedback: "I usually spend an entire Sunday afternoon writing copy for 10 new journals. Having the live storefront preview and instant tag chips ready to paste saves me at least 4 hours every week." Prize Categories Primary Track: Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Best Use of Gemma / Google Track: Powered by google/gemma-2-2b-it for lightning-fast instruction following and e-commerce copy generation. Meta Llama Track: Integrated support for meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct for edge-optimized conversion copy.

title: Building Croptera AI: My Journey to Bring AI into Agriculture
