title: GPL 2026/27: Hearts of Oak seal back-to-back wins as Berekum Chelsea shock Lions in Kpando
body: Hearts of Oak secured back-to-back Premier League victories after edging Vision FC 1-0 at the Nii Adjei Kraku Complex in Tema New Town on Saturday, while Berekum Chelsea stunned Heart of Lions with a 2-0 away win in Kpando. Kwesi Asmah emerged as Hearts’ match-winner, striking in the 86th minute to secure all three points in a tightly contested encounter. Asmah capitalised on a loose clearance inside the box before firing home with his left foot, extending the Phobians’ winning run following their narrow victory over Port City. Berekum Chelsea claimed their first away win of the season with a clinical 2-0 victory over Heart of Lions at the Kpando Stadium. Dramani Awuah opened the scoring in the 39th minute before Paul Attah Agyei doubled the advantage in the 69th minute, punishing the hosts despite their dominance in possession. The result leaves Heart of Lions with consecutive defeats, while Chelsea climb to seventh on the league table, gaining momentum ahead of their next fixture against Samartex. Hearts of Oak will look to build on their improved form as they continue their push for consistency in the Premier League.

title: How to Integrate the Travelport API into a Travel Portal
body: Originally published at sunnybadgujar.com . Travelport is the third of the big three GDSs, and the one with the most names: Galileo, Apollo, Worldspan, Travelport+. It also has two API families, a SOAP-based Universal API and newer JSON APIs, and a booking model built around a "workbench" with timers you have to respect. Here's how the integration fits together, in the order the decisions actually come up. This is the third guide in a set. I've already covered integrating the Amadeus API into a B2B travel portal and integrating the Sabre API . The core idea is the same on every GDS: a search result is a snapshot, the price must be confirmed before you take money, and booking and ticketing are separate steps. What changes is how you get access, how you authenticate, and how the booking itself is assembled. On Travelport, that last part is the most different. If you're still choosing a GDS, read Sabre vs Amadeus vs Travelport first. This post assumes Travelport is the right fit for your markets or your agency already has a Travelport contract, and now someone has to build it. First, untangle the names Travelport's history is a series of mergers, and the names in its documentation reflect that: Galileo (host code 1G) , Apollo (1V) and Worldspan (1P) are the GDS host systems Travelport runs. Most customers get their content from Galileo. Travelport+ is the current name for the Galileo-based platform. When a sales conversation says "Travelport+", it means 1G. Universal API (often "uAPI", also called the SOAP XML API) is the older, broad web-service interface covering air, hotel, car and rail. JSON APIs (the Flights, Stays and Pay APIs, presented on the developer portal as TripServices) are the newer REST interface. Versions before 11 were deprecated at the end of 2022, so v11 is the baseline. The host code matters in practice: your PCC belongs to one host, and you'll see values like 79JP_1G where the PCC and host are sent together. Universal API or JSON APIs? For a new air-focused portal, my default is the JSON APIs . They're REST with JSON, use standard OAuth tokens, are where Travelport's NDC content is delivered, and are far pleasanter to work with from .NET or Node than a large SOAP schema. The Universal API is still supported and still runs a lot of live portals. Travelport even put its uAPI schema-retirement process on hold in January 2025, so existing integrations aren't being forced to upgrade. Choose it when you're extending a portal that already speaks uAPI, or when a workflow you need isn't covered by the JSON APIs for your content. Don't guess on this: list the exact operations you need (search, price, book, ticket, cancel, exchange, refund, seats, ancillaries) and confirm with Travelport which interface supports each for your PCC. Whichever you pick, hide it. Wrap Travelport behind your own adapter from day one. Then a later move from uAPI to JSON, or the addition of a second GDS, is a change inside one component instead of a rewrite. Access: trial credentials, provisioning and the access group Like Sabre, Travelport has no sign-up-and-go production tier. Access comes in stages: Trial credentials from a sign-up form on the developer portal. Good for learning the request shapes. Pre-production and production credentials , issued at provisioning once there's a commercial agreement. That agreement normally sits with a travel agency or partner, not with the developer building the portal. You'll get a username, password, client ID and client secret, plus a welcome letter with your access group. The access group is the piece developers don't expect. It holds your organisation's Travelport configuration: the PCC, location, currency, which GDS and NDC carriers you can sell, and printer links. Each API user has at least one, and it travels with your requests so responses match your point of sale. A B2B portal working across markets may have several, so treat it as per-tenant configuration, never a constant. Authentication: one 24-hour token, cached The JSON APIs use OAuth 2.0 with the password grant. You post your credentials to the token endpoint and get back a bearer token valid for 24 hours: // C#: get a Travelport token (pre-production host shown) var form = new FormUrlEncodedContent ( new Dictionary < string , string > { [ "grant_type" ] = "password" , [ "username" ] = cfg . Username , [ "password" ] = cfg . Password , [ "client_id" ] = cfg . ClientId , [ "client_secret" ] = cfg . ClientSecret , }); var res = await http . PostAsync ( "https://auth.pp.travelport.net/oauth/token" , form ); // cache access_token until shortly before expires_in (86,400 seconds) // Every Flights API call then carries: // Authorization: Bearer {token} // XAUTH_TRAVELPORT_ACCESSGROUP: {access group from your welcome letter} // (or, in v11, TVP-PCC-CORE: {PCC}_{host}, e.g. 79JP_1G) // Accept-Version / Content-Version: 11 (where the operation requires them) Travelport is explicit that you should cache the token and not request a new one per call. Keep one per set of credentials, store it with its expiry, and refresh it a little before the 24 hours are up. Production lives on auth.travelport.net and api.travelport.net ; pre-production adds .pp . Make the hosts and credentials configuration per environment and per tenant. The core flow: search, price, workbench, ticket On the v11 Flights API the shape is: Search ( catalog/search/catalogproductofferings ). Results come back as catalog product offerings: each combines flights with a fare brand and its price and terms. There are also next-leg and flight-specific searches for building journeys leg by leg, and an Air Availability call that returns seats without prices. Price ( price/offers/buildfromcatalogproductofferings ). Travelport describes this as optional for most carriers and required for some NDC and low-cost carriers. My advice: price the selected offer every time before you take money. It's the step that tells you the fare you're about to charge is still the fare. Book in a workbench. A booking isn't one call. You create a reservation workbench, add the offer, add at least one traveller, then commit. The commit returns the record locator and creates a held booking: confirmed by the airline, not yet ticketed. Ticket in a second workbench. Open a workbench on the existing booking, add a form of payment, add the payment, and commit. That's when tickets are issued and money actually moves. There's also Unified Checkout ( book/reservation/reservations/build ), which adds the offer and travellers and commits in a single request without an explicit workbench. It's simpler for straightforward bookings; the step-by-step workbench gives you more control when you need to add extras or handle errors between steps. The timers that will bite you The workbench model comes with clocks, and your UX has to respect them: Search results stay in cache for 12 minutes for GDS content and 34 minutes for NDC content. Pricing and booking by reference only work inside that window. A customer who leaves a tab open and comes back 20 minutes later needs a fresh search, not an error. A workbench is valid for 30 minutes. If it isn't committed in time, it expires and its contents are discarded. Don't open the workbench when the customer lands on the checkout page; open it when you have everything you need to commit. Held bookings have a ticketing deadline set by the airline. Miss it and the booking is cancelled. Track it on every booking and alert a human before it passes. Get the order of operations right around money. Price, then take payment (or debit the agent's wallet), then commit the booking workbench, then ticket. If the commit fails after you've charged, refund automatically. If ticketing fails after booking, retry and escalate before the deadline. A charged customer with no ticket is the most expensive state your system can be in. Reference payloads, full payloads and NDC Travelport requests come in two styles. A reference payload points at identifiers from an earlier response ("price this offer from that search"). A full payload sends the complete itinerary without referring back, which lets you book something that didn't come from a Travelport search. GDS content supports both. NDC content, in most cases, only supports reference payloads. That has a design consequence: your offer model has to keep Travelport's identifiers from search all the way to booking, and it needs a content-source field so the booking code knows whether a full payload is even an option. NDC also needs its own provisioning and airline registration, its identifiers include the carrier code, and for NDC the form of payment is normally added at ticketing. Build the offer model for both content types from the start; retrofitting NDC into a GDS-only model touches search, booking, servicing and the admin panel. PCCs and access groups in a B2B portal A consumer site might run on one access group. A B2B portal rarely does: different markets, currencies or contracted fares often mean different PCCs. The rule is the same one I give for Sabre: resolve the access group (or PCC) per request from your own tenant and routing rules, and store it on every booking. When finance asks why two agents saw different prices for the same flight, that field answers the question. The rest of the B2B layer doesn't change with the GDS: server-side markup that turns net fares into sell fares, agent wallets as an immutable ledger, roles per agency, and rate limits per tenant. The Amadeus B2B guide covers those in detail, and all of it applies here. Keep Travelport behind an adapter Travelport's responses are deep and full of its own concepts: catalog offerings, product brands, workbenches, receipts. None of that should leak into your business code. Define your own types (an offer, a price breakdown, a booking result, a ticketing result) and write a Travelport adapter that translates both ways. The adapter also owns the workbench lifecycle, so the rest of your system just calls "book this offer for these travellers" and gets a result or a typed error. The payoff is the same as with any supplier: you can test the booking flow without calling Travelport, upgrade API versions in one place, and add Sabre, Amadeus or a direct airline feed as another adapter rather than a rewrite. I've written up that design in how to integrate multiple GDS providers into one booking engine . Pitfalls I'd flag before you start Start provisioning on day one. Trial credentials are for learning. Real pre-production access depends on the commercial agreement, and that takes time. Cache the token. One per credential set, refreshed before 24 hours. Never one per request. Treat the access group as data. Resolve it per tenant or route, and record it on every booking. Design around the timers. 12 or 34 minutes for search results, 30 for a workbench. Re-search gracefully instead of failing. Always price before you charge , even where Travelport says it's optional. Separate booking from ticketing. Track the ticketing deadline and alert a human before it passes. Carry identifiers end to end and mark each offer as GDS or NDC. Log every request and response. With credentials masked, and searchable by record locator. Support will need it daily. Travelport's workbench model feels unusual for the first week, then it starts to make sense: it's an explicit transaction around a booking, with a clear commit point. Get access, tokens and the money flow right first, respect the timers, keep Travelport behind your own interface, and it becomes a solid source of content for a portal you can grow. I'm Sunny Badgujar, a full-stack .NET developer who runs a live travel platform integrated with multiple GDS suppliers. I build travel portals and booking engines . The full version of this article, with an FAQ, is on my blog .

title: Provisioning k3s clusters over Tailscale
body: It has been a while since I wrote the last article about this deployment platform. The shape of it has changed since then, and I have been meaning to write down why. The old pipeline still exists in spirit. GitHub Organizations, GitHub Actions, k3s and SOPS are still there. The part that changed first was provisioning, the one I was least happy with. If you are new to this, the previous article describes the platform this one builds on and the decisions behind it. The previous setup used Ansible playbooks. They worked, but they were a second codebase with its own abstractions, and every new provider meant another set of assumptions about networking, users and firewall tools. Most of each playbook repeated the same work. Create a user, copy a key, install packages, configure a private network, bring up k3s. None of it was interesting, and all of it had to be right before the cluster could exist. So I wrote a small tool called tailk3s. You give it a list of servers and provider logins, and it gives you a k3s cluster on a Tailscale network. The repository is at github.com/ude-p/tailk3s . The cluster file You describe the cluster in an HCL file. If you have used Terraform, the format will look familiar. Each block is one server. node "cp1" { host = "203.0.113.10" role = "server" init_user = "ubuntu" init_key = env ( "SSH_KEY" ) } node "w1" { host = "203.0.113.20" role = "agent" join = "cp1" init_user = "ubuntu" init_key = env ( "SSH_KEY" ) } host is where the machine can be reached. role decides what it does. A server runs the Kubernetes control plane, which holds the API and the cluster state. An agent is a worker. It runs the applications. join tells an agent which server to join. init_user and init_key are the login the provider gave you. tailk3s uses them once, for the first connection, and removes the account when it is done. You run one of two commands. tailk3s plan --config cluster.hcl shows what would change without touching anything. tailk3s up --config cluster.hcl performs it. You can also describe a single node with flags and skip the file entirely. There is no state file to lose. Every step checks what the machine already looks like and skips work that is already done. Running up twice does nothing the second time. What Tailscale does A Kubernetes cluster needs its machines to reach each other. The control plane has an API that the workers call, the control plane servers talk to each other, and pods on different machines need a route between them. Those addresses can be public, but most clusters keep that traffic on a private network so it is not exposed to the internet. On a cloud provider, that normally means a VPC, private subnets and firewall rules, and every provider does it differently. Tailscale builds that private network for you, across providers. It is built on WireGuard, a modern VPN protocol. Each machine joins a network called a tailnet and gets a stable private address in the 100.x range, for example 100.117.36.53 . It can then reach the other machines at their addresses, whether they sit in the same data centre or on different providers. When a direct connection is possible, the machines talk directly. When it is not, Tailscale relays the traffic, so you do not have to open ports or arrange a route. The part that matters for this tool is identity. Every machine in the tailnet has a name, and it can be given a tag such as dev-server . A policy file, the ACL, decides which names and tags may reach which addresses and which users may connect. tailk3s uses that policy for two things. It gives every node a tag, and it adds one SSH rule that lets the orchestrator and administrators log in to those tags. I never copy an SSH key to a machine, and I never write provider-specific firewall rules. By the time Kubernetes is being installed, the network already exists. Every machine has the same kind of private address it would have had inside a single VPC, and that address does not change when the cluster moves to another provider. How it works The work happens in three phases. tailk3s prepares the tailnet, gets each machine onto it, and then finishes the cluster over it. The tool runs on your machine and joins the tailnet itself, as a node tagged tag:tailk3s . You do not need Tailscale installed on your laptop. It needs one thing from you, a Tailscale API key. It uses the key to read and update the access policy and to create the keys the machines join with. First, prepare the tailnet. Read the cluster file and check it. Machines that start a cluster are handled before the ones that join it, because a joining machine needs a control plane to exist first. Update the access policy. Every node will get a tag, which is a label the policy can match on. The policy needs an owner for each tag and one SSH rule that lets the tool and administrators log in to machines wearing them. If the policy already says this, the tool writes nothing. Create a joining key for each machine that is not on the tailnet yet. The key is a single-use ticket, and it expires after ten minutes. Then, get each machine onto the tailnet. Connect with the provider login and prepare the machine. Install the base packages, set the hostname, create the admin user, install Tailscale, and join the tailnet with the node's tag. This is the only time the provider password or key is used. Finally, finish the cluster over the tailnet. Connect again through Tailscale SSH. Close the public firewall. Only ports 80 and 443 stay open to the internet, and everything else is allowed on the tailnet interface. Then install k3s, configure it, and wait for the API to answer. If the machine joins an existing cluster, read the join token from a control plane and pass it along. The machines never need SSH access to each other. Write a kubeconfig file on your machine so kubectl works, and an SSH config entry so you can connect by name. Delete the provider login. The admin account has no password, and Tailscale SSH is the way in. A diagram makes this easier to see. Tailscale API (policy, auth keys) ^ | laptop ── tailk3s ───────┘ │ provider SSH │ tailscale SSH v v cp1 ─────── tailnet ─────── cp2 \ / \─────── w1 ────────────/ Two details are worth calling out. Node names carry a short hash of the address, so a node name can be reused across clusters without collisions. And the provider login is deleted at the end. The admin account has no password and is reachable only through Tailscale SSH. That is the point, but it also means the provider console is the recovery path if the tailnet is ever misconfigured. High availability HA is a file change. Add another role = "server" node that joins the first one. The first server starts with cluster-init: true , which selects embedded etcd. Every later server joins the same etcd cluster. Agents receive every control plane address in their server: list, so they are not tied to one machine being up. The API server's certificate includes the tailnet address and the hostname, which is what makes the tailnet the transport rather than an afterthought. There is no external load balancer to configure. k3s clients use the list of servers, and the network underneath is the tailnet. What this does not give you is machine-level reconciliation. tailk3s is a CLI, not a controller. If a server dies, provisioning a replacement is one command, but nothing does it for you. I am comfortable with that boundary. The machines are provisioned deliberately, and the workloads are reconciled continuously. What it gets right The obvious win is that there is no vendor lock-in. Any provider that gives you a Linux server and SSH works. Moving from one to another is a change to host values, not a rewrite of networking and firewall rules. There are a few less obvious wins. No private networking to build. No VPC, peering, NAT gateways or per-provider firewall rules. No configuration management layer. No playbooks, no inventory, no state file. Secure by default. Public ports are closed, the provider login is deleted, and there are no SSH keys to distribute or rotate. Fast. A node is a few minutes, and a cluster is the time it takes to install k3s. Readable. The cluster is one file, and plan is honest about what it will do. What it does not do It is not a general infrastructure tool. It does not create VPCs, load balancers, DNS records, volumes or provider accounts. You bring the server and an SSH login. It brings the cluster. It assumes a Linux machine with systemd, and it has only been exercised on Ubuntu. That is a deliberate constraint, not an accident, but it is still a constraint. It depends on Tailscale. If you do not want a tailnet, this tool is not for you. I think that is a reasonable dependency, because it replaces an entire category of provider-specific work, but it is a dependency. Finally, it is a one-shot provisioner. It does not watch the nodes. Drift in k3s configuration is corrected when you run it again, not while you sleep. Flux handles that for the workloads. Nothing handles it for the machines. Flux The cluster is now disposable. What matters is the state you want it to have, and that state should live in Git. Flux is the tool that makes the cluster follow Git. The idea is called GitOps. You keep the Kubernetes YAML files in a repository. Flux runs inside the cluster, watches that repository, and continuously compares what the cluster has with what the repository says. When the two differ, it changes the cluster to match. People call that reconciliation. You do not run a deployment command and hope it worked. You change a file, review the change, merge it, and Flux applies it. Flux is installed with one command, called a bootstrap. It installs its own components into the cluster, commits them to the repository, and keeps them running from then on. flux bootstrap github \ --owner = my-org \ --repository = infrastructure \ --path = clusters/prod \ --personal The layout I use has one directory per cluster, with shared pieces in a base directory. A file in each directory lists the applications and the cluster software that belongs to that cluster. The value is in the loop, not the tool. If someone edits a resource by hand, Flux notices and changes it back. If a component is deleted, it is recreated. The cluster stops drifting away from what is written down. Operators Kubernetes runs what you declare. You write a YAML file asking for three copies of a container, and the cluster keeps that true. The components that watch these declarations and act on them are called controllers. An operator is a controller built for one specific piece of software. It teaches Kubernetes how to run that software, including the parts that need care, such as failover or backups. Every cluster gets the same foundation. These are installed through Flux before any application lands. Tailscale operator. It lets a Kubernetes service be reached over your tailnet. A service is normally reachable only from inside the cluster. Exposing it usually means a public load balancer or a public hostname. With this operator, an internal tool can get a tailnet address instead. Longhorn. Persistent storage for pods. A pod that writes to a disk on one node needs its data to follow it when it moves. Longhorn keeps copies of each volume on several nodes, so a pod can be rescheduled without losing its data. It also handles snapshots and backups. The previous article ended by saying Longhorn was a maybe. It is now the default. CloudNativePG. Postgres, run by an operator. You declare a Postgres cluster, and it creates the instances, handles replication and failover, and takes backups. Point-in-time recovery means you can restore the database to a specific moment, not just to the last nightly backup. kube-prometheus-stack. Monitoring. It collects metrics from the nodes and the cluster, stores them over time, evaluates alert rules, and provides dashboards. cert-manager. TLS certificates. It requests certificates from Let's Encrypt, installs them, and renews them before they expire, so HTTPS becomes a resource you declare rather than a manual task. Each one solves a cluster-level concern. None of them belongs in an application repository, and all of them are easier to reason about when they are part of the same Git history as the cluster. appd Flux deploys what is in Git. Someone still has to write it. So I wrote appd to do that part. It is at github.com/ude-p/appdeploy . A normal web application needs several Kubernetes objects. A Deployment runs the container and keeps the requested number of copies alive. A Service gives those copies a stable address inside the cluster. ConfigMaps and Secrets hold configuration. An Ingress or Route publishes it on a hostname. Writing all of that for every service is repetitive, and Helm charts bring their own template language and values files. appd lets you describe the application once in HCL and generates those objects for you. The common blocks are app , stateful , job , cron , route , config , secret , volume and manifest . config "api" { env { source = ".env" prefix = "CONFIG_" } } secret "api" { env { source = ".env" prefix = "SECRET_" } } app "api" { image = "ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.0" replicas = 2 env { config = config . api secret = secret . api } port { service = 80 } health { path = "/health" port = 3000 } } route "api" { to = app . api host = "api.example.com" path "/" {} } appd run -o prints the YAML instead of applying it, which is the path that works with Flux. appd run applies it directly to the current cluster. appd explain documents the schema, and appd init writes a starter file. The motivation was the same as before. I was tired of copying the same Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret and Ingress between repositories, and I was tired of Helm values files that exist only to change an image tag. HCL is a better fit for the shape of the problem. It has blocks, it has expressions, and it does not need a templating function to concatenate two strings. I am also reducing the amount of configuration a user has to write, and rewriting the deployment path so that appd renders and Flux applies. Deploying directly from a CLI is convenient, but it bypasses the property that made Flux worth installing in the first place. The intended split is simple. appd describes an application, and Flux owns the cluster. What I think comes next Provisioning is becoming boring, and that is a good thing. A cluster that takes minutes to create and a Git repository that reconciles it means the interesting work moves up a layer. How fast you can get a correct environment, and how quickly you can understand what broke. On the second point, I want to build an operator that watches Kubernetes resources and explains them. Not another alerting rule. The system I have in mind correlates events, logs, metrics and ownership, and answers the question you actually ask during an incident. What changed, what depends on it, and what is the smallest safe fix. The model can read. It can propose a patch. It can run a server-side dry-run. It should not silently apply changes to production. The safeguards are the design. Read-only RBAC by default, scoped escalation, an audit trail, a human approval for writes, and an explicit ban on automatic remediation of stateful workloads. The other area I keep coming back to is GPUs. Kubernetes is a reasonable scheduler for GPU workloads, but it does not hide the hard parts. Device plugins, MIG partitioning, topology, NVLink, storage throughput, and the cost of leaving a card idle. I am learning this area now. I do not have deep experience in it yet, but I am looking for an opportunity where GPU infrastructure is the main problem, in an organization that treats it as a first-class discipline rather than a side project. For now, the pipeline is smaller and the clusters are faster, and that is enough for one post.

title: WAFU B U17: Black Starlets to face Ivory Coast in semi-final clash
body: Ghana’s U17 side, the Black Starlets, will face Ivory Coast in the semi-finals of the 2026 WAFU Zone B U17 Championship after the Ivorians secured second place in Group B following a 1-1 draw against Nigeria on Saturday. The West African rivals will lock horns in the first semi-final on Tuesday at 16:00 GMT, with a place in the final and qualification for the 2027 U17 Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco at stake. Ivory Coast finished second behind Niger in Group B to set up a crucial showdown with Ghana, who topped Group A after an unbeaten run in the group stage. Coach Kassim Ocansey’s side collected seven points from three matches, recording victories over Togo and Benin before playing out a goalless draw against hosts Burkina Faso in their final group fixture. The Black Starlets scored four goals and conceded just one to finish at the summit of their group. Ghana will now be aiming to maintain their unbeaten record against the Ivorians and secure a place at the continental tournament in Morocco. The team will also be determined to reach the final as they continue their quest for the WAFU Zone B U17 title. However, Ivory Coast will pose a stern test for the Black Starlets, with both teams aware that victory will guarantee their participation in the 2027 U17 AFCON, while the losing side will miss out on qualification through the tournament.

title: Grab an RTX 5090 for a discounted $5,300 as part of an MSI Infinite ZS prebuilt gaming PC — price includes other components worth about $2,300 on their own
body: This one will be short and sweet. So remember how there are apparently no more RTX 5090s available most anywhere, even though Nvidia's Senior Vice President just said that the company definitely hasn't stopped making them? If you had been saving up for Nvidia's greatest card, there's still hope for you. Best Buy has an MSI Infinite ZS in stock with an RTX 5090 ensconced within for $7,599 , making for roughly $5,300 for the RTX 5090 and $2,300 for the rest of the PC. Yes, over five grand is definitely a lot to ask for a graphics card, but it's worth ponying up the cash if you want the best gaming card in recent years (and likely future, too). Besides, it's not like these will be in stock anytime soon (if ever), and they were commanding $7,500 or more in stores before they vanished. Infinite ZS Gaming Prebuilt w/ RTX 5090: was $7599 now $229 The MSI Infinite ZS prebuilt with a Nvidia RTX 5090 and a Ryzen 9950X3D CPU is probably one of the last few chances of getting ahold of the mighty GPU for anything resembling an acceptable price. View Deal The rest of the PC around the humongous card is equally powerful. The Ryzen 9 9950X3D ($670) is probably the best desktop CPU in the current market, offering a high core count of 16 cores and 32 threads, fast clocks with a 5.7 GHz turbo speed, and 128 MB of cache. It'll run games and heavy applications with equal aplomb. That chip sits atop an MSI B840-VC motherboard ($250 est.) with PCIe 5.0 support thanks to its AMD B840 chipset. An MSI CoreLiquid 360mm CLC ($110) keeps the processor cooled. There are 32 GB of RAM ($450 est.) on tap — though MSI doesn't mention the speed, 6000 MT/s is a good, reasonable guess for a high-end machine. The machine is powered by an unspecified MSI 1300W Gold PSU ($170 est.), and all the hardware sits inside a MSI MEG Prospect 700RL case ($250 est.). A Windows 11 Home license currently sets you back about $130. For those keeping track at home, the PC core goes for over $2300. There are no weak spots we could find, too — pre-builts often skimp on one of their core parts, but there are no shortcuts here .

title: GMA donates 300 life jackets to boat operators, fishers in Dambai
body: The Ghana Maritime Authority (GMA) has handed over 300 life jackets to boat operators and fishers in Dambai to promote safety compliance and reduce fatalities on the Oti River. The donation, made at the Dambai Ferry Station, benefited three groups: the Boat Owners and Operators Association-Dambai, A1 Boats and the Inland Canoe Fishers Association, with each organisation receiving 100 life jackets. The intervention formed part of the Authority’s Life Jackets for Safety and Livelihood Initiative, which allows inland waterway operators to acquire life jackets at subsidised prices and pay in monthly instalments to ease the financial burden of obtaining essential safety equipment. The Deputy Director of the Technical Services Division and Head of Inland Waterways at the GMA, Captain Kodjo Adjarko Osei, said the high cost of life jackets had been a major challenge for some operators and contributed to non-compliance with water safety regulations. He said the Authority was addressing the challenge by improving access to affordable life jackets, stressing that their use was critical to preventing avoidable deaths during water transport accidents. Captain Osei noted that the intervention also supported the enforcement of the Authority’s “No Life Jacket, No Sailing” directive, introduced earlier this year during the launch of its Safety Guards Programme. He said making life jackets readily accessible was essential to ensuring that operators complied with safety regulations before embarking on journeys on inland waterways. The Krachi East Municipal Chief Executive, Mr Safo Nketiah, who spoke on behalf of the community, commended the Authority for its efforts to safeguard the lives of people who relied on waterways for their livelihoods. He noted that nearly 40 per cent of residents in Dambai engaged in lake-related activities, making the provision and use of life jackets crucial to protecting lives and sustaining economic activities in the area. Mr Nketiah urged the Authority to sustain such interventions to improve water safety awareness and encourage greater compliance among boat operators and fishers. Beneficiaries lauded the GMA for the intervention, describing it as a significant step towards improving safety on the Oti River. They pledged to use the life jackets for their intended purpose and comply with established safety requirements to protect lives and promote safer inland water transport. The initiative underscores the GMA’s commitment to enhancing safety standards on inland waterways by addressing barriers to accessing life-saving equipment and reinforcing compliance with maritime safety regulations.

title: Hubtel deployed AI to help ECG identify suspected electricity theft – CEO
body: The Chief Executive Officer of Hubtel, Alex Bram, has disclosed that the company worked with the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) to use artificial intelligence (AI) to help identify customers suspected of stealing electricity. He says the initiative was among the early applications developed by Hubtel’s AI laboratory, demonstrating how the technology could be used to address practical challenges facing businesses and public institutions in Ghana. Mr Bram revealed that ECG provided the company with an opportunity to test its AI capabilities using electricity-related data, which he described as valuable to the power distributor. “I think the biggest one that we announced was ECG. They gave us an opportunity to help them use AI to find people who could be stealing electricity. And that data was very helpful and still very helpful to ECG,” he disclosed. Speaking in an interview ahead of the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum, Mr Bram explained that Hubtel began experimenting with artificial intelligence in 2022 before formally establishing an AI laboratory in 2023. The company initially focused on developing its own AI models using machine learning and neural network technologies, working with businesses to test the systems it had built. “We opened the lab in 2023. We’re very lucky to have gotten an opportunity with some companies to work on their data, to experiment with some of the models that we built. Some were quite successful,” he said. The application of AI to improve productivity, strengthen public services and address economic challenges will form part of discussions at the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum , under the theme “AI and the Ghana Economy: Opportunity or Disruption?” The forum, held in partnership with Hubtel , will feature the Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Sam George; Economist and Technical Advisor at the Finance Ministry, Dr Theo Acheampong; Founder of AI for Ghana, Adam Watkins; Head of Engineering at Hubtel, Augustine Adjei; and Vice President of IMANI Africa, Bright Simons. It will air live on JoyNews and Joy 99.7 FM on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 8 p.m. AI’s potential to address electricity theft Electricity theft remains a concern for power distributors because unauthorised consumption can result in revenue losses and undermine efforts to improve service delivery. Artificial intelligence offers utilities the potential to analyse large volumes of consumption and billing data, identify unusual patterns and flag accounts that may require further investigation. Such systems could help electricity providers target their investigations more effectively instead of relying exclusively on conventional monitoring and inspection methods. His comments provide an example of a Ghanaian technology company exploring the application of AI to a challenge within the country’s energy sector. Hubtel’s AI ambitions faced challenges Despite recording some successes with its early AI experiments, Mr Bram disclosed that Hubtel eventually reconsidered its approach to developing AI models from scratch. He explained that the company encountered significant challenges recruiting the specialised professionals required to build and improve its systems. Hubtel initially sought to recruit approximately 30 machine learning engineers but struggled to find enough qualified personnel locally. “One, we struggled with manpower. So when we started, we wanted to recruit, I believe, about 30 machine learning engineers. We just couldn’t find 30 in Ghana,” he revealed. The company subsequently increased its recruitment budget substantially, but the search remained difficult. “We increased the budget almost twice, and we still couldn’t find machine learning data scientists who were from Ghana. We offered very generous terms. We still couldn’t find, so our tech was a bit behind,” he explained. Beyond the skills shortage, Hubtel also faced difficulties obtaining sufficient data to train and improve its AI systems. Mr Bram said attempts to establish data-sharing arrangements with other companies were frustrated by uncertainty over how information could be exchanged. “We realised there’s still no framework in Ghana for sharing data,” he said. He explained that these challenges became more pronounced as international technology companies commercialised increasingly advanced AI models at relatively affordable subscription prices. By late 2024 and into 2025, Hubtel had begun shifting from developing its own models towards using commercially available AI systems. Hubtel CEO Alex Bram speaks to CNN Marketplace Africa Lessons for Ghana’s AI development Drawing on these experiences, Mr Bram urged the government to ensure that its planned national AI compute centre is supported by sufficient data and skilled professionals. He welcomed Ghana’s decision to invest in AI infrastructure but maintained that building computing facilities without addressing the country’s data and skills challenges could limit the benefits. “So that data framework is important. If that AI compute centre is to succeed, because when a computer centre is there, without the data, it’s nothing,” he stressed. Mr Bram believes developing a national data-sharing framework, strengthening technical training and encouraging cooperation between government and private businesses will be essential to Ghana’s success in artificial intelligence. He argued that investment in AI should ultimately translate into practical improvements in how businesses and public institutions operate. Despite the difficulties Hubtel encountered, the CEO remains optimistic about Ghana’s technological future. He believes the country has an opportunity to build on its early investments and make artificial intelligence useful across sectors, including manufacturing, agriculture and public services. “I want to see more Ghanaians be better designers, be better manufacturers, be better farmers, be better agro-processors. Because they can find the answers to improving whatever it is that they are doing. If we get it right, we would be a country on the path of an accelerated development into a very, very bright future,” he said. For Mr Bram, the experience of applying AI to challenges such as suspected electricity theft provides a glimpse of the opportunities the technology could offer Ghana if the right investments and capabilities are developed.

title: Government appoints AI focal persons across ministries to drive national strategy
body: The Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Sam George, has disclosed that the government has appointed artificial intelligence (AI) focal persons across all ministries as part of efforts to prepare public institutions for the adoption of the technology. He says Cabinet ministers have already undergone AI training, while preparations are underway to equip senior civil servants with the skills needed to integrate artificial intelligence into government operations. “We’ve done the AI boot camp for cabinet ministers. We have AI-focal persons in every ministry now,” he revealed. Speaking in an interview ahead of the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum, Mr George explained that the government is taking steps to ensure that ministries, departments and agencies develop the capacity to deploy AI responsibly and effectively. He disclosed that Ghana has also undertaken an AI readiness assessment in collaboration with UNESCO to determine how prepared government institutions are to adopt the technology. “Working with UNESCO, we’ve done an AI readiness assessment model that has mapped out all of the government ministries and agencies and determined the various states of readiness for our various agencies,” he explained. According to the minister, the findings will help the government identify institutions requiring additional investment, technical support and capacity-building before introducing AI into their operations. He said the assessment would also guide engagements between his ministry and the Ministry of Finance on the resources needed to address gaps in institutional preparedness. The initiative forms part of Ghana’s broader national AI strategy, which seeks to harness the technology to improve economic productivity, strengthen public services and expand access to essential services. The country’s preparedness for artificial intelligence, its impact on jobs and the opportunities for economic growth will form part of discussions at the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum , under the theme “AI and the Ghana Economy: Opportunity or Disruption?” The forum, held in partnership with Hubtel , will feature Sam George; Technical Advisor at the Finance Ministry, Dr Theo Acheampong; Founder of AI for Ghana, Adam Watkins; Head of Engineering at Hubtel, Augustine Adjei; and Vice President of IMANI Africa, Bright Simons. It will air live on JoyNews and Joy 99.7 FM on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 8 p.m. Training senior public officials Beyond the appointment of AI focal persons, Mr George disclosed that the government is working with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and UNESCO to train senior civil servants, including chief directors and directors across public institutions. “We’re beginning the training, working with the UNDP and UNESCO, for our civil servants, our chief director and director levels,” he said. The training is intended to equip public officials with the knowledge required to understand and apply artificial intelligence within their respective institutions. Mr George believes preparing the public sector is essential because the successful implementation of Ghana’s AI strategy will depend not only on investment in technology but also on the ability of government officials to use it effectively. He explained that Ghana’s AI strategy provides a ten-year development framework with measurable objectives intended to guide the country’s adoption of the technology. “Our AI strategy gives us a 10-year plan of what we intend to achieve, measurable plans of what we need to achieve. We’ve started work on that,” he stated. The strategy identifies agriculture, healthcare, education and government services as priority areas where artificial intelligence could improve productivity and the delivery of essential services. AI to improve government decision-making The sector minister believes artificial intelligence could significantly improve how government institutions plan development projects and allocate public resources. He disclosed that the ministry is developing a national data exchange hub intended to connect 48 data registries across government institutions. The proposed system would allow information currently held in separate databases to be analysed collectively, helping policymakers identify development priorities using empirical evidence. The minister argued that decisions about public investments should be guided by the actual needs of communities rather than political promises or the preferences of influential individuals. “I think that where we should get to as a country is that our interventions in communities must be driven by hardcore empirical evidence,” he said. He explained that data from hospitals, schools and other public institutions could help determine where resources would have the greatest impact. The minister also outlined plans for a national AI compute centre, which he believes will provide the processing infrastructure required to analyse large volumes of government data and support AI applications across different sectors. According to him, the government has committed US$250 million towards the first phase of the project, which is being designed with capacity beyond Ghana’s immediate requirements. Mr George believes combining such infrastructure with improved institutional readiness could enable the government to deliver more efficient and responsive public services. Building a digitally inclusive government Despite the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence, the minister acknowledged that its successful adoption would require sustained investment in infrastructure, cybersecurity, data protection and human capacity. He disclosed that the government is reviewing Ghana’s cybersecurity and data protection legislation to respond to risks associated with the increasing use of AI and large volumes of personal data. Mr George said the objective is to ensure that Ghana takes advantage of emerging technologies while protecting citizens and strengthening the institutions responsible for delivering public services. He expressed optimism that the implementation of the national AI strategy would ultimately help create a more responsive public sector, where citizens can access government services with greater ease. Describing his vision for Ghana’s AI-powered future, the minister said he wants to see “a harmonised system that works for the benefit of the Ghanaian people.” For him, the appointments, training programmes and planned infrastructure investments are steps towards a broader transformation of the Ghanaian economy.

title: Ghana needs AI engineers and data scientists, not just computing infrastructure – Hubtel CEO
body: The Chief Executive Officer of Hubtel , Alex Bram, has urged the government to match its planned investments in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure with funding for specialised training, warning that Ghana’s shortage of skilled professionals could undermine efforts to develop a competitive AI industry. He believes investment in computing infrastructure alone will not be sufficient to drive the country’s AI ambitions without the engineers, data scientists and technical personnel needed to develop, operate and maintain such systems. Mr Bram says Ghana must pay particular attention to building expertise in machine learning, data science and data centre management as it prepares to establish a national AI compute centre. “The money is extremely important. The money to set up the starting data centres and the architecture and the infrastructure around it is very important. But whilst we do that, I think we also have to look at the skills,” he said. Speaking in an interview ahead of the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum, Mr Bram drew on Hubtel ‘s own experience to explain why developing the country’s technical workforce must be treated as a priority alongside investment in physical infrastructure. He disclosed that the company struggled to recruit qualified machine learning engineers when it began developing its own AI systems, despite offering attractive employment packages. The challenge, he believes, exposes a skills gap Ghana must address if it intends to compete in the rapidly expanding global AI economy. The availability of specialised skills, investment in AI infrastructure and the implications of the technology for Ghana’s workforce will form part of discussions at the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum , under the theme “AI and the Ghana Economy: Opportunity or Disruption?” The forum, held in partnership with Hubtel , will feature the Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Sam George; Economist and Technical Advisor at the Finance Ministry, Dr Theo Acheampong; Founder of AI for Ghana, Adam Watkins; Head of Engineering at Hubtel, Augustine Adjei; and Vice President of IMANI Africa, Bright Simons. It will air live on JoyNews and Joy 99.7 FM on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 8 p.m. Hubtel struggled to recruit 30 AI engineers Mr Bram revealed that Hubtel began experimenting with artificial intelligence in 2022 before establishing an AI laboratory in 2023 to develop its own models. The company initially sought to build AI systems using machine learning and neural network technologies, with the ambition of developing solutions tailored to local business needs. However, the initiative encountered difficulties when Hubtel attempted to recruit the technical professionals required to undertake the work. “One, we struggled with manpower. So when we started, we wanted to recruit, I believe it was about 30 machine learning engineers. We just couldn’t find 30 in Ghana,” he disclosed. According to him, the company increased its recruitment budget substantially in an attempt to attract qualified professionals, but the effort yielded limited results. “We increased the budget almost twice, and we still couldn’t find machine learning data scientists who were from Ghana. We offered very generous terms. We still couldn’t find, so our tech was a bit behind,” he explained. Mr Bram said the difficulties affected Hubtel’s ability to advance its own AI technology at a time when international companies were rapidly developing and commercialising more sophisticated systems. By late 2024 and into 2025, commercially available AI models had become considerably more advanced and affordable, making it increasingly difficult for Hubtel to justify continuing along its original development path. The company eventually moved away from building its own models from scratch towards adopting commercially available AI technologies. For Mr Bram, the experience highlights the challenge Ghanaian technology companies could face without a larger pool of trained AI specialists. Beyond the proposed AI compute centre The government’s national AI strategy includes plans to establish an AI compute centre intended to provide the computing capacity required to support the development and deployment of artificial intelligence applications. Communications Minister Sam George has disclosed that the government has committed US$250 million towards the first phase of the facility, alongside US$20 million for a proposed AI fund. Mr Bram welcomed the initiative, describing Ghana’s decision to develop an AI policy framework and invest in infrastructure as an important step. However, he maintained that the country must also develop the specialised human resources required to make the investment productive. “As a country, we haven’t been strong at having a large base of, for example, people that can manage data centres. There are so few data centres here. I think that number needs to go up a little bit. There’s also the skills required to build it,” he observed. He identified machine learning and data science as areas requiring greater investment in technical capacity. “Machine learning, data scientists. We need those skills. And I think we might have to improve our efforts on getting the skills,” he said. Data availability another challenge Beyond the shortage of skilled professionals, Mr Bram identified access to data as another obstacle Hubtel encountered in its attempts to develop AI systems locally. He explained that the company approached other large businesses to explore data-sharing arrangements but struggled because there was no clear framework governing how the information could be exchanged. “We realised there’s still no framework in Ghana for sharing data,” he said. According to him, the uncertainty made companies reluctant to share information, limiting Hubtel’s ability to obtain the data required to improve its AI models. He consequently urged the government to develop arrangements that would encourage the retention and appropriate sharing of useful data to support AI development. “So that data framework is important. If that AI compute centre is to succeed, because when a computer centre is there, without the data, it’s nothing,” he stressed. Mr Bram believes Ghana must therefore address three interconnected requirements: computing infrastructure, access to data and the availability of skilled professionals. Ghana has an opportunity to get it right Despite the challenges Hubtel encountered, Mr Bram remains optimistic about Ghana’s prospects in artificial intelligence. He believes the government’s decision to develop a national strategy and commit resources to the sector provides an opportunity to address existing gaps before they become greater obstacles. The Hubtel CEO wants deliberate investment in technical skills to extend beyond the development of national infrastructure to support the adoption of AI by businesses of different sizes. “I think Ghana is well on the path. I mean, starting with the policy building, putting some money where the policy is heading towards, investing deliberately in the skills, the digital skills required to manage and build and translate and take this AI out to, or this new technology out to everybody else, mass enterprises, micro enterprises and all that. I think we’re already on the path and that’s critical,” he indicated. He argued that training the workforce would be essential to ensuring that the benefits of the technology reach smaller enterprises and other productive sectors of the economy.

title: Zelensky warns Russia may expand missile threats from Belarus against western Ukraine
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Russia may use Belarus to intensify missile and drone attacks on western Ukraine, putting the region under a growing threat.
Speaking to journalists on Oct. 17 , Zelensky said Russia was already using drone signal repeaters in Belarus and that he believed Russian President Vladimir Putin needed the support of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko to station additional ballistic missiles in the country.
“But this is a direct involvement of Belarus in this war, and [that] is, in my opinion, very dangerous. And, of course, for Belarus too,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine's State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko has separately reported that equipment based in Belarus helps relay or amplify signals for Russian Shahed and Geran drones heading toward western Ukraine and Poland's border region.
In September, Ukraine's military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko said that units of Russia's 101st Missile Brigade, equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile system, had been deployed to Belarus.
A series of Russian attacks has struck cities and communities across western Ukraine in recent days, including in Volyn, Rivne and Lviv oblasts, resulting in deaths and injuries, damaged infrastructure and widespread power outages .
Zelensky also said Ukraine would increase air defenses across the country, distribute them according to the level of threat, and expand production of defensive turrets.

title: Meet Kyutai REKI: The 2.4B VLA Model Bringing Efficient Memory to Robot Manipulation
body: Kyutai, with Inria and École des Ponts, has released REKI , a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) for robot manipulation. The REKI vision-language-action model is pretrained only on public data. It also carries a cheap memory of its recent past. On three out-of-distribution benchmarks, only models about twice its size beat it. All weights are live on Hugging Face today. TL;DR Size: 2.4B parameters (2.2B Qwen3.5-2B VLM + 0.2B flow-matching action expert). Memory covers the last 3 frames, 1 s apart. Runs on: Benchmarked on 1 NVIDIA H100. 21.8 ms per action chunk, compiled, from 2 cameras at 256×256. Weights ship in BF16. No quantized variants announced. Performance: Best among VLAs pretrained on public data on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin Clean2Rand. Best: 90.4% on LIBERO-Plus, the top score in Kyutai’s comparison. Worst: 38.4% on RoboCasa365, well behind Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (57.4%). What is REKI? REKI is a vision-language-action model from Kyutai that maps camera views and an instruction to robot actions. It pairs a Qwen3.5-2B backbone with a 200M-parameter action expert. The expert generates action chunks by flow matching, integrated in 10 Euler steps. Robot state and flow time enter through adaptive RMSNorm. Each robot state layout gets its own small state MLP. How does REKI’s memory work? Most VLAs act on the current frame alone. Prior memory methods feed past frames to the VLM, unroll training, or add modules. Each option adds cost. REKI places memory inside the action expert instead. Before each frame’s action tokens sit 32 learned register tokens . They cross-attend the encoded prompt and views of that frame. They also self-attend the registers of earlier frames. Registers never read action tokens. So they depend only on observations, not flow time or robot state. They are computed once per frame and cached in a rolling window. The cost is small, per the project page : Reading cached registers adds 0.1 ms to a 21.8 ms chunk. The cache uses about 2 MiB of GPU memory per past frame. Training packs a 3-frame window into 1 batched pass. Memory also fixes a failure mode. Without it, arms often oscillate between 2 poses. On RoboTwin, oscillating episodes fall from 18.6% to 4.1% with memory. Kyutai attributes this to perceptual aliasing. How does REKI perform on benchmarks? REKI is pretrained once, then finetuned separately per benchmark. Scores below come from the model card and project page. LIBERO-Plus: 90.4%, ahead of Qwen-RobotManip (89.0%) and π0.5 (85.7%). RoboTwin Clean2Rand: 65.8%, behind only Qwen-RobotManip (68.5%). RoboCasa365: 38.4%, ahead of RLDX-1 (36.0%) and Qwen-RobotManip (35.9%). LIBERO (4 suites): 97.6%. RoboTwin 2.0 Easy / Hard: 85.9% / 84.6%. Pretraining helps most out of distribution. It adds 13.8 points on Clean2Rand and 30.3 under clutter. Memory adds 1.5 points on LIBERO-Plus and 5.4 on RoboCasa365. window.addEventListener("message",function(e){if(e.data&&e.data.mtpRekiHeight){document.getElementById("mtp-reki-frame").style.height=e.data.mtpRekiHeight+"px";}}); How does REKI compare with other VLAs? Feature REKI ( Kyutai ) Qwen-RobotManip ( Qwen ) π0.5 ( Physical Intelligence ) ABot-M0 ( AMAP ) Total size 2.4B 4.7B ( per Kyutai ) 3.3B ( per Kyutai ) 4.6B ( per Kyutai ) VLM backbone Qwen3.5-2B Qwen3.5-4B Gemma-based Not disclosed Pretraining data Public only Open-source + human video Includes own robot data Open-source (UniACT) Memory 32 registers, 3 frames In-context variant None None LIBERO-Plus 90.4 89.0 85.7 ( Kyutai eval ) 80.5 RoboTwin Clean2Rand (mean) 65.8 68.5 63.8 55.7 RoboCasa365 38.4 35.9 16.9 Not disclosed H100 latency, compiled 21.8 ms Not disclosed 33.8 ms ( openpi, Kyutai ) 46.1 ms ( Kyutai ) Weights Open, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 Not released Open, Apache-2.0 repo Open, Apache-2.0 repo Notes: Clean2Rand means are computed from the 6 conditions in Table 5 of the Qwen-RobotManip report . The Qwen report lists π0.5 at 84.4 on LIBERO-Plus. What data was REKI trained on? The mixture holds 1.0B frames plus 12.2M vision-language samples. Real-robot teleoperation provides 639.8M frames, simulation 193.9M and egocentric human video 170.9M. Sources include DROID, BridgeData V2, AgiBot World, EgoDex and EgoVerse. Pretraining ran 200,000 steps on 32 H100 GPUs. Kyutai keeps each dataset’s native control convention rather than remapping actions. How do you deploy REKI? Six checkpoints are listed: the pretrained base plus finetunes for LIBERO, RoboTwin (2 variants), RoboCasa365 and RoboCasa-GR1. Real-robot deployment uses the LeRobot async-inference gRPC protocol. On a UR5 arm, REKI was finetuned for 3k steps (1 hour) on 50 demonstrations per task. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser from reki import RekiPolicy policy = RekiPolicy.from_pretrained("kyutai/reki-2b-libero", device="cuda") policy.reset() # clears the register cache at episode start actions = policy.predict(images={"camera_top": img0, "camera_wrist_left": img1}, state=proprio, task="put the bowl on the plate") Key Takeaways REKI is a 2.4B VLA pretrained only on public data. It scores 90.4% on LIBERO-Plus, top in Kyutai’s comparison. 32 cached register tokens give memory for 0.1 ms extra. Memory cuts pose oscillations from 18.6% to 4.1% on RoboTwin. Weights are open but non-commercial (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Check out the Paper , Project Page , Model Weights and GitHub Repo . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.
