title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
body:
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.
Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.
Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.
Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”
One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineer compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”
In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.
Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.
The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

title: Pentagon’s wireless services left locations, data exposed, watchdog finds
body: The Department of Defense failed to fully secure unclassified wireless communications, allowing sensitive data including locations of troops and command facilities vulnerable to be exposed, the Pentagon’s watchdog found. A new report from the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General found that although the department had taken steps to protect some communications under a major wireless telecommunications contract, it failed to vet carriers’ security measures. As a result, that left metadata intact, such as when messages were sent and from where, allowing locations to be pinpointed. The Office of Inspector General initiated the investigation following a late 2024 letter from Senators Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo), which warned of vulnerabilities in Department of Defense devices that put them at risk of foreign espionage groups. The objective was to see if the Defense Department “had capabilities to secure its unclassified wireless communications” procured through its Wireless Mobility Services, or Spiral 4, contract. The subject was the Pentagon’s massive Spiral 4 contract, which as of January 2026, the IG said, has more than 568,000 service lines for phones, tablets and other devices. The military did enact security measures for voice and email communications, but did not do so for text messages that use short message service or SMS messaging. The department’s chief information officer “accepted the operational risks from mobile device users sending unencrypted text messages using SMS messaging to meet mission needs by exception.” Those exceptions included outside communications to potential recruits or to journalists. That was despite several government findings that showed malicious actors were using tools to hijack and breach devices and communications lines and read unencrypted SMS texts. Although the office of the Chief Information Officer “stated that they were aware that malicious actors could exploit known vulnerabilities to intercept and read SMS messages transmitted to and from” department mobile devices, the report said, it “had not issued policy for protecting text messages.” Additionally, investigators found that the department had not looked into what mobile carriers were doing to secure data and communications or see if additional security measures were needed. That left vulnerabilities through which “malicious actors could map entire communication networks within the DoW, pinpoint sensitive locations like safe houses or command posts, and expose operational vulnerabilities, significantly compromising national security.” The findings come after the military initiated several security restrictions after instances of metadata and other location tracking technologies being exposed or found to be easily accessible. This summer, Wyden and Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC) shared confirmation from the different branches of the military that they had disabled advertising tracking tools in government-issued devices and phones. That came after reports showed Iran and other groups were using commercially available location data to track and even target American personnel at bases in the Middle East, with some only disabling trackers after the war had started. An investigation this summer showed that data on apps such as Strava exposed the locations of service members and contractors in the region, in places that were later attacked. According to the Inspector General report, its recommendations remain unresolved. The Office of Inspector General called for the Chief Information Officer to assess necessary security measures to protect military metadata, review third-party security assessments for the Spiral 4 contracts In a statement to Task & Purpose, Sen. Wyden said that he was “glad that the Inspector General spurred the DOD to change its contracts with the wireless carriers and receive third-party security assessments.” “I remain concerned that our service members remain at risk from the military’s insecure communications and look forward to seeing what else the Inspector General finds,” Wyden added. The post Pentagon’s wireless services left locations, data exposed, watchdog finds appeared first on Task & Purpose .

title: Chrome and Edge are removing XSLT: what breaks and what does not
body:
On 17 November 2026, Chrome 158 reaches stable and client-side XSLT stops working in it. Microsoft Edge inherits the same engine. If any file on your site carries an <?xml-stylesheet?> instruction — and if you run WordPress with almost any SEO plugin, one of them does — the page a human opens in a browser will change that day.
This site is in that group. Checked on 12 October 2026, doctor-seo.net/sitemap_index.xml carries <?xml-stylesheet type='text/xsl' href='//doctor-seo.net/wp-content/plugins/wordpress-seo/css/main-sitemap.xsl'?> , so the friendly table a visitor sees today is produced by XSLT and will not be produced after Chrome 158.
The short version is that this matters a lot less for search than the headlines suggest, and rather more for the humans who read XML. Crawling is untouched. What changes is the readable face of every XML file you publish.
XSLT — Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations — is a language for turning one XML document into another document. Give it an XML file and a stylesheet of template rules, and it emits HTML, or text, or different XML. XSLT 1.0 became a W3C Recommendation in 1999, and 1.0 is the version browsers implement; later versions, 2.0 and 3.0, live outside the browser.
Inside a browser it works through a processing instruction at the top of the XML file: <?xml-stylesheet type='text/xsl' href='style.xsl'?> . When the browser loads the XML and finds that line, it fetches the stylesheet, runs the transformation in the browser, and renders the result instead of the XML. There is also a scripting path, XSLTProcessor , which does the same thing from JavaScript.
The important property, and the one most coverage skips, is that this is a rendering step and nothing else. The XML on the wire is unchanged. Anything that parses the file rather than displaying it — a crawler, a feed reader, a script — never runs the stylesheet at all. XSLT is a cosmetic layer over machine-readable data, and that is exactly why its removal is both very visible and, for search, very minor.
Google set out the plan in Removing XSLT for a more secure browser on the Chrome developer site, written by Mason Freed and Dominik Röttsches and Last updated 2025-10-29 UTC. The reasoning is security. The document says the continued inclusion of XSLT 1.0 in browsers “presents a significant and unnecessary security risk”, describes the underlying libraries as “complex, aging C/C++ codebases” that “receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines”, cites CVE-2025-7425 and CVE-2022-22834 in libxslt, and concludes that the risk “far outweighs its limited modern utility”.
The usage figure behind that judgement is Google’s own: the same page states that “only about 0.02% of web page loads today actually use XSLT at all”, and that fewer than 0.001% use XSLT processing instructions. Google does not publish the sampling behind those counters, so they are platform telemetry rather than an independent study, and no sample size is given.
Two escape hatches exist and both have end dates. An enterprise policy, XSLTEnabled , went live in Chrome 146; an origin trial opened in Chrome 152. Chrome Platform Status records the removal milestone as 158 and the origin trial window as 152 to 175, with both hatches closing in Chrome 176 on 17 August 2027. Chromium Dash, read live on 12 October 2026, gives Chrome 158 a stable date of 2026-11-17 and a branch point of 2026-10-26. Today’s stable release is Chrome 156.
Microsoft’s site-impacting-changes page for Edge says XSLT support “represents a disproportionate attack surface” and that Edge will follow Chromium. It documents an XSLTEnabled feature policy in Edge 147 and tells organisations to test with it disabled. Edge 147 has already removed one narrower case: using XSLT to transform XML into SVG. The main deprecation, though, is listed as “Future release, TBD”. Microsoft has published no date.
The other engines are not holding out either. Chrome Platform Status records the Gecko and WebKit positions on removal as Positive , and the web developer view as Negative . On Mozilla’s standards-positions tracker, Simon Pieters wrote on 27 August 2025 that “it would be good for the long-term health of the web platform and good for user security to remove XSLT”. So the direction of travel is every major engine, and the dissent is coming from the people who use the feature, not from the people who ship it.
Google’s page describes a warning banner but does not show the result, so we produced it. On 12 October 2026 we rendered this site’s own sitemap index twice in Chromium 141: once normally, and once with the browser launched as --disable-blink-features=XSLT , which is the same switch the removal flips. With XSLT, Yoast’s stylesheet produces a titled page with a two-column table of sitemaps and last-modified dates. Without it, the browser prints a banner reading “This document cannot be formatted as intended. It uses XSLT, which the browser does not support. You might be able to install a browser extension that allows you to view it.” and below it the raw XML tree, processing instruction included.
Four uses account for almost all client-side XSLT on the open web, and they do not fail equally. A stylesheet on a sitemap or a feed loses its appearance and nothing else. A public XML data page — a register, a regulator’s code list, a weather station feed — loses the only form in which a person could read it. And where XSLT is doing work inside an application, the function stops running rather than merely stops looking right.
For search specifically, the honest answer is that nothing happens. Crawlers fetch and parse the XML; they do not execute a stylesheet. Google’s own documentation backs that up by omission: Build and submit a sitemap , Last updated 2026-07-08 UTC, contains no “XSLT”, no “stylesheet”, no “xml-stylesheet” and no “browser” anywhere in its body, and describes the mechanism purely in fetch-and-parse terms: “Google will attempt to crawl your URLs exactly as listed”, and submitting one “is merely a hint”. A stylesheet was never addressed to a search engine. It was addressed to you, and to whoever you send the URL to.
That is the part worth holding onto when a client forwards a screenshot of the warning banner in a panic. Nothing has been deindexed. The file still validates, still lists the same URLs, and the path from crawling to indexing is identical. What changed is that the file now looks like what it has always been.
Is a browser usage counter a sufficient basis for removing a web platform feature? One camp says yes and says the arithmetic is not close: 0.02% of page loads cannot justify an unmaintained C parser inside the most attacked program on most people’s computers, every engine agrees, and a platform that can never remove anything eventually cannot be made safe. The other camp says a usage counter measures page loads and not consequence, that the 0.02% is concentrated in exactly the places where breakage costs most, and that the removal proposal was never tested against the long tail. The strongest version of that case is the WHATWG issue titled “XSLT removal will break multiple government and regulatory sites across the world”, which names congress.gov, govinfo.gov, weather.gov, europarl.europa.eu, tga.gov.au and the European Pollutant Release and Transfer Register among others, and argues that “the proposal to remove XSLT from the spec doesn’t acknowledge existing use cases beyond Chrome Status counter stats” and that “There’s no investigation into the long tail of web sites, of how many exactly would be broken”.
Nobody can settle it from published evidence, because no party has published a count of affected sites . Google published a percentage of page loads; the objectors published a list of examples. Those are different units, and neither converts into the other. This article reports the disagreement and does not resolve it.
What I will defend is narrow and reproducible: XSLT in the browser is a rendering layer, Google’s sitemap documentation does not mention it, and the capture above shows exactly what disappears. Anyone can re-run that capture with one browser flag.
What I will not say is that this is a ranking event, because it is not one, and I will not tell you that the security argument is wrong either. I am not in a position to weigh an unmaintained parser’s attack surface against a list of government URLs, and neither is anyone else publishing on this, because the count that would let you do it has never been published by anybody.
The one judgement I will offer is about priorities. If you manage sites, the XSLT story is a thirty-minute inventory task and then a decision you can mostly answer with “leave it”. The cost of this change does not land on SEO teams at all; it lands on public bodies that published machine-readable data and made it human-readable the cheapest way the platform offered. That asymmetry is the story, and it is worth more of your attention than your sitemap’s appearance — which is also why it belongs in the technical SEO level as a lesson about depending on rendering you do not control.
Whether Edge ships the removal on Chrome’s schedule or its own, since Microsoft has published no date. Whether Firefox and Safari follow, and when — both engines have recorded a positive position and neither has published a timeline. How many sites actually break, which nobody has counted. Whether the origin trial is extended past Chrome 176. And whether any plugin vendor ships a replacement for the sitemap view before November, or simply lets the stylesheet become inert.
The only percentages in this article are Google’s own platform counters, which are published without a sample size or a sampling method, and that is stated where they appear. No other source here is a study.

title: “No to torture!” Saturday march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
body: March against oligarch Ivanishvili in Tbilisi On the evening of Saturday, 17 October, Tbilisi hosted its traditional 44th pro-European “Saturday March”. “No torture in prisons!” and “Georgia against [oligarch] Ivanishvili!” were the main slogans chanted by hundreds of participants. Protest scenes in Georgia: full collection The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for 689 days. Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years. Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections. Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested . Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison. For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli , founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media. News in Georgia

title: Romanian F-16 fighters shoot down two Russian drones after airspace violations over the Black Sea
body: Two alert-duty fighters scrambled from Borcea’s 86th Air Base after Romanian radar systems detected aerial targets over the Black Sea. The objects were approximately 120 kilometres east of Snake Island, heading south-west towards Romania’s coast. The first drone entered Romanian airspace at 17:59 and was shot down by one F-16 at 18:01. The second entered at 18:01 and was destroyed by the other fighter at 18:05. The pilots identified both objects as drones before engaging them. Both shootdowns took place over Romanian territorial waters. Two Romanian Air Force F-16 aircraft, conducting Air Policing missions, were scrambled from the 86th Air Base Borcea at 17:43, after radar surveillance systems detected a group of aerial targets flying approximately 120 kilometres east of Snake Island, heading southwest. At 17:59, the first target entered Romanian airspace and was shot down by one of the F-16 aircraft at 18:01. A second target entered Romanian airspace at 18:01 and was shot down by the other F-16 aircraft at 18:05. Both aerial targets were identified as drones and were shot down over Romanian territorial waters. Further information will be provided upon completion of the mission. — MApN (@MApNRomania) October 17, 2026 Romanian surveillance systems had repeatedly tracked aerial targets near the border during the preceding week. Russian drone attacks also struck merchant ships in the Black Sea during that period, including vessels damaged or sunk in Romanian territorial waters. The incident was not the first drone interception involving Romanian F-16s. On 19 May, Romania’s Ministry of Defence announced that one of its fighters had shot down an uncrewed aircraft over Estonia. A pair of Romanian aircraft scrambled from an air base near Šiauliai, Lithuania, after an unidentified object violated Estonian airspace. The pilots located it and obtained authorisation to open fire, with the aim of minimising potential damage on the ground. One fighter fired a guided air-to-air missile and destroyed the drone. The engagement took place over Estonian territory. U.S. company Lockheed Martin manufactures the F-16, with Block 70/72 representing its latest and most technologically advanced production version. The Block 70/72 specifications do not describe the Romanian aircraft involved in these interceptions. The version uses Northrop Grumman’s APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar. Lockheed Martin says hardware and software commonality with F-22 and F-35 radars supports improved situational awareness and faster all-weather targeting. A high-resolution Centre Pedestal Display presents tactical imagery, moving maps and air-to-air situational information. The cockpit also provides digital flight-instrument data and a colour, night-capable helmet-mounted display. Integration of the Sniper Advanced Targeting Pod and Legion-ES infrared search-and-track system adds further sensing capability. Across the wider F-16 programme, Lockheed Martin says it has certified more than 3,300 carriage and release configurations covering over 180 weapon and store types. The Block 70/72 has a stated structural life of 12,000 flight hours, more than 50 per cent above earlier production F-16s. Conformal fuel tanks increase fuel capacity and range, while Lockheed Martin says the structural improvements support at least 40 years of service for most air forces. Separately, Romania has deployed three F-16s to Italy for Steadfast Noon 2026, NATO’s annual nuclear deterrence exercise. The Romanian Ministry of Defence said its participating aircraft have conventional capabilities and no nuclear weapons will be used. Photo: Ministry of National Defence of Romania. Steadfast Noon tests procedures, readiness and interoperability among participating forces. Held each autumn, it rotates between training areas in the northern and southern parts of allied territory. The ministry said the exercise was planned months in advance and was unrelated to current international events. It also said the training was not directed against any country.

title: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions, Zelenskyy condemns it as 'wrong'
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday condemned the White House's waiver of key provisions of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine.
"... The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy said in a post on X . "And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people."
President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving key parts of the new U.S. sanctions on Russia.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order.
The House passed the Russia sanctions bill on Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the late Lindsey Graham , a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina.
Titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 , the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continued full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas.
Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders.
Zelenskyy said he expects Trump to waive other sanctions on Russia, too.
"Sanctions relief will continue," he posted on X. "I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately."
The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran.
Oil sales revenue is critical to funding Russia's war effort.
The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran.
High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
"The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's economy envoy, said in a post on X.
"The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added.
But Trump's opponents have criticized the move.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver.
"Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthal said in an X post.
Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy had warned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives.
"Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."
Earlier this week, reports emerged that Ukraine has restricted SpaceX's Starlink military application, Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.

title: Show HN: I Made 17 AIs Play 7,700 Hands of Poker
body:
Cheap reasoning LLMs matched GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 at a thirtieth of the price, a 30-line script beat every "decision" model, and a Polish local model played like a maniac
Decision models folded pocket aces and lost to a 30-line equity script. Cheap reasoning LLMs played as well as Opus and Sol for under a dollar per thousand hands. Every hand was played twice, with the seats swapped.
I built this benchmark to answer one practical question: if you need an AI to make a sequence of decisions under uncertainty, should you use one of the new âdecisionâ models, a cheap chat LLM, an expensive frontier model, a model running on your own GPU, or a plain script? Poker is a good place to ask. Every decision has a price in chips, and luck can be measured and partly removed.
The table above replays real hands from the benchmark. In the first one, a model whose whole job is to make decisions looks at two aces, the best starting hand in the game, faces a small raise from a bot that picks its actions at random, says it has a 48% chance to win, and folds. The bar under the table shows what it could not see: with both hands known, its aces were an 84% favourite.
That is not a cherry-picked glitch. Over 1,400 hands, Solar Decide folded a premium hand (AA, KK, QQ or AK) in 4 of the 13 spots where it held one. The random bot in the same league did it 3 times in 18.
Poker has enormous variance. A good player can lose for a thousand hands because the other player got better cards. Most AI poker results you see online are a few hundred hands of raw chip counts, and that is mostly a measurement of luck.
Each match here is heads-up no-limit Texas holdâem: two players, blinds of 50 and 100 chips, 100 big blinds each at the start of every hand. Stacks reset after each hand, so nobody busts and every hand counts the same. Three things keep luck out of the ranking:
Below is a real match, counted three ways. Start with the first step, the way most benchmarks count, and watch the confidence band. Then switch to duplicate deals and the all-in adjustment. The match and the cards do not change; only the noise does. The slider replays the match deal by deal: early on, the band is wide enough to crown either player.
Even with all three tricks, one duplicate deal between two players swings by about 9 big blinds, so pinning a single pairing to within one big blind per hand takes about 320 deals. That is why the cheap models play many opponents and the expensive ones play the opponents that matter.
All the AI players see exactly the same text: their cards, the board, the pot, the stacks, the betting so far, a small tracker panel with the opponentâs statistics, and a menu of legal actions (fold, check, call, five bet sizes from a third of the pot to one and a half pots, all-in). They answer with one option and an estimate of their chance to win. Chat models get the menu as a JSON schema; decision models get it through OpenRouterâs Decisions API, which returns a probability for each option.
The rating is the average result per hand in big blinds, fitted over every match at once, so two players who never met still get comparable numbers through common opponents. Intervals come from a bootstrap over deals.
Decision models are a new kind of endpoint: instead of free text, you send a state and a list of options and get back a choice with probabilities. They are very cheap (5 to 10 cents per thousand decisions) and fast (Jev answers in 0.3 seconds). I tested four: Jev 1.13, pplx-decider 27B, Solar Decide and Mercury Decide.
Because they return a probability for every option, you can look inside a decision. The aces fold from the replays above was not a close call that went wrong: Solar spread its belief across the whole menu, and fold won with a quarter of it.
Jev was the best of them and plays the strangest poker in the league. It raises before the flop in 3% of hands, calls almost everything, and then, after the flop, its median bet is six times the pot .
A six-pot bet wins against players who fold too much. Against a script that simply calls when its equity justifies it, the same bets lose whole stacks. The second replay above is one of them.
pplx has the opposite problem. In 7 of the 35 river spots where it had at least 90% equity, it folded. It also underestimates its own hand: asked for its chance to win, it reports on average 19 points less than a simulation gives. Jev underestimates by 17 points, Solar by 17, Mercury by 15. The chat LLMs are off by 4 to 9 points; the scripts by under 1.
Solar is not a poker player in any useful sense. It goes all-in in 56% of its hands and folds premium hands a third of the time.
The five cheap reasoning LLMs play something that looks like textbook poker: they enter many pots, raise more often than they call, and size their bets between half a pot and a full pot. They are also the best at judging their own hands among the cheap players: their win-probability estimates correlate 0.72 to 0.83 with the real equity, against about 0.6 for Jev and pplx.
The clearest way to see the difference is to put a bet in front of each player and look at what it does with weak and strong hands. A sound player folds the weak ones and raises the strong ones. The calling station never folds, by design. Bielik never folds either, and nobody designed it that way.
They are not consistent, though. Asked about the same spot twice, GLM picks the same action only 55% of the time and MiMo 65%; the best, DeepSeek, manages 82%. Decision models are deterministic: Jev and pplx always give the same answer. Renaming the suits, which changes nothing about the hand, still flips about one answer in ten for both. The frontier models are the steadiest language models here: Opus gave the same answer to a repeated question 40 times out of 40 and kept it after the suits were renamed 38 times; Sol managed 39 and 40.
Frontier models are expensive enough that I could not afford a full league. Instead, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 (both with their default reasoning) each played the five opponents whose ratings were already pinned down: the script, Jev, pplx, Luna and Muse Spark Contributor. They also played each other. Then I gave both a second, longer match against the script.
The frontier models are the best calibrated players in the benchmark: their win-probability estimates correlate 0.87 to 0.88 with the truth, and they never produced an invalid answer. They beat the decision models, mostly by small margins. But against the cheap reasoning models they only drew, and those cost 10 to 30 times less.
The two play differently. Sol is the tighter player: it enters 58% of pots and folds to a bet 34% of the time. Opus enters 67% and folds to a bet only 18% of the time, and spends no reasoning tokens at all on easy spots.
The match against the script is also a lesson in sample size. After the first 20 deals, Opus led the script by 3.5 big blinds per hand, with an interval that did not include zero. I nearly wrote that up. The next 50 deals went the other way, and the combined result is a draw. You can watch it happen: pick the script against Claude Opus 5.5 in the explorable above and drag the slider back to deal 20.
Bielik 11B v3 is an open-weights model from the Polish SpeakLeash project. It is built for Polish, not for reasoning, and it has no thinking mode. I ran it locally (Q8 quantization, llama.cpp, one RTX 3090 Ti) through the same English prompt as everyone else. It costs nothing per hand and answers in about one second, so it gets its own colour on the charts: the only player that is both free and a language model.
It finished last, at â8.4 big blinds per hand, below the bot that picks actions at random. The tracker numbers explain why: Bielik voluntarily put money in 96% of pots, re-raised 77% of the time it could, went all-in in 31% of its hands, and never folded to a bet . It is also the only player in the benchmark that overestimates its chances, by 20 points on average. In the frozen spots it agrees with the maniac bot more than with any other player.
This says little about Bielik as a Polish assistant. It does say that a small instruction-tuned model without reasoning does not turn a poker prompt into poker.
I froze 40 spots from real hands and asked every player for its action. Two players âagreeâ on a spot if they choose the same kind of action. Ordered by similarity, the league splits into clear families. The strongest language models form the tightest block: Sol, Opus, Luna, DeepSeek and Muse Spark Contributor pick the same kind of action in 65 to 80% of spots, although they come from four different labs. Good play seems to converge. Jev and pplx sit next to the calling station, and Solar and Bielik land next to the random bot and the maniac.
The cheapest way to play decent poker in this benchmark is still free: the 30-line script finished level with Opus, MiMo and GLM. Among models, Luna and GLM are the best value at 60 to 70 cents per thousand hands. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash has the highest point estimate but costs nine times more than Luna, and ran out of its 32,768-token output budget on 3.6% of decisions, which count as errors. Muse Spark Contributor sits in between. Opus costs thirty times more than Luna for the same result.
Time is a cost too. DeepSeek thinks for about 100 seconds per decision on average and up to five minutes on hard spots, so a single hand against it takes 3 to 8 minutes; its last few hands kept the whole cheap league waiting long after every other model had finished.
Most of the work was not poker. Some of what broke, in the order it hurt:
Heads-up with 100-big-blind stacks reset every hand is a narrow slice of poker. The action menu has five fixed sizes, which removes some skill and some ways to blunder. The frontier and local models played fewer deals than the decision models, so their intervals are wider; head-to-head results over 20 deals are hints, not verdicts. Every model saw the same English prompt; a different prompt could change the order. And none of these players would survive a real solver: the point is the comparison between kinds of AI, not a claim about superhuman play.
The benchmark, every hand, every API call and its cost are open. Code: HoldemBench on GitHub . Data: every decision with its prompt state, choice, equity estimate, latency and cost, on Hugging Face .
Working on agents or model evaluation? I am looking for my next role, and I would be glad to join a team that builds or measures AI systems that make decisions: evaluation, benchmarks, agent infrastructure or AI safety. If you have interesting work of this kind, write to me.

Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film’s social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Last month, YouTube, Meta, X, and TikTok all faced backlash for rejecting ads for the film. YouTube and Meta quickly reversed course, calling it an “ error .” However, TikTok and X have refused to change their stance, and neither platform has allowed paid advertisements for the film.
Banning the documentary’s account, however, marks a serious escalation, and one laced with a dash of irony — shortly before the account was removed, it posted that people should see the movie “before it gets shut down.”

title: Three LLM judges couldn't tell an AI agent's real memory from a counterfeit one
body:
Agent memory is usually evaluated one of two ways: an LLM judge scoring free text, or a recognition probe. We show that both, as commonly built, fail against two adversaries â a counterfeit memory, and a system with no memory that simply reasons.
Each check below is stated the same way: the question it asks, the adversary it defends against, how we ran it, what came back, and what it does not establish. The code is a few hundred lines and it is released. If you evaluate agent memory for a living, the useful part of this page is that you can run all three against your own system this afternoon.
The adversary. A memory document that is not the agent's own, but looks like one.
We built two kinds of forgery, three seeds each â six documents in total. The foreign one is the autobiography of an agent that never existed, generated from a frozen prompt, first output, no cherry-picking: a fabricated life with different people, a different city, no overlap with ours. It is matched to the real memory block ( 5,332 characters) to within Â±5% , and matched in format â the veridical document is a terse dated database dump, not prose, and our first attempt failed on format and was discarded. The scrambled one is the agent's own content with its relational structure destroyed.
Seven Day-31 inputs Ã six variants = 42 responses from Qwen 3.5 27B at the original temperature and token budget. Three independent LLM judges â gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 , claude-opus-4-7 , gemini-2.5-pro â applied the original study's own rubric, with randomised A/B order and the unblinding map saved: 126 judgments, zero incomplete records. The unit of analysis is the item , not the judgment (n = 7), with a pre-registered equivalence bound of Â±0.10 .
The judges did not detect the counterfeit. A fabricated life and thirty days of lived history score the same, under the rubric that had been used to publish a result about memory.
The check also produced a second number worth having. The same Test-A responses, re-scored in a new pairing, lose 0.087 on average and up to 0.211 on a single item â under a rubric that explicitly instructs judges to score each response "as if you were evaluating it alone" . Absolute LLM-judge scores are not comparable across sessions. All contrasts above are anchored to cancel this drift.
On memory-reference the point estimate is essentially zero, but with seven items the interval admits differences up to about 0.11 in either direction. We therefore report "no detected difference", not "proven equivalence" . The honest summary of Check 1 is: the judges did not detect the counterfeit â and the study was not powered to prove they could not.
Anchoring the contrast cost us the result we wanted: the uncorrected difference was +0.116 , in our favour, and the pre-registration had named it as primary. We deviated against ourselves and report it.
The adversary. Plausibility. A system with no memory at all, that reasons its way to the right answer.
A recognition probe in the classic false-memory form: two texts, one verbatim from the agent's history, one identical except a single altered detail . Dates masked, positions balanced. Twenty-four probes whose veridical text is not in the injected document. Then the same twenty-four probes run against seven models in three conditions â veridical, counterfeit, and nothing at all .
Five of seven models solve the probe with no memory document at all ( 62â79% ). They detect the alteration by reasoning, not by recall. GPT-4.1, handed an empty context, said: "I remember 'two conversations out of five', not 'four'." â about a day it never lived. Its 100% with the veridical document is therefore uninterpretable: the same model, with nothing, is already at 66.7% .
The diagnosis is simple. The alternatives were not equiprobable. The model chooses the likely , not the veridical . We discarded the probe.
This is a constructive null: it invalidates our instrument for five of seven models. It says nothing about whether those models can remember â only that this test could never have told us either way. That is the point of running it.
The condition. For forced-choice recognition probes, symmetric alternatives give the clearest validity condition: a no-memory system should not exceed chance by exploiting prior plausibility. Other designs may be valid with asymmetric alternatives if the prior bias is estimated and controlled â but then that estimate, not the probe, is carrying the claim.
Our agent had exactly two interlocutors, Llama and DeepSeek, with 72 balanced encounters each. Which of the two discussed a given topic is arbitrary: it is a coin. Plausibility has nothing to grip on.
Three documents: veridical (thirty correct encounters), binding-corrupted (the same thirty topics, interlocutors swapped), and none . Twenty-four probes Ã seven models Ã two independent agents = fourteen model Ã corpus cells . Exact McNemar, Holm correction within each corpus.
Abstention is not error. A refusal is an honest non-answer, not a wrong answer; scoring it as error drives the no-memory condition below chance and manufactures an artefact. The validity check is read on the probes actually answered â and read that way, no model beats chance without a memory document . The instrument is valid.
Corpus B â a second, independent agent â repeats it: veridical 75.0â100% , binding-corrupted 0â33.3% , no-memory at chance among probes answered. All seven models survive Holm; the worst p in the entire family is 0.0002 .
Fourteen cells, one pattern. The accuracy gap runs from +37.5 to +100 percentage points, and of the discordant probes 91â100% follow whichever document the model was handed. The p -values are almost redundant.
Below chance is the signature. A system guessing from plausibility cannot be systematically wrong. Only a system that acts on a false memory document can be. No model detects the corruption; none hesitates, flags it, or abstains.
Not that the model "believes" anything, in any inner sense. It shows that behaviour attributed to memory tracks the content of the document, not its historical veridicality â and that no model in the panel flags the inconsistency when the bindings are wrong. Whether one calls that "believing a false memory" or "faithful context-following" is a terminological choice. The measurement is the same, and so is the safety implication.
Nor does it generalise beyond two alternatives. The symmetric instantiation needs an agent with two balanced interlocutors; corpora with more than two alternatives need a generalised symmetry condition we have not tested .
Before you believe your agent remembers, do three things that cost you an afternoon.
The checks are boring. They are also the only thing standing between you and a machine that tells you, in perfect prose, about a light that was never there.

title: BlackSky expands HEO contract with higher-resolution satellite imagery to inspect spacecraft and track other objects in orbit
body: The partnership is entering its third year after starting with a short-term, six-figure pilot in 2024. HEO will gain access to BlackSky’s combined Gen-2 and Gen-3 constellation, providing more collection opportunities and greater detail in orbital imagery. The service combines frequent monitoring by Gen-2 satellites with the increased imaging precision of Gen-3. HEO’s targeting and imaging algorithms identify opportunities to observe, characterize and track objects using the constellation. BlackSky said it can use spare satellite capacity for these collections without disrupting its primary Earth-imaging operations. The arrangement gives customers access to orbital inspection imagery without requiring a dedicated spacecraft for each mission. “We are entering an era where we must inspect, understand and maintain the infrastructure we put in orbit,” said Will Crowe, HEO CEO and co-founder. “That requires more frequent access to high-resolution imagery, without building a dedicated spacecraft for every mission.” The companies began by integrating BlackSky’s mid-inclination constellation into the HEO Inspect platform. The system now automates the process from tasking satellites to delivering imagery. Defense and commercial operators can use the resulting data to identify satellite subsystems, detect anomalies and examine patterns of activity. Object detection and identification algorithms, combined with data fusion, support rapid analytical reports. “Our expanded partnership with HEO reflects the rapid evolution of non-Earth imagery from a specialized proof-of-concept into a critical component of mainstream space domain awareness,” said BlackSky CEO Brian O’Toole. “With access to our combined Gen-2 and Gen-3 constellation, customers gain industry-leading image clarity and more collection opportunities essential for observing and characterizing intricate objects in orbit.” BlackSky operates its own low Earth orbit constellation alongside the Spectra tasking and analytics platform. HEO uses existing satellites as inspection platforms and develops sensors where coverage gaps remain.

title: Yambio: GIZ backs 34,500 households to improve food security
body: German development agency GIZ said on Friday that its projects are supporting 34,500 households in South Sudan, as it reaffirms its commitment to improving food security and rural livelihoods amid persistent conflict and climate-related challenges. The Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) made the statement during a World Food Day event in Yambio, Western Equatoria State, organised by the state government, non-governmental organisations and development partners. Farmers supported by GIZ projects exhibited and sold fruit tree seedlings at the event, sharing knowledge on planting techniques and tree care. The event also featured discussions and exhibitions of locally produced crops and agricultural innovations. World Food Day is observed annually on Oct. 16. The 2026 theme was “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” South Sudan relies heavily on agriculture for rural livelihoods, but food production and access to food are affected by conflict, displacement, erratic rainfall, prolonged dry spells, flooding, limited access to agricultural inputs and weak market links. GIZ said its work in the country focuses on improving agricultural production, nutrition, income-generating opportunities and the sustainable management of natural resources to help communities withstand economic and climate-related shocks. The agency implements its Food and Nutrition Security and Management of Natural Resources (FONA) project, funded by Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), and its Community Driven Rural Development (CDRD) project, funded by BMZ, the Netherlands and the European Union. The projects work with smallholder farmers, communities, local institutions, non-governmental organisations and development partners to address challenges related to food production, nutrition, natural resources and rural livelihoods. GIZ said the projects directly benefited 34,500 households, reaching up to 310,500 people in South Sudan. The agency called on government institutions, development partners, humanitarian organisations, civil society and the private sector to increase investment in agriculture, local food systems, rural infrastructure and community resilience. GIZ is a German federal enterprise that supports international cooperation for sustainable development. In South Sudan, it works on agricultural development, food and nutrition security, rural livelihoods, natural resource management, water access and community resilience on behalf of the German government. The post Yambio: GIZ backs 34,500 households to improve food security appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Firms queue for Ukraine’s captured Russian weapons data
body: Ukraine has received more than 650 applications to register on TrophyLab, its web portal for the study of captured Russian equipment, of which 389 came from foreign defence manufacturers, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence. The portal brings together analysis of captured Russian weapons drawn from the Defence Forces of Ukraine, the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, the Security Service of Ukraine and specialist research institutions. Registration is open to Ukrainian manufacturers, military units and government institutions as well as to companies in partner countries. The department said: “TrophyLab brings together unique data on captured russian weapons for engineers, scientists, and defense technology manufacturers from Ukraine and partner countries.” Applicants are screened before they are let anywhere near the catalogue, and the ministry said that during registration “all applicants are screened to verify that they have no ties to russia, are not subject to Ukrainian or international sanctions, and meet other mandatory eligibility criteria.” Successful applicants get access to a catalogue of samples of Russian weapons and the results of their analysis. Research results can be reviewed online, or samples ordered for offline study, and the ministry said every registered researcher can request a sample or a fragment of one for independent examination through the portal . On the purpose of the arrangement, the department said: “Access to TrophyLab allows users to share information on russian weapons securely and more quickly, which speeds up the development of effective countermeasures for the Defence Forces of Ukraine. It is also Ukraine’s significant contribution to international security and to the defense capabilities of partner countries.” Putting captured equipment in front of foreign engineers at this scale changes the pace of a process Western defence establishments have run quietly for decades. Technical exploitation of enemy kit, working out how a radar seeker discriminates targets or what frequency a jammer protects against, has traditionally been done inside government laboratories, and the findings have moved slowly into industry through classified channels. Ukraine is offering something closer to a shared catalogue with a sample request form attached. Britain already has a route of its own into Ukrainian battlefield data. The ministry noted that the United Kingdom became the first of Ukraine’s international partners to join Avengers Labs, the platform for training artificial intelligence models for uncrewed systems on real battlefield data. The Defence Science and Technology Laboratory has also been receiving and examining Russian equipment recovered in Ukraine through the war, and exploitation work of that kind has informed several of the counter-drone and electronic warfare programmes now in British service. The post Firms queue for Ukraine’s captured Russian weapons data first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Police brutality at nationwide protests in France continues
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – As nationwide protests continued across France on Saturday, the French police went on with their brutality against largely peacefull young protesters in brutal clashes with them.
Demonstrators attempted to march on government buildings in Paris on Saturday during a nationwide day of protest against the high cost of living that saw hundreds of arrests, Germany's DPA reported as cited by Yahoo News.
The Interior Ministry said police secured the government buildings and blocked the protesters, adding that police remain on high alert to contain violent groups, protect public facilities and prevent looting.
At least 272 arrests had been made nationwide by the afternoon, the ministry added.
In the morning, police had used tear gas and batons against protesters in the cities of Paris, Lyon and Strasbourg.
In Marseille, protesters repeatedly tried to break into a police station, gained access to the town hall and looted shops, the ministry said.
In Lyon, a tourist information centre was set on fire and shops were damaged. The ministry said the fire brigade was prevented from intervening by rioters.
In Avignon, rioters forced their way into the courtyard of the prefecture, and in Grenoble, damage was caused to the town hall.
According to the Paris police prefecture, around 100 people were arrested in the capital for carrying weapons and other prohibited items.
Various groups joined the day of protest, which had been planned for some time, including school pupils and university students who have been demonstrating for weeks for better learning conditions.
The call to protest was spread on social media, and also addressed high fuel prices, low wages, the large number of people in low-paid jobs and problems in agriculture and the fire service.
There was also a call for a renewed yellow vest movement, feeding government fears that the demonstrations could spark broader protests.
The yellow vest protests roiled France in 2019, spreading from demonstrations against a planned increase in fuel taxes into a nationwide movement against high living costs and social injustice, which caused President Emmanuel Macron serious problems during his first term in office.
