title: Drones hit gold mining site in South Kordofan
body: Drones operated by Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) attacked a gold mining site in South Kordofan state on Friday, damaging four gold-processing facilities, the Sudanese Mineral Resources Company said on Saturday. The attack targeted the market at the Bajon mine in Qadeer Locality, causing material damage, the state-owned company said. Preliminary assessments indicated that no deaths or injuries had been reported. Mohamed Abdelrahim, director general of the company’s environment and safety department, said the attack took place during the Friday holiday, when workers were absent from the targeted facilities. The company said it was coordinating with the relevant authorities to assess the damage and determine the extent of the losses. The incident was the second reported attack on the mine in less than a week. The site is a gold-producing centre that employs large numbers of artisanal miners. Eastern South Kordofan is home to thousands of artisanal gold miners operating in the localities of Qadeer, El Liri and Talodi. The mining areas lie near territory controlled by the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdelaziz al-Hilu, which is allied with the RSF. The post Drones hit gold mining site in South Kordofan appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says
body:
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt .
Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.
“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”
It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.
After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.
Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted onstage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.
“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models … OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”
However, Masad’s comments onstage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between Anthropic and Replit. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.
There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.
Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.
“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”
Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.
Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.
“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”
This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 p.m. PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. Its title has been updated, as well.

title: Microsoft and CMU Team Up to Train Early Career Software Engineers
body:
In between classes on machine learning and software engineering, Jace Watson isn't heading back to his dorm or finding a quiet place to study somewhere on Carnegie Mellon University's campus.
That's because Watson isn't even in Pittsburgh. He's in Seattle, working at his full-time job as a software engineer at Microsoft and taking classes through the Preceptorship for AI-accelerated Software Engineering (PRAISE) program , which CMU and Microsoft launched to train early career software engineers for the rapidly changing computer science landscape.
"When I started undergraduate, it was the beginning of AI being something that everybody had access to on their own computers. As I got closer to graduation, it started becoming clear how big AI tools would be in the workforce, but using AI wasn't a huge part of my education," Watson said. "When I joined Microsoft, these tools were part of my day-to-day, and I wanted to make sure I knew how to fully take advantage of them, which is why I sought out the additional education opportunity through CMU and Microsoft."
The CMU/Microsoft PRAISE program offers early career Microsoft employees a chance to take online courses in CMU's Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science while receiving hands-on mentorship at the company. At Microsoft, selected early career engineers, or preceptees, work with senior engineering preceptors to build AI-accelerated software engineering skills through structured guidance, mentorship and application to their day-to-day Microsoft work. Participants can also enroll in SCS classes focused on software engineering and artificial intelligence.
"This partnership with Microsoft is about providing the Griffin School of Computer Science's high-quality computer science learning to people who aren't in the traditional education system but are seeking guidance to navigate a rapidly changing landscape," said SCS Dean Martial Hebert . "SCS and Microsoft recognize that we all have a part to play in supporting and readying the nation's workforce, and the CMU/Microsoft PRAISE program is an innovative step in that direction."
The idea for the program came about following CMU alumnus Mark Russinovich's (ENG 1989, 1994) visit to SCS in October 2025. The chief technology officer, deputy chief information security officer and technical fellow for Microsoft Azure spoke about how AI tools help senior engineers, but noted that the same level of benefit isn't available for junior engineers.
"AI changes the work, but it doesn't eliminate the need for junior engineers or for human judgment and accountability," Russinovich said. "By combining Microsoft's engineering experience with CMU's academic expertise, PRAISE offers a model we're proud to lead and hope others in industry and academia will adopt."
From that discussion, SCS and Microsoft began considering how education could help junior engineers overcome the challenges of using AI in the workplace.
"It used to be that early career software engineers would do a lot of tasks that would build up their expertise," said Michael Hilton , a teaching professor in CMU's Software and Societal Systems Department (S3D). "Combining forces between academics and practitioners allows us to bring our expertise together and create solutions that draw on computer science research while standing up to the daily realities of software development."
This semester, Microsoft employees enrolled in the CMU PRAISE certificate program are taking Machine Learning in Production and Preceptorship in AI-Augmented Software Engineering I. These classes train students on how to incorporate machine learning into the software they write and to use AI tools while developing that software.
"That judgment for when to use AI should be viewed as ongoing education, which is why we're partnering with Carnegie Mellon University on curriculum as part of the PRAISE program," Microsoft wrote in their announcement of the partnership. "The intent is to set students up for success in the workplace and accelerate preceptees with formal curricula to complement the guidance from the preceptor on how to build and deliver with confidence."
In the spring semester, students will take DevOps: Engineering for Secure Development and Deployment and the second half of the Preceptorship in AI-Augmented Software Engineering course sequence. These courses can be applied to a master's degree in software engineering, allowing students to further their learning at SCS. CMU hopes to grow the program and add more students to the certificate program, perhaps one day opening the door to other industry partners.
"I am tremendously excited about the impact this program will have on junior engineers at Microsoft," said Jonathan Aldrich , an S3D professor who directs the PRAISE certificate program. "With so many companies worldwide faced with upheaval due to AI in software development, I believe this program will become a template for rapidly leveling up new developers across the industry."
To learn more about the program, visit Microsoft's Command Line .

title: No estimate given for Achilles delay after dock fire
body: The Ministry of Defence has declined to estimate how far the completion of the submarine HMS Achilles has slipped as a result of the 2024 fire in the Devonshire Dock Hall at Barrow-in-Furness, according to an answer given in Parliament. Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the estimated length of the delay, following an answer of 8 September. Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Work to recover from the impact of the fire in the Devonshire Dock Hall is progressing well. Achilles, the seventh and last boat of the class, remains at an advanced stage of build in Barrow-in-Furness. “The planned in-service dates for Royal Navy submarines are withheld as disclosure would, or would be likely to, prejudice the capability, effectiveness, or security of the Armed Forces.” Because in-service dates for Royal Navy submarines are withheld, the schedule Achilles was working to before the fire is not public either, so the size of any slip cannot be worked out from the published record, and the department gave neither a length of delay nor a cost. The Devonshire Dock Hall is the covered building hall at Barrow where British submarines are assembled, and the fire there in 2024 interrupted work on the yard’s output. Achilles is the seventh and final boat of the Astute class. The Astute class are nuclear powered attack submarines armed with Spearfish torpedoes and Tomahawk land attack cruise missiles, built by BAE Systems at Barrow-in-Furness around a Rolls-Royce pressurised water reactor fuelled for the life of the boat. Seven were ordered, and the first of class, HMS Astute, commissioned in 2010. The post No estimate given for Achilles delay after dock fire first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Where Are The Aircraft Carriers?: October 17, 2026
body: With a flight deck packed with carrier-based aircraft, including stealthy fifth-generation F-35Cs, the USS Theodore Roosevelt pulled into Yokosuka, Japan, on Friday. Roosevelt is the first non-resident U.S. carrier to visit the key naval port, strategically located on the east side of Japan, in more than four years. Yokosuka is home to the USS George Washington and America’s only forward-based Carrier Strike Group (CSG). The Roosevelt , which serves as the flagship of CSG 9, escorted by guided-missile cruiser USS Chosin and destroyer USS Decatur , completed the journey from San Diego in 19 days − maneuvering around a typhoon in the Western Pacific − and will participate in the upcoming combined exercise Keen Sword 27. Meanwhile, the USS George H.W. Bush departed Thailand after a five-day port call and returned to the Middle East, and the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived home after a nearly eleven-month combat deployment. In This Article Theodore Roosevelt Docks In Yokosuka, Japan; First Visiting Carrier In Four Years Abraham Lincoln’s Homecoming George H.W. Bush Leaves Thailand And Returns To The Middle East F-35C Lightning II Operates from A Ford Class Carrier For The First Time Big Deck Fleet At A Glance SHOW 2 MORE Here’s TWZ’s weekly carrier tracker monitoring America’s flattop fleet, including deployed CSGs and Amphibious Ready Groups (ARGs), using publicly available open-source information. Check out last week’s report here . TWZ/IAN ELLIS-JONES Theodore Roosevelt Docks In Yokosuka, Japan; First Visiting Carrier In Four Years Roosevelt and Chosin chopped into the U.S. 7th Fleet-Pacific Command (PACOM) area of responsibility (AOR) and arrived at Commander, Fleet Activities Yokosuka on the morning of October 16. The CSG will spend a few days in port before beginning participation in exercise Keen Sword, a “premier joint-bilateral field training exercise designed to increase readiness and interoperability between the Japan Self-Defense Forces and U.S. military forces,” according to the 7th Fleet press release . The brief visit allows the crew to complete maintenance, resupply, and disembark for liberty before resuming routine operations. “Our crew is honored to visit Yokosuka and experience the rich culture and hospitality of Japan,” the commanding officer of Roosevelt , Capt. Will Mathis, said in the release. “Port visits like this are vital for crew morale and mission readiness, allowing our Sailors to rest, recharge, and prepare to operate seamlessly alongside our allies during exercise Keen Sword.” Roosevelt arrives in Yokosuka, Japan. U.S. Navy photo Roosevelt moors at Commander, Fleet Activities Yokosuka. U.S. Navy photo The five-ship CSG, the composition of which a Navy official confirmed to TWZ , is currently operating on a disaggregated basis − a common practice employed by strike groups with multiple ongoing missions. The duo that departed the U.S. at the end of September linked up with another element of the group, Pearl Harbor-based guided missile destroyer USS Decatur , as they were steaming westbound past the Hawaiian Islands, based on public Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. Decatur arrived in Yokosuka the day after Roosevelt but was not mentioned in the press release. USS Carl M. Levin , also stationed in Hawaii, was the first ship from the group to deploy, according to DVIDS, the military’s content-sharing platform. Levin departed on September 9 and is operating at an undisclosed location. USS Paul Hamilton , the final ship assigned to CSG 9 to deploy, left San Diego on October 10 after onloading ammo at Bravo Pier and moored at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam on October 15, AIS data shows. Henry J. Kaiser class fleet replenishment oiler USNS Tippecanoe supported the group’s transit across the Pacific, conducting multiple replenishments-at-sea (RAS), and recently entered the East Sea/Sea of Japan via the Tsugaru Strait before going dark on AIS. Chosin alongside Roosevelt. Navy photo Decatur and Roosevelt at RIMPAC. Navy photo Tippecanoe conducts a RAS. Navy photo Multiple reports indicated that medium unmanned surface vessel (MUSV) Seahawk (2) deployed with the group, which would represent a significant operational achievement and the first time a drone boat was assigned to a CSG, but the MUSV quietly slipped out of Point Loma on October 8, more than ten days after Roosevelt . Seahawk reappeared on AIS and docked in Hawaii for a couple days before continuing its journey westbound in the Pacific on October 16. If Seahawk is assigned to CSG 9, it is currently disaggregated, and whether it will join Roosevelt to participate in exercise Keen Sword 27 is unknown. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao seemingly confirmed the deployment, saying during a panel at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) convention that “the Teddy Roosevelt carrier strike group just deployed on October 8 with a medium sized unmanned surface vessel. This is the first carrier strike group to ever deploy with a large size unmanned surface vessel.” However, Roosevelt was more than halfway to Japan on the date referenced. “This is a force multiplier, imagine having more guns out there,” he added. MUSV Seahawk leaving Point Loma in August. U.S. Navy photo Seahawk’s transit out of San Diego. Source: MarineTraffic/KPLER TWZ reached out to the Secretary’s office for clarification and to confirm the deployment but did not receive a response. “ Seahawk’s operations represent continued progress in the Navy’s efforts to integrate unmanned systems into Fleet operations. As with any emerging capability, we continue to learn, adapt, and refine how these systems are employed,” a Navy official told us. Abraham Lincoln’s Homecoming Surrounded by small boats, with hundreds of spectators lining the channel in San Diego Bay and thousands more watching online, the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived home from a historic ten-and-a-half-month combat deployment. The flagship of CSG 3 and her crew of more than 5,000 Sailors and Marines served as the tip of the spear in the war against the Iranian regime, first during Operation Epic Fury and then the subsequent blockades , and set a new record for the most consecutive days at sea without a port call. USS Abraham Lincoln pulls into San Diego Bay. U.S. Navy photo Lincoln pulled into Naval Air Station North Island and moored at Berth Lima on October 8, 321 days after casting off on November 21, 2025. Sailors in dress whites manned the rails as the carrier transited the bay, escorted on both sides by small boats and jet skis flying American flags, while family and friends eagerly waited pierside for their return. The video below, shared by the Pentagon, captures the moment. Family and friends welcome the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln home. Pentagon video. Lincoln now lays claim to the second-longest deployment in the modern carrier era, falling just five days short of the 326-day post-Vietnam record held by the USS Gerald R. Ford . The flattop traveled over 93,000 nautical miles during the cruise − more than four trips around the Earth, a post by the public affairs officer highlighted − and conducted 72 replenishments-at-sea, received 20-plus million gallons of aviation fuel, and flew more than 14,000 sorties that totaled 28,500 flight hours, a press release from the Navy highlighted. The release confirmed for the first time that Lincoln broke the previous record of 206 days set by USS Dwight D. Eisenhower during the COVID pandemic for days spent underway between port visits, as TWZ first reported . “The ship’s 208 uninterrupted days at sea between Guam and Oman, and its 286 consecutive days at sea between departing San Diego and arriving in Thailand, are record-breaking marks for modern aircraft carriers.” Lincoln’s cruise took her through both U.S. 7th Fleet and U.S. 5th Fleet AORs. During Operation Epic Fury, which began on February 28 and lasted almost 40 days, Lincoln took up station in the northern Arabian Sea as Commander, Task Force (CTF) 50 and pressured Iran’s southern flank. When major combat operations wound down, the carrier and her air wing patrolled and enforced the blockade line during both rounds that followed. Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 9, the “Navy’s premier next-generation air wing that served as the primary offensive power” for CSG 3, flew 14,037 sorties − including 4,000 combat missions − and dropped more than 1.37 million pounds of ordnance on thousands of targets while employing 1,499 precision weapons. “This concentrated firepower significantly degraded Iranian Navy capabilities,” a separate statement noted. “The rapid mobilization and combat execution of CVW-9 during Operation Epic Fury demonstrated the unmatched flexibility of a U.S. Navy carrier strike group,” Capt. J.W. Stigi, commander of CVW-9, said in the statement. “Pairing fifth-generation F-35C stealth and sensor fusion with fourth-generation workhorse strike and electronic attack platforms, Team Shogun destroyed Iran’s conventional Navy and secured vital maritime chokepoints in support of our commander’s objectives.” Kill marks painted on the island superstructure show CSG 3 destroyed 106 one-way attack drones fired by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), 34 Iranian Navy and IRGC ships, 23 inbound cruise missiles, and 10 enemy submarines. The strike group dropped 1,463 air-to-ground munitions in total, a Sailor explaining the marks said in a video on social media. George H.W. Bush Leaves Thailand And Returns To The Middle East The USS George H.W. Bush and her destroyer escort, USS Delbert D. Black , departed Phuket, Thailand, on October 9 after a five-day liberty visit. “Nearly 5,000 Sailors from across the strike group experienced the sights and sounds Thailand has to offer, deepening their understanding of the Thai people and strengthening interpersonal bonds,” according to a press release . George H.W. Bush departs Phuket, Thailand, on October 9, 2026. U.S. Navy photo “The Sailors and I had an amazing time in this beautiful country, and I sincerely thank the people of Thailand for their incredible welcome,” Capt. Justin T. Issler, the commanding officer of George H.W. Bush, said about the stop. “This port visit to Phuket was a tremendous opportunity for the crew. We are grateful to our Thai allies for hosting us, and we look forward to continuing our mission here in 7th Fleet, alongside Thailand and our other regional allies and partners.” USS George H.W. Bush arrives in Thailand. U.S. Navy photo USS George H.W. Bush anchors in Phuket. U.S. Navy photo Bush dropped anchor approximately two nautical miles south of Ao Makham Deep Sea Port on October 4 after 187 consecutive days at sea. After leaving Phuket, the carrier stopped broadcasting AIS while steaming due south at 10 knots. Imagery on DVIDS confirms that the CSG returned to the Middle East and operating in the U.S. 5th Fleet AOR to “support maritime security and stability,” joining the George Washington CSG once again as the second strike group in the region. Destroyer USS Mason , which deployed as the integrated air and missile defense (IAMD) commander for the CSG but has disaggregated at times, arrived in Singapore on October 5, likely for a port call. The Arleigh Burke class destroyer departed on October 9 and was last tracked heading northwestbound in the Malacca Strait, likely to rejoin the CSG. The other two destroyers assigned to the CSG, USS Ross and USS Donald Cook , remained in 5th Fleet during the visit. F-35C Lightning II Operates from A Ford Class Carrier For The First Time Marking a major milestone, an F-35C Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter made the first arrested landing aboard a Gerald R. Ford class carrier, the Navy’s newest and most advanced class of aircraft carriers that are being built to replace the aging Nimitz fleet. The trap was made by Lt. Cmdr. Robert Mason with the “Salty Dogs” of Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 23 aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy in the Western Atlantic on October 13. The first catapult launch followed the next day, pictures on DVIDS showed. F-35Cs approach for first landing aboard PCU John F. Kennedy. U.S. Navy video VX-23, based out of Naval Air Station Patuxent River in Maryland, is part of the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division and was putting Kennedy through the ongoing Aircraft Compatibility Testing to assess the “operational capabilities of the ship’s aircraft launch and recovery equipment.” A team from the Patuxent River-based F-35 Integrated Test Force, detached to the ship, conducted the evaluation using a specially instrumented example of the jet. One of the two pictured was externally equipped with an inert Joint Direct Attack Munition (JDAM) bomb. VX-23 F-35Cs flying over and on the flight deck of PCU John F. Kennedy. U.S. Navy photos The Navy took preliminary acceptance of Kennedy , which is still considered a Pre-Commissioning Unit, on September 29. This process allows the service to conduct at-sea testing and build underway proficiency while the shipbuilder, Huntington Ingalls Industries, completes final system checks ahead of expected delivery in spring 2027. Kennedy got underway on October 13 and returned to her homeport of Naval Station Norfolk three days later. The lead ship of the class, the USS Gerald R. Ford , does not currently embark F-35Cs and will need upgrades to field the Navy’s most advanced jet. Back in 2019, TWZ warned that the stealth jet wouldn’t fly from the troubled class for years. Because of this, Congress required that Kennedy be equipped to embark F-35Cs, which led to additional delays for the Navy’s next carrier. Big Deck Fleet At A Glance Overall, three U.S. carriers are deployed, three are working up in various states of readiness, three are in maintenance availabilities, one is post-deployment, one is being used primarily for training before deactivation next year, and another will be delivered in 2027. Two amphibious ready groups are deployed, one is forward-deployed, three are working up or in port, and three are in maintenance. Note: Positions are general approximations. Non-deployed LHA/LHD amphibious warships are not shown. Contact the author: ian@twz.com or @ianellisjones The post Where Are The Aircraft Carriers?: October 17, 2026 appeared first on TWZ .

title: Iron Duke refit cost a hundred million before withdrawal
body: The life extension programme for HMS Iron Duke cost £102.9 million and ran for 208 weeks between May 2019 and May 2023, and a further £4.7 million was spent on a towed sonar array conversion that was then cancelled, according to written evidence submitted to the Defence Committee. The figures were supplied by the Ministry of Defence in answer to follow-up questions from the committee’s High North inquiry, after members pressed the Minister during oral evidence on 15 July. The committee asked for the precise money spent on the deep maintenance of Iron Duke and HMS Richmond, and for the reason it was not then judged cost-effective to keep either in service. One of the questions put to the Minister ran: “We spent over £100 million on refitting Iron Duke a small number of years ago. In fact, I think the refit took longer than the payback of service. What is the precise reason that HMS Iron Duke was taken out of service?” A second asked: “We were going to fit a towed sonar array to Iron Duke as well. That plan was started and then abandoned. Could you tell the Committee how much money was spent on that plan?” The department set out the costs, dates and durations of the life extension programmes for both ships. HMS Iron Duke’s ran to £102.9 million from May 2019 to May 2023. HMS Richmond’s cost £72.0 million and ran for 126 weeks from October 2017 to June 2020. On why Iron Duke went, the department said: “HMS Iron Duke was taken out of service because the ship required significant additional structural repairs and investment which could not be justified given its remaining service life and the availability of other frigates to meet operational requirements.” On the abandoned sonar conversion, it said: “The Ministry of Defence keeps all capability programmes under regular review to ensure they remain affordable, deliver value for money, and align with operational priorities. The decision to cancel the Iron Duke conversion programme was based on a comprehensive assessment. Given the platform’s remaining service life, the time required to complete the conversion, and competing operational priorities, the benefits of proceeding did not justify the additional cost or extended period out of service. Resources were therefore re-prioritised to deliver greater operational effect. Approximately £4.7 million was spent before the conversion was cancelled.” On Richmond, the department said: “HMS Richmond was found to require a major refit to address structural defects. This would have produced limited availability before her planned out of service date. Focussing investment and resources on sustaining the remaining Type 23 frigates and supporting the entry to service of the Type 26 and Type 31 frigates was deemed better value for money.” Iron Duke came out of Devonport in 2023 after four years alongside, emerging with new diesel generators, upgraded Sea Ceptor and Artisan radar, and she was withdrawn in 2025 along with Richmond. The dates bear out the point the committee put to the Minister. Her life extension ran for 208 weeks and she gave the fleet about half that in sea service before coming off the operational list. The towed array conversion would have turned Iron Duke from a general purpose Type 23 into a towed array frigate, the variant that carries Sonar 2087 and does the deep anti-submarine work in the Greenland Iceland United Kingdom gap. The Royal Navy has been short of towed array hulls for years, with the general purpose ships retired first and the specialist ones held on while Type 26 is built, so converting one was a way of propping up the number before the new class arrives. Both ships went as part of the equipment reductions that have taken the frigate force down while the Type 26 and Type 31 programmes run. The first of class in both programmes, Glasgow on the Clyde and Venturer at Rosyth, are still working towards the point at which they can take on the tasks the departing Type 23s were doing. The post Iron Duke refit cost a hundred million before withdrawal first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: All-front ceasefire essential to ending regional war
body:
EHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh says ending the war on all fronts is a key condition for peace, stressing that continued fighting in any part of the region would mean the war persists across the region.
In an interview with Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen television network on Friday, Khatibzadeh – who arrived in Beirut on Wednesday for talks with Lebanese officials – said Iran remained committed to ending the Israeli war on Lebanon and had secured this objective in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, which Iran and the United States signed in mid-June this year.
He said Lebanon was among the key issues discussed between Iran and the US, adding that he sought to bring the two sides closer during his visit to Beirut. Khatibzadeh said that he held “good” talks with Lebanese officials, including Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, and officials at the Foreign Ministry.
The Iranian official stressed that Israel must end its war in Lebanon and the Levant, noting that developments in both regions are interconnected.
One of Iran’s conditions is an end to all wars, he said, adding that if fighting continues on any one of these fronts, it means the war continues on all fronts. That is why Iran remained committed to ending the war in Lebanon and managed to achieve that goal, he noted.
The Iranian diplomat also said that Washington and Tel Aviv violated the Islamabad understanding through their attacks on Iran and Lebanon, adding that US efforts to secure a ceasefire and end Israel’s war on Lebanon had reached a deadlock. He said Israel could not be trusted to honor its commitments and that Washington was responsible for restraining its regional ally.
Khatibzadeh described the US war against Iran as illegal under international law, saying Washington had failed to destroy Iran’s air defenses and deterrence capabilities. He said Iran had resisted an existential war and would continue defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
He added that Tehran was ready to address concerns raised by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the United States over Iran’s peaceful nuclear activities, citing more than 15 IAEA reports that he said confirmed Iran’s compliance with its commitments.
Khatibzadeh also said Iran had proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, emphasizing that Tehran did not seek war but would resist any imposed conflict.
He further described Hezbollah as a Lebanese political party established to end Israeli attacks and occupation, adding that Iran’s relations with its allies were based on shared beliefs, values and principles.

title: Ukraine hits Russian drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast
body:
Ukraine's General Staff reported on Oct. 17 that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast the day before.
According to the report , the strike targeted a production and storage facility belonging to Roboavia, a company that develops and manufactures drones for the Russian military, near the settlement of Lenina in Rostov Oblast.
Among the drones it produces are the Sarych, which uses video and thermal imaging equipment for surveillance, and the Klin , a loitering munition designed to strike targets, according to Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
Roboavia is linked to Russia's Era Military Innovation Complex, a Defense Ministry project focused on developing military technology. The General Staff said the strike was intended to interfere with drone production and deliveries to Russian forces. The extent of the damage and its result on operations remains unconfirmed.
The military also reported that Ukrainian forces struck a logistics warehouse used by a Russian missile brigade near Latyshi in Bryansk Oblast on Oct. 12.
The Ukrainian military said the strikes were aimed at aimed at disrupting UAV production and supply to Russian forces.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted facilities supporting Russia's war effort, including defense manufacturing plants and military supply infrastructure.

title: PwnEscape: Guest-to-Host KVM Escape (CVE-2026-99999)
body:
How a $1 million sandbox challenge led us to a vulnerability in Linux networking, repeatable host-memory disclosure, and ultimately a full guest-to-host escape.
On August 18, 2026, Vercel announced a $1 million challenge inviting researchers to break the isolation boundary of its Sandbox product (total prize pool). The announcement came just weeks after OpenAI had disclosed a remarkable security incident : AI agents running inside restricted evaluation environments had found ways around their network isolation, compromised internal infrastructure, and eventually breached systems at Hugging Face. The agents weren't supposed to have internet access in the first place.
But there was an important distinction. Escaping a sandbox's network restrictions is one thing. Escaping the virtual machine itself and reaching the host is another. Vercel's challenge explicitly invited researchers to attempt both. We were interested in the latter. (Although we ended up finding vulnerabilities that also allow the former - more on those findings in a later post)
The question was simple: how much could an untrusted guest influence the host kernel without ever exploiting KVM itself? We took the challenge, put our research infrastructure to work, and within three days discovered a primitive buried in Linux networking that allowed guest-controlled checksum metadata to rewrite an IPv4 header after the kernel had already validated it .
What initially looked like a 32-byte host-memory disclosure would eventually become a full guest-to-host escape in our own KVM and many many other Hypervisor environments. And the beautiful part about it was that the vulnerability wasn't even in the hypervisor, it was in the Linux networking stack.
Vercel later described it as the program's most important report , and its final tally recorded just one Critical finding. That Critical was what is now pwnescape. Together with a separate network-escape report, we had accomplished both network and host escape goals. Its important to emphasize Vercel's sandbox was already hardened beyond normal industry standards and had no misconfigurations we could spot. Although the vulnerability originated in the Linux kernel and wasn't a Vercel-specific flaw or misconfiguration, Vercel deserves tremendous credit for how they handled it. They moved quickly to protect their customers, launched their own independent research, identified and notified other affected hypervisor and sandbox providers, and worked closely with us to coordinate disclosure and fixes across the industry. Their efforts helped protect not just Vercel's customers, but the wider ecosystem.
This is the story of CVE-2026-99999, a Critical rated Linux kernel vulnerability leading to KVM escape.
We used Omega-Pwn, pwn.ai's experimental research harness combining our custom security architecture and automation with elements of OmegaClaw , developed by researchers at SingularityNET and BGI Labs for this ambitious project. Compared to traditional LLM harnesses, it enabled longer research horizons, persistent campaign state, parallel collaborative investigations, and the accumulation of hypotheses, failed experiments, and evidence across complex research sessions.
Humans led the research, framing the hard questions, engineering workflows, and directing investigations. GPT-5.6 Sol served as the primary reasoning engine for source-level analysis, exploring attack paths, and challenging assumptions. Omega-Pwn bridged human intuition and contextual insight with the analytical capabilities of advanced LLMs.
As far as we know, PwnEscape exposes an entirely new class of attacks in Linux networking: untrusted checksum metadata can rewrite security-sensitive packet fields after the kernel has already validated and acted on them, undermining assumptions across the networking stack far beyond the original VM escape.
The accepted Linux fix is upstream as 6785011f8b16 , ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum .
This is the first installment of PwnEscape . We are going to spend most of it inside sk_buff , checksum metadata, and IPv4 fragmentation, because that is where the actual failure happened.
Figure 1. Diagram showing guest-origin packet bytes and checksum metadata crossing through virtual networking into the host Linux networking stack.
Figure 1. The vulnerable component is the host networking stack. “KVM escape” describes the guest/host security boundary crossed in our isolated proof, not the source file that contained the bug.
Our previous kvmCTF research was about KVM's shadow-MMU behavior: an intricate interaction among mappings, reverse maps, and memory lifetime. This campaign began with a broader hypothesis. The security of a sandbox depends on much more than its hypervisor. A guest interacts with an entire host operating system, including device emulation, virtual networking, packet filters, memory allocators, and the APIs that glue those pieces together.
For pwn, that suggested an efficient research strategy: map the reachable boundary, search for places where untrusted state gets promoted to trusted state, and challenge the assumptions at every later consumer , not just at the initial parser. We used GPT5-6-Sol-assisted source inspection with human set the scope and decide what actually constitutes evidence. The particularly interesting question at this time was:
Can an asynchronous or deferred operation modify packet bytes after the kernel has already made security-relevant decisions about those same bytes?
Linux checksum offload offered exactly that possibility.
Linux does not always compute transport checksums immediately. Instead, it can carry a packet in a state where the checksum still needs to be completed. The relevant sk_buff bookkeeping includes:
This is normal, documented functionality. On the transmit side, a network device or the software helper skb_checksum_help() can calculate the checksum and store the result at the designated field. In well-formed TCP/UDP traffic, that field belongs to the transport checksum. In the ordinary kernel path, the metadata is supposed to describe the packet that actually exists. See the kernel checksum-offload documentation .
The critical point is that these values are not just descriptive metadata . They authorize a subsequent write into packet memory. If less-trusted software can influence them, their validity must survive every operation between admission and completion.
An sk_buff also has multiple notions of where packet data begins:
The distinction between the frame-relative view and the network-header-relative view is important. A packet can arrive with Ethernet and additional link-layer headers still in its linear data. Later, those headers are removed or skipped for L3 processing. Merely checking that a checksum start falls far enough into the original frame is not the same as proving that it follows the IPv4 header after normalization.
Figure 2. Diagram comparing frame-relative and network-header-relative packet coordinates before and after link-layer decapsulation.
Figure 2. The accepted packet's link-layer context is not the final IPv4 context. The issue is a mismatch of stored metadata and the current network-header boundary, not that the physical allocation magically moves. Our original reports cover the exact packet geometry; this figure focuses on the broken invariant.
The first public patch series makes the entry-path defect especially clear. In __virtio_net_hdr_to_skb() , the historical minimum-header check used skb_transport_offset(skb) , an offset relative to the current skb->data view. That protects against a checksum start that is trivially too early in that view. It does not by itself establish how far the start is from the network header when the packet contains additional link-layer structure.
The original reported hardening therefore proposed an additional network-relative comparison:
Those two inequalities are not interchangeable. The distinction is the essence of the L2/L3 coordinate mismatch. The patch review grew beyond this first formulation because nested headers, IP options, IPv6, and differing ingress callers require more careful validation than a single optimistic fixed offset. Our original input-side patch and Willem de Bruijn's later proposed broader input validation provide the source-level history.
For the eventual IPv4 consumer, the accepted guard expresses a particularly useful invariant. With N = skb->network_header , H = ip_hdrlen(skb) , C = skb->csum_start , and nonnegative checksum offset O , the eventual output location is W = C + O . Requiring C >= N + H before completion implies W >= N + H . The guard therefore prevents this completion from writing into the IPv4 header . It does not prove that W is the correct field within TCP or UDP; that is a separate protocol-validity question.
This is the first trust failure: checksum metadata from a less-trusted origin crossed into host packet processing without being constrained against the header that later code would actually use.
The most interesting part is the order of operations.
Host ingress sees and parses an IPv4 packet with an ordinary header. Fragment processing and routing can operate on that state. Later, output fragmentation reaches the pending checksum. In the historical code, ip_do_fragment() completed the checksum before obtaining the IPv4 header pointer and using the header length. The pre-fix ordering in net/ipv4/ip_output.c was effectively:
skb_checksum_help() is not inherently unsafe. It becomes unsafe here because malformed metadata allows its write to overlap bytes that were already parsed as an IPv4 header .
The header field that gives the leak its shape is IPv4 ihl , a 4-bit count of 32-bit words. The first byte of a normal IPv4 packet contains version and IHL. In our controlled research geometry, it could change from 0x45 (IPv4, five words = 20 bytes) to 0x4f (IPv4, fifteen words = 60 bytes), without changing the version nibble.
Figure 3. Bit-level diagram of the first IPv4 byte changing from 0x45, IHL 5 and 20 bytes, to 0x4f, IHL 15 and 60 bytes.
Figure 3. A two-byte header mutation can leave the packet looking like IPv4 while dramatically changing the header-length interpretation. 0x4500 and 0x4f00 are the before/after first words observed in the research case.
The IPv4 version nibble remains 4 ; only the four-bit header-length interpretation changes.
The earlier stages had not endorsed a 60-byte header. They had made decisions on a 20-byte header. But the later consumer read an updated field as though it were authoritative.
This is a time-of-check/time-of-use problem in the semantic sense , but not the usual race between threads. The execution can be fully deterministic. The “time” separating validation and use is the sequence of legitimate networking operations, with an attacker-influenced deferred write in between.
This is an example of vulnerability-oriented path diagram, not a claim that every network configuration takes precisely these exact hooks, although we have found numerous other methods to invoke these vulnerable paths.
This part is easy to explain poorly. Linux packet buffers need not contain all packet bytes as one contiguous linear object. An sk_buff has a linear head plus possible non-linear fragment data. After the relevant reassembly, the research case's logical linear data length was just:
The late checksum operation made the fragmenter believe that the IPv4 header was 60 bytes long. That means it treated the next 40 bytes after the original 20-byte header as IPv4 options. Eight of those bytes were genuinely inside the linear head, though they had been payload. The next 32 bytes were not part of the packet's logical linear data .
Figure 4. Memory-layout diagram showing a 28-byte logical skb linear head, a later 60-byte header copy, and the 32-byte disclosure beyond logical packet data.
Figure 4. skb_headlen(skb) = 28 while the later copy length is 60. The discrepancy is 32 bytes. This is a logical skb-data out-of-bounds read; it need not cross the boundary of the physical allocation or an individual slab object.
That final distinction is important. “Out of bounds” here refers to the sk_buff 's valid logical linear packet data , not necessarily to an access beyond the entire allocator object. The host may have physically mapped allocation tailroom past skb_headlen() . Reading those bytes and incorporating them into an outgoing network header still crosses a confidentiality boundary. They are host memory, not bytes the sender provided as part of the logical packet.
The IPv4 fragmenter can then generate outgoing fragments using the mutated header shape. The resulting transmitted packet exposes those bytes as apparent IP options. The problem has moved from an internal host state into an externally observable artifact.
That is the difference between the statements “this might read past a buffer” and “the host emitted data outside the sender's logical packet.”
We did not want to confuse an interesting hex dump with a host leak. The evidence design separated an identity case, where the packet's original header length remained unchanged, from the active case, where a later operation changed its interpretation. It checked whether the final transmitted packet was structurally valid, whether nonzero bytes appeared past the known logical data, and whether those bytes differed from the sender's controlled guard data.
The tests also used an independent application-level receipt alongside raw packet observation. Those two signals helped distinguish a genuine host-side rewrite and transmission from a packet-construction or packet-capture artifact.
The first bounded disclosure reproduced 32 bytes per active case . We treated the contents as sensitive and did not need to preserve unrelated raw host memory to demonstrate the boundary crossing.
We separately confirmed a host-availability failure on disposable, researcher-owned Linux 6.12 and 7.x. hosts .
A repeatable, attacker-controlled host-memory disclosure is already serious in a multi-tenant environment. It exposes information from a trust domain the guest is supposed to be unable to observe. It also changes the exploit-research problem: a working read primitive can help resolve uncertainty about host memory state and make additional memory-manipulation hypotheses testable.
In our owned KVM fixture , the research advanced beyond read-only disclosure. Using host-memory observations and carefully controlled allocation behavior, we demonstrated selected 64-byte host-kernel writes . We used the resulting capability in a bounded lab chain to execute a host-root helper and return a host-generated marker to the guest. Four separate true-cold boots completed that chain.
That is why we use the phrase guest-to-host escape for the isolated proof. It is not an inference from an out-of-bounds read, and it is not a claim of root command execution in any vendor's production environment.
Figure 5. Evidence ladder separating source hypothesis, controlled mutation, host-memory disclosure, selected kernel writes, and bounded host execution on owned machines.
Figure 5. Each rung is a different evidence claim. Source review alone does not prove a leak; a leak alone does not prove a write; a lab execution result does not become a production-execution claim.
The allocator-sensitive write chain, object-lifetime controls, and other hypervisor-specific adaptation are large enough to require a separate article. Although we suspect the security industry will use this post to figure out the other affected hypervisors and we expect exploits in weaker configurations to arrive in weeks, and exploits working in default hypervisor configurations to arrive in under a month. Part 2 of pwnescape will deal with what it took to move from the primitive to host control , rather than pretending that a 32-byte disclosure trivially becomes code execution, if the security community doesn't beat us to it.
What makes this research interesting beyond the particular kernel patch is the combination of three different trust transitions :
For our own research discussions, we call this pattern deferred-metadata trust inversion . That is a descriptive name for the mechanism. Its building blocks are known, and lots of the fundamentals the exploit abuses are publicly documented; the new and consequential result here is a concrete host-boundary exploit chain through these Linux networking interactions.
The recurring anti-pattern looks like this:
The corresponding audit question is not merely “did we validate the checksum offsets?” It is: “after every transformation, can a deferred writer still target bytes whose semantic meaning has already been trusted?”
The distinction matters for defenses too. A narrow check that prevents IPv4-header overwrites can stop the memory-safety path demonstrated here without proving that every protocol-specific checksum destination is correct. During upstream review, researchers also raised distinct concerns about later mutation of transport fields after policy checks. Those are related consistency risks, but they should not be folded into the proven 32-byte disclosure or claimed as fully addressed by the IPv4 fix .
The lesson generalizes as an audit technique for deferred work and mutable metadata. It is not evidence by itself that unrelated protocols, operating systems, or products are vulnerable .
The story of the fix(es) is worth telling because the shape of the remediation changed during review.
Our initial candidate series addressed two different points in the path: admission of virtio checksum metadata and the IPv4 fragmentation consumer. The public September patch series explains that rationale and includes the reviewer discussion. Subsequent review identified more checksum-completion consumers and debated the risk of a broad check in a central helper versus targeted checks at multiple sinks.
Michael S. Tsirkin's accepted upstream patch took the latter approach: a small IPv4-specific guard placed before checksum completion in each of five affected consumers. The helper was added in include/net/ip.h :
For a normal nonnegative csum_offset , that ensures the eventual checksum output location cannot fall inside the IPv4 header. The check does not try to certify that the target is a valid TCP or UDP checksum field; it makes the narrower claim needed to protect the already-trusted IPv4 network header .
The accepted commit, 6785011f8b16 , adds the guard to these consumer paths:
Figure 6. Diagram of ip_check_csum_start guarding five IPv4 checksum-completion consumers across the six files changed by the accepted Linux patch.
Figure 6. One shared ip_check_csum_start() helper, five protected checksum-completion sites. The shared helper is in the sixth modified file. The patch is expressly described as defense in depth.
The critical new ordering at each relevant site is validate the checksum start first, then complete the checksum . In ip_do_fragment() , the simplified post-fix sequence is:
One detail is especially important if you are backporting or reviewing related work: this commit is not a complete redesign of the virtio checksum API . The accepted commit message explicitly calls it a defense-in-depth measure and says broader ingress validation requires further work. The original discussion also considered TUN/AF_PACKET scenarios without a VM.
Michael reproduced the original issue during private review. Willem de Bruijn and other networking reviewers evaluated the accepted approach, including the cost of changing widely used checksum paths.
The patch was applied to net.git on October 8, 2026, and subsequently merged into the mainline Linus's tree Oct 14th, 2026. Stable backports and official CVE publication should be checked against the live kernel records at publication time;
We made deliberate evidence distinctions throughout: a suspected bug versus a demonstrated disclosure, a disclosure versus a host write, an owned-host root marker versus a provider-production result, and a code review versus an accepted upstream patch. Those are not bureaucratic labels. They are how you keep ambitious vulnerability research falsifiable.
That is also the point of the AI systems around the models. The research loop is much closer to is model or researcher proposes an invariant violation → build a bounded test → check controls and falsification cases → preserve evidence → iterate with expert researcher → ask independent reviewers to attack the conclusion → implement and retest an exploit . We use that loop to search a larger space without lowering the proof standard for under 700$ of API tokens.
We are keeping Part 1 focused on the public kernel fix and our owned-host evidence. We are also keeping the provider-specific coordination and private production telemetry separate until their disclosure status is explicitly cleared.
The popular mental model is that VM isolation lives in the virtual-machine monitor. Much of it does. But an attacker-controlled workload does not interact only with arch/x86/kvm/ . It interacts with a host OS full of optimized, highly composable interfaces. Some of those interfaces are performance contracts.
If the metadata crosses a trust boundary, every deferred consumer has to inherit the right invariants. And if the packet can be transformed after those invariants are checked, the invariants have to remain true in the new representation.
That is why a bug that looks, at first, like a malformed checksum hint can become a memory disclosure and a guest-to-host escape primitive. The problem was not how difficult IPv4 is to parse. It was that different parts of Linux were allowed to trust different versions of the same packet.
A huge thank you to Michael S. Tsirkin of Red Hat, Willem de Bruijn and Eric Dumazet of Google, David Ahern of NVIDIA, Jakub Kicinski of Meta, Chris Arges of Cloudflare, Greg Kroah-Hartman of Linux Foundation, and the wider Linux kernel community for their technical guidance, collaboration, and efforts to get this vulnerability fixed upstream.
We're equally grateful to Guillermo Rauch, Malte Ubl, Andy Riancho, Andrey Sibirev and the entire Vercel team for their exceptional collaboration and commitment to protecting the wider industry. Special thanks also to Eric Daniels (Modal) and everyone else who contributed, reviewed, reproduced, or helped along the way. This research wouldn't have been the same without you.

title: Starfighters Space Will Test Starlaunch 1 Suborbital Development Vehicle on an F-104 in December
body: Starfighters Space is preparing to conduct in December a captive-carry test flight of its new Starlaunch 1 suborbital development vehicle on one of the company’s F-104 Starfighter aircraft. Starfighters Space is preparing to take the next step in the development of its Starlaunch suborbital vehicle, with an F-104 Starfighter expected to carry Starlaunch 1 airframe on a captive-carry flight in December 2026. The mission will mark the transition from ground-based development to flight testing, after the completion of wind tunnel testing of the vehicle earlier this year. The company announced on Oct. 13, 2026, that it has finalized the airframe design for Starlaunch 1 and ordered flight hardware from Italian company Robby Moto Engineering. The hardware, which the company says will be inert, is expected to arrive at Starfighters Space’s hangar at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in November, where the team will assemble the vehicle and test its interface with the carrier aircraft ahead of the planned flight. “The planned captive-carry flight would move STARLAUNCH 1 from design and ground-based development into flight testing,” said Tim Franta, CEO of Starfighters Space. “Our approach is deliberately incremental: build the hardware, integrate it with the aircraft, fly it, collect data, and use those results to advance toward separation and powered flight. This work on STARLAUNCH 1 is also expected to generate engineering and operational experience to inform the future development of STARLAUNCH 2.” The mission is expected to take place between Kennedy Space Center in Florida and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)-licensed Cecil Spaceport in Jacksonville. During the captive-carry flight, STARLAUNCH 1 will remain attached beneath the wing of the F-104 throughout the mission, without attempting an actual release. In fact, the test is intended to demonstrate the vehicle’s behavior in flight, verify its integration with the aircraft and generate experience for future developments. The company says the data will also support work by its propulsion partner, Vaya Defense & Space, which could develop a hybrid rocket motor for Starlaunch. “December’s captive-carry mission would essentially be step one of a multi-flight campaign, building processes for our launch team while capturing data for the FAA and the Space Force as we move toward propulsive air launch,” said Piercarlo Ciacchi, Director of Flight Operations and Chief Pilot of Starfighters Space. “Our plan is to follow the December mission with a drop test over the Atlantic Ocean followed by a demonstration of the integrated propulsion system. Development of STARLAUNCH 2 would be informed by these missions, concurrent with the STARLAUNCH 1 development.” The F-104 Starfighter from Starfighters International, carrying the test article of GE Aerospace’s Solid Fuel Ramjet (SFRJ) test article on the left wing. | Source: GE Aerospace Additionally, the F-104 might also carry Starfighter’s recently-completed Wind Tunnel in the Sky hardware under the other wing on a customer-funded rideshare mission. This payload will also serve as a counterweight to balance the aircraft and improve its aerodynamic stability, which would be affected by a single, asymmetric payload. The press release mentions that the two systems share some components and interchangeable hardware, allowing the company to apply common integration procedures. The components, again produced by Robby Moto Engineering, are enroute to the company’s hangar at KSC , and will be assembled into two modular underwing flight articles. Starlaunch The company previously said that Starlaunch 1 is being developed as a sub-orbital vehicle designed to support short-duration microgravity missions and serves as a pathfinder for future air-launched concepts. The vehicle is based on the proven envelope of the AIM120 AMRAAM, says the company on its website . The company describes Starlaunch 1 as its “first proprietary design air-launch satellite delivery rocket.” The listed performance mention a total thrust of 41,000 lbf, an orbital inclination between 0° and 120° and a payload which can include multiple small satellites. The flight profile sees the F-104 climbing at 45,000 ft at Mach 2 , launching the rocket. Starlaunch 1 will be able to reach sub-orbital altitude, just above the Kármán line at 100 km, while the larget Starlaunch 2 will be able to reach low Earth orbit. In September 2026, Starfighters signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Vaya Defense & Space , a privately held developer of the patented Vortex-Hybrid rocket engine. The MoU covers two collaboration tracks. The cockpit of one of Starfighters’ F-104 as it flies at Mach 1.7 at 34,500 ft. | Source: Starfighters Aerospace The first one covers the flight testing of Vaya hypersonic test articles and other payloads on Starfighters’ Wind Tunnel in the Sky. The second will assess whether Vaya’s hybrid propulsion is suitable for Starlaunch. “Vaya has spent years maturing a propulsion technology that is throttleable, restartable, and non-explosive — which is close to an ideal profile for a vehicle carried under the wing of an aircraft,” said Franta. “Their shop is also a short drive from our hangar at Kennedy Space Center. That combination of technical fit and proximity allows us to develop and test hardware faster than either of us could alone.” Wind Tunnel in the Sky Starfighters Space announced the development of its Wind Tunnel in the Sky platform in July 2026 . The company described it as “a reusable airborne platform designed to help commercial, government, defense, and research customers evaluate advanced technologies during sustained Mach 2+ flight in real-world atmospheric conditions.” The system is being developed as a modular and reusable underwing platform able to host a variety of sensors, test articles, and other payloads for long-duration exposure to both high-speed and low-gravity conditions. The company expects to use it for aerodynamic test articles, avionics, sensors, communications systems, electronic equipment, advanced materials, and other technologies for hypersonic programs and microgravity research. The flight hardware will support an initial planned customer deployment while establishing capabilities that can be adapted for future missions, said the company. A statement also provided the dimensions of the system, which measures 3.65 meters in length and 178 millimeters in diameter with a form factor “based on a proven military air-launch vehicle.” The dimensions match the publicly released ones of the AIM-120 AMRAAM. “Using a proven aerodynamic configuration allows us to focus on payload integration, flight testing and mission execution rather than developing an entirely new external flight body,” said Ciacchi. “The modular design gives us the flexibility to support a wide range of customer requirements while maintaining predictable flight characteristics throughout our development program.” Starfighters’ TF-104G takes off from its former home at Grosseto Air Base, Italy, in 2023, ahead of the celebrations for the Italian Air Force’s 100th anniversary. | Source: Italian Air Force Rather than relying exclusively on ground-based wind tunnels, this system will exploit the F-104 Starfighter’s flight characteristics to subject the payload to real atmospheric conditions. The company says this also allows longer tests, as “a typical 45-minute mission can include up to a 10-minute Mach 2+ test window, providing significantly longer exposure than traditional wind tunnel test runs – which typically can last only seconds at a time.” “As demand for hypersonic and advanced aerospace systems continues to grow, access to specialized test infrastructure remains limited, increasing demand for complementary commercial flight-test capabilities,” said Tim Franta, CEO of Starfighters Space. “While ground wind tunnels remain essential for aerospace research and development, airborne testing can expose hardware to combinations of weather variation, vibration, acceleration, dynamic pressure, temperature and operational conditions that cannot always be fully reproduced in a fixed facility.” The F-104 as an airborne research platform Starfighters Space operates a fleet of F-104 Starfighters from Kennedy Space Center and Midland International Air & Space Port in Texas. Originally developed by Lockheed as a high-performance supersonic interceptor, the F-104 is now being used by the company for commercial flight testing, aerospace research and the development of its air-launch capabilities. The company plans to have a fleet of seven airworthy F-104s. In the past, Starfighters has purchased five F-104s from the Italian Air Force after the service retired the type from operational service in 2004, including three TF-104G-M two-seat trainers, as well additional aircraft from the Royal Canadian Air Force. “The F-104 is a remarkable aerial platform, capable of putting research projects into microgravity, high altitude, high speed, and high G environments. The jets can mimic the ascent, descent and flight profiles of spaceflight vehicles and high performance military aircraft, and — according to NASA estimates — can provide between 60-90 seconds of microgravity during parabolic maneuvers,” Starfighters website explains.

title: Show HN: Pay-per-Crawl – make AI crawlers pay per page in USDC, for 10 stacks
body:
Last night Pay-per-Crawl was a WordPress plugin that started as a comment on TikTok, with two real payments behind it. This afternoon the same gate runs on WordPress, Drupal, Laravel, Next.js, Node, Cloudflare, nginx, Caddy, Traefik and Python, and it is published on npm, PyPI, Packagist and drupal.org. Every edition settled two real payments on Base mainnet before we released it. We are proud of this one, so here is exactly what shipped and what it took.
The behaviour is identical on every stack. Humans and reverse-DNS-verified search engines read free. AI crawlers, SEO crawlers and scripts get an HTTP 402 carrying an x402 v2 header, a v1 body and an MPP challenge. They pay USDC on Base, and the page is served only after the settlement transaction hash comes back.
The owner keeps 100%, paid directly to their wallet. There is no custody, no ForgeMesh account and no API key. PayAI is the default facilitator and any facilitator URL works. Every edition carries the same 85-agent crawler catalog and serves the same discovery files: /.well-known/x402.json, llms.txt and agents.txt.
real $0.01 settlements on Base mainnet in one day
WordPress: free GPL plugin from forgemesh.io/wordpress , a GitHub release. It is submitted to wordpress.org and under review, so it is not listed there yet.
Next.js middleware: npm i @forgemeshlabs/pay-per-crawl-next
Express, Fastify, Hono, Koa: npm i @forgemeshlabs/pay-per-crawl-node
Cloudflare Worker in front of any origin: npm i @forgemeshlabs/pay-per-crawl-worker . The shared engine is @forgemeshlabs/pay-per-crawl-core , and there is an nginx njs snippet too. Source: github.com/forgemeshlabs/pay-per-crawl-js .
Python (FastAPI/Starlette, Flask/WSGI, Django): pip install forgemesh-pay-per-crawl , repo pay-per-crawl-py.
Go: go get github.com/forgemeshlabs/pay-per-crawl-go . It includes a Caddy module (http.handlers.pay_per_crawl, built with xcaddy) and a Traefik plugin.
PHP: composer require forgemesh/pay-per-crawl-laravel or composer require forgemesh/pay-per-crawl-drupal , both on the shared forgemesh/pay-per-crawl-core . Drupal has a project page at drupal.org/project/pay_per_crawl .
Every edition passed its own test suite and a 37 to 44 check HTTP matrix. Then each code base settled two real $0.01 payments on Base mainnet through PayAI before release. That is ten real settlements in one day. A few of the transactions: WordPress v1 , Python v2 , Go v1 , Laravel v2 . All public on Basescan.
We would rather show you a transaction hash than say the word tested.
Porting the gate turned up two real problems, and we fixed both in every edition before anything went to a registry.
A forwarded-IP spoof. A crawler could prepend a Googlebot address to X-Forwarded-For and walk through as a search engine. All editions now use the right-most hop, the one our own proxy appended.
Unanchored path exemptions. Free paths like /robots.txt were matched loosely enough that /robots.txt.html or /.well-known/../post could slip past the gate. The exemptions are now exact files, a sitemap regex, and normalised dot segments.
We are telling you because that is how we ship: attack our own gate first, then publish.
Drupal: the page cache answers before normal event subscribers ever run, so the gate had to become an HTTP middleware that sits above it.
Laravel: Sanctum drops middleware groups unless they are pushed after boot.
Traefik: its plugin interpreter cannot load assembly-backed keccak, so the Go edition carries a pure-Go keccak.
Edge editions pass static assets free by default, since nobody is scraping your favicon for training data.
Pro is $4.99 a month for up to 5 sites at proxy.forgemesh.io/wp , and it connects to any of the editions above: a hosted dashboard, a Monday digest, paywall monitoring with alerts, a crawler-intel feed of 104 agents, and a listing in the paid-sites directory with a badge. The gate itself is complete without it, and payments never pass through us.
Cloudflare Pay Per Crawl bills a few enrolled AI companies by card, with Cloudflare as merchant of record. Ours lets any x402 or MPP agent pay the site owner's wallet directly. If you also use Cloudflare, set its AI crawler control to Allow, otherwise crawlers are blocked before they get the chance to pay.
One TikTok comment, one night, one afternoon. Thank you to everyone who asked for it. Tell us which stack we missed.
Pick your edition above or start at forgemesh.io/wordpress. Pro ($4.99/mo, up to 5 sites) is at proxy.forgemesh.io/wp.
Related reading: Your WordPress site gets 175,000 bot visits a day. Now they pay. .

title: Sudan’s Burhan sends message to German chancellor on peace efforts
body: Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has sent a written message to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on bilateral relations and efforts to achieve peace and stability in Sudan, Sudanese officials said. Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi, who is Burhan’s personal envoy, delivered the message to German Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Serap Güler at the German Foreign Ministry in Berlin on Friday. Sudanese Foreign Ministry Undersecretary Muawiya Osman Khalid accompanied Minnawi. The message addressed ways to strengthen relations between Sudan and Germany, support peace efforts and promote Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue, the statement said. Sudan’s chargé d’affaires in Berlin, Idris Mohamed Ali, said the visit was part of ongoing communication between the two countries. He said Minnawi had briefed Güler on developments in Sudan and efforts to restore peace and stability. The German Embassy to Sudan said in a post on X that Germany remains committed to advancing peace efforts, six months after the Sudan Conference in Berlin. 6 months after #SudanConference in Berlin, is fully committed to advancing peace efforts in #Sudan . Minister of State Serap Güler met Darfur Governor Minni Minawi today and stressed urgent need for ceasefire and truly inclusive & civilian-led Sudanese dialogue #Quintet pic.twitter.com/q7iwZMNM8N — German Embassy to Sudan (@GermanyInSudan) October 16, 2026 Güler stressed the urgent need for a ceasefire and “truly inclusive and civilian-led Sudanese dialogue”, the embassy said. Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when fighting erupted between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), triggering a humanitarian crisis and repeated international efforts to end the conflict. The post Sudan’s Burhan sends message to German chancellor on peace efforts appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Show HN: Battle Isle 2 via spec
body:
Multiple people shared their old game reimplementation efforts recently, starting with projects where the author had access to source code of a port, to a version of Supreme Commander . Very cool work.
Sometime in spring, I started to look into one of my favorite games - Battle Isle 2 . A turn-based strategy game with very good presentation for its time: beautiful units, maps that use color well and a great electronic soundtrack. There are animated 3D rendered fights, mission briefings display as animated video calls. Blue Byte tried to make the best strategy game possible and I think they pretty much succeeded.
I still love playing the game to this day, it runs well under DOSBox and is available on GOG. The control scheme is a bit clunky, on mouse down the cursor moves to the bottom of the screen where you select the action. You can play with the keyboard, except single presses are often interpreted as double, making selecting units difficult.
A few years ago, kitana did a reimplementation for Windows, Battle Isle 2020 . I played it for a short time, the author has modernized the game very well - text-to-speech for announcements, scaled graphics, better AI, new missions - amazing work. I tried a reimplementation a few years ago and was looking at BI 2020 as a possible source. Back then, I couldn’t make sense of the PowerBASIC code , couldn’t find a compiler to build it and quickly gave up.
I decided to build a new port to fix controls and to be able to play on my phone. The first version runs in the browser and controls are much worse than in the original. I’m currently resolving some loose ends to have a playable version in a PWA.
Different from before, I decided to start with the spec of the game - all data files first, then the game logic. I now have good coverage of the data files. While there are a few missing fields, I think the spec makes almost the whole game playable. For the remaining few missing bits, I’m not sure they are even used in the game.
The game logic is trickier. If I did it again, I would follow the same pattern other AI ports are doing. I would have skipped the spec and gone straight for the new implementation, letting an agent port individual functions or parts of the code. I’m glad I started earlier as it allowed me to better understand how the game works. If you are interested, you can browse the partial spec for the data files. While I have the full spec in my repository, it’s not in a readable state yet.
In earlier stages, I let the agent ask me questions about behaviour and I controlled the game to find the answers. These answers were collected as the acceptance test suite that I’m still using. This is of course very slow. Eventually, I configured the agent to run the steps on its own, letting a small agent control DOSBox and trace what happens.
Agent control of DOSBox was dreadfully slow, taking ten minutes for a few clicks. It used accessibility APIs on macOS to trigger clicks and take screenshots of the window. DOSBox-X has a good debugger where the agent can trace what happens and GameLink support adds fast access to input and screenshots. I created a small local patch to allow parallel DOSBox windows to be controlled at the same time, better mouse handling and permissions to work well with agents.
The web port is not playable yet. It’s possible to move units, do attacks, undo moves. The spec already supports mission triggers, weather and construction, but the web implementation lags behind. If you’d like to try it, you’ll need your own Battle Isle 2 GOG copy. Run the exe to extract the CD image and ogg files, then upload them to the web version. The UI is very clunky, but you can then start any mission, move units around and make attacks.
You can also play around with some of the spec files - e.g. the full list of units extracted from the game, including their 3D meshes and animations, the spec of the unit files or maps . I’m cleaning up my findings to publish the rest.
I also prototyped a new 3D battle version, or you can configure it here :
Last, I fixed some bugs in existing missions and animations, you can download the fixes for the original game.

title: Egypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked
body: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, and parliament announced an emergency session on Sunday."It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed," Sisi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy. He said Egypt was not seeking to attack anyone, but was prepared to act in defense.Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognized government following the collapse of a truce.Sisi said Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited, to discuss issues including security and navigation in the Red Sea.Sisi requests emergency parliament session to discuss Saudi defense"I know this requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that authorisation if we are asked," Sisi said.Shortly after he spoke, parliament said it would hold a plenary session at 1 p.m. (1000 GMT) on Sunday in response to the request, though it did not disclose the agenda.Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist president Mohamed Morsi in 2013.Egypt also joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in 2015 to support the Yemeni government against the Houthis.
