title: Show HN: UOS – a workspace the server can't read (post-quantum, E2EE)
body:
A post-quantum, end-to-end encrypted workspace for people and organisations
uOS is a complete workspace â chat, mail, video meetings, files, documents, spreadsheets, presentations, boards, calendar, notes, tasks, AI assistants, shift planning and an app studio â delivered in the browser, on one identity and one security model. Its premise is simple: the operator of a service should not be able to read what its users create. In uOS, content is encrypted on the user's device, with keys the user alone holds, before it reaches our servers.
This paper is written for two readers. Decision-makers will find the product, the trust model and the business principles in Parts I and IV. Security reviewers will find the architecture, the cryptographic protocols, a per-application coverage matrix and a threat model in Parts II and III, with the exact primitives and parameters in the appendices. Where a guarantee has limits, the limit is stated next to the guarantee.
The software most people and companies rely on â office suites, cloud drives, team chat, mail â is built on a common arrangement: the provider runs the code, stores the data, and holds the keys. Encryption "at rest" protects against a stolen disk, not against the provider. Everything else rests on policy: privacy statements, contracts and certifications.
Policies are made in good faith, but they are not a technical boundary. They can change with a new owner, a new business model or a new law. They can be overridden by a court order in another jurisdiction. They cannot stop an insider with production access, and they do not survive a breach. For regulated organisations the consequence is concrete: every sensitive file stored in a mainstream cloud is, in principle, readable by someone outside the organisation.
A second pressure is arriving on a fixed schedule. Public-key algorithms in use today â RSA, elliptic curves â will be broken by a sufficiently large quantum computer. Adversaries do not need to wait: traffic and stored ciphertext recorded now can be decrypted later ("harvest now, decrypt later"). Security agencies in Europe and the United States have set timelines for migrating to post-quantum cryptography; data with a long confidentiality life needs that protection already.
uOS replaces trust by policy with trust by construction:
uOS runs in any modern browser on desktop and mobile, as a desktop-style workspace with windows or as a full-screen mobile layout. It is available in 28 European languages.
Platforms. A person has one core account â their cryptographic identity â and can belong to several platforms . A platform is an isolated workspace with its own members, roles, apps, branding and settings. There are four kinds: the personal core space, organisation platforms (for-profit and non-profit), and neutral collaboration platforms for work across organisations. A person's private workspace and their organisation's workspace are separate by design, including in who can ever recover the content (Section 10.4).
Client. An Angular single-page application that performs all key handling and encryption in the browser. Account private keys live in memory for the duration of a session and, by default, are never written to browser storage. The persistent browser storage is a device vault holding the forward-secrecy keys of that device (Section 8.2), encrypted under a non-extractable browser key, and â only if the user asks a browser to remember them â the sealed copy described in Section 5.6; other browser storage is cleared on every load. Application data is kept on the server â encrypted â so that a user can sign in from any device.
Server. A Go service that authenticates sessions, routes messages, enforces platform membership and organisation policy, and stores data. It is treated as untrusted for confidentiality : the system is designed so that a fully compromised server yields ciphertext and metadata, not content.
Storage. PostgreSQL holds ciphertext, public keys and operational metadata; encrypted file bodies are stored as opaque blobs. Redis holds short-lived state only â handshake challenges, presence, rate-limit counters. Session tokens and signing keys are held in server memory, never in Redis or on disk; a restart ends every session.
Transport. Everything a user does travels over one authenticated WebSocket ( /ws ), established with a post-quantum handshake (Section 6.3). Where a network blocks WebSockets, the client falls back to an HTTPS long-poll channel that runs the same handshake and carries the same encrypted, signed frames. The remaining HTTP surface is small and listed in Appendix C: login and key-derivation lookup, sign-in with a uID or a remembered browser, PIN checks, account rotation transfers, ticket-gated bulk upload of ciphertext, public invite and platform pages, and published Studio sites. The requests among these that carry anything sensitive â the login lookup and its answer, uID and remembered-browser sign-in, unlock, PIN checks, change of secrets and rotation â are themselves sealed with the hybrid KEM (ML-KEM-1024 + X25519) to a server key signed by the pinned server identity, so they do not depend on TLS either.
Desktop Agent. An optional program on the user's computer that connects outbound to the service, so no ports are opened. It lets the AI assistant work with local files and commands under explicit permissions, and can run AI models locally.
A uOS account is a set of key pairs, not a username and password on a server. At registration the browser generates random seed material â a 32-byte ML-DSA seed and a 64-byte ML-KEM seed â with a cryptographic random number generator. From this seed bundle it derives the account's post-quantum and classical signing and encryption key pairs, using domain-separated key derivation for each.
To make the account usable from any device, the seed bundle is stored on the server in wrapped form. The user chooses two secrets â Secret 1 (at least 12 characters) and Secret 2 , a passphrase (at least 20 characters) â and an account identifier in e-mail form. The browser derives a key-encryption key with Argon2id and wraps the seed bundle with it:
Each input is Unicode-normalised (NFKC) and trimmed before derivation, so the same secrets unlock the account on any operating system or keyboard; the fields are joined with zero-byte separators. The server stores the wrapped bundle, the salt, the public keys and a peppered HMAC of the identifier â never the secrets, a password verifier, or the plaintext identifier. On login, the browser fetches the candidate wrapped bundle, derives the KEK locally and unwraps. An unknown identifier receives a decoy of the same shape, derived deterministically from the identifier and a server secret, so repeated lookups return the same answer and do not reveal whether an account exists.
The wrapped bundle is released only to someone who proves the secrets. The lookup returns only the account's Argon2id salt. From the Argon2id output the browser derives, besides the KEK, a separate login key auth_key = HKDF-SHA256(Argon2id output, "uOS/login-auth/v1" â account id) ; the server stores only SHA-256("uOS/login-verifier/v1" â auth_key) and releases the wrapped bundle, through a request sealed with the hybrid KEM, only when the presented login key matches. Wrong keys, unknown accounts and decoys receive the same refusal, and attempts are limited per account and address (5 per minute) and per account overall (30 per minute), so a stranger cannot lock the owner out. Knowing an identifier therefore no longer yields an offline-guessing target: offline guessing needs the server's database. The mechanism uses only symmetric primitives, so it adds no quantum-vulnerable assumption. It is not OPAQUE: the server sees the login key during a login. Accounts switch to this gate automatically at their next login.
Other ways to open the bundle. Two further paths release the seed bundle without typing the secrets: a remembered browser (Section 5.6) and a uID , a FIDO2 security key or passkey the user has added (Section 5.7). Both open a sealed copy of the bundle in the browser and then run the same login handshake; neither lets the server see the bundle or issue a session by itself. The three secrets always keep working, and recovery setup, the recovery test and a change of secrets still ask for them.
A separate PIN, verified on the server against an Argon2id hash, gates sensitive actions â such as unlocking a returning session, enabling and reopening a remembered browser (Section 5.6), adding a uID (Section 5.7), changing secrets and rotating the identity â in addition to the session's signatures. Requiring the PIN to add a uID means that a stolen or unattended session cannot quietly enrol a key of its own. A uID itself is not unlocked with this PIN: the authenticator checks its own PIN or biometric, and changing the account PIN leaves uIDs in place.
Attempt limit. Every PIN prompt â unlocking, reopening and enabling a remembered browser, adding a uID, changing secrets, rotating, and checking or changing the PIN in the settings â counts against one counter per account on the server, so guesses cannot be spread across prompts. Each attempt is counted before the PIN is checked, so parallel guesses cannot outrun the counter. The first three attempts may follow one another at once; after the third wrong PIN in a row, each further attempt must wait 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and finally 128 seconds after the previous one, and the browser shows the seconds left. The tenth wrong PIN in a row locks the PIN: every PIN prompt is then refused, even with the right PIN, and the lock is lifted only by signing in again with the three secrets. A right PIN before that resets the count. A remembered browser at the PIN level has a lower limit of its own on top: five wrong PINs in a row forget it (Section 5.6).
Users can change their secrets or rotate their entire identity. A rotation creates a new key epoch, re-wraps every content key the account can open for the new key, and re-points every reference to the old key, in one transaction that can be resumed for 24 hours. Values sealed to an earlier key of the account â for example data still sealed to its v2 key after the move to v3-hybrid â are opened with that earlier key and re-wrapped as well, so that a later rotation cannot strand them; the new key is never used to open anything. The account's contact records, which name no account but a keyed hash of the platform and the owner's key, are re-encrypted and moved to the hash of the new key in the same commit. A mandatory PIN, a recovery-share gate and a deploy gate that checks the rotation, and account deletion, against the live database schema (Section 14.3) protect the process. Changing secrets replaces the wrapped bundle and invalidates old secrets and old recovery material.
Accounts created before the random-seed model, whose keys follow directly from their secrets, are upgraded at their next login . Before the workspace opens, a step that cannot be skipped asks for the PIN and runs a rotation to a fresh random seed bundle in the current suite. The wrapped bundle, the login verifier, the key-transparency entries and every content key are replaced in one commit, and nothing changes if the step fails. An operator can additionally set a date after which such an account can do nothing but this upgrade.
Clients authenticate the server, not only the reverse. The server's post-quantum signing keys are pinned in the client: during every handshake the server signs the client's challenge, and the client refuses any server key whose fingerprint is not pinned. Every frame the server sends afterwards is signed and verified. A network attacker who breaks or terminates TLS therefore cannot impersonate the uOS server to a client that is already running intact code . The pins, however, are part of the web client, and the web client is itself delivered over TLS: whoever controls TLS at the moment the app is loaded can serve different code, including different pins. The pins protect a client obtained intact â a cached release, a verified build or a native app â and do not by themselves protect against malicious code delivery (Section 13.2).
When a contact rotates their keys, the server fans out a key-change record signed by both the contact's old and new keys, and clients warn before sending to the new key; a server cannot fabricate a rotation of a key it does not hold. First contact is different: when Alice messages a new contact or shares a file with Bob, her client encrypts to the key the server serves for Bob. A malicious server could serve a key of its own for any contact whose key has not been verified. Key transparency closes most of this gap. Every account key epoch (registration, rotation, suite upgrade) is appended, in the same database transaction, to an append-only RFC 6962 Merkle log whose tree heads the server signs with its pinned identity key. Before encrypting to a contact key, a client requires an inclusion proof that the key is that account's latest entry, rejects key changes the log does not show, and checks every tree head for consistency with every earlier head it has seen â including heads its contacts report inside encrypted chat envelopes. At each login a client audits its own account: every entry must be its current key or linked to it by key-change records signed by both keys, and from the last head it verified (kept, signed, in its encrypted settings) it re-derives the root over every entry added since, so a key the server registers for an account is shown to its owner. This holds on every encryption path by construction. The client's encryption functions accept only a recipient obtained through the verified lookup, the session's own keys, keys the browser has just generated, or a short list of named non-account keys, and a build-time check rejects any other use. The paths are chat, attachments, mail, files, documents, spreadsheets, presentations, projects, boards, calendar, meetings, uLine, uShift, Studio and the Studio app database, profile shares, escrow share holders and rotation. A device prekey is used only when its device is signed by an account key proven in the log, and the device has signed the prekey. A call's offer and answer are accepted only from a proven identity key. When a recipient's key cannot be proven, group operations leave that recipient out and say so; operations that would otherwise lose someone's access, such as escrow shares and re-keys, stop instead. Organisation escrow keys are in the log too, as statements signed by the owner who set them (Section 10.4). The log cannot prove that a key is absent and does not bind accounts to people: a server that shows different logs to different users is detected only when their views meet, and a newly invented account impersonating a person still requires comparing a symmetric safety number out of band.
By default every visit needs the three secrets. A user may instead let one browser remember the account, at one of two levels chosen in the system bar: PIN on this browser (reopening asks only for the account PIN; valid for 90 days) or stay signed in (reopening signs in directly; valid for 30 days, shown with a clear warning). Enabling either level needs the PIN.
The browser then keeps the unwrapped seed bundle sealed twice: inside with a non-extractable WebCrypto AES-256-GCM key that never leaves the browser, outside with XChaCha20-Poly1305 under a key derived (HKDF-SHA256) from a random 32-byte share held by the server and, at the PIN level, from an Argon2id derivation of the PIN. To reopen, the browser proves possession of a second non-extractable key (HMAC over a single-use challenge) and, at the PIN level, the PIN, through two sealed pre-login endpoints; the server then returns its share, and the normal login handshake runs unchanged. The server never issues a session from this step and never sees the seed bundle.
Any remembered browser can be forgotten from another session; locking the account, changing secrets and rotating the identity forget all of them. Organisations can limit remembered browsers for their members: not allowed, PIN or uID only, or PIN, uID or stay signed in (Section 10.5).
A uID as the factor. At the PIN level the factor can be a touch of one of the account's uIDs (Section 5.7) instead of the PIN. The browser keeps a random 32-byte salt in its record and asks that one credential for a PRF output on SHA-256("uOS/uid/device-unlock/v1|" â salt) ; the outer key becomes HKDF-SHA256(server share â PRF output, info = "uOS/device-unlock/v1" â registration id) . Because the input is per browser, the factor is unrelated to the uID's sign-in key and differs between two browsers remembered with the same uID. To reopen, the browser sends a WebAuthn assertion over the device-unlock challenge itself; the server checks it as for a uID sign-in, including the signature counter, before it releases its share. A stolen device and the database together then leave no PIN to guess: the factor is a 32-byte secret that only the authenticator computes, after its own user verification. Wrong assertions are not counted, because only the authenticator can produce a valid one; a counter regression is refused and audited. Enabling still needs the account PIN; a PIN change keeps such a registration, while removing that uID, a lock, a change of secrets and a rotation forget it. The server stores only that the factor is a uID and which one.
A uID is a WebAuthn credential the user carries: a FIDO2 security key with the hmac-secret extension or a passkey whose provider supports the PRF extension. It opens a copy of the seed bundle sealed under a key that only the authenticator can recompute, after user verification on the authenticator (its PIN or a biometric). The normal login handshake then runs unchanged, as for a remembered browser; the server never issues a session from a uID and never sees the seed bundle.
Every uID is a discoverable credential with user verification required and the PRF extension; an authenticator that returns no PRF output or stores no discoverable credential is refused, and nothing is kept. The relying party is the host of the deployment ( uos.sh on the uos.sh service), so a credential answers only that origin: a look-alike domain receives neither an assertion nor a PRF output. Attestation is none , so any authenticator model is accepted and the server does not learn which. The WebAuthn user handle is a random 32-byte value per account, never the account id. Accepted algorithms are Ed25519, ECDSA P-256 and RSA (PKCS#1 v1.5); an account holds at most ten uIDs.
The PRF input is fixed because a discoverable-credential sign-in does not know the account before the assertion. The PRF output still differs per credential, and the random per-credential salt, held by the server, and the credential id in the HKDF info separate the boxes further and bind each box to its row.
This device, or a security key or phone. When adding a uID, the user chooses where it lives. This device means Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello or the Android screen lock: a passkey on the device or in its synced password manager. Security key or phone means a FIDO2 key such as a YubiKey or Nitrokey, or another device, such as a phone reached through a QR code. The PRF output is required either way, because it is what unwraps the keys on the device: without it there is no key to the box. A passkey store that returns no PRF output â some browsers keep passkeys in a store of their own that lacks it â is refused, with a hint to another browser or to a security key, rather than sealing the bundle under anything weaker. Passkeys in iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager sync to the user's other devices on that account, while a hardware key never leaves the key; both are phishing-resistant, but a synced passkey is only as safe as the account that syncs it. The server does not currently distinguish the two: it does not evaluate the backup flags in the authenticator data, and with attestation none it does not learn the model. An organisation that requires a uID (Section 10.5) therefore cannot yet require a hardware key; the interface points out that organisations may prefer one.
Adding a uID happens over the signed-in WebSocket and needs the account PIN (Section 5.2). The browser creates the credential, seals the bundle with the PRF output and sends the box with the attestation object; the server consumes the single-use challenge and checks the ceremony type, origin and cross-origin flag, the rpId hash, the user-presence, user-verification and attested-credential flags, and the key algorithm before storing the row. Signing in takes two sealed pre-login requests: a single-use challenge valid for 120 seconds, then the assertion. The server consumes the challenge, checks the ceremony type, origin and cross-origin flag, the rpId hash, user presence and verification, the signature over authenticatorData â SHA-256(clientDataJSON) with the stored key, the user handle, the signature counter (a counter that does not grow is refused and audited as a possible clone; passkeys that always report zero are accepted) and that the account is active, and only then returns the salt and the box. The browser derives K from the PRF output of the same assertion, opens the box and runs the normal handshake. Both requests are sealed like the other pre-login endpoints (Appendix C) and rate-limited per address and per credential. Wrong authenticator PINs never reach the server: the authenticator counts them itself.
A lock removes every uID of the account, because a uID that someone added with a stolen session and the PIN must not survive the panic button; a change of secrets and a rotation remove them in the same transaction, because the box holds the old bundle. Changing the account PIN leaves them in place. Removing the last uID never locks anyone out, since the three secrets keep working.
Post-quantum note. uID assertions are classical signatures (Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA), but they only authenticate a one-time challenge: forging one later gains nothing. The confidentiality of the seed bundle rests on symmetric primitives â the authenticator's HMAC-SHA-256 based PRF, HKDF-SHA256 and XChaCha20-Poly1305 â and, in transit, on the hybrid ML-KEM-1024 + X25519 sealing of the pre-login requests. Once the box is open, identity and session are the account's ML-DSA and ML-KEM keys in the normal handshake.
uOS combines a post-quantum and a classical algorithm for every asymmetric operation. Both must succeed; neither is accepted alone:
Hybrid construction is the approach recommended by European security agencies (ANSSI; BSI TR-02102-1, which also recommends ML-KEM-1024) during the post-quantum transition: an unexpected weakness in the young post-quantum algorithms is caught by the classical half, and quantum attacks on the classical half are caught by the post-quantum one. TLS protects the connection as well. Once the app is running, the confidentiality of content and of sensitive requests does not depend on TLS; the delivery of the app itself does (Section 13.2), which is why uos.sh also negotiates hybrid post-quantum TLS ( X25519MLKEM768 ) with browsers that support it.
Every key, ciphertext and signature belongs to a suite . A deployment accepts a fixed set of suites and writes exactly one; nothing is negotiated, so there is nothing to downgrade.
The v3-hybrid values are composite : the classical half is carried inside every public key, ciphertext and signature, so no field can exist without it, and stripping it yields a malformed value rather than a weaker one. The construction is uOS's own. A composite signature is an ML-DSA-87 signature with a suite-specific context string followed by an Ed25519 signature over a suite-prefixed message, so neither half verifies as a signature of another protocol using the same key. The KEM follows the design of X-Wing â the classical ciphertext and public key are bound into the combiner â but uses HKDF-SHA384 and is not wire-compatible with X-Wing; the signatures do not claim conformance with the IETF LAMPS composite drafts. Alignment with those standards is on the roadmap. Every key-derivation label is bound to its suite, so a ciphertext cannot be opened under another suite's derivation. New accounts, new keys and everything the server signs use v3-hybrid. An account still on v2 is moved to it at its next sign-in with its three secrets, from the same seed bundle, so nothing new has to be remembered; until then uos.sh still accepts its v2 keys. The v3-cnsa suite targets customers who must follow the US CNSA 2.0 profile, on their own or dedicated infrastructure only; it is built in and checked against the shared test vectors, and a first dedicated installation is the next step.
Shared known-answer test vectors pin every primitive and encoding across implementations: Go generates them, the TypeScript client reproduces every deterministic value byte for byte, and the Dart mobile code checks the v2 vectors.
A v2 identity receives the v2 handshake; a v3 identity receives the server's v3 key and the composite KEM. Handshakes are rate-limited per address and per account.
Content in uOS is encrypted under a random content key, and that key is wrapped â encapsulated with the hybrid KEM â for every person allowed to read it. Four patterns cover the product:
Live collaboration in uDoc and uSheet encrypts every update and awareness message under the document key with fresh nonces; the server rejects plaintext collaboration frames.
Large files are uploaded as ciphertext over a ticket-gated HTTP path: the client obtains a server-signed, short-lived ticket over the WebSocket and uploads the encrypted file with it. File sizes are padded to power-of-two buckets and file timestamps are coarsened to the hour, so storage metadata reveals less about the contents.
In uChat, the sender's identity travels inside each recipient's encrypted envelope, signed with the sender's identity key and bound to the conversation, a random nonce and the send time. Each recipient checks the signature against the key-transparency log; a copy that fails is marked and attributed to nobody, and an edit counts only when the original author signed it. The message table stores no sender: editing or deleting a message for everyone is authorised by a per-message secret that only the author's devices can derive, of which the server keeps only a hash. Messages sent before this scheme was introduced carry no signature; they are shown as before and can no longer be edited. Delivery is authorised with single-use tokens obtained through RFC 9474 RSA blind signatures (RSABSSA-SHA384-PSS-Randomized, 3072-bit dedicated key), so the server can check that a token is valid and unspent without being able to link it to the account that obtained it. Tokens carry a server-assigned, hour-aligned expiry of at most 12 hours; spent-token records, kept only to prevent replay, are deleted after 24 hours. Blocking and abuse reporting work on top of this model. Notifications do not record who contacted whom â only contact requests and join notices store a sender, because that relation is what they are about â a database trigger enforces this for every writer, and notifications are deleted 30 days after creation or 7 days after being read. Server logs of message delivery name neither the sender together with the conversation.
Sealed sender removes the stored sender graph; it does not hide who is connected at a given moment. The server still sees which authenticated session submits a message and when, and it knows the members of each conversation. Section 13.2 lists what remains visible.
Each of a user's messaging devices enrols its own key, signed by the account, and publishes signed, expiring prekeys (ML-KEM + X25519). Messages are encrypted to the recipient's device prekeys, so the compromise of an account key later does not expose messages in transit. To keep history readable on all of a user's devices, a device stores a copy of each received message on the server, re-encrypted to the account key. Stored history is therefore protected by the account key, not by forward secrecy: anyone who unlocks the account â for example by guessing its secrets from the wrapped bundle (Section 5.1) â can read the whole stored history. Forward secrecy protects messages in delivery. A shield badge in the chat shows when forward secrecy is active.
Organisation platforms distinguish direct , group , channel and confidential chats. Channels can only be created by administrators and are marked as escrowable; confidential chats are marked as such, can never be escrowed, and cannot change their class once set.
Online status is held in memory with a 90-second lifetime; last-activity stamps expire after 24 hours and last-seen stamps after 30 days. Nothing about presence is kept in the database.
uMeet runs its connectivity servers itself. Every call, including calls started from a chat in uChat, uses a media router (SFU) inside the uOS server, which forwards each participant's video in up to three qualities so every screen receives only the size it shows. A relay (TURN), also part of the uOS server, carries calls for participants whose network blocks direct connections. It refuses to forward anything to private, loopback or internal addresses. No third party takes part in a call.
The router and the relay carry media they cannot read. Every participant encrypts each audio and video frame with a sender key before it leaves the browser (AES-256-GCM, with the codec's first bytes left readable so the router can forward frames). A participant sends their key to each other participant separately, encrypted with the hybrid KEM to that person's key-transparency-verified key and signed with their identity key. When someone joins, every sender ratchets its key forward, so the newcomer cannot decrypt anything said before. When someone leaves or is removed, every sender switches to a fresh random key. In-call chat, reactions and raised hands are encrypted under the same keys. The server enforces host decisions (admitting from the waiting room, removing, locking, muting) by forwarding or withholding encrypted media. It never learns what was said or shown. The audio-level signal that would reveal who is speaking is not sent to the server; the browser works out who is speaking from the decrypted audio.
A sender key authenticates the group, not the individual frame: someone who holds a participant's key could in principle forge that participant's frames, as in the IETF SFrame design. Keys themselves are bound to identities by signatures.
Guests. A host or co-host can invite people without a uOS account with a guest link. The secret part of the link sits after # , so the browser never sends it with the page request. The server stores only its hash, an expiry and a usage limit. A guest's browser creates temporary identity and encryption keys for that one meeting and opens a connection that can reach nothing but that meeting. Guests always wait until a host or co-host admits them, and only then do participants send them their sender keys. From then on the guest's media and messages are end-to-end encrypted like everyone else's. A guest's keys are not in the key-transparency log, and a guest's name is only what they typed, so uMeet marks guests as not verified: the host decides who they are. For the same reason, a guest cannot verify the other participants. If the host has uOS e-mail the link, the server sees that link, which gets someone only as far as the waiting room.
The table states, for each application, what is end-to-end encrypted and what the server can see. "Visible" does not mean published: it means the server needs it to operate and could disclose it if compromised or compelled.
Studio apps. Apps built in Studio run in a sandboxed frame with an opaque origin under the uOS content security policy, so they cannot reach outside servers; everything else they use goes through the uOS host in the browser. The host gives every app per-user storage, the app database and rooms in the table above, and dialogs and notices that uOS itself draws with the app's name. Anything more â sending notices, setting reminders, the user's calendar, tasks, contact list, files, mail, documents and the other apps' data â the app must declare in its manifest; before it reaches other people, a member with the "Manage apps" right approves it together with the code; and each user must allow it on a consent card that is tied to that exact code and manifest; a change asks again. The host decrypts such data in the browser and hands it to the app inside its sandbox. Notices are sealed for each recipient's key, proven in the key-transparency log, or once for an app database scope, and signed by the sender, so the server can neither read nor forge them; it sees the app, the recipients, the level and the time, and when a reminder is due. For building, Studio offers a code workspace, a version history that is stored readable like the code, a component kit in the uOS look and six starter apps; its AI assistant is optional (Section 12).
uMail is internal to uOS. It delivers only between uOS accounts; it does not send mail to, or receive mail from, internet e-mail addresses, so no uMail message passes through SMTP. "External recipients" in an organisation's mail egress policy (Section 10.3) are uOS accounts outside that organisation's platform. The only e-mail the service sends is invitation and optional security notices (Section 15), composed by the server.
Notifications are sent as opaque wake-up signals; the device fetches and decrypts the content itself. Web Push is opt-in and carries no message content.
Every member joins through an invitation, and each invitation is signed by its creator; the invitation chain is recorded, so every member's path into a workspace is accountable. In organisation platforms only owners, administrators and HR can invite. Roles range from owner and superuser through administrator and moderator to member and guest, with per-platform permissions.
What each role may do is set in a per-platform rights matrix, which owners and holders of the manage roles right can edit: manage roles, manage platform, manage escrow, manage security, manage apps, moderate content, view members and invite members. Owners always hold every right, and the server checks the matrix on every request. Manage security â by default owner, superuser and administrator â controls the organisation's security policy (Section 10.5) and needs neither the platform nor the escrow right; the compliance controls of Section 10.3 need manage platform , the escrow key manage escrow .
Critical changes, such as ownership transfers and litigation holds, can require a quorum of owners. Each approval is an ML-DSA signature by a distinct owner, verified by the server and kept with the action for later audit.
Every change of the security policy (Section 10.5) is written, in the same transaction, to a policy audit table ( platform_policy_audit : the acting account, the policy, the old and the new value, the time) and shown in the Admin app's audit log next to role changes, ownership changes and verifications.
An organisation's compliance profile is a signed, versioned document with an append-only history. It controls which applications members can use (enforced on the server, not only in the interface), view-only and download restrictions, watermarking in Files, retention rules executed by a reviewed deletion queue, and a mail egress policy that allows, warns about or blocks mail to recipients outside the organisation. A litigation hold , created and released by owner quorum, blocks deletion of covered content types. Organisations record their jurisdiction; German organisations attest to their works-council agreement.
Organisations need to recover business records when an employee leaves or loses access; private individuals need to know that no one else can. uOS provides both, separately:
Escrow exists only on organisation platforms. It is absent â not switched off â on personal and collaboration platforms, and it never covers direct, group or confidential chats. Members are told when escrow applies. Every file, document, spreadsheet, board, calendar entry, note, task and e-mail whose content key is wrapped for escrow carries a mark reading "Recoverable by your organization", in lists and in the open item. Create forms show "Will be recoverable" when the platform covers the type, and chat channels carry an "Escrowable" mark.
The escrow key is signed and logged. Every escrow key is published as a statement naming the platform, the key, the threshold, the share holders, the time and the hash of the previous statement. The statement is signed with the identity key of the owner who set the key and recorded in the key-transparency log, in the same transaction that stores the key. Before wrapping anything for escrow, a member's app requires three things:
It never falls back to a key the server serves. At every login, owners' apps check the platform's whole chain of statements and show any change they did not make, naming who signed it. To obtain escrow copies for a key of its own, a server would have to create an owner account and sign with it, and both would appear in the log, where the real owners see them. Keys set before statements were introduced get no new escrow copies until an owner confirms them.
Organisation platforms have a security policy with two rules. Owners and the manage security right read and change it; every change is audited (Section 10.2).
Remembered browsers: not allowed, PIN or uID only, or PIN, uID or stay signed in (the default). A member's ceiling is the strictest setting among all the organisation platforms they belong to. The server enforces it when a browser is registered and when it is reopened, deleting registrations above it, and the client forgets such browsers after login (Section 5.6).
uID required to open this platform. When this rule is on, the platform can be used only from a session that began with a uID. The server cannot see how a seed bundle was opened, so it marks a session only from what it verified itself:
The rule is enforced per platform. Each event of an unmarked session is judged against the platform it names â its platform_id , otherwise the platform the socket was opened for â and refused with uid_required for a platform with the rule. Handlers that find the platform from a resource, such as a file or a board, refuse it in the same membership check. What the user needs to get back in stays reachable: the platform list, presence, their own settings and profile, uID and remembered-browser management, the key-transparency log and notifications. The user's other platforms are not affected, and the client shows a notice instead of the platform's apps. Sign-ins with the three secrets, reopenings with the PIN or at the stay-signed-in level, and Desktop Agent (device) sessions are not uID sessions, so an agent cannot work on such a platform. The server caches the rule for at most 15 seconds.
The rule can be switched on only from a uID session, so the person who sets it has shown they can still open the platform; there is no owner bypass, and while the rule is on, changing the policy again also needs a uID session. It is an access rule enforced by the server, not a cryptographic barrier: a member who signed in another way still holds their keys in the browser, and the pushes the server sends to a user (broadcasts) are not filtered by it. Uploads over HTTP need tickets issued over the WebSocket, which the rule gates. The rule exists only on organisation platforms.
Because the operator cannot recover accounts, users set up recovery themselves, and are asked to do so right after registration:
An account whose secrets and recovery material are both lost cannot be restored â by design. A service that can restore your identity for you can also impersonate you.
uOS includes AI across the workspace: the Vivian assistant with tools for calendar, files and documents; uSages personas; the uAssistant help; an assistant panel in every app; the Studio build assistant; and the Desktop Agent for local work.
AI conversations, reasoning traces, tool results and attachments are stored end-to-end encrypted to the user's key; Studio build conversations are encrypted under a project key that only the project's members hold, wrapped for each of them after a key-transparency check. Generating an answer, however, requires sending the relevant context to a language model. For that request, the server relays the context in memory without storing or logging it, and the provider the user or organisation has chosen processes it in plaintext. That the relay neither stores nor logs is a property of the server software â a policy, not a cryptographic guarantee: a compromised server could record the context of AI requests. Running a model locally through the Desktop Agent avoids the relay entirely. AI is optional: an organisation can switch AI features off for its platform, and each user decides, at first sign-in or later in the settings, whether their content may be sent to an AI provider at all; the server refuses every request that would send content to a provider unless both allow it. Providers are configurable per platform and per user â hosted providers in the US, the EU and elsewhere, a custom endpoint, or a model running locally through the Desktop Agent, in which case nothing leaves the user's machine. The interface discloses which provider receives a request.
The Desktop Agent executes local actions only within the paths and command rules the user allows, with confirmation for sensitive operations. It holds its own device key, pairs with a one-time token, and verifies every frame the server sends. At pairing it pins its owner's account identity key: the pairing code the user copies from the browser carries a fingerprint of that key, so a key substituted by the server is rejected. Tools that write, delete or execute â shell commands, file creation and edits, fetches to local-network addresses â run only after the owner approves the exact action in the browser; the browser signs the approval (tool, working directory, every argument, identifiers, decision, time) with the account identity key, and the agent verifies it against the pinned key, rejecting stale, replayed, altered or unsigned approvals. Changes of the working directory, and requests to open a web address in the local browser, are signed the same way, and the pin follows a key rotation only through records signed by both keys. The server relays approvals but cannot create them.
Automatic approval. For longer tasks, the confirmation dialog offers two ways to stop asking while an AI request of this tab is in progress. Per request , the user approves further actions of one kind â commands, file changes or local-network access â for that single AI request, for at most 15 minutes; this ends with the request, and a confirmation counts as part of it only while it is the only AI request this tab has in progress. All actions until I stop it approves every kind for every AI request this tab starts, with no time limit; it is held only in the tab's memory, never in browser storage, and ends when the user stops it, signs out or locks, switches account or platform, or closes the tab. In both modes the browser still signs each approval itself and logs it as automatic. Some confirmations always ask or are refused: a write to a place that runs programs by itself later â shell start-up files, autostart entries, launch agents, scheduled tasks, Git hooks and similar â always shows the dialog; commands that match a blocked pattern, and actions the browser cannot read, are refused before either mode is consulted; and a confirmation that arrives while no AI request of this tab is in progress â from another tab or device, an automation, or one the server made up â always shows the dialog.
Agent updates are installed only when their manifest is signed with the uOS release key (ML-DSA-87 + Ed25519) compiled into the agent, and never downgrade. Read-only tools within the working directory still run without approval, and their results reach the server and the AI; credential directories (for example ~/.ssh ) are never read.
A compromised user device or browser, physical coercion of the user, and weaknesses in the underlying standards themselves. Symmetric primitives with 256-bit keys are considered secure against quantum attack; if that assessment changes, the suite mechanism (Section 6.2) is the migration path.
Everything that protects the user runs in the browser and can be inspected there. The client's source code is kept in the repository github.com/uOS-sh/uOS under the UltimaOS Source-Available License 1.0; the Studio SDK and the Studio app templates are under the MIT licence. It is source-available, not open source. The repository is currently private: proven security experts, auditors and researchers receive read access on request, and the repository is to be opened to everyone after the Beta. Whoever has access may read, build and test the code to check the claims in this paper; running it as a service requires our written permission. Beyond inspection, each release is built deterministically â repeated builds of the same source produce identical files â and published with a manifest of the SHA-384 hash of every file ( /release-manifest.json ), while the page loads its code with subresource integrity. Every manifest is signed with the uOS release key â a hybrid ML-DSA-87 + Ed25519 key kept off the served infrastructure, whose public half is kept in the repository and whose key id is printed here ( 666MWqG6o0cwguPHVNYgspQDJ9bLtMvUTk/UxeA1YoY= ), so that a copy of the key obtained from the repository or from us can be checked. A verifier in the repository ( scripts/verify-release.mjs ) checks a host's signed manifest against that key and compares the served files byte for byte. The remaining step is publishing each release's manifest hash in an independently operated log, so that serving different releases to different users leaves public evidence.
The server's source is not public. In this architecture the server is not the user's trust anchor: the guarantees in Section 13.1 hold against a fully malicious server. What the server can accept and send is defined by the client and its protocol, which reviewers can inspect (Section 14.1). Security researchers, auditors and academics can request scoped access to the server source for review.
Every release runs automated gates before it reaches production: known-answer tests of every primitive across implementations; a coverage check ( scripts/check-rotation-coverage.sh ), run by both deploy scripts against the live schema of the target database, that fails if any column holding a key or data encrypted to an account is not handled by identity rotation, if a rotation statement no longer matches the schema, or if account deletion does not cover the same tables; and the authentication, cryptography, server and HTTP test suites. The production release is refused if any gate fails. The client is kept on a supported release of its framework â Angular 21 as of October 2026 â and at the date of this paper the dependencies shipped to the browser had no known security advisories ( npm audit --omit=dev reported 0).
The verification chain works the same way in both cases: every release is published with a manifest of its files, so an organisation running uOS itself can check that what it deploys is exactly what was released, and its users can check what their browser receives. In an on-premises deployment the organisation, not us, operates the server; the end-to-end guarantees in Section 13.1 then hold against that operator in the same way.
uOS is in Alpha. The following limitations are known and are being worked on; they are stated here so that no reviewer has to discover them.
The next steps, in order of priority. Everything in this list is planned, not yet available, unless the item says otherwise.
uOS starts from a position that most software treats as a trade-off: that a complete, collaborative workspace can be built without its operator being able to read it. Post-quantum cryptography, keys held by users, sealed metadata where possible and a clear account of what remains visible make that position concrete. We invite organisations, security reviewers and early users to test it with us.
Contact: patrick@ultimaos.com Â· https://ultimaos.com Â· Sign up and log in at https://uos.sh
The RSA blind signatures protect the unlinkability of delivery tokens, not the confidentiality of any content.
The sizes are the value bodies; every v3 value carries one additional suite-tag byte (for example, a v3-hybrid KEM public key is 1,601 bytes on the wire). v2 values keep their original untagged encoding, so existing data is unchanged.
Core account â a person's cryptographic identity. Platform â an isolated workspace with its own members and settings. Seed bundle â the random material from which an account's key pairs are derived. KEK â key-encryption key, derived from the user's secrets. CEK â content-encryption key of a single resource. Suite â a fixed set of algorithms and parameters. Epoch â one generation of a key, replaced on rotation. Escrow â an organisation-held recovery key for selected business content. Sealed sender â delivery without a stored sender identity. Forward secrecy â protection of past messages if a long-term key is later compromised. uID â a FIDO2 security key or passkey with the PRF extension that opens a sealed copy of the seed bundle for sign-in (Section 5.7). uID session â a session that began with a uID sign-in the server verified itself; organisation platforms can require one (Section 10.5).

title: Principles of Anchor Engineering
body:
Building software at agent speed with human judgement
I have often seen one engineer get much faster with AI coding agents; then adding a second engineer or a third on the same team doesn’t necessarily speed up development. Sometimes the “fast team” is just one person operating in a silo. What I wanted to understand was why teams didn’t seem able to move faster, even when they were trying.
What I found is that teams keep holding on to what they know while also trying to adapt to AI. The teams place agent-speed implementation within processes built for humans and thus slow it back down. The bottleneck is maintaining shared understanding, coordination, and a coherent direction while moving fast. Every person added needs more of all three, and the way we manage that traditionally doesn’t scale with agent speed.
Building the right thing and ensuring quality hinge on human judgement. It comes in the form of product definition, requirements, understanding how to apply architectural principles to solve problems in software engineering, as well as validating that our product can be released to customers.
Keeping up with agent speed requires setting aside the existing methods, processes, and points of friction we’ve put in place to manage and gate our own work. I’m not saying throw everything out the window, but if we want to build successfully and go faster, we have to work differently.
To come up with a solution, though, I did start by throwing a lot of things out the window, then added elements back. As an industry, we have rich expertise in software development, in honing judgement and knowing how to apply technology to real-world problems. But the mechanisms and tools we’ve applied to develop software need a clean slate rather than a simple tune-up. We need to be able to trust and verify that what we deliver matches what we designed.
In 2024, I wondered how new abstractions would change the code we write . That distinction between designing software and writing its code is central to Anchor Engineering.
I’ve been developing this method as the answer to all the callouts above: moving fast, high quality, enabling teams. I’ve been deep in a cave for the last few months building with a bunch of teams like this, with thousands of my own commits across those teams. I even ended up building an application that uses AI to narrate the scope of changes that go in each day - because reading that is a better use of time than reviewing 100 commits every day.
In this method, our human judgement is baked into the guiding context with an agent-specific focus on design: anchors.
AI does not care if the design you prescribe is high level or low level, it just needs to know what to build. This also means you don’t have to prescribe everything else for it to build the right thing; the anchors define what the right thing is, and you can let the agent fill in the rest.
It also serves as your team’s shared mental model and build plan. Both of these grew out of some of my earlier work on how AI context can be directed and kept in a specific “space” by storing text that served as anchors for specific behavior.
The shared context and mental model in the Anchor Book enable the team to work together closer to agent speed. For this, I recommend a small development team that stays in active conversation, whether working together in person or virtually. They all work off of the plan within the Book, and also update it as they navigate design and development progress. Engineers push and pull the Book as part of development which keeps them working in sync.
Here’s a first set of principles that guide this method. This post lays the groundwork; I’ll cover the details, examples, and mechanics of the method in follow-up posts.
The result of engineering with AI is a reflection of the judgement applied at each step in the process. Anchor Engineering puts that judgement into the Book and its anchors so it becomes durable direction for every AI building loop. Engineers and AI sessions then continue from the same decision instead of reconstructing it through repeated handoffs.
AI has made software development more accessible, but using it effectively still requires engineering expertise, judgement, and domain knowledge. You can install a coding assistant, set it up quickly, and it will build something . What it builds entirely depends on your tool selection and configuration - and the context and instruction. The quality and depth of your instruction depend on the quality and depth of your expertise in software engineering - think of system design, scaling, knowing what works well and what does not given circumstances. AI does not replace the need for an expert; it amplifies the impact of an expert in the system it builds.
Consider the analogy of an AI-written document; we’ve all seen documents that on the surface look like they contain reasonable prose, but end up lacking where it counts. If you know the subject matter, you’ll probably recognize it very quickly. Writing software with AI coding agents can follow the same pattern. The result might be fine for some uses, but its quality depends on the expertise you bring to guiding its creation.
Judgement is part of the input to the software building process, guides the building itself, and verifies that the resulting software is correct and is ready to be deployed.
The code should look like AI wrote it, because AI is what will maintain it.
This principle is a mental shift, and can be really freeing for us as engineers if we let it be; we stop editing and managing the code by hand. We own the goal, direction, and judgement in the process. AI writes, organizes, and iterates on the code.
We can appreciate beautiful code. Think of all the time we spent on this: the debates on your team about the best place to put brackets. We can mostly let this go. Correctness is critical; personal style is fleeting.
AI doesn’t care if code is organized around human aesthetic preferences; it does benefit from coherent patterns, clear and recognizable structures, well-defined constraints and use of standards it can recognize. Maintaining that helps AI maintain the code. Ultimately we humans care that the system is structurally sound, is correct, and satisfies the requirements.
This principle might sound familiar and dredge up memories of trying to keep documentation and code in sync. This is different, particularly when the artifact you use to build your system is your primary tool for updating it, coupled with the previous principle of not editing code outside of the AI build loop.
The Anchor Book I mentioned above is the home for all of your building artifacts - it represents the design and definition of your system: the anchors for each part of that design, the criteria by which your agent verifies those anchors are satisfied, and the planned chunks of work you can assign to your agents. It is not simply documentation in the traditional sense.
Another way to think about it: the Book defines your system, and you deploy your agents to instantiate it in whatever language you want. You can use the same Anchor Book to build a system in Rust, then Python, then Java (as long as the language fits the intended application). I have used the same Anchor Book to flip the language mid-development. Initially it applied Python. Then I decided Rust might be more appropriate, so I used the Book to change direction without changing the actual design. The implementation language changed; the system definition did not.
This artifact is living documentation and system definition and should be version controlled along with your code.
When you assess your processes, ask yourself: what function does this stopping point serve, and what faster mechanism can carry that function? I call the answer antifriction.
This means we’re replacing something in our process that creates a human bottleneck with something else that lets the process go faster, without sacrificing quality.
This is where I find people start getting nervous and return to known methods. It’s important to look forward, not backward in this paradigm. Here are two examples from my experience.
Consider task planning for a small, focused team working with AI agents. The Anchor Book holds the context for the work that needs to get done to implement a system. If we additionally go to the manual effort of breaking the design down into tasks for team members, planning them into sprints, and assigning them - we are just where we started, with no wins and duplicated planning. If each engineer on the team using the Anchor Book and AI agents can knock out the amount of work in a day that would normally be planned across 4 weeks, the effort does not pay off.
The antifriction is milestone tracking instead of task tracking, so that the team can continue to move forward while still enabling program management to track the project, manage dependencies, and identify risks.
Consider a team where the engineers guide their agents in developing code quickly, then depend on the team members to review their agent-written code. Teams review code to ensure issues are caught before they ship, verify code quality, maintain best practices and standards, etc. However, this is where speed goes to die. A team review is an asynchronous human gate, and putting it in a system with agent-produced code cancels out agent speed. As it is, on many teams a code review takes at least a day to get completed and teams still struggle to solve this with only human coders.
Instead, we enable our AI agents to apply automated testing and bug fixing loops and ensure that when the agent presents the resulting code to review, it has been through the testing gauntlet already. Having sound unit and integration tests, end-to-end tests, validation, etc. must take a front and center role in development (not that it shouldn’t have already). We make sure the AI agents eliminate as many errors as possible before completing the task, using not only AI adversarial and judge reviews but also deterministic testing. If you’re not mutation testing to test the output of your AI coding agent, you’re missing a great opportunity for a deterministic layer in your process; this step will test whether the tests the AI wrote catch deliberately introduced errors.
This is an appropriate point for a judgement check-in: the engineer who guided the agent should take a look at the resulting code and analyze it for structure and correctness, and validate that what came out of the AI building loop is what they expected.
The antifriction is removing the human team-gated reviews, and building out a comprehensive test plan for code changes. We keep a judgement step in the loop so that the engineer leading the AI building loop validates what was produced.
Code review also spreads knowledge and design context across a team; in this method, the Anchor Book carries that shared context and stays current as the team builds.
The method does not replace understanding with speed. It preserves the domain, design, operational, and implementation context required to build the system while reducing the time needed to assemble, share, absorb, apply, and update it.
I have talked with engineers off and on in the last year about what will happen to our mental model of the software we build if we are not “hands on” writing it, but instead defining it in terms of plain language text in markdown. Usually we build our mental models through writing the code, also through investing time in problem solving and designing, as well as explaining our approach and discussing with others. So how does this translate to a bunch of natural language directives to AI?
I designed the Anchor Book to be a structured artifact to ensure we can define a system with clear rules and outcomes with an implementation plan for AI agents. It tracks decisions, how they align with requirements and how those are realized in anchors, and then verified through tests in the code base. It also encodes human judgement within these mechanisms. Building the design into the Book means working with AI to ensure that what you are adding adheres to existing rules, or recognizing when it violates them and you need to solve the problem differently. This hands-on work creates a strong mental model in much less time than it would normally take to develop over the course of the project. We’re essentially compressing the time it takes to build and understand a full system, and creating the artifact that lives and grows as the system does. This means each person on the development team ends up with a crash course in the entire context for the system they are building - and a very rich mental model beyond the scope of what they’d normally need for task work.
Building at agent speed takes shared understanding, coordination, and a coherent direction. The Anchor Book is how I bring these together. In the posts that follow, I’ll show what goes into the Book and how a team uses it to design, build, and verify a system.

title: Crypto Super PAC Fairshake Pours Millions More Into Defeating Sherrod Brown
body:
Crypto’s biggest political spender is turning up the pressure on one of the industry’s fiercest critics. Fairshake has reported fresh spending to defeat Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio, pushing its total outlay against the former Senate Banking Committee chairman well past the $40 million mark.
A filing with the Federal Election Commission, signed Oct. 15, shows Defend American Jobs, the Fairshake affiliate that spends in Republican-friendly races, disclosed a $5.2 million media buy opposing Brown, followed by another roughly $1.95 million buy days later, plus media-production costs.
The filing lists Brown’s calendar-year-to-date total at about $46.66 million, cementing the Ohio contest as the most expensive target of the crypto industry’s 2026 campaign. The same filing showed parallel spending supporting Brown’s Republican opponent, Jon Husted, who inherited the seat after being appointed last year.
The sums dwarf what Fairshake is deploying elsewhere, underscoring how personal the Ohio race has become for the industry. The PAC earlier signaled plans to spend at least $30 million against Brown, a figure this filing shows it has already blown past.
Brown’s return to the Senate would hand crypto skeptics a powerful voice on the Banking Committee, the same perch from which he stalled market-structure legislation before losing his seat in 2024, a defeat Fairshake spent roughly $40 million to help engineer.
The renewed Senate blitz comes days after Fairshake broadened its map to the House. On Oct. 5, the PAC network announced it would back 32 House incumbents, 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats, framing itself as an issue-focused group that supports “pro-crypto candidates who support American innovation in both parties.”
It committed an initial $6 million, or $1 million each, to six of them: Republicans French Hill, Bill Huizenga and Bryan Steil, and Democrats Janelle Bynum, Steven Horsford and Derek Tran. All 32 voted to advance the Clarity Act when it passed the House in July 2025.
Fairshake, funded largely by Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz, entered September with roughly $120 million in cash and is expected to spend more than $100 million across House and Senate races this cycle. Its push runs alongside the Coinbase-backed advocacy group Stand With Crypto, which has rolled out its own slate of midterm endorsements .
The spending reflects the industry’s hardened resolve after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate, channeling its considerable war chest into reshaping the Congress that will decide crypto’s rules.
