title: Nigeria drove thousands of gold miners from a national park. But can it keep them out?
body: A military-backed operation shut down a major illegal gold mining site in Gashaka-Gumti National Park, driving more than 4,000 miners from Nigeria’s largest national park, according to the Africa Nature Investors Foundation (ANI). The miners had already fled by the time Nigerian soldiers arrived at the Kila mining area in July, according to Tunde Morakinyo, executive director of ANI, a Nigerian conservation organization working with the government to manage Gashaka-Gumti. He said no shots were fired during the operation, and bulldozers were brought in to fill the mining pits and shafts. As world leaders and conservation practitioners head to Armenia for the U.N. biodiversity summit Oct. 19-30, with the goal of protecting and conserving 30% of land and waters by 2030, the crackdown spotlights the complexity of safeguarding some of the most biodiverse places on the planet. Gashaka-Gumti is a stronghold for one of the rarest primates in the world: the Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes ellioti). The park is also home to more than 1,000 plant species and hundreds of bird and butterfly species, with some of the highest rates of endemism on the continent. A ranger patrols Nigeria’s Gashaka-Gumti National Park, where the Africa Nature Investors Foundation says it employs more than 180 rangers to help protect the park. Image courtesy of Africa Nature Investors Foundation. The operation followed years of growing friction over mining in the park. Tensions came to a head in late 2025. Two rangers were killed by miners in October 2025, according to Morakinyo. The…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: 'My soul is Iraqi, my heart is Emirati': Iraqi community comes together in celebration in Dubai
body: Thousands of Iraqis living in the UAE came together at Expo City Dubai on Saturday to celebrate their heritage and the close ties between their homeland and the Emirates. The second Emirates Loves Iraq community event brought Iraqi and Emirati guests together for a celebration of Iraqi culture, featuring traditional music, food and displays inspired by some of the country's most recognisable landmarks. Held at the conference centre at Expo City Dubai, the gathering was designed to strengthen cultural ties between the two countries while giving Iraqi residents an opportunity to reconnect with their roots and celebrate their shared identity. Families dressed in traditional Iraqi clothing enjoyed folk performances and cuisine, while others used the occasion to reunite with friends and members of the community. Sheikh Nahyan bin Mubarak, Minister of Tolerance and Coexistence, attended the event and praised the contribution of Iraqis to life in the Emirates. "This celebration for the Iraqi community in the UAE expresses their love for the UAE and the love of the UAE for Iraq," he said. "In the UAE, we are proud of the Iraqis living among us. We work to strengthen the bridges of love between the two nations." Sheikh Nahyan highlighted Iraq's rich cultural heritage and its historic contribution to human civilisation, describing the country as the birthplace of some of humanity's most important innovations. "The first wheel and the first letters were invented in Iraq. It is the place that witnessed the birth of civilisation. Iraq will always be a beacon of glory," he said. "Iraq is working towards peace and prosperity, and the UAE is committed to supporting Iraq's progress. The UAE loves Iraq." A home away from home For many Iraqis, the celebration was an opportunity to reflect on the lives they have built in the Emirates while maintaining a strong connection to their homeland. Mohammed Al Tawaiji, 48, who has lived in the UAE for 20 years, said he felt welcome from the moment he arrived. "I never felt that I was a stranger here. My soul is Iraqi and my heart is Emirati," he told The National . "I'm proud to be part of this country and to have witnessed its major development." He said the similarities between Iraqi and Emirati cultures had helped him settle into life in the UAE. "Iraqis and Emiratis both care about educating their younger generations and know how to live alongside people of other nationalities. There are a lot of similarities between the two nations, and that's why I never felt like a stranger here." Afnan Al Rawi, an Iraqi doctor who has lived in Dubai for 17 years, said the two communities shared traditions and values. "We have similar traditions, and the most important thing is that we love each other," she said. "Emiratis understand our accent well, and gatherings like this bring nations closer together and spread positivity." For younger members of the community who have grown up in the Emirates, the celebration offered a chance to explore their Iraqi identity. Ali Mohammed, 22, a student at Emirates Aviation University, was born in the UAE and considers it his home. "The UAE is definitely home for me. It is a great place to live, study and work," he said. "I never felt like a stranger here, and this event is great because I can reunite with my fellow Iraqis." Keeping traditions alive For some people, the event provided a rare opportunity to meet other Iraqis and enjoy familiar traditions. Afraa Al Rubaie, who has lived in Dubai for 25 years, said such gatherings were particularly important for people who had spent much of their lives away from their homeland. "It's hard to meet other Iraqis at work or in our residential areas, so this event is a chance to come together and enjoy our food, music and rich culture," she said. "Thanks to the UAE for giving us the opportunity to feel like we are in Iraq." She said the hospitality she had experienced in the Emirates reminded her of home. "Iraqis and Emiratis share the same hospitality and generosity. Here, we don't feel far away from our homeland because Emiratis always welcome us with a smile." The celebration also attracted Emiratis with personal connections to Iraq. Ibrahim Ali Binhatem, an Emirati writer, said his fascination with Iraqi history and culture began when he was young. His affection for the country grew over the years, and he eventually married an Iraqi woman and named their daughter Baghdad, after the Iraqi capital. "I have many Iraqi friends here in the UAE, and I've always loved the history and culture of Iraq," he said. "I used to read about Iraq and became fascinated by the traditions of Baghdad. I even named my daughter Baghdad." He said he attended the celebration to share in the community's pride in its heritage. "I came here to take part in this beautiful gathering with Iraqis. They are wonderful people with an incredibly rich history."

title: Crypto Firms Launch Quantum Alliance as 6 Million Bitcoin Sit Exposed
body:
A group of crypto companies is trying to settle one of the industry’s murkiest questions: what it actually means for a blockchain network to be safe from quantum computers.
Executives from nine organizations launched the Quantum Alliance on Thursday, an open standards body that will set criteria for judging quantum-resistance claims and create compatibility rules for networks as they migrate to new cryptography.
The founding contributors span base-layer protocols, privacy networks, rollups, hardware wallets and security auditing, including Quantus, Postquant Labs, Midnight Foundation, Keystone, Abelian and security firm Hacken.
Modeled on the Internet Engineering Task Force, the Alliance said proposals will advance on public evidence and working implementations rather than corporate size or token holdings, and everything it produces will be published openly.
Its work will run in four groups: blockchain migration, post-quantum zero-knowledge systems, wallet security and cross-chain compatibility. “In the future, ‘post-quantum cryptography’ will just be called ‘cryptography’ and everything else will be in a museum,” said Quantus founder and CEO Christopher Smith.
The problem it’s tackling is that there’s no agreed definition of “quantum-ready,” and no standard way to test one. A network can call itself quantum-resistant today with no shared understanding of what the claim covers or what evidence should back it, a gap the Alliance was formed to close.
The stakes are familiar to anyone following the beat. Nearly every major blockchain secures accounts with elliptic-curve signatures, and once an account’s public key is exposed on the ledger, a sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could theoretically reverse-engineer the private key and seize the funds.
The same cryptography guards stablecoin minting keys, bridges, oracles, and governance contracts, meaning one cracked privileged key could cascade across platforms. By the Alliance’s count, roughly 6.04 million BTC, about 30% of supply, sit quantum-exposed at rest.
The timelines keep tightening. The Quantum Alliance cites a cluster of recent forecasts pointing toward the late 2020s, including a model co-built by two Alliance contributors that flags March 2028 as an early window, and a Google Quantum AI study that slashed the estimated qubits needed to break Bitcoin’s cryptography to under 500,000.
No machine can do it yet. Google has also chipped away at key quantum bottlenecks, while figures like famed investor Kevin O’Leary have flagged the quantum threat as a catch hanging over Bitcoin’s long-term case.
The newly formed Quantum Alliance joins a widening industry scramble to address the risk. Coinbase recently urged Bitcoin developers to start the quantum migration now, suggesting preparations could take years. Meanwhile, a consortium backed by BlackRock, Strategy, and Coinbase has committed $15 million to the problem.

title: Here are the engineering lessons we learned when live-streaming sports to 32 million people
body: Live sports involve myriad unknowns, but one thing is certain: the live video feed must play flawlessly, and simultaneously, for all the fans tuning in. If some hear their neighbors cheering or groaning 5 seconds before each score, they won’t have kind words for their streaming platform. In 2023, Ashutosh Agrawal and his JioHotstar (then JioCinema) engineering teammates prepared for the Indian Premier League (IPL) cricket finals as intensely as the athletes. While the players ran on the pitch, the engineers ran their own training simulations and drills to ensure every fan could celebrate (or commiserate) in sync. A year ago, he joined us at P99 CONF to share how they built and tested the system behind that record-setting game, plus lessons learned that can help anyone preparing for high-uncertainty events (Black Friday, anyone?). Watch the complete talk, or read the highlights below. And if you enjoy these types of engineering case studies, join 30K of your peers for P99 CONF 2026, which is free and virtual. Grab a complimentary pass and join us October 21 and 22! Pre-game The IPL is the premier cricket tournament and one of the world’s most-watched sports. And Ashutosh is an IPL pro, from the engineering perspective at least. After working on the backend streaming platform since 2018, he’s learned that “with cricket, you never know what will happen.” In 2023, the final ended up drawing a then-record-breaking 32M concurrent viewers. But they were ready for even more. Just to be safe, the team builds and tests for roughly double the capacity they expect: “a scary number that scares the hell out of everyone on the team,” as Ashutosh put it. That year, they prepped for 50M to 75M. Aiming that high provides the headroom needed to absorb traffic spikes without requests piling up. Keeping the video feed flawless is their top priority. He explained, “You can sacrifice every other system and component in the line, but anything in the line of video delivery has to be a golden path — it cannot fail. Because if that fails, the entire promise of the platform goes away.” “You can sacrifice every other system and component in the line, but anything in the line of video delivery has to be a golden path — it cannot fail. Because if that fails, the entire promise of the platform goes away.” The first step in safeguarding that stream is identifying all the systems and components in that critical path. Although the actual video feed stems from CDNs, one of the biggest potential bottlenecks occurs before the final video delivery URL. Ashutosh explained: “The user has to be logged in and authenticated; we use SMS and OTP authentication. Sending out that many SMSs across the country in a short span of time is a problem statement of its own. And the key thing: the real peak on some of these systems isn’t during the final; it’s actually on the first day. That’s when a massive number of new users, or users who haven’t logged in for the last 360 days, show up, and they all try to log in within the first five or ten minutes. That’s where you see peak concurrency.” To handle the surges, they preemptively scale critical systems like authentication. Partners undergo rigorous load testing, and any who aren’t meeting the latency SLAs will be cut off during the event. Whenever one partner’s latency degrades, traffic is instantly redirected to the next partner in the hierarchy. A 200-point checklist The pre-game prep also includes an extensive system audit with a 200-point checklist. For example, for the database, they look at whether they’re running the latest version and check if there’s a maintenance window during game time. For other partners, they look at their key dependencies, redundancy, and timeout configurations. Timeouts between load balancers and services, services and application servers, application servers and the database, all the way up through the CDN are covered. Most of these checkpoints stem from lessons learned. “There was one incident where a service didn’t have keep-alive timeouts configured properly,” Ashutosh recalled. “During peak traffic, it was discarding connections instead of reusing them – so the load balancer started to crash because it couldn’t handle the request load.” That became a checkpoint for the next season. “If all your SMS partners die, what does your system do? It can’t just block traffic and lock users out; it has to let users in. We go to that extent to identify every point of failure.” Every developer or service owner uses the checklist exercise to identify the key points of failure, then they’re tasked with documenting their mitigation strategy. For example, “If all your SMS partners die, what does your system do? It can’t just block traffic and lock users out; it has to let users in, maybe in a non-authenticated way. That might require going back to Product to design something like a five- or ten-minute free viewing session without authentication, or a temporary token, deferring authentication to later. We go to that extent to identify every point of failure.” Testing, testing Next up: testing, lots of testing. They perform: Vertical testing , which is initially run on individual systems and services to ensure that each system can scale in isolation. Then, it’s performed on each partner (SMS partner, email partner, ad provider – anyone integrated into the critical path or surrounding paths). Multi-system load testing ensures clusters of systems work together properly. As Ashutosh explained, “A service might scale beautifully in isolation but reveal its true colors once you add dependencies.” For example, testing playback might involve testing a cluster with content systems, analytics, load-balancing systems for CDNs, and so on. Full user-like simulation , which simulates user behavior on the mobile app or website and looks at how that impacts all the associated systems. “A service might scale beautifully in isolation but reveal its true colors once you add dependencies.” That realistic end-user simulation is critical, according to Ashutosh: “It has actually helped us identify some critical system issues. For example, content systems get called from multiple places (the listing page, the details page, somewhere getting playback metadata). If a team forgets to account for that fan-in, those budget and scaling issues only show up in a full simulation. It stresses the system at a different level than a vertical load test does.” Latency budgeting When asked about their budget for end-to-end latency, Ashutosh shared their rule of thumb: Any system that’s entirely in-house (not talking to a third party) must operate within a budget of about 10 to 15 ms – purely server-side, no network involved – for a simple O(1) lookup and downstream response. In more complex cases (for example, with multiple database calls or a downstream third-party call), 40-50 ms is allowed. If anything in the critical path crosses 50 ms, they start thinking about what can be handled asynchronously . With client, network, CDN-to-origin, and last-mile latencies factored in, the user experiences 60-100 ms latencies. The strictest latency budget is reserved for the API that sits between a viewer tapping a video tile and the video actually playing. If something fails there, users end up hitting retry, or closing/reopening the app…and that hits the API even harder. That API response is difficult to cache since every call has to run CDN load balancing and check authentication in real time. “Even when a third-party call is unavoidable in that path, it runs under a strict circuit-breaking time budget – 5 or 10 ms – because it’s okay to fail fast and recover rather than wait to be correct,” Ashutosh said. Ashutosh summed up their thinking on latency budgets: “These response budgets help us question and challenge service owners: what can you optimize, how can you reduce load on the live system, how much more can you cache , how much can you pre-prep. Login obviously can’t be cached, but the moment you land on the homepage, we try to response-cache as much of the page as possible. With personalization, that gets tricky. So, we cache bits and components of the page separately, with the layout configuration cached separately from the content. That combination keeps page response times quick.” 3 tips for engineers preparing for big events Ashutosh closed by offering 3 recommendations for engineers prepping for high-uncertainty events, like Black Friday sales, other live events, and so on: “First: set your principles correctly. Get org-wide alignment with leadership and your team on what your priorities are. That alignment is critical because it drives decision-making before, during, and after the event. If you have a conflict of principles, you end up in a decision-making bottleneck, and that leads to a bad situation. So that’s number one.” “Second: challenge your systems. Don’t settle — don’t accept that 100ms response times are just okay. The technology has evolved massively, computing power has improved massively, and there’s no reason for server-side latencies to sit in the hundreds of milliseconds. Client-side latency, I understand that’s a different story — but server-side latency is very much within your control.” “Don’t settle — don’t accept that 100ms response times are just okay. Server-side latency is very much within your control.” “Third: identify your critical path and make sure it’s solid. Critical path identification is a genuinely tricky problem — it doesn’t just mean looking at the high-level systems. I mean things like: if there’s a synchronous call to send analytics data, that call should not be synchronous — it shouldn’t be anywhere in the critical path at all. Nothing that isn’t a true P1 or P2 dependency should sit in that synchronous critical path to the experience you’re trying to deliver. Optimize for that. It might mean saying no to things, or it might force you to re-architect some pieces. But that’s the most important piece, in my opinion.” Bonus round: Hear more from Ashutosh in this chat with Gergely Orosz on The Pragmatic Engineer .
